A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:16:49 UTC
17:16:49 KST

A decade of Lajee Celtic: The Palestinian club whose fans include Cantona
The football club founded in a West Bank refugee camp has built a global movement of solidarity.
London, United Kingdom – Nearly 200 people packed into Edami, a small Lebanese bakery in east London, to celebrate a decade of Lajee Celtic, a grassroots sports club based in a Palestinian refugee camp in the occupied West Bank.
What began as a football project has grown into an international symbol of solidarity.
In London, the room was filled with Palestinian flags, the aroma of Edami’s freshly baked manousheh, and Lajee Celtic shirts – which have been worn by celebrities, including football icon Eric Cantona and the actor Hannah Einbinder.
Martin, a Lajee Celtic organiser, travelled down from Glasgow for the celebration in September. He first visited Aida Camp, in the occupied West Bank, more than 10 years ago, a trip he described as life-changing.
“I don’t think anyone would really have expected that the project would have been as successful as it’s been,” said Martin, who requested to be identified by his first name. “But Celtic is a unique football club with its foundation, its Irish identity, the diaspora community, its universal support and then the values, which tie so much of that together.”
The relationship between Aida Camp, where Lajee is based, and Celtic supporters developed over years.
Mohammed al-Azzeh, director of the Lajee Centre, which provides services to the youth of the camp, remembers how it all began.
“We’d built up relationships with friends from Scotland and Ireland who had visited Palestine, and then in 2012, I travelled to Glasgow for the first time. We started to have conversations about creating a football academy,” he recalled.
By 2015, the idea was taking shape when a group of footballers from the camp travelled to Belfast to play a game.
Then came the 2016 Champions League draw. Celtic were paired with Israeli side Hapoel Be’er Sheva.
Supporters ignored warnings that displaying Palestinian flags could result in a fine. As the teams emerged, the stadium was transformed into a sea of Palestinian flags, an action led by Celtic ultras, the Green Brigade.
UEFA subsequently fined Celtic.
The Green Brigade responded by launching the Match The Fine For Palestine campaign. Not to pay the fine, but to support Palestinian organisations, including with the formation of a football academy in Aida Camp.
For al-Azzeh, it was a turning point.
“The support and solidarity shown in that game was really a pivotal moment,” he said. “And that’s what ultimately led to Lajee Celtic becoming what it is today.”
The team has brought together young Palestinians from villages around Bethlehem, refugee camps and communities in Hebron and Jerusalem.
“It means a lot, for us as Palestinians, to be in one place and meeting each other,” al-Azzeh said. “It becomes about more than just playing football.”
Lajee Celtic is competing in organised football for the first time. The club had been due to enter the Palestinian league three years ago, but the competition was cancelled when Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza began. Now, despite restrictions on movement between Palestinian cities and the wider disruption to football, the club has entered the Thousand Martyrs Cup, named after the 1,014 athletes killed in Gaza since October 2023.
Bassil Mikdadi, journalist and founder of Football Palestine, said that international reach has given Lajee Celtic a significance beyond the club itself.
“Lajee Celtic is a blueprint for ways in which fans of European clubs can directly support those on the ground in Palestine. It’s connective tissue,” he said.
For Martin, the popular shirts are more than merchandise.
“When people buy these shirts, they do so knowing that the money is funding football, sports and general youth development in Palestine. And then when the same people wear these shirts, whether they’re in Glasgow or London or New York, they’re each making their own individual solidarity action.”
Lajee Celtic created a link between clubs and communities inside Palestine and supporters and campaigners abroad.
“It has this kind of cross-cultural, cross-border solidarity,” he said.
That connection has become increasingly important as Palestinian football has struggled to continue since the genocide in Gaza.
For Mikdadi, the survival of grassroots clubs is essential: They are the groundwork for the national team.
“The success of the Palestinian national team in recent years … the base of that success has always been players provided by clubs in the West Bank and Gaza,” he said.
The club’s ambitions stretch beyond football. It has expanded into sports such as boxing and table tennis, while creating opportunities for young Palestinians across Palestine and the diaspora.
“Fundraising campaigns come and go all the time. But when you create a football club and when you have that sort of tangible idea at the heart of it, then you are creating a journey,” said Martin.
Mohammed al-Azzeh recalled a meaningful memory on a beach in Cape Town, South Africa, where the team played two friendlies in 2025.
Samir al-Amir, a coordinator with Lajee Celtic, had spent more than 19 years in Israeli prisons. When he travelled with the team to South Africa, it was the first time he had been able to leave the walls and checkpoints of the West Bank.
Al-Azzeh remembers watching him on the beach.
“He was acting like a young boy because it was the first time seeing the sea,” he said. “Without Lajee Celtic, I’m not sure Samir would have ever had that opportunity. That illustrates why the project is so important,” he said.

Ukraine Vows to Keep Striking Russian Refineries Despite Trump Deal – FT

17:12:00 KST

Ukraine intends to press ahead with long-range drone strikes on Russian oil refineries despite a bilateral agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel to US and international markets, the Financial Times reported.
A senior Ukrainian official dismissed US calls to halt operations against Moscow’s energy infrastructure, signaling that Kyiv will not adjust its asymmetric targeting strategy.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“We will burn [Russian] refineries,” the senior official told the Financial Times.
The vow comes as energy market analysts question Moscow’s physical ability to fulfill the commercial commitments announced by the White House, citing extensive degradation across the Russian petrochemical sector caused by repeated Ukrainian interdiction operations.
According to data cited by the Financial Times, Russian refineries are currently operating at approximately 60 percent of their installed capacity due to operational halts, emergency repairs, and equipment deficits resulting from Ukrainian strikes.
“The biggest question for me is: where are they going to get the diesel from?” said Michelle Brouhard, head of policy and geopolitical risk at energy intelligence firm Kpler. “Russia does not have an export problem. It has a refining problem.”
Russian refining deficit
Industry data highlights the extent of the contraction across Russia’s downstream petroleum sector over the past year.
Russia Exploits School Knife Attacks for Disinformation
Prior to 2025, Russia exported an average of 2.6 million metric tons of diesel fuel per month by sea, according to Kpler records.
However, maritime shipments fell precipitously throughout 2026 as successive Ukrainian drone waves damaged primary distillation units, cracking facilities, and storage hubs across European Russia and western Siberia.
With domestic refining capacity constrained, the Kremlin enacted strict restrictions on petroleum product outflows in July, effectively prohibiting domestic diesel exports to prevent localized fuel deficits and inflation within the Russian domestic market.
Outside rare exceptional consignments, seaborne diesel exports have effectively ceased.
The Financial Times also noted that the US has historically accounted for a negligible share of Russian refined petroleum consumption.
Washington has not imported Russian diesel fuel since July 2022, following early sanctions enacted in response to the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. During periods when American importers did purchase Russian diesel, volumes averaged approximately 77,000 metric tons per month, peaking at 210,000 metric tons in January 2022.
The Trump diesel pact
The dispute over refining strikes follows Trump’s announcement on Truth Social that Moscow had agreed to supply more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons thereafter.
Trump indicated that deliveries could scale up to 3 million tons within a short timeframe, though he acknowledged that shipments would depend on the condition of Russian refineries.
The US president claimed that the bilateral deal, alongside US naval operations in the Strait of Hormuz, would quickly alleviate fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a general license authorizing transactions involving Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The regulatory exemption was granted only three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which aimed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
The sanctions waiver granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since its July export ban, when Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov asserted that Russian fuel could ease international benchmarks only if granted unrestricted market access.
Trump has repeatedly urged Ukrainian officials to suspend strikes on Russian petroleum facilities, attributing high diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction rather than shipping disruptions in the Middle East.

'All human emotions': French astronaut Sophie Adenot returns to Earth
French astronaut Sophie Adenot said she experienced “the full range of human emotions, from the most joyful to the most difficult” during her eight months in space, speaking on Saturday in Cologne, Germany, in her first public appearance since returning to Earth.
French astronaut Sophie Adenot went through "all human emotions, from the most joyful to the hardest" during her eight months in space, she said back on solid ground on Saturday in Germany.
Adenot splashed down in the Pacific Ocean Thursday off the coast of California in the Dragon capsule that carried Crew-12, having returned to Earth from a mission on the International Space Station (ISS).
Read moreExclusive: French astronaut Sophie Adenot recounts her ‘miracle’ mission from orbiting ISS
She had spent a total of 235 days in space, breaking the record for the longest uninterrupted orbital stay by a European astronaut.
At 400km away from Earth, Adenot could see there are "no divisions, no borders" but "just a precious planet that we all share", she said Saturday on the tarmac of the European Space Agency (ESA) training centre in Cologne, occasionally in tears.
The 44-year-old astronaut looked visibly weakened on her arrival in Germany and was assisted by two ESA physicians.
In space, the body adapts to the absence of gravity, which leads to bone loss, muscle wasting, cardiovascular deconditioning and even visual problems.
Adenot must now begin an intensive recovery program of about three weeks to regain her pre-flight condition.
"It's a cocktail of astonishing emotions, it's incredible. It's great to be back on Earth, but it also comes with its share of challenges, especially physiological ones," she told a press conference.

She also described the "difficult" moment of Thursday's splashdown, when the capsule bringing back the four astronauts on her team had to endure "a lot of waves for 25 minutes".
"And when the commandos pulled me out of the capsule, the first thing I said to them was, 'Send me back to space, please!' It was much easier up there," she added.
During the mission, Adenot became the first French female astronaut to venture outside the space station for a spacewalk. In all, she undertook three spacewalks on August 18 and 25, and September 1.

Report: Trump struck Russia energy deal after Zelensky ignored requests to halt attacks on refineries
An unnamed US official says Ukraine’s strikes strained ties with Trump, while Kyiv alleges his envoys threatened to cut off intelligence sharing
President Donald Trump decided to strike a diesel supply deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky disregarded six US requests to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries, Axios reported, citing a US official with direct knowledge of the matter.
“Zelensky is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months,” the official told Axios.
According to the official, Trump wanted Ukraine to stop the strikes unilaterally because they were contributing to high fuel prices in the US.
Zelensky, however, told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that Ukraine was willing to halt attacks on Russian refineries if Moscow stopped targeting Ukrainian power plants.
The dispute also produced conflicting accounts of the pressure Washington placed on Kyiv. A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner threatened that Trump could end US intelligence sharing if Ukraine continued to disregard his requests.
The US official denied that any such threat was made. Instead, the official said, the envoys emphasized that Washington was supplying Ukraine with munitions and intelligence, and argued that Kyiv should avoid actions that hurt American consumers.
Zelensky told Axios after the announcement that the agreement caught him by surprise. He described it as “not fair and not honest” and an unjustified gift to Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump unveiled the surprise energy agreement on Friday following a call with Putin, saying Russia would supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets immediately, followed by 500,000 tons in November and another 1 million tons afterward.
He also said Russia would deliver a further 3 million tons within a short period, depending on the condition of its refineries. Trump presented the agreement as a way to lower diesel costs, highlighting the burden on farmers, ranchers and truckers.
His administration temporarily eased sanctions on Russian diesel exports to enable the deliveries, relaxing restrictions intended to limit Moscow’s revenue from energy sales during its war against Ukraine.
Hours after Trump announced the deal, a large fire broke out at the Novoshakhtinsk oil terminal in Russia’s Rostov region following Ukrainian drone strikes, in an apparent indication that Kyiv was continuing to target Russian energy infrastructure.

Simon de Pury: ‘The art market is ripe for disruption’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
08:00:00 UTC
17:00:00 KST

Simon de Pury: ‘The art market is ripe for disruption’
The star auctioneer Simon de Pury built his reputation by selling masterpieces to the world's wealthiest collectors. At 75, he tells Swissinfo the business model that made him famous has reached its limits: the art market's future depends on technology and tearing down its walls of exclusivity.
In the art world, Simon de Pury is something akin to a rock star, having been called the “Mick Jagger” of auctioneers. However, the comparison between the 75-year-old auctioneer (and art dealer, collector, photographer and DJ) and the youthful-looking 83-year-old Jagger is based more on de Pury’s public performances than on his looks and attire, although both men still sport rich and well-cared-for manes.
Impeccably dressed in his signature navy Caraceni suit, de Pury defies the typical image of the high-end art auctioneer with a style finessed over the course of a career spanning more than half a century.
In the documentary The Hammer, which premiered at the Zurich Film Festival in September, he appears completely at ease, cracking jokes with a selective audience of art collectors making six or seven-figure bids. One is left with the impression that this gentleman is an indefatigable social beast.
But de Pury confesses that even today he still gets nervous taking the stage. “I was very shy as a teenager and at the start of my career, at [auction house] Sotheby’s, conducting auctions was a challenge to overcome my shyness”, he tells Swissinfo in an interview at the luxury Baur au Lac hotel after the festival premiere of The Hammer.
Born into a patrician Genevan family, de Pury admits there is another, more reserved side to his personality and his private life. “That’s surely my Swissness,” he says. Home for him, though, is Monaco, where he has lived since 2000. In the documentary, there are only hints of a private life seen through discreet family pictures of his wife and four children.
Life of a salesman
The film follows the star auctioneer around several world capitals. Yet his career has gone far beyond hitting the hammer and visiting artists. He stayed with Sotheby’s for 16 years before being invited by Baron Heinrich Thyssen-Bornemisza to curate his private collectionExternal link – then one of the largest in the world – and oversee its transfer from his villa in Lugano, Switzerland, to its current site, the Museum Thyssen-Bornemisza in Madrid.
In 2000, de Pury acquired Phillips auction house (est. 1796), and renewed the old house’s standing in the market by focusing on contemporary art. In 2012, he sold it to the Mercury Group, a holding owned by two Russian oligarchs. Since then, de Pury has been on his own: his companyExternal link consists of only one assistant.
“When I sold Phillips, I thought I would never conduct another auction,” he says. “And now, at my advanced age, I conduct more auctions than I have ever conducted before.” In the week before we met in Zurich, he completed auctions in Dallas, Venice, Basel and Monaco; the next day he was off for another week of non-stop action.
Being at the high-end of the art market, and with an outstanding carbon footprint, de Pury still keeps his eyes open for new trends and shows a genuine concern about the elitism that pervades this exclusive universe. So much so that he has not shied away from embracing new technologies to expand access to artworks.
Swissinfo: The art market has changed continuously throughout your 50-year career. There are now new players: big galleries, global galleries, global art fairs and new big markets such as China. Do you miss the old art world a little bit?
Simon de Pury: No, I don’t. I feel that the art market is at a fascinating juncture and that it needs complete disruption. The art market is one that has best resisted all technological innovations, but now it’s at a stage where it has to embrace them. You can resist change, but at some point, change takes over. And I think this is what’s going to happen now.
Though the art market is much larger than when I first started my career, it remains small in absolute terms and still has huge growth potential. Art is universal in the same way that music is universal.
I feel that the art world has made itself difficult to access and has intimidated people, and that new technologies will make the market, and the knowledge that comes with it, accessible to everyone.
Swissinfo: You’re operating within the market in a very central position. And as we can see in the film, you are also working to cut off the intermediaries by putting the artists more directly in contact with their buyers. This is also a sort of disruption, isn’t it?
SdP: Auctioneers are going to be derelict because they are intermediaries. I’m excited to see how the art world will successfully transform the live auction experience by gamifying it, by making it accessible so that everybody can participate.
If a mega collector walks into Sotheby’s or Christie’s, then the expert will tell them all about a certain object and share their expertise. But that expertise can be shared with everyone. And with knowledge comes the hunger. The key is education; the more you know about a subject, the more you want to know, and the more you want to get into it. Spreading the knowledge is absolutely essential.
I think the disruption will probably not come from the traditional players, but from people with the tech savvy, with gaming savvy. And then, of course, you will need the expertise of the art market.
But if you bring the best of these elements together, you can completely revolutionise the art market. The current model is a result of the vision of Peter Wilson, who became chairman of Sotheby’s in 1958, and everything that he foresaw has happened. But now I think we’ve reached the limits of what that business model could bring. It now needs complete disruption.
Swissinfo: There is a new generation of collectors coming up. A big part is inheriting the collection of their parents, and they’re not selling it. Also, there are new players like tech billionaires and the emerging Asian market. Do you think they can play a role in this disruption?
SdP: It’s very important for the art market to always renew itself and renew its pool of buyers and collectors. Every year a whole range of very important collectors pass away.
I’ll give you an example. Take hip hop. I was fascinated by that whole jewelry in the scene, the bling jewels that they were wearing. It was a very innovative thing culturally in a field where there is not that much innovation.
Back then the big hip hop moguls were buying big cars, expensive watches, jewelry, and not buying any art at all. And then that changed. Who made that change?
The first one was Kanye West. I know that it’s a controversial name now, and he is indeed indefensible. However, he really was the first to ask contemporary artists like (Takashi) Murakami [in Graduation, West’s third studio album in 2007] or George Condo [My Beautiful Dark Twisted Fantasy in 2010] to design his album covers, and the first to collect art.
And then a number of key hip-hoppers like Jay-Z, Pharrell Williams, Puff Daddy, and many more all followed in his footsteps and focused on African American art. For a long time, the only African American artist with a high-profile in the market was Jean-Michel Basquiat, as if he was the only “artist of colour”. And then there has been this whole wave of fantastic artists like Mark Bradford, Kerry James Marshall… it’s a long list of artists whose market value has risen exponentially.
The tech community, with one or two exceptions, has not really entered the market yet in a way like the hedge fund guys, who became big collectors when they started making big money.
Swissinfo: Although many of them saw art much more as an investment, and not for the love of art.
SdP: Possibly, yes. But I feel it’s very important that the tech people get into the art market more actively, and they will when they understand that the only way to leave a long-term legacy is through art and culture. You can innovate all you want, but this will never leave as big and long-lasting an imprint as art and culture.
Another very important world that I love and that hasn’t entered the market yet is football. You only need somebody like [Norwegian footballer] Erling Haaland to start collecting to create a movement.
In the same way that hip-hoppers became tastemakers, football players will become tastemakers because whoever spends the most becomes a tastemaker. The same could go for the tech community. That’s why taste will always change and evolve.
Swissinfo: As for new markets, China is now the world’s second-biggest art market. But does China play a significant role today since Chinese collectors, in general, buy mostly Chinese art?
SdP: Initially, yes. The Chinese case is very interesting because, at the very start, some of the biggest collections of Chinese art were built by non-Chinese. [Swiss businessman] Uli Sigg was the key figure behind Chinese art. And when [Swiss curator] Harald Szeeman, at the head of the Venice Biennial in 1982, for the first time made a whole focus on Chinese art, it was all artists that had been discovered by Uli Sigg. And only then the Chinese started really collecting actively, and they moved on to also buying top Western artists.
More
Uli Sigg wants to help Chinese people ‘view their own art.’ Simple, right?
Swissinfo: But mostly Old Masters, right?
SdP: Yes, classical and modernist masters such as Modigliani but also cutting-edge contemporary art. During the Covid pandemic, when we could only look at art on the iPad and iPhone, the Chinese played a big role [in buying online].
That has quieted down at the moment, but I would say that Asian buying is absolutely key for the future of the art market. You always have to see which parts of the world are economically the strongest. Creativity usually flourishes in economically strong areas. I’m always fascinated to see how an economic upswing brings a cultural upswing.
Swissinfo: Where do you think this is happening now?
SdP: There is a new category of oligarchs that has been created in America. This will have an impact on the market as well as on future tastes.
The market has also become much more global. Some of the best contemporary art over the last few years has been made in Africa. There is this fantastic art fair called 1-54 [London, New York and Marrakech]External link, which has launched the careers of a number of African artists… so, location no longer is key for artists.
Swissinfo: Still, most of African art is still dealt in America and Europe. There are no big dealers or big players coming from Africa.
SdP: There are however quite a few African collectors now. I was two weeks ago in Rwanda, and I went to the Gihanga Institute of Contemporary Art that has just opened. The person behind it, Kami Gahiga, is partially working for Art Basel in charge of all African collectors. It’s all globally connected.
Swissinfo: We observe a consolidation of the market in which the bigger galleries and players are surviving and thriving while the mid-sized galleries, which include the ones dealing with Latin American and African art, have felt quite a squeeze. How do you see the picture right now for the mid-size and smaller galleries? That’s where usually new and original talent comes from.
SdP: That’s why I think that the market is ripe for disruption. Yes, there is a squeeze; it’s very difficult for the vast majority of galleries to cope financially. This means most galleries can no longer afford to go from art fair to art fair – and to be accepted by an art fair, you need to have a physical location as well.
It’s a model which is problematic because only the top players will be able to continue participating in it; a vast number of galleries will be left out. In the case of auction houses, whenever they become a little less profitable, they raise their commission, which is not a sustainable business. If I have to sell an object between 0 and $3 billion, I have to leave at least 28% on the table – these are absurd margins.
The market has to find ways of bringing these margins down. That will widen the market. And greater efficiency in selling will have to come through technology.
Swissinfo: And you’ll be happy to be part of this disruption, right?
SdP: As long as I am alive and kicking, I would love to be part of it, yes.
More
Art Basel keeps its lead as art fairs go corporate and scramble for markets

Vitosha – Nature just a step away from Bulgaria’s capital
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:59:20 UTC
16:59:20 KST

Author
Miglena Ivanova
Saturday 10 October 2026 09:30
Saturday, 10 October 2026, 09:30
PHOTO Pixabay
Font size
Vitosha-the mountain whose silhouette rises above Sofia—is one of the city’s favorite places to escape the hustle and bustle of urban life and one of the symbols of the capital city. It is no coincidence that one of Sofia’s central boulevards bears its name. Facing Vitosha, the boulevard creates a visual connection between the historic heart of the city and the mountain beyond. Despite the city’s urban expansion, the Vitosha ridge still stubbornly peeks out from between the buildings at various points across the city.
Cherni Vrah
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
“There’s nothing higher than Vitosha”, as the local Shopi saying goes. But in practice, with its highest point-Cherni Vrah (2,290 m)- it is the fourth-highest mountain in Bulgaria, after Rila, Pirin, and the Balkan Mountains. In 1934, the first national park in Bulgaria and on the Balkan Peninsula was established on its territory- “Vitosha” (today a nature park), currently covering an area of 27,079 hectares.
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
Vitosha boasts a fascinating geological history, natural phenomena, rich biodiversity, and opportunities for tourism and sports throughout all four seasons. We learn more interesting details about the mountain from Sava Popsavov, Chief Expert “Volunteers and Volunteerism Development”, and Anton Dimitrov, Tourism Specialist at the Vitosha Nature Park Directorate.
Sava Popsavov takes us back to the distant past, when the mountain was emerging with its distinctive profile:
PHOTO Facebook/ Vitosha Mountain
“Vitosha took on its present-day appearance during the Quaternary. This is the last geological period, which is still ongoing today. It began more than 2.5 million years ago. Around a million years ago, Vitosha took on its present-day appearance. If we go even further back in geological history, it can be said that it emerged from a sea during the Paleozoic Era, which covered the entire Sofia region and the surrounding plains.”
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
The stone rivers are among the most recognizable Vitosha landscapes.
“The stones themselves are large syenite blocks, formed as a result of spheroidal weathering under the constant effects of erosion and flowing water over immense periods of time”, explains Sava Popsavov. “The best-known stone rivers are in the valley of the Vladaiska River. A characteristic place is Zlatnite Mostove, or Golyamata Gramada, as it was formerly known-the toponym given to it by the local population. But, of course, there are also stone rivers in many other places, both on the northern and southern sides of Vitosha—along the Bistrishka and Yanchovska rivers, and at Matnitsa.”
Boyana Waterfall
PHOTO Facebook/ Vitosha Mountain
Among the most popular destinations in the mountain are also Cherni Vrah and Boyana Waterfall. For those who enjoy solitude in nature, the southeastern and southwestern slopes of Vitosha are more appealing, as they are the least visited due to their less-developed infrastructure.
Duhlata Cave
PHOTO akademic.org
Another interesting site in the mountain is Duhlata Cave, which until recently was considered the longest cave in Bulgaria and is impressive for its rock formations. However, it is accessible only through organized visits by speleologists.
''Zhivata Voda'' karst spring
PHOTO Miglena Ivanova
“We should also mention the karst spring ‘Zhivata Voda’ (Living Water), which is unique not only to Vitosha but to Bulgaria as well”, says Sava Popsavov:
“It is a system naturally formed as a siphon. What is specific about it is that a reservoir fills up and then gradually drains. When someone reaches the spring, they may find that water is flowing, or that there is no water at all. Once the water has drained away, some time passes before the natural catchment fills up again, so to speak. Then the water starts flowing again. There are all kinds of legends about this phenomenon. In the 17th century, the Ottoman explorer Evliya Çelebi described this phenomenon as the ‘fountain of happiness.’”
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
The nature park is also popular among adrenaline seekers.
“Vitosha offers much more than a classic walk,” Anton Dimitrov contends:
“Its proximity to Sofia makes Vitosha one of the most convenient places for outdoor sports throughout the year. During the warmer months, the most popular activities are mountain biking, mountain running, orienteering and rock climbing. For those who enjoy longer challenges, Vitosha hosts the iconic Vitosha 100 mountain marathon and cycling race. The mountain also offers opportunities for paragliding. In winter, it attracts skiing and snowboarding enthusiasts, and, when conditions permit, ski touring and other forms of winter mountain tourism.”
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
But the more accessible and popular a protected natural area is, the more important the question of its protection becomes. What role do the Vitosha Nature Park Directorate and the tourism community play in preserving its nature and biodiversity? Sava Popsavov has more:
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
“Vitosha Nature Park Directorate has been working on various projects for more than 10–15 years to restore and maintain biodiversity, park infrastructure and tourist trail markings. In addition to ensuring the safety of park visitors, these markings also help us preserve nature. We urge visitors to follow the marked trails and refrain from off-road driving or other similar activities that cause erosion, destroy valuable plant species and disturb wildlife.”
PHOTO Vitosha Nature Park
Besides mass tourism, another serious challenge is climate change. How is it affecting Vitosha, and are there already consequences that tourists can see with their own eyes?
“The snow cover definitely lasts for a much shorter period, and its boundary is much higher. There is also a shady spot known for its distinctive snowdrift, which is also the name of the locality- ‘Priaspata’ (between the Golyam and Malak Rezen peaks). There were many years when the snow lasted into the new season, and if it did not, it could at least be seen from Sofia until the end of August. Now, however, this snow has already melted by around late May or early June. Drying-up is also being observed at water catchments, as well as the drying of certain tree species. Mountain biking is replacing skiing as the mass sport. The main reason is that winters are no longer what they used to be”, concludes Sava Popsavov.

Trump pressured Ukraine to unilaterally halt strikes on Russian oil refineries – Axios
Axios reported this, citing a U.S. official familiar with the situation, Ukrinform says.
According to the report, Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries have been highly effective in recent months, triggering an energy crisis in Russia. In response, Russia banned diesel fuel exports, increasing pressure on global markets already facing disruptions caused by the war in Iran.
Zelensky told Trump and his envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, that Ukraine was ready to halt strikes on Russian oil refineries if Russia, for its part, stopped attacking Ukrainian power plants.
According to the U.S. official, Trump insisted that Ukraine halt the strikes unilaterally because they were contributing to higher gasoline prices in the United States. At the same time, the White House chief did not consider strikes on Russian oil refineries equivalent to Russian attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.
“President Trump decided to make a diesel fuel deal with Russia after Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky ignored half a dozen U.S. requests to stop attacking Russian oil refineries,” the source told Axios.
In an interview with Axios following the announcement of the deal, Zelensky said it came as a surprise to him. The Ukrainian President called it “not fair and not honest” and an unjustified gift to Putin, according to the publication.
The report says that during eight hours of talks in Miami on Friday, Witkoff and Kushner told the Ukrainian delegation that Trump planned to speak with Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports after Ukraine ignored repeated requests to stop attacks on Russian oil refineries, which had a direct impact on American consumers.
The publication notes that, according to a Ukrainian official, Witkoff and Kushner “threatened that Trump could cut off Ukraine from U.S. intelligence if it continued to ignore his requests.”
At the same time, a U.S. official said Witkoff and Kushner emphasized that the United States was a reliable partner providing Ukraine with ammunition and intelligence, and that Kyiv should therefore refrain from actions that harm American consumers.
During the talks, Witkoff and Kushner presented a package of measures for Ukraine’s postwar period. It included mechanisms to finance the country’s reconstruction and military development, as well as proposals to cover the budget deficit caused by the war. The participants also discussed a roadmap for Ukraine’s accession to the EU and Kyiv’s future relations with NATO after the war.
In addition, Witkoff and Kushner raised the possibility of creating a postwar security system between Europe and Russia that would satisfy both sides.
The U.S. mediators briefed Ukrainian and European representatives on possible energy deals with Russia. According to the official, Washington hopes these agreements will help lower energy prices and encourage Moscow to make concessions in peace talks.
The source told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner were considering visiting Moscow and Kyiv next week to discuss peace proposals. However, it remains unclear how the dispute that arose on Friday will affect their plans.
“Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop,” the U.S. official said.
As reported by Ukrinform, on October 9, U.S. President Donald Trump said that Russia, with U.S. approval, would supply 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to the global market and significantly increase its exports going forward.
President Volodymyr Zelensky stressed that gifts to Putin would not contribute to peace or benefit the civilized world, warning that Russia would “repay” them with further terror and treachery.

Vratsa Sinfonietta presents the story of Mara Belcheva and Richard Strauss

PHOTO Facebook/Vratsa Symphony
Font size
The little-known connection between Bulgarian poet Mara Belcheva and German composer Richard Strauss will be explored by the Vratsa Sinfonietta at the closing concert of the 57th Sofia Music Weeks International Festival, the orchestra announced, as quoted by BTA.
The concert, entitled Richard Strauss and Mara Belcheva – An Untold Story, will take place on 10 October at Bulgaria Hall in Sofia. The programme will feature music by Strauss, letters exchanged between the composer and Belcheva, and works associated with the European cultural circles of which she was part.
The audience will hear Strauss's Burleske for piano and orchestra, dedicated to Mara Belcheva, with pianist Nadezhda Tsanova as soloist. Tsanova is also the driving force behind the project.
Letters from the correspondence between Belcheva and Strauss will be read by Plamen Beykov, director of the Ruse Opera. The concert will be conducted by Hristo Pavlov, director of the Vratsa orchestra.

Ukraine's defence forces destroy over 4,700 aerial assets in September

Details: The aerial assets destroyed included 24 Kh-101 cruise missiles, eight Iskander-M/KN-23 ballistic missiles, 12 Kalibr cruise missiles, six Kh-59/69 air-launched missiles, six Iskander-K cruise missiles and eight Zircon anti-ship missiles.

Cockroach Janta Party names Ajinkya Shinde to lead its Jantar Mantar protest after founder Abhijeet Dipke and two associates are detained at Delhi airport. (Abhijeet Dipke, Ajinkya Shinde)
NEW DELHI: Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) on Saturday named its organisation in-charge Ajinkya Shinde to lead its protest at Jantar Mantar in New Delhi after founder Abhijeet Dipke, along with Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, was detained by Delhi Police at the airport.The party shared a pre-recorded video of Dipke, which he had filmed on Friday night in anticipation of a possible arrest ahead of the proposed October 10 demonstration demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation.
"Until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka are in detention, CJP’s Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead this protest at Jantar Mantar. Police guidelines require applications for demonstrations at Jantar Mantar to be submitted at least 10 days in advance.Authorities also cited alleged past violations of protest conditions, including demonstrations continuing beyond the stipulated time limits.

US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

US lifts sanctions on daughter of military-linked Myanmar businessman
Delisting comes days after Trump administration reportedly reopened talks with Myanmar’s government.
The United States has removed sanctions on the daughter of a Myanmar businessman accused of supporting the military-installed government.
The US Department of the Treasury removed Theint Win Htet from its sanctions list on Friday, according to its website, after she sued them in July.
The decision followed a Reuters news agency report that said US President Donald Trump’s administration has opened talks with Myanmar’s government, a break from years of US policy that sanctioned the generals responsible for a coup in 2021 against Myanmar’s democratically elected government.
In January 2024, the Treasury Department under former President Joe Biden’s administration targeted the Shwe Byain Phyu Group of Companies, which was founded by Theint Win Htet’s father, Thein Win Zaw, along with his family.
The department said the company supplied fuel to the military and owned at least 20 firms with close ties to the military leadership.
Theint Win Htet originally requested her removal in a lawsuit filed against the Biden administration. That case was dismissed last year. She then filed a second complaint in July, arguing that she has no role in her father’s business.
The sanctions had blocked her US credit cards, restricted her foreign bank accounts and forced her to abandon her master’s degree at Columbia University in New York. She now lives in Thailand with her mother, who was taken off the US sanctions list last year.
Theint Win Htet’s lawyer, Washington, DC-based sanctions specialist Erich Ferrari, filed a notice with the federal court in the US capital on Friday to voluntarily dismiss the lawsuit after her delisting.
‘Deplorable’
The group Justice For Myanmar has condemned the Treasury Department’s decision, saying Myanmar’s military is escalating attacks on civilians.
“It is deplorable that the US government continues to delist Myanmar cronies and their family members that provide funding for the junta’s terror,” the group said.
The Biden administration imposed sanctions on military officers and companies after the 2021 coup, which sparked a civil war that has killed about 100,000 people and displaced more than 3.5 million.
Washington lifted sanctions in July last year on several other Myanmar nationals and a company accused of aiding the military.

Super Hornet weapons computer can no longer be supported
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:48:24 UTC
16:48:24 KST

- The U.S. Navy intends to have Boeing design and qualify replacement parts for the obsolete AN/AYK-22 stores management processor used on its F/A-18 and EA-18G fleet.
- Other companies have until Oct. 28 to show they can do the work; the order’s value and schedule were not disclosed.
The U.S. Navy plans to have Boeing redesign parts of the computer that controls weapons and external stores on its F/A-18 and EA-18G fleet, after concluding that the current unit can no longer be supported because key components are no longer available.
Naval Air Systems Command’s PMA-265, the program office for the F/A-18 Super Hornet and EA-18G Growler, said in a notice posted Oct. 9 that it intends to award Boeing an order under an existing basic ordering agreement to design and qualify replacement parts for the AN/AYK-22 Stores Management Processor. The Navy did not disclose the order’s value, how many processors are involved or when the work would be finished.
The stores management processor sits between the jet’s mission computer and everything carried on its pylons, including missiles, bombs, fuel tanks and pods. It is the hardware that tells the aircraft what is loaded, manages weapon selection and passes the commands needed to release a store. The Navy said in the notice that the AN/AYK-22 is no longer supportable because some of its key parts have become obsolete, a problem the military calls diminishing manufacturing sources and material shortages, which occurs when suppliers stop making components that older systems depend on.
Although the Navy intends to go to Boeing without a competition, the notice is a sources-sought request, a step agencies use to check whether other companies could do the job. Interested firms have until Oct. 28 to send a one-page capability statement showing experience in finding and qualifying obsolete electronic parts for military aircraft, access to the required technical data and their quality certifications. The Navy also asked for published price lists, lead times and current stock levels for items that could meet the need.
The work is part of keeping the Super Hornet and Growler in service for decades after production ends. Boeing’s St. Louis line is due to deliver its last new Super Hornets in 2027 after the Navy’s final order for 17 jets in 2024, and Boeing no longer builds the Growler. Last month, the Navy paid Boeing $16.7 million to plan the shutdown of both production lines, including an inventory of government-owned tooling, on the same day it picked Boeing to develop the F/A-XX, the future carrier fighter meant to eventually replace both jets.
Existing Super Hornets are going through Boeing’s Service Life Modification program, which upgrades older jets to the Block III standard and extends their airframe life to 10,000 flight hours, with that work expected to continue into the mid-2030s.

US, Europe and Ukraine hold 'constructive discussions' on joint plan to end war
US, Ukrainian and European negotiators held talks in Miami on Friday to seek a common proposal to end the war in Ukraine, as President Donald Trump's decision to ease restrictions on Russian fuel drew criticism from lawmakers and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
US, Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Friday in a renewed diplomatic push to end Russia's war in Ukraine, with Washington seeking a way out of the dangerous stalemate.
The talks were overshadowed by US President Donald Trump's announcement of a deal with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to boost diesel supplies, underscoring how the conflict has become entwined with soaring energy prices.
Read moreTrump strikes diesel deal with Putin, reversing years of pressure on Russia over Ukraine war
US envoy Steve Witkoff posted to X after the meeting that the "constructive discussions" tackled "potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace".
Witkoff said the meeting included "the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO".
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and "longer-term arrangements for Ukraine's and Europe's security to prevent future conflict", Witkoff said.
He also noted the "productive" exchange discussed supporting Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession.
Witkoff did not say if the parties would meet on Saturday as originally planned.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned on Thursday that the conflict had reached a potentially explosive impasse, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
"The other way that stalemates end is through escalation," Rubio told reporters in Lisbon, warning that the conflict could spread to neighboring NATO countries.
"We do not believe that there is a military solution to this conflict," he added.
Trump has blamed Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries for surging fuel prices, although the US-Israeli war with Iran has been the principal disruptor of global energy supplies.
Following a telephone call with Putin on Friday, Trump said Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, with another 500,000 tons to follow in November.

The US Treasury Department said it was issuing a temporary license to allow Russian diesel to flow to global markets. It was not immediately clear whether Trump and Putin had discussed Ukraine during their call.
New proposals
The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff, a longtime Trump confidant, and Kushner, the president's son-in-law, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.
US negotiators have since been developing fresh proposals with Russian and Ukrainian officials, a source familiar with the discussions told AFP.
With winter approaching, the prospect of continued fighting and attacks on vital infrastructure has added urgency to the search for a settlement.
The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on buses in the frontline Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk that killed 30 people.
Territorial deadlock
Trump's repeated attempts to broker an end to the war have foundered over Moscow's sweeping territorial demands, particularly its insistence on controlling all of Ukraine's eastern Donbas region, including areas still held by Kyiv.
Zelensky has rejected surrendering Ukrainian-held territory, warning that Russia could use it as a springboard for another attack.
Russia, which launched its full-scale invasion in February 2022, now occupies roughly one-fifth of Ukrainian territory.
European officials have expressed concern over high energy costs and the wider economic consequences of the conflict, according to the US sources.
Witkoff and Kushner briefed the president on their latest proposals on Thursday at a meeting also attended by Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and other senior officials, Axios reported.
The US administration hopes to make diplomatic headway before November's midterm elections, with Washington also seeking to arrange broader talks involving Russia and Ukraine later this month.
The Kremlin has signaled that such three-way negotiations could resume in October, although no date has been announced.

Snow worries a key question ahead of Otepää biathlon world championships
With less than two months until the biathlon season starts, snow is the key question for organizers of the World Championships in Otepää, Valga County, in February.
Race director Borut Nunar said last winter's World Cup stage went ahead in terrible conditions; organizers are hoping for better weather in February.
Four months before the competition, everything expected was reviewed once more and gone through in cooperation with the International Biathlon Union (IBU) leadership. While everything else can be checked, the presence of snow cannot — yet it is the key question for organizers.
"Here I have to say the last World Cup, which was the last test before the World Championship, was not exactly a winter wonderland, but at the end I have to say a big thanks to the whole of Otepää and Estonia; they created a wonderful World Cup event with a terrible weather situation actually, and in February it should be normally easier, but you never know, and this is always our biggest concern, if the conditions are not the best for the athletes, because if you have happy athletes you have a happy World Championship," Nunar told ERR Sport.
At the same time, other winter sports events are to take place in Otepää this coming season. The biathlon World Championships will be the third major event. Before that, the Nordic combined World Cup takes place at the ski center, followed by the junior World Championships in skiing.
Snow has to be enough for all of them, and plans are in place for artificial snow just in case. Artificial snow requires low temperatures to create, which is why the cold snap matters.
"There is some snow reserve, about half of it is there," said Hillar Zahkna, chairman of the competition committee. "With the first cold spells we have to start making snow immediately, both for the track and for the store. Then also for the store at Kääriku. Then we hope for the best — if the weather is stable, we put the snow down."
The IBU Biathlon World Championships take place February 9-21, 2027 at the Tehvandi Sports Center in Otepää.

'Excuse Me, Is This Yours?': Before you boycott settlers, meet them - review
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:46:09 UTC
16:46:09 KST

Tuvia Tenenbom’s Excuse Me, Is This Yours? joins the debate over the West Bank (Judea and Samaria) not through resolutions, maps, or diplomatic declarations, but via the people who live there.
Last month, 12 Western countries announced plans to boycott trade with Israeli settlements, once again turning “the settlers” into an international political category. But who, exactly, are these settlers?
Tenenbom spent eight months living among them, moving from established communities to isolated hilltops, while also speaking with Palestinians, Samaritans, soldiers, politicians, rabbis, and activists. What emerges is considerably messier than the familiar portrait of a single ideological bloc.
Everyone has a different reason for becoming a 'settler'
Some settlers are intensely religious. Some are nationalists. Some are rebels against the Israeli state itself.
Others, Tenenbom discovers, moved across the Green Line simply because housing was cheaper. In Shaked, one resident tells him that most people now live there “because of convenience and cheaper housing, not because of ideology.”
Even attitudes toward Palestinians refuse to behave according to script.
One settler tells Tenenbom: “Culturally, I feel closer to the Arabs in the next village than to the Americans, including American Jews,” adding, “I don’t want the Palestinians to go.”
And then there is annexation.
The outside world often assumes that settlers uniformly demand it. Tenenbom finds something stranger. Politicians and settlement leaders repeatedly talk about sovereignty, yet Israel somehow never quite gets around to imposing it.
At one point, the author reduces the absurdity to a wonderfully Tenenbomian instruction: “You want it? Take it. And annex it. You don’t want it? Leave it. And move to Tel Aviv.”
Politics, theology, absurdity, and human contradiction
This mixture of politics, theology, absurdity, and human contradiction is the book’s strength. The author does not ask readers to love the settlers or hate them. He asks something less fashionable: to meet them first.
Of course, as is to be expected of Tenenbom, the book is also very funny. His classic Jewish humor is important because, without it, the subject could easily become unbearable. His voice, as always, is curious, mischievous, humorous, and occasionally exasperating. It keeps the narrative moving even when the politics become heavy.
Now that international governments are deciding what not to buy from people who live in the West Bank, Excuse Me, Is This Yours? asks whether we might first find out who these people are.
The book also examines and challenges the work of Yuval Abraham, co-director of the infamous NAZA documentary that recently won a coveted prize at the 83rd International Venice Film Festival and received a 25-minute standing ovation from a roomful of antisemites. ■
In addition to this latest book, Tenenbom is the author of the following six: Hello Refugees, The Taming of the Jew, I Sleep in Hitler’s Room, The Lies They Tell, Catch the Jew, and Careful, Beauties Ahead.
EXCUSE ME, IS THIS YOURS?
By Tuvia Tenenbom
Gefen Publishing House
488 pages; $30

The West Bank revolution: How Bezalel Smotrich changed Israel's map for the better - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:46:01 UTC
16:46:01 KST

Over the past four years, something remarkable has been happening in Judea and Samaria.
Since the current government took office at the end of 2022, it has approved the establishment or retroactive legalization of 104 Jewish communities there.
At the center of this transformation has been Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who also serves as a minister in the Defense Ministry. In 2023, he was given broad authority over civilian affairs in Judea and Samaria, including settlement planning, through the newly created Settlement Administration.
And he has used that authority to reshape settlement policy.
The 104 communities are not all entirely new. The figure also includes previously unauthorized outposts that were legalized and neighborhoods that were granted independent status.
Even so, the scale is extraordinary.
The government approved plans and funding for 34 communities over the summer
This past summer alone, the government approved plans and funding for 34 communities: nine in Samaria, seven in the Mateh Binyamin Regional Council area, seven in the Jordan Valley, six in Gush Etzion, four in the Hebron region, and one in the Dead Sea area.
It amounts to nothing less than a settlement revolution.
And it is taking place amid steady demographic growth. As of January 1, a total of 541,085 Jews lived in Judea, Samaria, and the Jordan Valley, excluding eastern Jerusalem. That represented an increase of 2.2% in a single year, twice the growth rate of Israel’s population as a whole.
Some of the government’s decisions have corrected anomalies that persisted for years. Communities that existed in bureaucratic limbo have finally received official status. Further, the government has moved to restore the four northern Samaria communities – Homesh, Sa-Nur, Ganim, and Kadim – that were uprooted under Ariel Sharon’s 2005 disengagement plan.
Twenty years after Israel withdrew from northern Samaria, Jews are returning.
But the importance of what is happening cannot be measured by numbers alone.
Look at the map.
Northern Samaria overlooks Israel’s densely populated coastal plain, where much of the country’s population, industry, and infrastructure are concentrated. Strengthening the Jewish presence there reinforces Israel’s hold on the mountain ridge overlooking its heartland while reversing the retreat initiated by disengagement.
Further east is the Jordan Valley, where seven more communities were included in this summer’s decision.
The valley provides Israel with strategic depth along its eastern flank and separates the Palestinian population centers of Judea and Samaria from Jordan and the wider Middle East.
Settlement cannot replace soldiers. But civilian communities, roads, and infrastructure help ensure a lasting Israeli presence in territory vital to the country’s security.
The same principle applies elsewhere. Shalem, east of Shechem (Nablus), will strengthen the Jewish presence in central Samaria, while six additional communities in Gush Etzion reinforce Jerusalem’s southern approaches and the historic Jerusalem-Hebron corridor.
Then there are the farms.
According to Smotrich, roughly 160 agricultural farms have been established throughout Judea and Samaria during the government’s tenure. Unlike conventional settlements, many consist of little more than a family or two, several structures, and herds of sheep or cattle.
But that is precisely what makes them significant.
A town may require hundreds of homes and extensive infrastructure to establish a substantial presence. A farm can maintain agricultural activity across thousands of dunams with a fraction of the population.
The Smotrich revolution is not merely about building houses
Their purpose is to protect state land, counter unauthorized Palestinian construction and cultivation, and extend Jewish activity into the open spaces between existing communities, along roads, and across ridgelines.
The Smotrich revolution is not merely about building houses.
It is also about controlling the spaces between them.
Just as important, Smotrich has changed the way the government handles settlement.
For decades, even right-wing governments often treated construction in Judea and Samaria as exceptional. Planning meetings were sporadic, approvals could languish for years, and international pressure routinely slowed the process.
Smotrich has sought to turn settlement development into a normal and continuous function of government. Planning procedures have been accelerated, longstanding communities legalized, and the Settlement Administration institutionalized inside the Defense Ministry.
The government has also put money behind the policy, including over NIS 1 billion for roads and infrastructure serving new and existing communities.
Without roads, water, and electricity, settlements can remain little more than dots on a map. Smotrich has sought to make them permanent facts on the ground.
That is the real significance of what has taken place over the past four years.
For decades, advocates of Palestinian statehood proceeded from the assumption that Judea and Samaria could eventually be divided, Jewish communities removed or isolated, and a sovereign Palestinian entity established in their place.
The Smotrich revolution has steadily closed off that option.
Oct. 7 demonstrated the potentially catastrophic consequences of allowing territory adjacent to Israeli population centers to fall into the hands of those bent on the Jewish state’s destruction. A Palestinian state in the hills of Judea and Samaria would overlook Jerusalem and much of Israel’s coastal plain, placing the country’s population centers within easy reach of those who seek the Jewish state’s destruction.
For supporters of Palestinian statehood, that is precisely why the settlement revolution is so alarming.
But for those of us who believe that establishing a hostile Palestinian terrorist state in Israel’s biblical heartland would be a historic and strategic disaster, it is precisely why the revolution matters.
Smotrich has not merely changed settlement policy.
He has changed the map, making a Palestinian state in Judea and Samaria virtually impossible.
And thank God for that.■
The writer served as deputy communications director under Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Ushakov further claimed that following the discussion, Trump instructed American officials to relay the diplomatic “signals” received from the Kremlin directly to the Ukrainian government.
Hardline stance despite diplomatic overtures
Putin’s refusal to consider peace talks comes despite intensive diplomatic maneuvering by Washington to initiate a negotiating framework ahead of winter.
Easing Diesel Sanctions Shows Weakness to Putin, Sybiha Says
On Friday, Oct. 9, high-level multilateral consultations convened by the US in Miami – bringing together US special envoy Steve Witkoff, Ukrainian negotiators, and representatives from Britain, France, Germany, the European Commission, and NATO – concluded after a six-hour session without a announced breakthrough.
While Witkoff characterized the dialogue as constructive, European and Ukrainian officials expressed skepticism regarding Moscow’s willingness to engage in substantive de-escalation.
Putin’s uncompromising posture in the phone call also aligns with public warnings issued by Ukrainian leaders.
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha warned on Friday that concessions to Moscow project Western weakness, asserting that Putin interprets economic and diplomatic overtures as appeasement rather than incentives for peace.
The Trump diesel pact
The phone call and Putin’s subsequent rebuff unfolded alongside controversy surrounding Trump’s announcement of a bilateral commercial agreement permitting Russian petroleum shipments into American and global markets.
Trump announced that Russia agreed to supply over 300,000 metric tons of diesel fuel immediately, with 500,000 tons scheduled for November and 1 million tons thereafter, potentially scaling up to 3 million tons depending on refinery operations.
Trump argued that the deliveries, combined with what he termed “total control of the Strait of Hormuz,” would curb fuel costs for American consumers and global markets amid energy market volatility fueled by the US-Israeli conflict with Iran.
Shortly after the announcement, the US Treasury Department issued a temporary general license authorizing the sale and import of Russian diesel fuel through April 7, 2027.
The sanctions waiver was enacted just three weeks after Trump signed into law the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026 on Sept. 18, which was designed to expand statutory penalties across Russia’s energy, banking, and defense sectors.
Hours before the license was issued, President Volodymyr Zelensky had directly appealed to visiting US lawmakers to strictly enforce statutory sanctions as a vital tool to compel Moscow to negotiate.
The sanctions relief granted Moscow an economic accommodation it had sought since July, when Russia imposed an export ban on domestic diesel following successful Ukrainian drone strikes that damaged major Russian refining facilities.
Trump had previously urged Kyiv to halt strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, attributing elevated diesel benchmarks to Ukrainian interdiction operations rather than the Middle Eastern conflict.

U.S. Navy warship gun program heads toward new contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:41:30 UTC
16:41:30 KST

- Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division asked industry for feedback on a hybrid fixed-price and cost-plus contract for its Gun Weapon Systems program.
- Responses are due Oct. 29, and the Navy has not disclosed the contract’s value, length or which gun systems it covers.
The U.S. Navy has asked defense companies for feedback on how it plans to structure a future contract for its Gun Weapon Systems program, the engineering effort behind the guns mounted on its warships.
Naval Surface Warfare Center Dahlgren Division in Virginia posted the request for information on Oct. 9. It asks potential vendors to comment on a proposed hybrid contract that would combine firm-fixed-price and cost-plus-fixed-fee work, and responses are due Oct. 29. The notice says the request is for planning only, and the Navy will use the answers to shape its acquisition strategy.
The posting does not say which gun systems the program covers, how much the contract could be worth, how long it would run or when a formal solicitation might follow. Those details, along with the specific questions for industry, are in attachments that were not included in the public summary. The notice lists the work under engineering services, with Dahlgren as the place of performance.
Under a hybrid structure, the Navy would pay a set price for tasks it can define clearly in advance and reimburse costs plus a fixed fee for work that is harder to scope, such as development and engineering tasks where the final effort is uncertain. The government often uses that mix on long-running engineering support programs.
Dahlgren is the U.S. Navy’s main center for surface ship weapons engineering, including the guns carried on destroyers, cruisers and smaller combatants. The largest of those is the Mk 45 5-inch (127 mm) gun fitted to Arleigh Burke-class destroyers, which can fire 16 to 20 rounds a minute.
Ship guns have taken on a larger role in air defense over the past three years. During operations against Houthi forces in the Red Sea, U.S. destroyers used their 5-inch guns to shoot down attack drones, and the Navy reported firing 160 main gun rounds in those operations. In one engagement, the destroyer USS Stockdale (DDG 106) used its 5-inch gun to destroy a low-flying Houthi drone that was detected late, according to U.S. Central Command. Guns offer a cheaper way to deal with small drones than surface-to-air missiles, which can cost millions of dollars each.

Silent killer: study finds most with high blood pressure unaware
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:33:37 UTC
16:33:37 KST

Men showed higher rates of hypertension, with 42% affected compared with 29% of women, after adjusting the figures for age groups.
A recent British study involving around 1.4 million people in England has found that more than a third of adults have high blood pressure.
Worryingly, the study shows that around 6 in every 10 people affected, 59%, do not know they are living with this "silent killer" and have not received any treatment.
These figures highlight a persistent failure to detect one of the main risk factors leading to heart and vascular disease and strokes, amid growing calls from health experts to step up early screening campaigns and save millions of people at risk of deadly complications.
A marked rise with age
Researchers from the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford analysed blood pressure readings taken in clinics as part of the "Our Future Health" programme, the largest health research initiative in the United Kingdom. The data covered participants who joined the programme between 2022 and 2025.
The study used World Health Organization criteria to define high blood pressure, classifying someone as hypertensive if their systolic reading is 140 millimetres of mercury or above, their diastolic reading is 90 millimetres of mercury or above, or if they are already taking blood-pressure-lowering medication.
The data showed a large variation in prevalence by age: 15% among adults aged 18 to 39, rising gradually to 71% in people aged 80 and over.
Men were more likely than women to have the condition, with rates of 42% for men compared with 29% for women, after adjusting for age groups.
Half of those on treatment do not reach the target level
The problem does not only concern undiagnosed cases. The study found that 50% of participants taking one or more medicines to lower blood pressure still had readings of 140/90 millimetres of mercury or above, the threshold used in the research to define high blood pressure.
According to the researchers, these findings show that difficulties in diagnosing and controlling the condition in England persist, despite clinical guidelines that have been in place for years.
They pointed out that current guidance from the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) requires several measurements before confirming a diagnosis and, in some cases, recommends starting with lifestyle changes before prescribing medication. They believe this approach may be leaving some cases without detection or effective treatment.
Calls for a more proactive approach
Wenyu Liu, a medical statistician in the Population Health Department at the University of Oxford and lead researcher on the study, said high blood pressure is often described as a "silent killer", arguing that the current methods of detecting and treating the condition need to be reconsidered.
Liu stressed that the "silent killer" crisis is not confined to older people, noting that more than 15% of younger adults aged 18 to 39 were found to have high blood pressure.
She noted that this younger group currently falls outside routine medical monitoring, as they do not meet the age criteria for the National Health Service (NHS) regular health check programme, which starts at 40. This, she said, makes an urgent update of early detection policies necessary.
Liu called for stronger population-wide prevention strategies, alongside directing treatment towards those most at risk of heart disease and other cardiovascular conditions.
For his part, Ian Turnbull, deputy chief medical officer for the "Our Future Health" programme, clinical researcher in Oxford University's Population Health Department and a general practitioner, said the results are in line with what doctors see in general practice, where many cases of high blood pressure remain undetected or are not treated optimally.
He highlighted the need for a more active approach to finding people with the condition, including examining whether treatment should start on the basis of an individual's predicted risk of heart and vascular disease, rather than relying solely on blood pressure levels.
British Heart Foundation warns of missed chances for prevention
Professor Bryan Williams, chief scientific and medical officer at the British Heart Foundation, described the study's findings as worrying, saying they reveal the scale of undiagnosed high blood pressure and the difficulties in controlling it among people who are already receiving treatment.
Williams said high blood pressure remains the main modifiable risk factor associated with cardiovascular disease, noting that it is linked to around half of all heart attacks and strokes in the United Kingdom.
He added that millions of people are living with the condition without knowing it, which means important opportunities for diagnosis and early intervention are being missed.
According to Williams, improving the detection and treatment of high blood pressure could help tens of thousands of people avoid preventable heart attacks and strokes. However, he believes this will require a rethink of how people at risk are identified, treated and followed up, to ensure blood pressure checks and effective therapy reach all groups.

Laser that warns B-2 pilots of contrails gets $34.6M deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:32:35 UTC
16:32:35 KST

- Ophir Corp. received a $34.6 million sole-source contract to repair the B-2 Pilot Alert System, with work running through October 2036.
- The lidar system detects when the B-2 starts forming a contrail so crews can change altitude and avoid visual detection.
The U.S. Air Force has awarded Ophir Corp. of Littleton, Colorado, a $34.6 million contract to repair the laser system that warns B-2 Spirit crews when their stealth bomber starts leaving a visible condensation trail.
The firm-fixed-price contract, announced Oct. 9, covers repairs of the B-2 Pilot Alert System, with work done in Littleton and expected to run through October 2036. The Air Force Sustainment Center at Tinker Air Force Base, Oklahoma, awarded it as a sole-source deal and obligated the full amount from fiscal 2026 working capital funds. The Pentagon did not say how many units will be repaired under the contract.
A B-2 is designed to be hard to find on radar, but a contrail, the white streak of ice crystals that forms behind jet engines at high altitude in cold, humid air, can reveal its position to anyone looking up. The Pilot Alert System is a lidar sensor, which uses a laser instead of radio waves, that looks behind the aircraft, detects when a contrail begins to form and tells the crew so they can change altitude.
The original B-2 design included tanks outboard of the main landing gear for a chemical meant to suppress contrails, but that approach was never used. The U.S. Air Force funded development of the lidar alert system in the mid-1990s as part of a retrofit of the bomber fleet. To avoid making the aircraft easier to detect, Ophir built the sensor around a continuous-wave laser instead of a pulsed one, which the company said would contrast too sharply with the background, according to a technical article by an Ophir executive. The company, founded in 1978, makes laser-based sensors for measuring air data, icing and wind.
The award will keep the system supported for about another decade on a bomber the U.S. Air Force plans to replace with the Northrop Grumman B-21 Raider. The service flies 19 B-2s from Whiteman Air Force Base, Missouri, after one was retired following a 2022 accident, and the fleet has been kept in service with new communications and other upgrades while B-21 production ramps up. B-2s carried out the June 2025 strikes on Iran’s Fordow and Natanz nuclear sites with GBU-57 bunker-busting bombs, a weapon only the B-2 can currently drop in combat.
