Expert Insights: Sixteen years to make a Danish friend. Was it worth it?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:29:33 UTC
16:29:33 KST

The author: Journalist Richard Steed has lived in Copenhagen since 2009. Arriving from Luton, he was briefly exotic – until the Danes discovered where it was: the backend of nowhere. Their insistence on practising English sabotaged any hope of him learning Danish. Left with one career option, he writes in English, flaunting selvfølgelig with pride. He writes a monthly column for The Copenhagen Post. You can also subscribe to his weekly newsletter, Danesplained, on Substack.
I’ve recently been asking internationals how long it took them to make their first Danish friend.
Five years, said one.
Eight, said another.
Then someone told me about an American woman who waited sixteen.
Sixteen years.
Only the reality show Paradise Hotel has lasted longer. It’s now on season 22.
And now, apparently, she’s off to Florida.
So, was it worth it?
I’m still waiting for her answer.
But it does raise the question.
Most people told me it took somewhere between two and eight years. And many internationals leave long before that.
You’re here on a three-year contract. Your partner can’t find a job. Danish lessons eat your evenings. You’re busy, tired, and not entirely sure you’re staying.
So why bother?
Because of what you get at the end of the queue.
It can feel like a long waiting list. But once you’re in, you’re in.
A Danish friend is thoughtful. They’ll remember your birthday, mostly because it’s been in their calendar since week three.
They’re calm. Steady. Reliable.
Right up until the julefrokost, when they become someone else entirely.
Then, on Monday morning, nobody mentions it.
Ever.
They don’t leave.
And that matters more than you’d think.
Make friends with other internationals and you’ll spend half your social life at farewell parties. One gets a job in Vienna. Another can’t meet the salary threshold and has to leave. A couple gets homesick and moves back to Toronto.
Danes, by and large, aren’t going anywhere.
They’re already home.
Make a Danish friend and they’ll still be there when everyone else has moved to Singapore.
And if you’re only here for three years?
It’s a fair question. Plenty of internationals decide it isn’t worth the effort and stay in the international bubble.
But a Danish friend gets you out of it. You start to see how Danes spend their time, what they argue about, and which rules everyone seems to know except you.
And thanks to my Danish friends, I’ve discovered we have rather more in common than you might expect.
A love of complaining, for one.
Who would have guessed?
And when your contract ends, the friendship doesn’t have to.
It may even be the reason you come back.
Assuming you’re allowed back in.
And here’s the part nobody tells you.
A Danish friend rarely comes alone.
Once you’re in, they quietly make sure their friends let you in too. Suddenly you’re at dinner parties, birthdays, and someone’s child’s konfirmation, wondering how it happened.
Before you know it, you’re part of a wider circle.
It took me three years to find my first Danish friend.
His name was Thorsten.
He took me under his wing and explained Janteloven, and what hygge actually means.
Candles, it turns out, are more than decoration.
They’re also part of a very specific moment in Danish history.
Thorsten told me how, when the BBC announced Denmark’s liberation on the evening of 4 May 1945, Danes tore down their blackout curtains and put candles in the windows.
They still do it every year.
He introduced me to Matador. He had the patience of a saint and the determination of an ox.
With me, he needed both.
Three years of waiting.
Worth every one.
Thorsten is no longer with us.
I think of him every time I light a candle.
So, sixteen years.
Was it worth it?
The queue is long, I’ll give you that.
But I’ve never met anyone at the front who asked for a refund.
Well.
Apart from one.
She’s off to Florida.

Kushner marks one year of Trump's Gaza peace plan, cites progress and challenges ahead
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump's son-in-law and adviser, marked one year since an agreement was reached on Trump's 20-point plan for Gaza on Friday, saying significant progress had been made in implementing the agreement over the past year.
Kushner highlighted several milestones, including the return of the 20 living hostages to Israel in October 2025, the return of the remains of the final hostage in January 2026, the establishment of the Board of Peace and an international stabilization force, and the formation of a technocratic Palestinian administration to govern the Gaza Strip.

Kushner: Progress is real, but challenges remain
"The situation is far from perfect, but the progress is real, and the world is better off because of it," Kushner wrote.
Looking ahead, Kushner said the coming year would require completing the disarmament process, establishing security, restoring essential services, and rebuilding communities throughout the Gaza Strip.
Kushner also thanked Trump, Steve Witkoff, the vice president, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, and several regional partners, including Egypt, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, and Israel, for their roles in advancing the agreement.
Hamas sees Gaza war survival as victory over Israel
One of the key points going forward that Kushner pointed out was the disarmament of Hamas, something the plan might be far from achieving following recent reports about a new Hamas operation that will involve establishing defenses in Gaza City.
According to Friday intelligence presented to Israel's senior political and defense leadership, including the prime minister and defense minister, Hamas's leadership views its ability to withstand the IDF over the past three years as a form of "victory," despite Israel's control of approximately 70% of the Gaza Strip.
Hamas considers Israel's territorial control "temporary," according to the information presented to officials.
"They are convinced that US President Donald Trump's points-based plan for the Gaza Strip, which his son-in-law Kushner is advancing, including a plan for economic development involving tens of billions of dollars in investment, is a direct continuation of Sheik Ahmed Yassin's vision from 1999," a senior security official said. "They believe in it even if it is delayed."
The senior security official added: "They tell themselves, and we can see this, that by launching an attack with men wearing beards, jalabiyas, and flip-flops, and through their steadfast resistance against the IDF even after three years, they have not been defeated. They have not surrendered to an army that everyone says is the strongest in the Middle East. Something no other Arab army in the Middle East has managed to achieve."
According to the official, Hamas is therefore preparing for an IDF ground maneuver toward Gaza City, despite tensions between the terrorist organization's local leadership and Khalil al-Hayya in Qatar.

One year after a U.S.-brokered ceasefire took effect in Gaza, Israeli strikes continue, much of the territory remains under Israeli military control and plans for disarmament and reconstruction have made little progress.
The agreement, which came into effect on Oct. 10, 2025, secured the release of the remaining 20 living Israeli hostages held by Hamas three days later and brought a halt to rocket attacks on Israel from Gaza.
But Israel has continued carrying out strikes in the Palestinian territory, killing around 1,450 people since the ceasefire, according to Gaza's Health Ministry.
Israeli forces now control about 70 percent of Gaza, compared with roughly 53 percent under the initial terms of the agreement.
The second phase of the deal, which envisaged further Israeli withdrawals, the disarmament of Hamas and the transfer of Gaza's administration to a Palestinian technocratic committee, remains stalled.
Hamas announced in July that it was disbanding its governing body and handing over administration to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), headed by Ali Shaath.
The group also agreed to give up its weapons, but disarmament has yet to take place. Hamas continues to exercise security control in parts of Gaza.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted that Hamas completely disarm before further withdrawals, rejecting a phased approach linking the two steps.
Reconstruction has also failed to get underway despite international funding pledges.
U.S. President Donald Trump's Board of Peace presented a $2.45 billion recovery plan in September, outlining projects to be implemented over six months. However, rebuilding remains stalled amid the political and security deadlock.
Most of Gaza's population remains displaced, living in tents, shelters or damaged buildings as winter approaches.
The anniversary comes ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 general election, raising further uncertainty about the agreement's future.
Analysts interviewed by Anadolu Agency said coalition negotiations following the vote could delay progress until early 2027, while Washington may face renewed pressure to intervene after the U.S. congressional midterm elections in November.
Egyptian political analyst Tarek Fahmy said the deadlock could persist for at least three months after the Israeli vote unless Washington steps in to revive negotiations.
Other analysts said a change of government in Israel might alter the approach to Gaza but was unlikely to produce an immediate breakthrough.
Meanwhile, mediators including Türkiye, Egypt and Qatar are expected to continue efforts to prevent further escalation and increase humanitarian assistance to Gaza.

‘Nuclear weapons not routine instruments of statecraft’: India’s warning to Pakistan at UN
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:24:24 UTC
16:24:24 KST

‘India will not bow to nuclear blackmail’: New Delhi hits back at Pakistan at UN (Anmol Sher Singh Bedi)
NEW DELHI: India on Friday warned Pakistan against using nuclear weapons as a tool of political pressure, asserting that New Delhi would not bow to nuclear blackmail and that any terrorist attack against the country would invite a fitting response.Exercising its Right of Reply at the United Nations General Assembly's First Committee, which deals with disarmament and international security, India said nuclear weapons must not be treated as “routine instruments of statecraft”.Senior Adviser (Disarmament) at India's Permanent Mission to the Conference on Disarmament in Geneva, Anmol Sher Singh Bedi, delivered the response following remarks by Pakistan on Jammu and Kashmir.
“Jammu and Kashmir is an integral and inalienable part of India,” Bedi said, rejecting Pakistan's claims over the region.He said India's military capabilities were defensive in nature and shaped by its security environment, rather than directed against any particular country.“We heard concerns about escalation. These are legitimate concerns. However, these are best judged by conduct over time. Nuclear weapons must not be treated as routine instruments of statecraft,” Bedi said.
He warned that relying on the threat of nuclear weapons to shield activities below the threshold of conventional warfare could increase the risk of escalation rather than promote restraint.“A posture that relies on nuclear overhang to limit the consequences of subconventional activity raises the risk of escalation and not the prospect of restraint,” he said.Bedi also outlined what he described as a recurring pattern in regional crises, involving provocation, denial of responsibility and subsequent appeals for restraint after a response.“Where those in power are neither elected by people nor accountable to them, their decisions carry no risk and impose no cost for those who take them. That is how crisis becomes an instrument of power. That is how instability becomes useful, and that is how the cycle keeps on repeating,” he said.
India reiterates three red lines
India said its position on terrorism and national security remained clear, identifying three principles that would guide its response to threats.“First, any terrorist attack against India will receive a fitting response. Second, India will not bow to nuclear blackmail. Third, India will make no distinction between those who sponsor terrorism and those who mastermind it,” Bedi said.He said India's actions in May 2025 followed a “grave provocation” and were undertaken in self-defence after the April 22 Pahalgam terror attack in Jammu and Kashmir, in which 26 civilians, mostly tourists, were killed.“These actions were measured, targeted, and designed to be non-escalatory,” Bedi said.India launched Operation Sindoor on May 7, 2025, targeting what it described as terrorist infrastructure in Pakistan and Pakistan-occupied Kashmir in retaliation for the Pahalgam attack. The Resistance Front, a proxy of Pakistan-based Lashkar-e-Taiba, was linked to the attack.Bedi also stressed that the use of non-state actors by a country did not absolve it of responsibility for their actions.“The use of force by states under the garb of non-state actors does not erase the state's responsibility. India's right of self-defense remains intact,” he said.
India raises Indus Waters Treaty, nuclear proliferation
India also referred to the Indus Waters Treaty, arguing that the agreement depended on mutual trust and cooperation between the two countries.“A state cannot undermine those foundations of trust and cooperation and at the same time insist that the privileges flowing from the relationship remain untouched,” Bedi said.Following the Pahalgam attack, India announced that the treaty would be held in abeyance until Pakistan credibly and irrevocably ended its support for cross-border and other forms of terrorism.On nuclear proliferation, Bedi invoked the legacy of Pakistani nuclear scientist Abdul Qadeer Khan and the international proliferation network associated with him, which supplied nuclear equipment and expertise to countries seeking to develop nuclear weapons.
The network contributed to international concerns that led to United Nations Security Council Resolution 1540, adopted in 2004, which requires states to prevent the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and their means of delivery to non-state actors.“This is relevant in the context of demands for unquestioned nuclear cooperation and transfer of advanced weapons and military capabilities. We urge all states and all responsible suppliers to exercise the highest degree of vigilance, not because of India, but for their own security,” Bedi said.

JSC Grindeks’ subsidiary in Lithuania Ltd Grindeks Kalceks has received the “Strongest in Lithuania 2026” (Stipriausi Lietuvoje) recognition, confirming the company’s financial stability, reliability and responsible business practices.
“Strongest in Lithuania” is an independent external assessment of a company’s creditworthiness and reliability and has been awarded in Lithuania since 2011. The certificate confirms that a company maintains a sound financial position, fulfils its tax obligations on time, and settles its obligations to business partners and employees in a timely manner. It is awarded to companies with a strong business reputation that contribute to the development of the Lithuanian economy and promote an ethical business culture. In 2026, a total of 1,439 companies in Lithuania received the “Strongest in Lithuania” certificate.
Director of Ltd Grindeks Kalceks Aurimas Motiejūnas comments: “This recognition reflects the professional approach of our team and the values that guide our work every day. Our priority is to maintain a strong and trusted position in the Lithuanian pharmaceutical sector while continuing to grow responsibly and uphold high standards of business ethics. At the same time, patients remain at the centre of what we do – our aim is to provide effective and accessible solutions that contribute to better health and quality of life. The company attributes the recognition to the professionalism and commitment of its employees, as well as to the consistent implementation of the Grindeks Group’s core values. Every team member contributes to the company’s performance, long-term development and reputation as a reliable business partner.”
In 2025, the Lithuanian subsidiary was also recognised by Creditinfo as a “Reliable Employer”, further highlighting the company’s financial reliability and responsible approach as an employer.
About JSC Grindeks
JSC Grindeks is the parent company of the international pharmaceutical group Grindeks. The Group is engaged in the research, development, manufacturing and commercialization of original medicines, generic medicines and active pharmaceutical ingredients.
The Grindeks Group comprises JSC Grindeks and its subsidiaries, including JSC Kalceks in Latvia, JSC Tallinna Farmaatsiatehas in Estonia and HBM Pharma s.r.o. in Slovakia. In total, the Group includes 38 subsidiaries and 11 representative offices.
JSC Grindeks specializes in the development and manufacture of medicines in the therapeutic areas of cardiovascular diseases, central nervous system disorders, oncology, dermatology and diabetes. JSC Kalceks focuses on the development and manufacture of medicines for the hospital segment, while JSC “Tallinna Farmaatsiatehas” specializes in the manufacture of ointments.
The Group’s products are exported to more than 100 countries worldwide. Key export markets include the European Union, Australia, the United Arab Emirates, Israel and CIS countries.

====================================================================================================

Why is Trump sanctioning the ICC — and what does it mean for Australia?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:19:19 UTC
16:19:19 KST

In Brief:
- Trump's toughest move yet against the ICC could complicate Australia's position.
- Allies have condemned the sanctions, while Australia weighs its response.
The United States has sanctioned the International Criminal Court (ICC), just hours after a Nobel Peace Prize decision that appeared certain to anger US President Donald Trump.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the US would ban transactions with what he called a "rogue court", vowing to cut off its resources and cripple its ability to operate in an escalation of a long-running campaign against the Hague-based tribunal.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said.
Trump later turned his anger on Norway, branding the Nobel committee's choice of South African jurist Navi Pillay a "disgraceful and embarrassing decision".
The move puts Australia, a US ally and founding supporter of the court, in a difficult diplomatic position as key allies split over how to respond.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
What the sanctions do
The ICC tries individuals suspected of the world's most serious crimes, including war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
The Trump administration has already sanctioned 17 people linked to the court, including its prosecutor and several judges.
The latest step goes much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the institution itself.
Jared Mondschein, director of research at the United States Studies Centre, said the move represented a significant escalation.
"This is perhaps the most aggressive move yet," he told SBS News, noting that earlier measures targeted individuals rather than the court as a whole.
US sanctions typically bar US-based companies from conducting business with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source alternatives and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The latest measures include a six-month grace period and exemptions for telecommunications, software, pension payments and detainee-related transactions, something Mondschein described as a window for negotiation.
Why is Trump sanctioning the ICC?
US wariness of the court is not new and has historically crossed party lines, Mondschein says.
"Both Democratic and Republican presidents have been concerned about the ICC and its jurisdiction over US citizens," he said, noting the US signed the Rome Statute that established the court but never ratified it.
The US has also long opposed efforts by the court to investigate alleged crimes involving American personnel in Afghanistan.
The ICC has issued an arrest warrant for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu over alleged crimes in Gaza.
"I think more than anything else, the goal is for the ICC to stop trying to prosecute US citizens as well as allies of the United States, including the leadership of Israel," Mondschein said.
"The Trump administration has concerns about the political bias of the ICC and it being overzealous in its prosecution of targets that are more politically motivated than legally motivated."
The US also has a law dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act", allowing it to use "all means necessary and appropriate" to defend US personnel or allies detained by the ICC.
What's the Nobel Prize got to do with this?
The announcement came just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, the South African jurist best known for her work in international human rights law.
Pillay, 85, spent much of her career defending anti-apartheid activists and last year, chaired a UN commission of inquiry that found genocide was occurring in Gaza.
Israel has rejected those findings.
Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, said Pillay had been "instrumental in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide are prosecuted".
He said awarding the prize to Pillay was "a clear message to those who are putting pressure on these institutions, to those who are sanctioning the judges and are attacking the institutions".
Speaking after the award, Pillay said: "We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack".
Israel condemned the award as the "grotesque weaponisation" of a prize to legitimise "anti-Israel hatred".
Pillay also appeared to acknowledge Trump's long-running interest in the Nobel Prize.
"If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump," she joked during a standing ovation.
Trump responded by saying the Nobel Prize had been "forever discredited" and claiming he had "never heard" of Pillay.
"This is an indelible stain on the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision," he said.
Mondschein said Pillay was a well-known critic of Israel, an issue that has long been a source of friction between the Trump administration and international legal institutions.
The award to Pillay was also a pointed snub to Trump, who had spent two years lobbying for the Nobel Prize.
'Tension' for Australia
The ICC has 125 member states, including Australia.
The United States, Russia, China, India and Israel are not members.
Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement they "strongly disagree" with the sanctions.
The European Union said it was "ready to take any necessary measures" to ensure the court could continue operating.
Australia, a founding supporter of the ICC and a key US ally, now faces a diplomatic balancing act, Mondschein said.
"It's a tension for Australia. It's also a tension for Japan," he said, noting the ICC's current president is Japanese.
Australia has not yet publicly responded to the sanctions.
"I don't think Australia has been in favour of these actions by the Trump administration," Mondschein said.
"They have been critical of them, perhaps not as critical as other countries.
"But this is something I don't think Australia really wants to telegraph too early.
"If anything, they want to consider all their options moving ahead."
The ICC said its future "now rests also in the hands of the states that created it".
"History will judge this moment."
— With additional reporting by Agence France-Presse and Reuters

Ukrainian strike drones attacked an oil transshipment terminal in the southern Russian port city of Rostov-on-Don early Saturday morning, Oct. 10, igniting a large blaze at the facility, Russian regional officials and independent media reported.
Residents across Rostov-on-Don reported multiple explosions and visible air defense fire beginning late Friday evening and continuing into the early morning hours.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Rostov Regional Governor Yuriy Slyusar confirmed an aerial attack and a subsequent fire in the regional center, stating that emergency responders deployed to contain the blaze and claiming no casualties were recorded.
Slyusar said Russian air defense forces intercepted at least 50 unmanned aerial vehicles across the Rostov region between Friday evening and Saturday morning.
Open-source intelligence analysts from independent Russian news outlet Astra geolocated footage published by local residents, verifying that the fire broke out at the “Yug Rusi” oil products transshipment terminal in Rostov-on-Don’s Zheleznodorozhny district.
The facility functions as a key logistics node for petroleum products, handling transshipment from the Novoshakhtinsk Petroleum Products Plant (NZNP) and other regional suppliers.
Operating with a designed annual handling capacity of approximately 2.5 million metric tons, the terminal processes fuel supplies utilized by the Russian armed forces and facilitates maritime export shipments generating foreign currency revenue.
Putin Touts 90% Dollar-Free CIS Trade as Russia Sidesteps Western Sanctions
Although commercially known as Yug Rusi since its commissioning alongside the first phase of the Novoshakhtinsk refinery in 2009, corporate filings by the Novoshakhtinsk plant designate the facility as the “NZNP oil loading terminal, Rostov branch.” The terminal was previously targeted by Ukrainian drone strikes in July.
Strategic targeting of Russian fuel and refining logistics
The strike in Rostov-on-Don forms part of a systematic Ukrainian asymmetric campaign targeting fuel depots, refineries, and chemical production hubs that sustain Moscow’s military operations.
The overnight attack follows coordinated long-range strikes on Oct. 9 that damaged Russian energy and industrial assets across western and central regions.
Drones struck the Redkino Experimental Plant in the Tver region, igniting a fire at the chemical facility, which manufactures Decylin-M – a specialized liquid fuel component utilized in Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 strategic cruise missiles – alongside fuel additives for aviation kerosene and diesel.
Concurrently on Oct. 9, Ukrainian strikes hit an oil depot north of Belgorod that supplies fuel to industrial enterprises and transport fleets across the border region, while a separate drone strike damaged a major Yandex data center in Kaluga, disabling multiple server modules for the second consecutive day following an earlier strike on a company facility in Sasovo, Ryazan region.
Extended-range interdiction
Ukrainian precision units have progressively expanded their operational strike radius against Russian petrochemical infrastructure deep inside Russia.
On Thursday, Oct. 8, Ukraine’s Special Operations Forces (SSO) announced they conducted a second deep-interdiction strike against the Omsk Oil Refinery in southwestern Siberia, situated roughly 2,500 kilometers (1,550 miles) from Ukrainian-controlled territory.
Operating alongside the domestic Russian insurgent movement “Chernaya Iskra” (Black Spark), SSO long-range strike drones navigated flight routes approaching 3,000 kilometers to strike distillation units at the Siberian plant.
Ukrainian defense and security officials have emphasized that degrading refining capacity, export terminals, and frontline fuel stockpiles directly constrains the mobility of Russian mechanized units while diminishing state export earnings that fund the Kremlin’s wartime budget.

‘How can you stop these kids?’ Indian capital on lockdown before protests
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi has pulled out all the stops to prevent Cockroach movement protests taking over New Delhi.
New Delhi, India – Heavy police barricades line the streets around Connaught Place, the colonial-era square near Jantar Mantar, on Saturday morning as police have begun detaining groups of protesters arriving for planned demonstrations.
They are here in support of the influential Gen-Z movement and Cockroach Janta Party, which have called for the resignation of India’s election chief, amid a bitter dispute over who gets to vote in the world’s most populous democracy.
Protesters are demanding sweeping reforms and a rollback of a controversial voter revision exercise which has struck 130 million names from the voter list.
For now, an eerie silence hangs over parts of central New Delhi. Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s government has gone to lengths to turn the city into a fortress, deploying nearly 30,000 personnel onto the streets.
Police have also detained the founder of the Cockroach Janta Party, Abhijeet Dipke.
Indian TV channels reported early on Saturday that officers met Dipke at New Delhi airport after he arrived from the financial capital Mumbai and asked him to call off the protest as authorities had banned it.
CJP leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka were also detained from their flight upon landing, the movement said in a statement.
On Friday, the government extraordinarily cancelled all trains to New Delhi; locked down more than 50 metro stations; imposed an internet shutdown; and sent personnel to thousands of students in local communities to warn them against participation in the protest.
Several students en route to New Delhi from different states of India were dragged out of trains and buses and detained by the police. Many have been placed under house arrest in cities hundreds of kilometres away from New Delhi.
The Cockroach movement says thousands have been detained across India as Modi’s government intensifies its crackdown. Yet undeterred protesters have pledged to keep returning to the streets.
‘Made EMERGENCY official’
Current restrictions in the Indian capital and the nationwide crackdown on protesters have evoked memories of the 1975 Emergency, when then-Prime Minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties, censored the press and jailed political opponents.
“Narendra Modi just made EMERGENCY official,” Dipke, the founder of the Cockroach movement, wrote in a post on X. “This intimidation is not going to work, Modi. The youth of this country are no longer scared of you.”
Neha Bora, the firebrand Gen-Z protest leader and the national president of the left student body All India Students’ Association, equated the Modi government with British colonialist forces that unsuccessfully clamped down on India’s independence movement. She called on the masses to join the protest.
On Saturday morning, young people were trying to respond to her call despite the police restrictions in place.
Santosh Kumar, 29, a street sweeper in the outer circle of Connaught Place, told Al Jazeera he feels frustrated seeing teenagers detained at police barricades.
“How can you stop these kids? They are detaining 10; 50 more are coming. Modi, the dictator’s time is up: He will not even stay until 2029 (the time of the next elections).
“This is the time we turn Delhi into Nepal and Bangladesh – learn from them and take back our country,” he said, referring to youth-led movements in those countries.
Sameer Irshad, 28, an engineer from Gurugram, approached the barricades near Connaught Place while pushing his 57-year-old mother Sheeba Abdi in a wheelchair.
Abdi told us: “This sort of crackdown, where we cannot peacefully express our dissent, is unseen in Delhi. Why has government turned this place into a fortress? Why are they so scared of citizens like me?”
Under house arrest
Last month, India was shaken by revelations of divisions within the supposedly autonomous body that is in charge of conducting elections, over controversial policies that critics say have disenfranchised tens of millions of people.
India’s Election Commission chief, Gyanesh Kumar, was accused of overruling concerns raised by the two other election commissioners about the integrity of ongoing changes in the voter database, an investigation by The Indian Express reported.
India is among the few countries to have taken an active approach to enrolling every last voter.
Critics say the ongoing revision of the voter list flips the foundational principle of Indian democracy: Demanding that citizens prove their voting rights, and disproportionately targeting Muslims, economically weaker sections, minorities and other vulnerable groups in Indian society.
Arif, a 24-year-old district coordinator for the Students’ Federation of India, another left-wing student organisation to have joined the protest call, was locked in his home in Saharanpur, nearly 200km (125 miles) from New Delhi, on Thursday.
“Several police officials started beating my door out of nowhere late at night, asking my parents for details of my whereabouts,” Arif, who did not want to give his full name, told Al Jazeera from his home in Saharanpur, where he is currently detained under the police’s watch around the clock.
“They just want to stop me from going to Delhi for protest. They are threatening to book me under criminal cases and destroy my future,” he said, adding that this is the first time he has been subject to such detention.
“I really wanted to be in Delhi, to fight and reclaim our democracy. The time for Modi is over,” he said.
Modi ‘at his weakest’
This week, Modi and his Bharatiya Janata Party (BNP) celebrated his 25 years in office, starting with his years as chief minister of the western state of Gujarat – where he oversaw the infamous 2002 Muslim pogrom – and later as India’s prime minister since 2014.
But Modi has never looked weaker in power than now, analysts and Indian political observers argue.
In July, the Cockroach-led protests choked key New Delhi streets and forced out Modi’s education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.
This time, Modi has taken more extreme measures to prevent protesters from gaining a foothold in central New Delhi, “because he wishes to retain the aura and image of a leader who never yields to public pressure, someone who is invincible”, said Nilanjan Mukhopadhyay, an author and biographer of Modi.
“Modi appears at the lowest point [of his political life] in public perception. This is extremely paradoxical because he has some of the most important autonomous institutions, large sections of the bureaucracy, and state wings in tight control and acting at his behest,” Mukhopadhyay told Al Jazeera.
In the face of growing protests, Modi is now “fast losing people’s perception of being a leader who leads them out of livelihood pits”, he said.
Prashant Bhushan, a senior lawyer at the Supreme Court and a rights activist who planned to join the protest on Saturday, told Al Jazeera that “Modi’s government looks quite scared of the people.
“People in India are rising and demanding answers. And when the government gets scared, they adopt draconian measures to stay in power,” Bhushan said. “But only more and more people will rise from repression.”

‘So safe you could drink it’: Scientists and pesticide victims fear an EU rollback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:10:25 UTC
16:10:25 KST

‘So safe you could drink it’: Scientists and pesticide victims fear an EU rollback
For decades, French farmers sprayed pesticides they were told were harmless. Many have since fallen ill, grappling with cancers and other diseases caused by exposure. As the EU prepares to vote on a package that would end regular safety reviews of most pesticides, victims, doctors and scientists warn it could keep harmful products on the market for longer.
For most of his life, José Nadan worked as a professional beekeeper in Morbihan, a coastal area in Brittany known for its medieval towns and fresh seafood. At the start of his career, he recalls a golden age of beekeeping, when each year, and “without much effort”, the number of hives would naturally increase.
But things took a turn for the worse in the 1980s, when the varroa mite made its way to France. A parasite, the mite weakens bees by suppressing their immune system and spreading deadly viruses that can collapse entire colonies. “We improvised trying to kill them with whatever we had until official products made their way onto the market,” Nadan recalls.
Nadan also spent many years keeping an orchard of cider apple trees he treated with a pesticide that, he was told, was organic and had no effect on humans. “The sales reps even said it was so safe you could drink it,” the 69-year-old says. “I never took the slightest precaution, spraying from my tractor as I drove along the rows of trees,” Nadan recalls. “Sometimes, because of the wind, I’d get some on my face. But I wasn’t worried.”
“I later found out it was a product like Roundup [a Monsanto weed killer] and contained glyphosate,” he says, a substance now known to be harmful to human health.
It was only after he retired that Nadan realised the consequences of being exposed to pesticides for all those years. Six years ago, he was diagnosed with prostate cancer.
His illness has officially been recognised as an occupational hazard caused by pesticides by France’s agricultural social security system.
In everything, everywhere, all at once
Pesticides are known to cause a range of health issues, including various types of cancer, respiratory diseases, neurodegenerative illnesses like Parkinson’s or Alzheimer's, cardiovascular diseases and infertility. They also impact children more than adults, leading to developmental delays and cognitive impairments.
And they are everywhere. A 2023 study in which hundreds of samples were gathered from different environments across 10 European countries found that pesticides were present in 100% of air, indoor dust and water samples.
Read morePesticides, cadmium, PFAS: France reckons with the hidden toxins in food (1/2)
Edmond Leduc, a retired doctor living close to the Belgian border in northern France, has lived next to crop fields treated with pesticides for 44 years. “The farmers working the fields practise intensive farming, so there is always a harvest,” he says. “When it’s potato season, they sometimes spray fungicides every two weeks.”
A lover of gardening, Leduc spent a lot of time outside and admits “not being very careful” in the early years. “I didn’t know the products I was inhaling were toxic.”
Leduc discovered he had lymphoma, a type of blood cancer, in 2018, and was diagnosed with prostate cancer in August of this year – two conditions linked to pesticides.
As one of Europe’s biggest agricultural producers, France is also one of its largest consumers of pesticides. And the number of requests by agricultural workers like Nadan, who are in close contact with the toxic substances, has shot up from 318 in 2024 to 975 in 2025.
Yet as the toll of pesticide exposure is becoming clearer, the EU is preparing to vote on a set of legal amendments that could make it harder to ban these harmful products.
The EU’s ‘safety lock’ at risk
Despite having a multi-layered system to assess the risk of pesticides, Europe still sees cases where they cause harm to both the environment and humans. Unlike the US, which uses a risk-based model that factors actual levels of exposure, the EU uses a hazard-based model, meaning it focuses on the inherent toxicological properties of a certain chemical before it’s approved.
But regulatory assessments are often delayed and take time, slowing down the process for pesticides to enter the market. To speed things up and cut red tape, the European Commission proposed a legislative package that would overhaul the current system. Known as Omnibus X, it would amend ten existing EU laws that cover pesticides, biocides, food residues, animal feed and official controls.
A key amendment aims to scrap the periodic re-evaluation of pesticides, which often end up causing greater damage than expected after being initially approved.
The EU ensures the move would have “no compromise on food safety or environmental protection”, but critics of the package disagree.
Read moreHow can you keep yourself safe from forever chemicals and cadmium in food? (Part 2/2)
“New scientific findings need to be taken into account regularly, because there is always a level of uncertainty [about the risk of a pesticide] before it hits the market,” says ecotoxicologist Martina Vijver, who was up in arms when news of the package dropped. “A periodic review is a safety lock, it’s crucial, because we can’t foresee every consequence.”
An insecticide known as chlorpyrifos, for example, was approved for use in the EU back in 2006. Sprayed on crops to control pests or on grains stored in warehouses, the chemical came to be one of the most commonly used pesticides in Europe. Residues of the substance were found in fruit, vegetables, dairy products and drinking water.
When its approval came up for renewal, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) reviewed the evidence and decided in 2019 that no safe exposure level could be set, and that chlorpyrifos didn’t meet the EU’s health requirements. Even in small doses, chlorpyrifos affects the human body’s neurological, reproductive, metabolic and immune systems. The substance was linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in children, including autism.
Even though the entire regulatory process spanned over seven years, once the ruling passed in January 2020, Member States had three months to dispose of all products containing chlorpyrifos.
“All pesticides are aimed at killing something,” Vijver explains. “If a substance is neurotoxic for insects, for example, that same neurotoxicity could apply to humans [...] Which is not so strange, because that’s the intention [of the pesticide].”
Denis Benoit, a former farmer in charge of pruning trees in the winter and applying pesticides from spring through summer, recalls going home with intense symptoms after a day’s work. “I had a fever at night and red patches on my arms,” he says. “It was because of the insecticides we were using, like D6.”
Like Nadan and Leduc, the 65-year-old from western France was also diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2019. “I do feel regret for having worked with those substances, but it was hard to find work at the time, and we were told they were only toxic in large doses,” he says.
‘Who sounds the alarm?’
For scientists like Vijver, the regular reassessment of pesticides is one of the few safeguards against such long-hidden harms, and it is precisely what the EU’s upcoming omnibus would remove.
Under the current EU system, a pesticide’s approval expires on a set date, and the company producing it has to show again that its product is safe to keep selling. If the approval no longer expires automatically, the product would stay on the market by default, removing the “safety lock” that Vijver refers to. The burden would then fall on the shoulders of regulators such as the EFSA or individual member states to sound the alarm.
“But who triggers the process? Doctors? Scientists? Or the guy who walks his dog and sees all the birds have died? That’s not our job,” says Vijver.
If passed, the legislation package would also increase the maximum grace period for farmers to substitute banned pesticides from 18 months to three years. Conditions for the exceptional use of banned pesticides, including endocrine disruptors, would also be loosened.
Sending a clear message of concern, Vijver took the initiative to write an open letter on September 17 and urged the European Parliament to pause the vote on the legislative package until an independent investigation into its potential health and environmental impacts is carried out. She gathered 573 other signatories from a wide range of disciplines, including environmental protection, medicine and public health – all of whom “have expertise” in the field, Vijver says.
“I’ve never done something like this before,” she admits. “As scientists, we are really worried. I would never have done this if I wasn’t really worried.”
Read moreEco-friendly French winemakers plant hybrid vines to curb pesticide use
The vote on Omnibus X is expected to take place at the end of October.
Victims take to the streets
Cancer victims and farmers marched arm in arm last weekend, flanked by doctors and activists, to protest pesticides. Organised by a handful of non-profits, the march saw 8,000 demonstrators gather outside a factory in northern France owned by Syngenta, the world’s largest pesticide seller.
Amid the crowd was Fleur Breteau, founder of the Cancer Colère collective, who made waves last year when she sparked a nationwide movement to block the reintroduction of the pesticide acetamiprid.
Read moreFrance's top constitutional court rejects return of bee-killing pesticide
Though the reintroduction of acetamiprid was eventually banned last summer, France passed an agricultural law in August this year that would partially reverse the decision.
Holding a placard that read: “Morgan, dead age 36, breast cancer,” Breteau told French daily Le Monde on October 3 that Morgan was her partner on agricultural issues and had passed away in June. “We’re losing peers every week,” she said.
“When I see the state of some of my fellow retirees, how sick and tired they are, I tell myself that all things considered, I am not doing too bad,” says former beekeeper Nadan, who now helps other agricultural workers as a member of a collective to support pesticide victims.
“I went to the funeral of a crop technician I was helping last week. He would go from farm to farm and survey treated fields, and fell ill shortly after retiring,” Nadan says. “He had a form of Parkinson’s that meant he could barely speak and was in a wheelchair. The disease progressed so rapidly that he didn’t have time to finalise his request to have the illness officially recognised as being caused by pesticides.”
For campaigners, cases like this are a stark reminder of what is at stake as Brussels prepares to rewrite its pesticide rules.
French environmental organisation Générations Futures has organised a weekend of protests and canvassing across the country, aimed at informing people about the EU legislative package that could loosen restrictions on pesticides.
“It’s never easy to bring EU issues into the public sphere because they aren’t very enticing. Our aim this weekend is to inform people about the Omnibus, spark debate, get people talking, which is definitely something its supporters want to avoid,” says Andy Battentier, campaign manager for Générations Futures.
“A third of the European Parliament is made up of right-wing and far-right MEPs, who favour scrapping standards [red tape],” says Battentier on the chances the legislative package will pass.
A first-ever “presidential debate” on pesticides organised by the NGO will also take place in Cambrai, northern France, this Saturday, with leftist representatives of presidential candidates for the 2027 election saying they will attend. Three hundred doctors in France have been awaiting a response from former prime minister Gabriel Attal, centre-right Edouard Philippe and Interior Minister Bruno Retailleau to debate “this major public health issue” – but their seats are likely to remain empty.
“23 million people in France suffer from either a chronic illness or cancer,” the doctors wrote in the letter sent on September 28. “Numerous studies have shown a strong link between these conditions and pesticides. As doctors, we work tirelessly to protect the health of our fellow citizens. What is the point of our efforts if we don’t tackle the root cause of the diseases?”
Back in Morbihan, Nadan still thinks about the bees he fought to save from the varroa mite, which weakens its host so slowly that by the time the damage shows, the colony is often beyond saving. Decades later, he and his fellow farmers fear the same may be true of the products they were told would protect them.
“Many farmers feel a sense of shame, especially because they have children who work in conventional farming,” he says, fearing the Omnibus would only “fuel the surge in cancers and other degenerative diseases” for generations to come.

World Mental Health Day: let’s talk and listen
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:10:09 UTC
16:10:09 KST

Anxiety and depression are the most common mental disorders. Such conditions can affect all aspects of our lives, including relationships with family, friends and community. They can result from or lead to problems at school and at work. And the economic consequences are substantial. According to a 2023 study, nearly half of Europeans declared having experienced an emotional or psychological problem such as feeling depressed or anxious.
World Mental Health Day on October 10 serves as a reminder that good mental health is important and how we can prioritise it in our lives. This year’s theme ‘Lived experiences heard: real voices, real change’ stresses how conversations about mental health make a difference.
At EU level, mental health is already a health priority. In 2023, it adopted a comprehensive approach to mental health, which is helping EU countries and interested groups to take swift action to deal with mental health challenges. It focuses on prevention, addressing behavioural risk factors and social, environmental, and commercial conditions that play their part in the development of mental health disorders.
In addition, of particular concern today are the pressures of the digital sphere and social media on our mental health. Modern platforms are highly addictive and designed to keep us engaged for as long as possible, particularly children.
EU laws and initiatives are already tackling addictive design, excessive screen time, exposure to illegal content, cyberbullying, and cyberviolence.
Last month, the EU also proposed the EU KIDS Act, based on the recommendations from the Special Panel on Child Safety Online. The proposal seeks to prevent access to social media platforms by children under the age of 13 and sets an EU-wide minimum age for minors to open an account of their own.
It’s not only the EU and national governments addressing mental health issues. We can all play our part in improving people’s mental well-being. On October 10, take the time to listen.

Ghent University honours Leonard Cohen with an international conference and a free exhibition
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:07:00 UTC
16:07:00 KST

Ghent University is honouring Canadian singer Leonard Cohen with an international academic conference and an exhibition. The Canadian was known to the general public as a singer, but he was also a writer and illustrator. Ten years after his death, international experts are examining his legacy. “It goes far beyond ‘Suzanne’ and ‘Hallelujah’.”
Ghent University honours Leonard Cohen with an international conference and a free exhibition
Leonard Cohen and Ghent share a special bond. Just a stone’s throw from the university library, the Boekentoren or the Books’ Tower, on St-Peter’s Square, the world-famous singer performed a series of sold-out concerts in 2010 and 2012. During those performances, Cohen expressed his love for Ghent on several occasions. He passed away 10 years ago.
Ghent University, in collaboration with two Canadian universities, is organising a conference on Cohen’s work. This is the first time such an event has taken place in the Low Countries. “Cohen is more than just the music most people know. He began as a poet and writer. He is a major figure in Canadian literature,” explains Professor Francis Mus. He is examining his legacy alongside 50 colleagues.
This is an interdisciplinary conference bringing together literary scholars, music experts, as well as researchers specialising in religious studies and translation. The participants come from both North America and Europe. “We want to explore what remains of his work and what significance it still holds.”
“Early versions of well-known songs”
Mus wanted more than just academic attention for the artist Cohen. There is also a unique, free exhibition at the Boekentoren featuring documents from the Canadian’s personal archive. “He kept a record of absolutely everything; it’s an incredibly rich collection. Here, you get to know him in all his facets,” says Mus.
The exhibition features photographs, fan letters, books and also graphic work by Cohen. The unused cover illustrations for his poetry collection “Flowers for Hitler” are on display. “Cohen was very provocative in that collection. He dared to hold up a mirror to society: this is what you’re all doing to one another. His later novels are regarded as key works in Canadian literature.”
The display cases also show how Cohen worked as a singer and musician. There are early drafts of songs that went on to become iconic. “We’re displaying the lyrics to ‘Chelsea Hotel’, which were scribbled on napkins. The general public is familiar with the song ‘Chelsea Hotel #2’, but there was actually another original version.”
“Cohen may not have been the most groundbreaking artist of his time – unlike Bob Dylan, for example – but his poetic tone continues to strike a chord with me. He used it to tackle social issues. He didn’t shy away from taboos. This is evident in the exhibition; there are several examples of censorship in his work,” says Mus.
“He had a distinctive, fundamentally human tone. He showed understanding yet was by no means naïve. It is precisely in this way that he remains relevant to me.” Mus is also organising a tribute concert featuring Cohen’s music at the Handelsbeurs on 7 October. That performance is sold out.
The conference is a collaboration between Ghent University and Acadia University and Memorial University in Canada. The free exhibition ‘The Mountain and the Volcano’ in the Boekentoren features documents from the Cohen Archive at the University of Toronto and is open daily from 6 to 8 October.

Low pensions and fewer workers pose a challenge to the pension system
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:03:57 UTC
16:03:57 KST

Author
Yoan Kolev
News
Low pensions and fewer workers pose a challenge to the pension system
The state should develop an active demographic policy, says economist Stoyan Panchev
Saturday 10 October 2026 08:25
Saturday, 10 October 2026, 08:25
PHOTO BGNES
Font size
More than 2 million Bulgarians rely on their pensions to get through the month. As of July 1 this year, the minimum pension in Bulgaria stands at EUR 347.51, while the maximum is EUR 1,738.40. Some 810,000 Bulgarians receive the minimum pension or less, while 9,195 receive the maximum amount. Meanwhile, the average monthly pension in the EU is around EUR 1,443, putting Bulgaria last among EU member states by this measure.
The issue of people’s incomes is always topical, while every attempt to reform the social sector raises more questions than answers. According to economist Stoyan Panchev, disparities in pension levels across different parts of the country are primarily due to income levels, which are unevenly distributed. He commented on the idea of a new regional division of Bulgaria, which has been periodically discussed for years. One proposal is to remove Sofia from the Southwestern Region and establish it as a separate “Capital” region:
Stoyan Panchev
PHOTO BGNES
“As far as I know, this is the direction things are heading. In practice, we should have four regions, one of them being the capital region (there are currently six regions – editor’s note). This is the right approach because Sofia distorts the economic data for the Southwestern Region. It is a specific region with a high concentration of economic, administrative, and other activity, so separating it out would certainly be beneficial. I am not sure to what extent this will affect incomes, since they reflect not so much the administrative division into regions as other processes. I believe that a policy of decentralization is needed in the country, which is clearly one of the many policies that are not being actively pursued, so that we can see some effect in this area.”
PHOTO BGNES
Stoyan Panchev noted that Bulgaria’s pension system is based on a pay-as-you-go model, which requires a certain number of pensioners to be supported by a certain number of working people:
“If we have a declining number of working people and an increasing number of pensioners, this will lead to a deficit in the pension system, making it increasingly difficult to finance. This means that if we want to address this problem in the long term, we need to work toward a much higher birth rate and many more people in employment in the future who will be able to overcome the deficit in the pension system.”
PHOTO BGNES
Stoyan Panchev believes that Bulgaria could introduce new ideas and mechanisms to promote demographic policies aimed at increasing the birth rate. He gave the example of how some of Hungary’s demographic policies could also be implemented in Bulgaria:
“For example, Hungary introduced a policy under which a woman with three or more children does not have to pay the so-called personal income tax. Perhaps we could arrange things so that in Bulgaria, mothers in this category would not have to bear most of the tax burden”, the economist said.
Currently, financial support for the birth of a child in Bulgaria is provided as a one-off payment of EUR 191.74 for a first child, EUR 460.17 for a second child, and EUR 230.09 for a third child, according to data from the Social Assistance Agency.
PHOTO Aflo Images
“It is important for Bulgaria to focus on studying what specific policies could be introduced to encourage higher birth rates, even by establishing a special body or commission to begin implementing them, because this is the most important policy a country can pursue,” Stoyan Panchev said.
Will the retirement age be raised?
The retirement age in Bulgaria is currently 62 years and 6 months for women and 64 years and 9 months for men. It will certainly increase in the coming years, the economist told Radio Bulgaria:
PHOTO BGNES
“ I would recommend doing this more quickly, because it is the least painful way to address the problem of having fewer working people relative to the number of pensioners. However, this should also be combined with demographic policies, because when you have such a large deficit in the pension system, you either have to stop indexing pensions, raise the retirement age, or find many more working people somewhere.”
The economist believes that, given the current state of the pension system, people who are now aged between 35 and 40, as well as younger generations, may not be able to retire at all, or at least not with a pension that would allow them to live a normal and dignified life.

The US' National Weather Service (NWS) has warned a life-threatening storm surge is expected from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Suwannee, Florida.
Hurricane Isaias made landfall in Florida on Friday evening, bringing 105 mph (around 169 kph) winds as it struck near the city of Destin.
Video footage on social media shows high winds and heavy rain battering the area, with one hotel appearing to have its roof ripped off by the storm in Pensacola, just along the coast from Destin in the Florida Panhandle.
The US' National Weather Service (NWS) has warned a life-threatening storm surge is now expected from Dauphin Island, Alabama, to Suwannee, Florida, and urged residents in the warning area to continue to follow advice from local officials.
"Extremely dangerous and damaging hurricane-force winds, especially in gusts, are expected over portions of the Florida Panhandle and southern Alabama where a Hurricane Warning remains in effect," the NWS said in an update late on Friday.
"Residents in these areas should have a safe room to ride out the storm and prepare for long-duration power outages," it added.
Strong winds are likely across large parts of the southeastern US, with Isaias also expected to bring heavy rainfall to much of the wider region over the weekend.
"Considerable flash and urban flooding, along with significant river flooding, will be possible. Landslides are also possible across the Southern Appalachians," the NWS said.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said that around 260,000 customers were without power as the category 2 hurricane made landfall.
The outages spanned from Pensacola to Panama City and the state capital, Tallahassee, he told reporters, adding that restoration crews would be mobilised after the storm had passed.

Klaipėda Port showcases the future of smart operations with a private 5G network trial and design
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:01:45 UTC
16:01:45 KST

Trials of a private 5G network at Klaipėda Port in Lithuania have successfully concluded, marking a key milestone in defining the port’s digital future. Santa Monica Networks and Latvian telecommunications provider LMT (LMT Group) have completed the comprehensive design phase for a potential port-wide private network and demonstrated concrete, practical applications directly to port company executives, illustrating how 5G technology can optimize daily workflows.
According to Mindaugas Žiūkas, Director of Santa Monica Networks, as the port increasingly digitizes its operations, reliable connectivity is becoming crucial as the foundation for a growing number of machines, devices, and daily processes, not just for human communication. “Numerous processes take place simultaneously at the Port of Klaipėda, making it clearly evident where technology can deliver practical benefits, such as boosting operational efficiency, automating more processes, and reliably managing machinery and data. For us, as a strategic IT partner, this is one of the most significant projects of recent years and an opportunity to leverage our expertise to help modernize the port that connects Lithuania to the world,” said M. Žiūkas during the event.
Autonomous systems demonstrate private 5G applications
Executives and IT specialists from companies operating at the Port of Klaipėda attended the demonstration. Santa Monica Networks, LMT, and their technology partners showcased specific private 5G use cases in a real-world port environment and discussed with port representatives how these solutions could further modernize the port.
Atlas demonstrated its autonomous drone-in-a-box solution, combining AtlasNEST with the AtlasPRO unmanned aerial system to enable persistent remote monitoring and autonomous operations. The integrated system enables remote deployment, operation, recovery, and recharging of the drone, supporting inspection, situational awareness, and monitoring missions in complex and hard-to-reach port environments.
LVR Flote, a provider of port technical services in Latvian ports, demonstrated its uncrewed surface vessel, the Otter USV, which is used for hydrographic surveys of the harbor bed. LVR Flote also presented a tool to improve the transfer and processing of large survey datasets and a data pre-processing tool that applies initial filtering before detailed quality control by hydrographers. Combined with 5G connectivity, these solutions are intended to reduce manual work, shorten the time between data collection and analysis, and support faster operational decision-making in ports.
“At LVR Flote, we see strong potential in using digitalization and data more effectively to support better, data-based decisions – whether in fleet management, hydrographic surveys or other operational areas. For any digital solution to work in practice, safe, reliable and secure connectivity is essential, especially in critical infrastructure such as ports,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote.
According to Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority, technological development is crucial for the port not only in terms of modernization but also regarding competitiveness.
“Today’s market rewards those who are fast, reliable, flexible, and resilient. A private 5G network could unlock even more opportunities for the Port of Klaipėda by enabling the implementation of advanced solutions, process automation, and increased operational capacity, while ensuring uninterrupted connectivity and secure data transmission, even in extraordinary situations. Resilient, modern, and flexible – that is how we envision the future of the Port of Klaipėda, and that is the port we are building every day,” says Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority.
Increasing use of digital solutions in port operations
A private 5G network would give the port greater control over connectivity management. The port could independently decide which processes are prioritized, which devices can connect to the network, and keep certain sensitive operational data within its own infrastructure. This contributes to an increase in security, and would help ensure controlled communication and coordinated action during incidents.
According to Aigars Runcis, Director of the Ventures Department at LMT, the solutions demonstrated in Klaipėda represent only a fraction of the potential applications for private 5G technology in a port environment. “Private 5G is not connectivity for its own sake – it is the foundation for smarter, safer, and more efficient port operations. Demonstrations in Klaipėda show how unmanned systems and mission-critical communications can already deliver practical benefits, while the same connectivity platform can support a wide range of other solutions as the port ecosystem evolves. Our goal is to help ports build infrastructure that enables continued digitalization and automation, while boosting operational efficiency and resilience,” said A. Runčis.
LMT brings practical experience in deploying private 5G networks in ports to the Klaipėda project. The LMT Group installed the first private 5G network in the Baltic states at the Baltic Container Terminal (BCT) in the Port of Riga. Covering an area of over 50 hectares, the network is already used in daily operations, ensuring connectivity for mobile machinery and facilitating mission-critical communications. The team is also applying this experience to develop solutions for other ports.

Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:00:50 UTC
16:00:50 KST

The owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.
Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind an X account calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.
The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.
The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.
Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’s Restore Britain party and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.
Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.
They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.
She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.
“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”
A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.
“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.
“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK. Social media companies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”
A number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.
A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.
“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.
Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.
Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.
That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.
The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.
Watson was approached for comment.

Lithuania’s rural regions bank on religious tourism
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
07:00:00 UTC
16:00:00 KST

The first international religious tourism forum was held in Lithuania’s northern Šiluva town, famous for its Catholic indulgences (atlaidai) ceremony. Organisers hope pilgrims will opt for longer stays in Lithuania and that the country's regions will attract more attention.
"The motivation of religious tourists is quite different, and they are less affected by the geopolitical situation. Interest in this area of tourism is growing rapidly," says Suleiman Farajat, a professor of cultural tourism at the University of Jordan.
More than 130 participants from different countries, including Poland, Uruguay, India, Argentina and Jordan.
According to forecasts by the United Nations World Tourism Organisation, pilgrimage tourism in Europe could grow by 6-7% a year.
Sigita Maslauskaitė-Mažylienė, Lithuania's ambassador to the Holy See, says pilgrimage tourism has every opportunity to showcase the country's cultural and historical identity to visitors.
"We should tell them not only why that Gothic church is important as a pilgrimage site, but also about the Ukrainian flag flying nearby, because it raises questions too. It is essential to link these two elements, and that is what makes us interesting," Maslauskaitė-Mažylienė says.
Around 100,000 pilgrims visit Šiluva in the northern Raseiniai district each year, most of them from Poland.
"They stay in the pilgrims' centre; we welcome them, they eat, attend Mass. This is an integral part of their visit. Then we organise excursions and, through educational activities, try to ensure that people have things to do," says Silvija Čižaitė-Rudokienė, head of the Šiluva Pilgrims' Centre.
Tourism experts say that in order to become an attractive religious tourism destination, municipalities with sites that attract pilgrims need to work together and create a joint range of experiences.
"A traveller is unlikely to come just to Šiluva. When someone arrives or lands in one Lithuanian city, they need to have a way to travel from one place to another, as well as opportunities to experience things along the way and at the different destinations they visit," says Olga Gončarova, head of Lithuania Travel.
Religious tourism is not seasonal, with people travelling at different times of the year. In recent years, the average age of travellers has also been falling, with most pilgrims now under 50. The main destinations are not the capital or the major cities, but the regions.
"I would like to highlight the opportunities for the regions and communities – what we create can be showcased to people coming from other countries," says Lidija Bajarūnienė, vice-president of the European Travel Commission.
Foreign tourists typically stay in Lithuania for two or three nights. Slower-paced religious tourists interested in itineraries spanning several municipalities are forecast to stay in Lithuania for four or five nights.
Up to 1.5 million foreign tourists visited Lithuania last year.

Powerful 7.7 quake hits Panama, damages buildings
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:58:47 UTC
15:58:47 KST

AP photo.
A powerful 7.7-magnitude earthquake struck southern Panama on Oct. 9, damaging buildings and roads, injuring several people and prompting tsunami warnings across parts of the Pacific coast that were later lifted.
The earthquake struck near Pitaloza Arriba at a depth of 12.6 kilometers, according to the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS).
The tremor was felt across much of the country, including the capital, Panama City, where thousands of residents rushed out of homes, offices and shopping centers.
Panamanian President José Raúl Mulino described the situation as a major disaster during a visit to Penonomé, one of the affected cities, where several buildings and roads sustained serious damage.
Mulino said some roads had completely collapsed, complicating efforts to reach affected communities, including Tonosí, near the earthquake's epicenter.
Authorities said 15 students at a school in Penonomé suffered minor injuries. A hotel partially collapsed in the city, while churches, hospitals and government buildings were also damaged.
No deaths or missing persons had been reported as of Friday evening, although emergency teams were continuing to assess the damage.
A second earthquake measuring 6.6 struck near Río Grande later in the day, while dozens of aftershocks kept residents on alert.
The initial quake triggered tsunami warnings for Pacific coastal areas, including parts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador and other neighboring countries.
The Pacific Tsunami Warning Center subsequently lifted the threat, although Panamanian authorities had warned coastal residents to move to higher ground as a precaution.
The government suspended classes nationwide and deployed emergency teams to affected areas.
Operations at Tocumen International Airport resumed after a temporary suspension for safety inspections, while the Panama Canal Authority said shipping traffic continued normally.

General Staff: Russia has lost 1,550,910 troops in Ukraine since Feb. 24, 2022
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:57:52 UTC
15:57:52 KST

Russia has lost 1,550,910 troops in Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion on Feb. 24, 2022, the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported on Oct. 10.
The number includes 1,420 casualties that Russian forces suffered over the past day.
According to the report, Russia has also lost 12,406 tanks, 25,515 armored combat vehicles, 160,946 vehicles and fuel tanks, 51,000 artillery systems, 2,201 multiple launch rocket systems, 1,699 air defense systems, 443 aircraft, 356 helicopters, 2,917 unmanned ground vehicles, 35 ships and boats, and two submarines.
Ukraine's General Staff has not revealed its own losses during the full-scale invasion, citing operational secrecy.
Independent Western think-tank reports agree that the Russian casualties significantly surpass Ukraine's losses, with the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimating the ratio to be "roughly 2.5:1 or 2:1."
A January 2026 CSIS report said Ukraine has likely suffered between 500,000 and 600,000 casualties from February 2022 to December 2025, of which between 100,000 and 140,000 are thought to be killed in action.
While Ukrainian officials rarely disclose the figure, President Volodymyr Zelensky told France TV on Feb. 4 that at least 55,000 Ukrainian soldiers have been killed in action since the beginning of the full-scale war, in addition to significant numbers who are missing in action.
The intensity of Russian drone attacks and the fighting has made it extremely difficult for Ukraine to retrieve the bodies of fallen soldiers, which are needed for DNA confirmation.

Center Party overtakes Isamaa to top party ratings

Center Party overtakes Isamaa to top party ratings
The opposition Center Party has risen to the top of Estonia's party ratings with 23 percent support, overtaking Isamaa, according to a recent poll.
Market research firm Turu-uuringute AS's October survey found support for Isamaa fell three points to 19 percent, just one percentage point ahead of the Conservative People's Party of Estonia (EKRE), now in third place.
Isamaa and EKRE are in opposition, and the fourth opposition party, the Social Democrats (SDE), placed next with a 14 percent rating, according to Turu-uuringute, down one percentage point on the previous month.
Center's support rose two percentage points to 23 percent between September and October.
The coalition Reform Party saw a fall in support, from 12 percent to 10 percent in October, while its partner in office, Eesti 200, polled at 2 percent, a rise on the 1 percent seen in September, according to Turu-uuringute.
The two coalition parties together polled at 12 percent, compared with 74 percent for the four opposition parties.
Of parties not elected to the Riigikogu, only Parempoolsed exceeds the electoral threshold of 5 percent. Parempoolsed rated at 8 percent in October according to Turu-uuringute, down from 9 percent the previous month. All other parties polled between 0 and 1 percent. Two percent of respondents with a voting preference said they would vote for an individual candidate.
The latest Turu-uuringute poll was conducted from 1 to 7 October, with 899 Estonian citizens aged 18 or over surveyed nationwide. One third of questionnaires were collected by phone and two thirds online. Support figures are calculated on the basis of respondents with a voting preference, which was 74 percent of those surveyed.
The next Riigikogu election is on March 7, 2027.
