Germany's firewall against the far-right AfD feels the heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:04:53 UTC
15:04:53 KST

Germany's firewall against the far-right AfD feels the heat
BERLIN, Oct 10 - Chancellor Friedrich Merz's warning this week that extremism was entering Germany's parliamentary system was the latest in a series of signs that mainstream parties' "firewall" to isolate the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has begun to buckle.
This week, at least four lawmakers from mainstream parties in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt appear to have defied party orders and voted to give the AfD, which wants to restrict immigration and restore energy ties with Russia, its first regional assembly speaker.
The ballot was secret but suspicion immediately fell on the 15 members of Merz's conservative Christian Democrats (CDU) in parliament, who had been told to abstain.
Karin Prien, deputy chair of the national CDU, said if CDU lawmakers were to blame, "there must be consequences".
The AfD itself, which has been leading the CDU in nationwide surveys for more than a year and declared its aim of winning a national election due in 2029, hailed a "political turning point".
"For the first time, it was clear that the so-called 'firewall' doesn't have to be stronger than the freedom of action of members of parliament," said Martin Reichardt, head of the AfD in Saxony-Anhalt.
COULD AFD WIN A NATIONAL ELECTION IN GERMANY?
The AfD's record victory last month has alarmed rivals, who consider it an anti-democratic party opposed to the values that helped Germany to rebuild after World War Two and renounce the horrors of Nazism and its nationalist, racist ideology. The AfD rejects their label of "extreme right" as a slur.
Across Europe and beyond, the result, which left the AfD just short of an absolute majority in the state parliament, was seen as one of the clearest indications yet that it could win a national election in 2029.
Merz's coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats in Berlin has been under increasing strain, riven by disagreements and sliding in opinion polls as voters, like many across Western Europe, blame the mainstream parties for declining living standards.
On Wednesday, the parties held talks to iron out differences over issues including pensions and tax, and said they were "determined not to hand our country over to extremists".
Set up over a decade ago during the euro zone debt crisis, the AfD has grown from a fringe movement into the most popular party in Germany in opinion polls.
Yet parts of the AfD - including its Saxony-Anhalt branch - have been designated as extremist by German security services, meaning that they are considered to be opposed to constitutional principles of human rights, democracy and the rule of law.
The Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution (BfV), the domestic intelligence agency, compiled a 1,100-page confidential report last year that found the AfD incited resentment of migrants, as well as racism and Islamophobia.
For its part, the AfD says it is restoring German national pride and values, and ensuring that migrants are not prioritised at the expense of German citizens.
So far, the "firewall" approach - under which the established parties have refused to cooperate with the AfD - has kept it from joining any coalition government.
In Saxony-Anhalt, where it needs three more seats for a majority, it is still unclear how it can form a government after talks over a possible coalition with the populist far-left BSW made no progress.
FEARS OF COOPERATION WITH AFD
However, the AfD's Ulrich Siegmund, who dismisses the firewall as "childish", says he can persuade enough members of other parties to defy party orders to enable him to be confirmed as state premier by the end of the year.
In this week's speaker ballot, the AfD's Tobias Rausch won 48 votes - four more than the combined total held by the AfD and the BSW.
Merz has ruled out any arrangement with the AfD, which he says aims to destroy the CDU, and the issue is expected to be discussed at a CDU's leadership meeting on Sunday and Monday.
But whether it remains realistic to refuse to cooperate with a party attracting almost a third of the vote, and more in the formerly communist eastern states where it is strongest, has become an urgent question.
CDU deputy leader Prien said any sign of accommodation could open divisions that could "jeopardise the very existence of the entire party".
The AfD has gained ground nationwide but remains weaker in western Germany than in the east, and appears unlikely to repeat its Saxony-Anhalt result in state elections next year.
However, the problems that have helped create the conditions for its rapid rise resist easy answers. War in Ukraine has cut off the supply of cheap energy that fuelled Germany's economy while competition from China has eaten away at its once-invincible industrial base.
Economists warn continually that fundamental reforms are needed to pensions and taxes to meet the needs of an ageing population, while deep divisions remain between the eastern and western regions, almost four decades after the fall of the Berlin Wall.
Marking the anniversary last week of German reunification in 1990, President Frank-Walter Steinmeier acknowledged that many felt overlooked by the political system and that a generalised feeling of insecurity had undermined confidence.
But, in an unusually bleak assessment, he said the bitter political climate was threatening to send Germany back into the chaos that ended the democracy of the prewar Weimar Republic.
"Today is about the survival of democracy," he said. "We must stand up for what remains important." REUTERS

UN warns of rising civilian toll in Ukraine as Russian strikes kill 100 in a week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:04:45 UTC
15:04:45 KST

The UN condemned a sharp escalation in attacks on civilians in Ukraine, reporting that more than 100 people were killed and at least 429 injured over the past week as Russian strikes hit residential areas, passenger buses and critical infrastructure.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, told the UN Security Council on Friday that attacks by the Russian Federation had reached “a new horrifying level” since the council’s briefing September 23.
“We strongly condemn all attacks against civilians,” said Khiari.
He said the pattern of escalating attacks had contributed to a "significant increase" in civilian casualties this year, with every month recording more casualties than the corresponding month in each of the previous three years.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, he warned that repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure were disrupting life for millions.
The official also expressed concern about reported attacks on telecommunications networks, retail businesses, food suppliers and logistics companies.
“All attacks on energy infrastructure and on population centers must cease immediately,” said Khiari, stressing the urgency of protecting vulnerable civilians before winter sets in.
Black Sea attacks threaten shipping
Khiari also expressed concern about civilian deaths and injuries resulting from intensified attacks by Ukrainian forces inside Russia.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded reports of 3,890 civilian casualties in Russia between January and September, including 496 deaths and 3,394 injuries, said Khiari.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” he added.
Khiari warned that the consequences of the war were increasingly extending beyond Ukraine and Russia, threatening regional security and international trade.
"Particularly worrisome, in the Black Sea, attacks on civilian vessels have multiplied and expanded in geographic scope," he said.
He welcomed diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and securing safe civilian navigation in the Black Sea, urging both to negotiate credible and sustainable arrangements.
Khiari warned that attacks on ports, transport networks, grain facilities and other agricultural infrastructure were contributing to rising global food prices.
He urged Russia and Ukraine to halt the escalating attacks on civilians and pursue renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
“The current cycle of escalating attacks against civilians must end now before the civilian toll reaches new, devastating levels,” he said.
Diplomacy and dialogue must prevail and be given a genuine chance to succeed, he noted.
“It is time to end this war,” Khiari added.

‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:51 UTC
15:00:51 KST

In the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate with Andy Burnham.
Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words in the cloud – and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”.
At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread.
“The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.”
A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them?
At conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued.
But while Labour MPs are relieved to have a leader with a clear political direction, many worry that offering big promises for after the next general election will not be enough to scratch the itch for dramatic change.
Downing Street believes part of the answer is what it describes as “everyday fixes” – cost of living measures that might not, on their own, amount to very much, but added up can make a difference and show the government is trying.
Overseen by the No 10 policy unit and the Cabinet Office’s cost of living taskforce, each department has “incubators” where proposals are dreamed up. Many are in the works, such as rules around car-parking apps and unbranded school uniforms.
They might not grab the media headlines, but strategists say they pick up engagement online, with 85m views across all social platforms last week alone. There will be more announced in the two-and-a-bit weeks running up to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.
“We want to show we can tackle the everyday frustrations that people assume are part of life,” one adviser said. But several admitted they had some qualms about the drumbeat of small interventions.
“We risk looking twee, frankly, if we aren’t successfully thinking about how to tie it to the bigger picture of structural change. Public control, tax, that is what we want to be able to point to as well as the everyday things.”
Another added: “We need to tread carefully. We have very small interventions now and huge ambitions for three years’ time. We also need medium-scale changes in the medium term, and that is what is missing at the moment.”
The government faces a difficult budget, with inflation and soaring borrowing costs as a result of the Iran war thought to have blown a £12bn hole in the public finances, forcing the chancellor to consider tax rises and spending cuts to fund plans to ease the cost of living.
The statement, which is expected to be “low key”, will focus on fiscal devolution, with a household support package centred on cutting energy bills and more help for small businesses. Next year’s spending review would require more revenue, sources said, but details would have to wait.
A No 10 aide said: “The budget is a moment of peak attention and potentially peak peril. We’re not able to do everything we want to, so we have to level with people and say we can’t fix everything all at once, but we’re trying.”
But for some MPs, there is a growing nervousness at the low level of ambition at this budget, especially on cost of living measures, which the Burnham government has made its main test.
One said: “If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we are screwed. As things stand, this looks like a Reeves budget with better vibes. I hope this isn’t all there is. But I really fear that actually it is.”
Treasury insiders acknowledge the need to “kickstart” longer-term changes at the budget – and that a “low-key” statement with the big decisions put off until next year may not be enough for the public. “The budget will be our first punch in the face moment,” a government aide said.
There was a “bit of friction” between the prime minister’s office and the Treasury over balancing fiscal responsibility with hope, the source added. “No 10 wants to signal intent: that we won’t get everything immediately, but we’ll get there.”
There were lingering questions about “how this all adds up when we’re under grey skies”, another adviser added. “It’s impossible to see how anyone can square the additional spending we need given the tightness of the fiscal envelope.”
Ministers and advisers are expecting a barrage of attacks from the Tories and Reform UK on welfare. But they believe the Milburn and Timms reviews, which will be published shortly after the budget – will help them fight back.
Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be “bumpy” but is optimistic that Burnham’s communication skills will help to make the case, and that the public will continue – for now – to give him the benefit of the doubt.
A source said: “We’ll take a bit of a hit over the budget. It’s going to be a tough couple of weeks. But then we have a run to the 10-year plan. If we get that right, we can potentially go into next year with people saying: ‘Yes, it’s difficult, but we trust this guy.’”
At the cabinet away day, Burnham told ministers: “Politics has become too suffocating. We need greater ambition. The country is not where it should be and nothing simple gets us out of that. We need to show a journey and a longer-term plan.”
Ministers were presented with polling that showed support for Labour’s social care policy, including adjusting the pensions triple lock, went up by a quarter after voters were shown a video of the prime minister explaining his plan.
A party strategist told them: “On social care and the triple lock we need to continually make the case, time after time. When we make the case we have the power to persuade.”
There is a political axiom that if you’re explaining, you’re losing. But Labour strategists are pushing back on that idea. The prevailing view inside government is that Burnham is the only one who can go out and make the case – on all of his big promises – to the country.
Not everybody inside the party thinks it will work. “I don’t know how convinced I am about giving people essentially the same message as before: we want to do more but we’re constrained,” one insider said.
But ministers hope that by focusing on policies which signal intent, they can get through these difficult months. “We need more time to lean into the big things we can do, like public control, but we need to be honest with voters. We set ourselves a target of tackling the cost of living, but so many things are out of our control.”
No 10 insight work shows that people were still prepared to accept the Iran conflict as an explanation for why things are so tough, rather than viewing it as an excuse. At the away day, Healey told his colleagues: “We are recognising those pressures, being honest about what we can do and taking practical action wherever possible to give people some breathing space at the budget.”
When parliament returns after conference recess on Monday, Burnham will give a statement, updating MPs on the past few weeks and taking questions. Throughout, he will aim to show the public he is on their side.
But one senior Labour figure cautioned: “We all hope that he has a plan for what comes next. The sense that he gets it and that he’ll keep trying won’t last for ever.”

UK accused of giving people of Gaza false hope over new refugee safe route
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

The Home Office is facing claims it gave false hope to the people of Gaza after it emerged that a new safe route for Palestinian refugees will only be open to those who have already escaped to Lebanon or Jordan.
Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, announced the reopening of a resettlement scheme for refugees at Labour’s annual conference last month. A statement from her department said: “Around one in four referrals will be for Afghan women and girls and Palestinian refugees, fleeing war and persecution.”
But the body administering the scheme has confirmed it would only refer “a very small number of extremely urgent cases”, all of which would be processed in Jordan and Lebanon.
The umbrella alliance Communities for Palestinians (CFP) said this crucial detail was not in Mahmood’s speech or subsequent Home Office statements, giving people in Gaza and their supporters the belief that they could also apply.
Vicky Moller, a co-founder of CFP, said: “The applause at Shabana’s announcement at conference was at the prospect of a resettlement scheme for Palestinians fleeing war and persecution. People understood that would mean rescuing people from Gaza.”
The Home Office has pushed back at the claims, saying the UK resettlement scheme that Mahmood has reopened has always been for people from outside their country of origin.
A Home Office spokesperson said: “To qualify for refugee status under international frameworks, individuals must be outside their country of origin.
“Palestinians who remain in Gaza would not initially be in scope for these routes. However, Palestinians who have fled Gaza could be referred to the UK through the International Refugee Assistance Project [Irap].”
Restrictions on eligibility for the scheme emerged after an exchange of emails between the CFP and Irap, which has been tasked with making referrals.
According to Irap’s website, it will refer “a very small number of extremely urgent humanitarian cases to the UK for consideration for resettlement”, adding: “These cases will be referred to Irap by humanitarian organisations in Jordan and Lebanon and Irap will then hold interviews to determine if these cases can be referred to the UK government.”
The programme focuses on “extremely vulnerable refugees whose lives have become unsustainable in Jordan or Lebanon”.
The non-profit’s website added: “Irap does not know how many people the UK government will accept under the Palestinian resettlement programme. This is ultimately a decision for the UK government and depends on funding as well as local authorities’ capacity.”
Other safe and legal routes administered by the UK have allowed small numbers of people to enter the UK from their country of origin, including previous schemes for Afghan refugees.
Palestinian refugees fall outside the remit of the refugee convention and UNHCR.
Unrwa was instead set up to serve Palestinian refugees who were defined as any person whose “normal place of residence was Palestine during the period 1 June 1946 to 15 May 1948 and who lost both home and means of livelihood as a result of the 1948 conflict”.
As a result, Palestinian refugees live in what refugee charities and NGOs refer to as Palestine – in other words, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip – as well as second countries such as Syria, Lebanon and Jordan.
Jon Featonby, the chief policy analyst at the Refugee Council, said ministers should recognise the particular circumstances that meant Palestinians could be refugees while living in their own country.
“The government is right to commit to safe and legal routes. They provide a vital way for refugees to reach safety without having to put their lives in the hands of smuggling gangs,” he said.
“But the warm words have to be accompanied by ambition, and that means supporting people in the thousands, not the hundreds. They must also recognise the particular circumstances of Palestinian refugees and be accessible to them no matter where they are in the world.”
A renowned expert in asylum systems has said resettlement programmes are usually designed as a solution for people who have already left their own country.
Dr Peter Walsh, a senior researcher at the Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford, said the UK government’s safe and legal route was always going to mean taking Palestinians from neighbouring states such as Egypt, Jordan or Lebanon.
“The Syrian scheme worked the same way: the roughly 20,000 people resettled to the UK between 2014 and 2021 all came from countries around Syria, with nobody to my knowledge being flown directly from Syria,” he said.
“Bringing people directly out of Gaza would be a different kind of programme, closer to an emergency evacuation … And crucially, such an emergency evacuation in Gaza would depend on Israel and Egypt letting people leave and on the Home Office finding a way to do security and biometric checks with no visa centre in Gaza.”

UK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say experts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:50 UTC
15:00:50 KST

National Savings and Investments (NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.
Competition in the savings market has been growing, leading to some of the highest interest rates for years.
However, in the current climate, attractive deals do not always hang around for long, says Rachel Springall at the financial data website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk. If a provider attracts enough savings cash it will pull a product from sale.
NS&I has upped the rates on its “British savings bonds”, which are rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds. They offer a fixed interest rate over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.
The deals are available to new customers and those with existing accounts that are maturing. With the growth version, interest is added each year and paid when the bond matures, while with the income version, interest is paid monthly.
Looking at the growth bonds, the new interest rate on the one-year product is 4.99% (up from 4.82%), while the two-year rate has risen to 5.07% (was 4.81%). The three-year rate has gone up from 4.83% to 5.1%, while the five-year rate has been increased to 5.17% (was 4.85%).
Those are pretty competitive rates, though as Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the advice firm AJ Bell, says, “you can still make more money elsewhere”.
At the time of writing, the top-paying one-year fixed-rate bond was paying 5.12%, while the highest-paying five-year fixed bond was offering 5.37%. But getting the very highest rates sometimes means signing up with less-well-known names. The one-year deal is from Union Bank of India (UK), while the five-year version hails from GB Bank.
If you have a very large sum that you need to stash somewhere – for example, the proceeds of a house sale or an inheritance – these NS&I bonds have one big thing in their favour: you can invest up to £1m per person in each bond issue. The minimum investment is £500.
As NS&I says, “most banks only guarantee your savings up to £120,000,” whereas it is backed by the Treasury and is “the only provider that secures 100% of your savings above this amount”.
Also, it means you are putting your money into the government’s savings bank, and “your savings will be invested back into supporting the UK”.
Money invested in NS&I’s British savings bonds cannot be withdrawn before the end of the fixed term.
That will not suit everyone, and it is a good idea to keep some money in a high-paying easy access account to cover things such as unexpected bills. Earlier this month the digital bank Starling announced that people who sign up for its Easy Saver account will enjoy a table-topping 5% interest rate. This account offers unlimited penalty-free withdrawals, but that rate (made up of a 2.5% variable standard rate, plus a 2.5% fixed interest bonus lasting for six months) only applies to those who open, or have opened, a Starling current account on or after 1 October. The rate applies on balances of up to £25,000.
Starling customers who signed up before then can benefit from a 4% rate when opening a new Easy Saver. That includes a 1.5% fixed interest bonus for six months.
Meanwhile, the savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.

Spa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont Blanc
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:49 UTC
15:00:49 KST

Mont Blanc is hiding behind the clouds, but the Aiguille du Midi spears the sky above a mountainside ablaze with russet, gold and tawny tones. The maples flare red; rowan trees are dusted with crimson berries.
Our little group has trundled up to Mont Lachat station (altitude: 2,115 metres) on the Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs improbably steep slopes from the French alpine town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. Operational since 1909, the railway was once intended to reach the 4,809-metre summit of Mont Blanc, but war, glacial terrain and waning funds put an end to that ambition. But even from Mont Lachat, the view is a showstopper. On one side, the Bionnassay Glacier slips scenically down the slope, a buzzard soaring over the milky-green glacial lake at its base, while on the other the Chamonix valley basks in soft autumnal sunshine.
Autumn is golden season in the Alps, when you can find quieter hiking trails, lower prices and air crisp enough to stir the senses without nipping your fingers. Once focused purely on winter sports, the region’s resorts have spent years building up their summer credentials to offer hiking and biking through flower-strewn meadows. Now they’re marketing their shoulder season, too, to meet a growing demand for off-peak escapes.
The little spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, 50 minutes from Geneva and sandwiched between its glitzier neighbours Chamonix and Megève, is perfectly placed to take advantage of this trend. Unlike many resorts, the town of 5,800 doesn’t fall silent once the snow (or summer crowds) melts away, in large part thanks to its thermal waters, which were discovered at the beginning of the 19th century.
A year-round gondola called Le Valléen now links the train station in the village of Le Fayet, farther down the slope where the thermal spa is located, to Saint-Gervais proper. Opened in late 2024, it means you can arrive by rail from London via Paris and reach the heart of the resort without needing a car. “If you go to Megève in the shoulder season there’s no one there,” says long-serving mayor Jean-Marc Peillex. “That’s not the case here. The secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy too.”
Saint-Gervais (850 metres) may lack Megève’s polish but it has its own quiet charm: a medieval fortified house, a 17th-century church with geometric stained glass windows, elegant belle époque buildings near the spa and a thriving market every Thursday. Several excellent restaurants stay open year round, and our hotel, the chocolate-box Coeur des Neiges, offers rooms at less than half the summer or winter rate, making it an ideal base for autumnal exploring.
From here we take the Mont Blanc tramway one stop to Motivon, at 1,400 metres, then hike for an hour without seeing another soul; the only sound is the gentle clanging of cowbells. Our destination is the Distillerie Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc, one of Europe’s highest microdistilleries at 1,365m. It’s actually set in a converted donkey shed with windows framing pine forests and plunging valleys, shelves fashioned from old skis and two gleaming copper distillation stills.
This is where Scotsman James Abbott, kilt and all, produces some 450 bottles a year of single malt whisky (in a Speyside style), along with vodka, the traditional herbal liqueur génépi and a superb mountain gin infused with ingredients such as blueberries and wild herbs from the nearby slopes.
“The locals noticed that when I went to parties, I took whisky, not wine,” James laughs. “They said: ‘Why don’t you make your own – you drink enough of it.’” It turns out he does it rather well: the whisky sells for €95, the gin for €50, and both go down beautifully after a day in the mountain air before we hop back on the tramway.
Although the tramway stops running from the end of September, there’s no shortage of scenic hiking trails fanning straight out from town which are accessible later in the year, plus a free, year-round bus service linking the villages that make up the commune of St-Gervais. We’re due to take it the next morning for a walk from Saint-Nicolas-de-Véroce, whose baroque church is resplendent with blue-and-gold interiors and frescoed ceilings, but a heavy rainstorm postpones our plans.
That’s not a problem when just down the road (or a free cog lift ride down the mountainside) are Les Thermes de Saint-Gervais, which have been soothing weary bodies since 1806, when notary Joseph-Marie Gontard discovered the springs. The mineral-rich waters, packed with sulphur, magnesium, calcium and zinc, bubble up from underground at 39C, feeding a three‑hour wellness circuit.
We drift between pools of different temperatures, move lazily from sauna to steam room, enjoy the rainforest spa and wallow outdoors as jets of water pummel our backs while the gondola glides silently overhead. Who cares about the rain?
By the time we emerge, the storm has cleared, so we continue to Saint-Nicolas. From here, a steep two‑hour trail winds up to the Refuge du Mont-Joly, a century-old wooden inn that smells of woodsmoke and melting cheese. Normally there are sweeping views of Mont Blanc from the terrace, but today the peaks are shrouded in cloud.
We might not be able to see the mountains but we can taste their produce, notably in the enormous portion of blueberry tart that follows a tartiflette big enough to satisfy a sumo wrestler. As I tuck in, snow begins to fall. By morning it will be gone, melted by the late-summer sun. But now it lies thick and soft outside, turning the world white, as if the Ice Queen from Narnia might step through the door at any moment. That’s autumn in the Alps for you.
The trip was provided by the Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist board. Doubles at the Coeur des Neiges from €108 room-only, or from €76 room-only at Plan B at Le Fayet. The Refuge du Mont-Joly is closed from the end of March to late May, and from November to mid-December.
The Tramway du Mont Blanc now stops at the Nid d’Aigle lookout (2,380 metres), after the line was extended in July

As Russia escalates its war, the EU realises its support for Ukraine won't be enough
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:00:45 UTC
15:00:45 KST

Russia's rapid escalation has thrown into doubt the European Union's multiple support programmes for Ukraine. Diplomats concede it is only a matter of time before leaders address the contentious matter.
The European Union is rapidly coming to terms with the limitations of its multibillion-euro support for Ukraine, as Russia's all-out escalation wrecks the country's finances, depletes its air defences and deepens its reliance on cash-strapped donors.
"This war will last longer than we thought," a European diplomat said, speaking on condition of anonymity. "There's a realisation that needs will continue to present themselves, but it's not yet clear how this will be addressed."
"We must send a clear message that the EU won't change its position and will double down on its support for Ukraine and pressure on Russia," another diplomat said.
Railways, bridges, cargo vessels, power stations, data centres, warehouses, medical centres, schools and kindergartens have all come under Russian airstrikes in recent days. Even the National Academy of Sciences has been targeted.
The relentless bombardment, a calculated mix of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, has killed scores of civilians, including over 30 people in Kramatorsk after a glide bomb attack set two public buses ablaze.
On Thursday, Russia plunged Kyiv into darkness, offering a grim preview of a winter that is likely to be the harshest, cruellest yet of the war.
This is "terror against people and life. And it is important that leaders do not ignore what is happening", Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
"Pure and simple: these are war crimes," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said, expressing her solidarity.
The escalation has hit the country's war-battered economy particularly hard, as the endless waves of drones disrupt ordinary activity, force businesses to close, raise material costs and eat away at profits.
Russia's blockade in the Black Sea has added further strain, preventing Ukrainian farmers from selling tonnes of grain to their global clients and depriving the state of an essential source of revenue.
The deterioration raises serious questions about the viability and durability of the EU's multiple support programmes, notably the €90 billion loan that leaders agreed last year to cover two-thirds of Ukraine's needs for 2026 and 2027.
The loan, it must be noted, was designed under the premise that the war would end sometime this year. Russia's escalation all but guarantees this will not be the case.
Ukraine's Finance Minister Sergii Marchenko has warned that the 2027 budget will be the most complicated since the start of the full-scale invasion. He has urged international donors to fill a staggering $78 billion (€70 billion) gap.
The Commission has refrained from endorsing the headline figure, which vastly exceeds the €45 billion it plans to provide next year under the support loan. Instead, it has promised to speed up disbursements, contingent on internal reforms.
"For 2027, the picture is indeed more challenging," Economy Commissioner Valdis Dombrovskis said on Friday after a meeting of finance ministers.
"It's clear that we are facing a sizeable funding gap. The exact quantification is still a work in progress."
Brussels has not formally reopened the debate on new support for Ukraine, as member states are currently embroiled in bitter negotiations over the next EU budget.
Officials and diplomats, however, privately admit it is only a matter of time before leaders are compelled to address the matter, which has become increasingly contentious amid rising debt, stagnant growth and far-right opposition.
The total absence of US aid, once a key provider of weapons, compounds the equation.
A group of EU countries has attempted to revive the debate on the immobilised Russian assets, arguing the €90 billion loan "will not be enough".
But Belgium, the main custodian of the assets, has pushed back. France and Italy, two key votes, remain reluctant to go down the uncharted avenue.
"On the assets, there's still some interest, but we still remember very clearly what happened in December," a senior diplomat said, referring to the dramatic summit where an asset-backed proposal fell apart. The loan was then set up as Plan B.
"As of now, there's nothing new or substantial on the table."
The option of issuing more joint debt to support Ukraine, as done with the €90 billion, has become politically unattractive amid spiralling borrowing costs.
Meanwhile, the option of ramping up bilateral contributions, which is much more straightforward, risks placing the burden on a few wealthy countries, namely Germany, the Netherlands and the Nordics.
With no easy solutions, Brussels is asking other allies, such as the UK, Canada and Japan, to step up to the plate as it figures out what to do next.
"We are assessing other possibilities in any case," Dombrovskis said. "We are committed to ensuring that Ukraine has the necessary funding for as long as it's necessary."

Palestine welcomed South African jurist Navi Pillay’s being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, saying the honour recognises her efforts to defend international law and document Israeli crimes.
The Foreign Ministry said on Friday Pillay’s win represented an elevation of “the voice of truth and the voice of the oppressed,” and recognised her efforts to advance peace and international law.
It said Pillay devoted her career to upholding law and justice and defending the rights of oppressed people in South Africa and around the world, including Palestinians.
The ministry praised her leadership of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, which she chaired from 2021 to 2025.
It said the commission helped document genocide, sexual violence, attacks on children and other Israeli violations.
The ministry said the prize was also recognition for defenders of international law and justice and encouragement for efforts to hold perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity accountable.
It added that Pillay has consistently defended the universality of law and equality among people, including Palestinians, and said the award underscored that “there can be no lasting peace without justice and equality for all.”
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that it awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to the 85-year-old jurist “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“This year's laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law,” it said, highlighting her work in international courts and as UN high commissioner for human rights.
Pillay, born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, under apartheid, began her legal career challenging racial discrimination and defending opponents of the apartheid system.
She served as UN high commissioner for human rights, as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She has also served as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice.
The UN commission she chaired concluded in a 2025 report that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza, a finding rejected by Israel.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

British Army deploys Nyan deep-strike drones in Estonia
Unknown

British Army deploys Nyan deep-strike drones in Estonia
A British unit at Tapa has deployed Nyan attack drone systems with a range of over 250 kilometers, boosting the allies' long-range strike capability, Postimees reported.
British Army spokesperson Melissa Terry told Postimees the allies brought Nyan drones to Estonia during this year's Exercise Spring Storm, adding they have already been used in exercises and training in Estonia.
"Nyan provides the British Army with a long-range precision strike capability as part of a broader deep strike capability. It is designed to complement existing fire support capabilities and provide additional options for engaging targets at long distances," Terry said.
Nyan is a U.K.-manufactured so-called One Way Effector, or single-use drone, with a range of over 250 kilometers, launched by a pneumatic catapult; as an attack drone it is comparable with the Iranian-designed Shahed.
It is made by defense company BAE Systems and is a jet-powered drone with a 2.9-meter wingspan, a maximum takeoff weight of over 75 kilograms, a payload of under 20 kilograms, and a top speed of approximately 220 km/h.
Terry added that the British Army uses two Estonian-made launch systems for Nyan: the Ely PL80 and the Threod CATA BT.
Estonia and the U.K. signed a defense cooperation action plan in Tallinn this July, superseding the previous armored unit concept which had been based on weapons such as Challenger 2 main battle tanks and Warrior infantry fighting vehicles.
Terry added that the deployment of Nyan in Estonia strengthens Britain's contribution to NATO deterrence and defense and allows for better integration of the new capability with targeting, mission planning, and digital fire control systems.
The British brought the Nyan systems to Estonia in the spring during Spring Storm, when various allied units were in Estonia at the time, which provided a better opportunity to test Nyan's integration into international division-level operations.
As a new solution, a unit was created which is equipped with highly mobile vehicles, modern weapon systems, and drones, specifically designed for the Estonian operational environment.

The Rugby League World Cup was officially launched on Saturday with representatives from all 10 men's teams and eight women's teams.
Samoa captain Junior Paulo hopes those in his side who lost last week's NRL Grand Final can use their pain to propel the Toa to a repeat of 2022, when they made the final.
What's next?
The men's tournament kicks off on Thursday night while the women's edition begins on Friday afternoon.
Junior Paulo knows what it feels like to pull yourself from the depths of grand final misery and glowingly represent your country at a Rugby League World Cup weeks later.
So he is happy to lend a helping hand to his Samoa teammates who are suffering similar heartache.
Parramatta's Paulo had big dreams of winning the NRL grand final in 2022, but they shattered when the forward's side suffered a 28-12 loss to Penrith in the decider.
He had to forge on, and weeks later found himself leading Samoa in a historic World Cup final against Australia.
Paulo will be looking to repeat the dose this time around after the tournament was officially launched at the Sydney Football Stadium on Saturday.
Samoa are one of 10 men's teams vying for glory, beginning when Australia face New Zealand on Thursday night, while eight teams will make up the women's tournament that starts with the Jillaroos taking on Samoa in Parramatta the following evening.
This year, four of Samoa's players — Newcastle winger Greg Marzhew, prop Pasami Saulo, and second-rowers Francis Manuleleua and Jermaine McEwen — will be feeling a similar pain to Paulo's back in 2022.
The Knights quartet lost to the Sydney Roosters in the grand final last Sunday.
"I was in the same shoes, losing to Penrith and then [having to play in the] World Cup," Samoa co-captain Paulo said.
"All you want to do is … be able to turn it around.
"So for them [Manuleleua and McEwen], they're eager to get back out and play some footy. Hopefully it means they bring the physicality that they do.
"It's time for us to bring them up to being ready to represent Samoa, but also making it enjoyable for them."
Regardless, Paulo cannot wait to lead a star-studded Samoan side when they begin their campaign next Friday against France before facing Papua New Guinea and Tonga.
All eyes are sure to be fixed on star half Jarome Luai after a headline-riddled season where he was announced as the first official signing for the PNG Chiefs from 2028 before later being released by Wests Tigers to join Parramatta for 2027.
"He's [been] just a bit misunderstood by many towards the back end of the year. People were very opinionated about him," said Paulo of his co-captain.
"He's locked in, putting his best foot forward and representing Samoa. He enjoys being in these camps, and you can just tell how locked in he is by the first day we got into camp.
"[I] just want to see him evolve as a leader, and grow into the leader he is now. All the boys will be backing him, and luckily, nothing fazes Romey [Luai] too much."
In the lead-up to the tournament, some members of the team also spent some time in Samoa, which Paulo said was an "indescribable" feeling as it reminded the players they are embarking on something for more than themselves.

Huckabee rejects Gaza genocide accusations at Arkansas October 7 memorial

U.S. Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee delivered a forceful defense of Israel at a ceremony marking the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas massacre, rejecting accusations of genocide in Gaza as American and Israeli officials gathered at the Arkansas State Capitol to honor the victims and reaffirm their support for the Jewish state.
"If Israel wanted to commit genocide, they could have done it in two and a half hours. They have the military capacity. Gaza is the size of Las Vegas. They intentionally did not," Huckabee told participants at Wednesday's commemoration in Little Rock.
The event, organized by the National Association of Christian Lawmakers (NACL) under the banner "October 7th: Remember, Pray, Stand With Israel," brought together elected officials, Israeli diplomatic and military representatives, and Jewish and Christian religious leaders.
Among those attending were Arkansas Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the ambassador's daughter, Attorney General Tim Griffin, Secretary of State Cole Jester and Israel's Consul General to the Southwest, Adi Farjon Israel.
The ceremony marked three years since Hamas terrorists launched their October 7, 2023, assault on southern Israel, killing approximately 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages into Gaza.
Speakers emphasized the importance of preserving the memory of the victims, countering antisemitism and challenging efforts to distort the historical record of the attacks.
Farjon Israel recalled that more than 100 Arkansas lawmakers had attended a presentation at the Capitol in 2024 featuring footage of the atrocities recorded by the Hamas terrorists themselves. "That matters, because three years later, some are trying to rewrite what happened on Oct. 7," she warned.
Sanders reaffirmed her state's support for Israel and the Jewish community. In a public statement marking the anniversary, she said: "We stand with the Jewish people and we pray for the victims, their families and the survivors."
Griffin also stressed the importance of combating antisemitism and ensuring that the atrocities of October 7 are not forgotten. "Our state has a special connection with Israel, and I have been proud to defend laws that combat antisemitism here in Arkansas. We will never forget the horrors of October 7, and we stand steadfast with our Jewish friends and neighbors," he said.
Jester praised Sanders for her support of Israel, describing her as one of the Jewish state's strongest advocates among American governors.
Albert Veksler, a leader of the Jerusalem Prayer Breakfast, spoke about the suffering experienced by Jewish communities and expressed concern over anti-Israel demonstrations around the world. "We can’t even understand the pain the Jewish people are going through these days, and the world is celebrating, and shouting, ‘From the river to the sea,’" Veksler said.
The ceremony also featured remarks and prayers from Rabbi Pinchus Ciment, regional director of Lubavitch of Arkansas; Harry Ehrenberg of the Arkansas Jewish Federation; and Pastor Happy Caldwell, a member of the NACL Governing Board.
Jason Rapert, founder and president of the National Association of Christian Lawmakers, who hosted the event, described the anniversary as both an occasion for remembrance and a call for continued action against antisemitism. "October 7th was an act of unspeakable evil, and three years later, we have a responsibility to make certain the world never forgets what happened," Rapert said.
"We gathered at the Arkansas State Capitol to honor the innocent lives lost, stand with the Jewish people, and make it absolutely clear that we will not be silent in the face of antisemitism, terrorism, or those who seek to distort the truth."
Rapert thanked Huckabee, Sanders, other state officials and Israeli representatives for participating, saying their attendance reflected Arkansas's longstanding ties with Israel.
He also emphasized the religious convictions underlying the organization's support for the Jewish state. "Scripture commands us to pray for the peace of Jerusalem, and we take that responsibility seriously," he said, adding that supporting Israel also meant confronting antisemitism and ensuring that the October 7 atrocities were neither forgotten nor misrepresented.
Following the ceremony at the Capitol's Second Floor Rotunda, invited guests attended a reception at the Arkansas Governor's Mansion and an evening dinner bringing together American and Israeli officials, lawmakers and representatives of Jewish and Christian communities.
The National Association of Christian Lawmakers, founded in 2020, brings together federal, state and local lawmakers who seek to advance biblical principles in public policy. The organization says it has established leadership positions in 43 states and developed a network of members and supporters across all 50 states and Puerto Rico.

World Insights: Okinawa murder case exposes price of Japan's U.S. security dependence
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
13:49:43 CST
14:49:43 KST

TOKYO, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- The Okinawa prefectural assembly has adopted a protest resolution and an opinion statement over a U.S. Marine's suspected robbery-murder of a local woman in the southern Japanese prefecture, demanding that the U.S. take effective measures to prevent similar incidents and calling for a fundamental review of the Japan-U.S. Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA).
Analysts said the case had once again exposed the consequences of Japan's long-standing security dependence on the United States and the unequal nature of their bilateral relationship. Meanwhile, Japan's continued military buildup in Okinawa is adding to security concerns among local residents, who have long borne the burden of hosting U.S. military bases.
CRIME REIGNITES PUBLIC ANGER
The suspect, identified as Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old U.S. Marine stationed in Okinawa, allegedly killed Anna Yagi, a 39-year-old local woman, and stole her wallet and other belongings at a hotel in the prefectural capital of Naha in the early hours of Oct. 3.
Okinawa police arrested him on Oct. 4. Japanese media, citing police sources, reported that surveillance footage showed a person whose physical characteristics matched those of Ballard. He has denied the allegations, responding "I don't know" to police questioning, according to the reports.
Following the arrest, the U.S. side expressed condolences to the victim's family and said it would cooperate with the Japanese investigation, but did not issue an apology.
The killing and the U.S. response have fueled anger among local residents. On Oct. 4, more than 100 people gathered in Naha to protest. One female demonstrator said she was constantly afraid that she or her daughter could become the next victim.
Anger has also spread across social media, with comments accusing the Japanese government of weakness and excessive deference to Washington, while some users likened Japan's position to that of a colony.
NIGHTMARE LINGERS IN OKINAWA
The anger in Okinawa is rooted in a long history of wartime trauma and the burden of hosting U.S. military bases.
Japan forcibly annexed the Ryukyu Kingdom in 1879 and established Okinawa Prefecture. During the final stages of World War II, Okinawa became a major battlefield as Japan sought to delay the U.S. advance toward its mainland, resulting in heavy civilian casualties. After the war, the islands came under U.S. administration.
Although the United States returned administrative control of Okinawa to Japan in 1972, the prefecture has continued to bear a disproportionate share of the U.S. military presence. Okinawa accounts for only about 0.6 percent of Japan's land area, yet it hosts approximately 70 percent of all exclusive-use U.S. military facilities and installations in Japan. Crime, noise and pollution associated with the bases have long troubled local communities.
According to Okinawa Prefecture statistics, U.S. military personnel and their family members committed 6,409 criminal offenses from 1972 through 2025. Cases involving U.S. military-related personnel have shown an upward trend in recent years.
Analysts say the recurrence of crimes involving U.S. military personnel is closely linked to the special legal status granted to U.S. forces under the Japan-U.S. SOFA, signed in 1960.
Under the agreement, the United States has the primary right to exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed by U.S. military personnel while on duty, while Japan has the primary jurisdiction over crimes occurring off duty.
However, if a U.S. service member is accused of a crime over which Japan has jurisdiction, but the suspect manages to return to a U.S. military base before being arrested by local authorities, custody legally remains with the United States until the person is formally indicted by Japanese prosecutors.
In practice, this arrangement can complicate Japanese investigations and the transfer of suspects to Japanese custody. Critics argue that the special treatment afforded to U.S. personnel undermines accountability and public confidence in the justice system.
The issue has remained contentious since a 1995 case in which three U.S. servicemen brutally raped an Okinawan schoolgirl, triggering widespread protests and calls for a revision of the agreement. Yet its fundamental provisions have remained unchanged.
Analysts point out that Japan's reluctance to pursue substantive revisions reflects its dependence on the United States for security. An editorial in Japan's Mainichi Shimbun criticized the government's hesitation over fundamental measures, including revising the SOFA, saying it exposed Tokyo's underlying fear of antagonizing Washington, its key security ally.
MILITARY BUILDUP ADDS TO CONCERNS
Beyond the burden of U.S. bases, Okinawa residents are facing new risks as Japan accelerates its military buildup, analysts say.
In recent years, Japan has stepped up its military expansion and designated Okinawa as a "forward base for combat readiness" amid shifts in U.S. security strategy and Washington's growing expectations that Tokyo assume a greater military role.
The government of Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi, who took office in October 2025, has been particularly active in promoting military expansion. During a visit to Ishigaki and Yonaguni islands in Okinawa Prefecture in November 2025, Minister of Defense Shinjiro Koizumi said plans to deploy a medium-range surface-to-air missile unit on Yonaguni Island were proceeding as scheduled.
In June this year, Japan's Akahata newspaper reported that the Defense Ministry planned to expand the number of beds at the Japan Self-Defense Forces' Naha Hospital and establish a medical evacuation system to transport casualties from outlying islands in Okinawa to mainland Japan.
Koja Genta, who was recently elected Okinawa governor with support from the ruling Liberal Democratic Party, has also said he is willing to adapt prefecture-managed airports, ports and other infrastructure to better support the government's military deployments "in times of emergency."
Local media and left-wing figures in Japan have criticized the government's approach, arguing that its pledges to ease Okinawa's burden and revitalize the local economy have not translated into meaningful relief. Instead, they say, the military presence is being reinforced, further entrenching Okinawa's role on the front line of Japan's defense buildup.
Tomoko Tamura, chairperson of the Japanese Communist Party, criticized the government for pushing ahead with military expansion while disregarding Okinawa's history of devastating wartime suffering, warning that the prefecture could once again become a battlefield.
Hiromori Maedomari, a professor at Okinawa International University, has also argued in an article that strengthening military deployments in Okinawa in the name of responding to a so-called emergency threatens local livelihoods and the regional economy, warning that Japan's continued reliance on military means could lead the country toward war.
For Okinawa, the latest killing is therefore more than an isolated criminal case. It has renewed questions about the unequal security arrangement with the United States, the Japanese government's ability to protect local residents, and the risks of turning the prefecture into an increasingly militarized frontier. ■

Lai casts Taiwan as a beacon of democracy in National Day address
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:44:11 UTC
14:44:11 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — President Lai Ching-te (賴清德) on Saturday outlined his vision for Taiwan as an example of democracy, resilience, and shared prosperity in a world facing conflict and authoritarianism in his National Day address.
Marking 30 years since Taiwan’s first direct presidential election, Lai recalled how voters went to the polls despite missile threats in 1996, fulfilling a long-standing aspiration for its people to determine their own future. Over the past three decades, Taiwan has undergone democratic transformation, experienced changes of ruling parties, and faced numerous challenges, Lai said.
Against this backdrop, Lai framed his vision for Taiwan around the themes of a city on a hill, salt of the earth, and light of the world. The imagery reflects democratic foundations, a commitment to freedom and peace, and its role in the international community.
He outlined plans to improve living standards and expand social welfare. He also called for individuals across the political spectrum to work toward a shared future for the country.
Lai said the government would work to ensure that economic growth translates into better living standards for the public. One priority is addressing Taiwan’s declining birthrate, with a growth allowance for children and young people aged 18 and under set to be introduced next year.
Housing affordability is another priority. Lai said the government plans to increase the supply of social housing through direct construction, rent subsidies, and additional units secured through urban renewal and floor-area incentives.
Turning to national security, Lai said Taiwan seeks peaceful relations with other countries while maintaining the defense capabilities needed to deter aggression. He cited China’s continued military and gray-zone activities around the nation, which he said were aimed at changing the status quo across the Taiwan Strait.
Lai pledged to continue defense reforms and strengthen domestic defense industries. He also highlighted the Whole-of-Society Defense Resilience initiative, which brings together government agencies and civil society to maintain essential services such as energy, communications, finance, food supplies, and healthcare during a crisis.
Beyond security, Lai highlighted innovation, economic cooperation, and social inclusion as pillars for Taiwan’s international role. He cited the country’s development from traditional industries to advanced semiconductor manufacturing as evidence that an economy with limited natural resources can become an important contributor to global prosperity.
To sustain that progress, the government is accelerating development in 13 key strategic industries, including semiconductors and quantum computing. The initiative extends beyond technology to cover critical minerals, biotechnology and healthcare, urban renewal, cultural and creative industries, and tourism.
A separate development and revitalization program aims to help small- and medium-sized enterprises and microbusinesses improve their competitiveness. Support includes financing, workforce training, digital transformation, net-zero upgrades, and access to international markets.
Lai stressed the benefits of technological development should extend beyond major technology companies. He called for closer ties between advanced and traditional industries, with large corporations helping domestic suppliers expand alongside their international operations.
Economic growth must also improve household finances, Lai said. He cited 11 consecutive annual increases in the minimum wage and five pay raises for military personnel, civil servants, and public school teachers over the past decade. He also pointed to salary adjustments for professional and supervisory positions this year.
With local elections approaching, Lai called for political competition to coexist with a shared commitment to the nation’s future. He acknowledged that political parties and voters hold differing views, but said disagreements should not divide society or undermine respect for democratic institutions.
Concluding his address, Lai called on Taiwan to remain open to the world and continue sharing the benefits of its development. He said the country should draw on the strength of its people and industries to contribute to global progress while upholding freedom, equality, and innovation.

US hosts ‘productive’ trilateral talks to end Russia-Ukraine war
US envoy Steve Witkoff says renewed negotiations aim to ensure lasting peace before winter approaches.
United States, Ukrainian and European officials have met in Miami, Florida, to discuss a proposal for ending the Russia-Ukraine war, US envoy Steve Witkoff said in a statement posted to X.
Witkoff said on Friday that “constructive discussions” tackled “potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace”.
Witkoff said the meeting included “the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO”.
The discussions covered energy resilience, grain exports, security guarantees and “longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflict”, Witkoff said.
He also noted the “productive” talks discussed “Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession”.
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday the conflict had reached a dangerous “stalemate”, with the failure to reach a negotiated settlement raising the risk of further escalation.
“The other way that stalemates end is through escalation,” Rubio told reporters, warning that the conflict could spread to neighbouring NATO countries.
Renewed diplomacy
Earlier on Friday, Russian President Vladimir Putin told US President Donald Trump that the resumption of talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.
The renewed diplomacy comes against a backdrop of deadly Russian attacks, including a strike on civilian buses in eastern Ukraine that killed 33 people. Authorities said the attack was the single deadliest attack this year.
The ongoing talks have been overshadowed by the US-Russia diesel deal on Friday. Trump blamed Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries for surging diesel prices.
The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.
Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”. Hours after the deal, a Ukrainian drone hit a Russian fuel site.
The Miami meeting follows visits to Moscow and Kyiv last month by Witkoff and Jared Kushner, as Washington seeks to revive negotiations that have yielded little progress.

Unknown

Abdelraouf Arnaout and Mohammad Sio
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Palestine on Friday welcomed South African jurist Navi Pillay’s being awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, saying the honor recognizes her efforts to defend international law and document Israeli crimes.
The Foreign Ministry said Pillay’s win represented an elevation of “the voice of truth and the voice of the oppressed,” and recognized her efforts to advance peace and international law.
It said Pillay devoted her career to upholding law and justice and defending the rights of oppressed people in South Africa and around the world, including Palestinians.
The ministry praised her leadership of the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, including East Jerusalem, and Israel, which she chaired from 2021 to 2025.
It said the commission helped document genocide, sexual violence, attacks on children and other Israeli violations.
The ministry said the prize was also recognition for defenders of international law and justice and encouragement for efforts to hold perpetrators of genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity accountable.
It added that Pillay has consistently defended the universality of law and equality among people, including Palestinians, and said the award underscored that “there can be no lasting peace without justice and equality for all.”
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced that it awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize to the 85-year-old jurist “for her efforts to promote peace and international law.”
“This year's laureate has significantly enlarged the scope and impact of international law,” it said, highlighting her work in international courts and as UN high commissioner for human rights.
Pillay, born into a family of Indian Tamil origin in Durban, South Africa, under apartheid, began her legal career challenging racial discrimination and defending opponents of the apartheid system.
She served as UN high commissioner for human rights, as a judge at the International Criminal Court and as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda. She has also served as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice.
The UN commission she chaired concluded in a 2025 report that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip, a finding rejected by Israel.
The Nobel Peace Prize will be presented in Oslo on Dec. 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel’s death.

UN warns of rising civilian toll in Ukraine as Russian strikes kill more than 100 in 1 week
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Diyar Güldoğan
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
The UN on Friday condemned a sharp escalation in attacks on civilians in Ukraine, reporting that more than 100 people were killed and at least 429 injured over the past week as Russian strikes hit residential areas, passenger buses and critical infrastructure.
Khaled Khiari, assistant secretary-general for the Middle East, Asia and the Pacific, told the UN Security Council that attacks by the Russian Federation had reached “a new horrifying level” since the council’s briefing Sept. 23.
“We strongly condemn all attacks against civilians,” said Khiari.
He said the pattern of escalating attacks had contributed to a "significant increase" in civilian casualties this year, with every month recording more casualties than the corresponding month in each of the previous three years.
Beyond the immediate loss of life, he warned that repeated attacks on Ukrainian cities and essential infrastructure were disrupting life for millions.
The official also expressed concern about reported attacks on telecommunications networks, retail businesses, food suppliers and logistics companies.
“All attacks on energy infrastructure and on population centers must cease immediately,” said Khiari, stressing the urgency of protecting vulnerable civilians before winter sets in.
Black Sea attacks threaten shipping
Khiari also expressed concern about civilian deaths and injuries resulting from intensified attacks by Ukrainian forces inside Russia.
The Office of the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) recorded reports of 3,890 civilian casualties in Russia between January and September, including 496 deaths and 3,394 injuries, said Khiari.
“All attacks targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure, wherever they occur, are a violation of international humanitarian law and must end immediately,” he added.
Khiari warned that the consequences of the war were increasingly extending beyond Ukraine and Russia, threatening regional security and international trade.
"Particularly worrisome, in the Black Sea, attacks on civilian vessels have multiplied and expanded in geographic scope," he said.
He welcomed diplomatic efforts aimed at reducing tensions and securing safe civilian navigation in the Black Sea, urging both to negotiate credible and sustainable arrangements.
Khiari warned that attacks on ports, transport networks, grain facilities and other agricultural infrastructure were contributing to rising global food prices.
He urged Russia and Ukraine to halt the escalating attacks on civilians and pursue renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
“The current cycle of escalating attacks against civilians must end now before the civilian toll reaches new, devastating levels,” he said.
Diplomacy and dialogue must prevail and be given a genuine chance to succeed, he noted.
“It is time to end this war,” Khiari added.

'Crashout', 'Ragebait' or 'Peak': Want to know which word is favoured by Germany's youth?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:30:23 UTC
14:30:23 KST

The three frontrunners 'Crashout', 'Ragebait' and 'Peak' are in the running to become Germany's youth word of the year 2026, with anglicisms particularly trendy. The winning term will be announced this Saturday at the Frankfurt Book Fair.
For weeks, young Germans have been able to vote on which word best reflects their generation. The favourites are "Crashout", "Ragebait" and "Peak". Together, they attracted votes in the mid six-figure range. The poll was open to 11- to 20-year-olds.
On Saturday, Langenscheidt, the publishing house behind the vote, will announce this year's winning term at the Frankfurt Book Fair. These are the favourites.
Crashout
If you "crashout", you've lost control. "Completely losing your composure, freaking out or emotionally exploding," is how the Langenscheidt jury defines the term, which has already made it into the top three.
The twist: it does not always mean that someone is genuinely overreacting. The word can also be used ironically, especially when an emotional outburst is triggered by something trivial.
Ragebait
This term refers to digital posts on social media: content deliberately designed to provoke a reaction. "With provocative takes, blatant false claims or completely wild opinions, people try to stir up anger," explains the Langenscheidt jury.
For responses are the currency on platforms such as Instagram or TikTok. Reactions bring clicks, comments, shares and reach. The more outrage there is, the more often a post is shown: the algorithm boosts it.
Peak
This originally English word can in fact be translated literally in German: it is about peak values, highlights and summits. "If something is peak, it is the best of the best – the absolute high point, maximum quality or simply 10/10," is how the Langenscheidt jury puts it.
The other most voted words of 2026:
Altogether, 43 percent of all votes cast went to the top three terms, according to an analysis by the publisher. Since 2008 it has been choosing the Youth Word of the Year.
For Langenscheidt's spokesperson there was a surprise. The popular 67 (Six Seven), which comes with a hand gesture, only made it into the top ten and not into the three most popular terms. It is less about a fixed meaning than about belonging. The trend went viral thanks to TikTok, basketball memes and above all the song "Doot Doot (6 7)" by US rapper Skirlla.
"We were actually sure that 67 would end up in the top three," said the publishing house's spokesperson. "Once again, it shows how unpredictable and fast youth language evolves." The fact that many of the words are Anglicisms, on the other hand, came as little surprise to the publisher – that was already the case back in 2023.
Another absolute classic, "Digga", was among the submissions once more, but the term has never yet taken first place.
In addition, the line "Du bist gut genug" ('You are good enough') from a song by KitschKrieg, Shirin David and Blumengarten made it into the top ten. The short sentence went viral on TikTok and other platforms and has also delighted audiences abroad. According to the Langenscheidt jury, there are now countless memes, remixes and parodies of it.
Another term, "Gute Käse", does not have a literal meaning but roughly stands for "really good" and "solid", and ranks among the ten most popular expressions. "Macker" can mean boyfriend, crush, mate or simply a guy, depending on the context. "Schere" comes from gaming and is used in the sense of "Sorry, my bad".
Yet another language made it into the top ten: the Turkish version of the word "super". The term became widely known through a viral video of an ultramarathon runner who, when asked "How are you?" after his race, simply replied "Süper".
"Mehrzweckeier" ruled out by jury
The jury also excluded a term this year that had been submitted many times: "Mehrzweckeier". The expression first appeared at a demonstration against the reintroduction of conscription. The placard originally carried the slogan "Merz leck Eier", which was confiscated by the police. The protester then faced an investigation for slander and defamation.
Afterwards, a campaign on Reddit called on people to submit the altered term "Mehrzweckeier" as a candidate for the 2026 Youth Word of the Year. The jury vetoed it "because the term stems from a campaign and at the same time is based on a personal insult", as the reasoning puts it. It therefore meets two key exclusion criteria, the jury said.
Gammelfleischparty: The very first Youth Word of the Year
In 2008, "Gammelfleischparty" was chosen as the very first Youth Word of the Year. It refers to an over-30s party and is a cynical comment on how young people see older generations.
As the years went by, terms such as "hartzen", "swag" and the acronym "Yolo" ('you only live once') were voted winners.
More votes than ever before
Thanks not least to social media and Susanne Daubner reading out the shortlist on the main German news programme Tagesschau, the vote on the Youth Word of the Year has attracted huge attention.

Flydubai co-pilot drifted towards 'extremism and terrorism' while studying at RMIT
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:29:30 UTC
14:29:30 KST

In brief
- Omani national Hammam al-Hammami become acquainted with individuals from a group called "My Centre", run by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza".
- The co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv last month.
The Omani Flydubai co-pilot who was accused of trying to crash a plane into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport last month was radicalised at an Australian mosque while studying in Melbourne in 2017, according to the United Arab Emirates attorney general.
Omani national Hammam al-Hammami, 29, allegedly attempted to hijack flight FZ1073 with 182 people onboard travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September before passengers and crew intervened.
A statement by UAE attorney general Hamad Saif al-Shamsi shared on UAE government social media said al-Hammami's radicalisation happened when was a student at the Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology (RMIT). During mosque visits, al-Hammami became acquainted with individuals associated with a centre known as "My Centre".
The statement said al-Hammami had revealed the centre was managed by a Lebanese man known as "Abu Hamza" and allegedly received support from an association linked to the Muslim Brotherhood.

The co-pilot "drew inspiration" from the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks in the United States and had also used two previous flights to Tel Aviv to "familiarise himself with the flight route and the airport", , according to the statement.
Al-Hammami, who joined Flydubai in January, had previously worked for several airlines in different countries, the UAE's investigation had found.
The statement did not appear to implicate Flydubai in any wrongdoing, and contained the most detailed account yet from prosecutors about what they believe to have happened. Flydubai was not immediately available for comment.
Bloodied and beaten
The aircraft was in Saudi airspace when the co-pilot attacked captain Smit Machchhar with a crash axe, typically kept in the cockpit for use during emergencies.
Bloodied and beaten, Machchhar managed to open the cockpit door, alerting passengers and crew to the assault.
The incident caused the airliner to plunge 4900 metres in 30 seconds before the attacker was overwhelmed and two other pilots who were on board landed the aircraft safely in Saudi Arabia.
Al-Hammami was transferred to the UAE, Flydubai's home country.
Investigators examined Flydubai's recruiting procedures and found al-Hammami had met all professional and security requirements, including holding a pilot's licence and providing a certificate of good conduct.
"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot," al-Shamsi added.
He said the 29-year-old had worked for airlines in different countries including Oman Air before joining Flydubai in January 2026.
The investigation found there were signs of al-Hammami drifting towards "extremism and terrorism" as early as 2017, while he was studying in Australia.
Royal Air Maroc has said that he underwent three months of training there in 2025 but that his application to work for the airline afterwards was rejected.
Al-Shamsi said al-Hammami had told investigators he had prepared psychologically and physically for the attack by viewing material promoting terrorism and taking boxing lessons.
Saudi Arabia has launched a separate safety investigation into flight FZ1073, sources had told Reuters.
