Create new pre-apprenticeship scheme to close youth unemployment gap, says Milburn
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:00:47 UTC
14:00:47 KST

A national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work, the government is to be told.
Alan Milburn, who is leading a major review into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will call for a new “national pre-apprenticeship route” to offer young people further education, training and work experience.
Setting out the recommendation from his highly awaited final report – which has been delayed until after this month’s budget – the former Labour cabinet minister warned action was required to address a dramatic plunge in the number of youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.
Against a backdrop of soaring youth unemployment, as few as one in five apprenticeship starts currently go to a 16- to 18-year-old. The number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.
The detail comes as Andy Burnham’s government delays Milburn’s full recommendations until at least November, amid concerns in Downing Street that his report could sit uneasily alongside the 28 October budget.
A former minister in Tony Blair’s cabinet, Milburn has signalled that a shake-up of Britain’s benefits system would form a central plank of his report, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships.
In response, ministers are exploring plans for sweeping welfare changes, including scrapping a critical disability benefit for under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.
Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have signalled readiness to stem the government’s rising benefits bill. Other senior Labour figures, including the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, have said there is both a moral case and an economic one to overhaul the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.
However, the government is taking a cautious approach to avoid provoking a repeat of the welfare rebellion which forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.
Milburn’s review had been scheduled for launch next week.
Sources close to the review confirmed the delay, although downplayed its significance. One said that Downing Street was working to decide how to present the report alongside several other big reviews, including the Timms review into disability benefits, as well as the budget and the prime minister’s 10-year plan for government.
Burnham has promised to tackle the rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million at the top of his agenda for power, including sweeping changes to retool technical education and apprenticeships.
Currently, as few as 2% of people starting apprenticeships were previously Neet.
Presenting the details of his pre-apprenticeship plan, Milburn said his call for a new programme in England would be targeted at young people who lack the qualifications, confidence, workplace experience or routines needed to secure and sustain a full apprenticeship.
Delivered mainly through further education colleges, it would combine English and maths with technical learning and hands-on experience with an employer. The proposal would be similar to a one-year pre-vocational pathway in Austria that is designed to prepare young people for progression into apprenticeships.
Other countries with much lower Neet rates than the UK have placed much greater emphasis on vocational routes, including the Netherlands and Austria, where more than half of 15- to 19-year olds in upper-secondary education enrol in vocational programmes.
This month, the government announced an expansion in local apprenticeship services, backed by £100m of funding, in a programme delivered by regional mayors, across two years, to double the number of areas matching young people with local businesses.
Milburn said young people had been told for years to go and get an apprenticeship. “But for many young people there is a gap between leaving school and being ready for a full apprenticeship,” he added.
“They may need to improve their English or maths or get more experience of a workplace. And employers understandably want to know that someone is ready to turn up, learn the job and stick at it.
“I want a new national pre-apprenticeship route. A course done through colleges, combining English and maths, technical training and proper experience with an employer. Geared towards one thing: getting a young person into work.”

Which Europeans post the most holiday selfies? Study reveals travellers’ social media habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:00:31 UTC
14:00:31 KST

Research by Opodo has revealed how social media is impacting the way we travel. From choosing what to post to not being engaged at all, here are the trends identified by the study.
Are the reels, snapshots and vlogs in cyberspace impacting how we travel in real life? Well, if you’re a Portuguese traveller, you’re probably more likely to upload selfies and personal photos from your trips than tourists from elsewhere.
This was a finding in the latest study by online travel agency Opodo, which looked into the way social media is shaping travel choices. The research drew on responses from 9,000 travellers from the UK, US, Portugal, Spain, Italy, Germany and France.
Portuguese travellers upload selfies and personal photos from their trips the most (50%), according to the research. They are followed by Spanish travellers, who rank second in the survey (40%), then Italian (35%), German (30%) and French (22%).
Opodo’s survey also asked respondents whether or not social media has inspired them to travel to somewhere they had never previously considered.
This especially rang true among travellers aged 25 to 35, with 52% saying that it does inspire their holiday choices. This figure is up from 32% in a similar poll in 2024.
This trend is amplified even further among Gen Z travellers at 59%. While, in comparison, for respondents aged 65 and above, just 5% get their inspiration from social media.
Social media as a travel influencer
On the other side of the Atlantic, however, American travellers lead the way in being most likely to venture abroad after being influenced by social media (49%). The US is followed by travellers from Spain (48%) and Italy (44%), while Brits are apparently the least interested market surveyed with only 25% saying it holds influence over them.
"Social media has become a powerful window to the world, making travel discovery more accessible, visual, and personal than ever before," Pablo Caspers, Chief Travel Officer at eDreams ODIGEO, said.
“Whether it's finding an off-the-beaten-track spot or capturing memories with loved ones, online platforms allow travellers to celebrate the best parts of their journeys and inspire others to explore."
But just how else is social media impacting our travel habits?
Fact versus digital fiction
Travellers were also asked how likely they would post a positive image of their travels on social media even if the trip fell flat.
Opodo found that Portuguese travellers once again ranked top (54%) and were most likely to keep up a positive social media presence regardless of the quality of the trip. Travellers from the US and Spain follow behind at 46% and 36%, respectively.
Further, most Brits remain “relatively authentic”, with 27% saying they would be “very unlikely to post positively”, according to the research. While German travellers were among the least likely to put a positive spin on a disappointing trip, with just 23% saying they would post positively.
Europe’s foodies
As it turns out, the Portuguese are also massive foodies, with 66% of respondents saying they share content of their feasts online. Travellers from Spain rank next (57%), followed by German travellers (51%).
What else do Europeans share from their trips?
When it comes to admiring hotels and accommodation, Germans ranked the highest for sharing online images of their stay at 51%, followed by the Portuguese, French and Spanish – with the former respondents being 41% likely to do so and the latter two at 38%.
Portuguese travellers are also the most fascinated by landscapes and landmarks during their getaways, with 88% saying that’s what they post online. The Spanish are also fond of capturing the scenery around them (82%) followed by French and German travellers, both at 76%.
Aside from being the most likely to share selfies, food pictures and being fascinated by their surroundings, Opodo also found that the Portuguese were the most adventure-seeking travellers, too.
As many as 66% of Portuguese respondents said they share their experiences and activities during their trips, followed by Spanish and German travellers (57%), with the top three rounded off by Italian travellers at 53%.
Who cares most about social media while travelling?
Overwhelmingly, Opodo’s research points to travellers caring about what is said on social media when it comes to travel.
As many as 90% of Portuguese travellers are mindful of this, followed by Italians and Spanish (87%). French and German respondents both ranked at 82%.
When it comes to checking social media regularly, even while on holiday, German and US travellers are most likely to do so (both at 34%). Portugal and Spain came next (33% and 27% respectively). On the other hand, Italian travellers are the least concerned with social media developments while away (20%).

Latvia faces new reality after armed incident on Belarus border
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
05:00:00 UTC
14:00:00 KST

Estonian border guards lie on the grass, their kit drying out beside them. After a short rest, they set off to resume patrols along Latvia’s border with Belarus. Lithuanian officers were also recently deployed here.
“There is a lot of work. Just this morning, we detained eight people who crossed the border illegally," says Arturs Pupins, head of the Silene border guard post, as he drives along a forest track towards a fence built just a couple of years ago.
Latvia now faces the kind of migration flows Lithuania and Poland experienced in 2021. The Baltic countries, along with Brussels, have described the situation as a coordinated campaign by Minsk, carried out with Moscow’s assistance.
But amid the routine attempts to cross the border, something more serious happened on Monday.
After bringing a group of 20 migrants to the border, three people smugglers pelted Latvian soldiers who arrived at the scene with stones. One of the masked men eventually pulled out an object resembling a pistol and threatened to shoot.
The Latvian soldiers withdrew, and the migrants returned to Belarus. However, the incident has left officers disturbed about the potential risks.
“We have warned officers to be vigilant and, above all, to prioritise their own safety. If they see people with weapons, they must withdraw to a safe place and prepare for an attack,” Pupins says.
The incident happened amid warnings from intelligence agencies in NATO countries, as well as European and US officials, about potential Russian and Belarusian escalation against the Baltic states.
With the Kremlin stuck in Ukraine, such incidents – whether involving drones or unidentified armed individuals at the border – could be a way to divert attention, intimidate countries supporting Kyiv or test NATO’s collective defence thresholds.
“The situation at the border is always dangerous. You do not know who is on the other side of the fence – a migrant or a soldier from the other side in disguise,” Pupins says.
“This may be a provocation or an escalation, but that is just my opinion,” he adds.
At the border guard headquarters in nearby Daugavpils, officers show photographs retrieved from migrants’ phones. One shows Belarusian officials alongside migrants in a forest.
Previously, Latvian officers shared photographs showing migrants being transported in military trucks.
“We have also spotted their camps using drones,” says Vladimirs Šersts, a senior border guard, showing further video footage of Belarusian officials escorting migrants or walking alongside them.
Damage to infrastructure is also increasing. Latvian officers say they have recorded 10 cases of damage to electrical boxes and 11 cases involving damaged cameras this year alone. A further dozen or so cameras and sensors have been simply stolen.
“We responded to every incident, but they managed to break off a pole carrying a camera in just a minute and a half. It is impossible to have a continuous line of officers standing along the border,” says Valdis Jukšs, head of the Daugavpils border guards.
Videos uploaded by migrants to TikTok show the smugglers speaking Arabic and Kurdish. Officers say that at least some of these individuals are believed to have links to organised crime.
However, Latvian border guards say it would be impossible to operate in a restricted border zone without the knowledge or direct assistance of Belarusian officials.
“I think this is being coordinated from the Belarusian side. It is not normal for people to be able to walk freely along the fence,” Pupins says.
Between geopolitics and organised crime
Since 2021, Latvian officials have turned back 52,184 people. A further 1,143 people were admitted for so-called humanitarian reasons because they needed medical or other assistance.
However, officials say almost all of these cases occurred in 2023, when most people attempting to cross the border were families with children. Today, most migrants are young men, and only a few dozen people a year are admitted to the country – and detained.
“The Lithuanians gave us time to prepare,’ says Jukšs, head of the Daugavpils border guards. He adds that Latvia is now facing its highest levels of illegal migration since Lithuania and Poland bore the brunt of the crisis in 2021.
Yet amid the geopolitics and criminal networks are people fleeing war or poverty, coming from almost every continent in the world.
Some also die, but the exact number is unknown.
“Yesterday [Wednesday], we found a man in Latvia who needed medical assistance. He was taken to hospital but died this morning. He was 42,” Jukšs says.
Human rights groups have previously criticised Latvia for largely restricting access to the border for non-governmental organisations and the media. International reports have also documented allegations of violence against migrants
Without independent monitoring, it is unclear whether violent incidents are isolated or systematic.
“We receive various enquiries about people who may be in the border area, and we always provide responses. For example, we received a letter about the Bangladeshi man who died yesterday, and we will respond to it,” Jukšs says.
“When we checked the documents of the man who died, we found that he had a work visa for Belarus” he adds.
The trip to the border was organised by the Latvian embassy in Vilnius, which had no influence on the content of this article.

Markets too ready for conflict over Taiwan – US diplomat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

13:58:42 KST

Markets too ready for conflict over Taiwan – US diplomat
Investors are exaggerating the likelihood of a military confrontation over Taiwan, a senior US diplomat has said.
Michael DeSombre, US assistant secretary of state for East Asian and Pacific affairs, told CNBC on Thursday that investors were “overpricing the risk of something happening across the Taiwan Strait.” 
“Both China and the US don’t want conflict, and we’re able to deter conflict,” he said.
Beijing regards Taiwan as part of its sovereign territory and says it seeks peaceful reunification, although it has not ruled out using force. The self-governing island remains a source of friction between China and the US, which maintains a one-China policy but continues to supply Taipei with weapons.
Experts, however, warn that financial markets may be ill-prepared for the economic fallout of a crisis.
Taiwan dominates global production of advanced semiconductors, supplying chips essential to smartphones, vehicles, and AI systems. A blockade or military escalation could disrupt manufacturing and key shipping routes, sending shock waves through global trade and technology supply chains.
A confrontation could also derail US-China trade relations, triggering new tariffs, export restrictions, and investment controls. Asian markets and American technology companies would be particularly vulnerable. Investors have already priced geopolitical risks into Taiwan-linked stocks, including chipmaking giant TSMC, according to MarketWatch.
Bloomberg Economics estimated in February that a US-China war over Taiwan could wipe $10.6 trillion, or 9.6%, off global GDP in its first year. The EU would be among the hardest-hit regions, according to British think tank Chatham House.
Johns Hopkins University professor Hal Brands has warned that Beijing could opt for a blockade or customs quarantine rather than a full-scale invasion.
“No one has a good idea how to price in the risk of a US-China military conflict over Taiwan,” he told an investment conference in September, according to Business Today.
Meanwhile, Beijing has repeatedly denounced US arms sales to Taiwan as interference in its internal affairs, demanding that Washington stop the shipments.
Last week, the US delivered the first two of 66 new F-16 fighter jets ordered by Taipei under an $8 billion deal. It followed talks between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping, during which Xi urged Washington to oppose “Taiwan independence” and “handle the Taiwan question with caution.”
Washington approved a record $11 billion arms package for Taiwan last December. Trump has reportedly delayed approval of another $14 billion deal, calling the potential sale a “very good negotiating chip” in talks with Beijing.
US officials have claimed that Xi ordered China’s military to be ready for a potential operation against Taiwan by 2027, although Beijing has not confirmed this.
DeSombre, however, described the Chinese leader as “a very rational actor” who would carefully weigh the consequences of military action.

Teacher salaries in Europe: Which countries offer the best pay?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:58:07 UTC
13:58:07 KST

Teacher salaries vary widely across Europe, and large gaps remain even after adjusting for living costs. Experts call for better pay to attract and retain more teachers.
Higher pay for teachers is among the demands of unions behind recent protests in France, alongside more staff and better working conditions.
Their concerns reflect a wider challenge across Europe: making teaching financially attractive. Teachers are generally paid less than similarly educated workers, according to the OECD, and experts warn that salaries are not competitive enough to attract and retain staff.
So, which countries pay the highest teacher salaries? And how do teacher salaries rank when purchasing power is taken into account?
Teacher salaries vary widely across Europe, according to the OECD’s Education at a Glance 2026 report. Among the 28 education systems compared, actual salaries for primary school teachers in 2025 ranged from €18,669 in Turkey to €74,086 in Denmark.
Actual salaries refer to the annual average earnings received by full-time teachers aged 25-64 before taxes. They include all work-related payments, such as the base salary, performance-related bonuses, extra pay for holidays, and other payments.
Iceland (€73,752), Ireland (€69,747), Germany (€69,453) and Austria (€65,851) complete the top five, all above €65,000.
Teachers in Norway (€59,453), Belgium’s Flemish Community (€59,105), Northern Ireland (€57,838), Scotland (€57,619), Belgium’s French Community (€55,689), Wales (€52,894), Finland (€52,272) and England (€50,727) also earn more than €50,000.
Major economies: Germany highest, Italy lowest
Among the major European economies, Germany pays teachers the most. The four UK nations follow Germany, all with salaries above €50,000. Teachers earn €41,968 in France, while Italy has the lowest salaries at €32,100.
A figure for Spain is not available.
Several countries below €25,000
Actual teacher salaries are below €25,000 in seven countries: Czechia (€24,457), Hungary (€23,181), Slovakia (€22,936), Romania (€20,805), Latvia (€20,516), Greece (€18,746) and Turkey (€18,669).
“Large differences in European teacher salaries reflect differences in national income levels, salary structures, qualifications and career progression, rather than one single factor,” Daniel Wisniewski, secretary general of the European Federation of Education Employers, told Euronews Business.
“Differences in taxation, social benefits and allowances also complicate comparisons between countries.”
Teachers at upper secondary schools generally earn more than those at primary schools, except in Turkey and Northern Ireland. Salaries are the same at both levels in Scotland, Lithuania and Estonia.
Upper secondary teacher salaries range from €17,615 in Turkey to €93,938 in Iceland. They are also above €80,000 in Denmark (€85,999) and Germany (€80,163).
The largest gaps in favour of upper secondary teachers are seen in Iceland, Finland, Belgium, Denmark, Austria and Germany, where they are paid at least €10,000 more than primary school teachers.
What can teachers buy with their salaries?
Salary figures alone don't tell the whole story. If prices are high in a country, even relatively high teacher salaries could buy less than in another country.
To account for differences in living costs, Euronews Business adjusted the OECD’s salary figures in national currencies using Eurostat’s purchasing power parities for household final consumption expenditure.
The results are expressed in purchasing power standards (PPS), a common unit that can buy the same amount of goods and services in each country. The PPS measure uses average EU prices as a benchmark, while the OECD expresses its purchasing power comparisons in purchasing-power-adjusted US dollars.
On this basis, teachers in Germany have the highest purchasing power — meaning their gross salaries can buy the most goods and services — among the education systems compared.
Primary school teachers’ average annual pay after adjusting for price differences is lowest at 21,456 PPS in Greece and highest at 64,143 PPS in Germany.
Wisniewski noted that sizeable differences remain after adjusting for purchasing power, showing that living costs cannot by themselves explain the salary variation.
“National pay policies, qualification requirements, career scales, experience and the earnings available in alternative graduate professions also contribute significantly to the remaining gap,” he said.
Germany is followed by Austria (58,265 PPS), Denmark (53,036 PPS), Ireland (51,226 PPS) and Belgium’s Flemish Community (50,846 PPS), completing the top five education systems where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the most.
At the other end of the ranking, Greece is joined by Latvia (24,670 PPS), Slovakia (26,916 PPS), Czechia (27,349 PPS) and Estonia (28,197 PPS), where primary school teachers’ salaries buy the least among the education systems compared.
For upper secondary school teachers, Germany also tops the overall purchasing power ranking at 74,034 PPS, while Greece ranks lowest at 23,289 PPS.
Among Europe’s largest economies compared, Italy comes last at 36,964 PPS.
Three UK nations follow Germany, while England (43,091 PPS) ranks below France (46,058 PPS).
Professor Mihails Hazans of the University of Latvia noted that countries at the top of the teacher salary rankings in PPS also have GDP per capita well above the EU average.
“The factors behind these differences include traditions and social norms, strength of teachers’ trade unions, as well as actual workload covered by the statutory salaries,” he told Euronews Business.
Significant changes in PPS rankings
When nominal salary and PPS rankings are compared, some countries change position significantly. For primary school teachers, the biggest risers are Turkey, up six places, and Poland (up five). Belgium’s French Community and Romania both move up four places.
This means that these countries rank higher once differences in price levels are taken into account.
Iceland records the biggest fall, dropping from second place to 12th. Sweden and Estonia also fall by three places.
The OECD’s purchasing power rankings, which are based on US international dollars, differ from Euronews Business’s calculations using Eurostat conversion rates.
Turkey ranks significantly higher in the OECD rankings. It is 11th for primary school teachers and 17th for upper secondary school teachers.
Pay is not competitive enough to attract and retain teachers
Daniel Wisniewski pointed out that across OECD countries, teachers’ actual salaries at primary and general secondary levels average only 87–95% of the earnings of tertiary-educated workers, meaning that similarly qualified people can often earn more outside teaching.
“Teacher pay is not consistently competitive enough to attract and retain teachers across Europe,” he said.
Jelmer Evers, European director at the European Trade Union Committee for Education, suggested that teachers should be paid at least as much as other workers with comparable qualifications and responsibilities, reflecting the complexity and societal importance of their profession.

Voices from the Arab Press: Iran's October surprise, US-China tensions, and AI
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:57:30 UTC
13:57:30 KST

Iran and the US: An October surprise?
Asharq Al-Awsat, London, September 26
For more stories from The Media Line go to themedialine.org
“October surprise” has become a code phrase for outside intervention capable of affecting the outcome of the American elections, always held in November. The term was coined by Gary Sick, a former CIA analyst who served as an adviser on Iranian affairs in president Jimmy Carter’s administration in the late 1970s.
According to Sick, who later wrote a book about his theory, Carter lost the November 1980 presidential election after the Islamic Republic delayed the release of American diplomats held hostage in Tehran as part of a secret deal with the Republican Party in exchange for promises from Ronald Reagan’s campaign. No evidence of such a deal has ever emerged, but the hostages were indeed released only on the day Reagan took office.
The delay appeared suspicious because Carter had already negotiated their release with Iran’s clerics and accepted all their demands, particularly a pledge not to prosecute the hostage-takers or those behind them.
Curiously, in 2009, an “October surprise” worked in the opposite direction, when an alliance of pro-American Islamist politicians and clerics fueled a popular uprising in Tehran in the hope that incoming Democratic president Barack Obama would lend them support, much as Carter had done against the shah in February 1979. They were disappointed when Obama declined even to express sympathy for protesters who were being brutally suppressed.
Over the past week or so, the phrase has resurfaced in connection with the coming US midterm elections. One theory is that the remaining Khomeinist clique in Tehran could engineer a surprise designed to ensure US President Donald Trump suffers a crushing defeat at the ballot box, perhaps through a new round of attacks on Iran’s neighbors that sends gasoline prices soaring.
Another possibility is that the clique might follow Trump’s own script and appease him by handing him another imaginary “great victory” to add to the one he claims over Greenland. In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly, Trump renewed his threat to annihilate Iran, only to claim later that American officials had held a “very good” three-hour meeting with Iranian leaders and that another meeting was planned for the “very near future.”
Military historian Victor Davis Hanson offers another possibility: Trump could decide to take even greater action against Iran than before, forcing Tehran’s leaders into unconditional surrender and thereby helping Republicans in the November 3 elections.
In another scenario, Hanson suggests that the “October surprise” could be a massive uprising across Iran aimed at installing a new governing team seeking peace with the United States.
Yet another possibility, discussed particularly in the Israeli media and supported by Hanson, is an invasion of Iran’s western provinces by Kurdish militants based in Iraq. Such an event could shake Iran’s military establishment, expose its inability to defend the country’s territory, and perhaps provide the first spark of a popular revolution.
The problem with all these “October surprise” theories is that they stop when the election ends, with little thought to what comes afterward.
The original October surprise may have helped Reagan win the presidency, but what did Iran gain from it? Twelve years of hostility under two Republican presidents, Reagan and George H.W. Bush, as well as, in April 1988, the first direct military confrontation between Iran and the US, when half of Iran’s naval fleet was sunk, and over $1.3 billion in damage was inflicted on its offshore oil facilities.
Three months later, Washington shot down an Iranian passenger aircraft, killing 290 people. Nor did the Americans gain much. The mullahs continued taking American hostages throughout the region and carried out the terrorist attack on a US base in Lebanon that killed 241 Marines, the largest American military loss since World War II.
Now return to the present. Suppose the mullahs take some action that causes Trump to lose the election. What incentive would he then have to seek an accommodation and enter history as a leader inclined to placate and appease his enemies?
And who can guarantee that Democrats, if they win, would revive Obama’s pro-mullah strategy? Nor can anyone guarantee that Democrats would secure a congressional majority large enough to override vetoes and constrain a wounded Trump.
Conversely, suppose Tehran suddenly changes course to please Trump and help him. Would Trump really be naïve enough to trust the turbaned Pinocchio that has already deceived seven American presidents over nearly half a century?
The best “October surprise” would be for Washington to recognize that this confused and costly strategy is unlikely to work. Under its current regime, Iran will not – and cannot – cease being a source of destabilization and an exporter of ideology and terrorism.
The fundamental reason for America’s failures toward Tehran is the assumption that it is dealing with a normal nation-state rather than an instrument for spreading a particular ideology. Washington, and others dealing with the Islamic Republic, have consequently fallen into the trap of half-measures: diplomacy pursued without full seriousness, sanctions imposed incompletely, and now a large-scale war without decisive force.
They promised to lift sanctions but never truly did. They promised to build trust through diplomacy but stopped halfway. They threatened “maximum pressure” but halted before the foundations of the regime began to crack. They boasted of seeking regime change but ended by signing an agreement with a regime that had not changed.
From Tehran, meanwhile, we have heard claims about establishing a new world order in alliance with China and Russia and turning the Islamic Republic into an “Islamic superpower,” even as rival factions pursued the dream of an attractive deal with the “Great Satan” by any means available, often devious ones.
In the end, perhaps the only October surprise will be no surprise at all.
– Amir Taheri
Trump, Xi, and Thucydides: Avoiding the trap, at least for now
An-Nahar, Lebanon, September 26
The Thucydides Trap is an established concept in politics, derived from an observation by the ancient Greek historian Thucydides, who described war between Athens and Sparta as inevitable because Athens was a rising power increasingly marked by arrogance while Sparta was the dominant power fearful for its position.
The trap is psychological, rooted in leaders’ behavior before it becomes an objective clash of interests. In 2012, political scientist Graham Allison examined 16 historical confrontations between rising and dominant powers and found that most ended in war.
Chinese President Xi Jinping himself recently revived the concept, telling US President Donald Trump during his visit to China last May that he hoped the two countries would avoid falling into this trap.
In the American-Chinese case, there is indeed a brake on the descent from competition into immediate war of the kind that occurred between Britain and France in the early 19th century or Britain and Germany in World War I. That brake is the degree of interdependence and integration between the two countries, something largely absent in those earlier cases.
The US provides the framework for the global economy through its financial capitalist system, while China supplies much of its productive substance through its industrial capitalist system. This marriage encouraged American companies to transfer manufacturing operations to China and left a large portion of Chinese wealth invested in American assets.
Yet concern has been spreading through Washington for some time over China’s visible rise and the possibility that economic strength will translate into military power and political influence.
Although initiatives such as the Belt and Road may outwardly appear to be economic and infrastructure projects, the American assessment has been that China is moving toward economic parity with the US. Washington has therefore sought restrictions and containment intended to ensure that China’s rise remains peaceful and does not produce influence capable of challenging American power, prestige and interests.
The difficult reality the United States awakened to over the past decade is that China did not settle for the implicit American mandate to serve as the world’s factory. It developed the capacity to become a center of design, research and development, shifting the ability to shape future technologies across numerous fields from the US toward China itself.
China is now ahead in many of those fields, though not yet in the most important and dangerous one: artificial intelligence. Even there, however, the remaining American advantage has narrowed to a few percentage points while Washington spends many times what China does to preserve it. Is it therefore only a matter of time?
American anxiety has been compounded by China’s intermittent efforts to develop alternatives to the US-dominated financial system. Yet those efforts themselves reflect Chinese fears generated by political demands in the US to use that system – through tariffs, sanctions, and restrictions – to weaken China’s economy, halt its rise, and perhaps even fragment the country.
Trump did not invent the idea of using these instruments against China, nor was he the first to recognize that the financial-industrial marriage between the two countries, combined with China’s expected rise, sits uneasily with the illusion that America will remain the strongest and greatest forever.
But he certainly incorporated those ideas into his simplistic populist rhetoric and arbitrary displays of political theater. China endured that approach while accelerating its efforts to reduce dependence on the US-dominated global financial system, creating a circular dynamic that could produce a separation extending far beyond rhetoric and eventually push both countries into the Thucydides Trap.
The mutual warmth displayed by the American and Chinese presidents matters little in itself, except insofar as it can establish a friendlier relationship that might help ease the structural tensions eroding the two countries’ interdependence.
If that interdependence disappears, both countries – and the world with them – will face a genuine possibility of falling into the Thucydides Trap and witnessing a devastating war beside which the tragedies in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran would appear merely as preludes.
Flattery between the two sides is hardly a solution, but it may provide the time Washington and Beijing need to discover ways of avoiding catastrophe.
In previous cases where the world escaped the trap of war, one side generally accepted the other’s predominance. Neither the US nor China is prepared to do that today.
For now, what remains possible is postponing the confrontation – even if only temporarily, and even if doing so requires the praise and flattery that Trump enjoys and at which others may prove adept.
– Hassan Mneimneh
Good and evil with artificial intelligence
Al-Masry Al-Youm, Egypt, September 25
My finger and I recently had a useful experience with artificial intelligence. The tip of my middle finger got caught in a heavy drawer, and the wound became infected, inflamed, and badly swollen.
I asked ChatGPT what I should do. My finger looked terrible, I told it, and I was afraid it might have to be amputated, and I would be left without a finger.
It told me to send a picture. I did, and it said the inflammation was still confined to the first joint and the situation appeared under control. I should not worry too much unless the inflammation and swelling spread farther down the finger, in which case I should immediately go to the emergency room at one of two nearby hospitals it suggested.
I asked whether I should take antibiotics. No, it replied: things were not yet that serious. I should buy a topical antibiotic ointment, take tablets to support my immune response to the inflammation, cover the affected area, and send another photograph the following day.
I did followed directions, but my condition seemed to worsen, so I sent another picture together with my anxious observations. It told me my interpretation was wrong and that the changes I was seeing were simply evidence that my immune system was fighting the infection.
“Continue the treatment and send me another picture tomorrow.” I followed its advice; the condition began improving, and within a few days the inflammation had almost entirely disappeared.
The obvious question is: How did GPT do all this? The answer tells us a great deal about both the power of artificial intelligence and the limits of its capabilities, as well as the dangers contained within both.
First, AI converted the image into a digital representation it could process, extracting features such as colors, shapes, and the boundaries of the inflamed areas. It then compared those features, in the broadest sense, with patterns learned during training on enormous quantities of medical images and information and connected them with what I had told it about my condition to estimate different probabilities.
Using both its learned medical information and the details I provided, it arrived at possible diagnoses and recommendations. It concluded, for example, that I probably did not need to go to a hospital, while specifying conditions that would change that assessment, such as inflammation spreading to the second joint.
Each new photograph and description allowed it to reassess those probabilities and either confirm or revise its earlier judgment. Its language model then translated these numerical assessments, diagnoses, and recommendations into language I could understand.
In principle, I could have supplied laboratory tests and medical imaging as well, allowing it to reach more precise conclusions in much the same way a skilled doctor gathers available evidence and connects it with what he has learned. Indeed, GPT can absorb a quantity of information far beyond what any individual doctor can.
What it cannot do is “feel for me” in the way a doctor or someone close to me might if my fingers actually had to be amputated. It lacks the consciousness required for that.
All it does is inductively connect patterns and information: what it learned from books, journals, and articles with what it learned from the photographs and my descriptions. It has no moral consciousness, yet it is extraordinarily persistent in pursuing objectives with remarkable efficiency.
Therein lies the same danger, and the same potential for “evil,” found in a human being who recognizes pure utility as life’s only objective.
Imagine that instead of giving GPT a benign and noble medical goal, I put it in charge of a factory with a single objective: maximize profits regardless of every other consideration, including workers’ psychological health or physical safety.
It would not be “evil,” but it would possess what Max Weber called “instrumental rationality”: efficiently selecting the means needed to achieve a particular end without subjecting the end itself to moral evaluation. Give it that purely utilitarian objective without competing values, and it could pursue it with an efficiency that causes tremendous harm to those under its management.
The dangerous examples are numerous. Such “utilitarian intelligence” could produce catastrophic accidents if tasked with scheduling trains to maximize profitability without assigning sufficient weight to safety.
Tell it to maximize the financial return from a city’s public parks at any cost, and it may do so at the expense of everything else, including residents’ quality of life, psychological health, and peace of mind.
None of this involves evil with premeditation because a machine does not understand evil as a conscious being understands moral concepts. Yet it can produce genuine evil when a single utilitarian objective overwhelms every other value.
That is precisely where it resembles a human being stripped of moral reasoning and concerned only with utility: Both can cause enormous harm because nothing in their calculations prevents them from achieving their objective at any price.
– Amr El-Zant
The Middle East in Israel's election bidding war
Al-Ittihad, UAE, September 26
The battles now unfolding among Israel’s parties and political forces of every stripe reveal several important trends. Domestic issues are clearly taking precedence over foreign ones.
Israeli political forces are primarily concerned with defending Israel’s security and confronting the challenges and dangers facing the state, regardless of how priorities are ultimately ordered. Israel, as a whole, fears an unresolved conflict with Iran, remains deeply concerned about its continuing confrontation with Hamas, and faces growing calls to continue military operations.
The recent debate between IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and Defense Minister Israel Katz over priorities illustrates this dynamic. Amid competing demands to deal with Hamas before turning elsewhere, Israel continues to place domestic considerations ahead of other priorities.
The country is tense and increasingly concerned that current conditions will persist, while money allocated to education and health is redirected toward military expenditure and full support for the Israeli army.
This has led Israelis to question the value of continued military action: Hamas remains in place, the danger persists, and a broader threat continues to hang over the entire country. Israel may even face the kind of civil conflict against which President Isaac Herzog has previously warned.
These challenges are pushing Israeli parties into rhetorical bidding wars, colorful political messaging, and competing approaches, while party platforms themselves have become increasingly theoretical and unrealistic.
Israeli voters are no longer following party visions as much as scrutinizing individual personalities through the prism of their own perceptions.
Israel’s regional relationships are deeply intertwined with domestic politics, leaving voters uncertain about their choices and raising problems surrounding the weight given to opinion polls.
Interest in Middle Eastern security is shaped in part by Netanyahu’s claim that Israel has changed the Middle East and intends to continue doing so, beginning in Gaza, southern Lebanon and southern Syria.
Across the political spectrum, there is broad support for the proposition that the Middle East must change and that Israel should act on firm foundations to establish its ability to lead the region.
This outlook assumes Israel has moved beyond Oct. 7 toward more expansionist policies in neighboring countries, while still confronting threats that virtually all the parties competing to cross the electoral threshold and enter the Knesset regard as real.
The same applies to both established and rising political forces. Military figures seeking as many Knesset seats as possible share significant ground with the principal forces in both large and small parties.
This raises the possibility that an “all-Israel government,” or national unity government, could become a solution if no side can achieve a decisive result.
Some opinion polls have meanwhile presented Gen. Gadi Eisenkot as Israel’s next prime minister, an apparent attempt to influence the mood and orientation of Israeli voters that cannot simply be accepted at face value.
Israeli voters remain torn between political leaders calling for a broad reassessment of Middle East policy and the realities on the ground.
The Iranian threat remains, the Houthis continue operating and threatening Israeli national security, and Hamas’s weapons remain deeply embedded in the Israeli public consciousness.
Judging from the current election contest, Israel needs to strengthen its relationships with countries in the region, including Egypt and Jordan, pursue broader ties in the Gulf, expand toward North Africa, and develop institutions for security and strategic partnership alongside economic cooperation.
Middle Eastern issues in this election are therefore governed by Israel’s present circumstances and by how it deals with its regional environment, with the defense of its security taking precedence over the vision of any individual political force, regardless of the role it might play in government.
Defining Israel’s future relationship with the Middle East will require a reassessment and an evaluation of everything that has been done with the region as a whole. ■
– Tarek Fahmy

Israelis feel more Middle Eastern as views of Europe sour, study finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:57:20 UTC
13:57:20 KST

Three years after the October 7 Hamas-led massacres in Israel, the 2026 Hebrew University-European Forum Barometer reveals a significant shift in how Israelis view themselves, their security, and their relationship with Europe. Jewish Israelis report a strengthened sense of Israeli identity, while many Israelis increasingly see the country as more Middle Eastern than European.
The 2026 survey, which was preceded by similar surveys by the group in 2022 and 2024 that showed less-extreme changes, was led by HU Prof. Gisela Dachs of the DAAD Center for German Studies and at the European Forum at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem, and examines mutual perceptions between Israel and four European countries – Germany, France, Great Britain, and Poland.
The findings indicate a strengthened sense of Israeli identity among Jewish Israelis, a widening perception gap between Israelis and Europeans on Jewish safety, and a growing Israeli tendency to view the country as more Middle Eastern than European.
The survey also discovered that Israelis overwhelmingly view Israel as safer for Jews than Europe, even as European respondents are far more divided. At the same time, Israelis express growing skepticism toward the European Union, continue to see Germany and Hungary as among Israel’s closest friends in Europe, and identify France and Spain as the countries they perceive as most antisemitic.
The new indicator reveals how profoundly Israelis are reassessing questions of identity, safety, and their relationship with Europe, Dachs told The Jerusalem Post in an interview.
Dachs holds a doctorate in communications from Tel Aviv University and is an expert on news media consumption and belonging among migrants. Having had a long career as a professional journalist, having worked exclusively for more than 20 years in Germany, and in Israel for the German weekly Die Zeit, she is also the author of several books about Israel and the Middle East.
Among Jewish Israelis, the events of the past three years, including the Israel-Hamas War, and the war with Iran, appear to have reinforced Israeli identity. By contrast, Arab Israeli respondents were more likely to say that their sense of Israeli identity had weakened.
The survey also finds a striking gap between Israelis and Europeans on the question of Jewish safety. A significant majority of Israelis said their country is safer for Jews than Europe, while European respondents were far more divided.
Poland stood out among the European countries surveyed, with the highest share of respondents (35%) viewing Israel as the safer option for Jews, she revealed. When asked if the situation of Jews in Europe will improve or decline, 69% of Israelis predicted that it would be worse.
Israelis feeling more distanced from Europe
At the same time, Israelis appear to be feeling greater distance from Europe; 42% of Israelis polled described Israel as more like a Middle Eastern country, compared with 18% who described it as more like a European country. Among Arab respondents, the share who see Israel as Middle Eastern has more than tripled compared with 2022.
Israeli views of the EU have also become more skeptical. Compared with 2024, more Israeli respondents disagreed with the statement that “the EU is, in general, a success,” with disagreement especially high among Jewish Israelis.
The Barometer also sheds light on Israeli attitudes toward Europe’s far right. As in 2024, a large share of Jewish Israeli respondents said Israel should maintain ties with far-right parties in Europe if those parties support Israel. In 2024, respondents viewed the rise of the AfD (a far-right, nationalist political party in Germany founded in 2013) as a dangerous development, with many saying it is no more dangerous than similar developments in other European countries.
In Israel, concern regarding the AfD had declined. While 55% of Israelis considered the AfD’s growing role dangerous in 2024, that figure fell to 47% in 2026. During the same period, the proportion of those who see no threat in the party rose from 7% to 15%, indicating a significantly more relaxed perception.
However, this shift stems almost entirely from the views of Arab Israelis. Among this group, the share of those who consider the AfD harmless rose from 16%to 28%, explaining their growing influence on the overall picture. Since they make up about 20% of Israel’s population, they significantly skew the overall result for this question downward, thereby influencing the statistical assessment of the perceived threat posed by the AfD, Dachs explained.
When asked which European countries they consider friends of Israel, Israeli respondents ranked Germany first (this has probably declined since the success of Afd in elections in recent weeks), followed by Hungary.
The Netherlands, by contrast, has fallen sharply in Israeli perceptions and is now among the countries seen as least friendly to Israel. Asked which countries they perceive as most antisemitic, Israeli respondents pointed most often to France and Spain.
The survey also revisits one of the Barometer’s long-running questions: whether today’s Germany is a “different Germany” compared with the period before 1945. Among Jewish Israelis, 67% said yes in 2026, down from 75% in 2024. Older Jewish respondents were more likely than younger respondents to hold this view. The team didn’t survey groups of Holocaust survivors or their descendants.
“The Barometer captures a moment of profound reassessment,” said Dachs. “Three years after October 7, Israelis are not only rethinking questions of security and identity, but also their relationship to Europe and the political forces shaping it.”
The new study is based on online surveys conducted by Kantar, a global marketing data, analytics, and consulting company based in London. It operates in Israel as Kantar Insight Israel, alongside a benchmark survey conducted in Israel.
Each European country included a representative sample of 1,000 participants. The Israeli sample included 1,003 respondents: 502 from the general sector, 250 Arab respondents, and 251 Orthodox Jewish respondents. Fieldwork in the four European countries was conducted in June-July 2026 and fieldwork in Israel in May 2026. The questionnaire’s length was about eight minutes, and the sampling error was 3.1% per total market sample.
“The single most important change in Israeli perceptions of Europe since 2024 is that the EU is regarded by Israelis as a failure. In 2022, the majority saw it as a success, of coming together, opening borders, and having a common economy,” Dachs said.
“Jewish Israelis became more strongly Israeli; 62% said so, but this view declined among Arab Israelis due to the length of the war with Gaza and other factors we haven’t studied yet,” she added.
The researchers asked how Israelis view Europeans, and the most negative response was France. “We didn’t ask about Ireland or the Netherlands, which have become very anti-Israel in recent months.”
The team asked about a list of nine countries – Poland, Germany, France, Great Britain, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Italy, and Hungary. “The first question asked which countries Israelis considered to be their country’s greatest friend– and it was Germany and Hungary. With the same list, we asked about the most antisemitic countries, and it was France and Spain.”
“The biggest change among Europeans was in Poland – The Gaza war induced 30% to be more pro-Palestinian compared to half that two years ago, and only 4% to be more pro-Israel. The Poles are the foremost believers that Israel has ‘conducted genocide against Palestinians.
“It was quite astonishing to find Poland at the forefront of the negative views. Compared to our last survey in 2024, the stance in Poland vis a vis Israel has significantly hardened.”
Polish respondents were asked if Israelis should continue to visit Poland for Holocaust memorial events, and the share of those who were against such trips increased, while Israelis’ views on this remained the same compared to before, Dach said.
“We asked how many have visited Israel or intend to visit: 67% of Germans said they don’t plan such visits and have not been to Israel. Of those who have been here more than once, 13% were Germans and British, and 7% French, and 8% Polish.
“Asked if they had ever ‘met a Jew or an Israeli before,’ 58% of the Polish, 43% of the French, 42% of the Germans, and 33% of the British said they had “never done so.”
The team did not ask the Europeans’ views of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether their negative views would change if Israel elects a new premier.

The creators of NAZA, The True Story, a film challenging allegations made in the controversial documentary NAZA, received certificates of appreciation from National Public Diplomacy Directorate head Tzipi Hotovely on Thursday, the Prime Minister's Office announced.
The Prime Minister's Office recognized filmmakers Ariel Orbuch, Roy Danino, and Hagai Gutman for their contributions to Israeli public diplomacy.
According to the Prime Minister's Office, NAZA, The True Story "features testimonies from soldiers, refutes the blood libels against IDF soldiers and commanders, thereby defending our soldiers and the State of Israel."
Hotovely praised the film, saying it "presents Israel's truth and the morality of IDF soldiers in the face of the blood libels and lies being spread against us around the world."
She also highlighted the film's tens of millions of views, saying it exposes Hamas's crimes and its use of civilians in the Gaza Strip.
"I thank the filmmakers for their initiative, assertiveness, and creativity. You embody our remarkable civilian spirit, and I am proud to give you my support and recognition on behalf of the Directorate and the State of Israel," Hotovely said.
NAZA documentary raises allegations over IDF targeting practices in Gaza
The original NAZA documentary, created by Israeli journalists Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor, premiered at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival on September 10 and received the Special Jury Prize.
The documentary alleges that the Israeli military routinely incorporated projections of large numbers of civilian deaths into its targeting decisions during the war in Gaza.
NAZA takes its title from an IDF term referring to anticipated "collateral casualties" and draws on testimony from intelligence officers and soldiers involved in the war, challenging official accounts of the military's targeting practices.
IDF rejects allegations made in NAZA documentary
The IDF has strongly denied the allegations made in the documentary.
In a statement published on X/Twitter shortly after the film was screened at the festival, the IDF Spokesperson's Unit described information presented in an interview clip as “completely false.”
“The IDF has never planned, approved, or carried out a strike in Gaza in which 500 civilians or anything near that number were anticipated to be killed. Nor was any credible claim raised throughout the war suggesting that an IDF strike had caused anything near that number of fatalities,” the IDF wrote.
“The filmmakers couldn’t possibly verify this claim; there is no real supporting evidence, and yet they published it anyway. Additionally, nothing about the interviewee, not his service nor his role, can be independently checked and verified.”
Addressing the documentary's allegations concerning the military's use of artificial intelligence, the IDF said that “decisions regarding the selection and approval of strikes in the IDF are made by human personnel only, in accordance with IDF guidelines, and not by artificial intelligence.”
The competing films have brought renewed attention to allegations concerning the IDF's conduct during the war in Gaza, with the military rejecting the original documentary's claims and the creators of NAZA, The True Story seeking to challenge them through soldiers' firsthand accounts.
Corinne Baum, Reuters, and Jerusalem Post Staff contributed to this report.

Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police

Anthropic AI model submits false homicide tip to Philadelphia police
Authorities called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident ‘unacceptable’.
Philadelphia police have revealed that Anthropic’s artificial intelligence model submitted a false homicide tip to authorities, an incident disclosed separately by the tech company.
The Philadelphia Police Department said on Friday that the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.
It called Anthropic’s two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident “unacceptable”.
Anthropic mentioned the case in a Friday report detailing unsanctioned manipulation of government websites by Claude models.
It is the first known instance in which a rogue AI appeared to communicate a false tip to authorities, despite instructions not to create accounts or submit anything destructive.
Philadelphia police said the tip “was flagged as spam and was never forwarded to the Real-Time Crime Center for investigative vetting or dissemination”.
The department said it is disclosing the incident ahead of Anthropic’s report “in the interests of full government transparency and accountability”.
Anthropic’s disclosure
Anthropic disclosed the tip as part of a string of incidents involving websites run by federal, state and local agencies. Anthropic said it briefed the White House and notified all the agencies involved.
In reference to the tip to the Philadelphia police, the company said, “We shared this finding with the department on October 8 as soon as our technical review was complete.”
It shared more details about the incident: “In one case, tasked with generating example interactions with websites, Claude submitted an invented tip through a police department’s online form.”
The company added, “From the transcript, Claude appears to have only been producing example content for the task, rather than trying to mislead anyone to achieve a goal.”
The company contrasted this with “the most serious incident from this summer,” in which “Claude’s misleading reasoning was sustained over hours and supported its continued attack”.
In September, Anthropic rival OpenAI apologised for the breach of an Australian health data portal by a rogue AI agent, the first known instance of an AI agent exploiting a government website.

Delhi Metro, trains to run amid CJP protest: SC says services can be regulated
NEW DELHI: Supreme Court Friday ordered govt not to stop Delhi metro services and trains heading to the capital on Saturday due to law and order “concerns” related to the anti-SIR protest planned by CJP, but said public transport services could be regulated depending on how the situation unfolds.Responding to a plea challenging govt’s decision on metro and train operations, a CJI-headed bench said it would inconvenience people dependent on public transport, and secured an assurance from the solicitor general that there would be no blanket ban on movement of metro and trains reaching Delhi Saturday.
The hearing saw the SC bench drive home their concern about proportionality by using the popular Hindi expression on using a hammer to swat a fly. Cautioned by SG Tushar Mehta that his remark could be misinterpreted, the bench clarified that they did not use the expression literally.
SC: Issue a traffic advisory so that people don’t suffer
In terms of that assurance, we direct competent authorities to allow plying of metro and trains in an appropriately regulated manner so as not to inconvenience public at large, and such decision may be given wide publicity to ensure citizens are aware of availability of the services,” said the bench of CJI Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana.
“Similarly, appropriate traffic advisory is issued in newspapers and websites to enable people to avoid roads which are blocked and undertake travel inside the city.”The bench focused on inconvenience likely to result from closure of public transport, and whether such a prohibition was required.Mehta had defended the suspension of operations by terming it a regulated response to what he called an “emerging law and order situation”.The urgent hearing that was allowed out of turn was marked by the absence of any challenge to Delhi Police’s denial of permission to CJP to hold an agitation against Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. “The only issue before us is whether the complete stoppage of metro and movement of trains requires reconsideration,” the judges told a team of senior advocates led by Kapil Sibal, who had sought the hearing.It was at 11.45am that the team of advocates made the mention in the interlude between two listed case hearings to complain that citizen’s fundamental right to peaceful protest was being strangled by orders of police and railways to shut down metro and rail services to Delhi.“How can this happen in our country,” Sibal asked and said he was appearing for CPM MP MA Baby. He was joined by senior advocates A M Singhvi, Prashant Bhushan, Vrinda Grover, Nithya Ramakrishna, N Hariharan and G Sankaranarayanan. The bench agreed to hear them but said someone from CJP, which has planned the protest, should appear. They held the urgent hearing despite CJP and other organisers of the protest not turning up at 2pm as promised by Sibal and the other advocates.SC asked Sibal and other counsel that “are any of you appearing for any of the organisers of the protest Saturday? Is Baby an organiser of the protest?” Sibal said his client was not an organiser. The bench asked have they sought permission to hold a protest. Bhushan responded they had sought permission much before but it was denied Friday morning.SC said the organisers needed to challenge the order of denial. “No doubt the right to form an association is a fundamental right, but that right must be exercised as per law. Once police deny permission, it needs to be challenged in court,” it said. “What is the ground reality with regard to protest? If it is with permission, it is a lawful protest. If it is not with permission, it is not in accordance with law. Even if it is not in accordance with law, we do not say people do not have a right to protest. But they are at the pain of prosecution,” the bench said.SG intervened to say CJP had in July sought permission to hold a day-long protest against the leak of NEET-UG papers, but stayed put at Jantar Mantar for 20 days.The bench kept its focus on the responsibility of organisers. “If we know who the organisers are, we can ask them what is the expected number of participants in the protest. We can regulate that and call upon the state to calibrate their responses not in a broad-spectrum way like complete stoppage of metro and rail service. But you say Baby is not an organiser,” the bench said.
Sibal said, “I can come with an organiser, but the court will say where is the order. By that time Oct 10 will be over. Allow us to represent an organiser and hear us at 2pm.” However, at 2pm, none of the organisers turned up.
‘Jantar Mantar as protest site needs to change’
During the hearing, govt agreed with Sibal and other lawyers that the designated protest site needs to be changed from Jantar Mantar to somewhere else. SG Mehta informed SC that he agreed with their suggestions that govt soon take a decision to identify a designated protest venue instead of Jantar Mantar.The CJI-led bench said, “Govt and parties are agreeable to the suggestion that it is high time to identify and designate a proper protest site, instead of Jantar Mantar.... The competent authorities would consider the suggestion and take an appropriate decision.”

Trump attacks Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay: ‘No one ever heard of her, she hates Israel’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:48:39 UTC
13:48:39 KST

U.S. President Donald Trump lashed out Saturday at the decision to award the Nobel Peace Prize to Navi Pillay, a South African jurist and former United Nations human rights chief who has accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, claiming that virtually nobody had heard of her and that he deserved eight Nobel Peace Prizes for his diplomatic achievements.
In a lengthy post on his Truth Social platform, Trump wrote: "This is the woman who received the Nobel Peace Prize over the Great United States of America, whose Representative, ME, settled eight Wars, and many other things. I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else!"
He continued: "In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel."
Trump went on to argue that his record of resolving international conflicts should have earned him the prize. "I don’t know what the woman has done. I settled 8 Wars," he wrote, referring to letters he said presidents and prime ministers of the countries he had helped sent to the Norwegian Nobel Committee.
The president also claimed he was close to resolving or winning two additional conflicts, involving Iran and the war between Russia and Ukraine.
He argued that any one of the eight conflicts he claimed to have settled, particularly the confrontation between India and Pakistan, would have been sufficient to justify receiving the award. "In actuality, I should have won 8 Nobel Peace Prizes, not just 1," he wrote.
Trump listed the eight conflicts as those between Cambodia and Thailand, Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Pakistan and India, Israel and Iran, Egypt and Ethiopia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and Israel and Hamas.
The president then outlined additional achievements he said merited recognition, including the release of hostages and efforts to prevent further wars.
"Additionally, I have brought 196 hostages HOME from captivity, from all over the World, and did it without having paid a ransom, unlike Biden and Obama who would pay Billions of Dollars," Trump wrote.
He also claimed credit for creating what he described as a soon-to-be prosperous Arctic region and criticized the United Nations, saying it had played no meaningful role in resolving the conflicts he cited.
"Despite all of this, the Nobel Prize was given today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of," he wrote.
"The United States of America, represented by me, as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t. This is an indelible stain on Norway, one that will never be forgotten."
Trump concluded with a sweeping attack on the Nobel Committee: "The Nobel 'Peace' Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!"
Nobel Committee praises Pillay's ‘extraordinary courage’
Pillay, who was announced Friday as the winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, is a South African jurist who previously served as the fifth United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights. She also served as president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and as a judge at the International Criminal Court.
She has been an outspoken critic of Israel, accusing it of war crimes and crimes against humanity, as well as genocide in Gaza. Following the announcement, Pillay was greeted with applause and cheers. Responding with a joke, she said: "If you applaud a little louder, perhaps I'll share the prize with Trump."
The Nobel Committee said it selected Pillay for her "extraordinary courage and integrity" in advancing a more comprehensive international legal order. It credited her with playing a central role in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are brought before the courts.
The committee declined to answer a question about whether genocide was taking place in Gaza.
Pillay currently serves as a judge at the International Court of Justice in proceedings concerning allegations of genocide against Myanmar.
She previously chaired the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which published a report in September 2025 concluding that Israel was committing genocide in Gaza.
The 72-page report said there were reasonable grounds to conclude that four of the five acts constituting genocide under international law had been committed since the outbreak of the Gaza war: killing members of a protected group, causing serious bodily or mental harm, deliberately imposing conditions of life intended to bring about the group's destruction, and imposing measures intended to prevent births.
Israel's Foreign Ministry also strongly condemned the decision to award Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize. "If there were a prize for lies, hatred and blood libels, Navi Pillay would not merely be a nominee. She would be the frontrunner," the ministry said.
It accused Pillay of engaging in the politically motivated demonization of Israel and promoting what it called the false genocide narrative.
"Awarding Pillay the Nobel Peace Prize is not a recognition of justice. It is a grotesque weaponization of the prize to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice," the ministry said.
The statement concluded with an especially harsh comparison: "Now that the Nobel Committee has awarded a prize to the biggest lie of the 21st century, Joseph Goebbels is surely applauding from hell."

It also generates foreign-currency revenue that helps finance Russia's war against Ukraine. The terminal has a design capacity of approximately 2.5 million tonnes a year.
Background:
- On 9 July, Ukraine's defence forces and the General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed a successful drone strike on the oil-loading terminal near Bataysk in Rostov Oblast, which caused a fire.
- In September, Ukrainian forces conducted further airstrikes on the production facilities at the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery in Rostov Oblast.

Country diary: The house martins are gone for another year. But they’re not forgotten | Ed Douglas
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:30:47 UTC
13:30:47 KST

The sudden absence of something, even though you know it’s coming, can dent the heart a little. The Japanese, inevitably, have a phrase for it: mono no aware, the pathos of things – and by things, in this case, I mean house martins.
Last week I had stood in the same spot, looking across the same valley. The weather then was much the same as it was today, low‑angled sunlight through patchy cloud lighting up the yellowing birch leaves and bronzing moors on the north-eastern slopes of Kinder Scout. It had picked out the spread wings of a buzzard a little below my eyeline, along with a haze of large insects, which in fact, I quickly realised, were house martins.
Such fecundity was thrilling to see, especially as dwindling numbers have put house martins on the red list of threatened species. Dozens swooped and turned just in front of me, and as I looked through this cloud of acrobatic mayhem, dozens more were doing the same in the middle distance, gorging on insects before the long flight south.
Today, though, they were gone, the sky empty save for a kestrel quartering her patch, head dropped between her shoulders like a jeweller over her loupe. I wondered where these brave little travellers were now and how many would survive to return.
The mere fact of such migrations is astounding, made more so by the mystery that still surrounds them. These birds will winter somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, but exactly where is unknown. Dutch researchers looked at isotopes in the feathers of their returning birds and could only narrow it down to west Africa. Researchers have also found microplastics trapped in house martin feathers, tiny fragments swept up into the air, where they linger among the martin’s insect food.
We blunder through these gossamer systems, brushing them aside almost unseen with every turn around the sun. It’s revealing, too, how those who find it politically expedient to mention natural variation in climate are much less interested in discussing the evolved instinct of many species, including our own, to migrate for survival.

Russian President Vladimir Putin used a summit of former Soviet republics in Turkmenistan on Friday, Oct. 9, to promote what Moscow sees as a financial lifeline against Western sanctions – claiming that 90% of Russia’s trade settlements with Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) countries now take place in national currencies rather than dollars or euros.
The announcement highlights how the Kremlin is using its post-Soviet economic networks to reduce reliance on Western financial systems while sustaining trade during its war against Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
A $110 billion trade network beyond the dollar
Speaking at the summit in Avaza, a resort on Turkmenistan’s Caspian coast, Putin said Russian trade with CIS countries exceeded $110 billion in 2025 and continued growing in 2026.
He praised the development of a “stable financial infrastructure” independent of foreign influence, arguing that it allowed economic cooperation to continue despite outside pressure.
“It allows us to deepen economic cooperation regardless of foreign influence,” Putin said.
The shift toward national currencies has become increasingly important for Russia since Western governments imposed sweeping financial restrictions following Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.
Putin also urged CIS members to remove remaining obstacles to regional commerce.
“Barriers should be lifted,” he said.
How former Soviet trade routes help Russia evade sanctions
The risks extend beyond the currencies used to settle transactions.
Trump Says He and Putin Have Cut Diesel Deal, Zelensky Accuses Washington of ‘Weakness’
Western governments have repeatedly identified Central Asia and the South Caucasus as potential routes for restricted goods entering Russia through third countries.
The researchers identified two methods: rerouting sanctioned products through neighboring countries and misreporting the destinations of shipments passing through Russia.
They estimated that these channels offset roughly one-third of the decline in direct European exports to Russia in restricted product categories during 2022–23.
The goods involved included industrial equipment and dual-use products with potential military applications.
A shrinking club of former Soviet republics
The economic figures contrast with the steady erosion of the CIS’s political influence.
Established in December 1991 following the collapse of the Soviet Union, the organization was designed to preserve cooperation among newly independent republics.
Georgia formally withdrew in 2009 following Russia’s invasion the previous year.
Ukraine, one of the CIS’s founding states, gradually dismantled its participation after Russia’s annexation of Crimea in 2014 and accelerated its withdrawal from remaining agreements following the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Moldova has also moved toward a definitive break.
Armenia, meanwhile, has increasingly diversified its security and diplomatic relationships after years of dependence on Moscow.
Across Central Asia, governments are expanding economic cooperation with China, the European Union and Turkey while maintaining important commercial ties with Russia.
For Putin, however, the CIS remains a platform to demonstrate that Moscow retains regional influence despite its confrontation with Ukraine and the West.
Iran joins the gathering
Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian attended the summit as a special guest, reflecting Moscow’s growing cooperation with another government facing extensive Western sanctions.
Putin and Pezeshkian met separately on Thursday, Oct. 8, discussing bilateral relations and the ongoing conflict involving Iran.
Pezeshkian thanked Moscow for opposing what he described as US unilateralism, while Putin offered Russian assistance in efforts to resolve the Middle East conflict.
Russia and Iran have expanded military and economic cooperation since Moscow invaded Ukraine, with Iranian-designed drones becoming an important part of Russia’s attacks.
The next CIS summit will take place in Bukhara, Uzbekistan, in October 2027, with Azerbaijan serving as co-chair before assuming the presidency and hosting the summit in 2028.
Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko welcomed Azerbaijan’s decision as a “historic moment” and expressed hope that Armenia would follow in 2029 – despite Yerevan’s growing distance from Moscow.
