Five Great Reads: unmarked graves, Happy Mondays, and a childhood without sugar
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:24:22 UTC
13:24:22 KST

Hello and welcome to the weekend.
This selection of reads from across the Guardian has chronicles of evolution, investigations and interviews which ask us to think about how we remember our loved ones when they are gone, and – of course – stories that leave you with a little something sweet.
Enjoy.
1. Unmarked graves
Peter Giesel was buried in an unmarked communal grave. The state government laid Giesel to rest in a cemetery on the outskirts of Sydney in a single plot with three others. This week, a Guardian Australia investigation found there are more than 100 cases like his across New South Wales. The Guardian revealed Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives such as Giesel’s sister, Nicole, have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.
Persons without means: This is the designation the state gives to those who are unable to afford their own funerals. Over the course of the investigation, the Guardian discovered at least 18 individuals known to homelessness services in Sydney who have been placed in unmarked graves in the last 10 years.
Notable quote: “How could such a heartless thing happen to someone who gave so much of his heart to others,” asks Giesel’s friend Elaine Grady (pictured).
An immediate response: When asked about the revelations, NSW Health delivered an apology to the dead and their loved ones, acknowledging they had not always been treated with the dignity and respect they deserved.
How long will it take to read: Less than seven minutes.
Further reading: Shared graves and stories such as Jayne and Barbara’s, have brought this issue to national attention.
2. A new ‘Lonely Generation’
Young people around the world are lonelier than ever, and examples of this are not hard to find. In online forums, users ask: “How do you deal with touch starvation?” Another asks: “The loneliness is unbearable, is anyone else experiencing this?” The answer to the latter question is yes. From Germany to Australia to the UK, studies show teenagers and young adults are finding social connections harder to form.
Why? The list is long. In her new book, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist Dr Michelle Lim examines why young people have turned toward solitude. She cites a long list of overlapping factors, including hyper-competitive education culture, social media, shifting family dynamics, the cost-of-living crisis, the grief many are still feeling from the Covid pandemic, and the rise of automation, “which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human”. Young adults are simply not being offered the opportunities to form meaningful connections, Lim says.
“People are getting used to being alone”: Lim’s biggest fear is what she calls “social atrophy”. Young people, she writes, can fall into what she calls the “loneliness loop”. When you experience loneliness, it can cause you to run away from further social interaction out of fear, making connections harder to come by.
How long will it take to read: Five minutes of solitude.
Further reading: Community-maxxing, and making new friends and connections as adults.
3. Drugs, drink and dancing with Bez from the Happy Mondays
Taking drugs, drinking heavily and dancing to the tunes of the Happy Mondays on stage made Bez famous. The story goes, as the Manchester music scene was exploding, band member Shaun Ryder urged Bez (whose real name is Mark Berry) to jump on stage with the band when they were supporting New Order. His “wild-eyed dancing” is now synonymous with the music itself, and as the band celebrate the 35th anniversary of their landmark album Pills ‘n’ Thrills and Bellyaches, Bez is back at it as the Happy Mondays go on a global tour.
A change for the good: After decades of partying, one might expect Bez to show signs of wear from his life on the road with a rock band. But when interviewer Emine Saner showed up at “his lovely cottage, down a rural track in Herefordshire”, Bez appeared unscathed by the years of drugs and drinking. Having given up cocaine and sugar, the former 24 hour party person now “juices every day, eats only organic food, drinks filtered water and works out with weights in his garden”.
Notable quote: “There’s sheep everywhere now,” Bez told Saner. At first, Saner took it as “a reference to our zombified society”, but he meant “actual sheep in the field” they just entered.
How long will it take to read: Just over five minutes, giving you enough time to Step On.
Further reading: Which is the best Happy Mondays song?
4. My sister Nicole married OJ Simpson
Denise Brown’s sister Nicole was murdered by OJ Simpson. On the last night the two sisters spent together, Nicole looked out the window to see Simpson driving by. “He’s constantly following me,” she told Brown. After her sister’s murder and the evidence of long-term abuse that emerged during the trial, Brown became a campaigner against domestic violence. She sat down with the Guardian to discuss what she wishes she had known before her sister’s death, and how she hopes her new book can save lives.
It’s rarely simple to leave: Brown says she told her sister all the wrong things. “You’ve got to leave him. You’ve got to get out of this situation. What are you doing?” she told Nicole. Brown now realises she was being unsupportive at the time, and has learned it is often not easy for a victim to leave. “Batterers usually threaten to take children away, threaten family members. When you are in a cycle like Nicole – like a lot of victims of domestic violence – was in, you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be.”
The car chase: The day after Nicole’s funeral, Simpson was scheduled to turn himself in to the police, but elected to go on the run. While millions watched on TV, Brown says she joined in the chase. “We were out of our minds. We got on the road, but he was so far ahead of us. I mean, come on, really?” She laughs at herself, but says: “It was a time of our lives that was insane.”
How long will it take to read: Five minutes.
Further reading: More stories of survival.
In Australia, domestic and family violence counselling is available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. In the UK, call the national domestic abuse helpline on 0808 2000 247, or visit Women’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found via www.befrienders.org
5. The generation raised on sugar rations
In the dark days after the second world war in Britain, many foods, including sugar, remained rationed. Adults had just 3 tbsp (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea and desserts. Children were offered even less, with the very young expected to have no sugar at all. But then the brakes came off, and sugar consumption in the UK almost doubled. Now scientists are looking back on this era to study the impact of sugar on our health.
Notable quote: “History created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime,” says Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.
What have they learned? Using data from the UK Biobank to compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK, scientists from the University of Southern California found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life. Another study, this one led by Zheng in Hong Kong, found reduced sugar exposure was associated with a lower risk of a growing list of health conditions. “In our work,” Zheng says, “we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing.”
How long will it take to read: A sweet three-and-a-half minutes.
Further reading: Everything you need to know about sugar.

If you would like to receive these Five Great Reads to your email inbox every weekend, sign up here. And check out out the full list of our local and international newsletters.

Hurricane Isaias makes landfall on US Gulf Coast, forcing evacuations, power outages
Unknown

Merve Aydogan
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Hurricane Isaias, the first of the 2026 Atlantic season, made landfall on the US’ northern Gulf Coast late Friday, bringing powerful winds and heavy rain to the country’s Southeast.
The National Hurricane Center said the storm came ashore near Destin, Florida, at about 8 pm local time (0000GMT) as a Category 2 hurricane before weakening to Category 1.
More than 610,000 customers were without power in the states of Florida and Alabama, according to PowerOutage.us.
Forecasters warned of a life-threatening storm surge of up to 9 feet (2.7 meters) from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, and up to 6 feet (1.8 meters) elsewhere along the Florida Panhandle.
Florida, Georgia, and Alabama declared states of emergency, while the Trump administration approved federal emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama.
Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey ordered tourists and non-residents in parts of Baldwin and Mobile counties to leave immediately. Officials said the evacuation window later closed because winds were too strong.
The storm is expected to weaken to a post-tropical system on Saturday as it moves inland, with rainfall of up to 15 inches (38 centimeters) in some coastal areas and a risk of tornadoes.

Oct 7 scars push Israel’s first-time voters to the right
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Oct 7 scars push Israel’s first-time voters to the right
NIR AM, Israel – Like hundreds of thousands of Israelis, Amihai will be of voting age for the first time since Hamas carried out its attack on Oct 7, 2023. When he casts his ballot in October, he has one priority above all – security.
From a field overlooking the sprawling ruins of the northern Gaza Strip, the 18-year-old says he plans to vote for a far-right party at the ballot box, three years after the deadliest day in Israeli history.
“I’m voting based solely on security – not for whoever will help me buy an apartment in 10 years, but for whoever can guarantee that I’ll even still be alive here in 10 years,” he told AFP.
Amihai, from Shomria in southern Israel, was speaking less than 2km from Gaza, swathes of which have been flattened by Israeli bombardment since the war with Hamas erupted in 2023.
He was attending an event calling for Jewish settlement of the Palestinian territory, and said that on Oct 27, he would be casting a vote for the ultra-nationalist party of National Security Minister Itamar Ben Gvir.
“After Oct 7, I want death for the terrorists, I want the terrorists here to suffer in prison, I want there to be deterrence,” the teenager said, alluding to a recently passed death penalty law that applies to Palestinians.
Sporting a cap and T-shirt in support of the minister, Amihai said he also wanted “emigration from Gaza, that the people of Gaza will be dying to leave” – another policy advocated by government ministers in recent months.
Roughly 550,000 Israelis aged between 18 and 22 will be voting for the first time in October, according to Israel’s Channel 12.
In a recent poll commissioned by the channel, 74% of first-time voters described their policy views as right or centre-right – an even higher share than the broadly right-leaning public at large.
‘Real future’
The trend stands in contrast to many Western democracies, where young people are among the most left-leaning voters – with some in recent years motivated by outrage over Israel’s actions in Gaza.
But the right-wing turn of Israeli Jewish youth has been building for around two decades, said pollster and analyst Dahlia Scheindlin.
“Older people... remember the hope of reaching full, comprehensive peace agreements with the Palestinians,” Scheindlin told AFP.
“Anybody who’s an 18-year-old now, his or her entire political consciousness is under (Prime Minister Benjamin) Netanyahu, it’s a very ultra-nationalist environment,” she said.
“Peace is not in people’s minds.”
At a gathering of young activists for the centre-left Democrats party in Tel Aviv in September, 18-year-old Gili said she felt society had turned its back on peace.
“I think especially young people, when they see something so huge happening, something that hurts so deeply and affects everyone, like what happened on Oct 7, then the first tendency is fear, to be afraid, and not to believe that peace is possible,” she told AFP.
“It’s logical that everyone kind of became more and more right-wing, and more and more extreme.”
Hamas’ Oct 7 attack resulted in the deaths of 1,221 people, according to an AFP tally based on official Israeli figures.
In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive that has killed more than 74,200 people in Gaza, according to the Health Ministry there, which is under Hamas authority and whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.
Gili and her friends at the rally said they supported the Democrats’ vision of a political agreement with the Palestinians.
“Conflict management is not a solution, and I don’t think the current situation can go on,” said Yuval, an 18-year-old from kibbutz Tel Yitzhak in central Israel. “Certainly not if we want to raise our children here, if we want to believe we have a real future for ourselves”.
‘Win decisively’
For yeshiva student Yishai Neeman, who hopes soon to enlist in a combat unit in the Israeli military, the horrors of Oct 7 and the wars that followed strengthened his resolve to fight for Israel.
He was at a synagogue when he heard of Hamas’ attack and spent his final years at boarding school running to bomb shelters.
From his home in the central city of Petah Tikva, the 19-year-old said he would be voting for the Religious Zionism party of far-right Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Neeman wanted peace, but felt it was not possible under the current conditions. Israel should annex the occupied West Bank, he said, and “erase their hope for a Palestinian state”.
Soon heading to fight himself, Neeman said he was not in favour of endless wars, but that Israel “can’t return once more to the understanding that preceded Oct 7”.
“That’s why now we must fight and win decisively.” AFP

AI data center demand lifts Taiwan connector industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:11:16 UTC
13:11:16 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s connector and cable assembly industry is reporting record revenue as investment in AI data centers drives demand for high-speed data transmission and liquid cooling components, CTEE reported Saturday.
Five companies, including JPC Connectivity Inc., Aces Electronics Co., Wonderful Hi Tech Co., Longwell Co., and Sinbon Electronics Co., reported record monthly figures in September. The broader trend was also evident in quarterly results, with at least nine companies posting record revenue for the third quarter.
JPC reported record revenue for both September and the third quarter. Monthly revenue exceeded NT$900 million for the first time, reaching NT$907 million, up 26.11% from a year earlier. Third-quarter revenue rose 22% year-on-year to NT$2.58 billion, according to UDN Money.
JPC said cloud service providers are moving away from their usual four-to-six-week ordering cycles toward longer-term commitments, extending its order visibility through 2028. Business is expected to improve further in the fourth quarter as shipments of components used in Nvidia’s Vera Rubin platform increase.
Longwell set new revenue records as well, with September revenue rising 15.68% year-on-year to NT$1.1 billion, the first time monthly revenue exceeded NT$1 billion. Third-quarter revenue reached NT$2.9 billion, up 16.1% from a year earlier, marking a quarterly high, according to UDN.
The growth followed the completion of product transitions for major cloud customers. Meanwhile, mass production of Nvidia’s Vera Rubin servers has begun, with shipments expected to increase significantly in the fourth quarter and continue rising next year.
Aces reported September revenue of NT$1.2 billion, up 22.66% year-on-year. Third-quarter revenue increased 23.1% to NT$3.4 billion, according to MoneyDJ.
Its growth outlook is also supported by high-power, high-voltage power cables for Bloom Energy. Orders began to ramp up in the second quarter, with shipments expected to continue increasing.
Wonderful Hi Tech posted the strongest year-on-year growth among the five companies in September, with revenue rising 58.4% to NT$1.1 billion. Third-quarter revenue reached a record NT$3.2 billion, up 57% from a year earlier. With strong order visibility, the company expects full-year revenue to exceed NT$10 billion, according to UDN Money.
Alongside its high-speed transmission cables, Wonderful Hi Tech is developing higher-value products for AI servers, including advanced power cables and leak-detection cables for liquid cooling systems. Customer testing has progressed smoothly, and shipments are expected to begin in stages before the end of the year.
Sinbon recorded its sixth consecutive monthly revenue record in September, with revenue reaching NT$3.4 billion, up 25.51% year-on-year. Third-quarter revenue totaled NT$9.8 billion, an annual increase of 28.9%, setting another quarterly record, according to CTEE.
The companies' results reflect rising performance requirements for AI data centers, where servers must handle larger volumes of data while consuming more power. Connectors link electronic devices and circuit boards, enabling signals and electrical power to pass between components, according to Sinotrade and Digitimes.
As AI workloads expand, data centers need faster connections to handle increasing data traffic and reliable power delivery for energy-intensive servers. The adoption of liquid cooling is also creating demand for cables and connectors that can operate reliably in more demanding environments, opening opportunities for suppliers of high-performance components.

India deploys police and restricts transport ahead of mass protest in Delhi

Indian police detain politicians at protests over election chief
India has deployed thousands of police and paramilitary personnel in central Delhi and restricted transport in and around the capital ahead of a youth-led protest demanding the resignation of Gyanesh Kumar, the country’s chief election commissioner.
Saturday’s rally, called by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a youth-based political movement, is expected to be the biggest yet in a wave of near-daily protests over a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
Organisers have billed it as a protest to “Save Democracy”.
Shutdown of central Delhi
Police have not authorised a rally at Jantar Mantar in central Delhi, which authorities usually designate for protests, because they said the request was not made on time and that the CJP had violated undertakings given during earlier protests.
Police have also warned that protesters will face a forceful law enforcement response if they violate the ban.
Roads to the site are blocked with multiple layers of metal barricades, as authorities shut 57 metro stations from Friday night, cancelled several long-distance trains and suspended mobile internet within 4km (2.5 miles) of the protest area until Saturday night, the Indian news agency ANI reported.
India’s Supreme Court said on Friday that some trains must still run and that blanket closure of metro stations is unlikely.
“The dictator would rather shut down the entire national capital and inconvenience millions of citizens than allow a peaceful protest at a designated protest site,” CJP chief Abhijeet Dipke said on X.
The CJP says at least 10,000 people, including protesters travelling to Delhi by train, have been detained across the country.
“You can detain the people, you cannot detain the movement,” said Neha Bora, national president of the All India Students’ Association, who has emerged as a leading face of the protests.
What kicked off the protests
Protesters want Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar to quit over a voter list revision that has removed more than 130 million names.
The Election Commission says the exercise removes duplicate and ineligible voters and aims to prevent “foreign illegal immigrants” from voting.
Critics say it has disproportionately affected marginalised and minority communities.
The protests escalated after the Indian Express reported that Kumar’s two deputies had formally raised concerns at least 14 times in the past 10 months over the revisions.
The Election Commission and the BJP have denied the allegations. The BJP says the opposition is misleading the country because it cannot win elections.
The CJP began online as political satire in May after Chief Justice Surya Kant called unemployed youth “cockroaches”, sparking nationwide outrage. Since then, the CJP has garnered a large following among India’s youth.
The July protests led Modi’s education minister to resign over exam paper leaks. The latest demonstrations come months before a series of state elections in early 2027, including in Uttar Pradesh, India’s most populous state, which the BJP governs.

“It lines up with price timelines,” he added.
Trump announced Friday that Russia would immediately supply 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by 500,000 tons in November, another 1 million tons afterward and potentially 3 million additional tons.
The US Treasury Department issued a temporary authorization for certain transactions involving Russian-origin diesel through April 7, 2027.

France’s dilemma: protesters demand spending as markets require fiscal restraint
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:00:47 UTC
13:00:47 KST

Eight years have passed since rising fuel prices brought the gilets jaunes (yellow vest) demonstrators to the streets of France, prompting the first big crisis of Emmanuel Macron’s time in the Élysée Palace.
As the French president contemplates his exit next year, turmoil has again gripped the streets in the form of student protests, but this time the financial markets are unhappy too.
Investors are concerned about the government’s failure to bring spending under control and end a long period of “fiscal incontinence”. Financial markets are unnerved by similar trends in the UK, the US and more recently Italy, causing jitters in global bond markets. But it’s France that has become the biggest worry, hemmed in by debts across the public and private sectors, limiting their scope to dig the country out of a deepening hole.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% for the UK respectively.
In Britain, the chancellor, John Healey, is on course to reduce the budget deficit this year and in 2027. His French counterpart, Roland Lescure, has promised to follow suit after a rise to 5.4% this year, but has yet to say how.
‘I am panicking’
One victim of the uncertainty is business investment. A survey by Medef, France’s largest employer federation, showed 82% of firms were pessimistic about the impact of the next government’s economic policy. In a warning to all politicians, 66% said their business would become vulnerable or even go bankrupt if economic policy remained deadlocked for the next five years.
A rescue operation could be mounted by the European Central Bank (ECB), but France would demand unconditional support when the ECB’s rules say bailouts must come with strict conditions.
Antonio Fatas, a professor of economics at Insead, the European business school, says the political and economic situation has pushed France to the edge of a financial collapse. “I am very worried about the economic situation because growth is low and it is difficult to see how the dynamics change. Then you have the debt numbers, which are bad, and the financial markets are thinking the government is not in control.
“If I look at the political situation, I am panicking. That’s because too many political parties are saying let France burn. They want a crisis, believing it will improve their share of the vote.”
There is much about the economic situation in France that mirrors what has happened in the UK and the US. A huge spending splurge during the Covid pandemic was followed by another round of subsidies to offset the worst side-effects from Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Investors have become wary of lending to all three countries, but the rise in interest rates is strongest in France.
Last week, the yield, or interest rate, on 10-year French bonds hit the highest level since July 2002, just short of 5%. Yields go up when bond prices go down.
Japanese investors, typically strong supporters of France as a haven for their savings, have been instrumental in the panic after they found better returns on home turf, heaping further pain on the French treasury.
Political turmoil
According to many metrics, it is difficult to see why France should be so badly affected. The French economy has many things going for it, from relatively low electricity prices to better than average infrastructure.
The schools that are the focus of recent protests are better funded than the OECD average.
On the debit side of the ledger, Macron’s plan to raise the pension age from 62 to 64, saving tens of billions of euros from an almost entirely socialised retirement system, stalled at 62 and nine months after parliament was deadlocked after the 2024 snap election. This might have mattered less if the economy was growing, but Macron’s much-vaunted economic revival remains stuck in first gear.
Laurent Warlouzet, a professor of history at the Sorbonne, says it is understandable that international investors are confused about France when Marine Le Pen, the frontrunner in presidential elections next year, says she will roll back the retirement age to 62 and at the same time introduce a “debt brake” via a referendum, restricting further borrowing.
He said: “The far right used to be a spendthrift populist force, especially under Le Pen’s leadership, broadening the appeal of National Rally voters in the country’s rust belts. In 2016–17, she still wanted France to leave the eurozone, which she regarded as a straitjacket.”
Warlouzet, the author of Liberty, Solidarity and Community: capitalism and European integration, 1945 to the present, added: “Nowadays, Le Pen has become an improbable fiscal hawk. How can she reconcile this with her voters’ demands for more nurses, teachers, police officers and judges?”
‘Too big to save’
Erik Britton, the director of Fathom Consulting, an international advisory firm, says the prospect of a runoff between Jean-Luc Mélenchon, the leader of the leftwing La France Insoumise (LFI), and Le Pen next April has spooked investors more than the failure to bring down the annual deficit.
“What has changed is the likely runoff. In the second round, it now looks likely that Le Pen will contest the presidential election against Mélenchon from the far left. Le Pen’s election might mean a 20% risk of Frexit: Mélenchon’s election, though less likely on current polling, would have a much higher risk of Frexit.”
Britton says the collapse of the centre ground would have implications far beyond its borders. “Where France goes, the euro area as a whole tends to follow. If it led to another test of the euro, all the considerations about debt and debt mutualisation would resurface, and bond yields would pop right across the euro area (perhaps with the exception of Germany) and beyond.”
It may seem improbable for financial market traders to consider France’s exit from the euro when it has occupied a central position in the single currency since its inception. Yet it is understood several eurozone finance ministers and ECB officials have made representations to the French government, urging it to devise a budget formula that will gain a majority in parliament and a win over leading lenders.
Without a budget, France may be left to fend for itself. And if that means traders boycott French bonds without a huge interest rate premium, the country may be forced to default on its debts. A bailout would also be expensive.
As the US Nobel prize-winning economist Paul Krugman said recently: “If France does need to be bailed out, it would be extremely expensive. As the second largest economy in the eurozone, France may have crossed the line from too big to fail to too big to save”
Dhaval Joshi, an independent City economist, said: “Ultimately therefore, France will have to make painful adjustments to bring its debt maths back under control. Just like Italy, Spain (and, of course, Greece) did a decade ago, from which these southern European economies have emerged much stronger.
“The crucial question is how much political pain France must go through before it makes, or is forced to make, this adjustment.”
The head of France’s central bank, Emmanuel Moulin, denied last week that France needed help from the ECB, but inflamed the situation by adding the rider, “not at this point”.
Albert Edwards, a senior global strategist at Société Générale, said France may survive the onslaught from bonds market traders – some of them termed vigilantes for their habit of sniffing out weak nations – should another country begin to look vulnerable.
“Although France has been in the crosshairs recently, the bond vigilantes’ focus is merely rolling from one market to another. Next month their attention might be back on Japan, the UK or indeed the US.
“It is the way of the bond vigilantes to jab away and test each market to find out which is the weakest before launching an all-out attack,” he said.

Growing up in a Malay family in Singapore, Hafeez Hassan feared dogs. He never expected to mourn one like a sibling.

Free Copenhagen event to connect international workers with Danish trade unions
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
04:00:00 UTC
13:00:00 KST

International workers and Danish trade union representatives will meet in Copenhagen on October 22 to discuss the challenges of working and building a life in Denmark.
The event, “Building Bridges: It’s Time to Connect International Workers and Danish Trade Unions,” will take place from 1:30 to 5 p.m. at the trade union 3F’s premises at Peter Ipsens Allé 25 in Copenhagen. Doors opens at 1:15 p.m.
Organized by the association InDe and the trade union PROSA, the event will bring together workers, unions and other organizations for a panel discussion and workshops.
The organizers say workers with foreign backgrounds are considerably less likely than Danish workers to belong to trade unions and unemployment insurance funds.
According to the organizers, unions often find international workers difficult to reach, while many internationals feel unions do not communicate effectively with them or adequately address their needs.
The event aims to give both groups a chance to discuss those concerns directly.
Panel discussion and workshops
Representatives from PROSA, InDe and 3F will open the event with a welcome and a brief introduction to the Danish trade union system.
A panel discussion, “Unions and internationals: a difficult relationship,” will follow. Scheduled panelists include Christian Sølyst from Akademikerne, an umbrella organization for unions representing workers with higher education, and Elizabeth Williams Oerberg from InDe. Bernardo Basilici Menini, editor in chief of The Copenhagen Post, will moderate.
After a break, participants will join workshops focused on four areas: IT, universities and research, blue-collar and service-sector work, and unemployment and job seeking.
The IT workshop will feature Heidi Ås from IDA, a professional association and trade union for engineers, IT specialists and science graduates, and Bjarke Friborg from PROSA, a union for IT professionals.
The university and research workshop will include Marina Kliuchko from PAND and Bersant Hobdari from DM, a trade union for academically trained workers. Andrew Mellor from InDe will facilitate.
Anthony Sylvester from 3F and David Rønbach from Community House will take part in the workshop for blue-collar and service-sector workers, facilitated by Sara Nardi from Belonging.
The unemployment and job-seeking workshop will include Eva Pihl from FOA, a union representing workers in areas including care and public services. The facilitator will be Soni Khanal.
Each workshop will begin with a short presentation about the participating organizations’ work for international workers, followed by questions and discussion. Participants will be able to ask about support and services, while union representatives will hear about workers’ needs and experiences.
The event will close with networking from 4 to 5 p.m.
The event is free and open to everyone, but participants need to register here.

‘Peddling lies and falsehoods’: India hits back at Pakistan at UN over Jammu and Kashmir
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:59:19 UTC
12:59:19 KST

NEW DELHI: India on Friday hit back at Pakistan at the United Nations, saying Islamabad was using the international forum to spread “lies and falsehoods” about Jammu and Kashmir and urging it to address alleged human rights violations in territories under its control.India exercised its Right of Reply during a discussion on decolonisation in the Fourth Committee of the UN general assembly after Pakistan raised the issue of Jammu and Kashmir.
“It is regrettable that Pakistan continues to abuse this august forum by peddling lies and falsehoods about the Union Territory of Jammu and Kashmir,” MP Mahima Kumari Mewar said while delivering India's response.
Mewar criticised Pakistan over its record of military dictatorship, elections, the imprisonment of elected leaders, religious extremism and alleged state sponsorship of terrorism. She said Islamabad should refrain from “preaching homilies” at the United Nations.“Jammu and Kashmir is and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India,” she said.India also called on Pakistan to end grave and ongoing human rights violations in territories under its illegal occupation. Mewar alleged that people in these areas were resisting military occupation, repression, brutality and the exploitation of local resources.
She further claimed that Pakistani armed forces and their proxies had killed dozens of civilians in recent months as they protested for basic rights, freedoms and necessities.Mewar is part of a 15-member parliamentary delegation visiting the United States for a familiarisation programme at the United Nations. The delegation held engagements at the world body and met members of the Indian diaspora at a reception hosted by the Consulate General of India in New York.India flags accountability, human rights at UNIndia's response to Pakistan came amid a broader push by New Delhi on human rights, accountability and development during recent United Nations engagements.At the 63rd session of the UN Human Rights Council in Geneva, which concluded on October 7, India reiterated its position on protecting human dignity without discrimination.“There must be no hierarchy of human life, no selectivity in protecting human dignity and no double standards. We regret the absence of a clear focus on the human rights of victims of terrorism,” Ambassador Arindam Bagchi, India's Permanent Representative to the United Nations and other international organisations in Geneva, said in a video outlining India's interventions.India also called for progress on the proposed International Covenant on the Right to Development. First Secretary Anuj Swarup urged states to work towards its early conclusion, while counsellor Gaurav Kumar Thakur said reform of global governance, development cooperation and stronger representation for developing countries remained priorities.On climate issues, India backed farmers' access to climate-resilient seeds and called on developed countries to fulfil their climate finance commitments. Its interventions on artificial intelligence included Prime Minister Narendra Modi's MANAV vision, with First Secretary Anupama Singh calling for AI to become more accessible and inclusive, particularly across the Global South.“AI must be democratised and become a medium of inclusion and empowerment, especially across the Global South,” Singh said.India also raised the protection of Indians working abroad, including safeguards against wage theft and passport confiscation, and highlighted its contributions to UN trust funds supporting technical cooperation and the Universal Periodic Review.On Jammu and Kashmir, counsellor Kshitij Tyagi reiterated India's position and referred to the displacement of Kashmiri Pandits in 1990, alleging that terrorists armed and trained by Pakistan had driven them from their homes.“Jammu and Kashmir was, is and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India. It happened in 1990 to the Kashmiri Pandits, driven from their homes by terrorists Pakistan armed, trained and sent across the border. Pakistan would better serve its people by focusing on development, rather than by coveting territory of others or exporting terror, because neither these nor its theatrics in this Council would help repay the loans its economy survives on,” Tyagi said.
India also reiterated its commitment to racial equality, citing Mahatma Gandhi's struggle against racial discrimination, and called for continued international cooperation on development and human rights.Separately, MP Priya Saroj delivered India's national statement at the 81st session of the UN General Assembly's Sixth Committee on the criminal accountability of United Nations officials and experts on mission. India called for stronger cooperation between the UN and member states, effective accountability mechanisms, due process and protection for victims and witnesses.

China successfully launches 27th batch of SatNet communications satellites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:52:28 UTC
12:52:28 KST

BEIJING, October 10. /TASS/. China has successfully launched 27th batch of SatNet communications satellites into low-Earth orbit, the China Aerospace Science and Technology Corporation (CASC) reported.
According to a post on its official account on WeChat, a Chinese social media and messaging platform, the launch took place aboard a Long March-12 (CZ-12) carrier rocket at 3:27 a.m. Beijing time on Saturday (7:27 p.m. GMT on Friday) from the commercial launch site at the Wenchang Space Launch Site in the Hainan Province in southern China.
The CZ-12 is a two-stage, liquid-propellant rocket with a liftoff thrust of 5,000 kilonewtons. It has a payload fairing diameter of either 5.2 or 4.2 meters, is 62 meters long and can carry at least six metric tons into a sun-synchronous orbit at an altitude of 700 kilometers. This was the rocket’s ninth launch and its fifth in the current year.

India: Delhi braces for Cockroach protest amid strict curbs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:50:00 UTC
12:50:00 KST

India's 'Cockroach' leaders detained ahead of major protest
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 10, 2026
What you need to know
- Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke and other party leaders detained on landing in Delhi
- 43,000 police and security personnel deployed across Delhi
- Internet services suspended in central Delhi
- Massive restrictions in place on metro and railway services
- CJP called for a rally — that has not been authorized by police — to oppose ongoing revision of voter lists and demand resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar
Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:
Indian media houses say their journalists were briefly detained during Delhi protests
Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.
Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.
It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.
In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. Press freedom groups have raised concerns about the use of criminal laws against journalists and the impact of such measures on independent journalism.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother has died — reports
Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.
Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.
News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.
Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.
IN PICTURES: Dissent and detention
CJP appoints interim protest leader to press on with rally
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.
CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.
The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.
"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.
"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.
In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."
Supreme Court bar association calls for intervention after lawyers are detained
The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.
This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.
The arrested lawyers include those protesting outside the premises of the Supreme Court of India, as well as lawyers inside their chambers, legal news website, Bar and Bench, reported.
The Supreme Court Bar Association passed a resolution condemning the use of "excessive force against, and detention of, senior and young advocates, particularly women advocates, who were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area today."
The advocates' body expressed "grave concern" and requested the CJI to take action to ensure that the "whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate are ascertained."
How have India's opposition politicians reacted to the Delhi protest crackdown?
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has slammed the measures taken by Indian authorities to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party's protest from going ahead.
He called out a "war-like deployment" of security personnel and said that the suspension of the internet in a key part of Delhi was among the "most regressive" and "repressive" measures.
"A government confident in the fairness of its elections would welcome questions about them, whereas one that turns its capital into a fortress to avoid them only deepens the very suspicions it seeks to suppress. The government should provide answers, not lathis (sticks); expression, not repression," Tharoor wrote on X.
He also called for the release of the protesters who had been detained.
Tharoor said India's Gen Z "deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ," in a play on words.
Leaders of the CJP on Friday likened the clampdown on their planned protest to a "state of emergency."
A state of emergency was declared in India by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were invoked by the Congress leader for 21 months, during which civil liberties were suspended, much of the opposition was jailed and media was censored.
Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) National Convenor and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also mounted an emergency-related attack against Modi's government.
"This is worse than the Emergency. It's official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear," he said, referring to the arrests of CJP's three main leaders.
Modi's party accuses opposition of attempts to 'incite tension'
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday accused opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal of "attempting to incite tensions" in the country.
"The Govt of India will deal strictly with the attempts you are making to incite tension, and BJP workers, remaining constantly among the people, will effectively thwart your designs," BJP President Nitin Nabin told news agencies on Saturday morning.
"Your repeated electoral defeats in various states and the resulting desperation suggest that, in some way, you do not wish to see this country move forward peacefully. However, I warn you today that the BJP and the patriotic citizens of this country will give you a fitting and stern response," he said.
Nabin suggested that "foreign forces" were behind the opposition leaders and that the protests were an attempt to "destabilize" India. BJP leaders have made similar claims before without offering proof.
"I issue a clear warning to you today: the foreign forces upon which you rely for your politics up for sale—and the alliances with such forces through which you seek to destabilize India—will never allow your nefarious intentions to succeed," he said.
More detentions reported as protesters attempt to push through security blockade
It's past noon here and Indian news channels are playing visuals of protesters trying to reach central Delhi, despite the mass preventive detentions taking place.
Several groups of young people have been seen running through the streets, trying to dodge police personnel and barricades.
News agency ANI reported, citing police sources, that 200 more people were detained in the key Connaught Place area as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site.
What to know if you're joining us now
Here's the situation right now:
- The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, which called Saturday's protest, have been detained
- Police have reportedly detained more than 500 people heading toward Jantar Mantar in anticipation of demonstrations
- Heavy barricades have been erected across central Delhi and along the national capital's borders to prevent protesters from entering the city
With this, it is unclear at the moment whether the planned protest will be able to take place.
But the CJP isn't the only group protesting against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
The left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star, Neha Bora, have been leading protests in the capital all week.
Also on the ground are the Gandhi siblings, lawmakers Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, who are leading the opposition alliance's protests against the poll body in New Delhi.
Rahul Gandhi is the leader of the opposition in the lower house of the Indian parliament and possibly Prime Minister Modi's biggest challenger in the 2029 elections. According to Indian media reports, Gandhi is scheduled to attend a political meeting in the southern city of Chennai today.
Gyanesh Kumar, Modi government 'will go,' says Rahul Gandhi
India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday reiterated his demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down and critized the Modi government.
"Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. Then the repair of democracy will begin," the Congress leader wrote on X as he shared a video of himself addressing INDIA bloc MPs in the Central Hall of Parliament.
Late on Friday, Gandhi and a delegation of opposition lawmakers met President Droupadi Murmu to submit a four-point memorandum.
The memorandum outlined what Gandhi called Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah's "gross subversion of India's electoral system" and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
IN PICTURES—Central Delhi turns into a fortress under unprecedented security
Delhi police say they've detained 500 protesters headed for 'Cockroach' march
Delhi Police said in a statement that around 500 people were detained on Saturday as they arrived for the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party, news agency ANI reported.
"Around 500 people coming in different groups from various locations have been detained," ANI quoted the Delhi Police statement as saying.
The police added that an additional 50 people had been arrested and described them as "anti-social elements with criminal antecedents" who had been taken into custody to ensure that they "did not disturb" public order or "incite trouble."
Visuals aired by Indian news channels earlier showed police in central Delhi chasing young protesters before forcing them into vehicles and taking them away.
'Cockroach' party founder Abhijeet Dipke detained
Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained by Delhi police, Indian media reported, as a preventative measure to block the planned protest against India's election chief in central Delhi.
According to reports by several media outlets, including India Today, authorities detained Dipke on board a flight after he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. The news outlet quoted Dipke as saying, "I'm not afraid of you," while police officers urged him to cooperate.
The CJP's X handle soon released footage of the detention. "Shame on you Narendra Modi, Amit Shah," the caption read, referring to India's prime minister and home minister, respectively.
Authorities have also detained CJP's co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, as well as the group's legal aid head, Ratna Singh.
Right before being arrested, Dipke posted a video on Instagram, showing tens of Delhi police officers lining up outside his airplane to enter. "Love you, we'll do it together, Inqalab Zindabad," one of Dipke's associate is heard saying in the video's background.
'Inqalab Zindabad', meaning 'long live the revolution,' is a famous slogan used by Indian freedom fighters during their struggle against British rule. It has regularly been used by the Cockroach party against the Modi government.
The preventative arrests are part of a major crackdown on protesters this weekend.
Most of central Delhi, where the government is headquartered, is under an internet blackout and riddled with barricades, which authorities are using to identify and stop potential protesters.
BJP calls CJP, INDIA bloc 'anarchists'
Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) National President Nitin Nabin held a press conference in New Delhi, denouncing the CJP and opposition party protests over voter list irregularities as an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country."
He described the INDIA bloc of opposition parties and the Cockroach movement as "two anarchic groups."
"Your 'anarchist competition,' vying to see who can create more instability in the country, will not succeed," Nabin said, accusing both groups of "a plot to destabilize the country."
"I want to say that you are undertaking these efforts, driven by your political agendas, at the behest of foreign forces," he said without elaborating on who the foreign forces were.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained, reports say
Popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained by the police ahead of the Jantar Mantar protest, according to the CJP and Indian media reports.
"Dhruv Rathee has been detained. The Dictator is TERRIFIED of young people who question its wrongdoings and refuse to stay silent," the CJP wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Modi.
According to reports, Rathee was detained at his home in Gurugam. Earlier this week, the CJP officially launched Rathee as part of its "fight to save democracy" campaign.
The Germany-based YouTuber participated in a CJP protest in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru on Thursday.
CJP legal head Ratna Singh is also reported to have been detained at her home in New Delhi on Saturday.

Detained Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke's grandmother is reported to have died on Saturday.
Indian media reports said that Dipke's paternal grandmother had been suffering from a prolonged illness and had been unwell in recent days. She died in her native village in Maharashtra, reports said.
News agency ANI, citing police sources, reported that the Delhi Police had informed Dipke of his grandmother's death. It was now up to the CJP leader to decide whether to continue his protest while under detention or travel back for the funeral rites.
Dipke was detained aboard his plane after it landed in New Delhi on Saturday morning, ahead of the protest. He was traveling from Mumbai.
IN PICTURES: Dissent and detention
CJP appoints interim protest leader to press on with rally
The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has indicated that it will press on with its protest despite its leaders and supporters being detained.
CJP's National Organization In-Charge Ajinkya Shinde will lead the protest at Jantar Mantar until Abhijeet Dipke, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka remain in detention, the group said in a statement on X.
The CJP also shared a video of Dipke purportedly recorded on Friday night, anticipating a potential detention.
"If you are seeing this video, it means Ashutosh, Saurav and I have been arrested," Dipke says in the video.
"After us, Ajinkya will lead this movement," he says.
In a separate post, the CJP alleged that its three detained leaders had been taken to an undisclosed location, were being denied access to lawyers and had been cut off from "all contact with others."
Supreme Court bar association calls for intervention after lawyers are detained
The formal association of advocates at India's apex court called for urgent intervention by Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant after several lawyers were detained by Delhi police.
This comes amid a reported crackdown on protesters attempting to reach the national capital, specifically central Delhi, to protest against India's chief election commissioner over alleged misconduct.
The arrested lawyers include those protesting outside the premises of the Supreme Court of India, as well as lawyers inside their chambers, legal news website, Bar and Bench, reported.
The Supreme Court Bar Association passed a resolution condemning the use of "excessive force against, and detention of, senior and young advocates, particularly women advocates, who were peacefully protesting in the Supreme Court area today."
The advocates' body expressed "grave concern" and requested the CJI to take action to ensure that the "whereabouts and safety of every detained advocate are ascertained."
How have India's opposition politicians reacted to the Delhi protest crackdown?
Congress MP Shashi Tharoor has slammed the measures taken by Indian authorities to prevent the Cockroach Janta Party's protest from going ahead.
He called out a "war-like deployment" of security personnel and said that the suspension of the internet in a key part of Delhi was among the "most regressive" and "repressive" measures.
"A government confident in the fairness of its elections would welcome questions about them, whereas one that turns its capital into a fortress to avoid them only deepens the very suspicions it seeks to suppress. The government should provide answers, not lathis (sticks); expression, not repression," Tharoor wrote on X.
He also called for the release of the protesters who had been detained.
Tharoor said India's Gen Z "deserves better than an undeclared Emer-GenZ," in a play on words.
Leaders of the CJP on Friday likened the clampdown on their planned protest to a "state of emergency."
A state of emergency was declared in India by former Prime Minister Indira Gandhi in the mid-70s. Emergency powers were invoked by the Congress leader for 21 months, during which civil liberties were suspended, much of the opposition was jailed and media was censored.
Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) National Convenor and former Delhi chief minister Arvind Kejriwal also mounted an emergency-related attack against Modi's government.
"This is worse than the Emergency. It's official.. we are living under an absolute dictatorship ruled by Modi. Arresting cockroaches straight off their flight shows an unprecedented level of fear," he said, referring to the arrests of CJP's three main leaders.
Modi's party accuses opposition of attempts to 'incite tension'
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Saturday accused opposition leaders including Rahul Gandhi and Arvind Kejriwal of "attempting to incite tensions" in the country.
"The Govt of India will deal strictly with the attempts you are making to incite tension, and BJP workers, remaining constantly among the people, will effectively thwart your designs," BJP President Nitin Nabin told news agencies on Saturday morning.
"Your repeated electoral defeats in various states and the resulting desperation suggest that, in some way, you do not wish to see this country move forward peacefully. However, I warn you today that the BJP and the patriotic citizens of this country will give you a fitting and stern response," he said.
Nabin suggested that "foreign forces" were behind the opposition leaders and that the protests were an attempt to "destabilize" India. BJP leaders have made similar claims before without offering proof.
"I issue a clear warning to you today: the foreign forces upon which you rely for your politics up for sale—and the alliances with such forces through which you seek to destabilize India—will never allow your nefarious intentions to succeed," he said.
More detentions reported as protesters attempt to push through security blockade
It's past noon here and Indian news channels are playing visuals of protesters trying to reach central Delhi, despite the mass preventive detentions taking place.
Several groups of young people have been seen running through the streets, trying to dodge police personnel and barricades.
News agency ANI reported, citing police sources, that 200 more people were detained in the key Connaught Place area as they tried to reach the Jantar Mantar protest site.

- The leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party, which called Saturday's protest, have been detained

Also on the ground are the Gandhi siblings, lawmakers Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi, who are leading the opposition alliance's protests against the poll body in New Delhi.

Gyanesh Kumar, Modi government 'will go,' says Rahul Gandhi
India's main opposition leader Rahul Gandhi on Saturday reiterated his demand for Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar step down and critized the Modi government.
"Gyanesh Kumar will go. This government will go. Then the repair of democracy will begin," the Congress leader wrote on X as he shared a video of himself addressing INDIA bloc MPs in the Central Hall of Parliament.
Late on Friday, Gandhi and a delegation of opposition lawmakers met President Droupadi Murmu to submit a four-point memorandum.
The memorandum outlined what Gandhi called Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Home Minister Amit Shah's "gross subversion of India's electoral system" and called for the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
IN PICTURES—Central Delhi turns into a fortress under unprecedented security
Delhi police say they've detained 500 protesters headed for 'Cockroach' march
Delhi Police said in a statement that around 500 people were detained on Saturday as they arrived for the protest called by the Cockroach Janta Party, news agency ANI reported.
"Around 500 people coming in different groups from various locations have been detained," ANI quoted the Delhi Police statement as saying.
The police added that an additional 50 people had been arrested and described them as "anti-social elements with criminal antecedents" who had been taken into custody to ensure that they "did not disturb" public order or "incite trouble."
Visuals aired by Indian news channels earlier showed police in central Delhi chasing young protesters before forcing them into vehicles and taking them away.
'Cockroach' party founder Abhijeet Dipke detained
Cockroach Janta Party's (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been detained by Delhi police, Indian media reported, as a preventative measure to block the planned protest against India's election chief in central Delhi.
According to reports by several media outlets, including India Today, authorities detained Dipke on board a flight after he landed in Delhi on Saturday morning. The news outlet quoted Dipke as saying, "I'm not afraid of you," while police officers urged him to cooperate.
The CJP's X handle soon released footage of the detention. "Shame on you Narendra Modi, Amit Shah," the caption read, referring to India's prime minister and home minister, respectively.
Authorities have also detained CJP's co-conveners Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, as well as the group's legal aid head, Ratna Singh.
Right before being arrested, Dipke posted a video on Instagram, showing tens of Delhi police officers lining up outside his airplane to enter. "Love you, we'll do it together, Inqalab Zindabad," one of Dipke's associate is heard saying in the video's background.
'Inqalab Zindabad', meaning 'long live the revolution,' is a famous slogan used by Indian freedom fighters during their struggle against British rule. It has regularly been used by the Cockroach party against the Modi government.
The preventative arrests are part of a major crackdown on protesters this weekend.
Most of central Delhi, where the government is headquartered, is under an internet blackout and riddled with barricades, which authorities are using to identify and stop potential protesters.
BJP calls CJP, INDIA bloc 'anarchists'
Bharatiya Janata Party's (BJP) National President Nitin Nabin held a press conference in New Delhi, denouncing the CJP and opposition party protests over voter list irregularities as an attempt to "create a highly dangerous and serious situation in the country."
He described the INDIA bloc of opposition parties and the Cockroach movement as "two anarchic groups."
"Your 'anarchist competition,' vying to see who can create more instability in the country, will not succeed," Nabin said, accusing both groups of "a plot to destabilize the country."
"I want to say that you are undertaking these efforts, driven by your political agendas, at the behest of foreign forces," he said without elaborating on who the foreign forces were.
YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained, reports say
Popular YouTuber Dhruv Rathee has been detained by the police ahead of the Jantar Mantar protest, according to the CJP and Indian media reports.
"Dhruv Rathee has been detained. The Dictator is TERRIFIED of young people who question its wrongdoings and refuse to stay silent," the CJP wrote on X, referring to Prime Minister Modi.
According to reports, Rathee was detained at his home in Gurugam. Earlier this week, the CJP officially launched Rathee as part of its "fight to save democracy" campaign.
The Germany-based YouTuber participated in a CJP protest in the southern Indian city of Bengaluru on Thursday.
CJP legal head Ratna Singh is also reported to have been detained at her home in New Delhi on Saturday.

Axios: Trump has struck diesel deal with Putin because of Ukraine's refusal to halt refinery strikes
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
06:50:00 EEST
12:50:00 KST

Axios: Trump has struck diesel deal with Putin because of Ukraine's refusal to halt refinery strikes
US President Donald Trump has decided to strike a deal with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin to supply Russian diesel fuel to the United States because Ukraine refused to unilaterally halt its attacks on Russian oil refineries.
Source: Axios, citing a senior US official familiar with the situation
Details: According to the official, Trump's decision came after Zelenskyy ignored half a dozen requests to stop strikes on Russian oil refineries.
Quote: "Zelenskyy told Trump and his envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner that he was prepared to stop attacking Russian oil refineries if the Russians halted attacks on Ukrainian power plants.
The US official said Trump wanted Ukraine to unilaterally stop attacking Russian refineries because the strikes were contributing to high gas prices in America.
Trump didn't see the attacks on refineries as equivalent to Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid, the US official said."
Details: The official added that "the attacks on the refineries cause pain in Russia, but it causes pain for the US, too".
"Zelenskyy is misreading the room. By continuing to hit refineries, he is eroding the good will that he has built with Trump over the last six months," the official said.
According to Axios, during eight hours of talks in Miami, Trump's envoys told the Ukrainian delegation that the president would speak to Putin and lift sanctions on Russian diesel exports.
A Ukrainian official told Axios that Witkoff and Kushner had threatened to cut Ukraine off from US intelligence if it continued the strikes. The US official denied that any such threats had been made and said the US was a reliable partner that provided ammunition and intelligence.
In addition, Witkoff and Kushner briefed the Ukrainian delegation and European representatives on potential energy deals with Russia which the US hopes will encourage Moscow to make concessions in peace negotiations.
"Putin is hitting [Ukraine] hard but we think he is open to a discussion on ending the war. We want to work on a new proposal that will be good enough for him in order to get him to stop," the US official said.
Background:
- In September and October, Trump repeatedly urged Zelenskyy to scale back attacks on Russian oil refineries, linking the strikes to fuel shortages and rising prices in the US.
- On 8 October, Zelenskyy announced that talks would take place in the US involving a Ukrainian delegation. This delegation included Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People party; Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service; Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; and Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
- Ahead of the meeting, Axios reported, citing US and Ukrainian officials, that US President's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning to present "new ideas and proposals" in Miami to break the diplomatic deadlock.
- On 9 October, US President Donald Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move. He stressed that this "happy birthday present for Putin" will provide Russia with billions more to continue the war
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine's negotiating team in the US was being used as "cover" while Trump and Putin reached agreements on fuel supplies.
- Yuri Ushakov, an aide to Vladimir Putin, said that the Russian leader had rejected the prospect of peace talks and stressed that Russia will continue fighting until it has achieved "all its objectives" during a phone call with US President Donald Trump.

India's 'Cockroach' leaders detained ahead of major protest
Published October 10, 2026last updated October 10, 2026
What you need to know

- Internet services suspended in central Delhi

Here is our rolling coverage of developments from India on Saturday, October 10:
Indian media houses say their journalists were briefly detained during Delhi protests
Indian media outlets, including Scroll and Newslaundry, reported that their journalists had been detained by police while covering the 'Cockroach' party protest. The journalists were later released.
Newslaundry reported that police seized its reporters’ phones, while other reports said journalists were physically assaulted.
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ), an independent nonprofit organization that promotes press freedom and defends journalists' rights worldwide, has called on Delhi Police to immediately release all detained journalists and media workers.
It has also urged police to return their equipment, investigate reports of physical abuse, and allow the press to cover the ongoing protests in New Delhi and the police response without interference.
In the 2026 World Press Freedom Index published by Reporters Without Borders (RSF), India ranked 157th out of 180 countries, down six places from 2025. 'Fire Tisch': Mamdani faces pressure from socialist allies to oust NYPD chief after ICE shooting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:46:31 UTC
12:46:31 KST

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is facing increasing pressure from some on the leftmost flank of his voting coalition, and an ICE shooting Thursday led democratic socialist allies to add their voices to a major demand: dump police commissioner Jessica Tisch.
“The NYPD’s Strategic Response Group must be disbanded as quickly as possible, and Commissioner Tisch must step down,” said Darializa Avila Chevalier, who won her Democratic primary with Mamdani’s endorsement. The democratic socialist, who is expected to join Congress next year representing Upper Manhattan and parts of the Bronx, was referring to the heavily armed police department unit that often responds to protests.
Another 17 democratic socialist elected officials and nominees — including congressional nominee Claire Valdez — signed a letter Friday which stated that Tisch “must end police assistance for ICE operations and disband NYPD’s Strategic Response Group — and if she won’t, she must be fired.”
The calls for Tisch’s removal follow strident criticism of the mayor from pro-Palestinian activists on Wednesday night who called him names, including “traitor” and “Ziohran,” when he showed up at an Oct. 7 Israeli peace vigil mourning the loss of both Jewish and Palestinian lives. The demonstrators assailed him for not doing more to advance the pro-Palestinian agenda that has long been central to his political beliefs, raising questions over whether he could lose parts of his base as he pledges to be a mayor for all New Yorkers.
The demand for Tisch’s removal came after an ICE agent shot and wounded a Dominican man in his car on Thursday afternoon while his 5-year-old son was in the back seat. Avila Chevalier, who joined protests against ICE on Thursday, wrote on X that the NYPD “spent more time protecting a militia that just shot someone than protecting New Yorkers.”
Mamdani's decision to retain Jessica Tisch drew support from Jewish organizations
Mamdani’s decision last year to retain Tisch — a self-described “proud Zionist” who comes from a prominent Jewish family — was seen as a reassuring move by moderates and establishment Jewish organizations including UJA-Federation of New York and the Jewish Community Relations Council. (70 Faces Media, the parent company of the Jewish Telegraphic Agency and New York Jewish Week, receives UJA funding.)
A number of progressives were skeptical of the decision at the time, citing her background as an appointee of Mamdani’s predecessor, Eric Adams, and her past criticism of campus pro-Palestinian protests. Some viewed her as an impediment to criminal justice reform.
Meanwhile, some on the left have dinged him for not yet following through on campaign promises 10 months into his term, including dissolving the Strategic Response Group, or backing down from his vow to arrest Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, a plan which he later said he did not have the power to execute.
Anti-Zionist groups including Pal-Awda, Within Our Lifetime and a number of student organizations who rallied against Mamdani at the Oct. 7 vigil accused him of succumbing “to Zionist pressure.” Protesters called him a “traitor” and a number of chants rang out including, “Mayor Mamdani you can’t hide, we charge you with genocide,” drowning out speakers at the vigil and forcing the organizers to move it behind police barricades to keep the protesters from overrunning the event.
Among those protesters’ many gripes with the mayor was his decision to retain Tisch. One sign at the demonstration depicted Mamdani with the text, “Chief Executive of the NYPD SRG” with a Star of David in the middle, and a name tag on the mayor’s chest reading, “Ziohran.”
Criticism was also directed at Mamdani for not stopping Israeli real estate events at synagogues, and for his strategy to combat antisemitism, released last week, which allocates funds to a number of community-based organizations aimed at preventing hate crimes. Some critics have charged that some of the funding will aid Zionist organizations.
“The Jewish community is a large part of New York, and it should be cherished. But you cannot fund these Anti-Defamation Leagues that prioritize Zionism over Judaism,” a John Jay College student protester, who declined to be named, told JTA during the demonstration.
On Thursday, the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City chapter — which Mamdani has called his “political home” — wrote that Tisch “must end NYPD complicity with ICE” and that if she “cannot put a stop to these injustices, she must be fired.”
“Abolish ICE. Disband the SRG. Fire Tisch,” wrote Illapa Sairitupac, a fellow democratic socialist who won the Democratic nomination for a Lower Manhattan State Assembly district. Mamdani endorsed both Sairitupac and Avila Chevalier this past year.
Mamdani allies question whether pro-Palestinian protesters represent his voter base
While some protesters at the vigil said they were Mamdani voters — and one speaker even identified herself as a former intern for the now-mayor — some of the mayor’s allies have stressed that the crowd protesting him was not representative of his base.
“If I had to gamble, I would gamble that the vast majority of them were people who never supported him,” activist Abby Stein told JTA on Thursday night, during the Mazals gala held by left-wing group Jews for Racial & Economic Justice. Mamdani was due to attend the JFREJ event, but because of the ICE shooting was instead in the Bronx, where he denounced the federal agency and demanded that it cease its operations in New York City.
Many of the signs excoriating Mamdani at Wednesday’s protest outside of City Hall were signed with the name of the Maoist Communist Union, an organization that opposed Mamdani before he took office. Some protesters were handing out copies of Spartacist, the Trotskyist International Communist League’s journal.
“We certainly didn’t support Mamdani or vote for him,” said Erica Jones, among the Trotskyist protesters. “We knew he was running as a Democrat and he would be as big of a sellout as AOC and Bernie Sanders and all the rest of those who claim to have, at one time, stood for socialism but in reality, stand for the capitalist masters who are oppressing us all.”
Mamdani ally criticizes protesters' tactics but shares concerns over NYPD chief
Stein, a member of the DSA in addition to JFREJ, called out some of the protesters’ rhetoric and the choice to crash the Israelis for Peace Oct. 7 vigil. But she also acknowledged that there was overlap between their demands and her views, including over the police commissioner.
“There are things that people are upset over that I think are legit — like keeping Jessica Tisch on, for example,” Stein said. “A lot of us were not very happy about it.”
Ultimately, Stein said there is “always going to be something to protest” with any politician, and pointed to a quote from New York’s mayor in the 1970s and ‘80s, Ed Koch: “If you agree with me on 9 out of 12 issues, vote for me. If you agree with me on 12 out of 12 issues, see a psychiatrist.”
