Black-Jewish alliance isn’t nostalgia. We need it to defend democracy - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:46:16 UTC
12:46:16 KST

At the recent 2026 Atlanta Summit for Black Pastors and Rabbis, I joined 100 rabbis, Black American clergy, Black Jewish leaders, scholars, activists, and community leaders in signing a Sacred Covenant affirming a renewed national commitment to unite against antisemitism and racism.
I was honored to stand shoulder to shoulder with Georgia Sen. Rev. Raphael Warnock, Amb. Andrew Young, journalist Van Jones, Rabbis Rick Jacobs, David Saperstein and Heather Miller, Rev. Mariama White-Hammond of the New Roots African Methodist Episcopal Church and many other leaders to discuss how to further our alliance.
Amid surging antisemitism and discrimination, conversations were heavy, but I was reminded that this partnership isn’t nostalgia; it’s a living commitment each generation must choose. I was also struck by the particular weight carried by my Black Jewish colleagues, whose experiences can show the complexity of navigating both Black and Jewish spaces. The Black-Jewish alliance is not simply a partnership between two distinct communities; it is lived every day by Black Jews whose experiences remind us that neither community is a monolith.
History of the Black-Jewish alliance
When I speak with Jewish peers about events like this, they’re sometimes surprised to hear that the Black-Jewish alliance is still so alive. They tell me that the allyship seen in the civil rights movement was frozen in time, and that following the Hamas raids inside Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, some Jews have felt abandoned by progressive allies, including those in the Black community. Disagreements over Israel and Gaza, debates about the meaning of solidarity, and diverging views on what is or is not antisemitic deeply challenge us.
Despite these areas of friction, in my experience, the Black-Jewish alliance is far from a relic of the past. The history of this alliance runs deeper than most people know and continues to this day.
As the director of the Religious Action Center of Reform Judaism, I take tremendous pride in sharing the story of our founding, including the 1959 stipulation by philanthropist, civil rights activist, and Reform Jewish leader Kivie Kaplan that the Washington, D.C. building he gifted to be our Reform movement’s home serve as a hub for the civil rights movement. My predecessor and the RAC’s founding director, Rabbi Dick Hirsch, invited his friend Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to use our space as his office when in town, and I fervently wish our building’s walls could talk.
Because of this special history, the Voting Rights Act of 1965 was partly drafted in our conference room, rooted in the bloodshed in places like Selma, Alabama, and Neshoba County, Mississippi, by people including future Rep. John Lewis, as well as Andrew Goodman, James Chaney, and Michael Schwerner, two white Jewish men and a Black Christian man whose sacrifices continue to inspire. Equally inspiring is the work of many Black Jews, such as Charles McDew and Julius Lester, who made significant contributions during the civil rights movement, but are too often overlooked. That commitment to showing up for each other brings us to the ballot box today.
Voting rights continue to connect both communities
Through my seats on the boards of the NAACP and The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights, I work every day with Black Jewish colleagues and leaders in the Black community to protect voting rights more than 10 years after the Supreme Court’s decision in Shelby County v. Holder decimated the Voting Rights Act; stand against antisemitism and racism in the face of attacks like the racially motivated 2022 Tops Grocery shooting in Buffalo and the assault this year on Temple Israel in West Bloomfield, Michigan; expand health care in the face of narrowing Affordable Care Act coverage; reform our broken criminal justice system that still sees the disproportionate incarceration of Black men; and protect critical programs like the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program.
Today’s moments of crisis also echo the past: The recent arson attack against Beth Israel Congregation in Jackson, Mississippi, recalls the Ku Klux Klan’s bombing of the congregation in 1967 over its rabbi’s civil rights work. When the building was set afire this past January, the Black community quickly came to the aid of the congregation at an “All-City Call to Prayer and Action.”
Voting rights continue to connect both communities. Democracy keeps Jews and all people safe, and it’s on the line. That’s not a political calculus; it’s a Jewish imperative. For more than 60 years, the RAC has existed to turn the Reform movement’s moral commitments into civic power, and nothing tests that mission more than the current assault on the right to vote, voter ID laws, racial gerrymandering, and attacks on vote-by-mail that threaten Jews and the Black, LGBTQ+, Latino, and immigrant communities alike.
As the Sacred Covenant we signed in Atlanta declared, “The Black-Jewish covenant cannot be sustained by nostalgia alone…. Sacred memory must become present responsibility.”
We must continue this alliance, in partnership with Black-led organizations, to ensure our communities are safe and our voices are heard.
That’s the Judaism I was ordained to practice: One where liberation only makes sense in solidarity with others who are still not free.

Montenegro expels founder of pro-Kremlin war blog Rybar over security concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:46:13 UTC
12:46:13 KST

The founder of the influential Russian war blog Rybar was arrested in Montenegro and then expelled with three other Russians on Friday for national security reasons, police and the state security agency said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, who is also a former Russian Defense Ministry official, was detained with others, including his wife, in the Adriatic resort of Risan on charges of spreading "Russian influence," Pobjeda newspaper reported, citing sources.
Rybar, one of the most popular blogs on Russia's war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers, posted a message saying Zvinchuk and the others had been in the country legally and were planning to film at a monastery there.
Rybar faced British sanctions
"Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released," Rybar said.
The Russian embassy in Podgorica said it had demanded clarification on the reasons for the arrests.
The blog is part of a network of sites and media feeds covering a wide range of Russian activities.
Britain imposed sanctions on 10 individuals linked to Rybar in July, saying the media company was resourced by the Russian state and "responsible for spreading false narratives about Ukraine and interfering in European elections, including in Moldova and Armenia."
Moscow has regularly denied accusations of misinformation and sabotage campaigns, saying the West is spreading anti-Russian propaganda.
Montenegro has long had fraught relations with Moscow. In 2016, authorities there accused Russia of plotting with a group of Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, a charge the Kremlin denied.
Ties soured further when the small Adriatic republic joined NATO in 2017.
Montenegro, a candidate for membership in the European Union, enforced sanctions against Russia over the war in Ukraine in 2022, banned Russian state media and expelled Russian diplomats for spying. In retaliation, Moscow declared it an enemy state.
'Montenegro is protecting its interests'
Montenegro's Prime Minister, Milojko Spajic, earlier announced the arrests and said there had been warnings that the country would face attempts to destabilize it and hybrid warfare - acts that fall short of direct military conflict.
"The message after today's successful operation ... is clear," he said. "Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future," he added.
Montenegrin police and the ANB state security agency said four Russian nationals they identified only by initials "were uncovered and processed."
"It was determined that these persons cannot continue their stay in Montenegro ... (and) it was decided to expel them from Montenegro for reasons of national and internal security of the state," the statement read.
A police source confirmed the four were Zvinchuk and the other Russians.
In October 2024, the US State Department offered a reward of up to $10 million for information leading to the identification of 19 individuals involved in managing Rybar-led social media channels, saying they had promoted Russia's political interests in the US ahead of the 2024 presidential elections.

Trump takes suit against Hillary Clinton over 2016 election to Supreme Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:46:13 UTC
12:46:13 KST

President Donald Trump asked the US Supreme Court on Friday to revive his dismissed lawsuit against his 2016 Democratic rival Hillary Clinton accusing her of conspiring along with former FBI Director James Comey and others to rig that year's election by linking his campaign to Russia.
The Republican president filed his appeal after a federal judge threw out the case and imposed nearly $1 million in sanctions against Trump and one of his lawyers for bringing a "frivolous" suit. A US appeals court subsequently upheld the dismissal and sanctions.
Trump's lawyers wrote in the appeal that Supreme Court review of the case is needed in order to protect the presidency. They wrote that the decisions by the lower courts reflect "a deeply troubling trend of federal courts using sanctions and disciplinary threats to punish the president and his lawyers for legitimate legal positions that those courts (erroneously) reject."
In 2022, when he was out of office after losing the 2020 election, Trump sued Clinton, Comey, former British intelligence officer Christopher Steele, the Democratic National Committee and numerous others in a lengthy complaint filed in federal court in Florida.
Trump, who has a history of suing adversaries, alleged that in the lead-up to the 2016 election, Clinton conspired with allies to discredit him with a "false narrative" that he and his campaign colluded with Russia. The lengthy suit alleged "racketeering" and a "conspiracy to commit injurious falsehood," among other claims.
Trump defeated Clinton in that election despite losing the national popular vote and served his first term from 2017 to 2021.
US government officials have accused Russia of meddling in the 2016 election, and an investigation led by former FBI chief Robert Mueller documented extensive contacts between members of the Trump campaign and Russian operatives who sought to influence the election in his favor. Trump has called the idea of Russian interference a "hoax."
Since losing to Democrat Joe Biden in 2020, Trump has made false claims of widespread voting fraud in that year's election. Trump regained the presidency by defeating Democrat Kamala Harris in 2024, and has continued to make those false claims.
'Political manifesto'
US District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed Trump's lawsuit against Clinton, citing numerous inadequacies, including that Trump waited too long to bring some of the claims. The judge likened Trump's lawsuit to a "two-hundred-page political manifesto outlining his grievances against those that have opposed him."
Middlebrooks later ordered Trump and his lead attorney in the case, Alina Habba, to pay nearly $1 million in fees and costs, imposing the sanctions for bringing a case that the judge said was intended "to dishonestly advance a political narrative." The judge also faulted Trump and his lawyers for a "continuing pattern of misuse of the courts."
Middlebrooks found that the lawsuit used abusive litigation tactics, contained "knowingly false" factual allegations and asserted "frivolous" legal theories.
The Atlanta-based 11th US Circuit Court of Appeals upheld the judge's rulings in 2025, including the sanctions.
"Many of Trump's and Habba's legal arguments were indeed frivolous," the 11th Circuit stated.
In Friday's filing, lawyers for Trump and Habba said the time limit for filing the lawsuit should have been extended because he chose to defer suing during his first term in office in order to carry out his constitutional responsibilities as president.
"This court's intervention is necessary to protect the presidency, and to prevent judicial disagreement from becoming a license to punish its advocates," the filing stated.
Russia's effort to tilt the 2016 election in Trump's favor
Mueller, serving as a special counsel appointed by the Justice Department, issued a 2019 report on his investigation. The report stated that Russia "interfered in the 2016 presidential election in sweeping and systematic fashion," but also stated that "the investigation did not establish that members of the Trump campaign conspired or coordinated with the Russian government in its election interference activities."
Mueller said in his report that he found "numerous links" and that the Trump campaign "expected it would benefit" from Russia's effort to tilt the election in Trump's favor.
Trump's then-Attorney General William Barr appointed a different special counsel, John Durham, in 2019 to look into potential missteps by the FBI.
In a 2023 report, Durham concluded that the FBI lacked "actual evidence" to investigate Trump's 2016 presidential campaign and relied too heavily on tips provided by Trump's political opponents to fuel the probe.
Trump's Justice Department last year indicted Comey, one of several adversaries of the president hit with criminal charges, accusing him of making false statements and obstructing Congress after he was accused of lying about authorizing leaks to the news media. A federal judge subsequently dismissed the indictment, finding that the prosecutor who Trump handpicked to prosecute Comey had been unlawfully appointed.
Steele, working for an opposition research firm that was hired by a law firm on behalf of the Clinton campaign and the Democratic National Committee, produced a dossier that alleged ties between Trump's campaign and Russia as well as other salacious accusations, all of which Trump denied.

"Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel Prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of. I've never heard of the person," Trump said during a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York.

"In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations. They were of no help to me," Trump said. "The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't."
Trump blasts Norway over Nobel Peace Prize decision
He then directed his anger at Norway, where the Nobel Peace Prize committee is based.

Trump concluded by returning to his own record on peace and his criticism of the Nobel process.
"Based on my record of peace — a record like no one ever has had — I'm just saying how crooked the whole Nobel Prize deal is," he said.

Celebrity chef who signed Hospitality for Humanity pledge shares stage with Israelis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:46:00 UTC
12:46:00 KST

When celebrity chef and Bay Area food ambassador Samin Nosrat appeared this week at San Francisco’s JCC alongside two Israeli chefs, it was nearly three years since she pledged not to buy or promote Israeli food.
The Chez Panisse alum and author of 2017’s smash hit “Salt Fat Acid Heat” joined Israeli chefs Itamar Srulovich and Sarit Packer, the couple behind a beloved London restaurant, to discuss their latest cookbook, “Honey & Co. Daily: Easy Food for Your Everyday Pleasure.”
In promoting the event, Nosrat urged people to join her in the JCCSF’s sukkah to enjoy bites from Loquat, a Jewish bakery in the Hayes Valley neighborhood of San Francisco that she calls her favorite. The celebration of Jewish and Israeli food culture came two days shy of the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attack on Israel.
Hospitality for Humanity pledge
Nosrat was among those who signed the Hospitality for Humanity pledge in 2023, which, in accordance with the boycott, divestment and sanctions movement, committed signers to “not purchasing, using, or promoting Israeli agricultural or food products … so long as Israel continues its system of apartheid, occupation, settler colonialism, and genocide.” Israel rejects the genocide charge.
The boycott drew signatures from more than 1,100 people across the industry. When the New York Times covered the saga in November 2023, it listed Nosrat as one of its most prominent supporters.
The pledge targets Israeli products, not Israeli people, and Srulovich and Packer are longtime friends of Nosrat’s.
Nosrat did not return several requests for comment, nor has she publicly disavowed the boycott, which has scrambled Israeli and Jewish food businesses’ relationship with other Middle Eastern cuisines. New York magazine depicted this tension in August in its Habibi City series, which proposed that Israel’s war in Gaza had ushered in a golden era for Southwest Asian and North African restaurants, at the peril of cuisines considered Jewish or Israeli.
Bay Area restaurants have felt the pressure, too. Guy Eshel, the Israeli owner of Sababa, a popular pita eatery in San Francisco’s Financial District, told J. that he recently sold his shop, citing the dual pressures of a struggling downtown and anti-Israel sentiment. Mica Talmor, an Israeli chef who ran Oakland’s Pomella until last year, said that stress related to Oct. 7 and its aftermath contributed to the restaurant’s closure.
Nosrat shares Jewish ancestry
In the years since signing the boycott pledge, Nosrat, a first-generation Iranian American raised by a Muslim mother and Baha’i father, revealed a family secret: Her paternal ancestors were Jewish.
She found out by accident. Nosrat had gone looking for her estranged father’s will as he lay on his deathbed. The search returned a hidden YouTube channel with hours of her father “ranting.”
In those recordings, “he revealed we had Jewish ancestry, which had always been kept from us,” she told podcast host Sam Fragoso last year while promoting her new book, “Good Things.” “I was like, this is so cool, this is amazing. Like, there’s just things where I’m like, wow, I wish I had known this about myself.”
Rabbi Tarlan Rabizadeh, who oversees the Maas Center for Jewish Journeys at the American Jewish University in Los Angeles, said she has seen many Iranian students discover they have Jewish roots.
“It’s not easy being a minority religion in a majority Muslim community,” Rabizadeh said. “So a lot of people either hid their Judaism or converted, and then their great- great-grandkids didn’t find out until someone revealed it on their deathbed.”
Religion was central to the Nosrat family story. In the mid-1970s, as the pressure in Iran intensified, Nosrat’s parents fled to escape the persecution of Baha’is.
Her father’s death, combined with her own depression, the lingering effects of the COVID pandemic, and a growing self-doubt following the success of “Salt, Fat, Acid, Heat,” triggered a personal excavation.
“So many people at this point in time are deeply searching for a sense of meaning and sort of trying to answer for themselves this question of ‘what is a good life?’” Nosrat told Fragoso.
She found answers in Jewish teaching, and one 20th-century rabbi in particular. A friend slipped her a copy of Rabbi Abraham Joshua Heschel’s 1951 book “The Sabbath.” Heschel, a Poland-born American rabbi, was one of the foremost Jewish voices of the Civil Rights Era and marched alongside the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr. in Selma, Alabama.
Nosrat was taken by Heschel’s description of “Judaism being a religion not of things, but basically of time.”
“A huge practice in that is the carving out of this sabbath. I think he calls it a cathedral in time,” Nosrat told Fragoso. “I have tried to figure out what I am doing with my life and why. The answer … has ultimately been about figuring out a way to maximize or value my time the best I possibly can, and to share this message of how important time is for all of us.”
Whether that search has changed how she views the boycott, Nosrat hasn’t said.
'Jewish identity is central to politics in the US'
Historian Arash Azizi, a lecturer at Yale University who is writing a book on the relationship between Israel and Iran, said the discovery of Jewish roots tends to have a more profound effect on people than finding out they are, say, from some other region in the world.
“It’s because Jewish belonging is a much more contentious issue than, let’s say, Italian belonging,” Azizi said. “Jews are a small population relatively, but the Jewish identity is central to politics in the US and other places. So, it’s not surprising at all that declaring Jewish identity would be a bigger deal.”
Azizi said he has been “disturbed” by how the war in Gaza has forced people, particularly those in the public eye, to take a position unlike with any other global event.
“This is the be all and end all for so many people, and it speaks to the monochromatic nature of culture wars in America,” Azizi said. “Americans think they’re talking about the world, but it’s always about themselves. The Israeli-Palestinian conflict is used as a cudgel in these parochial culture wars.”
For Talmor, the event with Nostrat reaffirms her view that food should not be politicized to the point of excluding people.
“Criticizing a government is one thing. Shutting out its people, its artists, its farmers and its chefs is another,” she said. “I’d rather see chefs sit at the same table and talk than draw lines around who gets a seat.”
Aliza Sokolow, an Emmy-winning food stylist based in Los Angeles, said she supported Nosrat’s effort to “come and learn,” despite her Israel boycott pledge.
“I’m going to reach out and invite her to Shabbat next time she’s in town,” Sokolow said.

Bladder cancer frequently misdiagnosed as UTIs in women
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:45:07 UTC
12:45:07 KST

Women's bladder cancer symptoms dismissed as UTIs, perimenopause amid calls for more awareness
In short:
In Australia, three in four people diagnosed with bladder cancer are men, but the five-year survival rate for women is much lower.
It is common for women to face diagnostic delays, with symptoms easily misdiagnosed as urinary tract infections (UTIs) or perimenopause.
What's next?
Experts are calling for greater awareness about bladder cancer symptoms, as well of the importance of referrals for women with recurrent bladder infections.
Four years.
That is how much time passed between when Andrea Harris first presented to her GP with a suspected bladder infection, and when she was diagnosed with advanced, muscle-invasive bladder cancer.
Ms Harris went back to the doctor multiple times over these four years, wanting to understand more about the root cause of her symptoms.
At one stage, Ms Harris recalls being "in tears" in the doctor's office, pressing for more extensive testing.
"I'd have a seven-day lot of antibiotics, and I'd be good for six or seven weeks and then I'd start to get symptoms again," she said.
By the time she was finally diagnosed in March 2024, Ms Harris's cancer had advanced to stage three.
In Australia, three in four people diagnosed with bladder cancer are men, but experts are concerned about the number of women, like Ms Harris, presenting with late-stage bladder cancer.
Alison Zhang, a medical oncologist at Macquarie University Hospital, said although bladder cancer symptoms, like blood in the urine and a frequent need to wee, were similar in both sexes, they were easy to misdiagnose as urinary tract infections (UTIs) or perimenopause in women.
Bladder cancer in Australia
About 3,345 cases of bladder cancer were estimated to be diagnosed in Australia last year.
But unlike most other cancers, the five-year survival rate has dropped since 1987.
Women diagnosed with bladder cancer in Australia face about a 50 per cent chance of living five years post-diagnosis, while men have an almost 60 per cent chance.
"Women tend to present later with later-stage disease, which is a real problem," Dr Zhang said.
Magdalena Simonis, a practising GP and women's health expert from the University of Melbourne, said men often had their bladder cancer symptoms — especially blood in the urine — escalated quickly as UTIs were far less common in men, and therefore unlikely to be the cause.
"If a man shows up with microscopic, that is, invisible blood in the urine, or visible blood in the urine, we would immediately advance that person to further investigations," she said.
"When a woman presents with the symptoms of bladder cancer, the symptoms are not dissimilar to those of a UTI; they might have a burning sensation with urination or blood in their urine."
Christine La Rose, a patient and support lead for advocacy group BEAT Bladder Cancer Australia, said there needed to be "more focus, more urgency and awareness" on improving outcomes for women.
Ms La Rose, a bladder cancer survivor herself, faced a short diagnostic delay after initially being told the blood in her urine had been caused by a UTI.
"Blood in the urine should never be ignored; it should always be investigated,"
she said.
Other common symptoms of bladder cancer include a sudden change in urine colour, loss of appetite and weight loss.
Need for better referral pathways
There are a few things that experts agree will help improve outcomes for women.
The first, Dr Zhang said, was to increase community awareness about the symptoms of bladder cancer.
The second, Dr Simonis said, was that women who presented with recurrent UTIs — more than two within six months or three within a year — needed their symptoms investigated further with additional testing and/or a referral to a urologist.
"Women have traditionally been dismissed if they've got pain or ongoing symptoms," she said.
"Any level of discomfort that is continuous is something that we shouldn't really put up with."
Dr Simonis said GPs needed to consider risk factors of bladder disease, such as smoking and age, when treating female patients presenting with UTI-like symptoms.
"If they're a smoker, and they've got ongoing symptoms and recurrent symptoms, then alarm bells should ring a lot earlier," she said.
Ms La Rose said although bladder cancer was "traditionally seen as an older man's disease", she had met women in their 20s, 30s and 40s who had been diagnosed with it.
"You know your body best. If something doesn't feel right, go get it checked out,"
she said.
"Go back or go and get a second opinion. You really need to advocate for yourself and push for answers."
Margaret Blake was one of the many Australian women who needed to do just that.
Ms Blake saw three different GPs within the space of six months, concerned about her frequent need to urinate and finding blood in her urine.
She said her third GP was the first one to take her symptoms seriously, referring her for a series of tests, which eventually led to her bladder cancer diagnosis.
Survivors Ms Harris, Ms La Rose and Ms Blake all live with the ongoing consequences of treatment.
Ms La Rose has a neo-bladder, built by a surgeon using a piece of her intestine, which she is grateful to be able to empty easily and maintains a good quality of life.
"I'm really lucky. And I also know how lucky I am to still be here, given the diagnosis," she said.
"I know that if I'd waited any longer, the outcome could have been much much worse."

Merve Aydogan
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
US President Donald Trump on Friday attacked this year's Nobel Peace Prize winner, describing her as "a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of."
Trump said he himself had "never heard of the person," referring to South African jurist Navi Pillay, who chaired a UN commission of inquiry that concluded Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
"Today they gave out the Nobel Peace Prize to a person I never heard of. The person nobody did. It’s a mystery person," he said at a Republican campaign rally in Syracuse, New York ahead of the Nov. 3 midterm elections, adding: "But congratulations anyway."
Trump repeated his assertion that he "settled eight wars," citing the conflict between India and Pakistan as an example.
"Any one of these eight wars, you get the Nobel Prize. I did eight. No president’s ever done any," he said.
He then escalated his criticism of the Nobel Peace Prize Committee and Norway, the country it comes from.
"The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway," he said.
He claimed the prize had been "forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization."
"We will not forget Norway," said Trump, adding that the omission was "just another sign of how Norway and all these others are ripping off our country."
 
Trump accuse 'enemies of civilization' of discrediting prize
Later Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform: "I know nothing about this woman, and neither does anyone else! In fact, to the best of my knowledge, no one ever heard of her other than the fact that she, very obviously, hates Israel.”
Saying he should have gotten the award, Trump added: “The Nobel ‘Peace’ Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of Radical Ideologues who are Anti-Democracy, and Enemies of Civilization!”
Trump has long made the case that he is deserving of the Nobel Peace Prize and criticized how to date he has not been awarded it.
Pillay served as a judge and president of the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, as a judge at the International Criminal Court, and as the United Nations high commissioner for human rights from 2008 to 2014.
She chaired a UN inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory from 2021 to 2025. That commission said Israel had committed genocide in the Gaza Strip, a finding Israel rejected.
The Nobel Committee said she played a central role in efforts to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, and that her work had widened the effect of international law.

Russian presidential aide says Putin-Trump conversation was substantive, friendly
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:29:33 UTC
12:29:33 KST

MOSCOW, October 10. /TASS/. A phone call between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US counterpart Donald Trump lasted an hour and a half and was substantive and friendly, Russian Presidential Aide Yury Ushakov told reporters.
TASS has compiled the key takeaways from Ushakov’s statements.
Details of phone call
Russian and US officials began preparing for the call on October 7, when Ushakov spoke by phone with US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff. Witkoff conveyed Trump’s birthday wishes to Putin.
"Steve Witkoff also said that Trump wanted to congratulate Putin personally by phone. We then began looking for a convenient time for the call, <…> taking into account the time difference between Moscow and Washington. We also had to consider Putin’s planned departure for the CIS summit in Turkmenistan on the morning of October 8.
"We eventually agreed that the best option would be to speak as soon as our president returned from that trip."
"President Trump postponed some events that had been scheduled for today, and so the phone call took place late in the evening on October 9."
Putin and Trump had a "very substantive," even friendly conversation that lasted an hour and a half.
"Donald Trump immediately warmly congratulated Vladimir Putin on his birthday and wished him success and well-being. He also remembered to convey greetings from his wife, Melania," Ushakov said.
"Nobody wanted to hang up first. In light of that, I hope the US president will not be offended if I quote his words that he was ‘ready to continue communicating with Vladimir Putin today, this evening, tonight and the next day.’"
Putin and Trump expressed satisfaction with the communication channels functioning between the two countries through their presidential administrations, intelligence services and other relevant agencies.
"As for the substance of the conversation, I, of course, cannot satisfy your curiosity, dear colleagues. I also cannot go into detail about the specific issues the presidents discussed."
Kiev’s actions and the situation on the battlefield
Putin told Trump that Russia’s position on the goals and objectives of its special military operation remains unchanged. Russia also remains ready for a political and diplomatic settlement to achieve a lasting and sustainable peace.
Ushakov said the possibility of resuming trilateral talks involving the United States and Ukraine had been discussed during the presidents’ previous conversation, with negotiations potentially restarting immediately after Russia’s State Duma elections. "The situation is different now," he said.
Kiev’s attempts to disrupt parliamentary elections in Russia had effectively undermined the possibility of immediately resuming negotiations. "And now, as the president said, we will consider when these negotiations can be resumed," Ushakov added.
Putin also spoke in detail about Russia’s response to Ukrainian attacks.
"Vladimir Putin spoke in detail about the measures we are taking in response to terrorist attacks by the Kiev regime, which has opted for escalation and every possible means of prolonging the conflict," Ushakov said.
Putin told Trump that Russian forces have full control of the initiative along the line of contact and are advancing confidently.
"It was emphasized that Kiev’s attempts to halt the advance of Russian forces along the entire line of contact by launching strikes deep into our territory have no chance of success. Our armed forces have full control of the initiative and are advancing confidently," Ushakov said.
Prospects for an in-person meeting
Putin said he values the attention the US leadership is devoting to dialogue with Russia despite its domestic agenda and involvement in Middle Eastern affairs.
The presidents did not discuss specific dates for their next in-person meeting.
Putin and Trump currently plan to attend the APEC summit in China and may find an opportunity to meet there.
"An important international event is coming up in China - the APEC summit. At least for now, both the Russian and US leaders are interested in attending. Accordingly, if both leaders are at the same international venue, I assume they will find an opportunity to meet, shake hands and talk," Ushakov said.
Economic initiatives and petroleum products
"The two leaders discussed preparations for major economic initiatives in detail, including potential supplies of Russian petroleum products to US and global markets. The Russian and US presidents have already issued a special statement on the matter," Ushakov said.
Humanitarian cooperation
Putin thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her contribution to reuniting children with their families in Russia and Ukraine.
Regarding concerns about the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki, in the Kherson Region, it was agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in regular contact with Melania Trump’s staff.
The situation surrounding Iran
"Vladimir Putin specifically emphasized that diplomatic options on the Iran track have by no means been exhausted: an agreement with Tehran can and should be reached through negotiations," Ushakov said.
Putin also told Trump that Moscow’s offer to transfer Iran’s enriched uranium to Russia remains on the table.
Witkoff hopes to meet Putin soon
"Steve Witkoff asked me to add his own and Jared Kushner’s (a US businessman and Trump’s son-in-law - TASS) warmest wishes to our president, whom he sincerely respects and hopes to meet soon," Ushakov said.

Taiwan exceeds WHO hepatitis C targets ahead of 2030
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:25:10 UTC
12:25:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s hepatitis C treatment rate reached 92.7% by the end of last year, meeting the World Health Organization’s target ahead of schedule, the Health Promotion Administration said Friday.
WHO’s gold-tier targets require diagnosing at least 80% of people with chronic hepatitis C and treating at least 70% of those diagnosed. Its 2030 targets raise these thresholds to 90% and 80%, respectively, both of which the country has already exceeded after a decade of efforts.
By December, 92.4% of people in Taiwan with chronic hepatitis C had been diagnosed, while 92.7% of those diagnosed had received treatment. Expanded screening has played a key role in identifying infections and connecting patients with care.
The country offers free hepatitis C screening to people aged 39-79, following an expansion in 2020 and a lower minimum eligible age last year. By December, 7.86 million people in the target population had been screened, according to the Ministry of Health and Welfare.
Those who test positive can receive direct-acting antiviral drugs, which have a cure rate of nearly 99%. The National Health Insurance Administration began covering the drugs in 2017 and expanded coverage in 2019 to include patients regardless of the severity of their liver fibrosis.
Efforts have also extended to groups at higher risk of infection. Treatment rates have reached 95% among dialysis patients, people receiving methadone replacement therapy, and people living with human immunodeficiency virus, or HIV.
Hepatitis C is a viral infection that can cause chronic liver disease. While acute infections may produce symptoms such as fever, nausea, vomiting, and jaundice, many infections can go unnoticed because they may produce few or no symptoms, according to the Centers for Disease Control.
About 70- 80% of infected people develop chronic hepatitis, which can progress to cirrhosis or liver cancer. Taiwan has expanded medical services in rural and mountainous areas while monitoring chronic liver disease and cirrhosis deaths linked to hepatitis B and C.

Isaias weakens to Category 1 hurricane after Florida landfall, NHC says
Oct 9 - Hurricane Isaias weakened to a Category 1 storm on Friday, rapidly lost wind speed after hitting the Florida coast, the US National Hurricane Center said while warning of storm surges and snapped power lines as it moves through the Deep South.
The hurricane, crossing the western Florida Panhandle after making landfall near Destin as a Category 2 storm, was about 65 miles (105 km) west-northwest of Panama City, Florida, packing maximum sustained winds of 90 mph (150 kph), the NHC said in an advisory.
The center warned of possible storm surges, urban and river flooding and flash floods across the region, with considerable impacts likely across much of southern Alabama and the Florida Panhandle into southwest Georgia.
Isaias, the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, is expected to continue weakening but produce gusty winds well inland through Saturday even after it becomes post-tropical, the NHC said.
Alabama's emergency management agency said the hurricane has downed trees and power lines, making travel hazardous in Houston County, which is under a flash flood warning.
"Due to the impacts of Hurricane Isaias, all Houston County roads are closed until further notice," it posted on X. "These road closures will remain in effect until conditions are deemed safe for travel."
Isaias is expected to cross Alabama and go into the Tennessee Valley over the weekend, the NHC said.
President Donald Trump, asked about hurricane preparations, told reporters outside the White House, "We're watching it very closely, the hurricane," adding that it was "under control."
More than 412,000 people in Florida and nearly 243,000 in Alabama lost power as the storm hit shore, according to power outage tracking firm PowerOutage.us.
"Emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to Isaias," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on X.
Florida's emergency services urged residents to shelter in place and watch for hurricane conditions across the north of the state. REUTERS

Israeli attacks leave more dead in Gaza as ceasefire nears one year
Israeli attacks have left more Palestinians dead in Gaza as the ceasefire approaches its first anniversary, without bringing an end to the violence.
At least eight Palestinians were killed and several others wounded in Israeli strikes and gunfire across the enclave on Thursday and Friday, according to local medical sources and rescue workers.
On Friday, Israeli troops reportedly shot dead a Palestinian man near refugee camps in central Gaza, wounding several others.
Seven people were reported killed on Thursday, including three in drone strikes on a vehicle and a tent sheltering displaced Palestinians in Gaza City.
“Two people, a woman and a child, were killed and others were wounded when Israeli aircraft bombed a residential building” in Gaza City, the Civil Defense Service said. Another woman was killed by artillery fire, while a separate fatality was reported in central Gaza.
The Israeli military told AFP that three of those killed were members of armed groups and said it was checking reports concerning the other four deaths.
The US-brokered ceasefire took effect on October 10, 2025. Israel has continued to conduct strikes, saying it is targeting militants and accusing Hamas of violating the agreement.
More than 1,450 Palestinians have been killed and over 5,000 wounded since the truce began, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. UK-based aid group Islamic Relief said on Thursday that an average of one Palestinian has been killed or wounded every 90 minutes over the past year, with at least 320 children among those killed.
The agreement envisioned Israeli troop withdrawals and reconstruction, but progress has stalled over Hamas disarmament demands. The group said it had agreed in principle to a US-backed proposal but would not surrender its weapons until Israeli forces had withdrawn completely. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has demanded that Hamas disarm before further withdrawals. He has also said he ordered the IDF to expand its control to 70% of Gaza, up from roughly 53% when the ceasefire took effect.
Nearly all of Gaza’s 2.1 million residents have been displaced during the war, which has left much of the enclave in ruins. Around 82% of its structures have been damaged or destroyed, according to Islamic Relief, while reconstruction has barely begun.
Israel’s military campaign has killed more than 74,200 Palestinians and wounded over 175,000 since October 2023, according to Gaza’s Health Ministry. The war began after Hamas-led militants attacked southern Israel, killing around 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.
Netanyahu has also faced scrutiny over reports that he received advance warnings of the October 7 attack but downplayed the threat. Haaretz reported that UAE President Mohamed bin Zayed had warned him of a possible major Hamas operation roughly ten days beforehand. Netanyahu’s office dismissed the allegation as an “absolute lie.” The Israeli leader traveled to Abu Dhabi in late September to seek a denial of the claim that he had been warned.

12:22:53 KST

Major fire reported at oil terminal linked to Russia's Novoshakhtinsk refinery after suspected drone strike
A large fire broke out at an oil-loading terminal in Russia's Rostov-on-Don overnight on Oct. 9–10 amid a reported drone attack, according to footage published by the Exilenova+ monitoring channel.
An OSINT analyst with the independent Russian outlet ASTRA identified the burning facility as the Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal in Rostov-on-Don's Zheleznodorozhny district, based on footage supplied by local residents.
The terminal handles petroleum products for export, including shipments from the Novoshakhtinsk Oil Refinery, which belongs to the Yug Rusi group of companies.
Videos circulating on multiple accounts on Telegram appeared to show large flames and thick smoke rising from the site. Exilenova+ later reported that the terminal was still burning.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the footage or determine the extent of the damage.
Russian regional authorities acknowledged a fire and reported that air defenses were operating, but did not confirm damage to the terminal, and Ukrainian military officials had not claimed responsibility for the reported attack.
ASTRA also reported damage to a residential building in Rostov-on-Don's Donskaya Sloboda complex, identifying its location through footage posted by residents. It remained unclear what struck the building amid reports of continued drone activity and Russian air defense operations.
The Yug Rusi oil-loading terminal is separate from the Novoshakhtinsk refinery's main processing facilities. According to the refinery's published specifications, its Rostov-on-Don terminal has an annual capacity of 3.5 million metric tons for receiving and shipping petroleum products.
The reported attack follows a Ukrainian strike on the Novoshakhtinsk refinery on Sept. 25, which sparked a fire at the facility, according to Ukraine's General Staff.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian oil refineries, storage depots and fuel infrastructure in recent months in an effort to disrupt fuel supplies to the Russian military and reduce Moscow's energy revenues.
U.S. President Donald Trump has urged Ukraine to halt strikes on Russian oil facilities, arguing that the attacks contribute to rising global diesel prices.
Zelensky has said Ukraine is prepared to stop targeting Russian energy facilities if Moscow agrees to halt its own attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure, insisting that any pause must be reciprocal.

UN warns of worsening humanitarian crisis in Ukraine as winter approaches
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:01:26 UTC
12:01:26 KST

Diyar Guldogan
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
The UN on Friday warned that repeated attacks on civilian areas and critical infrastructure in Ukraine are deepening the humanitarian crisis ahead of winter.
Gemma Connell, director of the Crisis Response Division at the UN Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA), urged Russia and Ukraine to protect civilians, facilitate aid deliveries, and ensure safe evacuations for people trapped in frontline and occupied areas.
Connell delivered a briefing to the Security Council on behalf of Tom Fletcher, the UN under-secretary-general for humanitarian affairs and emergency relief coordinator.
“The past 48 hours have brought more death and destruction across Ukraine,” said Connell, describing attacks on residential neighborhoods, public transport, and essential civilian infrastructure in multiple regions.
Repeated attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure have brought back scheduled and emergency power cuts, including in Kyiv, according to Connell.
“Winter preparedness cannot wait for winter,” she told the council.
The UN’s $358 million Winter Response Plan aims to assist more than 2 million of Ukraine’s most vulnerable people with heating, shelter, food, healthcare, cash, and other essential support.
Connell said funding must arrive in time for aid agencies to position supplies, repair homes and heating systems, and help communities prepare for freezing temperatures.
She stressed, however, that humanitarian assistance alone cannot compensate for continued destruction of civilian infrastructure.
“Ultimately, no amount of preparedness can substitute for protecting the infrastructure civilians depend on in the first place,” she said.
Connell outlined three immediate priorities for the parties to the conflict: they must protect civilians and the infrastructure on which civilian life depends, in line with international humanitarian law; agree on practical arrangements to ensure humanitarian aid reaches civilians wherever they are and to enable safe and voluntary evacuations when needed; and humanitarian personnel must be protected, with credible investigations and accountability when incidents occur, she said.

What's next?

Pauline Hanson has used a speech at a conservative conference to urge voters to abandon the Coalition, while acknowledging she would work with them if it meant removing Labor from government.

Loading
"The Liberals signed us up to Paris and net zero. The Liberals legislated the safeguard mechanism, and Labor locked the targets into law and made them even worse," she said.
"They signed us up to this mess, so why would we trust them to get us out of it?"
Ms Hanson pledged to hold a royal commission into net zero climate targets, should One Nation be elected.
And she further criticised the Coalition for creating the office of the eSafety Commissioner, a position she has pledged to abolish on the grounds it infringes on free speech online.
Both Ms Hanson and Mr Taylor addressed CPAC — a spin-off of conservative conferences held in the US and UK — on Saturday morning, taking aim at the Albanese government and pitching themselves as the conservative alternative.
It was the first time a Coalition leader has addressed the annual forum, although notable Liberal figures like Tony Abbott and Jacinta Nampijinpa Price have addressed it in recent years.
But while Senator Hanson sharply criticised the Coalition, Mr Taylor made almost no mention of One Nation.
His speech made just one apparent indirect reference to Senator Hanson, referencing her dominance of the One Nation party and brand.
"Good government isn't built around one figure. You need a strong team," he said.
And he opened the speech by referencing a number of "mistakes" the Coalition made in government, acknowledging to the audience that "some of you may have doubts".
He pointed to areas like immigration policy, climate change and government spending during the pandemic as policy failures under Coalition governments.
"We made the mistake as a government of signing up to net zero," he said.
"Your frustrations about where we let you down in the recent past are understandable and reasonable. Believe me, I share them."
Both leaders reserved their strongest attacks for the Albanese government — Mr Taylor arguing it was leaving Australians "poorer, weaker, and demoralised", and Senator Hanson calling it "wretched and corrupt".

"One Nation will work with the Liberals and Nationals to remove this horrible Labor government and deliver something better," she said.

In a later press conference, she clarified that the offer extended to supply and confidence only — not a formal coalition.
"We will give them the numbers if they need it to form government, but I hope it's going to be the other way around," she said.
"So if we have the numbers, they will give us the numbers to form government. I don't want seats around their [cabinet] table."
She referenced her time in prison after a 2003 conviction for electoral fraud, later quashed on appeal, under the Howard government, but said she would put "personal grievances aside".
"Yes, I do have reasons to hold a grudge, but I also have children and grandchildren," she said.
"Their futures and your futures matter more."

"My message to you today is, look, we do wear lots of different colours. I get that," he said.
"There's lots of different people here.

Ukraine, US and European talks in Miami end early
Talks between representatives of the United States, Ukraine, European countries and NATO in Miami on ways to de-escalate and end the war have ended earlier than planned.
Source: Alex Raufoglu, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty's senior Washington correspondent; the US President's Special Envoy Steve Witkoff
Quote from Raufoglu: "Miami talks concluded sooner than planned. 'No second day,' sources tell me."
Details: Witkoff said that participants in the meeting had "held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace".
"The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine's and Europe's security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine's post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession," he wrote.
Witkoff stressed that the productive exchange of views had helped identify areas of work ahead of the United States' next contacts with Russia.
Background:
- On 8 October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that talks would take place in the US involving a Ukrainian delegation. This delegation included Davyd Arakhamiia, leader of the Servant of the People party; Rustem Umierov, Head of Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service; Kyrylo Budanov, Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine; and Serhii Kyslytsia, First Deputy Head of the Office of the President of Ukraine.
- Ahead of the meeting, Axios reported, citing US and Ukrainian officials, that US President's Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were planning to present "new ideas and proposals" in Miami to break the diplomatic deadlock.
- On 9 October, US President Donald Trump said he had had a "highly successful discussion" with Kremlin leader Vladimir Putin and reached an agreement on lifting sanctions on Russian diesel fuel.
- Zelenskyy strongly criticised Trump's actions, describing the easing of sanctions as an "absolutely terrible" move. He stressed that this "happy birthday present for Putin" will provide Russia with billions more to continue the war
- Zelenskyy said Ukraine's negotiating team in the US was being used as "cover" while Trump and Putin reached agreements on fuel supplies.

Chile declares part of Santiago disaster zone after heavy rains
Floods in Las Contes, affluent suburb of capital Santiago, leave 6 people injured, force evacuations, sweep vehicles through streets
Maryam Ashalem de Andres
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
ISTANBUL
Chile on Friday declared part of the capital Santiago a disaster zone after torrential rains triggered flash floods and mudslides, leaving at least six people injured and forcing evacuations, according to local media reports.
The declaration for Las Condes, an affluent suburb of the capital, allows public agencies to adopt extraordinary measures to coordinate emergency assistance, assess damage, and support recovery efforts.
Heavy rain on Thursday sent torrents of water and mud through streets, swept away vehicles, and inundated homes.
The Mapocho River also overflowed, while flooding made roads impassable and prompted emergency crews to respond to calls for help.
Las Condes Mayor Catalina San Martin said 14.4 centimeters (5.7 inches) of rain had fallen in recent days, around nine times the average October rainfall, leaving the ground saturated and raising the risk of additional flooding and landslides.
At least six people were reportedly injured, including a one-year-old who suffered fractures.
Firefighters rescued or evacuated more than 1,000 people as emergency teams worked to assist residents, clear debris, and restore access to affected areas.
The National Disaster Prevention and Response Service also declared a red alert for 10 municipalities in mountainous and foothill areas of the Santiago Metropolitan Region due to the risk of additional landslides.
Authorities urged residents to follow official safety instructions as emergency services continued to assess the damage and respond to potential new incidents.
The flooding affected homes and infrastructure in the area, with emergency crews working to remove mud and debris from streets and help residents whose properties were damaged.
The disaster comes during spring in the Southern Hemisphere, when intense rainfall can trigger flash floods and landslides, particularly in areas where the ground has become saturated.
The government said the disaster zone declaration would help coordinate public services and provide assistance to affected households as recovery efforts continue.

Under new regulations, Türkiye bans children under 15 from social media
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
02:51:25 UTC
11:51:25 KST

Merve Aydogan
10 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
Türkiye has barred social network providers from offering services to minors under the age of 15, according to new Cyber Security Directorate regulations published Saturday in the Official Gazette.
The regulation said providers "cannot provide services to children who have not reached the age of 15."
Providers must also offer differentiated services and take necessary measures for users 15 and older, according to the regulations, adding that they should consider the minor’s best interests and their physical, mental, psychological, social, and emotional development.
Age verification must prioritize personal data protection, using methods that determine only whether a user meets the age threshold rather than establishing identity, it added.
Saying that providers must make the reliability of verification methods, their algorithm structures, and child-focused service policies "clear, auditable and testable for users, parents and the directorate," it stressed that they must create clear, user-friendly parental control tools.
The regulations come under new legislation on social media passed by the Turkish parliament this April.

South Australia's campaign for a third-straight Sheffield Shield title is off to a winning start with victory over Victoria.
The Redbacks won by an innings and 40 runs at Junction Oval.
Debutant Noah McFadyen, who scored a century in SA's only innings of 508, took the final wicket with a caught-and-bowled to clinch the win.
South Australia has started its Sheffield Shield campaign in the same way it ended the last one, beating Victoria at Junction Oval.
The two-time defending champions wrapped up their dominating start today, beating the home side by an innings and 40 runs.
Fittingly, debutant Noah McFadyen took the last wicket of the game when he had David Moody caught and bowled, after top-scoring with 134 in SA's innings.
McFadyen had hit two sixes to go from 88 to 100, finished with 16 fours and five maximums.
The 23-year-old all-rounder had match figures of 3-65, including Moody's wicket to clinch the game.
Resuming at 7-175 and needing another 89 to bat again, Victoria was dismissed for 224.
Victoria made 244 in its first innings and SA took the game away from them with 508.
Fergus O'Neill top-scored in Victoria's second innings with 62, while Nathan McAndrew and Henry Thornton took three wickets apiece.

Asia-Pacific Community: China's Yunnan-grown coffee gains ground on New Zealand cafe menus
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
10:33:51 CST
11:33:51 KST

WELLINGTON, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- Cafes across New Zealand's major cities are pouring more cups brewed with coffee beans from China's Yunnan Province, whose diverse, distinctive flavor profiles are winning over local coffee lovers.
Coffee drinkers in New Zealand have long associated quality coffee with well-established growing powerhouses: Brazil, Colombia and Ethiopia. But a new origin is making inroads on the global coffee circuit -- China's Yunnan.
MQ Coffee, headquartered in Auckland, New Zealand's largest city, is among the businesses helping Yunnan coffee gain a foothold in New Zealand. Wang Yanqi, co-founder of MQ Coffee, said that the quality of Yunnan coffee has improved significantly in recent years, and overseas consumers are paying increasing attention to China as a coffee-producing origin.
MQ Coffee currently carries out coffee product customization, production and packaging of drip coffee bags, and coffee training in New Zealand, while introducing Yunnan coffee to local consumers and coffee professionals through cupping sessions, professional training and origin exchanges.
"Personally, I think Yunnan specialty beans are getting better and better year by year," said Zhang Xue, a coffee taster and coffee trainer in New Zealand, adding that Yunnan specialty coffee is becoming increasingly attractive in terms of flavor expression and quality consistency.
Yunnan has formed six core coffee-producing regions: Pu'er, Baoshan, Lincang, Dehong, Xishuangbanna and Nujiang. Pu'er coffee and Baoshan small-bean coffee have been included on the mutual recognition and protection list under the agreement on China-EU geographical indications.
According to Kunming Customs statistics, in the first eight months of 2026, Yunnan exported 11,000 tonnes of coffee worth 450 million yuan (about 67 million U.S. dollars), mainly to 42 countries and regions including Vietnam, Malaysia and Germany, ranking first nationwide by export value. In 2025, Yunnan exported 195.6 tonnes of green coffee beans to New Zealand, worth 10.2 million yuan.
Some Yunnan coffees deliver good sweetness and body and retain distinct coffee flavors with milk added, making them well-suited to milk-based coffee drinks familiar to New Zealand consumers. Meanwhile, finely processed Yunnan coffees can develop richer layers of floral and fruity aromas via pour-over and drip brewing, Wang noted.
New Zealand's coffee market is operating with a relatively mature industry chain covering importation, roasting, wholesale and retail. For Chinese coffee products that have just entered the local market, building stable sales channels, expanding consumer groups, and turning consumers' initial novelty into lasting competitiveness remain key challenges to address, according to local coffee market observers.
To raise recognition of Yunnan coffee, MQ Coffee has organized New Zealand coffee professionals and enthusiasts to visit Yunnan's growing regions to learn about local coffee farming and processing practices.
For repeat purchases from foreign consumers, Yunnan coffee must further boost its competitiveness in product quality, pricing and supply stability, Wang said. ■

Red Cross to fund evacuation of around 90 rural households from Donetsk region
The Donetsk Regional Military Administration’s Department of Agricultural Development and Land Relations told an Ukrinform correspondent.
“About 90 households in the Donetsk region have so far submitted applications and the required documents to receive financial assistance from the International Committee of the Red Cross to evacuate livestock, poultry and equipment. They are already receiving the funds, and the process is underway,” the department said.

The first payment is intended to cover the costs of transporting animals, poultry and equipment, while the second payment is transferred to the recipient’s account after the relocation has been confirmed.

The detention of agricultural workers in the Donetsk region was linked to their inability to find transportation to evacuate their animals, and this problem is now being addressed,” the Department of Agricultural Development and Land Relations of the Donetsk Regional Military Administration said.
As reported, the ICRC financial assistance program is aimed at supporting economically vulnerable households in evacuating livestock, essential agricultural equipment and means of livelihood from communities where mandatory or partial evacuation has been announced.
The project has been launched in the Kramatorsk district of the Donetsk region, as well as in the Zaporizhzhia and Dnipropetrovsk regions. The amount of financial assistance is UAH 65,000 per household.

Mexico: Court finds three men guilty of murder of Australian, US surfers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10

Mexico convicts 3 in murders of Australian, US surfers
October 10, 2026
A Mexican court on Friday convicted three men in the 2024 murders of two Australian brothers and their American friend, who were killed during a botched robbery which sparked international outrage.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico when they were shot dead in Baja California state.
They were camping in a remote beachside area near the city of Ensenada when they were attacked during a suspected robbery. Their bodies were found days later, in a well, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
What was said in court?
The judge on Friday ruled that the three Mexican defendants had acted with premeditation. They are yet to be sentenced for the murders.
The prosecution has asked for an "exemplary sentence" of 210 years for each of the three convicted, even though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.
Debra Robinson, mother to the Australian brothers, burst into tears when the court passed the guilty verdict.
"While no verdict can ever bring back our boys or ease the heartbreak of losing them," the convictions marked "an important step towards justice and accountability," their father Martin Robinson said in a statement on behalf of the family.
Victim begged for mercy
Case prosecutors described the killings of the three surfers during the closing arguments on Thursday, by recalling the testimony of the girlfriend of one of the main suspects.
She had said that Rhoad had begged for his life while her boyfriend had bragged about "how beautifully" his victims cried before he robbed them.
The triple homicide shocked Mexico and drew international attention when it came to light.
Baja California is one of Mexico's most violent states, riddled with organized crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity doesn't usually affect tourists.

First hurricane to hit US in two years: Isaias slams Florida with 105 mph winds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
02:17:12 UTC
11:17:12 KST

Hurricane Isaias struck the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday night, becoming the first hurricane to make landfall in the United States in two years, as residents who had not evacuated rushed to complete their preparations against destructive winds, dangerous storm surge and torrential rain.
The storm made landfall near Destin in the Florida Panhandle, close to the Alabama border, with sustained winds of around 105 mph (170 kph), according to the National Hurricane Center.
Isaias had earlier intensified into a Category 3 hurricane but weakened to Category 2 before reaching shore. Despite the weakening, forecasters warned that it remained capable of causing extensive damage and life-threatening flooding.
Rain began falling along parts of the Gulf Coast on Friday morning, and tropical storm conditions spread across the region as the hurricane approached.
The National Hurricane Center warned that Category 3 hurricanes, classified as major hurricanes, can cause devastating damage. Although Isaias weakened before landfall, its powerful winds and heavy rainfall remained serious threats.
The storm was expected to weaken rapidly as it moved inland, potentially becoming a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon while tracking northward through Alabama toward the Mississippi border.
"Preparations should be completed quickly, as weather conditions will deteriorate rapidly," the hurricane center warned in an advisory issued early Friday.
"Although the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, Isaias will likely still be a major hurricane when it reaches the coast," the earlier advisory said.
Dangerous storm surge, flooding and tornadoes
Beyond the powerful winds, forecasters warned of a dangerous storm surge reaching 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters) in some coastal areas, along with heavy rainfall and the possibility of tornadoes.
Rainfall totals of 4 to 8 inches (100 to 200 millimeters) were expected across parts of the region during the weekend, with isolated areas potentially receiving as much as 15 inches (380 millimeters).
Such rainfall could trigger flash flooding, particularly in low-lying communities and areas already saturated by earlier rain.
Isaias is the first hurricane to strike the U.S. coastline since Hurricane Milton hit Florida on October 9, 2024, exactly two years earlier.
As the storm approached, residents were seen boarding up windows, filling sandbags and securing their homes.
Thousands of National Guard troops were deployed to assist with preparations and emergency response operations.
Several counties issued mandatory evacuation orders for vulnerable coastal communities, while videos shared on social media showed heavy traffic on roads leading away from the threatened areas.
Double red flags were raised on beaches, warning of extremely dangerous water conditions.
The governors of Florida and Alabama declared states of emergency across dozens of counties, allowing authorities to mobilize additional resources ahead of the storm.
On Dauphin Island, a barrier island off the Alabama coast, authorities encouraged residents to evacuate voluntarily.
Mayor Jeff Collier said he did not expect extensive damage but emphasized that hurricanes can change course or intensify unexpectedly.
"These things are very fickle, and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength, we just have to be prepared for the worst," he said.
An unusually quiet hurricane season
Isaias is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, which has been unusually quiet.
For the first time in 75 years, no Atlantic hurricane had formed by the end of September, making this one of the latest starts to hurricane activity in decades.
The storm is the ninth named system of the Atlantic season, but the previous eight never developed beyond tropical storm strength.
Most of those storms formed between mid-August and September.
The latest seasonal forecast had projected between seven and 13 named storms, with two to six potentially strengthening into hurricanes.
In an average Atlantic hurricane season, approximately 14 named storms form, including seven hurricanes.
The Atlantic hurricane season officially runs from June 1 through November 30.
Although Isaias was expected to lose strength as it moved inland, forecasters warned that heavy rainfall, flooding and damaging winds could continue affecting communities well beyond the immediate coastline.
For residents who remained in the storm's path, authorities emphasized that the danger would not end once the hurricane's center moved away.

Ukraine attacks Russia with spy balloons
Ukrainian spy balloons have been spotted over central Russia’s Yaroslavl Region for the first time, according to the regional Security Ministry.
Local authorities said several of the small flying objects were successfully shot down on Friday, urging residents to report anything suspicious that they see in the sky or suspected debris to emergency services.
The balloons “had been launched from the territory of Ukraine,” according to officials. Small reconnaissance balloons can be used to distract enemy air defenses, but they can also serve as reconnaissance platforms, including to pinpoint the locations of air defense systems or help direct strikes against other targets.
Yaroslavl Region has been targeted by Ukrainian long-range strikes in recent weeks. In mid-September, the Russian military shot down 65 drones over the region in a single day during a large-scale drone raid targeting a local refinery.
Although Friday’s incident was the first of its kind reported in Yaroslavl Region, the Russian military has encountered Ukrainian spy balloons and even explosive-laden balloons in the past.
In September 2025, the Ukrainian military attempted to strike several Russian regions with dozens of meteorological balloons carrying explosives.
The Wall Street Journal claimed in a February article that Kiev had been using high-altitude balloons in attacks on Russia since the Ukraine conflict escalated in 2022. However, according to the Russian Defense Ministry, such attacks were first detected in autumn 2024, with another surge in reported incidents in late summer 2025.
The recent balloon attacks come as Russia has stepped up strikes on missile and drone warehouses, as well as unmanned aerial vehicle assembly facilities, in response to continued Ukrainian strikes on Russian civilian and energy infrastructure, which Moscow describes as terrorist acts.
After Ukraine’s Vladimir Zelensky recently threatened to step up attacks on Russian oil refineries, Moscow vowed to intensify strikes on Ukraine’s military-related facilities while maintaining that it never targets civilians.
On Wednesday, the Russian military targeted a Smart Ammunition facility used to assemble and store FP-5 Flamingo cruise missiles, FP-9 tactical ballistic missiles, and components for both weapons, as well as other sites across several Ukrainian regions, including a drone workshop in Kirovograd Region and the JTI Ukraine tobacco factory in Kremenchug, which Russian officials say is used to manufacture small-arms ammunition.

Super Micro contractor pleads guilty in scheme to divert AI servers with Nvidia chips to China
A contractor linked to Super Micro Computer has pleaded guilty in a scheme to illegally export computer servers containing advanced Nvidia AI chips to China, a federal court filing showed on Oct 9.
Ting-Wei “Willy” Sun pleaded guilty to four counts, including conspiracies to violate US export controls, smuggle goods from the US, defraud the country and obstruct justice. He entered the plea on Oct 9 in the US District Court in Manhattan.
The United States and China are competing for dominance in artificial intelligence, with both investing billions of dollars in a technology seen as critical to economic growth, national security and military and cybersecurity capabilities.
In March, US prosecutors charged Sun and two others associated with Super Micro, including a co-founder of the AI-server maker, with conspiring to divert about US$2.5 billion worth of American AI technology to China in violation of export laws.
The scheme began around October 2023, with Sun and others conspiring to export servers from a US manufacturer, widely believed to be Super Micro, to China without the required licences, according to the indictment.
Asked for comment on the guilty plea, California-based Super Micro referred to its prior statements that the company was not named as a defendant in the indictment and that it had no impact on its business operations. 
Super Micro terminated Sun and cut ties with the other defendants earlier this year.
A lawyer for Sun declined to comment.
Also indicted were the co-founder Yih-Shyan “Wally” Liaw and Ruei-Tsang “Steven” Chang, who was a sales manager at Super Micro’s Taiwan office, while Sun was a contractor.
A lawyer for Liaw - who co-founded Super Micro in 1993 and joined its board in 2023 - did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Chang’s lawyer could not immediately be reached for comment.
The indictment described Sun as a broker and “fixer” who facilitated orders and took steps to conceal the scheme. 
He helped stage “dummy” servers in December 2025 and made false statements to a US Department of Commerce officer during an inspection of supposedly stored servers, which had already been diverted to China, according to the indictment.
Washington has restricted sales of advanced AI chips to China, citing national security concerns. The indictment said Nvidia’s B200, H100 and H200 graphics processing units, and servers containing them, were subject to the restrictions. REUTERS
