Trump's diesel agreement with Putin accused of contradicting Russia sanctions law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
02:09:00 UTC
11:09:00 KST

President Donald Trump's Friday announcement that Russia will supply diesel fuel to the global market marked an apparent pivot from recent efforts to pressure Moscow to end the Ukraine war by targeting Russian energy exports.
Trump claimed the move, unveiled with less than a month left in an affordability-focused midterm election, would swiftly bring down record-high diesel prices.
But commentators and critics were quick to highlight contradictions between the new policy and prior efforts by the U.S. to clamp down on Russian oil sales.
Those efforts most recently included the enactment of the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, empowering Trump to impose tariffs up to 100% on the top purchasers of Russian crude oil or gas, among other restrictions. Trump signed the bill into law just three weeks ago.
"Congress just passed a law giving Trump the power to impose new tariffs on major buyers of Russian oil & gas," Scott Lincicome, vice president of the libertarian Cato Institute, said on X after Trump's Friday announcement.
"Can America tariff America?" he quipped.
Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Ukraine Caucus, accused Trump's latest move of being "directly contrary to Congress's intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill."
Peter Harrell, visiting scholar at Georgetown University Law Center's Institute of International Economic Law, in an X post said that the relaxation of Russian diesel restrictions "pretty much proves the point that the Graham Russia Bill was not going to force the Trump Administration to increase economic pressure on Moscow."
Some of the criticism crossed party lines.
"Through the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act, we gave the president significant authorities and leverage against China and Russia to bring Putin's war to an end with a negotiated settlement," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said in an X post. "Unfortunately, while I understand the desire to bring down diesel prices, I am concerned the lifting of sanctions on Russian oil will only fund the Kremlin's war machine—emboldening more violence and destruction, as we have seen in recent days," McCaul said.
The White House did not immediately respond to CNBC's questions about the diesel agreement with Russia.
Less than a year earlier, the Trump administration slapped sanctions on multiple Russian oil companies in response to what it called "Russia's lack of serious commitment to a peace process to end the war in Ukraine."
Trump also had previously slammed NATO allies for continuing to buy Russian oil. In a September 2025 Truth Social post, he wrote, "the purchase of Russian Oil, by some, has been shocking! It greatly weakens your negotiating position, and bargaining power, over Russia."
Later that month, Trump again harangued world leaders for doing business with Russia.
"They're funding the war against themselves. Who the hell ever heard of that one?" he said in a speech at the United Nations General Assembly. "They can't be doing what they're doing. They're buying oil and gas from Russia while they're fighting Russia."
Trump announced the diesel deal in a Truth Social post Friday afternoon after what he described as a "highly successful discussion" with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Under the agreement, Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, then another 500,000 tons in November, followed by 1 million tons "immediately thereafter" and 3 million more depending on refinery conditions, Trump wrote.
The Treasury Department soon after said that Trump directed the Office of Foreign Assets Control to immediately issue a "temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market." OFAC specified that the sanctioned transactions will be authorized for about six months, until April 7.
Russia seemed to celebrate the move. "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world," an X account associated with Putin's economic envoy Kirill Dmitriev said in response to the announcement.
But Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, whose military has started targeting Russian oil refineries, said in a searing statement that the U.S. easing sanctions on Moscow "plays into Russia's hands."
"Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness," Zelenskyy said. "Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged."
"We count on America's fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia," he said.
"A strong one, not a weak one," he added.
Trump thanked Putin later Friday afternoon for enabling "massive amounts of oil" to come to the U.S.
"We need oil for the world, and this is diesel, which is what we need, so we're very happy to get it," Trump told reporters before heading to Syracuse, New York.
The Trump administration has previously eased some Russian energy sanctions temporarily, though more narrowly than Friday's announcement.
Earlier this year, in an attempt to stabilize markets after the start of the Iran war, the Trump administration issued limited, 30-day waivers allowing countries to buy sanctioned Russian oil that was already in transit.
But some interpreted the latest move as a more significant step.
"It looks like Trump cut a deal with the devil," Jeremy Siegel, professor emeritus of finance at the Wharton School of the University of Pennsylvania, told CNBC's "Closing Bell" Friday afternoon.
"It's not a permanent solution at all. It's sort of a short-term Band Aid," Siegel said. "And cutting back on or eliminating sanctions on Russia for the invasion in Ukraine, I think, is a very unfortunate consequence."

Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida
October 10, 2026
Hurricane Isaias has made landfall as a Category 2 storm near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) said Friday evening.
The storm is the first hurricane of the Atlantic season.
What do we know about Hurricane Isaias?
The NHC warned of "life-threatening storm surge impacting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash flooding spread inland."
The weather system is also bringing extreme winds, with a tornado watch issued for parts of Florida and southern Georgia.
Isaias was originally a strong Category 3 storm before making landfall. It later weakened to a Category 1 storm.
After the storm made landfall, the Florida Division of Emergency Management said the tornado watch for parts of North Florida has been extended until at least 6 a.m. local time Saturday (10 a.m. UTC).
The NHC said the hurricane has maximum sustained winds of 105 miles per hour (165 kilometers per hour).
Evacuations took place in coastal communities as the hurricane approached.
All flights at the Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport have been canceled due to the storm. Destin is in the panhandle region of northern Florida.
Florida, Georgia and Alabama have all declared a State of Emergency due to the extreme weather system.
US Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said "emergency declarations have been approved in Florida and Alabama to ensure federal resources are available to respond to #Isaias."
Florida Governor DeSantis urges residents to 'buckle down'
In a press conference, Florida Governor Ron DeSantis urged residents to "buckle down at this point. Don't be getting out on the roads."
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier also warned those "thinking about using this storm's power outages and evacuations to break in, loot, or steal: don't even try it."
"During an emergency, these crimes become first-degree felonies, punishable by up to 30 years in prison," Uthmeier said.
According to power outage tracking site PowerOutage.com, roughly 480,000 customers altogether were without electricity as of Friday evening in Florida, Georgia and Alabama.
Alabama Governor Kay Ivey said Uber, Comcast and Home Depot have offered to help Alabamians during the storm. Uber, for example, is offering free round-trip rides to state-approved evacuation shelters in Mobile and Baldwin counties.

"I don't really care how he goes, as long as he goes," Trump said, referring to Hasan.
What did Hegseth and the Pentagon say about Hasan's execution?
Trump's remarks comes a day after the Pentagon said it would livestream the execution of 56-year-old Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist who murdered 13 people and injured 32 others in Fort Hood in Texas in 2009.
In a video shared by the Pentagon regarding the execution, US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said "We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequence for these types of things."
Hasan is currently being held on death row in Fort Leavenworth in Kansas. His execution is slated for December 3.

JD Vance says he would not watch livestream of execution

"I absolutely support the sentence of death, but livestreaming executions is what jihadists do. America is better than that," said Republican Representative Austin Scott of Georgia.
Public executions are common in Taliban-controlled Afghanistan and the so-called Islamic State (IS) also engaged in public beheadings when the group controlled large swathes of Syria and Iraq in the 2010s. Iran is another country that carries out public executions.
Republican Congressman Rob Bresnahan of Pennsylvania said "an execution shouldn't be a livestreamed spectacle."

Democratic Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut said Pentagon chief Hegseth is "turning the Fort Hood execution into a gruesome inhumane spectacle."
The UN human rights office (OHCHR) also strongly condemned the ideaof a livestreamed execution, while the president of the United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the plana "barbaric promotion of a culture of death."

Former US Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer condemned US President Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as “very unwise,” warning in an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post on Friday, Oct. 9, that the move would help finance Moscow’s war machine while undermining Washington’s own efforts to negotiate peace.
Pifer, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine from 1998 to 2000, said the agreement would send American money directly into Russia’s economy, enabling the Kremlin to purchase more weapons for its continuing attacks on Ukraine.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“This is a very unwise decision,” Pifer told Kyiv Post.
“First of all, it means that American dollars will be going to purchase Russian fuel, and that’s going to help the Russian military machine buy more missiles and bombs to use against Ukraine.”
The former ambassador argued that Trump’s decision was particularly damaging because Washington was supposed to be increasing pressure on Moscow to negotiate an end to its invasion, not offering the Kremlin economic relief.
“Second of all, it completely undercuts Trump’s own effort to mediate a solution to the Russia-Ukraine war, at a time when the US should be putting more pressure on Moscow to negotiate seriously,” Pifer said.
“In fact, he’s relieving that pressure, because this will make it harder to achieve peace between Russia and Ukraine.”

Little relief for US fuel prices
Pifer, now a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and an affiliate of Stanford University’s Center for International Security and Cooperation, also challenged the economic rationale for Trump’s agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, arguing that the initial diesel shipments were too small to significantly affect US fuel prices.
“If you look at the amount of diesel fuel that he hopes to buy – 300,000 tons in October – that amounts to less than one half a day’s consumption of diesel fuel in the United States,” he said.
“That’s not going to have that big an impact on the price of diesel.”
Trump announced Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons afterward and an additional 3 million tons depending on the condition of Russian refineries.
The administration subsequently issued a temporary authorization allowing certain transactions involving Russian diesel, reversing restrictions intended to deprive Moscow of energy revenues.
The White House has presented the agreement as a way to ease soaring diesel prices for American farmers, truck drivers and consumers.
However, energy analysts have questioned whether the additional supplies will produce lasting price reductions, given the scale of American demand and global refining constraints.
Pifer expressed hope that the administration might reverse course.
“It’s a very unfortunate decision. I hope that there’s a chance that it will be reconsidered,” he said.
Will Republicans challenge Trump over Graham sanctions?
The former ambassador also questioned how Republican lawmakers would respond to Trump’s decision after Congress passed legislation designed to increase economic pressure on countries purchasing Russian energy.
“It will be interesting [to see] the Republicans, who had passed the Graham sanctions bill, which was to apply greater sanctions on countries that buy Russian energy – how they’re going to react when Mr. Trump now says the United States will be buying Russian energy,” Pifer said.
Trump’s agreement came just three weeks after he signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18.
The legislation was intended to expand economic pressure on Russia’s energy sector and financial networks supporting its invasion.
The new diesel arrangement has raised questions about the administration’s willingness to enforce those restrictions even as Ukraine continues pressing Washington to cut off Moscow’s war revenues.
‘No evident movement by the Russian side’
Asked about the prospects for the latest US-led peace negotiations, Pifer expressed deep skepticism.
The talks were taking place in Florida, where US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting Ukrainian and European officials to explore possible ways to end Russia’s full-scale invasion.
One proposal under consideration involved a partial ceasefire covering energy infrastructure.
But Pifer expressed little hope for progress, citing Russia’s unwillingness to compromise.
“I have not had much expectation that these talks would produce anything, because while Ukraine, I believe, has shown a readiness to make some painful decisions to try to find a compromise to end the war, there has been no evident movement by the Russian side,” he told Kyiv Post.
He pointed to previous statements by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as evidence that Moscow had not softened its negotiating demands.
“The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said six weeks ago that Russia’s position had not changed from the one announced by Vladimir Putin in December 2024,” the former US envoy said.
“And that suggests that Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner have failed to get the Russians to move on any significant issue.”
The former ambassador said he saw little reason for optimism about the current diplomatic process.
“So I do not have many hopes for this negotiation process at this point.”
Pifer warned that Trump’s decision to ease sanctions would only reinforce Moscow’s resistance to compromise.
“This decision makes it even harder, because Moscow sees the US easing pressure rather than pushing the Kremlin to negotiate seriously,” he said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also sharply criticized Washington’s decision, saying Ukraine’s negotiating team in Florida was being used as a “smokescreen” while Trump reached a separate energy agreement with Putin.
“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said Friday.
“And that is definitely unfair. And it is a weak decision by strong partners.”

US, Ukrainian, European officials discuss ending Russia's war at Miami meeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
01:50:28 UTC
10:50:28 KST

U.S., Ukrainian and European officials met in Miami on Oct. 9 to discuss efforts to end Russia's war against Ukraine ahead of winter, on the same day Washington moved to ease restrictions on Russian diesel exports.
Discussions were described by U.S. Special Envoy Steve Witkoff as “constructive”, and covered preparations for winter, including protecting Ukraine's energy infrastructure and maintaining grain exports, as well as security guarantees and longer-term arrangements aimed at preventing future conflict. The topics of Ukraine's postwar reconstruction, economic recovery and potential accession to the European Union were also reportedly covered.
In addition to the United States, representatives from the E3 group of France, Germany and the United Kingdom, the European Commission, Ukraine and NATO took part.
Ukraine's delegation included Presidential Office head Kyrylo Budanov, Foreign Intelligence Service chief Rustem Umerov, presidential adviser Sergiy Kyslytsia and lawmaker Davyd Arakhamia, a negotiating team that has traveled to the U.S. and engaged in such discussions in the past.
Zelensky said on Oct. 8 that the negotiations were expected to last two days, Oct. 9–10, and that he anticipated a briefing from the delegation upon its return to Kyiv on Monday, Oct. 12.
In a post on X, Witkoff said that the talks helped identify areas for further consideration ahead of Washington's next engagement with Russia, but announced no concrete agreements. His statement did not indicate whether further meetings would take place on Oct. 10.
Ukrainian representatives had not publicly released their own account of the meeting at the time of publication.
The meeting coincided with U.S. President Donald Trump's announcement that Russia would supply millions of tons of diesel to the United States and global markets following a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
The U.S. Treasury Department subsequently issued a temporary authorization permitting purchases of Russian diesel, drawing criticism from Kyiv and European officials over the potential financial benefit to Moscow.
The Kyiv Independent reported earlier on Oct. 9 that Russia was seeking sanctions relief as part of negotiations over a possible halt to attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure. Moscow also wants to link a potential energy truce to ceasefire arrangements in the Black Sea.
The discussions come as Russia intensifies attacks on Ukraine's energy facilities ahead of winter, threatening electricity and heating supplies across the country.

Hurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida with severe effects expected across several states
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
01:44:33 UTC
10:44:33 KST

Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf coast on Friday as a dangerous category 2 storm, hammering communities in Alabama and the Florida panhandle with damaging winds, heavy rain, flooding and life-threatening storm surges.
The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, said at a news conference, adding flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region”.
In Pensacola, about 50 miles (80km) west of Destin an Agence France-Presse reporter witnessed howling winds rip the roofs from some homes and businesses, snapping tree branches as the power went out.
“Things are flying really fast, and I’ve never seen wind this fast before, so it’s intense, it’s scary,” Jonathan Ramos, a 40-year-old government employee, said from his hotel in Pensacola, where the power went out.
“I don’t recommend people coming down here for fun to do this.”
President Donald Trump told reporters at the White House late Friday night: “We’re watching it very closely, the hurricane,” adding that it was “under control”.
Forecasters had expected Isaias to weaken from its peak earlier on Friday as a major category 3 hurricane because of shifts in wind speed.
But even as a weaker storm system, the NHC warned of a life-threatening storm surge affecting the Gulf Coast as dangerous hurricane conditions and flash floods spread inland. The hurricane is expected to cross Alabama and into the Tennessee Valley on the weekend, the agency added.
Warnings included a storm surge of up to 7ft (2.1 meters) along the Alabama-Florida line, and powerful wind gusts reaching parts of northern Georgia.
In the Florida Panhandle, Isaias’s early impacts also came into view. In Panama city beach, Noaa officials observed a water level 5.4 feet (1.64 meters) above average. About 125 miles west, at the Pensacola city hall, a wind gust up to 102 mph (164km/h) was recorded.
Powerful gusts of wind and heavy rainfall appeared to down the canopy of a Crestview gas station on Friday evening, according to a video captured by meteorologist Nick Stewart. The tattered cover hung on top of a filling station.
“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,” Florida governor Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard “throughout the region”.
The governors of Mississippi, Alabama and Florida all declared states of emergency ahead of the storm’s arrival, urging some residents of coastal communities to evacuate and many more to prepare for the storm’s likely violent arrival.
Alabama governor Kay Ivey announced shortly before the hurricane made landfall that Donald Trump had approved the emergency declaration for her state. “This will help cut tape for our federal partners to aid in any response,” Ivey said.
The Mobile office of the National Weather Service warned parts of Florida could see “extremely dangerous” tornado-like winds.
By Friday evening, nearly 500,000 customers had lost power across Alabama and Florida, according to PowerOutage.com.
“Things are going to get really, really treacherous,” Jamie Rhome, deputy director for the National Hurricane Center, told the AP.
Florida’s national guard deployed roughly 5,000 soldiers and airmen to aid with the response, the AP reported. Some prisons were also evacuating their incarcerated populations. Most flights were grounded at several airports in Florida’s Panhandle.
The state guard has deployed about 400 soldiers to assess the hurricane’s damage and assist with route clearance, among other duties.
The Florida fish and wildlife conservation commission has readied 10 airboats, 18 shallow-draft boats, nine ATVs and six larger platform vessels in the event of damage or flooding.
Uber has also partnered with the state to offer free-round trips, up to $40 each way, to and from state-approved evacuation shelters.
Isaias is notable as one of the two latest-forming Atlantic hurricanes on record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.
Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the US.
In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company’s website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm’s severity.
Kelsei Frazier, a Florida native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.
“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier. “Which is a pretty big deal.”
Associated Press contributed reporting.

Trump renews bid to fire Fed’s Cook with fresh White House inquiry

Trump renews bid to fire Fed’s Cook with fresh White House inquiry
- Trump has opened a fresh White House inquiry into Fed Governor Lisa Cook, accusing her of false mortgage statements and seeking a possible firing before congressional elections.
- Cook’s lawyers say there is no legal basis to remove her, and they plan to show she did not commit mortgage fraud at the Nov 5 closed hearing.
- The move renews fears over Fed independence after a Supreme Court ruling set a “cause” process for removal, while critics call Trump’s action a “kangaroo court”.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – United States President Donald Trump launched a new inquiry into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook weeks before congressional elections, convening an investigative committee and ordering an unprecedented White House hearing into allegations she made false statements on mortgage applications.
Trump has been trying to fire Cook for more than a year, as he moves to exert more control over a central bank he says is refusing for political reasons to lower interest rates. Lawyers for Cook said on Oct 9 any fair hearing would show there is no legal basis for firing her.
“As President, it is my job to ensure the laws are faithfully executed, including by firing subordinates who cannot be trusted to tell the truth and follow the law,” Trump said in a notice on the White House website on Oct 9.
“To assist me in carrying out that responsibility, the committee shall investigate the allegations against Governor Cook and report to me whether there is ‘cause’ for Governor Cook’s removal,” according to the notice dated Oct 7.
The committee will hold a closed, in-person four-hour hearing at the White House on Nov 5 “to consider the evidence and allegations against Governor Cook”, the presidential memorandum said.
The hearing falls two days after elections that will determine if Trump’s Republican Party maintains control of the US House and Senate, whose members are charged with confirming presidential nominees to the Fed.
A successful removal of Cook would create a vacancy on the Fed’s seven-member Board.
If the hearing is “anything close to objective, the conclusion will be that Governor Cook did not commit mortgage fraud, leaving no cause to remove her from the Federal Reserve Board”, Cook’s lawyers Abbe Lowell and Norm Eisen said in a statement.
“Governor Cook welcomes the opportunity to present the facts so she can clear her name and demonstrate there is no legal basis to fire her.”
They said they had engaged with the White House about the process.
Trump first tried to fire Cook, the first black woman to serve on the central bank’s board, in August 2025.
No US president has ever tried to fire a sitting Fed governor before. Central banks are widely seen as needing political independence to ensure their ability to fight inflation as needed.
Supreme court ruling on Fed removal
Cook sued, saying she had done nothing wrong. The case led to the US Supreme Court ruling earlier in 2026 that the president could not remove a Fed governor at will, and needed to follow a clear process laying out a “cause” for firing and allowing for a defence.
The ruling left Cook in her position, but kicked the case against her back to a federal district court, where Judge Jia Cobb in September set a Nov 6 deadline for the lawyers of Trump and Cook to submit a joint proposal for the proceedings.
Cook was appointed to the Fed board in 2022 by former US President Joe Biden, a Democrat, and was re-appointed in 2023 to a term that lasts until 2038.
She has always cast her vote with the majority on the Fed’s policy-making committee, which in September raised interest rates under the leadership of Kevin Warsh, whom Trump appointed to succeed Jerome Powell in May.
“Trump appears to believe that the reason the Fed has turned hawkish is because his chosen chairman Warsh is boxed in by a hawkish and politically hostile Fed board,” Evercore ISI analyst Krishna Guha wrote.
Trump’s creation of the inquiry committee “constitutes a re-upping of his threat to Fed independence and will be counter-productive in terms of the President’s desire for lower interest rates”.
Trump’s chief economic policy adviser Kevin Hassett, Equal Employment Opportunity Commission chair Andrea Lucas and acting Office of Government Ethics director Keith Sonderling will comprise the newly formed committee, the memorandum said.
Those members, their representatives or Department of Justice personnel will question Cook for “no longer than four hours”.
The committee will make its recommendation to Trump on whether he has cause to remove Cook “as soon as practicable” after a Nov 10 deadline for Cook to submit any post-hearing statement, the memo said.
Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee that oversees the Fed, called the hearing a “kangaroo court” and part of Trump’s “dangerous quest to illegally take over our nation’s central bank”.
Trump has contended that Powell, who has remained at the Fed as governor, may have engaged in financial misconduct related to the Fed’s building renovations. The allegation sparked a now-closed Department of Justice criminal investigation and was rejected in September by an independent watchdog agency. REUTERS

CAIRO, Oct. 10 (Xinhua) -- China defeated Thailand 2-0 in the semifinals of the Badminton World Federation (BWF) World Junior Team Championships in Cairo on Friday evening, setting up a title clash with Malaysia on Saturday.
The Chinese team overcame an early deficit to secure victory at the Cairo Stadium Indoor Halls Complex, winning two straight sets under the tournament's relay scoring format, in which players compete across five disciplines and accumulate points for their teams.
Yin Yiqing, an 18-year-old Chinese player, said the match was challenging because China was trailing when she entered the court. "We had prepared thoroughly for the team competition format and practiced it many times during training," she told Xinhua after the match.
"I think I performed quite well today. I was able to stay in control of the match, manage the pace effectively, and put into practice what I had worked on in training," she added.
Her teammate Luo Jingyu, also 18, acknowledged the difficulties he faced in the men's singles and praised the strength of the Thai team.
"Today's match was quite challenging. As the first player to compete in the men's singles, I faced some difficulties, but I tried my best," Luo said, adding that he hoped to improve his performance in the next match.
Looking ahead to Saturday's final, Luo said, "If I get the chance to play, I will give it my all and fight for every point. I hope Team China can achieve a great result in the end."
Malaysia advanced to the final after defeating Indonesia 2-0 in the other semifinal earlier on Friday.
The team competition, also known as the Suhandinata Cup, runs from Oct. 5 to 10 in Cairo and will be followed by the individual championships. ■

Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
US President Donald Trump’s top envoys have begun two days of negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives in Miami, focusing on preparations for the coming winter and potential ways to de-escalate the Ukraine conflict on terms that would be acceptable to Moscow.
US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Friday’s discussions as “constructive,” saying American representatives had discussed prospects for a “lasting peace” with Kiev and its most hawkish European backers, including Britain, France and Germany, as well as officials from the European Commission and NATO.
The talks covered “near-term measures related to winter preparedness,” including energy resilience and grain exports, as well as longer-term security guarantees, post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s potential accession to the EU, according to Witkoff.
“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on X.
Today, representatives from the United States, the E3, the European Commission, Ukraine, and NATO met in Miami and held constructive discussions on potential avenues to de-escalate and conclude the war with Russia ahead of winter and advance efforts toward a durable and lasting peace. The discussions covered a broad range of issues, including near-term measures related to winter preparedness (energy resilience, grains exports), security guarantees, as well as longer-term arrangements for Ukraine’s and Europe’s security to prevent future conflicts, and support Ukraine’s post-war reconstruction and economic prosperity, including EU accession. The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia. Participants reaffirmed their shared commitment to continuing diplomatic efforts toward a sustainable peace that strengthens security and creates opportunities for lasting stability and prosperity.
— Special Envoy Steve Witkoff (@SEPeaceMissions) October 9, 2026
The negotiations were scheduled to continue on Saturday, and no concrete agreements or breakthroughs have been announced so far.
The US delegation is led by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Kiev is represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, deputy chief of staff Sergey Kislitsa and senior lawmaker David Arakhamia.
The European delegation reportedly includes Bjoern Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany. NATO is represented by Geoffrey van Leeuwen, chief of staff to Secretary General Mark Rutte, according to European media reports.
The talks follow reports that Witkoff and Kushner were preparing to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the diplomatic deadlock. According to Axios, the pair could travel to Moscow later this month for further talks with Putin.
One proposal under consideration reportedly involves a partial ceasefire covering strikes on energy infrastructure, amid growing anxiety among Kiev’s European backers over the economic and energy consequences of the conflict.
“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source previously told AFP.
The Miami meeting also coincided with a 90-minute phone conversation between Trump and Putin on Friday, during which the leaders discussed Ukraine, Iran and a major agreement to resume Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets.
Zelensky lashed out at Trump, effectively accusing Washington of stabbing Kiev in the back by striking a separate diesel deal with Moscow. Zelensky branded the move “a weak decision by strong partners” and accused the US of using talks with the Ukrainian delegation in Miami as a “smokescreen” while negotiating with Putin behind Kiev’s back.
Trump has repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for American consumers. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Trump promised Putin that he would convey Moscow’s position to the Ukrainian delegation in Florida.

Building trust requires tackling deep-seated misgivings among bureaucrats and citizens. Easing visa restrictions, facilitating dialogue and collaborating on shared goals are the places to start

Brian Wong is an HKU-100 assistant professor in philosophy at the University of Hong Kong. 
Last month, President Xi Jinping travelled to New Delhi to attend the Brics summit – his first visit in seven years. On the summit’s sidelines, Xi and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi had an in-depth conversation that explored topics of shared interest between them, such as leveraging open-weight artificial intelligence (AI) for mutual benefit.
Even so, such sanguine signals were soon drowned out by a spate of downbeat headlines. One recent story warned of the “asymmetric” relationship between the two, with China’s manufacturing dwarfing India’s. Another reported Delhi’s renaming of 28 sites in Ladakh, situated near the heavily contested Line of Actual Control.
For keen observers of Sino-Indian relations, such dynamics are by no means a new phenomenon. Positive reassurances from the top leadership are welcome, yet they take time to percolate through to the policy level. Impediments to warming ties, on the other hand, are aplenty – especially concerning territorial claims.

US Justice Department scrutinises Binance compliance with 2023 settlement deal

US Justice Department scrutinises Binance compliance with 2023 settlement deal
- The US Justice Department is checking whether Binance broke its 2023 settlement, while also probing possible Iran sanctions breaches linked to black-market oil sales.
- Binance agreed to a US$4.3 billion penalty in 2023 and must report misconduct. If it breached the deal, it could face revived charges and more fines.
- DOJ official Tysen Duva urged crypto firms to self-report fraud and praised public-private cooperation. Binance said it is improving controls and will keep working with law enforcement.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – The United States Department of Justice (DOJ) is scrutinising whether Binance Holdings breached a landmark settlement with the US government, as the authorities probe activity on the platform for potential Iran sanctions violations.
Tysen Duva, head of DOJ’s criminal division, said in an interview this week that officials were reviewing Binance’s compliance with its 2023 agreement.
Duva declined to discuss specifics and did not say that Binance was in violation of the settlement, under which the company agreed to a US$4.3 billion (S$5.5 billion) penalty, pleaded guilty to violating banking rules and accepted increased compliance controls.
In September, the US Attorney’s Office in Manhattan, which is leading the probe and working with the criminal division in Washington, sought forfeiture of US$61 million that it said was generated from Iranian black-market oil sales and laundered through Binance.
Federal prosecutors have been investigating whether the operator of the world’s biggest crypto exchange committed violations of US sanctions on Iran by not stopping certain trading on its platform, Bloomberg has reported.
“There is an ongoing investigation there that we are involved with,” Duva said in the interview. “But beyond that, we’re not going to get into specifics about exactly what the status of the facts are, how it’s developing.”
The DOJ said it does not comment on ongoing investigations in response to follow-up questions.
Neither the company nor its employees have been accused of wrongdoing and probes can end without charges or lawsuits being filed.
“We are continually working to enhance our controls, and we are fully committed to cooperating with law enforcement,” Binance said in a statement.
Self-reporting
Duva also praised Binance and other digital asset companies for helping the US thwart cyber scams and frauds, especially those committed by transnational criminal organisations.
He has been encouraging companies to come forward and self-report, favouring settlements over what could become costly prosecutions.
“I want to focus really on the positive part of the relationship that we’re trying to build with the crypto companies and tech companies,” Duva said.
“The early returns have been great with social media, with crypto exchanges, and we’re very excited to really press that and continue this. A big part of this is these public-private partnerships.”
More broadly, DOJ is urging companies to self-report possible fraud, favouring settlements with companies that proactively disclose potential violations over what could become costly and time-consuming prosecutions, Duva said.
Binance is required under the 2023 settlement to report to the government any evidence or allegations of misconduct related to federal laws governing money laundering, banking transactions and sanctions violations.
If Binance is found to have breached the deal, the company could be subject to prosecution for the criminal activity that was resolved under the settlement, potentially facing revived charges and billions of dollars in additional fines.
Since the 2023 settlement, Binance has sought to emphasise its cooperation with law enforcement and regulators. The company said in a blog post in February that overall, more than 1,500 people, or about 25% of its global headcount, worked on compliance.
Binance’s former chief executive Zhao Changpeng pleaded guilty to failing to maintain an effective anti-money laundering programme and ended up serving four months in prison.
Zhao, also known by his initials, CZ, was pardoned by US President Donald Trump in October and has been travelling the world promoting adoption of cryptocurrency in places ranging from Dubai to Pakistan. Bloomberg

Two Renoir paintings recovered after France museum heist, mayor says
The recovered Renoir paintings, valued at millions, were stolen in a daring heist at Cagnes-sur-Mer last month.
Renoir paintings worth $10.5 million missing after museum heist
Two paintings by the French Impressionist artist Pierre-Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in southern France a month ago have been recovered, the town’s mayor said.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city’s history,” Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, near Nice, said on Friday. “Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief.”
Six people have been arrested in connection with the theft, local authorities said. Masson did not say where the paintings were found or in what condition.
How the theft unfolded
Two thieves broke into the Renoir Museum a little before 6am on September 8, cutting through a fence to enter the grounds, smashing a window and using an electric saw to cut the clips securing the frames, Masson said at the time.
He described them as “well equipped” and “well informed”.
The museum alarm sounded at 5:48am, and municipal police arrived five minutes later, forcing the thieves to flee.
They had taken four paintings, valued by the mayor at about nine million euros ($10.5m).
Two of the stolen works – Renoir’s “Portrait of Madame Pichon” and “Coco Reading” – were later found dropped in the museum garden, the prosecutor’s office said at the time.
The two works that remained missing were “Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano” and “Young Woman at the Well”, the office said.
Police said last month that the thieves were not first-time offenders and had scoped out the premises.
The Marseille prosecutor opened a theft investigation into an organised gang, and the national office for trafficking in cultural goods joined the probe.
A string of museum heists
The museum, opened in 1960, is in the painter’s last home, where he died in 1919.
“This incident should serve as a warning about the protection of our museums,” Masson said after the robbery.
The theft came less than a year after jewels worth about $100m were stolen from the Louvre in Paris in a daylight robbery.
The four suspected robbers have been arrested, but the jewels have not been found.
In August, Italian police said they had recovered paintings by Renoir, Cezanne and Matisse worth more than $10.4m that were stolen from a museum in March.

How much fibre do you really need? Here’s what an expert says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
01:18:06 UTC
10:18:06 KST

IN BRIEF:
- Fibre-maxxing has swept the algorithm, but it has multiple health benefits.
- Experts say it's important fibre is consumed as food, and not supplements.
Are you getting enough fibre in your diet?
The recommended daily fibre intake is 30g for men and 25g for women, but Australian men and women consume on average about 21g and 18g of fibre per day, respectively. So, you're probably not.
Dietitians have been calling for Australians to increase their fibre intake for decades, and now the challenge has made its way to social media.
Enter the fibre-maxxer: A person committed to hitting, and even exceeding, their daily fibre target.
Online fibre-maxxers promote eating more fruits and vegetables and increasing dietary fibre intake by adding seeds, grains and vegetables to regular foods. This includes putting chia seeds in soft drinks, beans on avocado toast, grains in homemade bread, or adding a cup of legumes to rice.
News that makes sense
Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox.
Can you have too much fibre?
Program director of human nutrition and associate professor at Adelaide University, Evangeline Mantzioris, said that while fibre-maxxing was probably "one of the more positive" social media-fuelled food trends, some elements could be "problematic".
"We actually do need to increase the amount of fibre in our diet," Mantzioris told SBS News.
She said the daily intake suggestion of 25 to 30g per day was based on attaining the best health outcomes, including a reduction of colon cancer, "which is one of the most preventable diseases we have".
"But I understand some are suggesting intakes up to 50 grams a day, possibly more, and there isn't a lot of good evidence that having such extremely high levels may provide any additional benefits."
While there is no upper limit on how much fibre you can eat, more fibre means your body produces more flatulence.
"One of the biggest problems, I guess, is gas, right? No one wants to be gassy out in public."
Another issue, Mantzioris said, is fluid intake.
It was imperative to drink a healthy amount of fluids throughout the day, as without fluids, high fibre can cause constipation, rather than ease it.
"I describe it as it's a bit like trying to clean the bathroom with a dry sponge or a wet sponge. The wet sponge is going to work a lot better than the dry sponge," she said.
"Any increase in fibre will result in an increase in wind, and what we normally tell people to do is to do it slowly."
Don't "go from nothing to 40 grams of fibre in one day". Instead, Mantzioris said, gradually increase high-fibre foods in your diet. This will also help ensure it is a "sustainable" transition for your gut microbiome, the complex community of trillions of microorganisms that live in your digestive tract.
"We know that the bacteria in our gut use that fibre for their survival, and we know that the fibre that comes from whole foods like fruit, vegetables, legumes, beans, nuts, and seeds gives you the healthiest type of microbiome possible", as opposed to the bacteria that thrive on "sometimes foods", which are unhealthy for your body.
"So it's sort of like this lovely symbiotic relationship between your bacteria and you, and the more healthy food you give them, the better off they are, and the better off you are."
Why fibre should come from food
"It's all about balance," Mantzioris said, stressing that fibre intake should come from food, not supplements, which she said some fibremaxxing influencers might be recommending.
"By using supplements, you're missing out on all of the additional nutrients that are in the foods that they originally come from."
She said the best way to avoid "overdosing" on fibre would be to get it from food.
"And get it from a range of different foods — there are a lot of different types of fibres, and they each play a different role in our bodies."
"It's important to eat beans, to eat fruit, eat vegetables, and to eat cereals, to get the maximum benefits from all the different types of fibres, as well as the nutrients that come with all those foods that we know promote health," she said.
What is fibre?
Fibre is a nutrient found in many foods that reduces your risk of chronic disease and keeps your digestive system healthy.
Adequate dietary fibre is essential for proper gut function. It has also been related to risk reduction for some chronic diseases, including heart disease, certain cancers and diabetes.
There are three kinds of fibre: soluble fibre, which slows down digestion, like oats and barley; insoluble fibre, like whole grains, which bulks your stool and speeds up the movement of food through your digestive tract; and resistant starch, found in boiled and cooled potatoes, which ferments in your gut and acts as a prebiotic to feed beneficial bacteria.
Mantzioris said there were "a few reasons" why fibre intake was so consistently low in Australia.
Only about 5 per cent of Australians are meeting the minimum requirements for vegetables in their diet, at 5 serves a day.
"And of course, fibre vegetables are a great source of fibre," Mantzioris said.
She pointed to the ever-increasing popularity of high-protein diets, or "the protein craze".
"When you're consuming more of one food, you're dropping out another essential food group, which is providing you with essential nutrients."
"They're focusing on their protein intake, and we know that roughly 98 per cent of Australians meet their protein requirement".
Beans, she said, were a great example of a high-protein food with multiple benefits.
"The benefit of that protein source is that it also gives you the fibre, and all the antioxidants that we need to fight disease, to reduce oxidative stress in the body and reduce inflammation."
"Every different colour you have in the plant foods represents a different nutrient that's useful for the body."
Finally, she said, "There's an aversion to carbohydrates in our society."
"People see carbohydrates as the problem food when it comes to trying to manage their weight — and all of the carbohydrate-rich foods also provide us with a lot of fibre."

Brazil prosecutors sue Shell for US$108 million over deadly 2024 floods
- Brazil prosecutors filed a US$108 million lawsuit against Shell’s Brazilian unit over the deadly 2024 floods in Rio Grande do Sul.
- The floods, caused by heavy rain, killed nearly 200 people and displaced 500,000. Prosecutors say Shell should answer for its climate impact and emissions.
- The case, backed by Instituto Preservar, is seen as a major step in climate litigation. Experts say it is the first suit by a national prosecutor against an oil major for a climate disaster.
AI generated
BrasIlia – Brazilian prosecutors on Oct 9 filed an unprecedented lawsuit against oil giant Shell’s subsidiary in the country, demanding US$108 million (S$138 million) in compensation over deadly 2024 floods.
Torrential rains sparked historic flooding in southern Brazil in April and May that year, leaving nearly 200 people dead, 500,000 more displaced and massive damages.
According to the lawsuit, Shell’s liability should match its contribution to global warming – estimated at 2% of historical global greenhouse gas emissions.
“This civil suit is aimed at holding the defendant company accountable, in terms of its environmental and climate-related responsibilities, for collective material and moral damages stemming from the extreme weather event that hit Rio Grande do Sul state,” public prosecutors said, according to court documents seen by AFP.
They said the British energy giant should be held responsible because of its past and current greenhouse gas emissions associated with exploration, production and sale of fossil fuels.
The US$108 million in compensation accounts for both material and moral damages.
The filing of a new climate-related suit by Brazilian prosecutors – in conjunction with Instituto Preservar, a Brazilian non-governmental organisation – marks a new phase in the global battle in the courts against oil giants.
“This is the first time a national public prosecutor is suing an oil major for a climate disaster,” Maria Antonia Tigre, director of global climate litigation at the Sabin Center for Climate Change Law, told AFP.
Shell is already being sued in Britain by victims of a typhoon in the Philippines. AFP

What is celebrated on October 10 in Ukraine and around the world
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-10
03:58:38 EEST
09:58:38 KST

What is celebrated on October 10 in Ukraine and around the world
Kyiv • UNN
In Ukraine, Standardization and Metrology Workers’ Day is observed. Around the world, it is World Mental Health Day, World Migratory Bird Day, and World Homeless Day.
On Saturday, October 10, Ukraine observes Standardization and Metrology Workers' Day, while around the world it is World Mental Health Day and World Migratory Bird Day. Orthodox believers commemorate the holy martyrs Eulampius and Eulampia on this day, UNN reports.
Standardization and Metrology Workers' Day
The holiday was established by a decree of the President of Ukraine in 2002. It is a professional holiday for specialists who ensure measurement accuracy, product quality control, and compliance with technical standards in industry, medicine, and other fields.
World Mental Health Day
It has been observed annually on October 10 since 1992. Its aim is to draw attention to psychological well-being, access to assistance, and overcoming prejudice against mental disorders.
What other international holidays are observed on October 10
This year, October 10 also falls on World Migratory Bird Day. It is observed on the second Saturday of May and October to remind people of the need to protect migratory birds, their routes, and their natural habitats.
Other commemorative dates include World Homeless Day, intended to draw attention to the problem of homelessness, and World Porridge Day, dedicated to promoting this dish and addressing nutrition issues.
Church Holiday and Folk Traditions
According to the New Julian calendar, on October 10 the Orthodox Church honors the martyrs Eulampius and his sister Eulampia. According to church traditions, they lived in Nicomedia and suffered because they refused to renounce the Christian faith.
In folk traditions, this day was associated with preparations for winter. Household heads finished their autumn work, checked their supplies, and prepared their homes for the cold. They also tried to predict what the coming winter would be like based on the weather.
Name days on October 10 according to the new church calendar are celebrated by Andrii, Anton, Vasyl, Kyrylo, Pavlo, Serhii, Stepan, Yukhym, and Yakiv.

The parents of Australian surfing brothers murdered in Mexico have said “no outcome can ever undo this tragedy” after three men were convicted of the 2024 killings.
Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33 respectively, and their friend Carter Rhoad, 30, were on a surfing trip to Mexico’s Pacific coast when they were shot dead in Baja California state in a suspected robbery.
The deaths of the trio sparked an outpouring of grief and condemnation in Australia and the United States.
Jesus Gerardo – known as “El Kekas” – was accused of leading the attack. His surname has not been disclosed for legal reasons. He and two other defendants, Irineo Francisco and Angel Jesus, were found guilty on Friday local time.
The judge ruled the three Mexican defendants acted with premeditation.
Martin and Debra Robinson, the brothers’ parents, travelled from Australia to the port city of Ensenada for the trial, which began on 7 September.
“They took our sons from our lives forever,” said Debra Robinson, who testified on the final day of the trial. “What hurts us most is that, in their final hours, they were treated with such cruelty.”
She burst into tears when the guilty verdict was pronounced.
Speaking outside the court after the verdict, Martin Robinson thanked family and friends for their support, and also thanked the judge, court staff, the Australian embassy in Mexico and the Australian federal police.
He said: “No outcome can ever undo this tragedy, but we hope today marks an important step towards justice and allows us to continue honouring their lives and the extraordinary young men they were. They will never be forgotten.”
Debra Robinson said: “I don’t feel any different today as I did yesterday or I will tomorrow, because … Callum and Jake are not here. A verdict is a good thing, but it doesn’t bring them back.”
She said she had no feelings towards the three guilty men. “I have tried to hold on to the memory of my children, my sons, and I try really not to think about them. And I don’t actually want them to have any notoriety. We don’t actually really speak their names. They’re not part of our grief really.”
Martin Robinson said a foundation in their sons’ names would carry on their legacy.
The Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation aims to “help people live bigger, shine brighter and love harder in their honour”.
Rhoad’s mother, Page, and his fiance, Natalie Weirtz, also participated in the hearing in a video call from the United States.
“The accused are guilty and must be punished so that no other family suffers the same pain,” Weirtz said. “Since Carter’s death, I feel paranoid and isolated.”
Sentencing is scheduled for 16 October.
The prosecution requested 210 years’ imprisonment for each of the accused, though the maximum sentence in Baja California is 60 years.
The surfers were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked in April 2024. Their bodies were found in a clifftop shaft, with gunshot wounds to their heads.
In November 2025, Ary Gisell Silva, the then-girlfriend of the main defendant, was sentenced to two decades in prison after admitting that she instigated the robbery.
Baja California is one of Mexico’s most violent states, plagued by organised crime and drug trafficking, although cartel activity does not usually affect tourists. Other foreign visitors have, however, been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers, Dean Lucas and Adam Coleman, were killed in 2015 while travelling through the north-western state of Sinaloa. Their bodies were later burned.

Paris and Berlin are contradicting each other on the fate of a much-heralded joint main battle tank development project. French Chief of Defense Staff General Fabien Mandon has claimed Germany withdrew from the program, while the German government says the opposite.
Known as the Main Ground Combat System (MGCS), the project was launched back in 2018 with the aim of replacing both the French Leclerc and German Leopard 2 main battle tanks. It was a collaboration between the Amsterdam-headquartered KNDS – the EU’s largest tank maker – the German Rheinmetall weapons manufacturing giant, and the French Thales industrial group. Berlin even purchased a 40% stake in KNDS in June, with another 40% held by Paris, when the project was still in full swing.
On Thursday, Mandon told French lawmakers that the plans for the project had essentially fallen through. “The outcome isn’t good. We had hoped to build a future tank in cooperation with the Germans, but unfortunately, we have to acknowledge that the Germans have withdrawn from the project,” he said during a hearing on next year’s budget.
According to Le Monde, the chief of the defense staff said Berlin made a political decision to halt cooperation. He reportedly stated that “the two army chiefs of staff had co-signed a joint document outlining their shared needs,” but the two neighbors were “no longer dealing with purely military choices.”
A German Defense Ministry spokesperson denied that claim, stating that Berlin merely wants to “adjust” the program to include the “lessons” of the Ukraine conflict. “We remain committed to equal partnership in the MGCS and are focusing on future technologies for armored combat,” the official said, according to Reuters.
Madon himself stated in a press release published after the hearing that an industrial proposal submitted in early 2026 “was incompatible with the need to replace the current tanks by 2037,” prompting Berlin to opt for a national effort to replace its Leopard 2 tank.
The general also maintained that a decade of work had “not been in vain” and the MGCS project was not scrapped but rather “pushed back to the late 2040s.” Paris would now launch its own national development of “an interim” replacement for its Leclerc tanks, he added.
The MGCS was intended to become a comprehensive platform for land warfare, with multiple weapon systems derived from it. The troubled project has reportedly been plagued by delays linked to political and industrial disputes. It is said Paris was aiming for a lighter combat vehicle suited for African deployments, while Berlin sought better heavy armor suitable for a major conflict, including with Russia.
The total cost of the project remains unclear, although a French parliamentary budget report suggested that Paris authorized a total of €212 million ($237.3 million) for the program over 2025 and 2026. The German government has not published any specific figures related to the project’s funding, but said in 2024 that the two partners were “each contributing 50% of the costs.”
Another major Franco-German armament program collapsed just months ago. Dubbed the Future Combat Air System (FCAS), it aimed to produce a next-generation fighter jet by 2040. The venture failed in June after an estimated €3.2 billion in sunk R&D costs due to irreconcilable disputes between aircraft makers Dassault and Airbus.

Anthropic AI model sent fake murder tip to Philadelphia police
SAN FRANCISCO - An artificial intelligence model developed by Anthropic submitted a fabricated tip about an unsolved homicide to Philadelphia police, US authorities said on Oct 9, criticising the company for taking two months to report the incident.
The Philadelphia Police Department said the false submission was made in July through PhillyUnsolvedMurders.com, a public website where people can share information about unsolved killings.
According to Anthropic’s account, as relayed by police, the model was running a test that involved interacting with randomly selected websites when it reached the site and filed false information about an unsolved murder.
The AI model presented itself as someone who might have knowledge of the case.
The incident echoed other recent cases, including one where an OpenAI agent undergoing a security evaluation broke out of its testing environment and breached systems at AI platform Hugging Face.
The episode heightened concerns about the AI industry’s increased use of AI agents, systems programmed to take multi-step actions without human supervision.
Anthropic published a report on Oct 9 outlining multiple types of “unintended” actions that its models have taken, including the incident involving the Philadelphia Police Department website.
Other organisations impacted included the White House and other US government agencies, the report said.
The newly revealed incidents “had minimal real-world impact” and were “significantly less severe” than other cybersecurity incidents previously reported, Anthropic said.
The company outlined four categories of incidents that it found during an internal review of its Claude model: exploiting “basic” coding flaws, submitting forms on websites, bypassing requirements for tokens or fees, and using short URLs to get around other limits.
Anthropic has turned off internet access for Claude during all internal testing for now “until we have confirmed that our security and monitoring measures... reliably catch behaviours like these,” the report said.
Police said the tip, dated July 18, was flagged as spam and never reached the department’s Real-Time Crime Center for vetting.
They added that there was no sign that police systems had been breached or department data compromised.
Anthropic discovered the incident on Sept 28, shut down the automated testing process responsible and added a new validation step for future tests, police said.
The company alerted the department on Oct 7, and the two sides met the following day.
“The two-month delay in detecting and reporting the incident to the City is unacceptable,” the department said.
Police said their safeguards had limited the impact, but that these “do not diminish the seriousness of an AI system presenting fabricated information as though it came from a person with knowledge of a homicide”.
“Unsolved cases involve real victims, grieving families and investigators working to secure answers,” the statement added. 
Anthropic also said it briefed the White House on these cases and notified each agency involved, reported Bloomberg.
On Oct 9, Trump administration officials said they were now requiring that AI companies notify affected parties and address security incidents involving their models.
“Earlier today, Anthropic contacted the SI Force to disclose the details of various prior incidents that it discovered in late September involving the unauthorised and fraudulent use of government and other systems,” the White House said in a statement from the Super Intelligence Force, a new government unit tasked by US President Donald Trump with overseeing AI development and safety.
“The company informed us that these events occurred in the past, the activity has ceased, and there is no ongoing similar activity,” the statement said.
Axios reported on the government requirement earlier. AFP, BLOOMBERG
