Book Publishers Are Quietly Using More AI. Staff Are Revolting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:28:49 UTC
04:28:49 KST

In headline after headline this year, American book publishers have appeared to be fighting back against generative AI, from suing Google for copyright infringement to canceling books by authors suspected of using LLMs.
But behind the scenes, at least three of the Big Five US book publishers—HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette—have been quietly incorporating AI tools into their publishing processes without public disclosures or author consent.
According to interviews with more than two dozen workers, all of whom spoke under the condition of anonymity to avoid jeopardizing their employment, publishers are now using LLMs like Claude and ChatGPT to email literary agents, write publicity and back-cover copy, design cover art, and generate marketing materials, often at the direction of their executives.
At the same time, multiple editorial staffers say the widely publicized cases of authors accused of using LLMs to help write their books—like Hachette’s horror novel Shy Girl or Macmillan’s crime thriller Call Me, I’ll Hide the Body—are just the tip of the iceberg. “Every single imprint has a story of someone very esteemed who had a book canceled because of blatant AI use” without ever making the news, one editor says.
At HarperCollins senior leaders purchased Claude licenses from Anthropic months ago “but very quickly realized they didn’t know how to implement them,” according to a current employee. Dozens of junior- and senior-level staff were then “voluntold” to become “AI Champions” and were tasked with discovering use cases in monthly brainstorming sessions with staff across the company.
This spring, when some HarperCollins employees expressed concerns about the legal, ethical, and environmental impacts of AI at one of these brainstorming sessions, a person leading the meeting dismissed their qualms as “the cost of doing business,” according to someone who attended the meeting. Soon after, a statement was added to the new AI section of the HarperCollins online employee portal, noting that “while AI does have an environmental impact, it’s a small part of most individuals’ total digital carbon footprint.”
Some HarperCollins staffers were unnerved by the brainstorming sessions. “It was such a slap in the face,” says one employee. “We’ve been making valid business cases for years to be paid a healthy salary, and instead they spent that money on software that most of us don’t really want.” (The average entry-level salary for New York City publishing employees at the Big Five and Scholastic was $47,583 in 2023.) In addition to Claude, staffers say HarperCollins has also purchased licenses for ChatGPT and Jasper, an agentic platform that promises “to run end-to-end marketing workflows.”
At least one HarperCollins division has been “all in” on AI since gaining software licenses, according to one staffer, including AI-generated marketing videos. But according to workers at HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster, and Hachette, one of the most common use cases for LLMs so far is generating publicity copy.
Readers encounter publicity copy everywhere from Amazon and Goodreads to back covers, and it’s used to pitch books to booksellers, journalists, content creators, and critics. However, “using AI to generate publicity copy is short-sighted,” a Big Five publicist tells me. “Publicists have a duty to engage in good faith with readers and our colleagues in the media, who I’m sure have a low threshold for tolerating AI-generated pitches.”
On the other hand, Meg Reid, publisher of the independent Hub City Press, says LLM-written marketing and publicity unfortunately “feels pretty inevitable” for the Big Five. “That’s one place we’re probably going to see a bigger shift between corporate publishers looking for efficiencies and smaller publishers insisting that the humans involved are the whole point.”
Meanwhile, earlier this year, literary agents began suspecting specific Big Five editors were using AI to write rejection letters. “Among colleagues, we compared emails on different books from the same editors, and they all had the same classic signs of AI writing, like ‘not this, but that’ and the rule of three,” one agent says. Employees at Simon & Schuster, HarperCollins, and Hachette tell WIRED they believe the agents’ suspicions were correct.
A spokesperson for Hachette says the company “support[s] the use of AI tools for operational purposes, when they help our authors’ books reach more readers,” but that it “[does] not support creative uses of AI, including communicating with our authors and partners.”
Wibke Grutjen, global chief marketing and communications officer at Simon & Schuster, says “employees across all functions have access to a limited number of enterprise-level AI tools,” but using them is not mandatory. Grutjen said the company prohibits the use of any AI tool “that has not been vetted and approved” and that “the goal is always to free up more time for our employees to spend on deeper focus and creative work on behalf of and alongside our authors.”
HarperCollins did not respond to requests for comment.
Months ago, workers at Simon & Schuster attended a workshop with representatives from OpenAI. “The person leading the workshop genuinely had no idea what we did,” an attendee says, but one of the AI company’s recommendations for how to use ChatGPT in the book trade was, in fact, composing emails to literary agents. The practice has also grown among editors at HarperCollins and Hachette, employees say.
In May 2024, staffers say Simon & Schuster held a contest among employees to come up with the best use cases for AI, with a $10,000 prize for the winner and $5,000 each for two runners-up. Since then, the company has “rolled back some of the AI-pushing because employees kept complaining about it in town halls,” says one employee. According to several staffers, AI assets are also cropping up in cover art, with some foreign presses distributed by Simon & Schuster openly acknowledging AI use when sharing designs.
All of the agents I spoke with expressed fears that publishers might paste text from their authors’ manuscripts into the LLMs in order to generate things like rejection letters and publicity descriptions. “We’ve added AI clauses to our contracts saying ‘this material can’t be run through an LLM,’” says one agent, who did not want to be named to avoid professional repercussions. “Ostensibly, that was meant to protect authors from tech companies, but it also applies to the company buying and publishing the book. If they're not using a closed-loop model, they could be feeding an LLM with an author’s unpublished writing.” Unlike the LLMs most people use online (Google Gemini, ChatGPT, et al.), a closed-loop model operates on an individual computer or network that’s “air-gapped” so it can’t share data with the AI company’s cloud servers. One source at HarperCollins says multiple editors have asked managers if they could paste a full manuscript into an open-loop LLM and were told not to by the company’s legal team.
Hachette employees are also bracing for the company’s AI policies to “evolve” under new chief information officer Carl Hixson, due to his previous role as chief technology officer at SRMG, a Saudi state-backed company that has publicly embraced agentic AI.
Some staffers across the Big Five say they’re reluctantly experimenting with LLMs only because executives gutted their teams through layoffs and subsequently tripled their workloads.
“It’s skeleton crews everywhere you look,” says one employee. “Large teams have been reduced to just five or six people, give or take, and we’re doing double or triple the number of books. No wonder people are taking shortcuts. I don’t judge them for that. I judge the company for shoving the shortcuts down our throats and saying, ‘Do this or we fall behind.’”
In just the past few weeks, word spread among Simon & Schuster workers that the company was conducting an experimental trial with Skan AI “at the apparent urging of KKR”—the investment firm that purchased Simon & Schuster in 2023. According to its own website, Skan AI “gives leaders the evidence base they need to reduce costs, prioritize automation, and meet board-level transformation mandates.”
In response, Simon & Schuster employees began gathering signatures on an open letter to their CEO, Greg Greeley, expressing their “strong opposition” and “seeking a commitment to not bring Skan AI or other similar software into S&S workflows, either now or in the future.” Beyond the software’s surveillance capabilities, many workers were also concerned with Skan AI’s “automation discovery” tools being used to shadow and replace them.
News of the open letter was published in New York magazine’s Book Gossip newsletter on October 6. On the same day, Greeley sent a memo to Simon & Schuster employees confirming that the company has been exploring Skan AI’s Blueprint product but that “no decision has been made to use Blueprint or any other productivity-monitoring or workflow-analysis tool,” and that he “had not seen the materials relating to this early-stage exploration” before concerns were raised to him the day before. Pangram, which, for better or worse, has become the go-to AI-detection platform, indicates that at least some of Greeley’s memo was written by AI.
Almost two years ago at the UBS Global Media and Communications Conference, HarperCollins CEO Brian Murray said AI presents “more opportunities than risks” for book publishers and that he saw AI playing a role in increasing the number of translated books and audiobooks published by HarperCollins in the future. Since then, multiple editors say they’ve seen LLM-translated manuscripts with AI-use disclosures at the annual Frankfurt and London book fairs, where US publishers buy international publishing and translation rights from foreign literary agencies.
In August, Michael Reynolds, executive publisher at Europa Editions, an independent press in New York best known for publishing Elena Ferrante’s Neapolitan Quartet of novels, told a room full of booksellers at the New Voices New Rooms conference in Baltimore he was excited about the possibilities for AI in translation and “seemed baffled by critiques of it,” according to attendees. Europa Editions is already controversial among literary circles for leaving the names of its human (for now) translators off the covers of its books.
“The C-suites at Big Five publishing companies have more in common with the C-suites at other major American companies than they do with the editors and publicists and translators who work for them,” says Dan Sinykin, author of Big Fiction: How Conglomeration Changed the Publishing Industry and American Literature. “They’re always looking for ways to maximize profit, and right now they’re trying to see what they can get away with before there’s a revolt.”
Most of the industry professionals I spoke with just want publishers to provide clear AI usage guidelines and disclosures, at the very least, to help mitigate the current chaos. “We need publishers to be clear about what is being used and when,” says Emma Dries, an agent at Triangle House Literary who previously worked in editorial at HarperCollins and Penguin Random House. A current HarperCollins staffer, meanwhile, says there has been no direction “about what to say to authors or agents about any of this, because I think they know it would start a shitstorm.”
“Short of these tools being banned, which would frankly be my preference,” Dries continues, “everybody should be communicating more.”

09 October 2026•Update: 10 October 2026
US President Donald Trump said Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel fuel to American and global markets following talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump said on his Truth Social platform that he had concluded a "highly successful discussion" with Putin, resulting in an agreement to increase Russian diesel supplies.
"I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump said.
He added that another 3 million tons would be delivered "within a short period," depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
"Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be coming down, in record numbers, and fast!” Trump said.
The president described lower fuel prices as a priority, particularly for American farmers, ranchers, and truckers.
Fuel prices, and their ripple effect on the economy, have emerged as a key issue in the US midterm congressional elections, set for Nov. 3, just a few weeks away.
Trump also cited what he described as the US’ "total control" of the Strait of Hormuz and reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to develop nuclear weapons.
Trump later told reporters that he was "very happy" to get the deal, adding: "We needed oil prices … already dropping like a rock."
 
US Treasury issues license for sales
Shortly after Trump's announcement, the US Treasury Department said on US social media platform X that its Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) was “immediately issuing a temporary general license to allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market.”
The Treasury later issued a general license authorizing transactions related to the sale, delivery, offloading and importation of Russian-origin diesel fuel through April 7 of next year.
The US and Israel launched a war against Iran on Feb. 28, prompting Tehran to respond with missile and drone attacks across the region and effectively closing the Strait of Hormuz.
The conflict has continued for more than seven months, driving up global energy prices as commercial oil traffic through the strategic waterway has effectively halted.
The US and Iran signed a framework agreement in June following mediation efforts by Pakistan and Qatar to halt hostilities and pave the way for negotiations.
Implementation of the agreement has since stalled amid disagreements, including over security and navigation in the Strait of Hormuz.

Montenegro, a country of fewer than 650,000 people, has been seeking EU membership since 2008. The Balkan country joined NATO in 2017 despite protests from opponents who recalled the military bloc’s 1999 bombing campaign against Yugoslavia, of which Montenegro was then a part alongside Serbia.

German Bundestag recognizes Germany’s special historical responsibility to Ukraine for Nazi crimes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:23:00 UTC
04:23:00 KST

German Bundestag recognizes Germany’s special historical responsibility to Ukraine for Nazi crimes
The votes took place during a plenary session of the Bundestag on Friday, October 9, an Ukrinform correspondent reports.
The motion submitted by the governing CDU/CSU and SPD parliamentary groups emphasizes that Germany’s special historical responsibility to Ukraine also entails a present-day political obligation.
“Germany’s special historical responsibility to Ukraine gives rise to a political obligation to preserve the memory of the crimes committed during the National Socialist occupation. Today, Germany and its partners stand for Ukraine’s freedom, sovereignty and self-determination. Germany stands alongside Ukraine as it defends its territorial integrity, national independence and democratic future against Russia’s war of aggression, which is illegal under international law,” the document states.
It also explicitly links Germany’s historical responsibility to its current assistance to Ukraine.
“This responsibility finds concrete expression in comprehensive support for Ukraine’s self-defense; efforts to secure the return of Ukrainian children and adolescents abducted by Russia; support for reconstruction and the strengthening of democratic and legal institutions; and assistance to Ukraine on its path toward EU accession, as well as in maintaining strong transatlantic relations,” the motion states.
The coalition motion calls on the federal government to continue providing Ukraine with comprehensive political, economic, financial, humanitarian and military support as it defends its sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity against Russian aggression. It specifically calls for continued military assistance in coordination with European and transatlantic partners, including the provision of necessary weapons systems, ammunition, equipment, training capabilities and logistical resources.
The second adopted document, a motion submitted by the Alliance 90/The Greens parliamentary group, states the point even more directly: “Germany recognizes its special historical responsibility toward Ukraine and other countries in Central and Eastern Europe.”
The document also states that “Germany bears a special historical responsibility toward Ukraine and for peace throughout Europe.”
In view of Russia’s war of aggression, the Bundestag motion calls on the federal government to continue supporting Ukraine “at all levels, and to a greater extent,” in defending its right to self-determination, independence, freedom, territorial integrity and sovereignty, and to strengthen political, financial, humanitarian and military assistance.
One notable feature of the vote was that the German parliament adopted both competing motions. The opposition Greens’ motion was supported by the Greens and the Left Party, while the CDU/CSU, SPD and the right-wing populist Alternative for Germany (AfD) abstained. The motion submitted by the CDU/CSU and SPD was supported by the governing parties, while the Greens and the Left Party voted in favor and the AfD abstained. Thus, every parliamentary group in the Bundestag except the AfD supported at least one of the two motions, and neither motion received any votes against it.
Ukraine’s Ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, who watched the debate and voting from the Bundestag’s visitors’ gallery, called the outcome unique, noting that parliament had ultimately approved two separate motions, one from the governing coalition and one from the opposition.
“According to the usual logic of parliamentary politics, this should not have happened. But it did. Instead of playing politics, the German Bundestag’s parliamentary groups – all except one – decided to make history. They allowed both motions to proceed, and not a single vote was cast against either of them,” the Ukrainian ambassador wrote on Facebook.
He said the Ukrainian side had spent several years working on the issue of Germany’s historical responsibility and the idea of a corresponding Bundestag resolution.
“We spent several years working on the issue of historical responsibility and on the idea of a Bundestag resolution. In the end, we got two. But most importantly, we recorded a fundamental and profound change in attitudes,” the ambassador said.
Makeiev also drew a parallel with the Bundestag vote in autumn 2022, when the German parliament recognized the Holodomor of 1932–1933 as genocide.
“I was in this same gallery in autumn 2022. I saw how Germany’s democratic parliamentary groups can demonstrate unity when it comes to what matters most. Back then, the Bundestag recognized the Holodomor of 1932–1933 as genocide. I remember the special sincerity and unity that prevailed in that chamber. Today, I felt the same thing again,” the ambassador said.
Summing up the parliament’s decision, Makeiev wrote: “On October 9, 2026, the German Bundestag officially recognized Germany’s special historical responsibility to Ukraine for the crimes of National Socialism.”
As Ukrinform reported, Ukraine’s Ambassador to Germany, Oleksii Makeiev, previously said in an interview with the agency that German leaders were increasingly speaking about the country’s historical responsibility specifically toward Ukraine, rather than only toward Russia. He said this was the result of systematic efforts by Ukrainian diplomacy to encourage Berlin to reassess historical narratives.

I found an AI slop book written about me
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:19:32 UTC
04:19:32 KST

Someone made an AI slop book about me. I'm not alone
A few months back, I was doomscrolling before bed when I received a WhatsApp message from a friend with a link to Amazon.
As someone who has spent years reporting on technology, and now solely on artificial intelligence, it's pretty common to get tips about something weird that was generated with AI.
Unusually, this tip was about me. Sort of.
The listing was for a book entitled Conspiracy Nation Exercises: Redefine Living Through Cam Wilson Teachings.
I couldn't know for sure it was something, and not someone, who'd decided to write a book about me, but there were signs.
The title closely resembled a book of mine that I co-wrote and published last year.
The "author", Leni McAllister, doesn't seem to exist, and the short blurb has the tell-tale signs of AI-generated writing.
Identifying "slop" becomes a sixth sense after you've seen enough of it.
Em dashes. The distinctive tempo. The blurb even had the "it's not X — it's Y" that AI seems to love.
So, I bought the book.
Two days later, it arrived in the mail. I didn't expect it to be so absurdly big. Like A4-sized-big.
I was able to quickly flick through its meagre 89 pages, although even that number gives a misleading impression about its seriousness. The text was double-spaced and printed in a very large size.
The moment my bemusement turned to hurt was when I realised that they had chosen Comic Sans — the most unserious of all fonts, and one more closely associated with primary school projects — as a suitable match for my "teachings".
'They pop up everywhere'
I'm not a full-time author but, by all accounts, making a living publishing in Australia is extremely gruelling.
I was holding something that probably took longer to leaf through than it did to generate. Filled with things I didn't say, poorly written and bizarrely laid out, it was extremely frustrating.
It felt like the exact opposite of the care and love we poured into our book.
It also felt like a physical slop that existed not to be enjoyed or understood, but to deceive a prospective reader just long enough to convince them to click "buy" online.
I then discovered an infestation of other books online using an identical template, just for different authors and books.
One author who'd put out her debut book around the same time as me, Natalie Kyriacou, responded with exasperation when I sent her a link to Nature's Last Dance Exercises: Redefine Living through Natalie Kyriacou Teachings.
It turns out she already knew about this because she'd heard from those who mistakenly bought the fraudulent version of her book off Amazon.
"We have been trying to remove them but they pop up everywhere," she says.
So I sent Amazon a list of questions. The next day, the listing for "my" book was taken down.
The listing had broken Amazon's guidelines, I was told, although the exact rule that was broken wasn't clear. The company took others down, too.
"We have proactive and reactive methods that help us detect content that violates our guidelines, whether AI generated or not. We invest significant time and resources to ensure our guidelines are followed, and remove books that do not adhere to those guidelines," an Amazon spokesperson said in an email.
But when I asked for any information about who was behind it, the company didn't provide it.
"Looking into this for you," one staff member said.
I didn't hear back.
'Platforms should bear responsibility'
But I was lucky.
Others have struggled to get AI books taken down, sometimes books that aren't just about them, but are attributed to them.
Australian Society of Authors chief executive Lucy Hayward says this has become so common as to be unremarkable.
"On the publication day for an author, you'll often see that there's already an AI-generated version of the book that's already been on sale," she says.
Hayward says there are obvious ways it hurts authors: they lose sales to the fakes, they get poor reviews because someone bought the slop and blamed them, it confuses people trying to buy the book, and they give up.
She says jobs many authors have done as side hustles, like copywriting, have been particularly affected by the spread of generative AI, and fraud is contributing to dropping reading rates.
Hayward says there are some simple fixes, such as requiring platforms like Amazon to effectively police these kinds of derivative works and requiring retailers to label AI-generated content so readers don't get tricked.
"Platforms should bear responsibility," she says.
But her remedies go further.
Hayward says AI companies need to do licensing deals with authors to compensate for the books they've taken and to do more to protect their intellectual property.
The government has been quietly consulting on two proposed changes to copyright law to facilitate AI training in Australia.
Both plans would make training opt-out for authors and other creatives, meaning that the burden was on the individual, not the company, to stop their work being used to train AI.
AI companies say an opt-out system is necessary to allow legal AI training in Australia, something the federal government explicitly says it hopes will happen.
Haywood and other creators think the onus should be on AI companies to secure approval from creatives to use and protect their work
Creatives remain vulnerable
When I looked this week, I found dozens more AI-generated books still for sale.
It's not just on Amazon, either. Other platforms reportedly have similar issues.
I can't see any more ripoffs targeting me. Perhaps I should be offended; if my book was more popular, surely there'd be more imitations.
But it's telling that of all of the utopian AI futures that we're promised — abundance, the end of disease, happiness — tech executives' blue-sky thinking is still leaving creatives vulnerable.
Even though AI-enabled rip-offs are already happening en masse, authors are hoping there's more that can be done to protect their work in future.
Or, to quote "Leni McAllister" quoting "Cam Wilson": "This is not an ending. It's an invitation."

Quick hits: Maddinson makes historic 33-ball duck as Aussie batters flounder
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:18:12 UTC
04:18:12 KST

Nic Maddinson's unlikely Test return has ended with a historic duck as Australia's battered floundered despite a South African DRS debacle.
Here are the quick hits from the opening day of the first Test between Australia and South Africa.
1. Maddinson makes historic duck on return
With almost a decade having passed since the last of his three Test appearances, veteran opener Nic Maddinson could have been forgiven for thinking his days in Australian whites were over.
But after being parachuted into the squad earlier this week, the 34-year-old's sensational return to the Test arena was cemented at the toss in Durban, with Pat Cummins confirming Maddinson would be the replacement for the injured Cameron Green.
In an even bigger surprise, he was in line to open his side's innings, with the also recently recalled Matt Renshaw dropping down the order.
Maddinson did not play at all in the last Sheffield Shield season, with his last First Class appearance having come back in March 2025.
And with Australia winning the toss and batting, he was put to the test immediately.
Maddinson looked both nervy and underdone in his drought-breaking Test knock, unable to get off the mark during his first 32 balls before being dismissed by his 33rd, the New South Welshman chopping onto his stumps off the bowling of Marco Jansen.
Unfortunately for Maddinson, it was a historic return as well as a miserable one, his 33-ball effort setting a new record for the longest duck by an Aussie opener in Test cricket.
Overall, it was the second-longest no score by an Australian in the history of the format, only behind Mike Whitney's 42-ball 0 in 1981.
2. South Africa in DRS debacle
Only minutes earlier, Maddinson had been gifted a huge slice of luck.
With the opener swinging across the line wildly, a Wiaan Mulder delivery thudded into his front pad. There was a big appeal, but umpire Richard Kettlebrough was unmoved.
South African captain Temba Bavuma indicated Maddinson had gotten some bat on ball and opted against the first review of the series.
And there certainly were two noises but replays showed Maddinson's willow had gotten nowhere near the ball, instead clipping his pad.
The South Africans watched the big screen ruefully as it showed the three reds that would have sent Maddinson back to the pavilion.
It was an unconvincing start for the South Africans as far DRS was concerned, with Bavuma also burning two reviews on appeals that didn't have a whole lot going for them.
First, Marnus Labuschagne survived a referral on a ball that swung too sharply and was projected to be missing leg stump.
Then, the hosts wasted a second review when a steepling Marco Jansen delivery caught Renshaw on the arm. The ball had looped up to wicketkeeper Kyle Verreynne, who took a simple catch, and the South Africans were convinced it had brushed the Australian's glove.
It hadn't.
The replays showed Jansen had found nothing but arm guard and the hosts had just one review remaining.
3. Labuschagne departs on stroke of lunch
It was a gut-wrenching end to an innings of serious promise for Labuschagne.
The Queenslander, so desperately in need of a score to get his Test career back on track, reached the final over of the morning session on 37 and with one eye on kicking on after the first break.
He was able to see off the first five balls of the set, but fell on its last.
Angling into the right-hander, Mulder was able to sneak one past Labuschagne's outside edge and into the front pad.
It looked touch and go whether the ball made impact in-line with the stumps, but the umpire's finger was up.
Labuschagne didn't look overly hopeful sending the decision upstairs, but DRS showed how close he was to getting outside the line of off stump, with the Australian only having to leave the field because of the umpire's original call.
It is not the kind of luck you need when you've gone more than three years without a Test century.
4. Smith makes anticlimactic entrance
With all that had been made of Steve Smith's return to the country his Test career had so shockingly unravelled eight years earlier, the understated reception he received when entering the game felt at least a little anticlimactic.
There was no chorus of boos from the few spectators in place for the morning session as Smith joined Labuschagne at the crease, tasked with steadying the Australian innings with both Maddinson and Head back in the sheds.
And Smith began his innings like he had so often in the past: fidgety, idiosyncratic and paranoid, but set on getting himself into the game.
After seeing off the opening pace barrage, Smith stamped his authority on the morning with two big sixes back over the head of spinner Keshav Maharaj in the space of four balls.
Smith made it to lunch, but only lasted three balls after the first break.
He was struck on the finger by a rearing Marco Jansen length ball, before edging the very next delivery through to the slips.
Smith was out for 25 and Australia had lost two wickets in four balls either side of the lunch break.
5. Bad light robs Renshaw of drought-breaking milestone
Coming in at number five, Renshaw was a bright spot in an otherwise dark day for the Australian batters.
The southpaw watched on as South African spearhead Anrich Nortje removed Alex Carey and Beau Webster in the space of three balls, and looked supremely confident in his new home in the middle order.
He made his way to 46 before bad light ended the day with over an hour left of scheduled play and just 65.2 overs bowled.
Renshaw will begin day two four runs away from his first Test 50 in more than 3,500 days, tasked with continuing to rebuild Australia's innings alongside Cummins.

Verstappen controversially won qualifying for the sprint at the Singapore Grand Prix

Max Verstappen won qualifying for the Singapore Grand Prix sprint, finishing ahead of Russell and Leclerc. The stewards did not penalize him for the incident under yellow flags.
Red Bull driver Max Verstappen secured pole position for the sprint at the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix. Despite a dramatic incident involving a possible rules violation under yellow flags, the stewards decided not to penalize the Dutch driver. This was reported by UNN, citing Formula 1.
"Max Verstappen claimed pole position for the sprint in Singapore, beating Mercedes' George Russell and Ferrari's Charles Leclerc in a tense session under the floodlights at the Marina Bay Street Circuit," the report said.
Verstappen timed his final lap perfectly, surpassing the times of each of his rivals and finishing the session with a time of 1 min 31.156 sec.
His lap on soft tires allowed him to beat Russell by 0.120 sec, while Leclerc was another tenth of a second behind and took third place.
Franco Colapinto of Alpine finished 11th after Russell pushed him out of the top ten on the final lap, while Nico Hülkenberg of Audi took 12th place.
However, it should be noted that the session was preceded by controversy. During the first qualifying session (SQ1), single yellow flags were displayed after Sergio Perez of Cadillac crashed into the barrier, and Verstappen subsequently appeared to overtake Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari, prompting Hamilton to report over the radio: "Max overtook me under yellow flags."
Verstappen commented: "I will let Lewis through again. I think I overtook him before the yellow flags appeared, but I just want to be on the safe side."
A document published after the stewards' hearing into the incident explained: "When Car No. 3 (Verstappen) was exiting Turn 7 on a fast lap, a single yellow flag was shown. Car No. 44 (Hamilton) was ahead of Car No. 3 and was warned of the approach of Car No. 3."
The stewards considered that Verstappen had "reacted appropriately to the yellow flag" and acknowledged that, although he had breached the rules, it was an "unfortunate consequence of a significant difference in approach speeds."

Lebanese army receives ammunition from France under military cooperation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:15:32 UTC
04:15:32 KST

Lina Altawell
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The Lebanese army said Friday it has received a shipment of ammunition from France as part of ongoing military cooperation between the two countries and efforts to strengthen its capabilities.
The ammunition was delivered to the Port of Beirut as "a donation from the French authorities," the army command said in a statement.
The army said the assistance formed part of ongoing cooperation between the Lebanese and French armed forces.
It added that the donation was intended to support the military as it carried out its responsibilities amid challenges facing the country.
The statement did not specify the type, quantity or value of the ammunition. 
EU, US military assistance
The French donation came a day after the Lebanese army received assistance from the EU, including engineering and transport vehicles, electricity generators and other equipment, according to Lebanon's official news agency.
The agency said the European assistance was intended to strengthen army units and meet their logistical needs as they carried out missions across Lebanon.
In late September, the Lebanese army announced that it received 47 Humvee military vehicles and five trucks at the Port of Beirut under US military assistance programs.
The deliveries came amid continued Israeli attacks on Lebanon and the security and military challenges they pose to the Lebanese army. 
Israeli attacks continue despite agreement
Israel has carried out attacks on Lebanon since March 2, killing and injuring thousands of people, according to the supplied account.
On June 26, Beirut and Tel Aviv signed a US-sponsored framework agreement in Washington providing for a gradual Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory.
The agreement also provides for the deployment of the Lebanese army in areas vacated by Israeli forces.
Despite the agreement, Israeli attacks on southern Lebanon have continued, and Israeli forces remain in control of areas there, including territory occupied for decades and areas seized during more recent military operations.

She's finally beaten Ledecky, now Pallister wants Olympic gold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:11:30 UTC
04:11:30 KST

After finally beating Katie Ledecky, swimmer Lani Pallister is focused on 2028 Olympics
Swimming superstar Lani Pallister wasn't meant to be a distance swimmer.
At the beginning of her career, she was focused on the butterfly events.
It was only when Pallister mistakenly selected the 800 metres freestyle on a race program (instead of the 100m butterfly) that her career path would change.
"I ended up swimming it [800m freestyle], qualified for my first junior team, and now I'm on the senior team, and short course world record holder for the event," Pallister told ABC Sport at the Australian Short Course Championships earlier this month.
It's been a packed year for the 24-year-old, but a satisfying one.
Her success at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, where she won gold in the 400m, 800m and 1,500m, saw her become the first woman at the Games to complete the treble.
But her performance at this year's Pan Pacific Swimming Championships in August, less than two weeks after the Glasgow Games, was her most remarkable breakthrough, beating United States powerhouse Katie Ledecky for the first time in the long course 800m freestyle.
"When you achieve a feat like that, you don't believe it until your hands are on the wall," Pallister said.
"It's not as much about just beating the one person in particular, but I think when you have someone as monumental as Katie, that definitely plays into the feelings and the sense of achievement off the back of it."
Pallister puts this success down to a change in coaching, making the shift from Michael Bohl to Dean Boxall over a year ago.
"The past 18-month journey with [Dean] has been unbelievable, and I've achieved things in swim times I didn't think possible for myself," Pallister said.
It is a change that could take her to the Los Angeles Olympics in 2028, earning redemption for the heartbreak she has experienced in the past few years.
Rebuilding after Paris
It hasn't been an easy journey for Pallister, with illness and mental health taking a toll on her swimming career.
In 2021, she developed an eating disorder and a series of illnesses that saw her miss qualification for the Tokyo Olympics.
After seeing improvement in her times in the lead-up to the Paris Olympics in 2024, COVID struck, causing Pallister to pull out of the 1,500 and 400m races and finish sixth in the 800 metres.
She thought her swimming career could be over at 22.
But after changing coaches, breaking world records in short course events, and finally claiming her win over Ledecky, Pallister is excited for the future and focusing on LA.
If everything goes right, an individual Olympic medal could finally be on the cards.
"I really wanted to focus on staying humble," Pallister said.
"There's a lot of work and a lot of things that are going to happen between now and the LA Olympics and I think that week over in LA in 2028 is going to be about consistency, repeat performance and just preparing."
Pallister will be 26 years old by the time the LA Games arrive, and 30 when Brisbane rolls around.
Age doesn't worry her though; moving to Boxall's squad has given her a fresh perspective.
"Female distance swimmers are slowly getting a little bit older," Pallister said, referring to Ledecky, who broke her own 800m world record at 28.
Any thought of retirement is far from Pallister's mind, and with a home Games in Brisbane in sight, it is tempting to hold on.
"At the end of the day, swimming's one of those sports, when you know you're done, you'll be done," Pallister said.
"With friends and family, in a city that I grew up swimming [in], it's probably the perfect way to end, and I think there's a lot of athletes that are in my age group that are kind of thinking the same thing."
Defending her title
Before the LA and Brisbane Games, however, Pallister will be continuing her busy year, having qualified for the 2026 World Aquatic Championships in December.
The championships will be held in China, with Pallister returning as the defending champion and short course 800m world record holder.
At the Australian Short Course Championships, she claimed victory in the 200, 400, 800, and 1,500 metres, meaning her World Championships will be busy.
"The biggest goal for me this year is going back to a World Championships and defending my back-to-back title in the 800," Pallister said.
"When you have the opportunity to race on the international stage and get more race practice under the belt, particularly before the next two years going into LA, it is something that's really important."

"If it's all through livestream, I'm not going to be watching it," Vance said.

Head of Russian military propaganda network to be expelled from Montenegro over suspected anti-EU operation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:08:56 UTC
04:08:56 KST

Montenegro has ordered the expulsion of Mikhail Zvynchuk, head of the pro-Kremlin military information network Rybar, and four other Russian citizens over national security concerns following a security operation targeting suspected Russian hybrid influence activities, Vijesti reported on 9 October.
Zvynchuk is the founder and head of Rybar, a prominent Russian military-focused information network known for its Telegram channels covering Russia's war against Ukraine. The network promotes pro-Kremlin narratives and has been associated with Russian propaganda and influence operations.
Montenegrin police announced on 9 October that the five Russians had their residence rights revoked and were ordered to leave the country on national and internal security grounds.
Montenegro investigates suspected Russian hybrid activity
The operation involved Montenegro's police and National Security Agency (ANB), which seized drones, high-resolution recording equipment, cameras, and several mobile phones for further examination, according to Vijesti.
According to Montenegrin authorities, the five had arrived in the country less than two days before the operation. The investigation is being conducted with support from international partners.
Montenegrin police identified the five Russian citizens as Zvynchuk, his wife Valeria Zvynchuk, Sergei Belous, Pavel Lekatorchuk, and Kira Doroshenko. Authorities said the case had been referred to prosecutors in Podgorica and Kotor.
The European Union has sanctioned Zvynchuk over activities that undermine or threaten Ukraine's territorial integrity, sovereignty, and independence. He has also been sanctioned by the United Kingdom, Switzerland, Australia, and Ukraine, according to Vijesti.
Suspected influence operation targeting EU integration
Vijesti reported, citing security sources, that Montenegrin authorities suspected the group of planning a documentary intended to undermine public support for the country's European integration.
According to the outlet, the planned material would portray Montenegro's expected alignment of its visa policy with EU standards as a politically imposed measure that threatens tourism, economic stability, and national interests.
Security services had monitored the group's arrival before carrying out the operation in Risan, in the Bay of Kotor area, Vijesti reported. The equipment seized from the group will undergo expert analysis to establish its intended purpose and use in Montenegro.
Medvedev threatens imprisoning “European and American idiots” for prisoner exchanges
Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev responded to the operation by suggesting Moscow might need to expand its pool of prisoners to exchange for Europeans and Americans to secure Zvynchuk's return.
“We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots,” Medvedev said, according to Vijesti.
Montenegro, a NATO member and EU candidate, has aligned itself with EU sanctions against Russia following Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. The expulsion comes amid broader European concerns over Russian intelligence activity, propaganda, and other forms of hybrid interference.

Strong earthquake shakes Panama, prompting tsunami alert
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:03:00 UTC
04:03:00 KST

Strong earthquakes, aftershocks shake Panama
October 9, 2026
A powerful magnitude-7.7 earthquake struck Panama on Friday morning.
According to the US Geological Survey (USGS), the quake's epicenter was located approximately 10 kilometers (6 miles) southwest of the remote community of Pitaloza Arriba, near Panama's southern tip.
The quake struck at a depth of 10 kilometers. Shallow earthquakes (up to 70 kilometers deep) are considered more dangerous and destructive.
The USGS later reported that a second powerful earthquake, measuring 6.6 in magnitude, struck the country following a series of aftershocks.
The tremors were strongly felt in the capital Panama City, causing buildings to shake and sending people rushing into the streets.
"We felt it very strongly. It knocked things over in the kitchen, but we're okay, though we're very scared," Rosendo Domínguez, 60, who is from Herrera province, where the earthquake struck, told The Associated Press by phone. “Everyone is outside, scared."
Panamanian President Jose Raul Mulino described the earthquake as a "major disaster" which had destroyed roads near the epicenter.
What do we know about damage?
Mulino did not say whether there were any casualties.
According to Omar Smith of the National Civil Protection Service, damage was concentrated in the central provinces of Veraguas, Herrera and Los Santos.
Smith reported several injuries, as well as partial collapses and cracks at the cathedral in the district’s main square, as well as damage to the governor’s office building and the Dos Continentes hotel.
Meanwhile, local news outlets reported that the colonial-style Church of San Atanasio in Panama’s Los Santos province collapsed. The church was declared a National Historic Heritage Site in 1938.
Tsunami warning lifted
The US Tsunami Warning System issued an alert stating that hazardous tsunami waves were possible along parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador, and Mexico within the next three hours.
The system also reported a tsunami threat to Hawaii. The warning was lifted later on Friday afternoon.
Initially, there were no reports of damage to the Panama Canal. The Panama Canal Authority stated that the waterway was operating as usual.
Tocumen International Airport in Panama City briefly suspended operations and activated evacuation protocols before reopening later on Friday afternoon.
Panama is located along the so-called "Ring of Fire," a line of seismic faults encircling the Pacific Ocean where most of the world's earthquakes occur.

Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:01:17 UTC
04:01:17 KST

- Category
- War in Ukraine
Russia Keeps Striking Ukraine’s Energy Grid—Now It Wants Sanctions Relief to Stop, Report Says
Russia is seeking sanctions relief from the United States in exchange for a possible agreement to suspend attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, while also pushing to include a ceasefire in the Black Sea as part of a wider arrangement.
According to The Kyiv Independent report on October 9, citing American and Ukrainian officials familiar with the discussions, Moscow has privately signaled that it could consider an energy ceasefire but is seeking additional concessions before agreeing to the proposal.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Russia’s demands emerge amid an escalation of strikes against Ukraine’s energy facilities, which have left communities across the country facing significant electricity disruptions.
A senior Ukrainian defense official told the publication that Moscow is attempting to cause as much damage as possible to Ukraine’s energy infrastructure to improve its bargaining position ahead of potential negotiations.
While discussions over a possible agreement continue behind closed doors, Russian officials have publicly expressed little interest in suspending attacks on energy infrastructure.
According to The Kyiv Independent, on October 8, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov dismissed the prospect of negotiating a ceasefire limited to the energy sector.
“Kyiv is not currently proposing a long-term settlement, but rather a ceasefire in an area that is its Achilles' heel—the energy sector,” Peskov said.
Nevertheless, two Ukrainian officials and one American official told The Kyiv Independent that Moscow had privately indicated a willingness to consider the initiative, although it was linking any potential agreement to further demands.
Washington has been urging both Kyiv and Moscow to stop targeting each other’s energy infrastructure, with the proposal emerging as a key element of US-led efforts to advance negotiations.
Several Ukrainian officials also indicated that US President Donald Trump is seeking tangible diplomatic progress on Ukraine ahead of the upcoming American midterm elections.
Following their most recent trip to Russia, Trump’s representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner reportedly concluded that an agreement to suspend strikes on energy facilities remained possible.
The proposal was also raised during two visits to the United States in September by Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev, who held discussions with Witkoff and Kushner. According to US and Ukrainian officials briefed on those meetings, Dmitriev made clear that Moscow wanted sanctions restrictions eased as part of any potential deal.
However, the precise measures Russia is seeking to have lifted have not been identified. Ukrainian officials familiar with the negotiations acknowledged that sanctions relief had been raised but said they remained unaware of which specific restrictions Moscow wanted removed.
One European diplomat informed about the discussions suggested that Russia might be seeking the release of frozen Russian assets as part of the arrangement.
“If they get sanctioned funds released… the likelihood that these will be used to escalate (war) is almost guaranteed,” the diplomat told The Kyiv Independent. “No one really thinks they are genuinely seeking to adhere to a ceasefire.”
Moscow’s demands are expected to become a subject of further discussions between Ukraine and the United States as diplomatic efforts continue.
A Ukrainian delegation is due to meet with Trump’s representatives in the United States on October 9 to examine proposals for suspending attacks on energy infrastructure and establishing a ceasefire in the Black Sea, the outlet reported.
The Ukrainian officials are also expected to be briefed on Washington’s recent contacts with Moscow and request further details about the sanctions relief Russia is seeking in exchange for a potential agreement.
The discussions come amid a separate diplomatic initiative by the Trump administration that could also involve easing sanctions against Russia. The Atlantic reported on September 29 that Washington was considering offering Moscow sanctions relief in exchange for the release of political prisoners, potentially creating an opportunity to restore economic ties between the two countries despite Russia’s ongoing war against Ukraine.
The proposal was developed by Trump’s envoy to Eastern Europe, John Coale, who reportedly presented the initiative to the US president several months earlier. Trump is said to have approved the proposal, although the initiative remains in its preliminary stages.

Germany Concerned About Threat Russian Satellites Pose to Starlink
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:57:52 UTC
03:57:52 KST

The ability of Russian satellites to perform coordinated active maneuvers raises concerns about a potential attack on Starlink satellites.
Major General Michael Traut, commander of the German Space Command, spoke about this in an interview with Reuters.
According to him, in May 2026, a group of Russian military satellites tracked a Western satellite assisting Ukraine, demonstrating capabilities that could threaten commercial satellite constellations.
General Traut stated that a direct attack on a Starlink satellite would constitute a significant escalation, but Moscow could employ gray zone tactics.
He described a hypothetical scenario in which a Russian satellite would shift into Starlink’s orbital path and then break up into debris. This would force the satellites to perform evasive maneuvers, consuming fuel and potentially shortening their operational lifespan.
According to the U.S. Space Force, in May, Russia maneuvered four military satellites — Cosmos 2610–2613 — bringing them closer to a commercial radar imaging satellite operated by the Finnish company ICEYE.
ICEYE CEO Rafal Modzewski told Reuters that the company subsequently changed the position of its satellite, after which the Russian satellites performed additional maneuvers.
According to him, this incident demonstrated that satellites are increasingly likely to maneuver close to one another to observe or potentially cause damage. Modzewski noted that this incident underscores the need to monitor activity in orbit and raises questions about the need for protection.
According to Western military officials, Russia’s interference with Western space systems has significantly intensified since its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
They note that this includes jamming via ground-based assets and in-orbit surveillance to gather intelligence and test the West’s limits of tolerance.
In early September, the U.S. simulated a Russian nuclear explosion in space and its impact on satellites. The simulation shows that the radiation belt created by the explosion could cause 11,000 satellites to fail within a week.
Separately, the authors suggest that Moscow could use a space-based nuclear threat against Starlink to force Washington or SpaceX to limit their support for Ukraine.

The Fourth Law and Odd Systems have unveiled Project Foundation, a semiconductor initiative to mass-produce uncooled thermal sensors in Europe and the United States.
The companies say the project aims to quadruple European thermal sensor output and double US output within three years, expanding production capacity for defense and civilian applications.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
The initiative plans to develop proprietary uncooled long-wave infrared (LWIR) sensors, also known as microbolometers, and manufacture them at scale. The companies say the goal is to strengthen European and US control over thermal sensor supply.
The sensors are intended for drones, cars, factories and robots, with production planned through partner semiconductor foundries and dedicated facilities.
The first two planned fabrication facilities, First Foundation and Second Foundation, would be located in Europe and the United States, respectively. They would share a common technology base and proprietary sensor designs.
Odd Systems develops and manufactures thermal and daytime cameras for drones and other robotic systems. Its flagship product, the Kurbas thermal camera, is supplied to more than 70 Ukrainian drone manufacturers, according to the companies. The Fourth Law builds technologies that enable drones to continue their missions when communications are disrupted, with an initial focus on defense.
Drawing on Isaac Asimov
Both companies were founded by Yaroslav Azhnyuk, whose earlier ventures include Petcube, Fuel Finance and Ozero Design. Petcube has featured in Kyiv Post’s coverage of Ukrainian startups.
Russian Refinery Seeks Air Defense Operators Amid Escalating Drone Strikes
The two companies were established in Kyiv in 2023 with a team of engineers, operators and veterans. They operate across Ukraine, the rest of Europe and the United States.
According to the companies, the founding team has 14 years of camera development experience, including work on more than one million consumer smart cameras.
Project Foundation is headquartered in Eindhoven, the Netherlands, which the companies described as a major European semiconductor technology hub.
“Building thermal cameras has shown us what manufacturers need from the sensor inside: performance, a reliable supply and a price that works at scale,” Project Foundation CEO Igor Nakonechnyi said in the press release.
The companies said the project had attracted interest from investors and partners, with financing arrangements to be announced once confirmed. They did not disclose an investment amount.
The project’s name follows the group’s practice of drawing on Isaac Asimov. The Fourth Law refers to his Laws of Robotics, while Project Foundation draws on the Foundation series and its theme of preserving knowledge through periods of upheaval.

Strong 7.7 magnitude earthquake felt in Panama, Costa Rica, tsunami waves possible, USGS says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:56:03 UTC
03:56:03 KST

A magnitude 7.7 earthquake struck southern Panama on Friday, damaging buildings and sending thousands into the streets, but the country appeared to escape widespread destruction or deaths.
The US Geological Survey said the earthquake hit at a depth of 12.6 km (7.8 miles), with an epicenter in a sparsely populated area about 200 km (124 miles) from the capital, and that some casualties were possible.
In the following hours, even as more than 40 aftershocks rattled the isthmus nation, the Panama Canal and Cobre Panama copper mine reported normal operations, and the Tocumen International Airport lifted a suspension on flights.
Office workers in the upscale business hub of downtown Panama City fretted about getting home in the snarl of traffic after the quake sent thousands into the streets.
Juan Sanchez, a 37-year-old employee of the Ministry of Economy, waited for a bus he said he doubted would arrive.
"They evacuated all of these buildings. Everyone is outside. Now the problem is, how do we get home?"
President Raul Mulino traveled to Penonome, a city about halfway between the epicenter and Panama City, where some buildings collapsed and a church was damaged.
Prolonged termors
Nestor Luque, director of Panama's geosciences institute, attributed the quake to the Azuero Sona Fault System that he said contained a massive buildup of pressure that is occasionally released.
"The seismic signals have traveled throughout the national territory, and that is why it could be felt everywhere."
In Panama City, Luque said he counted 40 seconds of vibrations, though other areas may have felt even longer tremors.
Sabina Rios, who was on the sixth floor of an old US military-era building in Panama City, said the shaking was unusually strong and prolonged.
"The quake felt strong and lasted a long time, the longest I’ve felt in years,” Rios said.
Victor Pinzon, a 48-year-old maintenance worker, told Reuters he had watched high-rise window cleaners ride out the shaking. “It’s a miracle they didn’t get killed,” he said. “They looked like they were swinging in a hammock.”
Strong earthquakes are not common in Panama, and some elderly residents were in tears as they evacuated into the streets.
“We’re scared. It’s just the two of us old folks here. The house has cracked, and we’re afraid it could fall on us,” said Ricardo Brown, 74, in Herrera province in southern Panama, where he said he saw a number of damaged homes.
Omar Smith, who heads Panama's civil protection agency, told news outlet Telemetro Reporta that impacts had also been reported in Chitre, the capital of Herrera, and along the coast in Los Santos province.
The USGS estimated economic losses could amount to 1% to 10% of Panama's gross domestic product, and electricity provider Naturgy reported power outages in six provinces.
Panama was due to hold a national evacuation drill on Monday of next week to test the country's emergency response.
Shipping through the Panama Canal remains uninterrupted
The Panama Canal Authority said the canal was operating normally and that staff were inspecting for earthquake-related damage, later adding that ships are passing through the canal without interruption.
Panama is set to hold a national evacuation drill next Monday to test the country's earthquake response.
Vessel passage at the Panama Canal was not interrupted on Friday after a strong earthquake caused infrastructure damage in the Central American country, the waterway's authority said.
Operations at the canal were normal while technical teams inspected facilities, the authority said in a release, adding that an emergency protocol had been activated.
The quake prompted tsunami warnings for parts of the coasts of Panama, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Peru, Nicaragua, Guatemala, El Salvador and Mexico.
About 90 vessels, including bulk carriers, tankers, and container ships, were on Friday at both ends of the canal waiting to pass or to dock at any of the berths serving storage terminals and trans-shipment services, according to monitoring data from LSEG's Workspace.

Ukrainian drone alert disrupts Russian government flights returning from Putin’s Turkmenistan trip
Several aircraft from Russia’s Rossiya Special Flight Detachment, which transports the country’s leaders and senior officials, circled over Moscow on the evening of October 9 because of the threat of a Ukrainian drone attack.
Five of the detachment’s aircraft were unable to land immediately. At least three were returning from Turkmenistan, where Russian President Vladimir Putin had attended a Commonwealth of Independent States summit, several Russian news outlets and Telegram channels reported (1, 2, 3). All three were Il-96s, the type used to transport the president, Agentstvo reported.
According to Flightradar24, two Il-96s with registration numbers RA-96020 and RA-96022 circled over Moscow and the surrounding region. They departed Turkmenbashi Airport at 2 p.m. and 2:15 p.m. and landed at Moscow’s Vnukovo Airport at 6:06 p.m. and 6:21 p.m., respectively.
A third Il-96, with registration number RA-96025, departed Turkmenbashi at 3:52 p.m. and flew over Moscow even though it was scheduled to land at Vnukovo. It was eventually diverted to St. Petersburg’s Pulkovo Airport and later departed for Moscow.
Restrictions were imposed at all Moscow airports around 3:40 p.m. and fully lifted by 6:40 p.m. According to estimates from Ostorozhno, Novosti, more than 200 flights were delayed and more than 100 canceled amid the restrictions.
It is unclear which aircraft Putin was aboard. At 1:52 p.m., TASS reported that the president had ended his visit to Turkmenistan and boarded one of the Rossiya detachment’s aircraft, which was preparing to depart Turkmenbashi. Agentstvo suggested that Putin may have been aboard RA-96025. He had flown to Turkmenistan on that aircraft on October 8.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky had threatened to “close the skies” over Russia in early September. Putin called the statement “a signal of intent to commit state terrorism.” In response to Ukraine’s threats, Russia’s Transport Ministry said the country’s aviation services would prevent “significant disruptions” to civil aviation.

NEW DELHI: Aam Janata Unnayan Party (AJUP) chief Humayun Kabir on Friday said he would move to Dubai on a 10-year golden visa after completing the mosque he has promised to build in West Bengal’s Murshidabad district, following his son’s crushing defeat in the Rejinagar bypoll.Kabir, the MLA from Nowda, said the mosque, modelled on the Babri Masjid, would be completed by December 6, 2028. Reform's Suella Braverman: UK antisemitism ‘not going to get better’ amid systemic Islamism crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:55:22 UTC
03:55:22 KST

Islamism is a “systemic” and “deep-rooted” problem in the UK, while antisemitism is “not going to get any better,” former British home secretary Suella Braverman told The Jerusalem Post.
The Post spoke to Braverman, 46, ahead of the publication of her first book, the memoir Patriot: Empire, Betrayal and Hope. Released on October 1, it explores Braverman’s time as a barrister-turned-MP-turned cabinet minister, and her wider views on the issues in the UK, such as Islamism and political weakness. She served as home secretary under the Conservative government, before leaving the party for Reform UK in 2026.
Braverman noted that there are “systemic, profound, deep-rooted, social and cultural and institutional problems with Islamism in the United Kingdom.”
“Whether it’s in our schools, our police force, our political parties, our broader institutions – there’s a crisis. And it’s been caused by cowardice and appeasement by political leaders, most recently conservative political leaders who actually – instead of just failing to stand up to Islamism and extremism – actively engaged with it.”
She cited an example from her book of how former prime minister David Cameron invited the Muslim Brotherhood’s spokesman to lunch at Chequers, the prime minister’s official country residence.
“That’s a group that should be prescribed, not embraced by governments,” she continued.
Braverman says political courage, strong leadership can counter Islamist extremism
Despite the pervasiveness of the problem, Braverman said she does believe it can be fixed.
“We don’t need to surrender to the fate of our country being taken over by Islamists and extremists. It’s not going to be easy. It does require a high level of courage and political leadership. But I do think it is possible with a clear formula,” she said.
In fact, in Braverman’s view, the solution to Islamism in the UK is “not complex” but simply requires “a high level of political determination.” And that’s not something that can be found under a conservative leadership, she opined.
“They had 14 years, and it got worse under the conservatives during that time,” she noted.
The Conservative Party’s failure to address the worsening issues of radicalization and Islamism was the reason Braverman left the cabinet.
“There were Islamists demonstrating in our streets in marches day in, day out. I wanted to ban them and actually stop antisemitism. The prime minister of the day didn’t agree with me, and he sacked me instead,” she recalled.
“I blame the Conservative Party and many of the people still in the party for the problems that we are enduring today.”
But is there enough public concern about these issues that it could sway a future election?
Braverman claims Islamist extremism accounts for 75% of MI5's caseload
Braverman acknowledged that her views are derived from running the Home Office, dealing with counter-terrorism, working with MI5 – in fact, she revealed that Islamism makes up 75% of MI5’s caseload – which does not mirror the everyday experience of most people, and most voters.
“I am beginning to see that with the crisis of illegal migration and the insecure borders that the UK has had now, coming up to a decade – the consequences of that are making people more alert to the issues of Islamism, because the two are connected,” she said.
She pointed out that a large proportion of the people entering the UK illegally have “Islamist tendencies and intentions.”
“There’s no doubt that among them will be Iranian hostile actors coming illegally into our country who want to terrorize British citizens.”
The boat issue has made Islamism in the UK a more pressing issue, she said, because it’s on television every day.
“When people start considering that crisis in more detail, they can join the dots and see that our illegal migration crisis is a cause that will exacerbate our security threat.”
If she were here, home secretary again now, Braverman is very clear on what her first steps would be.
“First of all, we’d have to secure our borders and take a robust approach to who is coming into the country, and stop illegal migration. That would very quickly reduce the national security threat that we’re facing.
“When it comes to the existing threat of Islamism in our country, we need to make the law clear that the damaging aspects of Islamist culture are unlawful.”
Braverman calls for UK bans on burkas, polygamy, and first-cousin marriage
She cited banning the burka, polygamy, and first-cousin marriage as priorities.
“Banning the burka would be unequivocal. It’s clear in law that it’s unlawful, and there would be police powers to enforce against it. It is an obstacle to communication and integration, and is a simple symbol of female oppression. It has no place in 21st century Britain,” she said, adding that people who wanted to wear the burka and their families “would leave the country.”
“Polygamy; first-cousin marriage, which has led to a high level of severe deformities among children born of these unions, should be made illegal. Sharia courts – all of that must go.”
Braverman also said that Islamist preachers who are routinely invited and platformed at mosques and public events in the UK must be put behind bars and be deported “if they’re not British,” and that the Muslim Brotherhood needs to be proscribed.
She also believes the Muslim call to prayer should not be permitted in large public spaces.
“This is a Christian country, not a Muslim one,” said Braverman. “People need to speak English in the country.
“Constitutionally, we are not actually a secular country. We are constitutionally and institutionally a Christian country. And our head of state is the head of the Church of England,” she continued.
Braverman nevertheless stressed that she is not calling for other religions to be banned. She is a Buddist, and her husband, Rael, is Jewish.
“We are a Christian country, and I’m trying to encourage people to have that confidence in their Christian faith and the Christian heritage of this country.
“However, having said that, we are not banning non-Christians. And we are in many ways de facto a secular society. So people of other faiths are free to practice their faith. They’re free to participate in their religion’s customs and rituals. But there has to be a line whereby they do that in a way that’s consistent with British values and the Judeo-Christian values of Britain.”
Braverman says fear of Islamophobia accusations prevents politicians from confronting Islamism
While she said there is a desire by many to return to these values in Britain, Braverman said that many in politics are afraid of cracking down on Islamism for fear of being labeled Islamophobic.
“On the Right, my Conservative colleagues were terrified of being called Islamophobic,” she said. “They wanted to do everything they could to avoid that accusation, from inviting the Muslim Brotherhood to lunch at Chequers, to biting their lips when it came to calling out grooming gangs.
“On the Left, it’s slightly different. For example, we’re seeing the Labour government do appalling things right now. They have basically come out against Israel, opened a refugee route for Palestinians and people from Gaza, recognized Palestine, and put an arms embargo on Israel. All of that – that’s not because they don’t want to look Islamophobic. That’s because they want to shore up the Muslim vote.
“It’s all about cynical politics,” she continued, arguing that Labour’s policy is more about suppressing the Greens by pivoting against Israel and securing a Muslim vote.
All of this – the cynical anti-Israel politics, the permissibility around Islamism, and the decrease in Christian values – have led to a situation where the UK is arguably not safe for Jews, Braverman said.
“Almost every week, there are more Jewish people who seriously question whether they have a place in the United Kingdom. The Labour Party has now nailed its colors to the mask, which is that they are anti-Israel, anti-Zionist, and have joined the hate movement calling for Intifada.
“They don’t see Israel as an ally anymore; they see Israel as the aggressor in the wrong. I think that is morally devoid and heartbreaking.”
Because of this, Braverman believes that antisemitism in the UK, “which is already at unprecedented levels,” is not going to get any better.
“I think if we don’t turn it around at the next election, there’s no hope,” she said, adding that the next general election will be the most consequential of her lifetime.
“I think the choice will be very, very clear and binary. And it will either be four more years of socialism, and more immigration, higher taxes, more poverty, more humiliation on the world stage, more antisemitism.
“Or we can begin the fight back and the recovery. I’m with Reform because I genuinely believe that the only vehicle that can stop Labour and stop socialism is Reform.
“The Conservative Party isn’t viable as a serious proposition to win. So to anyone on the Right, to anyone who wants to bring an end to this kind of madness and chaos and nonsense that’s going on in the UK, there is only one way.”
Braverman rejects antisemitism allegations against Reform UK and Nigel Farage
When asked for her response to accusations of antisemitism in the Reform party, including those against its leader, Nigel Farage, she replied: “I would never join ranks with people who are antisemitic. I’ve taken a political stand over antisemitism. I was sacked as home secretary over antisemitism. I’m not going to join a party, or try and make someone prime minister, who I thought had a gram of antisemitism in them.”
She also noted that many leading figures in the party are outspoken friends of Israel.
Deputy leader Richard Tice, for example, has traveled to Israel to show support, and is a strong advocate against antisemitism, against Islamism, and for the Jewish community.
“And the same with Nigel and obviously Robert Jenrick [elected as a Conservative Party MP who joined Reform in January 2026], and myself,” she said.
In fact, Braverman wanted to stress that she has “always been a friend of Israel and will always continue to be a friend of Israel.”
She visited Israel after the October 7, 2023, Hamas-led massacres, showing her solidarity with the country, and meeting with survivors, heroes, and families.
“I was incredibly inspired, frankly, by the resilience of the people in Israel. and Israel as a whole, and particularly the young people who were fighting to defend their nation.
“If there is a Reform government, which I hope there will be soon, we will reestablish diplomatic relations with Israel.”
Braverman backs recognizing Jerusalem as Israel's capital, moving UK embassy
While Braverman said she could not speak about Reform’s official stance on recognizing Jerusalem as Israel’s capital and moving the embassy there, she noted that she has personally supported this in the past.
Regarding recognition of a Palestinian state, Braverman said it is “an ideal,” but currently not realistic.
“Hamas needs to be totally degraded, disarmed, and disabled. There must be no authority in Palestine that has access to arms or the ability to attack Israel. There must be zero tolerance of extremism, antisemitism, and Islamism in a potential future Palestinian state. There needs to be authority with whom neighbors, whether it’s Israel or Jordan or Egypt or any other country, can do business.
“We need to know they’re honest brokers, that they’re legitimate, that they have free and fair elections, that they’re not going to distort figures and statistics and elections and stop aid. And they’re not going to divert aid to the construction of tunnels. If those conditions can be met, then I think Israelis would support living side by side with a peaceful neighbor.
“But if those conditions are nowhere near being satisfied, then I’m afraid no, we cannot allow Palestine to be an independent state; we cannot recognize it. And right now, it seems that we’re very, very far away from that.”

Moldova to change laws to produce arms for itself, parliament head says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Moldova to change laws to produce arms for itself, parliament head says
CHISINAU, Oct 9 - Moldova's pro-European government intends to press for changes in legislation to allow for the production of weapons, but needs them for its own defence and has no intention of providing them to neighbouring Ukraine, the head of parliament said on Friday.
Parliament Chairman Igor Grosu, the No. 2 official in Moldova's state hierarchy, said the changes were needed to proceed with the manufacture of dual-purpose weapons, like drones.
"I would very much like for us to produce them for ourselves. We need them, particularly for dual-use purposes," Grosu told a two-day international security forum, citing drone use for national security, emergencies and agriculture.
Grosu, head of President Maia Sandu's Action and Solidarity Party, which holds a majority in parliament, dismissed any suggestion that they might be meant for use by Ukraine in its 4-1/2-year-old war with Russia.
"Of course not! Why would we?" he told reporters. "We would produce them for ourselves."
Sandu's administration, which wants Moldova to join the European Union by 2030, has been fiercely critical of Moscow's invasion of Ukraine.
Moldova, lying between Ukraine and EU member Romania, has been buffeted by the war. Increasing numbers of drones and missiles, believed by authorities to be Russian, have intruded into the country's airspace in recent weeks, with debris crashing on its territory.
Grosu told the forum that 88 such violations of Moldova's airspace had been recorded since Russia's February 2022 invasion.
"With such figures, people are asking a simple question: Can our state defend us?" he said.
"We cannot provide this defence overnight. And we cannot in four years make up for 30 years of failing to finance our defence. To protect our airspace we need radar, equipment, trained personnel, communications, infrastructure and procedures."
Sandu told the forum on Thursday that Moldova's position in the region was "vulnerable". She said domestic defence production was a key part of future defence planning and changes to legislation would soon be submitted to parliament. REUTERS

"I want to thank President Putin, to be honest with you," he added, but nonetheless called Washington Ukraine's "strong partner."
Democratic Senators Jeanne Shaheen, Chuck Schumer, and Elizabeth Warren condemned the six-month authorization for global purchases of Russian diesel, calling it "a total betrayal of Ukraine, our European allies and American national security."
In a joint statement, they accused Trump of funding Russia’s war effort to offset fuel price increases caused by the U.S. war with Iran. They also said the decision undermined bipartisan legislation passed weeks earlier to curb Russian energy revenues.
"Putin only responds to strength, which means cracking down on Russia and the enablers of its war against Ukraine," they said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky also criticized the decision, saying it would provide Russia with additional revenue to finance its war against Ukraine.

"This only fuels Putin and enables him to wage more war," Zelensky said. "And at the very moment when we are talking about peace, America is allowing Russia to export diesel."
