"God willing, may they all return to Russia, Ukraine, America and Britain, and may Palestine be cleansed of these filthy Zionist terrorists," he continued.
Despite the controversy surrounding those statements, IISNA has remained a registered charity in Australia. The organization has also previously received government support for community events and educational initiatives.
The revelations have drawn renewed attention to al-Hammami's years in Melbourne after UAE Attorney General Dr. Hamad Saif Al Shamsi announced Friday that the suspect had intended to seize control of the Flydubai aircraft and crash it into the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport, with the aim of causing the greatest possible number of casualties.
According to the investigation, the first signs of al-Hammami's extremist beliefs emerged in 2017, while he was studying in Australia. Investigators said he was exposed to radical literature and online material glorifying terrorist organizations and suicide attacks, and eventually became inspired by the September 11, 2001, attacks in the United States.
The suspect has confessed to acting alone, but Emirati authorities are continuing to investigate his connections and the possible involvement of accomplices. His account of contacts in Melbourne has opened another line of scrutiny into his ideological development, although the extent to which individuals he encountered in Australia influenced his plans remains unclear.

British nuclear subs have only fire hoses as drone defense – media
British sailors are drilling to fend off potential drone attacks against £4 billion ($5.3 billion) Vanguard-class subs using fire hoses as the only onboard “air defense weapon,” The Sun has reported.
The hoses, known as “center fed reels” are placed on submarine decks as a precaution when the vessels are moored at the British naval base Clyde in Scotland, the UK’s most sensitive military site, the tabloid reported on Thursday, citing anonymous sources. The equipment has pistol-grip nozzles that would allow sailors to direct water at approaching drones.
“You have to use what you’ve got,” the tabloid cited one of its sources as saying.
The Royal Navy’s four Vanguard-class ballistic missile submarines are the only British platforms equipped to carry and launch Trident II nuclear missiles, which deliver the UK’s only operational nuclear weapons. According to The Sun, the Navy insists that layered defenses, including “physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone capabilities,” protect the subs.
The report comes as the Royal Navy is facing what a former senior commander has described as its worst crisis in 350 years.
The UK’s entire fleet of nuclear-powered Astute-class attack submarines are not fit for combat duty, retired chief of the Naval Staff, Lord Alan West, told The Sun earlier this year. Five of the vessels are facing maintenance and availability delays, while the sixth, according to the Royal Navy, is still undergoing sea trials ahead of returning to service.
West described the number of ships the Navy has as “pathetic.” The fleet has just five operational frigates and no amphibious assault ships, while former Prime Minister Keir Starmer’s government retired four frigates, two assault ships, two tankers, and a nuclear-powered submarine during his time in office, The Sun reported in July.
This year, the UK has pledged an additional £15 billion in military funding, citing alleged threats from Russia. London has also seized and aided in seizing ships it has accused of being part of the so-called Russian ‘shadow fleet’ – a practice Moscow has denounced as “piracy.”
Russian President Vladimir Putin has dismissed claims that Moscow wants to attack NATO and has accused Western European leaders of escalating tensions with Moscow, pointing to their statements about preparing for a possible war with Russia in 2029 or 2030, repeated military exercises in the Baltic Sea, and attempts to detain Russian vessels. “This is all escalation,” he said last week.

At least 1,471 Palestinians have been killed since then, with daily demolitions carried out and civilians targeted.
“What we see on the ground is that the ceasefire exists in name only. A ceasefire is absolutely meaningless when civilians, including children, are being killed every single day,” Alexandra Saieh, Head of Policy and Global Influencing at Save the Children, told The New Arab.
"The reality is, there is no ceasefire."
Saieh said they see Israeli airstrikes, shooting, and drone attacks that are killing children and other civilians every single day in the enclave.
“The ceasefire has left Palestinians in Gaza teetering at the edge of survival,” she noted.
The organisations asserted that “the killing and deprivation in the enclave must not be normalised under the cover of a ceasefire agreement”, also noting the Israeli military has moved the its 'Yellow Line' further into Gaza, restricting the movement of Palestinians and dividing the enclave further.
“There was never a real ceasefire in Gaza. The genocide is not over: every day Palestinians are forced to survive in conditions that can only be described as unliveable,” Riham Jafari, advocacy and communications coordinator at ActionAid Palestine told The New Arab.
Jafari explains that instead of a truce, the Israeli army has “continued to kill and injure hundreds of people, pursuing its strategy of death, expulsion and colonial domination”, noting the unprecedented levels of violence in the occupied West Bank.
“The world must not normalise what is happening in Gaza. The impunity must end. There must be full accountability and justice for all atrocities that have been committed.”
The terms of the October ceasefire said that Israel was meant to withdraw from major cities in the enclave, Palestinian prisoners were to be freed, and large amounts of humanitarian aid were to enter the enclave daily through crossings; however, Israel has continued to target Palestinians with daily attacks and frequent strikes.
Israel also continues to prevent vital aid, including medicine, from entering the Strip, putting the thousands of Palestinians' lives at risk.
“There are still severe shortages of the most basic things in hospitals here, including IV fluids, anaesthetic medicines, and surgical consumables, which can directly affect whether we can provide surgical services,” Sally Saleh, MAP’s Head of Emergency in Gaza, told The New Arab.
Saleh notes there are also heavy restrictions on medical items classified by Israel as “dual use”, including laboratory equipment, reagent components for laboratory machines, imaging equipment, neonatal intensive care units and ventilators.
Activists say Israel regularly uses the "dual use" classification, alleging that it could be used for attacks or military purposes, as a way to prevent aid from entering Gaza and putting a stop to the recovery and reconstruction process.
“From a health perspective, these restrictions can have very dire consequences, such as delays in diagnosis, disease surveillance, and treatment,” Saleh notes.
Three years since the outbreak of the genocidal war, Palestinians have faced little reprieve, forced to live in tents for shelter as over 80 percent of structures across the enclave have been damaged.
Despite promises of peace and reconstruction, with multiple agencies declaring Israel’s war a genocide, Gazans are still waiting for the war to be officially over.
“The reconstruction and rebuilding of Gaza should not be conditioned on political or security outcomes,” Saieh asserts.
“Palestinians in Gaza have the right to rebuild their homes and to recover, and they have just not been allowed to do that.”

An investigation had begun four hours earlier, when military police found an abandoned vehicle near the facility at around 10pm on Wednesday.
Military police, joined by officers from Cambridgeshire police, discovered a small hole in the perimeter fence, before finding and arresting the two men inside the base.
The suspects, both Latvian nationals currently resident in the UK, were initially arrested on suspicion of trespass on a prohibited site and causing criminal damage. They were then further arrested on suspicion of an offence under section 4 of the National Security Act 2023, namely entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
They have since been released on bail, with strict conditions, as the police continue their investigation.
Commander Helen Flanagan, the head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said they were “very aware of the recent heightened interest and concern around military sites”, but that there was nothing from their investigation so far to suggest a connection to an incident near RAF Fairford in September.
“Our investigation continues and we are working closely with colleagues from the Ministry of Defence police and Cambridgeshire constabulary on this. A key line of inquiry remains to identify any potential motivation behind why the men were at that location, and this includes whether it may be connected to any criminal activity,” she added.
Officers have since carried out two searches at addresses in the Peterborough area in connection with the investigation. The abandoned vehicle was also taken to a nearby police location.
Located west of Huntingdon, RAF Molesworth is home to Nato’s Intelligence Fusion Centre and the US Joint Intelligence Operations Center, Europe.

Ukrainian journalists say Austria detained them “like terrorists”: prosecutor says suspicion unsubstantiated
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:45:53 UTC
02:45:53 KST

Austrian police detained Ukrainian investigative journalist Mykhailo Tkach and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko in Vienna yesterday, on 8 October. Both were later released, but the circumstances of their detention remain unclear, and the prosecutor’s office said suspicion against them had not been substantiated so far.
The detention lasted more than 12 hours, the first time Tkach had been held that long while on a reporting assignment abroad. The case unfolded alongside a separate Austrian espionage investigation involving two men suspected of working for Ukraine’s military intelligence. Authorities have not said whether the cases are connected.
Tkach describes detention
In a video published by Ukrainska Pravda, Tkach said seven people wearing masks and carrying weapons approached their car at a traffic light about 3–5 kilometers from central Vienna, broke its windows, and pointed weapons at them.
He said the people did not identify themselves or explain their actions. The journalists were pulled from the car, forced face down onto the road, searched, and had their hands taped behind their backs, according to Tkach. He said he initially thought they were being kidnapped because he did not see identification or have time to notice police markings. He realized they were police only after seeing police vehicles.
“As I felt it, they detained us like terrorists,” Tkach said.
He added that people shouted and pointed weapons, and there was no communication. He said one person put a knee on his neck and shouted at him to be quiet. He also saw glass from the broken window fly into Bondarenko’s face.
In a second report, Ukrainska Pravda said Tkach’s account of a document presented to him listed three allegations: espionage in the interests of Ukrainian military intelligence, participation in a criminal organization, and, as far as he remembered, causing harm to Austria. He said investigators did not explain the evidence behind the allegations.
Vienna prosecutor’s office spokesperson Nina Bussek told the Austrian Press Agency (APA) that suspicion against the two journalists had arisen during other investigations but had not been substantiated. She said it currently appeared that the suspicion was not holding up. Austrian officials have not publicly addressed Tkach’s account of the force used.
Diplomatic response and calls for an investigation
Tkach and Bondarenko were in Vienna on an assignment to find Ruslan Kravchenko, Ukraine’s former prosecutor general, Ukrainska Pravda reported. Kravchenko was dismissed on 15 September amid an investigation by Ukraine’s National Anti-Corruption Bureau and Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office into alleged protection of fraudulent call centers. He denied involvement. Der Standard reported that it remained unclear whether the journalists’ detention was connected to their reporting on him.
Ukraine’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Heorhii Tykhyi confirmed Tkach’s release and said the Ukrainian consul had requested access to him, according to NV. Musaieva said Bondarenko had been injured and hospitalized.
A statement signed by Ukrainian media and civil society organizations, including Euromaidan Press, called for an immediate, transparent, and independent investigation of law enforcement’s actions. The signatories also demanded an independent review of the force used, the return of seized equipment, and necessary medical and legal assistance.
Separate espionage investigation
Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner confirmed the arrests of four Ukrainians, according to ORF. The two men detained on 5 October were placed in pretrial detention until 21 October on suspicion of secret intelligence activity against Austria. APA reported that they were suspected employees of Ukraine’s military intelligence service. Both deny the allegations.

Greenpeace warns of oil spill threat following Aframax Rio tanker fire, saying Russian authorities lie about pollution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:45:05 UTC
02:45:05 KST

Greenpeace specialists have released a report analyzing the consequences of the fire on the tanker Aframax Rio, which was seen burning in the Black Sea off the coast of Sochi on Oct. 6. According to the environmental organization, the fire was most likely caused by burning bunker fuel rather than by the oil the tanker was transporting. However, a spill of petroleum products has already created an oil slick of about 25 square kilometers in the area, and although the fire does not appear to have affected the cargo, the threat of a larger oil spill remains.
After analyzing satellite images from Oct. 7 and 8, Greenpeace reached the conclusion that:
“If 100,000 metric tons of crude oil had been burning, such a fire would have lasted several days. The first reports that the burning had ended came in roughly 10–12 hours after the fire began. They were confirmed by satellite images taken 16 hours after the start of the fire.”
The experts also noted that the oil being transported by the ship is held in 10–15 isolated compartments. Had the contents of such tanks been burning, the compartments would have caught fire gradually, one after another, and each new ignition would have resembled an explosion from the outside. No such explosions were observed.
Additionally, ignition of the transported oil would have seriously damaged the tanker, yet images suggest that the hull of the Aframax Rio remains intact.
Finally, the oil slick that appeared in the Black Sea after the fire covers an area of about 25 square kilometers. Had the compartments with the transported oil been damaged, the volume of pollution would have been significantly larger.
Greenpeace stresses that there has been no official confirmation that the tanker is carrying oil. However, if it is indeed loaded, then a spill remains possible:
“If there is indeed oil in the tanker, the threat of a major spill remains until the entire contents are pumped out of the tanks. We do not know the condition of the vessel’s hull, so it is impossible to assess the likelihood of a further spill. The images also show that on both Oct. 7 and 8, petroleum products continued to enter the water from the tanker. This may be caused either by incomplete burning of the bunker fuel or by a loss of integrity of the tanks containing oil.”
Greenpeace notes that censorship inside Russia hinders accurate analysis of the scale and gravity of the pollution in the Black Sea:
“The statements by Russian authorities that this incident did not lead to environmental pollution are false. Even if only bunker fuel caught fire, this is a serious incident with a complex environmental impact. The film on the water’s surface destroys plankton — the basis of the marine food chain — and poisons and kills marine animals and birds. Heavy petroleum products sink to the bottom over time, destroy bottom-dwelling organisms, and will contaminate the water with toxic compounds for a long period. Toxic soot formed as a result of the fire will settle on the water’s surface and possibly on land.”
Earlier, The Insider reported that the Aframax Rio sails under the Liberian flag, is owned by the Marshall Islands–registered company RIO ENTERPRISES SA, and has called at Russian Black Sea ports — in particular, it spent three days at Taman in May 2026. The tanker is on Ukraine’s sanctions list and most likely belongs to Russia’s “shadow fleet.”

Ukraine Struck Samara Station: 170,000 Metric Ton Oil Storage Tanks Burned Down
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:44:39 UTC
02:44:39 KST

As a result of a strike by Ukrainian forces on the Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station (LPD) in the Samara Region of the Russian Federation, four RVSPK-50000 storage tanks, each capable of holding up to 170,000 metric tons of oil, were destroyed.
This is evidenced by satellite images published by the Telegram channel Absolutely Reliable Source.
The attack took place on October 7 and was the second since the beginning of October 2026. During the first attack, four to five RVS-20000 tanks and one RVS-50000 tank sustained significant damage.
In addition, tanks with a capacity of 20,000 cubic meters and a process pipeline were damaged at the oil blending facility at that time.
The RVSPK-50,000 is a vertical steel tank with a floating roof, having a nominal capacity of 50,000 m³, or 314,500 barrels of oil. In terms of mass, this is approximately 42,500 metric tons.
Due to their size, such tanks are complex engineering structures, and their construction takes a long time — usually more than a year.
The Samara Linear Production and Dispatch Station is part of the Transneft system and serves as a major hub for the transportation, storage, and blending of crude oil. It occupies an area of over 216 hectares, and its tank farm is the largest in Europe.
The station houses 71 storage tanks with a total capacity of over 1.6 million cubic meters of crude oil. The complex also includes the Samara-1 and Samara-2 oil pumping stations and a separate oil blending station.
The blending station produces oil streams with specified quality characteristics. To achieve this, crude oil with varying sulfur content is blended in the required proportions to maintain the specifications of Urals-grade oil for supply to refineries and for export.
Four main oil pipelines converge at this hub: Almetyevsk–Kuibyshev, Kaltasinsky–Kuibyshev, Nizhnevartovsk–Kurgan–Kuibyshev, and Guryev–Kuibyshev.
These pipelines carry oil from Western Siberia, Tatarstan, the Orenburg Region, and Kazakhstan.
Under normal operating conditions, approximately 130-140 million metric tons of crude oil were transported through the Samara station annually, accounting for about a quarter of Russia’s total production.

NYPD Releases ICE Shooting Bodycam Footage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:42:34 UTC
02:42:34 KST

A day after a federal immigration agent shot a man in New York City, the New York Police Department released footage from one of their officers responding to the shooting.
The release came amid a growing outcry over the shooting of 28-year-old Oscar Belgal, which has prompted calls for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to immediately release body cam footage of the ICE agent involved in the shooting and for ICE to end their operations in New York City altogether.
The NYPD’s video, which did not capture the shooting itself, showed two police officers showing up to a scene where a man was sitting on the ground, with one person holding on his neck to avoid further injury.
One ICE officer, who was wearing a neon construction vest, an ICE badge and holding an assault rifle, was making a phone call and did not talk to the NYPD officers.
While responding to the scene, one NYPD officer asked if the victim should be transferred to a hospital, but ICE officers did not respond to his question.
“Are we putting him in [the police vehicle] or what?” The police officer asked. Multiple police officers eventually lifted the person on the ground onto the police vehicle which drove to the nearest hospital.
Earlier on Friday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the ICE officer involved in the shooting had been equipped with a body camera and that there was footage relating to the incident. “As the investigation moves forward, as I said, we’ll release the information,” he said.
TIME has reached out to ICE regarding when the body camera footage from the ICE officer will be released.
What’s ICE’s protocol for releasing bodycam footage?
ICE’s policy requires its officers to activate cameras during routine enforcement activities, including while making arrests, executing search warrants and responding to emergencies. In an event when a serious injury or a death occurred during the operation, a panel of ICE internal leaders will review the footage and decide whether footage should be released. According to ICE’s internal policies released in February 2025, this process should take within 72 hours of recording, or as soon as operationally feasible
But the release isn’t always guaranteed. According to the policies, ICE can withhold footage from body cameras if there are “specific and compelling circumstances justifying an objection to public release that cannot be resolved by redaction or other means.” The decision would lie in the hands of the ICE director.
The released footage from ICE will also have ICE officers’ faces and identifiable information redacted to protect its officers’ privacy, according to the policy.
The agency spent tens of millions this year in purchasing and equipping its officers with body-worn cameras, following a pair of deadly shootings in Biddeford, Maine and in Houston over the summer. The ICE officers involved in both shootings did not wear body cameras when conducting operations.

The Baltic countries insist on banning the transit of Russian grain through the EU — journalist
Kyiv • UNN
The prime ministers of Estonia and Latvia and the president of Lithuania called on the EU to ban the transit of Russian grain. The issue will be considered next week.
Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda sent a joint letter to European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen regarding a ban on the transit of Russian grain through the territory of the European Union. This is stated in the joint letter from the countries’ leaders, reports UNN.
Details
As noted in the letter, Russia is deliberately attacking Ukrainian ports, civilian vessels, railways, trains, and key trade routes. It states that by striking infrastructure that enables Ukraine to export and sustain its economy, Russia is making Ukrainian trade significantly more difficult, more expensive, and less safe, while Moscow continues to seek access to international markets and increase its revenues.
"The situation in the Black Sea is of particular concern. Russia’s attacks have seriously disrupted grain supplies to global markets. By undermining Ukraine’s ability to export grain, Russia is actively seeking alternative routes for its own grain exports through the EU, including via the Baltic Sea," the letter states.
The countries’ leaders emphasize that the EU must not become a channel through which Russia offsets the economic consequences of its own aggression.
"Deliberately undermining Ukraine’s ability to conduct trade while simultaneously redirecting its own exports through the EU in order to generate profits is unacceptable. We must not allow Russia to use our infrastructure and internal market to implement this strategy. We must also prevent the export through the EU of grain stolen by Russia from the temporarily occupied territories of Ukraine. As an urgent measure, the EU should ban the transit of Russian grain through EU territory and strengthen economic measures that impose significant costs on Russia’s ability to sustain its military operations. In addition, measures supporting Ukraine are of decisive importance, including strengthening the ‘Solidarity Lanes’ between the EU and Ukraine," the letter states.
It is noted that the issue is planned to be raised at the European Council meeting next week.
We remind you
EU ambassadors approved new sanctions against Russia’s military-industrial complex and 77 State Duma deputies of the Russian Federation elected from the occupied territories of Ukraine, and also extended restrictions related to the use of chemical weapons.

At least 31 civilians were killed and 19 others were wounded when a drone strike blamed on Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) hit a camp for displaced people in southeastern Blue Nile state, a local medical group said Friday.
In a statement, the Sudan Doctors Network said the attack targeted a gathering of displaced people in the Abu Shandi area of Wad Al-Mahi locality.
The group said four children were among those killed, while six children and eight women were among the injured.
It condemned the attack, saying the victims were unarmed civilians who had fled the conflict in search of safety.
The network described the strike as a war crime and a violation of international humanitarian law, holding the RSF responsible.
It called on the U.N., humanitarian agencies and international human rights organizations to urgently condemn the attack and take action to protect civilians.
There was no immediate comment from the RSF on the allegations.
Blue Nile state has witnessed escalating violence in recent weeks, with the RSF and its ally, the Sudan People’s Liberation Movement-North (SPLM-N), launching attacks in several areas.
On Oct. 3, Sudanese authorities accused the RSF of carrying out drone strikes targeting the governor’s residence and civilian sites in Damazin, the state capital.
Sudan has been engulfed in fighting between the army and the RSF since April 2023, leaving tens of thousands dead and around 13 million displaced, according to U.N. and international estimates.

IRGC reports fire aboard LPG carrier in Strait of Hormuz, warns against unauthorized transit
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:35:29 UTC
02:35:29 KST

IRGC reports fire aboard LPG carrier in Strait of Hormuz, warns against unauthorized transit
TEHRAN— Iran’s Islamic Revolution Guard Corps (IRGC) Navy has reported that a large, liquefied petroleum gas (LPG) carrier caught fire after being struck while attempting to navigate an unauthorized route south of the Strait of Hormuz, as senior Iranian military commanders reiterated that the strategic waterway remains under Iranian control and warned against foreign interference.
In a statement issued on Friday, the IRGC Navy identified the vessel as the NV Sunshine, a large LPG carrier owned by Nhat Viet, and said the incident had occurred hours earlier. According to the statement, the vessel sustained a major fire in its engine room and propulsion system while attempting to transit the route.
The IRGC Navy said its operations in the Strait of Hormuz were being conducted in accordance with the directives of Leader of the Islamic Revolution Ayatollah Seyyed Mojtaba Khamenei and the Iranian public’s demand for the exercise of national sovereignty over the strategic waterway.
The force said it would not permit 'aggressor military forces' to establish a presence in the area and would respond firmly to attempts to undermine its management of the strait.
IRGC Navy accuses US of escalating maritime tensions
The IRGC Navy held the US military responsible for incidents of this kind, adding that Washington’s interference in maritime affairs had contributed to growing risks for regional shipping.
According to the statement, the United States has interfered in shipping and insurance arrangements, misleading companies and offering substantial financial inducements to influence their decisions. The IRGC Navy warned that further incidents could occur if such interference continued.
It also cautioned shipping companies against relying on 'unauthorized arrangements,' saying companies found to have violated the applicable restrictions would face sanctions and that punitive measures would be imposed on vessels associated with them.
The warning extended beyond the Strait of Hormuz itself. The IRGC Navy said enforcement would no longer be geographically limited to the waterway and that vessels using unauthorized passages could be pursued throughout the region.
Vahidi: No foreign power has the right to interfere in Hormuz
The announcement came as IRGC Commander Major General Ahmad Vahidi reaffirmed Iran’s position that security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz must be maintained by the countries of the region, without interference from outside powers.
In a message released on Thursday to mark IRGC Navy Day, Vahidi described the security of the Persian Gulf and the strait as a strategic red line for Iran, rejecting any attempt by extra-regional powers to threaten the area or establish a dominant military presence there.
“Our strategy in this arena is clear, principled and unchangeable: security in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz is indigenous and regional, and no extra-regional power has the right to threaten, establish a domineering presence in, or interfere in it,” he said.
Vahidi described the Strait of Hormuz as a vital artery for global energy supplies, emphasizing that its security was directly linked to Iran’s national interests, public security and national dignity.
He said the IRGC Navy was operating in coordination with the Iranian Army’s Navy and was prepared to respond decisively to any hostile miscalculation involving unauthorized vessel movements through waters under its management.
The commander cited precision-guided missiles, attack drones, fast-attack vessels, electronic warfare systems and coastal defense networks among the capabilities underpinning the IRGC Navy’s operational readiness.
“Any threat from the US-Israeli camp will be met with this force’s vigilance, unified command and comprehensive readiness,” Vahidi said.
He also called on IRGC naval personnel to maintain their readiness to defend Iran and the strategically important waterway under the command of Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, commander-in-chief of the Iranian Armed Forces.
Izadi stresses readiness across southern coasts and islands
Separately, Major General Mostafa Izadi, deputy commander of the IRGC, underscored the readiness of Iran’s Armed Forces to defend the Strait of Hormuz and safeguard the country’s interests and rights in the strategic waterway.
Izadi made the remarks on Thursday evening during a visit to IRGC Ground Force personnel stationed along Iran’s southern coasts and islands.
He said the IRGC Ground Force, Navy and Aerospace Force maintained a presence on the islands and in areas north of the Strait of Hormuz, with their personnel prepared to defend the strategically sensitive region.
The deputy commander pointed to operational planning, advanced tactics, combat engineering, troop deployment and the positioning of military equipment as key elements of the forces’ defensive capabilities.
He also emphasized coordination between the IRGC and the regular Army, saying personnel from both branches were responsible for guarding and defending the Strait of Hormuz.
Izadi reiterated that Iranian forces controlled the strategic waterway and expressed hope that their combat readiness would be further enhanced on the islands and across the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
A strategic waterway at the center of regional security
The latest statements underscore Iran’s emphasis on regional security arrangements and its opposition to an expanded military role for powers from outside West Asia in the Persian Gulf and the Strait of Hormuz.
The strait connects the Persian Gulf with the Gulf of Oman and is a critical route for international energy shipments. Its security has significant implications for regional stability, maritime transport and global energy markets.
Iran’s military leadership has repeatedly stressed that the countries bordering the Persian Gulf should assume primary responsibility for regional security. The latest warnings link that position to the operational readiness of Iranian forces and their stated determination to prevent unauthorized maritime movements and counter what Tehran regards as external threats.

US harbouring of Assad ex-general undermines Syria justice drive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:34:31 UTC
02:34:31 KST

Breadcrumb
US harbouring of Assad ex-general raises questions over Syria justice drive
A former Syrian general may hold information about Syria’s chemical weapons programme that could help investigators establish responsibility for alleged crimes committed under the former regime, raising questions about how intelligence gathering involving him could affect efforts to secure accountability.
Bassam al-Hassan, a former general who served as a strategic affairs adviser to ousted dictator Bashar al-Assad and acted as a liaison between the presidential palace and Syria’s Scientific Studies and Research Centre (SSRC), is reportedly living in Lebanon under an arrangement involving US and Lebanese authorities.
The BBC and US broadcaster NPR reported that al-Hassan has been permitted to remain in Lebanon because of his willingness to provide information about the disappearance of American journalist Austin Tice and other intelligence matters. Hassan is wanted for crimes against humanity and is subject to US sanctions.
The BBC has reported on links between Hassan and the operation in which Tice was abducted in Syria in 2012. His potential knowledge of the former regime’s chemical weapons programme, however, raises broader questions about what information he may hold and whether it could contribute to investigations into alleged crimes under Assad.
Nabil Halabi, a Lebanese lawyer, told The New Arab that US investigators may also want to question Hassan about chemical weapons stockpiles and their locations. He speculated that this could be one reason why Hassan has been allowed to remain in Lebanon rather than being extradited to Syria.
Intelligence gathering and accountability
Halabi said the FBI’s interest in Hassan may extend beyond establishing what happened to Tice. This could extend to information about Syria’s chemical weapons stockpiles, including whether undeclared storage sites exist.
"If the FBI wants to question him, for example, about chemical weapons stockpiles and where they are located – which, of course, goes beyond the issue of Austin Tice – these questions could raise sensitive issues and put the new Syrian leadership in an embarrassing position," Halabi said.
He added that questioning Hassan in Lebanon could allow US investigators to gather information outside the Syrian judicial system and not put the Syrian authorities in an "awkward" situation. However, there is no confirmed evidence that chemical weapons intelligence is the reason for the arrangement allowing Hassan to remain in Lebanon.
Hassan’s former position could make him a potentially significant source of information about the former regime’s military and security structures. Any information he does have could help investigators understand how decisions were made, who was involved and where further evidence might be found.
The Syrian Network for Human Rights (SNHR) has also highlighted the potential significance of his position, including his links to the SSRC, which was associated with Syria’s chemical weapons programme.
In November 2023, French judicial authorities issued an arrest warrant for Hassan in connection with alleged crimes against humanity and war crimes linked to the 2013 chemical attacks. He has not been convicted of those offences.
The issue has renewed relevance amid continuing efforts to establish the full extent of Syria’s former chemical weapons programme. Any information Hassan provides would need to be independently verified and assessed alongside documentary, forensic and witness evidence.
Fears of evading justice
For SNHR, the main concern is not intelligence cooperation itself, but whether any arrangement could prevent evidence from being used in criminal proceedings or shield individuals from accountability.
The organisation has argued that the pursuit of information about Tice must not come at the expense of the rights of Syrian victims. At the same time, it has stressed that intelligence gathering and criminal accountability are not inherently incompatible.
Accountability does not necessarily require al-Hassan to be extradited to Syria, SNHR told The New Arab. What matters is that any allegations against him are examined by a competent and independent court that can guarantee a fair trial.
The organisation warned that if arrangements with intelligence agencies were to prevent such proceedings, victims could be left with the impression that cooperation with foreign governments allows former officials to evade justice.
Hassan could also possess information relevant to Syrians who were forcibly disappeared during the former regime’s rule, including details of detention decisions, officials involved, and the locations of detainees or burial sites. Such information would need to be verified rather than accepted at face value, SNHR said.
Families' right to know the fate of missing relatives should not depend solely on intelligence negotiations or wait for criminal proceedings to conclude, it added. Relevant information should be shared with appropriate missing-persons bodies and accountability mechanisms, with safeguards for witnesses and sensitive data.
A wider challenge for transitional justice
The case highlights the broader challenge facing Syria as it attempts to address abuses committed during decades of Assad family rule and the brutal, 14-year civil war.
Syrian commentator Robin Yassin-Kassab told The New Arab that Hassan’s presence in Lebanon was unlikely to deteriorate Syrian-Lebanese relations, noting that numerous former regime officials were already believed to be living in Lebanon.
Lebanese authorities have returned groups of Syrian military personnel who fled after the fall of Assad, but the extradition of former general Adel Issa this August marked the first reported handover of a senior former-regime military figure to face trial in Syria.
Yassin-Kassab also argued that the Syrian authorities had, in some cases, accepted the principle of dealing with individuals accused of wrongdoing when they could provide information or help consolidate the government’s power. He cited the cases of former regime figures Fadi Saqr and Mohammad Hamsho as examples of the tensions between political expediency and accountability.
More broadly, he said Syria had yet to establish a comprehensive transitional justice process capable of addressing the legacy of the former regime.
"Unfortunately, there is no comprehensive transitional justice process in Syria. It simply hasn’t happened," Yassin-Kassab said.
"There have been some high-profile arrests and trials, which are, overall, a good thing. But there has been no comprehensive programme involving truth, reconciliation, rebuilding, proper accountability, the establishment of a historical narrative or the protection of documents."
Without such a process, he warned, violence and resentment risk remaining entrenched in Syrian society.
The question surrounding Hassan is therefore not simply whether US investigators can just obtain useful intelligence from a former Assad insider, but whether information gathered through such arrangements can contribute to a wider effort to establish the truth about abuses under the former regime and ensure that those responsible can be held accountable.
The case of Austin Tice
Tice, a freelance journalist and former US Marine, disappeared near Damascus in August 2012 while attempting to leave Syria after reporting on the country’s civil war.
The Assad regime repeatedly denied knowing his whereabouts. But last year, the BBC presented evidence suggesting that Tice was detained in Damascus under Hassan’s supervision.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa last month met with Tice’s mother in New York City, on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly. He said his country’s authorities had "some initial leads" on Tice’s disappearance but added that he could not disclose everything at this stage because of security and intelligence considerations.
The search for Tice remains a significant issue for US authorities, and information from Hassan could help investigators establish the circumstances of his disappearance and identify those responsible.
But any intelligence obtained from the former general could also have implications beyond Tice’s case, particularly if it sheds light on the former regime’s security apparatus or chemical weapons programme.
Whether that information can be used to advance accountability will depend not only on what al-Hassan knows, but also on whether it can be independently verified and made available to appropriate judicial and investigative processes.

Florida execution called off after DeSantis withdraws death warrant for first time
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:32:18 UTC
02:32:18 KST

Ron DeSantis cancelled a planned execution in the state on Friday, days before a 74-year-old man was due to be killed by lethal injection.
The move – the first time Florida’s governor has withdrawn a death warrant in his nearly eight years in office – comes just over a week after the botched execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee.
DeSantis, who has aggressively used the death penalty during his time as governor, signed a letter on Thursday withdrawing the death warrant for William Lee Thompson. The Republican did not give a reason for the withdrawal, which comes at a time of increased national and international scrutiny on the use of the death penalty in the US.
Pike, 50, survived two lethal injections on 30 September. She was taken to a hospital and declared brain dead on Monday, before waking up and beginning to speak on Tuesday. On Thursday her lawyer said she was “up and walking” in hospital, but said her arms were severely injured.
Adding to the attention on state executions, this week the Pentagon announced that it would livestream the execution by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, who was sentenced to death for killing 13 people at Fort Hood in 2009.
William Lee Thompson, 74, had been scheduled to be killed by the state on Tuesday, for the murder and kidnapping of Sally Ivester in 1976. Lawyers for Thompson said he is suffering from dementia.
A second Florida execution scheduled for Tuesday is still set to take place. In that case, James Robertson, 63, is due to be executed for the first-degree murder of Frank Hart, then a fellow inmate, in 2008. Robertson waived all appeals, and told investigators he killed Hart so he could be moved to death row.
DeSantis did not provide a reason in the letter for withdrawing Thompson’s death warrant, but had temporarily stayed his execution last month pending a psychiatric evaluation. Florida prison officials, however, had still been preparing for Thompson’s potential execution next week.
Grace Hanna, executive director of Floridians for alternatives to the death penalty, said Thompson’s attorneys had told DeSantis he was “incompetent for execution due to his dementia”.
“He did not know where he was, stated that ‘Bush’ was the president, and, at times, did not even recognize that he had been sentenced to death,” Hanna said. “In accordance with state law, he underwent an evaluation last week. Officials never released the findings or explained today’s withdrawal.”
Thompson’s attorney, Bri Lacy, said they were relieved by the result.
“Mr Thompson suffers from dementia and his health is failing – both of which were gravely concerning with an impending execution,” Lacy said in an email to Associated Press.
“Now that Mr Thompson is no longer under a death warrant, we hope FDOC [Florida department of corrections] will relocate him to an adequate medical facility and provide the care he needs.”
A spokesperson for DeSantis did not immediately return an email seeking comment. Thompson will remain on Florida’s death row, and a new death warrant could be signed for him in the future.
Florida carried out 19 executions last year, a record in the state since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. In July, Florida became the first state in nearly a decade to execute two prisoners in one day.

Why power outages in Ukraine’s regions are occurring regularly - Ukrenergo explains the situation
Kyiv • UNN
The outages are caused by the destruction of generation capacity, strikes on the grids, and air-raid alerts. Ukrenergo urged people to consume electricity sparingly.
Since the beginning of October this year, consumption restrictions have regularly been introduced in several regions of Ukraine. This applies to industry, household consumers, and businesses alike. The reasons for the outages were explained by Ukrenergo, UNN reports.
Details
According to the company, there are several reasons:
-  the systematic destruction by the enemy of generation facilities in certain regions, which has led to a high level of energy shortages in these areas; 
-  continuous strikes on substations and transmission and distribution lines, in particular near large cities with high levels of energy consumption; 
-  constant air-raid alerts in regions where the enemy is carrying out massive attacks on high-voltage substations and lines, preventing emergency repair and restoration work from being conducted quickly. 
The combination of these factors is why consumers in some regions of Ukraine are being forced to remain without power at a time when there are no restrictions in the rest of the regions, while electricity is being exported to avoid the problem of excess capacity
Energy workers are doing everything necessary to restore power after every Russian missile strike or every jet-powered "Shahed" attack. At the same time, they called on Ukrainians to conserve electricity in regions where restrictions are currently being imposed out of necessity.
The lower the load on the grid, the shorter the periods of forced outages will be

Police steadfastness during wartime

Public trust and institutional strengthening

The Leader also called for comprehensive improvements in the capabilities of the security forces, emphasizing the need to strengthen human resources, equipment, and technological infrastructure.

Blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk is a former serviceman who worked in the press service of the Russian Ministry of Defense. He founded the Telegram channel “Rybar,” which has more than 1.5 million subscribers, and actively supports Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.
Police said that Zvinchuk and the others were detained in the coastal town of Risan, where they were staying at a hotel. Law enforcement officers confiscated “modern digital equipment and devices,” including a drone, two cameras, and several phones.
Montenegrin Prime Minister Milojko Spajić, who reported the detentions earlier on Friday, said: “Our institutions are doing their job, Montenegro is protecting its interests, and no one will jeopardize our European future.”
“We warned that attempts to undermine Montenegro’s stability and destabilize the situation in the country through hybrid actions constantly accompany our European path,” he added.
The country, which was once an ally of Moscow, is now a NATO member and aspires to join the European Union.
In addition
Earlier, a message appeared on the Rybar Telegram channel saying that the group had planned to film a video at a monastery, having notified the authorities in advance. It also stated that the channel was in contact with the Russian Foreign Ministry, which was handling the matter.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said that Russian diplomats would determine the reasons for Zvinchuk’s and the others’ detention and help protect their rights. Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said that the Russian embassy in Montenegro was handling the matter.
Zvinchuk, who fervently supports Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, is one of Russia’s most popular military bloggers.
After arriving in Montenegro, Zvinchuk posted a video in which he said that he had entered the country despite being on the EU sanctions lists. He attributed this to the inattention of a border guard who apparently failed to notice his sanctioned status. Montenegro—a country with a population of about 630,000, located on the southern coast of the Adriatic Sea—is regarded as the next candidate for EU membership. This Slavic state, where the majority of the population is Orthodox, was historically an ally of Moscow, but went against Russia’s position and joined NATO in 2017.
After the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022, thousands of Russians moved to Montenegro. The country joined the EU and other Western countries in imposing sanctions on Russia, and has been introducing a visa regime for Russian citizens since November 1.
Pro-European Montenegrin officials have repeatedly warned that Russia may resort to “hybrid” operations to derail the country’s accession process to the bloc.
Montenegrin police said that a “timely and coordinated response” had prevented any harmful actions that could have been carried out on the country’s territory.
Meanwhile, in Moscow, Dmitry Medvedev—Russia’s president from 2008 to 2012 and now deputy chairman of the Russian Security Council—said that a “hunt has been declared” for all Russians traveling to Europe, adding that “anyone can be arrested.”
Medvedev, known as a fierce critic of the West and one of Russia’s most radical officials, also suggested that the Russian authorities could take retaliatory measures by arresting citizens of European countries and the United States.

Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:27:54 UTC
02:27:54 KST

Iran questions France’s nuclear double standards
TEHRAN— Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baqaei has criticized 'France’s contradictory approach' to nuclear weapons, questioning why Paris considers its own nuclear deterrent essential to national security while insisting that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, despite Tehran’s stated commitment to the peaceful use of nuclear energy.
In a post on X, Baqaei contrasted French President Emmanuel Macron’s remarks on the importance of military power and deterrence with his categorical opposition to Iran acquiring nuclear weapons.
During a test of a ballistic missile capable of carrying a nuclear warhead, Macron declared: “To be free, therefore, one must be feared, and to be feared, one must be powerful.”
Yet, as Baqaei noted, the French president has also insisted that Iran must never possess nuclear weapons, neither now nor in five or ten years.
The Iranian spokesperson argued that the central issue was not France’s possession of a nuclear deterrent, but the apparent double standard under which a rationale presented as essential to French security is treated as a threat when applied to Iran—even in discussions concerning a civilian nuclear program subject to international oversight.
Baqaei argued that the underlying problem was the desire of certain nuclear-armed powers to preserve their exclusive hold on strategic power and the authority to determine which countries may legitimately exercise it.
He said these powers seek to retain their own nuclear arsenals, presenting them as instruments of security and freedom, while invoking the prospect of a nuclear threat to justify restrictions on other countries, including those pursuing peaceful nuclear technology.
According to the Iranian diplomat, such an approach reflects a selective interpretation of security rather than a universal commitment to peace.
“A peace in which nuclear powers regard their own weapons as the guarantors of their freedom and security, but label the same logic a threat when invoked by others, is not true peace,” Baqaei wrote, arguing that this disparity amounted to a monopoly on power rooted in a sense of superiority.
Baqaei maintained that an international order that fails to recognize the equal right of all nations to security and peace risks reinforcing the dominance of a limited group of powerful states rather than safeguarding international stability.
His remarks placed the debate over Iran’s nuclear program within a broader question of consistency in international security policy: whether the principles invoked by nuclear-armed states to justify their own deterrence strategies should be applied fairly in their dealings with other countries.
Iran maintains that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes and has repeatedly called for its nuclear activities to be assessed on the basis of international law and safeguards obligations.
Baqaei’s criticism thus challenged France to reconcile its stated commitment to preventing nuclear proliferation with its own reliance on nuclear weapons as instruments of deterrence, arguing that lasting peace cannot be built on a system in which security is treated as a privilege reserved for a select group of powers.

The US and China Cannot Slow the AI Race, But They Can Make It Safer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:27:00 UTC
02:27:00 KST

The most important shift in artificial intelligence (AI) is not that models are becoming more intelligent, but that they are becoming more capable of acting.
Much of the first wave of AI safety governance focused on misinformation, bias, deepfakes, privacy violations and harmful content. Those risks remain. But increasingly capable AI agents can plan, write and execute code, use tools, obtain credentials, and interact with external systems. Recent incidents in which OpenAI’s autonomous systems slipped past their constraints show that as agents gain tools and autonomy, the boundary between a model and the outside world becomes harder to enforce.
That makes AI safety a collective-action problem. The AI superpowers face a prisoner’s dilemma. If one laboratory slows while competitors continue, it may lose its edge. Disclosure creates a similar tension: reporting failures can make the wider ecosystem safer, but the discloser bears the costs and may expose vulnerabilities to attackers. Governments face the same strategic impasse as the firms. Washington fears that slowing its AI development will allow China to catch up; Beijing fears that doing so will leave it further behind.
Yet cooperation can be narrow on AI safety. The United States does not need to trust China, share frontier models with China, or slow its own AI development to have a national security interest in such cooperation. It has an interest in ensuring that AI-enabled cyber incidents are contained before they cascade through third countries, shared software infrastructure and global supply chains. China has the same systemic interest.
This collective action has significant implications for middle-power countries. Helping others repair a vulnerability can be a form of systemic containment and a public good.
The Accelerating AI Race
The AI arms race is intensifying.
U.S. President Donald Trump has rejected calls to slow U.S. AI development, framing continued technological leadership as essential to winning the AI race. On September 29, he convened major technology companies at the White House, where six firms – OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, xAI and Nvidia – signed a voluntary accord built around four layers of oversight: internal capability assessments, internal audit teams, independent external auditors, and board-level review. His administration ordered federal agencies to replace the term “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence,” presenting the technology as a source of economic and strategic leadership.
Taken together, these moves point to a U.S. approach combining continued AI power with developer responsibility, voluntary industry controls, external scrutiny, and ex-post legal accountability.
China approaches the problem through a more centrally coordinated system. In May 2026, guidelines on AI agents, issued jointly by the Cyberspace Administration of China, the National Development and Reform Commission, and the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology, made “safety and controllability” a baseline requirement for agent development and deployment. Governance is tiered, with tighter filing, testing and recall requirements for agents used in sensitive sectors.
On September 14, China’s AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0 reiterated “safety and controllability” while updating its classification of AI risks and associated technical and governance measures.
Despite their institutional differences, the two approaches converge on one point: neither country wants safety policy to halt AI development, and both increasingly recognize that greater autonomy creates new problems of control.
Common Ground and Shared Risks
AI systems rest on overlapping technological foundations. Chinese AI development has relied heavily on U.S. chips and, in some cases, U.S. cloud infrastructure. Export controls may weaken those hardware links, but the stronger case for joint risk management lies in the software and services AI systems share.
Standards, certificates, identity infrastructure, model repositories, and open-source libraries support trust across networks. A compromised root certificate or a maintainer’s credentials can put the entire dependency tree at risk.
AI risks vary along two dimensions: severity of harm and whether responsible actors can recognize it in time. The biggest danger is severe and invisible harm, where nothing visibly breaks for days or weeks, yet time compounds the severity of the incident. An AI agent could quietly corrupt records, act on instructions planted in its memory or in documents it consults, or appear cooperative while accumulating access beyond operator intent. Infrastructure may operate normally while the means to disrupt it are already in place.
The dependencies and shared risks determine which code a system runs, which credentials it accepts, and which updates it trusts. Harm can cross borders quietly even when models and their owners remain separate.
That makes the speed of response critical. Delays in detecting a breach, assigning responsibility or authorizing a shutdown can allow damage to spread. Both China and the United States therefore need warnings to reach personnel with the authority and technical means to respond.
Make the Race Safer
There is no obvious diplomatic agreement that can resolve the paradox built into the AI race: it rewards speed and secrecy, while safety depends on collective restraint and disclosure.
China-U.S. cooperation should instead focus on measures that improve safety without requiring either side to slow unilaterally, transfer its most advanced models, or expose commercially and strategically sensitive capabilities. Four areas stand out:
1. Keeping humans in control
Before the Trump-Xi summit, American and Chinese security experts in a long-running bilateral dialogue proposed red lines around nuclear systems, human control over consequential cyber operations, and a dedicated mechanism for AI incidents.
When an AI agent can search, authenticate, write code, call external tools, and act within minutes or seconds, where should human intervention occur? Requiring approval for every step would undermine the autonomous value of AI agents; waiting until something goes wrong may make intervention too late.
The harder questions concern permissions, escalation thresholds, shutdown mechanisms and which actions should always require explicit human authorization. Researchers could cooperate on these engineering challenges without sharing model weights, training data, or proprietary frontier capabilities.
2. Test the guardrails, not each other’s secrets
Sandboxing, monitoring, permission controls, and model-level refusals are often treated as established safeguards.
The underlying technical risk is broad: with appropriate tools and access, advanced models could identify previously unknown vulnerabilities and develop exploits across well-protected systems without step-by-step human direction. The key question is not whether a developer has guardrails, but whether they still work as agents become capable enough to search for ways around them.
While frontier AI labs in the U.S. have voluntarily disclosed instances of their models escaping from sandboxed environments, public reporting from China on comparable containment failures remains limited. This lack of transparency shouldn’t stop the two sides from working together. Washington and Beijing could develop compatible methods for testing sandbox escape, scope violations, unauthorized tool use, shutdown resistance, and failures of human intervention. Independent auditors, potentially from trusted third countries, could help verify the results.
3. Contain first, attribute later with care
Cyber attribution has always been challenging. AI makes it harder.
A defender discovering unauthorized access may be looking at a state-directed operation, a criminal actor using AI, a human-directed autonomous agent, or an agent that has exceeded its instructions while pursuing a legitimate task.
Between strategic rivals, that ambiguity is especially dangerous when the trust deficit widens. An autonomous system interacting with critical infrastructure could be mistaken for reconnaissance or preparation for attack before either government understands what happened.
American and Chinese experts have already identified this risk: autonomous cyber exchanges could move faster than governments can determine whether an operation was deliberate, accidental, or unauthorized.
Washington and Beijing are unlikely to agree routinely on the attribution of contentious cyber incidents. They could instead develop common technical expectations about the evidence that should be examined before an AI-enabled incident is escalated politically, including agent logs, credential use, tool-invocation records, model provenance, human authorization, and network telemetry. In the first hours of a major cross-border incident, governments and trusted responders should be able to exchange technical indicators, containment measures, and patch information without first deciding who is responsible. Exchanging such information need not imply an admission of responsibility.
4. Close the AI remediation gap
Cybersecurity has struggled with remediation for decades. Critical infrastructure is fragmented across hospitals, utilities, telecommunications networks, ports, government agencies, and private vendors. A vulnerability may be understood and a patch may exist, yet deployment can still take days or weeks.
AI compresses the time between vulnerability discovery and exploitation. A capable model may identify a weakness, develop a working exploit, and begin using it faster than organizations can patch their systems.
This creates an emerging AI remediation gap: offensive capability increasingly operates at machine speed, while much of the world still responds at the slower pace of human decision-making and institutional coordination across multiple stakeholders.
Most countries will not train the world’s most capable AI models themselves. Their defensive capacity may therefore depend increasingly on capabilities developed in a small number of frontier ecosystems. If frontier defensive capability arrives only at another power’s discretion – or not at all – exposed systems have no reliable recourse in a crisis.
Closing this gap requires extending access to frontier defensive capability to these countries.
An affected operator or national CERT (Computer Emergency Response Team) could provide malware samples, vulnerable code, selected system logs, or configuration information through a trusted technical intermediary. A frontier defensive model could then help analyze the incident, validate vulnerabilities, generate and test patches, and return a remediation package, while the underlying model and its most sensitive capabilities remain with the provider.
The United States and China also have reasons to support such a system out of self-interest. An AI-enabled vulnerability left unpatched elsewhere can spread through open-source software, cloud infrastructure, model repositories, digital certificates, and global supply chains before reaching systems in either country.
Middle Powers as Security Intermediaries
Many middle powers sit outside the central China-U.S. frontier-model competition while remaining exposed to its consequences.
The upcoming APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen offers a practical platform to move this agenda beyond bilateral China-U.S. cooperation. All 21 APEC economies, including the United States and China, share an interest in preventing AI-enabled cyber incidents from cascading through the region’s tightly connected digital infrastructure, software supply chains and trade networks. Their ability to detect and repair such incidents, however, varies widely.
The Shenzhen gathering of APEC leaders need not produce a common AI regulatory regime. It could instead task APEC’s technical bodies with developing several practical measures. They can build independent evaluation capacity, strengthen national and regional CERT networks, host trusted remediation infrastructure, and serve as intermediaries between frontier capability providers and countries that lack equivalent defensive capacity.
For the Asia-Pacific, this would turn the AI remediation gap from an abstract vulnerability into a regional capacity-building agenda. It is not simply about managing the rivalry between Washington and Beijing. It is about preventing that rivalry – or failures in the technologies produced by it – from becoming a regional systemic risk. The region has an interest in shaping the mechanisms for containment and remediation rather than waiting for the two AI superpowers to define them alone.
Competition Will Continue, But Cooperation Must Get Priority
AI competition will continue. Even the September Trump-Xi summit produced agreement on a bilateral communication channel for AI-related incidents, it also shows the differences: the U.S. readout called it the “U.S.-China Super Intelligence Dialogue” but Beijing’s readout called it the “China-U.S. AI Dialogue.” The naming difference shows how limited the shared vocabulary is.
At such a time, crisis communication becomes more important, not less. A hotline is not a safety regime; it is communication infrastructure. But both parties need minimum agreement to work together to make the AI race safer, for themselves and for everybody else. Disclosure itself can create security risks, so the appropriate principle should be calibrated reciprocity: enough information should move quickly enough to reduce common danger, while details that could create new vulnerabilities or expose sensitive capabilities remain protected.
The objective should be simple: to stop technical failures from becoming geopolitical crises, accelerate remediation, and extend defensive capability where it is most needed.
The U.S. and China do not need to agree on who should win the AI race. They need to agree on what red lines cannot be crossed in the competition, and how middle power countries can engage.

Committee to Protect Journalists urges Austrian authorities to explain detention of UP journalists
The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) has urged Austrian authorities to urgently explain why Mykhailo Tkach, head of investigative journalism at Ukrainska Pravda, and cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko were forcefully detained in Vienna on Thursday.
Source: CPJ
Details: Fiona O'Brien, CPJ's regional director for Europe and Central Asia, said there is a lack of transparency regarding the detention.
Quote: "It is shocking to hear of two journalists being detained in such an aggressive manner in a European capital city, and with so little transparency as to why they were held for so long and questioned. While we are relieved to see that both Mykhailo Tkach and Yaroslav Bondarenko have now been released, we call on the Austrian authorities to provide a full explanation as to why they were treated this way."
More details: CPJ contacted Austrian prosecutors for comment, but has not yet received a response.
Background:
- On 8 October, it was reported that Tkach had been detained in Vienna while carrying out an assignment from the editorial team involving tracking down the fugitive former prosecutor general Ruslan Kravchenko.
- Tkach was in Austria with his colleague Yaroslav Bondarenko.
- It later emerged that the Ukrainian consul had been granted access to Tkach and had spoken with him.
- On 9 October, Ukrainska Pravda Editor-in-Chief Sevğil Musaieva reported that Tkach had been released after being detained in Vienna, but the editorial team was unable to contact him, and that cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko was injured during the detention.
- Austrian Interior Minister Gerhard Karner stated that Tkach was released following his detention in Vienna, but cameraman Yaroslav Bondarenko remained in custody. The minister said the Ukrainians were detained on suspicion of espionage.
- Tkach said that armed masked men smashed the windows of his car and dragged him and Bondarenko out onto the road as they were arrested in Vienna. One of the men then knelt on Tkach's neck as he repeatedly insisted he was a journalist.
- The journalist also said that they were accused of three offences following their detention in Vienna: espionage on behalf of Ukrainian military intelligence, involvement in a criminal organisation and causing harm to Austria.
