Pezeshkian Calls for Regional Integration, Multipolar Cooperation at Turkmenistan Summits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:24:51 UTC
02:24:51 KST

Pezeshkian Calls for Regional Integration, Multipolar Cooperation at Turkmenistan Summits
TEHRAN— Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has called for deeper regional integration, stronger economic and transport connectivity, and closer cooperation among neighboring countries, proposing a new “CIS+1” framework to expand Iran’s engagement with members of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS).
Addressing the CIS leaders’ summit in Turkmenistan on Friday, Pezeshkian emphasized that regional security, economic development and political stability are inseparable, arguing that countries must strengthen their collective capabilities rather than allow external pressures and geopolitical rivalries to undermine cooperation.
His remarks came as he attended two major regional gatherings in Turkmenistan: the CIS leaders’ summit and an extraordinary summit of Caspian Sea littoral states focused on environmental challenges. On the sidelines, the Iranian president held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Secretary General Nurlan Yermekbayev, and Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov.
Across his speeches and bilateral meetings, Pezeshkian emphasized a common set of priorities: expanding trade and transit links, accelerating joint projects, safeguarding the Caspian Sea, strengthening ties with neighboring countries and advancing a multilateral international order based on dialogue, sovereignty and mutual respect.
'CIS+1’ framework to strengthen regional connectivity
Pezeshkian described the CIS summit as an opportunity to reinforce existing relationships and open a new chapter in regional cooperation, thanking Turkmenistan for inviting Iran as the gathering’s first special guest.
He proposed establishing a “CIS+1” format to provide a structured framework for cooperation between Iran and CIS member states in trade, energy, transportation, investment, mining, technology, tourism, water management, environmental protection, and scientific and cultural exchanges.
The initiative, he said, could also facilitate joint responses to challenges such as climate change, water scarcity, organized crime, and drug trafficking.
Pezeshkian argued that recent regional and international crises, including the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the US-Israeli military attacks against Iran, had demonstrated the interconnected nature of security and stability.
Countries cannot expect to preserve their own security and pursue economic development while insecurity, economic pressure and instability spread elsewhere in their neighborhood, he said.
The Iranian president also criticized the use of trade, banking, technology, energy and international financial systems as instruments of political pressure, warning that such measures have consequences extending beyond bilateral relations and can undermine regional commerce, investment and economic development.
He maintained that resilience against external shocks and disruptions depends on connecting national capabilities and infrastructure.
“Our shared interests lie not in competition between routes, but in connecting routes,” Pezeshkian said.
Iran positions itself as a regional transit hub
The Iranian president highlighted Iran’s geographical position as a natural link between Central Asia, Eurasia and international markets, particularly through its southern ports on the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman.
He singled out Chabahar Port as a strategic gateway capable of connecting Central Asian countries with South Asia, Africa and Europe.
Pezeshkian also welcomed the prospect of implementing a Turkmenistan proposal at the United Nations General Assembly for a transport corridor linking Central Asia, South Asia and Europe through the Caspian region, saying Iran’s infrastructure and geographical position could contribute to the initiative.
He called for the North-South and East-West transport corridors to be developed as complementary components of an integrated regional network rather than competing projects.
The president also urged regional countries to expand cooperation in oil, natural gas, electricity and renewable energy, while exploring practical financial arrangements and barter mechanisms to facilitate trade and sustain economic exchanges despite external restrictions.
He said stronger regional connectivity should be accompanied by genuine multilateralism, with countries in Central Asia, the South Caucasus and neighboring regions playing a more active role in shaping an emerging multipolar world.
“We want connectivity instead of fragmentation, cooperation instead of exhausting competition, interdependence instead of one-sided dependence, and security based on trust and shared interests instead of threats,” Pezeshkian said.
He stressed that regional diplomacy must go beyond summit declarations and become an effective mechanism for managing crises, preventing conflicts from spreading and translating political commitments into practical cooperation.
Pezeshkian calls for coordinated action to protect Caspian Sea
Addressing the extraordinary summit of Caspian littoral states, Pezeshkian warned that declining water levels, climate change, pollution and damage to natural habitats pose serious threats to the region’s environment, economy and coastal communities.
He said the Caspian Sea’s interconnected ecosystem could not be protected through isolated national efforts, calling for joint scientific research, information-sharing and coordinated environmental policies among its five coastal countries.
The Iranian president identified the Tehran Convention as the principal legally binding regional framework for protecting the Caspian marine environment and urged its signatories to strengthen implementation rather than limit their efforts to monitoring environmental deterioration.
He called for a transition toward 'joint crisis management,' backed by scientific evidence, sustained political commitment and concrete measures.
Pezeshkian welcomed the decision to establish a high-level commission comprising deputy heads of government from the Caspian littoral states and proposed a long-term regional program under the Tehran Convention to address the sea’s falling water levels.
The proposed program, he said, should include coordinated scientific monitoring, marine pollution control, biodiversity protection, restoration of wetlands and natural habitats, adaptation of ports and coastal infrastructure, support for fisheries and local communities, and the provision of adequate funding and technology.
The president also warned against allowing the Caspian to become an arena for geopolitical rivalry or intervention by extra-regional powers, arguing that lasting security depends on respecting the sovereignty and legitimate interests of all littoral states.
He called for the condemnation of attacks on coastal facilities, ports, vessels and other maritime infrastructure, citing the attack on Iran’s Anzali port during the US-Israeli war against Iran and an armed Ukrainian attack on an Iranian commercial vessel. He warned that such incidents could endanger regional stability and cause environmental damage extending beyond national borders.
Pezeshkian urged the coastal states to choose scientific cooperation and collective action over passively accepting the Caspian’s environmental decline.
“Our choice is cooperation; our choice is science; our choice is protecting the Caspian,” he said, describing preservation of the sea as a shared historical responsibility toward future generations.
Iran and Russia reaffirm strategic partnership
In his meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Pezeshkian called for accelerating bilateral cooperation in trade, energy, agriculture, transportation, and other economic sectors, as well as strengthening humanitarian and people-to-people ties.
The two presidents reviewed progress in bilateral relations and emphasized the need to expedite the completion of joint projects and implement agreements under their comprehensive strategic cooperation framework.
Pezeshkian described the current period as an important opportunity to deepen ties, expressing satisfaction with the progress achieved and calling for faster implementation of bilateral plans.
He also welcomed Moscow’s opposition to unilateralism and called for greater coordination between Tehran and Moscow in support of multilateral cooperation at the regional and international levels.
Turning to the conflict involving Iran, the Iranian president reaffirmed Tehran’s commitment to diplomacy, while criticizing repeated US attacks following negotiations.
“We are in talks, but every time we negotiate with the US, they attack again. However, we will not withdraw from the negotiating table or abandon dialogue,” Pezeshkian said.
He explained that Iran had submitted proposals and that Washington had presented new ones. Tehran was reviewing and revising the proposals, he said, adding that once the revisions were finalized, the parties would meet through existing intermediaries to discuss and consolidate them.
Pezeshkian stressed that Iran’s objective was to end the war while ensuring that the rights of the Iranian nation were respected under international law. He warned, however, that a settlement based on unilateral demands would not be acceptable.
Putin, for his part, welcomed the expansion of relations with Iran and said cooperation between the two countries was growing. He emphasized the need to resolve the regional crisis through diplomatic means, noting that Iran had put forward new proposals aimed at ending the war.
SCO needs to strengthen independence, implement commitments
In a separate meeting with SCO Secretary General Nurlan Yermekbayev, Pezeshkian called on the organization to ensure that its decisions were guided by the collective interests of its members rather than the domestic policies or external pressure of the United States.
He said multilateral organizations such as the SCO and BRICS were established to provide common frameworks for cooperation in finance, trade, economics, security and political affairs.
Allowing Washington’s policies to influence decisions taken by these organizations, he warned, could undermine their unity and effectiveness. He specifically questioned why some SCO decisions concerning Iran continued to be shaped by considerations of the US position.
Pezeshkian urged member states to strengthen independent regional cooperation and pursue dialogue rather than coercion, emphasizing that relations with neighboring countries should not be constrained by the preferences of distant powers.
He also called for greater attention to implementing agreements, arguing that summit declarations would have little value without concrete action.
Yermekbayev agreed on the importance of multilateralism but emphasized that implementing decisions required practical mechanisms and consensus among member states. He proposed compiling a list of outstanding agreements with Iran so they could be pursued through ambassadors and national representatives.
The SCO secretary general also reaffirmed the organization’s commitment to peace, respect for territorial integrity, and the non-use of force. He noted that all countries have the right to peaceful nuclear energy while adhering to nuclear non-proliferation principles.
Tehran seeks stronger ties with Armenia and Azerbaijan
Pezeshkian’s discussions with the leaders of Armenia and Azerbaijan further underscored Iran’s emphasis on strengthening relations with neighboring countries and expanding regional cooperation.
In his meeting with Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan, the Iranian president highlighted the considerable potential for expanding bilateral relations and called for sustained coordination, communication and mutual trust.
He stressed that the two neighboring countries should take advantage of their geographical proximity and existing opportunities to deepen cooperation across a range of sectors. Pezeshkian reaffirmed Iran’s readiness to develop relations with Armenia and expressed hope that bilateral engagement would continue to expand.
In talks with Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev, the two sides reviewed bilateral relations and explored ways to make fuller use of existing economic and political capacities.
Both presidents emphasized the importance of accelerating the implementation of joint agreements, completing ongoing projects and strengthening cooperation in trade, the economy, transit and regional affairs.
They also called for continued dialogue and constructive consultations between officials to advance shared interests and reinforce good-neighborly relations.
The meetings reflected Tehran’s broader approach of prioritizing engagement with neighboring countries as a means of promoting regional stability, expanding economic opportunities and improving connectivity across the South Caucasus and Central Asia.
Pezeshkian also met with Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedov, during which the two presidents stressed the need to accelerate the implementation of previously agreed projects and make better use of existing opportunities to strengthen bilateral ties.
Regional cooperation and issues concerning the Caspian Sea were also discussed. Both sides underscored the importance of closer coordination among Caspian littoral states, protecting the sea’s environment and expanding joint initiatives in pursuit of the shared interests of countries in the region.
From regional dialogue to practical cooperation
Taken together, Pezeshkian’s speeches and meetings in Turkmenistan outlined an agenda centered on regional integration, economic interdependence, environmental responsibility and diplomatic engagement.
His proposed “CIS+1” format would provide an additional mechanism for connecting Iran with Central Asian and Eurasian economies, while expanded cooperation with Russia, Armenia and Azerbaijan could help advance shared infrastructure and trade objectives.
At the same time, his calls for protecting the Caspian Sea and strengthening the SCO highlighted Tehran’s argument that regional institutions must translate common interests into practical action and resist the destabilizing effects of geopolitical rivalry.
The broader message from the Iranian president’s participation in the two summits was that geography has already connected the countries of Central Asia, the South Caucasus and the Caspian region. The challenge, he argued, is to turn that geographical reality into a durable framework for shared security, sustainable development and regional prosperity.

Jetten condemned the announced sanctions, describing the escalation as "disappointing," but welcomed diplomatic efforts that had prevented the measures from taking immediate effect.

EU considers measures to protect court
Costa reaffirmed the EU's commitment to supporting the ICC, stressing that international justice was essential to upholding international law.
He said the bloc deeply regretted the announced US sanctions and urged Washington to use the coming six months to resolve the dispute through dialogue.
Asked whether the EU would invoke its Blocking Statute to mitigate the impact of the sanctions, Costa said the bloc would adopt "adequate measures" to protect the ICC, its members and staff.  
He added that the six-month period would be used to determine which measures were necessary.
The EU's Blocking Statute seeks to shield EU companies and individuals from complying with certain foreign sanctions.
The remarks followed an announcement of sanctions against the court by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Rubio threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats."
The ICC, based in The Hague, is an independent international tribunal responsible for prosecuting individuals accused of genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and the crime of aggression.

“Cult of Death”? Check your calling card, Mr. Rubio
TEHRAN — US Secretary of State Marco Rubio addressed Iran in parts of his Wednesday evening speech at the Acropolis in Athens. Taken as a whole, his speech was a selective reading of history; a flimsy version of Samuel Huntington's "Clash of Civilizations." When the argument is flimsy, a theatrical stage must inevitably be built out of historical symbols. The audience is meant to be impressed by the backdrop, not by the force of the reasoning.
The same logic applies to the war. When a war is launched without careful calculation, on the basis of impulsive, gut-feel decisions, a civilizational and historical veneer must later be tailored to justify it. Rubio's colleague, US Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, has gone even further, seeking to legitimize the same action with religious and evangelical language.
I do not intend here to critique every aspect of Rubio's speech. Other observers have, to some extent, already done so, particularly from a historical perspective. What is striking to me is where Rubio called the Islamic Republic of Iran a "cult of death."
The phrase reminded me of George W. Bush's "axis of evil" after September 11. The pattern is the same: manufacturing a label to evade accountability. Most of the perpetrators of those attacks were Saudi nationals, and no documented link to Iran was ever proven, yet the then-US president chose to point the finger at Iran. Twenty-five years later, the victims' families remain aggrieved by Riyadh's lack of accountability and by the appeasement of the matter by US administrations — Republican and Democratic alike.
Labeling Iran a "cult of death" is, first and foremost, an insult to the intelligence of that speech's audience. One need only review the record of the seven-month war:
Who attacked a school in Minab on the first day of the war? Who targeted Iran's bridges, roads, and civilian infrastructure?
Thousands of civilians were killed in these attacks, some 300 of them schoolchildren alone. The unarmed vessel Dena was also sunk in waters near Sri Lanka, killing more than a hundred sailors. Trump later stated bluntly that we did it for fun.
Nor is this record limited to that. Who threatened, even at the UN General Assembly, the complete annihilation of the Iranian nation and civilization? And who, by supporting Israel's operations in Gaza, became complicit in the killing of more than 20,000 children?
Ten days ago, the US Secretary of War said bluntly at the Marine Corps base in Quantico, Virginia: " Lethality is our calling card." The remark was shocking, but at least it was honest. An army that sets in motion under the slogans of counterterrorism, freedom, and democracy — what has it brought the targeted nations in practice but death and destruction?
So with this record, who truly deserves the label of "cult of death"? Answering that question requires no complex research. It requires only a modicum of courage and a refusal to close one's eyes to reality.
The Trump administration claims that all this killing was carried out to prevent Iran from acquiring a nuclear weapon. The bitter irony of our time is that the only country in history to have used the atomic bomb, killing hundreds of thousands, regards itself as the world's nuclear policeman.
When the Israeli regime, even after the genocide in Gaza, calls itself "the most moral army in the world," it is hardly surprising that the US Secretary of State should also call Iran a "cult of death."
The issue here is not the misreading of history. It is the attempt to turn history into a license for war and atrocity.

NHS faces exodus of ADHD and autism services staff to private clinics
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:24:16 UTC
02:24:16 KST

The NHS is facing an exodus of staff quitting its ADHD and autism services to join private clinics amid huge demand from children and adults to get a diagnosis.
The loss of specialist personnel to the private sector has already forced one NHS trust in England to limit access to its neurodevelopmental service to only the most urgent cases.
The brain drain of psychologists, psychiatrists, nurses and other staff are leaving the NHS “weaker” and making it more likely that people will be forced to seek private healthcare.
The NHS care watchdog announced on Friday it will start inspecting private clinics that offer diagnostic assessments for ADHD and autism, which are unregulated. The Care Quality Commission’s move follows the publication of the government-commissioned review of mental health and neurodiversity urging ministers to ensure all service providers are properly regulated amid claims of a “wild west” of private firms offering diagnostic tests.
Scores of private clinics have been set up in recent years offering assessments and treatment for ADHD and autism. They have capitalised on the large number of people who have been unable to access NHS care because services have been overwhelmed by an explosion in demand for diagnoses of neurodiversity, creating long waits for help and large backlogs.
Adrian James, the CQC’s interim inspector of mental health care, said: “This new responsibility will … close a significant gap in our oversight, meaning that people receiving these diagnoses can have far greater confidence in the service they are receiving.”
Prof Peter Fonagy’s report – thought to be the biggest inquiry of its kind in the world to date – voiced concern that private firms face the temptation of “financial incentives” to wrongly diagnose and treat patients whose symptoms mean they should not qualify for either.
The CQC already regulates services offering diagnosis and treatment. But the change means non-NHS clinics offering only diagnostic assessments will in future have to register with them.
Yvette Cooper, the health secretary, said the tighter regulation means “people can be confident that assessments are high quality and that the NHS is not being overcharged by independent or private providers”. About 810,000 children and adults in England are waiting for an assessment for ADHD or autism.
The risks to the NHS of losing staff to the private sector was highlighted last week when the Health Service Journal revealed that the Herefordshire and Worcestershire health and care NHS trust had been forced to restrict children and young people’s access to its neurodevelopmental service for that reason.
A paper presented to the trust’s board reported: “Neurodevelopmental staffing is reduced significantly, with the majority of leavers choosing to take up employment with ISP [independent sector providers] and RtC [Right to Choose] providers for ND [neurodiversity].”
Right to Choose gives NHS patients the right to have an NHS-funded ADHD or autism assessment with a private provider to help them receive care more quickly.
The trust responded to the exodus last month by limiting access by under-18s to only those with the most serious symptoms. It will revert to a normal service on Monday. A total of 1,298 people have already waited at least two years for an ADHD or autism assessment with the trust.
Thea Stein, the chief executive of the Nuffield Trust and a member of the government’s ADHD taskforce, said NHS services suffered when staff joined private operators, as also happens in physiotherapy and child and adolescent mental health services.
She said: “Some staff stay with the NHS part-time when they get a private-sector job, but many will walk away entirely, leaving the health service in a weaker position and under greater pressure.
“Concerning inequalities will widen further if the NHS can’t keep fully staffed teams or expand them to meet increasing demand for ADHD support. If these services continue to haemorrhage staff, some people will get much quicker support if they can afford to pay for private care,” Stein added.
The NHS Alliance, which represents trusts, confirmed the continuing exodus of staff. “We’re increasingly dealing with one ADHD workforce spread across different providers, both in the NHS and private sector,” Rebecca Gray, the director of the alliance’s mental health network, said.
“The significant growth in the private sector market, where people accessing services can often be seen more quickly than in stretched NHS services, will make working in the independent sector attractive to some staff.”
The Independent Healthcare Providers Network (IHPN), a trade body that represents many non-NHS firms, welcomed the CQC’s enhanced new role.
Sean Phillips, the IHPN’s head of policy, said: “While all of IHPN members who deliver ADHD and autism assessments are CQC registered – with 83% rated good or outstanding – we have long called for greater ‘end-to-end’ oversight of neurodevelopmental provision and it’s welcome to see that the CQC have confirmed they will now be regulating all providers of ADHD and autism assessments.”

Paul McCartney’s 1973 Hit Inspires 60 Artists to Help Children in Ukraine and Other War Zones
Paul McCartney has contributed a lyric from his 1973 song Band on the Run to inspire a charity art exhibition and auction featuring original works by more than 60 contemporary artists, with proceeds supporting children affected by armed conflicts, including those in Ukraine.
According to The Art Newspaper on October 8, the former Beatles musician selected the line “Well the rain exploded with a mighty crash as we fell into the sun” from the song Band on the Run of the 1973 album by McCartney and Wings.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Participating artists, including Genieve Figgis, Alvaro Barrington, and Joshua Donkor, have been invited to create original artworks inspired by the lyric.
The works will be presented as part of the third edition of Sound & Vision, an annual charity exhibition and auction organized by War Child UK in collaboration with arts organization AOAP Projects.
The exhibition will take place at London's Iconic Images Gallery from November 6 to 8, while an online auction will run from October 27 through November 12.
“We couldn’t be more grateful to Paul McCartney for donating his lyric from Band on the Run,” said Charlotte Nimmo, War Child UK’s fundraising engagement director.

The exhibition's curator and founder of AOAP Projects Gemma Peppé said participating artists “have had a lot of fun” interpreting McCartney's lyrics through their work.
Funds raised through the auction will support War Child UK's humanitarian programs, including specialized mental health services, education, child protection, and emergency assistance.
The organization operates in areas affected by ongoing armed conflicts, including Ukraine, Sudan, and Gaza, providing assistance to children whose lives have been disrupted by war.
Separately, American singer Chappell Roan has partnered with MAC Cosmetics to launch a new lip makeup collection, with proceeds going toward humanitarian relief efforts, including support for people affected by Russia’s war against Ukraine.

According to FT, Zelensky argued that it could also improve targeting that is needed to down Russia’s ballistic missile launchers ahead of winter, when Moscow is expected to intensify its campaign against critical Ukrainian infrastructure.

Jonathan and David: When elections turn friends into enemies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:22:55 UTC
02:22:55 KST

Because Rosh Chodesh falls on Sunday, this week we set aside the regular haftarah for Parashat Bereishit and read Machar Chodesh (I Samuel 20:18-42), the extraordinary story of David and Jonathan.
At first glance, it is a story about friendship. But it is really about what friendship demands when loyalty comes at a price.
King Saul has become convinced that David is a threat, and intends to kill him. David turns to Jonathan, Saul’s son, and asks him to discover whether the danger is real.
Jonathan agrees.
Jonathan is not simply helping a friend escape an angry king. He is helping the man who may one day take his own place on the throne.
Saul himself makes that painfully clear. When Jonathan defends David, his father explodes at him: “For as long as the son of Jesse lives upon the earth, neither you nor your kingdom shall be established” (I Samuel 20:31).
Saul is telling his son, in effect: You are protecting the man who stands between you and the crown.
Jonathan knows that his father may be right. And yet he protects David anyway.
The two devise a secret signal. Jonathan will shoot arrows near David’s hiding place. If he tells the boy accompanying him that the arrows are on this side of him, David will know it is safe to return. But if Jonathan says that the arrows are beyond the boy, David will know that Saul intends to kill him and that he must flee.
When Jonathan gives the second signal, David understands that he is in danger.
That is a difficult lesson in any election season
JONATHAN KNEW perfectly well what was at stake. He simply refused to let it determine how he saw David. He would not reduce his friend to what David’s rise might cost him.
That is a difficult lesson in any election season, and perhaps especially in Israel today.
As the Jewish state prepares to go to the polls on October 27, political divisions are sharpening, and arguments over the country’s leadership and future are becoming increasingly intense.
There is nothing wrong with disagreement. Jews have never had a shortage of it. The danger begins when disagreement changes the way we see the person on the other side.
David was far more than Jonathan’s political opponent
Someone who votes differently is no longer simply wrong but suspect; his motives and character open to question.
David, of course, was far more than Jonathan’s political opponent. If Saul was correct, David’s success meant the end of Jonathan’s own hopes for the throne. Yet when the moment of decision came, Jonathan chose loyalty over self-interest.
The haftarah makes that choice explicit in its closing scene. After Jonathan warns David to flee, the two men do not part as rivals for the throne. They reaffirm the covenant between them.
“Go in peace,” Jonathan tells him, “since we have both sworn in the name of the Lord, saying, ‘May the Lord be between me and you, and between my descendants and your descendants, forever’” (I Samuel 20:42).
Jonathan does not know what the future will bring. He does not know when, or even whether, he will meet David again. But he knows that their covenant must survive whatever happens next.
The kingdom would change hands. Saul would fall, and David would rise. But Jonathan had already made his choice: the struggle for the crown would not decide whom he called a friend.
In the weeks ahead, Israelis will argue fiercely about the election and the country’s future. Jews elsewhere will have their own arguments – about Israel, politics, and the direction of the Jewish community.
Those disagreements matter. But they need not determine how we see one another.
If Jonathan could refuse to let politics turn a friend into an enemy, surely we can do the same.

'Echoes of Rashi': Exploring R. Shlomo Yitzhaki's ideas and their relevance today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:22:48 UTC
02:22:48 KST

Rashi, Rabbi Shlomo Yitzhaki, lived in France from 1040 to 1105. His commentary transformed the way we study Torah. It was the first comprehensive Hebrew commentary to move systematically, verse by verse, through the Torah, combining close attention to the plain meaning of the text, or pshat, with midrash and the teachings of the Sages.
Rashi’s range was remarkable. Alongside his mastery of Torah and rabbinic literature, his commentary reflects deep linguistic sensitivity and an impressive familiarity with everyday life, including agriculture, commerce, crafts, tools, and trades. He often draws on this practical knowledge to clarify a difficult word, image, or biblical description.
Rashi’s commentary quickly became the foundational commentary on the Torah. For centuries, generations have encountered the Torah through his explanations. Even today, virtually every traditional Chumash – no matter how many additional commentaries it contains – places Rashi alongside the biblical text.
In my new book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, I explore some of the larger ideas that emerge from Rashi’s commentary. These messages are as relevant today as they were in the world of Genesis. Jewish history often moves in recurring patterns; challenges faced by earlier generations return in new forms, and the lessons they learned continue to guide us.
What follows are several of these ideas, each carrying particular relevance to our current condition and the challenges we face.
The trail and the trial
Immediately upon arriving in the Land of Israel, Abraham faces a severe famine. Rashi explains this hardship was a test: would Abraham question the divine command that had brought him to this land, now that his arrival was followed not by blessing but by crisis?
Sometimes, the trail ends but the trials are only beginning.
Herzl imagined the creation of a Jewish homeland would offer Jews refuge from the antisemitism they had endured for centuries. No longer living as guests in foreign lands, Jews would finally possess a country of their own.
Yet, as in the days of Abraham, our return to this land did not end our trials. We have faced relentless violence, hostility, and opposition.
These hardships can lead people to question whether we are truly meant to live here. Abraham teaches the opposite. Faith in the journey does not mean that the trials end when we arrive. Sometimes, arrival itself begins new trials.
For many who have moved to Israel, this story is personal. Aliyah may represent the fulfillment of a lifelong dream of living in our homeland. Yet many discover that the journey to Israel was only the beginning. The trail to Israel leads to trials testing our faith in this land and our commitment to remain here.
A seat filled for a reason
Abraham comes to Hebron to purchase a burial place for Sarah, making the first recorded Jewish acquisition of land in Israel.
To complete the transaction, he must negotiate with Ephron, a newly appointed city judge. Rashi comments that Ephron was elevated to this position on the very day Abraham arrived.
This was no coincidence. Divine providence operates not only through miracles but also through political appointments and public events. The person needed to facilitate Abraham’s purchase was placed in position precisely when Jewish history required him.
The modern return to Israel was likewise shaped by a long chain of political developments. Some stretched back centuries, including the rise of the British Empire, which later played a decisive role in events leading toward Jewish statehood. World War I brought the collapse of the Ottoman Empire and redrew the political map of the Middle East.
Later, the emergence of the US as the dominant global power and American support for Israel created conditions that helped make Jewish sovereignty possible.
Rashi’s comment reminds us that history is shaped not only by people who occupy positions of power, but also by the timing of their arrival. Sometimes a political seat is filled because Jewish history needs the person sitting in it.
Questioning our origins
On the day Isaac was weaned, Abraham hosted a great celebration.
Rashi comments that many women brought their infants to Sarah so that she could nurse them. Skeptics had questioned whether Sarah, at her advanced age, could have given birth to Isaac. Others questioned Isaac’s paternity, since Sarah had recently been taken into the palace of Abimelech. By nursing other children, Sarah demonstrated that her body had miraculously been restored to motherhood.
These questions were not merely personal. If Isaac was not truly the child of Abraham and Sarah, Abraham would have no biological successor. His family would have no future, and the promise of the land would have no one to inherit it. Challenging Isaac’s pedigree was therefore a way of challenging the larger story that began with Abraham.
Our enemies have revived a similar strategy. They do not merely dispute Israeli policies or borders. Some challenge the pedigree of the Jewish people itself: whether we are an ancient nation, whether we had a historic presence in this land, and whether our connection to it stretches back thousands of years.
Rashi reminds us: Denying Jewish pedigree was already a way of denying Jewish continuity and Jewish claims to this land.
A Rainbow-less generation
The iconic rainbow appears after the Flood as the sign of God’s covenant with humanity never to destroy His world.
Rashi explains that its appearance signals that the world is once again vulnerable to divine judgment. The rainbow reminds us that God remains faithful to His covenant and will never again destroy the world through a flood.
Rashi then adds a striking comment. Some generations were so righteous that they did not require the rainbow. Their merit was sufficient to protect them from divine punishment.
Among the generations he mentions is that of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai, who lived during the harsh Roman persecutions of the second century. It was a generation that endured enormous pressure yet remained committed to preserving Jewish faith and identity.
We may be living through another kind of rainbow-less generation.
In the decades following the Holocaust, the Jewish people rebuilt shattered families and communities, returned to Israel in vast numbers, and established a sovereign Jewish state. More recently, our soldiers and their families have displayed extraordinary courage, sacrifice, and faith.
A generation capable of rebuilding after devastation and defending Jewish life at enormous personal cost possesses a reservoir of merit difficult to measure. Perhaps this is the kind of generation that does not need a rainbow to plead its case.
The home front
After defeating the coalition of kings and rescuing Sodom, Abraham refuses payment from the king of Sodom.
Yet Rashi notes that Abraham insists that those who remained behind to guard the camp and protect the people and possessions should receive their share. They may not have fought on the battlefield, but their contribution was indispensable. Without those who protected what lay behind the front lines, the campaign could not have succeeded.
Our current war has reminded us how essential the home front – the oref – is to national defense. Our cities and civilian population have come under sustained attack, forcing families to display enormous psychological strength and resilience. At the same time, the prolonged mobilization of reservists has placed extraordinary burdens on spouses, children, workplaces, and communities. Many reservists have spent months away from home, while their families have shouldered responsibilities that would normally be shared.
Abraham understood that victory belongs not only to those who fight at the front. It also depends on those who hold everything together behind them. Then as now, the battlefield can succeed only when the home front remains strong.■
The writer is a rabbi and educator at Yeshivat Har Etzion (Gush). Find his latest book, Echoes of Rashi: Bereishit, at mtaraginbooks.com

The unique vision of young Dimitar Nenov in Four Sketches for Large Orchestra
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:20:50 UTC
02:20:50 KST

Author
Tsvetana Toncheva
Article
Highlights of Bulgarian Musical Culture
The unique vision of young Dimitar Nenov in Four Sketches for Large Orchestra
Friday 9 October 2026 20:00
Friday, 9 October 2026, 20:00
Dimitar Nenov (1901 – 1953)
PHOTO archives.bnr.bg
Font size
An undisputed intellectual and spiritual aristocrat among Bulgarian musicians, Dimitar Nenov was one of the key figures in the emergence of Bulgaria’s professional school of composition. Music exerted a powerful fascination on him from his earliest childhood, yet as an adolescent his intellectual interests were remarkably broad, encompassing literature, art, philosophy, mathematics and physics. His life was marked by hardship and adversity. Still very young, he found himself at odds with his parents, who insisted that he abandon music and pursue what they regarded as a “serious” profession.
At the age of 19, Nenov left for Dresden to study architecture. His choice of city was far from accidental: Dresden offered him the opportunity to study piano and composition at the Conservatory alongside his architectural training, despite his family’s disapproval. At the time, Germany exerted a powerful attraction on many Bulgarians, including musicians, artists and writers, who encountered the avant-garde currents of European culture there and subsequently helped introduce new and modernist tendencies into Bulgarian cultural life.
For Dimitar Nenov, his student years were exceptionally arduous. He arrived without a scholarship, with barely enough financial support to sustain himself, and without even knowing German. In order to pay his university fees and afford accommodation, he worked seven hours a day as a cinema pianist and as an accompanist at a ballet school.
He repeatedly postponed his university exams because he had to earn his living and was overwhelmed by work. At the same time, however, the young architect was establishing himself as a sought-after concert pianist, giving numerous recitals and appearances in cities across Germany, Denmark and Czechoslovakia. It was during this period that he produced his earliest compositions: piano pieces, songs, his First Symphony, Poem, Ballad, Cinema Suite, a violin conata, two piano sonatas, and Four Sketches for Large Orchestra.
The perfection of poetic expression in Dimitar Nenov's Miniatures for Piano
Although written when he was only 24, Dimitar Nenov’s Four Sketches for Large Orchestra is distinguished by its formidable craftsmanship and considerable artistic stature. Information about the genesis of the score can be found in a 1938 letter Nenov addressed to the eminent Bulgarian violinist, musicologist and public figure Konstantin Zidarov:
“Several fine films gave me the idea of writing characteristic music for individual scenes. I made about ten sketches. And a fine Grotesque... Later, in 1926-27, I orchestrated three of them for large orchestra, together with the Grotesque. Thus my Four Sketches for Large Orchestra (1924-25) took shape: Aspiration, Yearning, Grotesque, Dance.”
The affinity between the first two sketches, Aspiration and Yearning, is unmistakable. Their very titles are synonyms, and not coincidentally so. These two pieces have prompted scholars to seek semantic and associative parallels between Nenov’s music and the work of the great Russian composer Alexander Scriabin, particularly his celebrated Poem of Ecstasy, which incorporates, in Scriabin’s own terminology, a “theme of dreams and longings” and a “theme of flight”.
In striking contrast to the Scriabin-inspired first sketches Aspiration and Yearning stands Nenov’s third sketch, Grotesque, a vivid counterweight to their dreamlike atmosphere, marked instead by a dynamic and theatrical character.
The final movement of Four Sketches for Large Orchestra, Dance, impresses with its melodic and rhythmic diversity and its richly coloured orchestration, evoking the music of another celebrated Russian composer, Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. The associations with the whirlwind-like “Festival at Baghdad” from the immensely popular symphonic suite Scheherazade are particularly striking.
According to the distinguished Bulgarian composer and conductor Konstantin Iliev, Dimitar Nenov’s Four Sketches for Large Orchestra, each distinguished by its own distinctive musical imagery, nevertheless form a stylistically coherent cycle in which “Grotesque refracts the Yearnings into Dance”.
This youthful score stands as one of the earliest compelling manifestations of Dimitar Nenov’s extraordinary talent: a highly intellectual and aristocratic artist of profound sensitivity, whose great personal drama lay in being compelled to devote himself to architecture while his reason, his heart and his entire being were irresistibly drawn towards music.

Netanyahu's Oct. 7 records probe: What was allegedly altered, and why is it stalled? | Explainer
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:19:48 UTC
02:19:48 KST

Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil, who served as Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's military secretary before, during and after the October 7, 2023, Hamas massacre, publicly alleged Thursday for the first time that at least one official record from the morning of the attack had been altered inside the Prime Minister's Office. He identified former chief of staff Tzachi Braverman as the person allegedly responsible.
The allegations prompted calls across the political spectrum for an investigation. But the matter has already been investigated, and the case has been awaiting a decision by prosecutors for more than a year. With Israel approaching elections, no decision is expected for at least another month.
What exactly is Braverman suspected of doing, what did Gil reveal, and why has the investigation yet to produce a decision? Here is what we know.
Has an investigation been opened?
Yes. Police opened an investigation into Tzachi Braverman over suspicions that official records from the Prime Minister's Office had been falsified.
Braverman was questioned under caution in November 2024 and denied the allegations. His attorney, Jacques Chen, maintained that Braverman had acted within his authority to correct a clerical error in the records.
Although the investigation has been completed and the case transferred to the prosecution, no decision has been made on whether to file charges.
What exactly was investigated?
The investigation centered on suspicions that Braverman personally altered the recorded time of a telephone conversation between Netanyahu and his then-military secretary, Avi Gil, on the morning of October 7, 2023.
According to the allegations, the time of the call was changed from 6:40 a.m. to 6:29 a.m., an 11-minute difference during the critical opening moments of the Hamas attack.
Investigators examined claims that Braverman initially instructed a stenographer in the Prime Minister's Office to change the time recorded in the transcript. When she refused, he allegedly made the alteration himself.
The dispute concerns the official documentation of Netanyahu's communications that morning and the chronology of the information he received as the attack unfolded.
What is the status of the investigation?
The case was transferred to the prosecution for a decision approximately one year and three months ago. Since then, prosecutors have not announced whether Braverman will face criminal charges.
Despite renewed public attention following Gil's interview, a decision is not expected within the coming month because of the election period.
The central question is therefore no longer whether authorities will investigate the allegations, but whether the existing evidence is sufficient to justify an indictment.
What did Avi Gil reveal Thursday night?
In an interview with Channel 12 News, Gil confirmed two reports previously published by journalist Nadav Eyal in Yedioth Ahronoth: the alleged alteration of records at the Prime Minister's Office and a warning about the possibility of war delivered by former Shin Bet director Ronen Bar.
Gil said he first became concerned during the war, when he learned that records and transcripts were being collected inside the Prime Minister's Office in violation of established procedures.
"During the war, while we were preparing the ground maneuver, I was approached and told that records were being collected in the Prime Minister's Office, contrary to regulations," he said. "I contacted the attorney general. At the height of the war, stenographic transcripts and protocols were being collected. I didn't want to accuse anyone. I wanted to stop it."
Gil said he asked the attorney general to formally clarify the rules governing access to the records.
He described a subsequent incident in January 2024, when a stenographer approached him privately and said she had been instructed by the chief of staff to change the recorded time of Netanyahu's 6:40 a.m. conversation.
"She came into my office, closed the door and told me," Gil said. "That says everything. She understood that it was unusual. I believe she was distressed."
According to Gil, the stenographer refused to make the change because the original computer record documented the conversation as having taken place between 6:40 a.m. and 6:44 a.m.
"She said, 'I'm not allowed to change it. The computer shows 6:40 to 6:44.' Those are facts, and they are not in dispute," he said.
Gil questioned why anyone would seek to alter the documentation of a four-minute conversation from the morning of October 7, particularly months after the attack.
"The first thing I ask myself is why anyone is dealing with the stenographic record of a four-minute conversation on the morning of October 7," he said. "Who cares about it, and what was said in that conversation that made it so important?"
Gil said he had shared his assessments with the appropriate authorities but distinguished those assessments from what he described as an established fact.
"Someone was dealing with certain narratives. It was important to them to examine something that happened on October 7, sometime in mid-January 2024," he said. "This is changing a stenographic record, changing the truth."
He said he immediately documented the incident in a handwritten note to the attorney general.
"I didn't wait. We were between two meetings, and I sat down and wrote a note to the attorney general in my own handwriting, updating her on the matter," he said.
Gil described the alleged alteration in unequivocal terms.
"This is forgery. Factually, an instruction was given to change the time of a conversation," he said.
He also urged any future commission of inquiry, as well as the state comptroller, not to rely solely on written transcripts when reconstructing the events of October 7.
"I have one recommendation for the commission of inquiry that will be established, and for the comptroller: Don't settle for transcripts. Demand the original recordings."
How did Netanyahu respond, and how did his account change?
Netanyahu responded Thursday by accusing Gil of knowing about indications of an impending attack on October 7 and failing to wake the prime minister in time.
The accusation echoed similar claims Netanyahu has directed at former Shin Bet chief Ronen Bar, who has said he intends to sue the prime minister, and former IDF chief of staff Herzi Halevi.
In a statement issued through Likud, Netanyahu's party accused Gil of attempting to divert attention from his own failures.
"Tonight, Channel 14 revealed that Avi Gil is trying to divert attention from his personal failures that night with lies," the statement said. "Like others, Avi Gil knew about the impending attack and chose not to wake the prime minister in time."
According to Likud, at 3:55 a.m. on October 7, Gil received a text message from an intelligence officer in the Prime Minister's Military Secretariat describing several warning signs.
These included the activation of SIM cards in Hamas facilities in central Gaza and Khan Younis, the activation of Hamas emergency communications systems and unusual activity involving Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif.
"Avi Gil did nothing with the information," Likud said. "Gil's interviews are attempts to obscure the simple and painful truth about his failure to perform his duties."
However, Netanyahu's latest accusation contrasts with a statement he issued in March 2025, when he defended the conduct of his military secretariat.
At that time, Netanyahu said an intelligence officer in the secretariat had received a message during the night of October 7 describing several warning signs, but also indicating that Hamas was operating normally and that the head of the IDF Southern Command would discuss the situation only the following morning.
"The intelligence officer immediately forwarded the message, word for word, to the military secretary," Netanyahu said in March 2025. "However, in light of the message's assessment that this was not an urgent event, he chose not to wake him."
The statement concluded: "Prime Minister Netanyahu has full confidence in the military secretariat of his office."
The difference between the two statements has become a central point of contention, with Netanyahu's critics accusing him of changing his account of the intelligence warnings and the actions taken by his staff before the massacre.
How have political leaders responded?
Opposition leader Yair Lapid accused Netanyahu of attempting to rewrite the history of October 7 rather than accept responsibility for the failures that preceded the attack.
"The truth that emerged from Maj. Gen. Avi Gil's testimony is simple and indisputable: Netanyahu was warned and ignored it, and since then he has evaded responsibility, whined that no one woke him up and done everything possible to rewrite history," Lapid said.
"If he remains in office, there will be more October 7s, and our children will not be safe," he added.
Yisrael Beytenu chairman Avigdor Liberman called for an immediate criminal investigation into Netanyahu and members of his office.
"I call on the attorney general to order an immediate investigation against the prime minister and his associates on suspicion of treason and conspiracy," Liberman said.
He also urged the IDF chief of staff to prevent any attempt to use the military for political purposes, accusing Netanyahu's camp of trying to change the public agenda immediately before the elections.
Democrats chairman Yair Golan described Gil's allegations as an extraordinary development.
"This is an earthquake. Maj. Gen. (res.) Avi Gil's testimony is among the most serious ever heard in Israel," Golan said.
"The blame and responsibility of Netanyahu for the massacre of 1,200 people and the abduction of 251 have never been clearer," he added, accusing the prime minister of committing a grave offense against Gaza border communities, former hostages and the Israeli public.
For now, the investigation into the alleged alteration of official records remains unresolved. Braverman has denied wrongdoing, prosecutors have yet to decide whether to file charges, and Gil's public account has renewed scrutiny of how Netanyahu's office documented the crucial first minutes of October 7.

Drone strike kills 30 people in Sudan’s Blue Nile region
Drone reportedly linked to RSF targets Wad al-Mahi, killing dozens near displacement camp, including women and children.
At least 30 displaced people, including women and children, have been killed and dozens of others have been wounded following a drone attack in southeastern Sudan.
The governor of Wad al-Mahi province told Al Jazeera on Friday that a drone belonging to the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) targeted the centre of the province, killing 26 women and four children.
Governor Mahjoub Al-Sheikh described the attack as “cowardly”. He said the drone was launched from “inside Ethiopia”, according to the AFP news agency.
Al Jazeera Arabic’s Sudan correspondent, Wadah Al-Tahir, explained that the attack was the latest in a wave of drone strikes targeting the Blue Nile region and this time Wad al-Mahi province near the city of Damazin was struck.
Friday’s attack was just outside a displacement camp, near an informal gold mining site, where women earn a daily wage using chemicals and their bare hands to clear gold nuggets from the earth extracted by men.
The latest frontline in the war between the Sudanese army and the RSF is the border region with Ethiopia, which is facing its own internal conflict that threatens to escalate.
Sudan has repeatedly accused Ethiopia of harbouring RSF fighters and bases – Ethiopia has denied the allegations.
Local sources say the porous border between the two countries is a key supply line for the paramilitary and its allies, AFP reported.
The RSF launched its offensive towards Damazin but the advance could put the army in a bind, forcing it to defend territory on both the Blue Nile front and in the Kordofan region, where a year of deadly drone strikes has left the two sides deadlocked.
Aid workers estimate that Sudan’s civil war has killed more than 200,000 people since it started in April 2023, creating one of the world’s largest hunger and displacement crises.
Nearly 100,000 people have been displaced in Blue Nile state this year alone, according to United Nations figures.

Russian search engine Yandex struggles after Ukrainian strikes on data centres
- Published
Russian tech giant Yandex has said it was struggling to maintain services after two of its five data centres were struck by Ukrainian drones in the past two days.
Often dubbed "Russia's Google", the company runs the country's most popular search engine, as well as a food-ordering and taxi app used by tens of millions of people.
President Volodymyr Zelensky said the attacks were in response to weeks of Russian strikes on Ukrainian data centres.
Both sides have stepped up attacks on infrastructure in recent months as the war between the two drags on. Kyiv says its strikes are aimed at revenue streams for Moscow's war machine, and that the latest attacks could force Russia to divert resources to Yandex.
Yandex said that its data centre in Sasovo, in the Ryazan region, had been "seriously damaged as a result of a drone attack" overnight into Thursday, with its operations "completely suspended".
Another data centre in Kaluga, a region south-west of Moscow, had also been attacked on Friday morning, it said, with part of that site's infrastructure "taken out of service".
Yandex said on Friday that its data centres were "critical" for the normal operation of its services and that it was "very difficult to predict" when they would be back online.
It said teams were working "day and night" to keep services running, but "unfortunately it is not a simple task".
The tech giant said none of its employees had been injured in the strikes. The regional governor in Kaluga said nine people had been injured in a drone attack on the city's infrastructure.
The exact scope of the disruption to the company's services is unclear - though it told state news agency Tass that some of its AI chatbot functions were temporarily unavailable, while its smart home devices may also experience problems.
Yandex previously said its Kaluga data centre was one of Russia's largest - covering an area of 130,000 sqm (1,399,000 sq ft) and consuming as much electricity annually as 220,000 UK households.
Its data centre in Sasovo, meanwhile, houses two of three supercomputers used to develop the company's AI model. It is unclear whether the supercomputers survived the attack.
Ukraine's defence ministry confirmed the data centre attacks, saying they could "force Russia to divert resources to repair the damaged capacity".
Zelensky said Kyiv was responding to similar Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centres in a "mirror-like fashion".
Last month, a Russian drone hit a business centre in Kyiv, killing four people and damaging a data centre. Due to the strikes, about 100,000 households in Kyiv and the region suffered internet outages.
Some Ukrainian firms have already begun moving data from damaged servers to facilities abroad.
Moscow has justified the attacks by saying the data centres were used by Ukrainian military intelligence.
But Ukraine accuses it of deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure. Russia has stepped up strikes on energy infrastructure ahead of the winter, as it has done in previous years of the full-scale invasion, which began in 2022.

Briefing the UN Security Council, Grundberg said hostilities have intensified in recent weeks following advances by Ansar Allah, also known as the Houthis, toward Mokha and the coast along the Bab el-Mandeb Strait.
He condemned Houthi attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure in Saudi Arabia, including recent strikes on Abha International Airport and King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that killed and injured civilians.

"While the situation in Yemen remains highly fluid, one fact is clear: civilians, especially women and children, are once again bearing the brunt of escalating violence," he said.
Grundberg cited the International Monetary Fund's ranking of Yemen as the world's poorest country.
He urged all parties to comply with international humanitarian law, including requirements to distinguish between civilians and combatants, avoid disproportionate harm and take all feasible precautions to protect civilians.
He stressed that children were entitled to special protection and that their recruitment and use in armed conflict were prohibited.
Grundberg also called for the protection of medical facilities, humanitarian personnel and operations, and people no longer participating in hostilities.
The envoy warned that Houthi threats against Saudi-linked commercial vessels in the Red Sea undermined freedom of navigation.
He said the threats were becoming increasingly intertwined with disputes over maritime trade routes and pressures on international energy markets.
Grundberg acknowledged that regional security, freedom of navigation and international trade were legitimate concerns.
However, he stressed that international efforts must also reflect conditions inside Yemen and the needs and aspirations of its people.
He warned that shifting military calculations were influencing the parties' assessments of when and how to pursue negotiations.

Grundberg said military pressure could strengthen negotiating leverage but stressed that military action and diplomacy were not mutually exclusive.
"Ultimately, gains on the battlefield cannot substitute for the negotiations that will be required to settle the conflict," he said.
As mediator, Grundberg said his responsibility was to create space for a Yemeni-led political settlement.
He stressed that the parties owed a political solution to approximately 40 million Yemenis who had endured more than a decade of conflict.
"Unless war is to become Yemen's permanent reality, the time to consider political strategies is now," he said.
The envoy also expressed concern about the continued detention of UN personnel and staff from nongovernmental organizations, civil society groups and diplomatic missions.
He called for urgent action and continued Security Council support.
"Without a credible political process that sustainably resolves the conflict, it will continue to resurface, deepen regional tensions, and threaten broader stability," Grundberg warned.
He urged Security Council members to maintain unity, sustain their attention on Yemen and collectively support mediation efforts to end the conflict.

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:13:43 EEST
02:13:43 KST

Since the beginning of the year, more than 4,300 people, including 161 children, have been forced to evacuate from border communities in Sumy region, according to Head of Sumy Regional Military Administration Oleh Hryhorov.
"More than 4,300 people have been evacuated from border communities in Sumy region since the beginning of the year. Among them are 161 children… Take care of yourselves and your loved ones. If your town is under constant shelling, it's important to make the right decision and save your life," the administration's head said.
To support evacuated residents in Sumy region, transit centers are operating in Sumy, Romny, Shostka, and Shostka district. In total, 28 temporary shelters have been set up for internally displaced persons, with 740 vacant spots currently available; for long-term housing, the community is offering 33 houses, two apartments, and 20 spots in dormitories.
In addition, financial support is provided for internally displaced persons. Specifically, monthly state assistance amounts to UAH 2,000 per adult and UAH 3,000 per child or person with a disability. In addition, there are one-time payments, including UAH 2,000 from the regional budget for each evacuated child and UAH 12,300 in one-time international aid from partners.

Tesla drops 'Full Self-Driving' brand name in Europe after regulator pushback
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:12:32 UTC
02:12:32 KST

Elon Musk's automaker Tesla has changed the brand name of its "Full Self-Driving (Supervised)," or FSD, system in Europe to "Assisted Driving" after German regulators called the branding "somewhat misleading."
The package is still sold under the Full Self-Driving (Supervised) branding in the U.S. as a $99 per month subscription for Tesla owners.
Tesla is gunning for approvals across Europe, where EV sales have been on the rise this year amid soaring fuel costs caused by the war in Iran, and where Tesla sales have shown signs of recovery from a sales slump last year.
On Tuesday, the German Federal Ministry of Transport, known as the BMV, said in a statement that Tesla's brand name "FSD" was "somewhat misleading," adding that "It is not a system that takes over the entire driving task. Rather, it is a driver assistance system that can support certain driving tasks such as accelerating, braking, and steering. The driver must remain attentive at all times."
Tesla has been pressuring automotive regulators in Europe, especially in the Netherlands, for rapid approval of their system. Reuters reported that in some cases, Tesla's "browbeating" pushed regulators to reduce the intensity of their safety tests and reviews of the company's technology.
The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, the U.S. automotive safety regulator, is also investigating Tesla's FSD to determine if it is safe for drivers to use in fog, glaring sun or other reduced visibility conditions, and is investigating Tesla to determine whether FSD caused Tesla drivers to commit traffic violations — some that resulted in collisions.
In December 2025, a judge in California determined that Tesla had engaged in deceptive marketing around its Autopilot and FSD systems, falsely implying they were fully automated driving systems. Tesla has countersued the California DMV to try to shed that "false advertiser" label in a Los Angeles superior court. That litigation is ongoing.
Autonomous systems expert Missy Cummings, an engineering professor at George Mason University and outspoken critic of Tesla and other autonomous vehicle developers, said renaming FSD isn't a strong enough measure to ensure the systems are safe for broad release in Europe.
In an email to CNBC, Cummings said European agencies are "ignoring both past and ongoing NHTSA investigations" into safety defects with Tesla's FSD.
"The EU is struggling to keep up in the AI marketplace," she said. "Musk sees this and is definitely bullying them as a result."
She criticized the Dutch regulator, known as RDW, for approving Tesla FSD for release in Europe, "based on secretive data," adding that, "The public should demand transparency in any approval of a transportation system with embedded AI."
Tesla and RDW did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
In its second-quarter earnings update, Tesla said it had 1.48 million "active" FSD subscriptions but did not say how many were activated from free trials or other incentives.

The United Arab Emirates said Friday that a FlyDubai co-pilot had planned to seize control of an aircraft and carry out a "suicide attack" on Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv.
Federal Attorney General Hamad Saif Al Shamsi said an investigation into the Sept. 30 flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv found that the 29-year-old Omani co-pilot had planned the attack in advance, according to the official WAM news agency.
The suspect "had begun carrying out a premeditated terrorist plot to seize control of the aircraft and use it to launch a suicide attack targeting the passenger terminal at Ben Gurion Airport in Tel Aviv, with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life," Al Shamsi said.
The attorney general said investigators had examined the suspect's "ideological and professional background."
According to Al Shamsi, investigators found that signs of "extremism and terrorism" had emerged in 2017 while the suspect was studying in Australia.

Syrian authorities trying keep Arabs, Kurds from clashing in Hasakah city
Unknown

17:11:47 UTC
02:11:47 KST

BEIRUT, October 9. /TASS/. Syria’s internal security forces have been deployed to the city of Hasakah, the administrative center of the governorate of the same name, to prevent clashes between the city’s Arab population and Kurds, the Al-Ikhbariya television channel reported.
According to the TV channel, demonstrations of the city’s Arabs erupted after the Friday prayer. The demonstrators installed Syrian national flags in the city squares. The police clashed with activists who were attempting to provoke riots in a number of neighborhoods. Several law enforcement officers sustained injuries.
The situation in Hsakah is under the control of the central authorities, the TV channel said, adding that police cordons around Kurd-populated neighborhood in the city’s northern part have been reinforced. However, despite enhanced security measures, crowds of Arabs from neighboring settlements of Al Rashidiya, Al-Haddadiyah, and Al-Shaddadi have managed to get into the city, exacerbating the situation.
The political council of the Kurdish-led Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF) coalition called on the city’s residents, ethnic Arabs, Assyrians, and Kurds, to stay calm and not to yield to potential provocations. "The SDF insists that the government in Damascus is responsible for maintaining civil peace and public order," it said in a statement. "We call on social and political forces, parties, tribal and religious leaders to prevent the dissemination of hostile rhetoric and rumors intended to incite unrest."
Protests triggered by the shooting of a Kurdish young man were held in the city of Ain al-Arab (Kobani) in the Aleppo governorate on September 12. This was the first incident after the dissolution of Kurdish armed units that had been announced by SDF commander Mazloum Abdi on August 25. Kurdish fighters were incorporated into the Syrian army and law enforcement forces in northeastern Syria.

Colombia: Italy Supports the Restoration of Cartagena’s Historic City Walls
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:11:31 CEST
02:11:31 KST

Italy is supporting a project for the conservation of the historic city walls of Cartagena de Indias, in northern Colombia. The Italian Embassy, the Italian Agency for Development Cooperation (AICS), and the city government are finalizing the guidelines for the national ideas competition “Imagine the Future of Cartagena’s Walls,” open to architecture students and architects up to age 30. The initiative aims to gather proposals to improve the connection between the San Ignacio and San Francisco Javier ramparts, two key points of the city’s fortified system, which is recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Entries may be submitted through November 5. The competition is part of an international cooperation project funded by the Italian government with a grant of 3 million euros, earmarked for heritage preservation, the promotion of sustainable tourism, and the strengthening of the local economy. The planned interventions include the restoration of several sections of the walls, such as the La Tenaza spur and the Murallita del Diablo, as well as the construction of an elevated walkway connecting the two bastions. The project also includes work on the Cathedral of Santa Catalina de Alejandría and the Santo Domingo bastion. Proposals must consider not only architectural aspects but also the relationship between the city walls and public spaces, the landscape, local culture, and the city’s residents and visitors. Participation is open to individuals or groups of up to three people, with at least one member from Cartagena. Ten projects will be selected, from which the three best will be chosen. The selected ideas will be exhibited and may contribute to the subsequent phases of the project.

🔴 FlyDubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport, inspired by 9/11, UAE prosecutor says
Unknown

FlyDubai co-pilot planned suicide attack on Tel Aviv airport inspired by 9/11, prosecutor says
The Omani co-pilot who attacked the captain of FlyDubai flight 1073 had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport in a suicide attack, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said Friday. The Israel-bound flight carrying 182 people made an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia after a descent so extreme that part of its rudder was torn away.
The co-pilot who attacked the captain of a FlyDubai jet last week had planned to crash the plane into Tel Aviv's international airport, the United Arab Emirates' top prosecutor said on Friday.
In the aftermath of the incident, people on board – the majority of whom were Israeli – described a sudden plunge in altitude and a fight for control of the aircraft, which was forced to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. The passengers were repatriated on a second flydubai flight hours later.
The unnamed Omani co-pilot, now in custody in the UAE, had drawn inspiration from al Qaeda's September 11, 2001 suicide attacks on the United States, and carried out his attempt "with the aim of causing the greatest possible loss of life", according to the Emirati prosecutor's findings published by state media.
The prosecutor found that the co-pilot had first begun to be radicalised while studying in Australia "through reading extremist literature and following online content glorifying terrorist organisations and suicide attacks".
He said last week's flight had been the co-pilot's third to Tel Aviv, and that he had used the two earlier trips to plan the attack.
Read moreWho are the mystery pilots who successfully landed endangered FlyDubai flight 1073?
During the flight, the suspect used an emergency axe to attack the plane's Indian captain, Smit Machchhar, who fought back and tried to call for help.
Another pilot assigned to the return flight who was also on board "noticed the cockpit door opening and closing repeatedly in an unusual manner", according to the findings.
After gaining entry, he "intervened with the assistance of a cabin crew member and several passengers, and together they rescued the injured captain and restrained the suspect".
The return flight captain and his co-pilot then landed the plane at Tabuk Airport in Saudi Arabia.
No sign of intentions
Israel and the UAE have become close partners since normalising ties under the US-brokered Abraham Accords in 2020, and Israel carries out stringent security checks on those travelling to the country.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu previously said that the co-pilot – identified in reports as Hamam al-Hammami – must have got around restrictions preventing individuals from nations that do not recognise Israel operating flights to the country.
The UAE prosecutor's "findings showed that he had met the professional and security requirements for employment, including holding a pilot's licence, providing a certificate of good conduct and completing the required checks".
"However, none of the procedures revealed any indications of his extremist views or his intention to carry out a terrorist plot."
The co-pilot had previously worked for Oman Air and Royal Air Maroc, but media outlets reported after the incident that he had been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about his extremist views.
After the incident, Netanyahu had hailed the passengers and the plane's captain for their bravery in averting what would have otherwise been a catastrophe.
He later ordered a "thorough review of all security aspects of foreign civil aviation to Israel" in response to the incident.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP)

UNITED NATIONS, United States - The United Nations on Oct 9 called US plans to live-stream the execution of Nidal Hasan, the gunman who killed 13 people at the Fort Hood military base in 2009, “abhorrent” and said it could be a violation of prohibitions against torture.
“These kinds of public executions we’ve seen in other countries, whether it’s Iran or Afghanistan... can constitute a form of cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment, or punishment,” UN spokesperson Stephane Dujarric told a daily UN briefing in New York.
“Showing it live is tantamount... to it being public, and could be a violation of the prohibition against torture,” he said.
“A government executing someone in public, or in front of live cameras, frankly, is abhorrent.”
Hasan is set to become the first person to be executed by US military firing squad since 1945.

China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

02:09:00 KST

China, EU reach deal to 'moderate' China's car exports to EU
October 9, 2026
European Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic announced on Friday that China and the European Union had reached a deal that could cut Chinese exports of hybrid cars to the EU by more than half.
This announcement followed two-day talks in Beijing aimed at reducing the EU's growing trade deficit with China.
Earlier, Sefcovic said this week's talks were the culmination of three months of intensive work.
What do we know about the EV deal?
According to Sefcovic, the deal would "moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the EU."
He added that this opens the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half, based on projections over a four-year period.
"By this step, we're actually preventing several millions of cars exports from China to the European Union," Sefcovic said.
Although he did not offer details on how the agreement will be implemented, Sefcovic said he believed the two sides had achieved a very good result.
What else was decided?
Sevcovic added the two sides also reached an agreement to reduce Chinese import duties on €4 billion ($4.5 billion) worth of EU exports, including car parts, olive oil and footwear.
They also agreed to simplify China's process for granting export licenses for rare earths and permanent magnets.
The agreement will require approval from the leaders of all 27 EU nations, who will discuss the outcome at the start of their summit in Brussels on Thursday.
Rebalancing EU-China trade
According to UN Comtrade data, Chinese exports to the EU totaled $560 billion (€500 billion) last year, up from $517 billion in 2023. Exports to major economies, including Germany, Italy, Spain, and Poland, each rose approximately 10% from a year earlier. Shipments to Hungary increased by 43%.
Meanwhile, China imported $268.3 billion (€240 billion) worth of European goods last year, down from $269.4 billion the previous year. Purchases from Denmark, Ireland, and France led the way.
Last month, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen warned lawmakers at the European Parliament that the trade gap had reached a tipping point. She said the EU would use all available tools to rebalance the relationship.
