Taiwan’s overseas representative offices marked Double Ten National Day with receptions in India, Turkey, the Netherlands, the Philippines and the US, underscoring efforts to bolster diplomatic ties, expand trade and deepen cooperation in technology and other key industries.
Taiwan’s representative office in India on Thursday held a National Day reception in New Delhi, with several hundred people attending, including officials from India, diplomats and Taiwanese businesspeople, the office said.
At the event, Representative to India Chen Mu-min (陳牧民) announced that the Taiwan-India Parliamentary Friendship Association would resume operations.
Photo: CNA
So far, 23 Indian lawmakers have agreed to join the group, which would become an important new force in promoting cooperation between Taiwan and India, Chen said.
Trade relations between Taiwan and India are continuing to grow rapidly, with bilateral trade reaching a record US$12.5 billion last year, he said.
Trade in the first eight months of this year reached US$12.9 billion, a 60 percent increase from the same period last year, he added.
Taiwan’s representative office in Turkey held a National Day reception on Wednesday, with more than 300 guests attending, including Turkish lawmakers from across party lines, senior government officials and diplomats, the office said.
Taiwan hopes to deepen cooperation with Turkey’s public and private sectors by promoting joint ventures, jointly developing artificial intelligence (AI) applications and cultivating high-tech talent, Representative to Turkey Huang Chih-yang (黃志揚) said.
By combining Taiwan’s technological and industrial strengths with Turkey’s strategic location and market advantages, the two sides could build a bridge linking East Asia and the Mediterranean, Huang said.
Taiwan’s representative office in the Netherlands on Wednesday hosted a reception attended by more than 250 Dutch political and business figures and members of the Taiwanese community, the office said.
Representative to the Netherlands Tien Chung-kwang (田中光) thanked the Dutch government and parliament for their firm support of Taiwan, including publicly backing Taiwan’s participation in the WHO at the World Health Assembly in May and sending the Royal Netherlands Navy frigate De Ruyter through the Taiwan Strait in June.
Peace and stability in the Taiwan Strait are in the global interest and particularly important to trading nations such as Taiwan and the Netherlands, Tien said.
The Taipei Economic and Cultural Office (TECO) in Atlanta, Georgia, held a National Day celebration on Wednesday, with nearly 300 people from the political, academic and business sectors attending, the office said in a statement on Thursday.
The office will continue working with local state governments, chambers of commerce, schools and businesses to bolster cooperation in AI, healthcare, aerospace and disaster resilience, TECO Atlanta Director Lin Chu-en (林主恩) said.
Taiwan-US ties have continued to deepen over the past year, with Taiwan’s economy continuing to grow on demand from high-tech industries, Lin said, adding that the US has become one of Taiwan’s most important trading partners.
Cooperation between Taiwan and six US states — Alabama, Georgia, Kentucky, Tennessee, North Carolina and South Carolina — has become increasingly practical, covering high-tech talent development, scholarships, Chinese-language education, cultural exchanges, research collaboration and industrial investment, Lin said.
TECO Houston also hosted a National Day reception on Wednesday, drawing more than 300 guests from the political, business, academic and Taiwanese expatriate communities in the southern US, the office said in a statement.
Taiwan and the US are working together to build a “joint fleet” by further reinforcing bilateral trade, investment and supply chain integration, TECO Houston Director Yvonne Hsiao (蕭伊芳) said.
By combining Taiwan’s manufacturing strengths with US innovation and talent, the two sides aim to build secure and resilient supply chains for semiconductors, AI and drones, Hsiao said.
Taiwan-US technology cooperation is about helping both sides succeed and promoting the global economy, she added.

Ethiopian federal police yesterday fanned out across the regional capital of Tigray after anti-government forces pulled out, driving in vehicles and calling on residents over loudspeakers to help establish a new administration following the rebels’ withdrawal.
Over the last weekend, government-allied fighters had entered Mekelle, the capital of Ethiopia’s northern Tigray region, after the rebel Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF) announced its withdrawal.
The TPLF had joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed. Fighting escalated late last month, undermining the 2022 peace deal. The rebels seized the Mekelle airport and the city, one of Ethiopia’s largest.
Photo obtained by Reuters
Then on Saturday last week, the rebels said their forces had pulled out — similar to what they did in the previous two-year war, which ended with a peace agreement in 2022, apparently to spare the city from destruction.
Still, local government offices remained shut yesterday in Mekelle as the city awaited new authorities, with police and the government-allied Tigray Peace Force in charge of security. Members of the city’s new civilian administration had arrived with federal police on Thursday, but said they were awaiting instructions.
The Tigray Peace Force imposed an overnight curfew on Wednesday.
No administration had taken office in Mekelle by yesterday morning.
Tigray’s TV and radio stations have been off the air since the TPLF withdrawal.
Ahmed’s government promised to restore banking, electricity, telecommunications and water services, but gave no timetable. It also outlined plans to register people involved in the conflict and help them return to civilian life.
Further north, a government-allied commander and a conflict monitoring group have separately reported Eritrean troops entering Ethiopia, raising fears of a wider conflict.
Eritrean personnel entered Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday, Tigray Peace Force commander Ermiyas Ababu said, citing reports from his personnel in the area.
The Armed Conflict Location & Event Data monitoring group said Eritrean troops crossed the border at Zelambesa on Wednesday and came under drone attack at Guada while traveling toward Idaga Hamus.
It attributed the strikes to Ethiopia’s military.
Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Gebremeskel said in a statement: “We are not in the business of refuting wild allegations or narratives.”
He accused Ethiopia of threatening regional peace through its pursuit of “sovereign access to the sea,” but did not explicitly confirm or deny the crossing.
Eritrea has previously denied Ethiopian allegations that it supports the TPLF — its enemy during the 2020-to-2022 Tigray war, when Eritrean troops fought alongside Ethiopian federal forces.
During that war, the Associated Press documented accounts from survivors and witnesses accusing Eritrean soldiers of killings, rape and looting.
Eritrean President Isaias Afwerki dismissed allegations of abuses by his forces as “a fantasy” in 2023.
Eritrea announced last week that it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara.

The Ethiopian Ministry of Foreign Affairs on Monday said it remained committed to dialogue with its neighbors.

China Youth Corps ruled a KMT-affiliated body
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:43:01 UTC
01:43:01 KST

The Supreme Administrative Court on Thursday upheld a 2018 ruling by the Ill-gotten Party Assets Settlement Committee designating the China Youth Corps (CYC) as an “affiliated organization” of the Chinese Nationalist Party (KMT).
The decision, which cannot be appealed, means NT$5.61 billion (US$176 million) in assets frozen by the committee would not be returned to the CYC.
The CYC said in a statement late on Thursday that it could not accept the decision and “strongly objected to the court stigmatizing more than 70 years of its public service work as ill-gotten KMT assets.”
Photo: Liu Hsin-de, Taipei Times
The KMT condemned the ruling, accusing the judiciary of acting as a rubber stamp for the ruling Democratic Progressive Party’s (DPP) targeting of political opponents.
The Executive Yuan-supervised committee was set up following the 2016 enactment of the Act Governing the Settlement of Ill-gotten Properties by Political Parties and Their Affiliate Organizations (政黨及其附隨組織不當取得財產處理條例) by the then-DPP government.
The law aims to address assets acquired by political parties and their affiliated organizations during the KMT’s authoritarian rule over Taiwan.
In its 2018 ruling, the committee said the CYC benefited from the KMT party-state system’s resources and privileges under martial law and that the KMT controlled the CYC’s personnel, finances and operations until 1999.
It determined that although a leadership change saw the CYC break away from KMT control in 1999, continued ambiguity over asset ownership meant it could not conclude the two organizations had fully separated.
Following the ruling, ownership of 61 plots of land and buildings belonging to the CYC was ordered transferred to the state and the organization’s assets were frozen.
The CYC appealed the ruling, arguing that it was established and initially run by the government in 1952, under the supervision of the Executive Yuan and the Ministry of National Defense, and that its key leaders were appointed through the government rather than by the KMT.
It said that it became an independent civilian organization after ending its affiliation with the Ministry of National Defense in 1969, pointing to the defeat of a KMT-backed candidate in its 1999 leadership election as evidence of its independence.
However, the Taipei High Administrative Court in 2024 ruled that the CYC was effectively controlled by the KMT, despite being formally under the ministry, and that the KMT’s control continued after the CYC became a civilian organization.
The court also agreed with the committee that the CYC’s 1999 break from KMT control did not mean it had fully separated from the party, as asset ownership remained unclear.
In its ruling, the Supreme Administrative Court said it found no reason to overturn the lower court’s decision, citing sufficient evidence and correct application of the law.

Doctor accused of falsifying record
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:52 UTC
01:42:52 KST

Allegations that a China-trained doctor is illegally practicing medicine with a fake US medical diploma need to be verified, officials said yesterday, although they did not rule out launching a probe into the matter.
In a post on Threads, a member of the public said that they recognized a Tainan-based internal medicine doctor as an acquaintance who studied medicine in China.
She had cut all ties with her friends shortly after graduating, the post said.
Photo: Taipei Times
The person is practicing medicine with a diploma from the University of California, Riverside under a different name, but records of medical certification for her under either name could not be found online, it said.
Ministry of Health and Welfare Medical Affairs Department Deputy Director Liu Yu-ching (劉玉菁) said that Taiwan does not recognize higher-education qualifications in medical fields from China when it grants doctors’ licenses.
The restriction applies to medicine, dentistry and traditional Chinese medicine, Liu said, citing the Act Governing Relations Between the People of the Taiwan Area and the Mainland Area (台灣地區與大陸地區人民關係條例).
Holders of a medical diploma issued by foreign countries other than China might qualify for a license to practice medicine if the degree-conferring institution is accredited by the Ministry of Education, she said.
Applicants must study in a field relevant to the type of license they apply for, and meet standards for academic credits earned and scholastic performance before being allowed to take a medical license test, she said.
The evaluation for eligibility to take the test is conducted by a panel of experts, she added.
The applicants must pass a Ministry of Examination-administered certification test to become a doctor in Taiwan, she said.
The health ministry has not verified the accusations on social media against the Tainan-based doctor, she said, adding that officials would, if necessary, seek information from the Ministry of Examination.
The doctor’s medical license would be revoked if the examination authority cancels her qualification after establishing that she had submitted forged documents, Liu said.
The claims that no record of the doctor’s medical license could be found would be investigated, she said.
Deputy Minister of Examination Huang Ching-chang (黃慶章) said that would-be doctors must pass background checks to qualify to sit the license test.
Candidates with Chinese diplomas are not allowed to take the exam, while those who hold degrees from other foreign nations are rigorously scrutinized, including a review of their academic and international travel records, Huang said.
The examination ministry would initiate a probe into the doctor accused of using forged qualifications if it receives a complaint or request for investigation through official channels, he said.
With some exceptions, Taiwan does not recognize academic degrees conferred by China’s Jinan University, which the doctor supposedly attended, because of the institution’s affiliation with the Chinese United Front Work Department, said Liao Kao-hsien (廖高賢), director-general of the Ministry of Education’s Department of Higher Education.
Holders of degrees in medicine, dentistry or traditional Chinese medicine issued by a foreign country must pass an education ministry qualification assessment before taking the national licensing examination, subject to statutory exemptions, Liao said.

GlobalFoundries rallies after US$2bn TSMC deal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

GlobalFoundries Inc shares gained as much as 7 percent after the chip manufacturer announced a five-year, US$2 billion deal to provide US production capacity to Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (TSMC, 台積電).
Under the agreement, announced on Thursday, GlobalFoundries is to help supply components known as silicon interposers. The US company is to rely on manufacturing at its facility in Malta, New York, and said it has the option to expand capacity “as customer demand grows.”
An interposer is a small layer of silicon that sits between a chip and its packaging. It is home to the wires that carry electronic signals and power needed to make that chip functional. The components are increasingly important as semiconductors become larger and companies combine multiple chips into the same package.
Photo: Bloomberg
GlobalFoundries expects to expand capacity at its Malta facility and establish the first US-based source of silicon interposers supporting advanced packaging technologies, including embedded deep trench capacitor components, it said.
The company expects to begin ramping up volume production of the TSMC components in the first half of 2028.
The multi-year US$2 billion agreement will expand capacity for advanced packaging ecosystem and support growing demand for AI and high-performance computing technologies, GlobalFoundries said.
The deal provides TSMC with an additional US-based source of production at a time when the Taiwanese company is working to expand its US footprint. TSMC is the dominant chip foundry — a business that produces semiconductors for outside customers — and serves clients such as Nvidia Corp, Apple Inc and Advanced Micro Devices Inc.
Shares of GlobalFoundries rose as high as US$51.45, marking their biggest intraday gain in three weeks. The stock had been up 38 percent this year through Wednesday’s close.
GlobalFoundries’ foundry business is generally focused on less sophisticated chips, what it calls “essential semiconductors.” Greater interest in technology like silicon interposers for packaging is giving the company a role to play in more advanced AI components.
“Advanced packaging is becoming increasingly critical to delivering the performance, power efficiency and scale required for next-generation AI systems,” GlobalFoundries senior vice president Ed Kaste said in the statement.

Respect for gay community lacking
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:50 UTC
01:42:50 KST

The recent controversy surrounding a police raid on a gay bar on Saturday last week in Taipei’s Ximending (西門町) area flies directly in the face of the city government’s long-standing efforts to project an image of Taipei as a diverse and inclusive city. With its rainbow-themed public spaces and tourism marketing, Taipei has long been proud of its support for diverse communities. However, in light of this incident, it must be asked: Should a city’s inclusivity be measured by the number of rainbows on its streets, or by how the authorities actually treat LGBTQ people?
According to the Wanhua Precinct, police were investigating a case involving public indecency in accordance with the law. However, their conduct during the operation has drawn sharp criticism, with reports of patrons being handcuffed, ordered to squat and officers making inappropriate remarks. LGBTQ groups have called on the Taipei City Government to investigate the conduct of the operation and address the stigma and insecurity that the city’s queer venues have long faced.
It is the police’s duty to investigate and crack down on crime, and gay bars should not be treated as spaces beyond the reach of the law. Equally, however, standards regarding due process, human rights and dignity must not be weaker for cases involving LGBTQ establishments. The legal grounds for enforcement and whether its execution respects the principle of proportionality and the dignity of the public are two separate questions. They must both be seriously examined.
Taipei has over the past few years promoted rainbow tourism, but genuine inclusivity cannot exist only within the confines of tourism brochures and event stages. Whether LGBTQ communities receive the same respect as other citizens when it comes to police checks, searches or other exercises of state authority is the real measure of how far we have come on equal rights.
There is no need to rush on pronouncements of guilt. Instead, the Taipei City Government should release full footage from the operation to address the concerns raised. Any misconduct should be dealt with through accountability and corrective action.
The incident should also prompt a review of police training to prevent prejudice from influencing law enforcement. Taipei’s rainbows are decoration; they do not prove that equality has been achieved. When the events are over and the flags have been put away, the real test is whether the city’s LBGTQ communities can retain their full dignity when dealing with the authorities.
Ken is a social worker.

Photo: AP
The prominent local businessman denied the allegations.

Photo: AFP
“Allegations do not constitute proof of wrongdoing, and any action taken by Fijian authorities must uphold due process, the presumption of innocence and the rule of law,” it added.
An investigation by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project in 2024 alleged that Zhao operated as a key pointman for Beijing’s interests in Fiji and was a naturalized citizen of the Pacific nation.

His lawyer, Nikheel Nambiar, said he denied those claims and that allegations of influence-peddling for Beijing were “false and misleading.”

China has over the past few years sought i to deepen its influence among Pacific Island nations, to the consternation of the US and its ally Australia.

Meta bans ads from TikTok on its apps
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:48 UTC
01:42:48 KST

Meta Platforms Inc banned advertisements in the US from ByteDance Ltd (字節跳動), the former controlling owner of TikTok, intensifying the competition with the popular social video site.
On Thursday, Meta began implementing a complete restriction on ads and paid marketing messages placed on its platforms by ByteDance, the Chinese company that remains in charge of key parts of TikTok in the US.
The ban is to take effect in the US, Canada, Egypt, Indonesia, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam, according to Meta, and also extend to third-party advertisers running campaigns that link to TikTok and other ByteDance properties in those countries.
Photo: Bloomberg
“We don’t have to run ads from a competitor whose goal is to pull people off our apps,” Meta spokesperson Chris Sgro said in an e-mailed statement. “Declining promotional services to a competitor is a normal business practice across industries. We will continue to compete on product quality and user experience.”
Meta and TikTok have competed neck-and-neck for years, even with a key imbalance in that rivalry: TikTok has been able to operate in Meta’s most important market, the US, while Meta has been unable to do so in TikTok’s most crucial market, China. However, that competition took a more heated turn in August after Meta agreed to a historic US$18 billion settlement with US states requiring it to implement new safety features for minors across its Instagram and Facebook apps.
Since then, Meta has been pressuring TikTok and Google’s YouTube to commit to making similar changes, suggesting it cannot solve industrywide child safety problems on its own.
TikTok has remained publicly silent on the matter, ratcheting up the tension between the companies as Meta grapples with what it sees as yet another competitive disadvantage.
Last month, TikTok enacted a number of measures to make it harder to shift from its app to other social platforms, including by eliminating dedicated Instagram links from its users’ profiles. It also rejected ads from Meta demanding that TikTok commit to comparable concessions on child safety.
Soon after the settlement with the state attorneys general, Meta ran ads in top newspapers upping its pressure campaign. Meta executives have also called out TikTok publicly for failing to show up at a recent Office of the Surgeon General event on the harms of excessive screen use, and for dropping out of a national security meeting with the House Select Committee on China to avoid broader scrutiny amid its child safety litigation.
Other consumer tech platforms have also introduced friction between its products and its competitors. The Information reported last month that OpenAI told advertising partners that it would not accept ads for image and audio-generation products that competed with its own.

Thailand’s Queen Suthida has flown a Gripen fighter jet solo for the first time, the royal household revealed yesterday, watched by her husband, King Maha Vajiralongkorn, himself a keen pilot.
The 48-year-old queen took off in a single-seat JAS 39C from a military air base in southern Surat Thani Province on Thursday, footage released by the royal household showed.
The outing followed weeks of simulator training at the base and about 10 hours in a two-seat Gripen, media reports said.
Photo: Royal Household Bureau via AFP
A former Thai Airways flight attendant who married the king in 2019, days before his coronation, Suthida began flying in 2010 and has logged nearly 1,190 hours.
She regularly flies as copilot to the king on royal trips, including landing at Bhutan’s notoriously difficult Paro airport, the reports said.
Thailand already operates a squadron of Gripen C/D fighters made by Sweden’s Saab, and last year signed a deal for three Gripen E jets and one Gripen F worth about US$556 million, with deliveries due by 2030.
After she landed, the king handed the queen a bouquet and pinned a Golden Gripen Order patch on her left arm, which reports said made her Thailand’s first female Gripen pilot.

Coast guard struggling to staff its expanding fleet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

The Coast Guard Administration (CGA) has increased its fleet by 21.3 percent since 2022, but is struggling to recruit personnel to crew the vessels, the Legislative Yuan’s Budget Center said yesterday, as the agency is increasingly tasked with countering Chinese “gray zone” incursions.
The CGA increased its fleet from 169 vessels in 2022 to 205 as of July under two vessel-building projects, but its recruitment shortfall has exceeded 30 percent since 2024 and is approaching 40 percent this year, it said.
The fleet added three patrol vessels and 34 patrol boats, while the number of pelagic patrol vessels decreased by one, the report said.
Photo: I-Hwa Cheng, AFP
The larger fleet means the CGA needs to recruit 136 additional personnel this year and 128 next year, plus 15 people annually from 2028 to 2031, it said.
These staffing requirements do not include personnel needed for the Maritime Rights Protection Coast Guard Vessel Construction Plan (海域維權海巡艦艇建造計畫), it said.
From 2021 to last year, the CGA’s annual personnel requirements ranged from 142 to 306 people, while the number of candidates recruited ranged from 140 to 229, and the number who reported for duty ranged from 121 to 208.
The resulting annual shortfall ranged from 21 to 98 people, or 15 to 34 percent of the recruitment target, the report said.
The CGA’s recruitment target for this year is 344 people, an increase of 202 from 142 in 2021, it said.
As of the end of August, results had yet to be announced for the Civil Service Senior and Junior Examinations and the Grade 3, 4 and 5 Special Examinations for Coast Guard Personnel.
The report said it would continue to monitor the number of candidates selected and how many reported for duty.
However, the rate of shortfall for examinations whose results had been announced was about 40 percent, reinforcing concerns over recruitment, it said.
The CGA should draw on the experiences of the US and Japan and make greater use of technology to support coast guard operations, helping to address personnel shortages and maintain its maritime law enforcement capabilities, the Budget Center said.
In response, the CGA said it commissions the Central Police University and Taiwan Police College to recruit and train personnel for its vessels according to schedule, while replenishing its workforce each year through special examinations and other recruitment channels.
To encourage more young people to join, it has increased six types of allowances, including those for seagoing and hazardous duties, and sought budget approval for additional contract positions to recruit vessel operations personnel, it said.
Staffing levels aboard its vessels comply with regulations, it added.

16:42:46 UTC
01:42:46 KST

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) yesterday condemned a senior diplomat facing corruption charges who has not returned since going on a trip to Japan, and said it is preparing to fire him.
Paul Chen (陳盈連), who is a senior diplomat at the ministry’s Institute of Diplomacy and International Affairs and previously served as director-general of the Taipei Economic and Cultural Office in Guam and Taiwan’s representative to Fiji, was indicted by the Taipei District Prosecutors’ Office in June on charges of breaching the Anti-Corruption Act (貪污治罪條例).
He is accused of fraudulently claiming NT$3.43 million (US$107,608) in rent subsidies while stationed in Los Angeles and embezzling public property during his tenure in Guam.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs
According to a Chinese-language Mirror Media report, Chen pleaded guilty and returned the illicit funds during the investigation.
However, when the Taipei District Court was scheduled to hold a hearing in the middle of last month, it discovered that he had flown to Japan and subsequently traveled to the US.
Chen applied for personal leave to visit Japan from Sept. 12 to 20, but has not returned to Tainan, the ministry said.
The institute made multiple attempts to contact Chen and asked his spouse for assistance, demanding a written explanation by a specified deadline, but received no response, it said.

Education as a tool for preventing drug abuse
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:44 UTC
01:42:44 KST

As the local elections heat up, the issue of drugs has become a focal point of public discussion. Political considerations are inevitably part of election-related debates — but if they can prompt society to re-examine drug policy, it might not be a bad thing. Rather than arguing over who is tougher on drugs, we should instead consider what constitutes the most fundamental anti-drug policy.
Early approaches to drug control focused heavily on enforcement, punishment and incarceration. However, practitioners found that incarceration alone was not enough to address addiction. Consequently, policies have expanded to incorporate management, treatment and harm reduction.
Drug enforcement disrupts supply, addiction treatment helps people recover and harm reduction minimizes harm to individuals and society — each is a vital part of the equation.
However, drug seizures might represent only a fraction of the drugs in circulation, while addiction treatment requires sustained investment of resources.
Beyond asking how we stop drugs from coming in and how we help people quit after they become addicted, we should take the question one step further: How can we ensure that children never want to try drugs in the first place?
Tainan’s experience warrants attention. Since 2021, the Tainan Bureau of Education has promoted drug awareness campaigns. In 2022, Tainan’s anti-drug program — initiated by a senior prosecutor and backed by the city government — mobilized resources from the judiciary, academia, lawyers and civil society organizations to produce 10 short anti-drug videos for elementary and junior-high schools across the city.
The education bureau also scheduled the videos to be shown at the beginning, middle and end of each semester, supplemented by anti-drug educators and realistic teaching aids featuring emerging drugs. Two minutes might seem brief, but when these messages appear repeatedly in children’s daily lives — serving as a constant reminder that drugs should be avoided — they can help develop an internal framework for making sound judgements about drugs.
Even more encouragingly, some elementary schools have begun developing their own anti-drug education programs, showing that anti-drug efforts have begun shifting from being something government-mandated to a voluntary undertaking on the part of schools. If this grassroots momentum continues to spread, it could foster a culture in which schools, teachers, students and families all play a role.
Hating drugs should mean rejecting drugs and the harm they cause, not discriminating against those struggling with addiction. The central government should continue to provide treatment and opportunities for people with substance abuse disorders to reintegrate into society. For children, the focus should be on building psychological resilience and a strong defense against drugs from an early age.
Once drugs infiltrate society, the costs associated with enforcement and treatment are immense. By contrast, starting with everyday education entails relatively limited costs, but could yield lasting preventive benefits.
If “don’t use drugs” can become as natural a habit and value choice for children as observing traffic lights before crossing the street, only then would we have the kind of anti-drug policy that is worth long-term government investment.
Yang Yung-nane is a professor in the Department of Political Science and vice dean of the College of Social Sciences at Cheng Kung University.
Translated by Kyra Gustavsen

Eswatini’s king yesterday pledged to deepen his country’s “enduring friendship” with Taiwan during a return visit to Taipei after President William Lai’s (賴清德) trip to the southern African nation in May that China tried to block.
King Mswati III arrived early yesterday for a state visit until Saturday next week. He is to attend today’s Double Ten National Day celebrations in Taipei.
The trip is his 20th visit to Taiwan and comes as the two countries celebrate 58 years of diplomatic ties.
Photo: Tu Chien-jung, Taipei Times
Eswatini would continue to advocate for Taiwan’s meaningful participation in the UN, the monarch said.
“We deeply value the enduring friendship and cooperation between our two countries, and we look forward to strengthening these bonds for the benefit of our peoples,” the king told a welcoming ceremony on Liberty Square.
Lai said the two sides had always collaborated from a position of trust and were partners who “support each other and grow together.”
Cooperation with Eswatini has expanded under Taiwan’s diplomatic initiative to promote shared prosperity with its allies, with increasingly close exchanges between the two countries’ peoples, Lai said.
In separate remarks, Lai thanked the king for supporting the establishment of a Taiwan Industrial Innovation Park in Eswatini and expressed hope that more Taiwanese companies would invest there, making the country a gateway to African markets.
The two leaders also witnessed the signing of an agreement on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters, which Lai described as a milestone in law enforcement cooperation.
Mswati emphasized turning existing bilateral agreements into practical cooperation and encouraging partnerships between businesses.
“We need to put them into action,” he said, calling for officials to study how the agreements could be implemented effectively.
Mswati’s itinerary includes observing a joint ground-air military exercise alongside Lai, a visit to an agricultural research center and an investment dinner hosted by Minister of Foreign Affairs Lin Chia-lung (林佳龍), the Ministry of Foreign Affairs said.
Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokeswoman Mao Ning (毛寧) said the king was interfering in China’s internal affairs and “ignoring the long-term interests of his people.”
The former Swaziland is one of just 12 small states, mostly in Latin America, the Caribbean and the Pacific, that have formal diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
In April, Taiwan accused China of pressuring three other African countries to block overflight permission for Lai’s aircraft, causing him to postpone a plan to join celebrations of the 40th anniversary of the king’s accession.
That was the first time a Taiwanese president had canceled an entire foreign trip due to denial of airspace access, an apparent new Chinese strategy to curb the nation’s international ties.
Lai made a surprise trip in May, using an “arrive, then announce” approach.

Pig farms urged to heed rules about feed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:41 UTC
01:42:41 KST

Twenty-four cases of illegal transportation of kitchen waste have been identified so far this year, the Central Emergency Operation Center for African swine fever (ASF) said on Thursday, calling on pig farmers to abide by epidemic prevention regulations.
The government continued to clamp down on the illegal use or transportation of kitchen waste by pig farms after the Mid-Autumn Festival break to prevent ASF, the center said.
As of Wednesday, 24 cases of illegal kitchen waste transportation had been detected so far this year, 22 of which resulted in fines, it said.
Photo courtesy of the Pingtung County Government
The two other cases — in Taichung and Miaoli County — are under investigation, it said, adding that penalties would be issued according to the results.
The 24 cases involved 23 pig farms, with one of the farms caught twice, the center said.
Of the 23 pig farms, six had 200 or more pigs, while 11 had 20 to 199, it said.
The six other farms had 19 pigs or fewer, the center said.
That means 17 non-compliant farms had 199 pigs or fewer, accounting for about 73.9 percent of all non-compliant farms, it said.
Eight non-compliant farms had 20 pigs or more without livestock farm registration, accounting for 34.8 percent, the center said.
The center said it would ask local authorities to conduct follow-up inspections and penalize the eight farms for failing to register in accordance with the Animal Industry Act (畜牧法).
Farms that are not big enough to register should be listed for epidemic prevention management, it said.
Registered pig farms with non-compliance records should be listed for high-risk site inspections based on their kitchen waste sources, transportation routes, operational scale and registration status, it said.
Real-time temperature and video monitoring systems have been installed at 243 pig farms that have permission to feed pigs with kitchen waste, the center said.
GPS trackers have also been installed on 453 vehicles to monitor kitchen waste disposal, it said.
The Taichung City Government during a joint inspection on Friday last week found that a farm with 23 pigs in Longjing District (龍井) was having kitchen waste illegally transported to it, the center said.
The farm also illegally mixed pig feed with rice, ham and large bones, it said.
The Taichung Animal Protection and Health Inspection Office has collected blood samples from three pigs at the farm and confirmed that the samples tested negative for ASF, the center said, adding that a 15-day movement ban has been imposed on the farm.
Since the beginning of this year, transporting kitchen waste to pig farms without prior approval has been subject to a fine of NT$200,000 (US$6,275) for the first offense, NT$500,000 for the second offense, and NT$1 million for the third offense and each subsequent offense as stipulated in revised penalty guidelines issued pursuant to the Act on the Prevention and Control of Infectious Animal Diseases (動物傳染病防治條例), it said.
Farms that feed pigs kitchen waste without prior approval would face fines of NT$200,000 for the first offense and increased fines for subsequent offenses, capped at NT$3 million, as stipulated by penalty guidelines for the Feed Control Act (飼料管理法), the center said.
Those who illegally transport kitchen waste to a pig farm and illegally feed it to pigs would be fined according to the two pieces of legislation, or NT$400,000 for the first offense up to a maximum of NT$4 million for subsequent offenses, it said.

Last month, a young woman filed a lawsuit against Cornell University, alleging that two years ago the university had failed to protect her from being raped by seven men at a fraternity house near the university campus. She also sued the fraternity.
The lawsuit has plunged the university into a crisis and invited criticism of the district attorney, Matthew Van Houten, who decided there was not enough evidence to bring criminal charges against the seven men.
At this point, we can only guess why neither Cornell nor Van Houten did more in response to the young woman’s allegations. But there is little question that we are living through a time when men feel some impunity when it comes to attacking women.
Illustration: Louise Ting
Violence against women is hardly new. Nor is the impunity that some men feel in attacking them.
However, the man now occupying the White House has contributed to a lower and more dangerous standard for what men can do to women with impunity.
US President Donald Trump was found in civil court to have sexually abused the writer E. Jean Carroll. He has repeatedly insulted the physical appearance of female journalists, politicians and public figures. He was caught on a hot microphone boasting about using his fame to forcefully kiss and grope women without consent, stating that being a star allows men to “do anything” and “grab ’em by the pussy.”
When women have spoken out against him, Trump has resorted to smear campaigns, as he did with Carroll, Stormy Daniels and former US secretary of state Hillary Rodham Clinton. When women have stood up to him, he has exploded in anger against them, as he did with Fox News anchor Megyn Kelly, TV talk-show host Rosie O’Donnell, former US vice president Kamala Harris and US Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez.
His administration is the most belligerently misogynistic of any in memory. It has openly equated testosterone levels to strength, conducted a cage match on the White House lawn as part of its celebration of the US’ 250th anniversary, fired senior female officials, and accused the Democratic party of being run by “a bunch of childless cat ladies.”
Nor do I think it irrelevant that Trump, US Vice President J.D. Vance and Trump’s erstwhile pal Elon Musk inhabit what has been termed the “manosphere” — a place where the main events are dominance and submission. The whole point is to humiliate weak men and to subjugate women.
An implicit promise of the 2024 Trump campaign was to restore patriarchy to the US. Fifty-four percent of men supported Trump in that year’s election.
After Trump’s re-election, sexist and abusive attacks on women — such as “your body, my choice” and “get back in the kitchen” — surged across social media, according to an analysis from the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.
A remarkable number of Trump’s cronies are sexual harassers and predators. Trump was introduced at the Republican national convention by Ultimate Fighting Championship chief executive Dana White, who was once caught on tape slapping his wife in a nightclub.
Vance has claimed men in the US are “suppressed” in their masculinity.
Before becoming Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth paid off a woman who accused him of sexual assault. (Hegseth’s own mother accused him of abusing women, though she later disavowed her words. He has denied the claims.) And as secretary, Hegseth has championed “high-T” men and blocked promotions of female officers.
One of Musk’s companies, SpaceX, reportedly paid US$250,000 to a flight attendant who said Musk had exposed himself to her, though he denies the allegation. In a lawsuit filed last year, former employees accused him of “treating women as sexual objects to be evaluated on their bra size.”
After kissing Trump’s derriere, Mark Zuckerberg, the third-richest person in the US, called for more “masculine energy” because the corporate world was becoming “culturally neutered”. He told podcaster Joe Rogan: “Having a culture that celebrates the aggression a bit more has its own merits that are really positive.”
The Trump regime celebrated toxic masculinity by smoothing the way for Andrew and Tristan Tate to be released from Romania to the US. The Tate brothers had been accused of luring women to Romania and then forcing them to work as pornographic webcam performers. Britain is also investigating the Tate brothers for rape and human trafficking. US marshals arrested the Tate brothers in Miami on 18 July, following an extradition request from the UK. They have denied all charges.)
“I’m a Trump fan because I’m a man,” Tate has said. “You have to support Trump if you’re a man.”
Trump’s authoritarian manosphere is organized around a hierarchy topped by heroic male warriors. Winning is all about getting other males to submit to the dominant male. Women are relegated to subservient roles.
Anything that challenges the traditional heroic male roles of protector, provider and controller of the family is considered a threat to the social order. LGBTQ+ people are believed to weaken the heroic male. Hence, Trump’s executive order declaring that the US government will recognize only a person’s sex assigned at birth, limit the definition of a “male” or “female” to their reproductive cells, and potentially withhold federal funding from programs that acknowledge transgender people or “gender ideology”.
I do not want to oversimplify a complex social phenomenon or engage in the same kind of gender stereotypes that the manosphere promotes. Male domination is hardly the only characteristic that unites Trump, Vance, Hegseth, Kennedy, Musk and the tech bros. Misogyny is not unique to authoritarian men.
Nor do I presume to know what happened at the Cornell fraternity house two years ago. But I do not think it unreasonable to see it related to a climate of distrust bordering on hate, fostered by Trump and his administration against people who seem weak or feminine.

The Lancet yesterday published Taiwan’s hepatitis C elimination strategy, which the Health Promotion Administration (HPA) said marked international recognition of the national effort to suppress the disease.
Minister of Health and Welfare Shih Chung-liang (石崇良), Deputy Minister of Health and Welfare Chuang Jen-hsiang (莊人祥) and HPA Director-General Shen Ching-fen (沈靜芬) coauthored the study, which the journal published online as a letter in its correspondence section.
The publication follows an announcement by the Ministry of Health and Welfare late last year that Taiwan had reached its elimination goals ahead of schedule following a 10-year effort, the HPA said.
Photo: CNA
The WHO’s Western Pacific branch has confirmed receiving Taiwan’s hepatitis C study and thanked the nation for its participation in the global public health campaign against the disease, HPA Cancer Prevention and Control Division Director Hsieh Pei-chun (謝佩君) said.
The report is still undergoing internal review by the regional office and it remains unclear when the official results would be released, Hsieh said.
Taiwan had identified an estimated 92.4 percent of people with chronic hepatitis C by December last year and reported a 92.7 percent treatment rate among those diagnosed, exceeding the WHO’s diagnosis and treatment targets and Path to Elimination gold-tier benchmarks, which are achieving a 90 percent diagnosis rate and an 80 percent treatment rate by 2030, the HPA said.
The HPA since September 2020 has offered free hepatitis B and C screenings for people aged 45 to 79 and expanded eligibility to include people aged 39 to 79 in August last year, it said.
The National Health Insurance Administration has offered coverage for oral hepatitis C drugs since 2017 and waived all requirements related to hepatic fibrosis severity to encourage early treatment, the HPA said.
Taiwan achieved a 95 percent hepatitis C treatment rate across all high-risk groups, including people undergoing dialysis or methadone treatment, as well as people with HIV, while the national harm mitigation program provides sterilized needles, it said.
It has implemented rigorous standards to ensure blood supply and medical needles are not contaminated by the virus, the HPA said.
Taiwan is expanding its healthcare resources in mountainous regions, as well as improving the integration of national, local and community-level care, and creating a centralized monitoring network for health to support effective policy, it said.
It has also rolled out a hospital monitoring program to track long-term mortality trends associated with chronic liver disease and cirrhosis caused by hepatitis B and C, it said.
The measures have contributed to reductions in liver cancer incidence and mortality figures in the past few years, the HPA added.

Environmental research academy honored by ARTDO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:42:35 UTC
01:42:35 KST

The National Environmental Research Academy won this year’s Human Resource Development Excellence Award from Manila-based ARTDO International, the academy said yesterday.
The award is the first major international recognition of training of environmental personnel in Taiwan since programs were first launched in 1991, the academy said.
Academy president Chang Shun-chin (張順欽) said that it has been providing professional environmental certification training for more than three decades.
Photo courtesy of the Ministry of Environment via CNA
The training includes 22 programs, which have among them issued about 280,000 certificates since they began, Chang said.
The Human Resource Development Excellence Award went to the Green Human Resource Development Strategy, which was developed based on the academy’s rich experience in talent training, he said.
It integrated the academy’s environmental protection training management system by introducing batch issuance, digital signatures and QR code verification mechanism, he said.
That facilitated a complete digital service process from training and testing to certification, he added.
ARTDO International said that the academy won due to its contributions to human resource development through digital transformation and environmental sustainability.
With the strategy, the academy implemented a secure, integrated electronic certification platform, it said.
The platform issued more than 10,000 digital certificates, “significantly improving service delivery, saving applicants more than 17,000 cumulative waiting days, reducing administrative burden, lowering public expenditure, and promoting environmental sustainability through reduced paper consumption and carbon emissions,” it said.
Applications for electronic certificates accounted for about 60 percent of all certificate applications since digital issuance began last year, Chang said.
Digital certification saves time for trainees and companies seeking to hire talent, he said.
Companies recruiting environmental personnel can check applicants’ training backgrounds documented in the academy’s database by scanning the QR code printed on their certificate, he said.
ARTDO International was established in 1974 as the Asian Regional Training and Development Organization, with the Taipei-based Chinese Society for Training and Development as one of the founding members, the academy said.
Its members include government agencies, educational institutions, multinational corporations and human resources experts from more than 30 areas, including the UK, New Zealand, Australia, the Middle East and the Asia-Pacific region, it said.
This year’s awards ceremony was held at the Asian Regional Training and Development Organization’s 53rd international conference in Sabah, Malaysia, on Sept. 7, the academy said, adding that Taiwan hosted three of the conferences in 1992, 2011 and 2018.

====================================================================================================

New Procedure Lets Maintainers See ‘Blind Spot’ in F-16 Engine That Caused Crashes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:41:38 UTC
01:41:38 KST

The Air Force has figured out a way for maintainers to inspect what had been a “blind spot” in F-16 engines, after problems in that area led to the catastrophic crashes of two jets in recent years.
A spokesperson for the Air Force Life Cycle Management Center confirmed the new procedure to Air & Space Forces Magazine last month. Task & Purpose first reported the development.
AFLCMC’s propulsion directorate developed the new process, which does not require any modifications to the engine or new equipment, the spokesperson added. The inspections is meant specifically for Pratt & Whitney F100 engine models—some F-16s are powered by GE Aerospace F110 models.
The F100 engine consists of 13 “stages,” each with variable vanes and compressor blades. Air flows through the stages, which rotate to accelerate, compress, and then regulate the airflow before releasing it into the engine’s combustion chamber. If a vane is turned or misaligned, however, it creates “abnormal aerodynamic forces” and “irregular wake patterns” that put stress on the compressor blades in the following stages, according to Air Force reports. That can lead to vanes or blades cracking or breaking, causing the entire engine to fail.
Maintainers can inspect many of the F100 engine’s stages using a borescope—a camera mounted on a flexible tube. There are even borescope ports for them to do so. But the fourth and especially the fifth stages are hard to reach. Before the development of this new inspection process, the Air Force said it was impossible for maintainers to inspect them without completely disassembling the engine, something only done at depots and not while the engine is installed on the aircraft.
This blind spot proved dangerous. An F-16 crashed near Holloman Air Force Base, N.M., in April 2024, and another jet, belonging to the U.S. Air Force Thunderbirds, crashed in the California desert in December 2025. Subsequent investigations determined that in both cases, the F-16s’ engines had failed because of misaligned vanes in the fifth stage.
The pilots in both crashes were able to safely eject, but both jets were completely destroyed and the total damages exceeded $54 million.
Notably, both F-16 engines in question had experienced foreign object debris, or FOD, events in the years prior to the crashes. In both cases, maintainers noted damage to early stages of the inlet fan but found no issues with the fourth, seventh, or eighth stages—and the F-16’s technical orders did not require maintainers to remove and disassemble the engine core to inspect the fifth and sixth stages after a FOD event if no damage is found in the surrounding stages.
While investigators were unable to conclusively say if the FOD events led to the vanes becoming misaligned, the Air Force has now updated its technical orders to require the new inspection procedure to check the fifth stage of the engine after every FOD event.
“Additionally, the program office has worked with Pratt & Whitney to redesign the vane arm to be more impact resistant. The new design is qualified, on order, and will be installed via forced retrofit as soon as available,” the AFLCMC spokesperson said.

Diyar Güldoğan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
 UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres condemned US sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, warning that the measures could undermine its work and deal "a serious blow" to international efforts to ensure accountability for grave crimes. 
"Today's decision marks a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar. Accountability for international crimes and delivery of justice to victims are central to our global commitment to peace, security, human rights and fundamental freedoms," said a statement issued by his spokesperson, Stephane Dujarric. 
Guterres is "deeply alarmed" by the expected impact of the sanctions on the court as a whole, particularly its ability to carry out its mandate, the statement said. 
The UN chief also reiterated his support for the court's independence and called on countries to uphold their obligations under international law. 
US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, hours after Navi Pillay, a former ICC judge and UN human rights chief, was awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. 
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court," Rubio said in a statement. 
Rubio said Washington had deferred the designation "in hopes that the ICC would change course or would otherwise be restrained by States Parties," but neither had "taken meaningful steps to address our concerns." 
Guterres reiterates his "unwavering support" for the independence of the Court and its officials, Dujarric said.  
"The Secretary-General calls upon all States to uphold their commitments under international law and to support efforts aimed at ensuring accountability for the most serious crimes of concern to the international community," he added.  
The UN remains committed to cooperating with the ICC in accordance with the Relationship Agreement between the UN and the ICC, Dujarric said.

Why Delhi Police denied permission

The restriction covers all mobile internet technologies, while services elsewhere in Delhi are expected to remain unaffected.Entry and exit gates at 57 metro stations will remain closed from 9pm on Friday until further notice. Interchange facilities will continue at affected stations, except New Delhi metro station. Among the stations affected are Rajiv Chowk, Central Secretariat, Patel Chowk, Kashmere Gate, Janpath, Mandi House, ITO and Supreme Court.Several train services scheduled to arrive at or depart from New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations between 4am and 2pm on Saturday have also been reported cancelled.Other preventive measures include:
Deployment across Central Delhi: The New Delhi district has been divided into 20 zones, each to be monitored by senior police officers. Additional women personnel from Uttar Pradesh and Haryana have also been called in.
Surveillance and monitoring: Police will use facial recognition systems, additional CCTV cameras, rooftop spotters and drones. More than 200 content creators are reportedly under scrutiny over online mobilisation linked to the protest.
Checks across the capital: Police have stepped up surveillance at borders, hotels, guest houses, railway stations, bus terminals and airport approach roads. Vehicle restrictions in New Delhi may also be imposed depending on the security assessment.
Detention arrangements: Six designated centres, including Chhatrasal Stadium, Rajiv Gandhi Stadium and Yamuna Sports Complex, have been identified to hold detained protesters.
Liquor shops across Delhi have also been ordered to remain closed on October 9 and 10 as a preventive measure.
Police told to exercise restraint
During a briefing, the police commissioner instructed personnel not to react to provocative behaviour or engage in unnecessary verbal confrontations. Officials were also warned against situations in which their interactions with protesters could be recorded and circulated online.
Unlike the deployment during the INDIA bloc protest, police teams have now been authorised to carry lathis or batons. CAPF units have been instructed not to issue weapons for the deployment, with letters sent to the concerned directorates regarding the arrangements.Senior officers will remain available on the ground to respond to developments. Police have also said that any proposal to shift the demonstration to Ramlila Maidan would require a separate application and a decision by the authorities.

DHS defends ICE shooting in NYC, says officers believed they were in danger
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:36:31 UTC
01:36:31 KST

DHS defends ICE shooting in NYC, says officers believed they were in danger
The shooting prompted protests in New York City as officials defended ICE and Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the incident.
The United States Department of Homeland Security has defended Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) shooting of a man in New York City while his child was present. Federal officials used the incident to criticise sanctuary-city policies that limit cooperation with federal immigration authorities.
New York officials have condemned the shooting and have called for ICE to end its operations in the city.
The shooting took place on Thursday afternoon when ICE officers attempted to arrest a man identified by New York City police as Oscar Belgal.
Homeland Security officials gave their account of the incident on Friday during a news conference, saying that Belgal refused to exit his car when approached by officers and then accelerated, striking two ICE vehicles.
They said officers then opened fire, grazing Belgal’s neck while his five-year-old child was in the back seat.
According to Homeland Security officials, Belgal received first aid and was taken to hospital before being transferred to a secure detention facility outside New York state. They did not disclose where Belgal is being held.
Department of Homeland Security (DHS) Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the agents did not know the child was inside the vehicle when they fired.
ICE senior official Marcos Charles said agents had attempted to arrest Belgal as part of an investigation into suspected gang involvement in an earlier shooting of a US Customs and Border Protection officer.
According to US officials, Belgal is an undocumented migrant from the Dominican Republic who had previously evaded arrest and received a five-year sentence for grand larceny in April 2025.
“[Belgal] was a thug,” Mullin said at the Friday news conference. “The absolute worst of the worst.”
Mullin confirmed that officers were wearing body cameras but the footage has not been made public. New York City police released bodycam footage on Friday of police officers on the scene who had responded to a 911 call about the incident.
In other violent incidents involving federal immigration officers, video evidence has contradicted initial accounts from ICE and Homeland Security officials, including in Minneapolis, where footage of the fatal shootings of Alex Pretti and Renee Good challenged federal officials’ descriptions of the encounters.
The latest shooting prompted protests on Thursday night in the Bronx, where the shooting took place, with demonstrators condemning ICE and calling for the agency to be abolished. Tensions rose after NYPD officers clashed with some of the protesters.
New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani condemned the shooting and said he had called US President Donald Trump to demand an end to ICE enforcement in the city.
Speaking to reporters late on Thursday at the scene of the shooting, Mamdani said he had tried unsuccessfully to secure Belgal’s release in phone calls with Trump and Mullin.
“These actions are making the city less safe,” Mamdani said. “ICE is rotten to its core.”
Mullin accused Mamdani of prioritising politics over public safety and said Trump had offered to transfer Belgal to New York police custody if they pursued charges. Mullin said Mamdani refused this offer.

Yemen urges UN Security Council to take action against Houthis

09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Yemen's government urged the UN Security Council on Friday to take decisive action against the Houthis, accusing the group of escalating attacks, recruiting children and displacing civilians while threatening regional security.
"Today's session is held at a time when we are witnessing ongoing escalation from the terrorist Houthi militias," Yemen's permanent representative to the UN, Abdullah Ali Fadhel Al-Saadi, told the council.
He said the escalation threatened the lives of Yemenis, the security of neighboring countries and the region, and one of the world's most important waterways.
Al-Saadi cited Yemeni government figures indicating that more than 100 children had died in September alone.
He also accused the Houthis of continuing to recruit children and deploy them to front-line positions. He stressed that children should be attending school and living with their families rather than being drawn into fighting.
"The humanitarian cost of this escalation uncovers the true nature of the project we are facing today," Al-Saadi said.
The envoy said Houthi attacks in recent weeks had forced thousands of Yemenis to flee their homes, pushing the number of internally displaced people above 200,000.
Many families had been displaced for a third or fourth time, he added.
Al-Saadi also reported that approximately 3,000 people had fled to Djibouti and said those affected urgently needed humanitarian assistance.
He accused the Houthis of targeting residential neighborhoods, markets, schools, camps housing displaced people and other civilian infrastructure.
 
- 'Threat is no longer an internal Yemeni affair'
"The threat of the Houthis is no longer an internal Yemeni affair that can be contained within our borders," Al-Saadi said.
"It is threatening freedom of navigation. This is not a future possibility. It is a reality that is expanding if they continue to enjoy impunity."
The envoy urged the Security Council to adopt a "clear decision" holding the Houthis responsible for the escalation and ensuring the implementation of existing council resolutions.
He called for practical measures to restrict funding, smuggling networks and transfers of weapons, technology and technical expertise to the group.
Al-Saadi also urged international action against those supporting the Houthis, specifically accusing Iran of backing the group.
He praised Saudi Arabia for providing a "practical example of solidarity" with Yemen and called on international partners to increase economic and humanitarian support for the government.
"In conclusion, a real peace is the peace that ends the coup and that restores the control of state institutions over our national territory," he said.
Al-Saadi said restoring state authority was essential to protecting citizens' rights, freedom and dignity and preventing Yemen from becoming a threat to regional and international peace and security.

Background

Why EU sanctions have missed company behind Russia's tank industry?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:34:56 UTC
01:34:56 KST

Why have EU sanctions missed the company behind Russia’s tank industry?
Russian tanks move during the "Zapad-2025" (West-2025) joint Russian-Belarusian military drills at a training ground near Borisov, Belarus, on Sept. 15, 2025. (Olesya Kurpyayeva / AFP via Getty Images)
Nezir Sinani
Executive director of the B4Ukraine Coalition
With more than four years of full-scale war and 12 years since Russia first invaded Ukraine, it seems the European Union has developed an extensive arsenal of tools to sanction Moscow, but one problem appears to persist: the visibility problem.
Consider two companies that share a name.
The first is Research and Production Corporation Uralvagonzavod in Nizhny Tagil, Russia's only tank manufacturer. It has been under EU sanctions since March 2022 for supplying the T-72B3 tanks used against Ukraine. Its EU entry names its owner: Rostec, Russia's state defense conglomerate.
The second is Moscow-registered Concern Uralvagonzavod. Since 2020, Russia's company register has listed it as the tank plant's sole executive body, or basically the entity running it. Its chief executive, Aleksandr Potapov, is on the EU sanctions list. Its Moscow address appears in the EU's export-control entry for the plant. When listing a Rostec executive in June 2026, the Council of the EU itself described the Concern as "subject to Union restrictive measures."
Yet the Concern is not named on any EU sanctions list.
"At that pace, the gap would probably close by year 2030 — a remarkably leisurely timetable for a sanctions regime meant to constrain a war already underway."
That matters because of how EU sanctions reach beyond the names on the page. A listing does two things: it freezes a company's assets in the EU and, more importantly for a Russian arms maker with little to freeze in Europe, it bars anyone in the EU from making funds or economic resources available to it: no payments, no supplies, no contracts.
It has long been the law that these prohibitions also cover entities owned or controlled by a listed person. The Council's Best Practices clarified that a stake of 50% or more counts as ownership and that holdings of several listed shareholders are added together.
In March 2026, in EM System (C-84/24), the Court of Justice confirmed that such a stake creates a presumption of ownership or control. One that can be rebutted, but that is the starting point.
The rule, however, is built to reach downwards — to the companies a sanctioned entity owns or controls, yet whether it reaches the company that runs a sanctioned factory is not clear.
The Concern may still be off-limits through a different and less visible route.
Rostec itself is not under an EU asset freeze. It sits instead on a separate list, Annex XIX of Regulation 833/2014, whose ban on transactions extends to companies Rostec owns by more than 50%. Whether that ban covers the Concern, or any other Rostec subsidiary, depends on ownership percentages that nobody outside Russia can check.
Uralvagonzavod's own latest available annual report, dated Aug. 20, 2020, declines to disclose its shareholders, citing a 2019 Russian government resolution that allows companies to withhold such information.
A European supplier is therefore asked to apply an ownership test to data Moscow has made secret — and, if it gets the answer wrong, it has a ready defense: there was no way to know.
The stakes extend beyond one tank maker.
Ukraine's military intelligence service maintains a structure map tracking 553 entities affiliated with Rostec. Of those, 145 (26%) are subject to some form of EU restrictive measure.
Seven of Rostec's eight top-level holding companies — including Russian Helicopters, the Kalashnikov Concern, Technodinamika, High Precision Systems, United Aircraft Corporation, and United Engine Corporation — are individually sanctioned.
An independent investigation by the Independent Anti-Corruption Commission (NAKO), working from a separate dataset of 482 Rostec-linked entities, reached a similar figure: 23%.
The Uralvagonzavod group shows that gap up close. Ukrainian intelligence attributes 32 subsidiaries to it, with 21 not being named on any EU list.
Many are support businesses — catering, workwear, and a hotel, but the unnamed include Chelyabinsk Tractor Plant–Uraltrak, which Ukrainian intelligence identifies as the main producer of engines for T-72, T-90M, and T-14 tanks; a research institute for tracked military vehicles; an armored-vehicle repair plant working under defense ministry contracts; and the design bureau behind the flatcars that carry T-90M tanks.
The EU has added four of the group's companies since 2024. At that pace, the gap would probably close by year 2030 — a remarkably leisurely timetable for a sanctions regime meant to constrain a war already underway.
Each new sanctions package is a negotiated political act, yet ownership rules require no negotiation: they are already the law. They only work, however, if those expected to apply them can see what they are applying them to.
For a workable alternative, Europeans can simply look across the Atlantic. The U.S. Commerce Department's Entity List lets officials add dozens of Rostec-linked companies to an export-control regime without the political weight of a full sanctions designation — a faster instrument used precisely because full designations are slow.
The EU has comparable tools, but it does not use them visibly enough to be trusted by outside observers.
Three steps would fix this.
First, publish what the authorities already know: where the Commission or national competent authorities have assessed that an unlisted entity is owned or controlled by a sanctioned Rostec company, say so — and where Russia withholds the ownership data needed to make that call, treat the secrecy itself as a reason to list the entity by name.
Second, name the companies that run sanctioned plants: management companies such as Concern Uralvagonzavod sit above the factories they control, where the ownership rule offers no transparency, and should be designated directly.
Third, when the next package is drafted, prioritize the defense-critical subsidiaries still missing from the list — starting with the plant that builds Russia's tank engines.
By doing so, the EU can address the contradiction of sanctioning the factory that builds Russia’s tanks while forgetting about the one that actually runs it.
Editor's note: The opinions expressed in the op-ed section are those of the authors and do not purport to reflect the views of the Kyiv Independent.

US sanctions against International Criminal Court draw opposition as countries warn of impact on its work
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:34:51 UTC
01:34:51 KST

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Six European countries, Canada and Japan on Friday expressed regret over the US announcement of sanctions against the International Criminal Court (ICC), warning that the measures could significantly affect its operations, staff and their families.
In a joint statement, the foreign ministers of Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, the Netherlands and the UK, along with their Canadian and Japanese counterparts, said they "strongly disagree" with Washington's announcement.
"We, the undersigned States Parties to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court (ICC), reaffirm our continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC," the statement said.
The ministers welcomed the court's preparations to respond to potential sanctions, saying the measures would help it continue carrying out its mandate under the Rome Statute.
"Nevertheless, if put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," they warned.
The eight countries also pledged to pursue "constructive and inclusive dialogue" with countries that are not parties to the Rome Statute ahead of the Assembly of States Parties scheduled for December.
"We will continue to work together to support the Court's vital work, uphold the rules-based international system, and advance accountability," the statement said.

====================================================================================================

Ryanair lashes out at Air France and Lufthansa over ownership probe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:34:26 UTC
01:34:26 KST

Michael O'Leary, group CEO of low cost airline Ryanair, takes part in a press conference in London on September 23, 2026. | Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images
BRUSSELS — Ryanair has accused rivals Lufthansa and Air France-KLM of trying to ground the low-cost carrier by alleging that its ownership structure violates EU rules.
The two legacy airlines, which face growing competition from budget carriers, belong to the European Network Airlines Association, a lobby group that has filed a legal challenge over Ryanair's share ownership.
“Now they're in the Irish High Court seeking to have our license suspended and Ryanair grounded,” Ryanair CEO Michael O’Leary said Thursday in Brussels.
Advertisement
The association confirmed to POLITICO that it has spent months urging EU and Irish aviation authorities to investigate whether Ryanair complies with the bloc’s ownership and control rules.
Under those rules, airlines must be majority-owned and effectively controlled by EU nationals or entities to hold an EU operating license. ENAA argues that Ryanair no longer meets those requirements, pointing to the airline’s March announcement that only 30% of its shares are held by EU nationals. O'Leary, an Irish citizen, holds 4% of the stock.
When the Irish Aviation Authority seemed “reluctant to engage on the matter,” ENAA took the matter to court. If Ryanair loses the case, it could be forced to change its ownership structure. The carrier's operating license would only be suspended if it does not comply with the verdict.
An aircraft operated by Irish low cost airline Ryanair makes its way past BER airport's control tower in Schoenefeld on June 29, 2026. | John Macdougall/AFP via Getty Images
Ryanair has rejected the allegations, arguing that its non-EU shareholders do not have voting rights, which means the airline is under EU control.
In an emailed statement, Ryanair accused its rivals of attempting “to restrict competition and choice for EU air travel” by challenging its operating license.
Grounding risk seen as remote
Augusto Viansson Ponte, a London-based director at Alton Aviation Consultancy, doubted that the legal case would be easily dismissed, but also said it was unlikely that Ryanair would lose its operating license.
Advertisement
“ENAA’s request is sufficiently well-founded to justify examination, but it is way too early to say that Ryanair is violating the rules,” he said.
Regardless of the legal outcome, Viansson Ponte said that a "likely first step would be corrective measures, not immediate grounding."
Even if the court rules against the budget airline, Ryanair would have several options to address any compliance problems, the analyst said.
“Ryanair could restrict non-EU [share] purchases, facilitate transfers of shares to EU investors, implement targeted share buybacks or restructure its licensed subsidiaries for example,” he said, adding that the process “should be manageable” for the airline.
Enemies in court, friends in Brussels
Despite their spat, Ryanair, Lufthansa and Air France-KLM all belong to the Brussels-based Airlines for Europe (A4E) lobby, and all are pushing for a reform of the Air Services Regulation, which sets the rules for operating in the EU, including ownership and control.
The lobby’s members jointly support providing “more flexibility … and tackle the risks linked to this change,” they said in feedback to the Commission.
Advertisement
“The potential way forward is to allow institutional investors from selected third countries to hold a limited percentage of shares … which would count towards the EU share of ownership,” the joint position adds.
If EU lawmakers adopt the proposal, “that would allow a greater access to liquidity in those markets for airlines,” said easyJet CEO Kenton Jarvis, whose company is set to be acquired by U.S. investment firm Apollo.
However, the legal battle between the Irish budget airline and legacy carriers may fracture A4E. O’Leary threatened on Thursday at an A4E press conference to leave the lobby group unless the legal case is dropped by the end of the year.
A4E later acknowledged that its members “may have differing views on certain issues, [but] we share a common interest in advancing our collective work for the benefit of European passengers, particularly in an increasingly complex and costly regulatory environment.”
Neither Lufthansa nor Air France-KLM commented on O'Leary's threat to leave A4E.

‘A Ceuta-style surge is possible’: Border tensions on NATO’s eastern flank
