Paramount-Warner Bros. merger puts Ellison’s Israel ties, political pressure in spotlight
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:07:23 UTC
01:07:23 KST

Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery has brought CNN and CBS News under common ownership, with financial backer Larry Ellison’s support for Israel and former British Prime Minister Tony Blair’s appointment as an adviser adding political dimensions to the media merger.
The transaction closed on Oct. 6 following the required regulatory approvals, according to the company’s completion announcement.
The combined company, named Skydance, brings together Paramount and Warner Bros. studios, HBO, Paramount+, CNN, CBS News and major sports broadcasting assets.
The agreement announced in February valued Warner Bros. Discovery’s equity at approximately $81 billion and its enterprise value, including debt, at $110 billion.
The financing plan included $47 billion in new shares backed by committed investment from the Ellison family and RedBird Capital Partners, according to a company filing. 
Trump’s pressure on Netflix
The bidding contest unfolded alongside public pressure from US President Donald Trump on rival bidder Netflix.
In a February Truth Social post, preserved in an online archive, Trump demanded that Netflix dismiss board member Susan Rice, a former senior official in Democratic administrations, or “pay the consequences.”
The post also shared criticism from activist Laura Loomer urging Trump to block Netflix’s proposed Warner Bros. transaction.
Netflix subsequently announced on Feb. 26 that it would not match Paramount’s higher offer.
Co-chief executives Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters said the price required made the acquisition “no longer financially attractive.” The company attributed its withdrawal to the terms of the deal, without citing Trump’s pressure. 
Ellison’s support for Israeli soldiers
Larry Ellison, the Jewish-American co-founder of Oracle and father of Skydance chairman and chief executive David Ellison, has made substantial financial contributions supporting Israeli soldiers. His family background is documented by the Jewish Virtual Library.
At a November 2017 gala, he gave $16.6 million to Friends of the Israel Defense Forces, which was the organization’s largest single gift at the time, according to Jewish Telegraphic Agency reporting citing the organizers.
The donation was designated for welfare facilities at a training campus for mixed-gender infantry units.
“We should do all we can to show these heroic soldiers that they are not alone,” Ellison said at the event. 
Blair’s Gaza role and controversies
Skydance’s Oct. 6 board announcement named Blair as a board adviser acting in a personal capacity, with a role in shaping strategic priorities. The announcement did not assign him an editorial position.
Blair also holds responsibilities concerning Gaza. A Jan. 16 White House statement named him to the founding Executive Board of Trump’s Board of Peace and the Gaza Executive Board, whose responsibilities include governance, reconstruction and financing.
His involvement in Gaza planning has previously prompted Palestinian objections.
On Jan. 1, 2024, the Palestinian presidency rejected reported efforts to assign Blair a role in relocating Palestinians from Gaza and declared him unwelcome in Palestinian territories, according to an official statement carried by Palestine News and Information Agency (WAFA).
In July 2025, the Financial Times reported that two institute staff members participated in discussions on a Gaza redevelopment project involving Boston Consulting Group consultants and Israeli businessmen.
The institute said it had never authored, developed or endorsed a proposal to relocate Gazans, according to the report.
Blair subsequently endorsed Trump’s September 2025 Gaza plan in a public statement, describing it as “bold and intelligent.”
In an April 28 Security Council briefing, he advocated a transitional period of international support and disarmament arrangements acceptable to Israel, alongside reconstruction and eventual Palestinian self-government.
His institute’s relationship with Larry Ellison predates the media appointment. Its 2021 financial review described a philanthropic partnership with the Larry Ellison Foundation supporting digital infrastructure initiatives.  
Binding editorial safeguards
The merger includes specific obligations concerning CNN and CBS News.
Under a settlement with 12 state attorneys general, the company must establish a five-member News Editorial Independence Board within 180 days of closing, according to its Sept. 30 regulatory filing.
The board will comprise established journalists, set guiding editorial principles and resolve specified disputes concerning bias, fairness and compliance with those principles.
David Ellison has also pledged noninterference.
“We believe in editorial independence and we will never interfere,” he said, according to CNN’s Oct. 6 broadcast transcript.
CNN also reported that Ellison supported its legal challenge against the Trump administration over press access.

In Russia, they want to raise the upper age limit for military service for women: details of the bill
Kyiv • UNN
The bill proposes raising the upper age limit for women’s service from 45 to 50. The changes also concern the period of time spent in the reserve.
The Russian authorities have proposed raising the maximum age for women’s military service. The relevant draft law has been published in the State Duma’s database, reports UNN.
Details
The draft law proposes raising the maximum age for women to remain in military service from 45 to 50, as well as extending the reserve service age limits for female officers and women with other ranks: from 50 to 55 and from 45 to 50, respectively.
The authors of the draft law state in its explanatory note that amid the Russian-Ukrainian war, the majority of personnel in medical units are female service members, "including those who have reached (are reaching) the maximum age for remaining in military service."
The draft law also states that the current maximum age for remaining in military service does not always allow individuals to complete the required period of service to qualify for a pension and other support measures.
Recall
In Russia, conscripts are increasingly facing a ban on traveling abroad, with restrictions in some cases appearing directly during border control.

Khader, whom El Adeb says is 17, was taken into custody in Jordan on Sept 29 and is cooperating with the bureau’s investigation, people familiar with the matter have told Reuters. Attempts by Reuters to reach Khader, members of his family or representatives for him have been unsuccessful.
Reuters has spoken to a handful of former associates of Khader - whose alleged hacker nickname was Rey - including El Adeb, who is better known under his old hacker nickname, Pryx.
The two were publicly known members of the cybercrime group Hellcat, which emerged in 2024 and took responsibility for several attention-grabbing hacks, including a break-in at France’s Schneider Electric, where the hackers demanded US$125,000 (S$160,000) worth of baguettes as ransom.
Rey and Pryx were identified as Khader and El Adeb by the Israeli cybersecurity research firm Kela in a report circulated in March 2025 and reviewed by Reuters. The report tied Pryx to El Adeb in part by showing that Pryx’s criminal ventures shared infrastructure, software tools and communication channels with a security-focused website called Pato, whose guide once listed El Adeb as its author.
Reuters reached El Adeb through an email address listed in Kela’s report. In a video interview from the Gulf emirate of Ras Al Khaimah, El Adeb acknowledged being Pryx and identified Khader as Rey, but he said that, unlike his friend, he had put his cybercrime days behind him.
El Adeb, who chain-smoked the Emirati cigarette brand Manchester Red through the hour-long interview, said he quit cybercrime before he turned 18 and is now setting up a cybersecurity business called VulOne with a cofounder.
“I’m clean now,” he said.
El Adeb said he was born in Tunisia and that his parents moved to the United Arab Emirates for work. He said he and Rey met online when they were 11 or 12 and beginning to experiment with hacking. He said they bonded over their shared support for the Palestinian cause and that they vandalised websites to act out their preteen political sensibilities.
“We thought it was cool when we were kids,” El Adeb said. “But then we grew out of it. We started to think that hacktivism is cringe.”
El Adeb ‘proud’ of cybercriminal background
Less cringe, he said, was making money.
El Adeb said Khader and other young cybercriminals formed Hellcat and went on a digital rampage, breaking into organisations around the world. Analysts say the group was noteworthy for publicly humiliating victims, something El Adeb described as “trolling.” He declined to say how much he earned from Hellcat’s cybercrime spree.
Reuters could not fully corroborate El Adeb’s account of his past or his exchanges with Khader. El Adeb said he “nuked” most of their messages after Khader was detained. But his recollections of their relationship line up with published research from security professionals, interviews El Adeb has conducted as Pryx and a podcast featuring Pryx released earlier this year, in which he said he had left cybercrime.
Other young hackers have publicly claimed to have gone straight while allegedly continuing to hack and steal. In an interview in 2025, Khader said he had quit hacking. Pepijn van der Stap, another suspected ShinyHunters hacker, repeatedly told journalists he had put his days of theft and extortion behind him. He was arrested by Dutch police on Sept 15 and is being investigated over allegations that he tried to organise murders abroad.
Attempts to reach representatives for Van der Stap were unsuccessful.
El Adeb insisted he was out of the game, describing himself as a “retired threat actor.” But between drags of his cigarette, El Adeb said he felt no shame or regret over his hacking.
“I’m proud that I had this experience,” he said. “I’m actually very happy and proud that I had actual cybercrime experience in a field that is filled with people that claim they know stuff but they never actually experienced real hacking.” REUTERS

A tornado in Sicily overturned cars and seriously injured people
Kyiv • UNN
A tornado destroyed a house and damaged a school in Marsala and neighboring towns. A married couple were hospitalized in serious condition; the authorities will allocate funds.
On Friday, vehicles were overturned and two people sustained serious injuries as a tornado swept through the Sicilian city of Marsala and neighboring settlements. Experts called the event almost unprecedented for the Mediterranean island, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
The storm caused panic among local residents: the tornado destroyed a house and also damaged a school and other buildings in Marsala and the neighboring towns of Petrosino and Mazara del Vallo.
"It was almost like an American tornado; nothing so destructive has been seen here in the memory of the current generation," Salvatore Cocina, head of Sicily's Civil Protection Service, told Reuters.
As early as the beginning of September, the agency warned that the hot summer had caused a great deal of heat to accumulate, which could trigger extreme weather events in the autumn.
"This once again highlights the problem of extreme weather events that have become characteristic of recent years due to the climate crisis," Cocina said.
Video released by local media shows a school in Marsala with shattered windows and a partially collapsed roof, as well as passenger cars and trucks overturned onto their sides and power-line poles blown down by the wind.
A couple caught at the epicenter of the storm while traveling by car was hospitalized in serious condition.
The president of the Sicily region, Renato Schifani, promised to allocate special funds to address the consequences of the emergency; a warning about possible extreme weather events also remains in effect for Saturday, as rains and storms continue to hit the island.

India: Delhi police must facilitate right to peaceful protest amid lockdown-like restrictions in capital

Responding to the sweeping and disproportionate restrictions imposed by the Delhi Police and the Government of India ahead of planned protests in the capital on Saturday 10 October, Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India, said:
“Peaceful protesters must be able to demand accountability from those in power without facing intimidation, arbitrary detention, or sweeping restrictions on their freedoms.
“From denying permission for a peaceful demonstration, halting all Delhi-bound trains, and sealing the city’s borders, to issuing an internet suspension order near the protest site, and pre-emptively arresting activists – India’s authorities are leaving no stone unturned in their bid to prevent this march from happening. The right to protest is protected in India’s constitution. The authorities must immediately lift all these arbitrary restrictions, which violate India’s obligations under international law. Demonstrations should not depend on obtaining prior permission from the police. At most, organizers may be expected to notify the authorities of their plans.
Peaceful protesters must be able to demand accountability from those in power without facing intimidation, arbitrary detention, or sweeping restrictions on their freedoms
Aakar Patel, Chair of Board, Amnesty International India
“With more than 30,000 security personnel reportedly being deployed in the city, it is critical that police protect the public, not punish people for exercising their rights. Security measures are there to protect people, not punish them for exercising their fundamental rights. We urge the authorities to exercise the utmost restraint and take all necessary steps to protect and facilitate the right of peaceful assembly.”
Background
The protesters, led by the Cockroach Janta Party, student unions and opposition parties, have been protesting since 2 October to demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation amid controversy over the Election Commission’s Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls. More than 130 million people have been deleted from electoral rolls since 2025.
The Delhi Police stated that permission to hold a protest at Jantar Mantar on 10 October had not been granted.
Student union members and activists associated with the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) have been detained, placed under house arrest outside Delhi or intercepted and detained while travelling to the capital by road and rail.
Restrictions on travel into Delhi will reportedly be put in place from the night of 9 October to the early hours of 11 October, with Delhi Metro stations scheduled to close, bus services set to be suspended, and the capital’s borders to be sealed to buses, trucks, tractors and other large transport vehicles.
A 24-hour mobile internet shutdown has been ordered in central Delhi from Friday night. The suspension will cover a 4km radius around the protest sites, according to a notification issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Delhi Police’s Special Cell.
Meanwhile, the Supreme Court on Friday provided partial relief by directing the Government of India not to completely suspend train services to Delhi or shut down Delhi Metro stations. The court directed the government to regulate these services in accordance with the principle of proportionality, ensuring that public transport remains accessible, and commuters are not inconvenienced. The Supreme Court has asked the Centre to consider designating an alternative venue to Jantar Mantar for peaceful protests, emphasizing the need for a location equipped with adequate facilities and amenities for protesters.
Approximately 22,000-armed personnel from across the country have reportedly been brought to Delhi, in addition to more than 10,000 Delhi Police officers expected to be deployed.

U.S. sanctions ICC, vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick" without changes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:02:02 UTC
01:02:02 KST

U.S. sanctions International Criminal Court, vowing to dismantle it "brick by brick" without changes
The Trump administration imposed fresh sanctions targeting the International Criminal Court on Friday, taking action against the court itself after previously penalizing more than a dozen of its judges and prosecutors.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement announcing the measures.
The move came just hours after the Norwegian Nobel Committee announced it was awarding the Nobel Peace Prize to Navanethem "Navi" Pillay, a South African-born human rights official who served as an ICC judge from 2003 to 2008. Pillay also led a U.N. inquiry that determined last year that Israel committed genocide in Gaza. Israel strongly disputed the report's findings.
Neither the United States nor Israel is a party to the Rome Statute that established the ICC. Washington has long objected to the court's investigation of alleged war crimes by U.S. personnel in Afghanistan and its arrest warrants for Israeli leaders over alleged crimes in Gaza.
The court maintains it can prosecute crimes committed on territory under its jurisdiction, even when the accused is a national of a country that has not joined.
Rubio has previously described the ICC as a "fatally politicized supranational court" that has "maliciously abused its authority." He vowed Friday to dismantle it "brick by brick" if necessary.
Under the designation, the court's assets under U.S. jurisdiction are blocked, and U.S. companies and individuals are generally barred from doing business with the court. For now, the Treasury Department is allowing some services to continue and giving the court 180 days to maintain certain operations while its member countries address Washington's objections.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns," Rubio said. "If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly."
The ICC condemned the designation as an attempt to interfere with its work and intimidate those who cooperate with it, calling it "an assault on the rule of law."
"The Court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality," ICC President Tomoko Akane said. The court also appealed to its 125 member states to help ensure it has adequate resources to continue operating, warning its future now depends in part on the governments that established it.
The court's member states include most U.S. allies in Europe, including every NATO member besides Turkey, as well as Canada, Japan and Australia.
The foreign ministers of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands, and the U.K. said in a statement later Friday that they "regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States."
"[I]f put into effect, these sanctions will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families," the countries said. "They work every day to bring those accused of the most serious international crimes to justice and to support their victims."
Pillay, the Peace Prize recipient, left the court in 2008 to become the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights, and currently serves on the International Court of Justice, which is separate from the ICC.
She was also the chair of the U.N. Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the panel determined that there were "reasonable grounds" to conclude that "the Israeli authorities and Israeli security forces have committed and are continuing to commit" acts of genocide. Israel's foreign minister called the report "fake" and said it "relies entirely on Hamas falsehoods, laundered and repeated by others."
Pillay referenced the U.S. campaign against the ICC in a video following news that she had won the Peace Prize.
"We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack," she said. "This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the decision to award the Peace Prize to Pillay showed that the Nobel Committee "has lost its moral compass."
"It has awarded its highest honor to a bigot who built her career around inventing and propagating blood libels against the one and only Jewish state," Netanyahu's office said in a post on X.
The U.S. action against the ICC also follows a speech Rubio delivered Wednesday in Athens against the backdrop of the Acropolis, where he criticized Western governments for transferring national authority to international bureaucracies.
"[W]ith every passing year, we seemed to outsource more of our sovereignty, transferring our decisions to global bureaucracies far beyond the reach of our control," he said.

Trump launches probe into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook

Trump launches probe into Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook
Trump began efforts to remove Cook as one of the governors on the US Fed Reserve Board in 2025 and litigation on the matter is still on.
United States President Donald Trump has announced a committee to investigate Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook and whether alleged false statements on mortgage documents constitute grounds for her removal under federal law.
The White House announced the new committee on Wednesday, but published the notice on its website on Friday.
The three-member committee, which will be tasked with reviewing evidence and reporting to the president on whether he has sufficient cause to remove her, will include the assistant to the president for economic policy, the chair of the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission and the director of the Office of Government Ethics.
The notice says there will be a hearing on November 5, where Cook will be required to appear and answer questions.
Political pressure
Trump began efforts to remove Cook as one of the governors on the US Federal Reserve Board in August 2025 after Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte accused her of misrepresenting two different properties on a 2021 mortgage application before she joined the central bank. She was appointed to the Fed Board in 2022 by then-President Joe Biden. Cook’s term runs until 2038.
Trump announced Cook’s removal amid the allegations, but Cook sued, and a federal judge blocked her firing in September 2025. Cook remained in office while the case continued.
In June, the Supreme Court declined to let Trump remove Cook while the litigation continues.
The case led to the US Supreme Court ruling earlier this year that the president could not remove a Fed governor without adequate cause and needed to follow a clear process to lay out the reasons and provide evidence.
The ruling left Cook in her position, but kicked the case against her back to a federal district court.
The case has been closely watched as Trump has put political pressure on the central bank to cut interest rates, including launching investigations into then-Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell, whose term ended in May.
In December 2025, Trump said he would only appoint someone who agreed with him on cutting interest rates. He appointed Kevin Warsh as Powell’s replacement.
Amid ongoing tensions with Iran, pressure on the oil market and rising inflation, the Fed last month raised the benchmark interest rate by a quarter of a percentage point to 3.75–4 percent, the first hike in three years. With the final rate decision before the midterm elections later this month, CME FedWatch, which tracks the likelihood of monetary policy decisions, forecasts that rates will likely remain unchanged.

====================================================================================================

We took a social media scientist to
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:00:35 UTC
01:00:35 KST

Aaron Sorkin’s new movie The Social Reckoning, the hotly anticipated follow-up to The Social Network, tells the story of whistleblower Frances Haugen, a Facebook employee who showed that the company knew its platforms harmed some users.
Haugen, played in the film by Mikey Madison, shared Facebook’s internal data with journalist Jeff Horwitz (played by Jeremy Allen White) at the Wall Street Journal. The resulting investigation, “The Facebook Files,” was published in 2021. It and other reporting led to congressional investigations, lawsuits and more action against Facebook—much of which is ongoing.
It also gave urgency to research investigating how social media affects people’s mental health, especially that of children. Among these scientists is Laura Edelson, a social media safety researcher at Northeastern University, who has studied Facebook’s moderation practices during the January 6 insurrection, the way that misinformation spreads on Facebook and social media privacy across multiple platforms. We took Edelson to see The Social Reckoning to find out what the film gets right about social media’s potential harms.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
“It was really, frankly, surreal seeing a series of events that you lived through on the big screen,” she says.
[An edited transcript of the interview follows.]
In the movie, we learn about Facebook’s 2018 transition to an algorithm based on “meaningful social interaction” (MSI), which had disastrous consequences for some users. What is MSI, and how does it work?
Before 2018, Facebook primarily maximized [its algorithm] for duration of use. They cared about how long your Facebook session was and how many times [you returned] over a day or a week. MSI [maximizes for] users who are interacting, who are clicking things, who are typing. It is very different from a passive, just viewing, just scrolling state.
When you are clicking a lot of things and you’re responding a lot, you can see how that could apply both to congratulating someone on their new puppy or [to commenting], “This is the dumbest idea ever. You should go die.” As much as those two [actions] are very different things, you’re actually in a similar state of being deeply engaged and paying a lot of attention. That is obviously very, very different than an algorithm that just tries to get you to be there for as long as possible. It’s going to select different things to show you.
Content that is going to be very interactive is going to be the kind of content that is more extreme content. And that’s true whether it’s something that makes you happy or whether it’s something that makes you angry or scared.
Why did Facebook make the shift to MSI?
The why is because that is what they sell. Facebook sells ads. But more specifically, what they sell is user interaction with ads. That’s not to say that no Facebook ads are sold on a per-view basis, but mostly it’s this interactivity, this click-through rate, that’s the thing that is important to Facebook’s bottom line.
The movie seems to cast blame on Facebook for increasing political radicalization in 2019–2021, including the January 6 riots. Do you think it fairly portrays Facebook’s role?
New mediums have profoundly destabilizing effects on political structures. I think it is not surprising that social media had a similar effect. It’s hard to wrap your head around because what happened was absolutely an amplification of existing underlying patterns. But there is a point at which moderate content literally cannot compete—that becomes a point at which, if you are a politician, it is genuinely difficult to spread a moderate political message because it will perform badly on the dominant medium of communication. And that’s not a left thing or a right thing. That [means that] the more extreme your message is, the better it will perform on both social media. I see that repeatedly in every study I ever do of content.
In one study we observed that on January 6, a lot of [content posted to Facebook] got taken down. And then, on January 12, a larger tranche of stuff was taken down. The thing was: the vast majority of these takedowns happened too late to have much of an effect [on what people saw in their news feeds]. It had some very small impact, but moderating after the content has already been up for days just doesn't change user experience on your platform very much.
It matters not just what you moderate but when you moderate. If your fact-checking takes several days, if your system that identifies content that might violate your rules takes several days, you might as well not do it just because it’s not going to matter much in terms of user experience.
Several studies suggest that social media shows people more extreme content but does not necessarily change their views. Is that true?
It's very hard to set up an experiment that is causal, and that is what you’d have to do to answer that question. You need to set up a controlled experiment where you take a population and then you randomize and then you show them different stuff. An experiment from this year did that in a long-term way. And the researchers actually did find an effect. They found that when [the researchers] changed what was in someone's feed, [the participants’] political beliefs changed.
This movie depicts Facebook in 2021. How have social media algorithms changed since then?
Things are quite different in 2026. That is not to say that some of the problems that were very visible in 2021 are not still with us, but one of the things that has happened is: Facebook is a much smaller and more marginal place. TikTok, Instagram Reels and YouTube Shorts are the places where more people are spending more of their attention.
[Political content] is not as uniquely advantaged [on those platforms] as it was on Facebook [because of] the difference in monetization of how ads are sold on short-form video platforms. They are more likely to be sold on a per-view basis. The algorithm for TikTok is much more durational. To keep someone on a platform of that type for as long as possible, it’s going to wind up favoring different kinds of things.
It’s creating different kinds of problems; [for example], the eating disorder problem continues to be very real. There remains a big conspiracy theory problem, particularly around things that get monetized. But the political extremism problem is not as severe—not because anybody really did anything [to address] it but because this other form of social media that just was able to capture people’s attention longer and better became more dominant, and it’s prone to different problems.
What are your final thoughts on the film?
It got a lot of small things that I knew about right. The movie made it very legible why Jeff did what he did and why Frances did what she did. But I did not find that movie very enlightening as to why Mark Zuckerberg does what he does.
I think we all like to think, when there are such obvious bad things happening in the world, that it’s because there’s a villain twirling their mustache and making the bad thing happen.
But I think a lot of bad things in the world happen because good people let them. Or good people have other reasons for finding that bad thing to be tolerable. I think it would be more useful to understand that as a way of getting to “How can we make social media safer for people?”

How your personality “acts as an invisible architect for your career,” according to new research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:00:19 UTC
01:00:19 KST

Young adults who are willing to wait for larger financial rewards tend to apply to college programs associated with longer study durations and steeper earnings growth, while those who avoid risk lean toward fields where graduates experience more predictable salaries, according to a study published in PNAS. The findings suggest that individual economic preferences predict postsecondary educational choices. This pattern indicates that educational sorting reflects how young people evaluate time and uncertainty, operating alongside academic performance and family background.
The research was conducted by an international team of six economists who contributed equally to the work. Their investigation examines how fundamental economic preferences predict real-world educational investments. In economics, two behavioral traits are central to these decisions: patience and attitudes toward risk. Patience refers to a person’s willingness to wait for larger rewards down the road, while risk aversion describes a preference for stable outcomes over uncertain prospects that carry financial risks.
Economists typically view higher education through the framework of human capital theory, which treats schooling as an investment. Under this model, students spend years out of the workforce gaining skills with the expectation of earning higher wages later in life. Individuals who place greater value on future rewards are theoretically more willing to postpone earnings to complete longer degrees. At the same time, because career paths offer widely varying degrees of earnings stability, people who dislike uncertainty are expected to shy away from fields with unpredictable financial prospects.
Empirical evidence linking these economic traits to higher-education decisions has remained scarce. Testing these theories requires measuring how people handle risk and delayed rewards before they make their educational investments. It also requires gathering those measurements across large groups of students and observing their actual choices. Because laboratory-style experiments with real money are difficult to combine with official educational records, prior research has often relied on smaller samples or brief survey questions rather than incentivized choices.
“While psychologists have long known that personality influences our choices, proving that specific cognitive traits dictate major life paths has remained an empirical challenge,” study co-author Ernst Fehr, a professor of economics and director of the UBS Center for Economics in Society at the University of Zurich, told PsyPost. “Historically, it has been nearly impossible to capture a person’s baseline traits before they make massive life decisions and then objectively track their real-world trajectories over decades.”
Rather than following participants for decades, the team measured their preferences just before they applied to higher education and drew long-term earnings data from an older generation of graduates. They conducted the study in Denmark, which Fehr described as a “pristine real-world laboratory.” Higher education in Denmark is tuition-free, and students receive monthly government stipends to support living costs regardless of family wealth. This arrangement allowed the scientists to examine how personal preferences predict educational investments without major distortions from borrowing limits.
The authors invited a random sample of 18- and 19-year-olds from Danish population registries in 2018, catching them just before they submitted higher-education applications. The final analysis focused on 3,132 young adults who completed upper secondary school, had official ninth-grade exam scores, and applied to programs receiving at least ten applicants from the study. In all, the applicants sorted across 76 educational options, consisting of 72 postsecondary degree programs and four upper secondary school tracks.
The researchers measured patience through an online experimental task involving 16 financial choices. In each decision, participants could take a sum of money earlier or save some of it to receive more later, such as eight weeks versus 16 weeks, with the delays and interest rates varying across decisions. One decision was randomly chosen to be paid out for real, with an average payment of about 250 Danish kroner (roughly 40 U.S. dollars) sent to participants’ phones. The researchers ranked participants on a percentile scale from 1 to 100 based on their average savings rate.
To measure risk aversion, participants completed an investment exercise featuring 15 financial scenarios. In each situation, they could keep an amount of money with certainty or invest part of it into a lottery offering a chance at a larger return alongside the risk of a loss. By observing the share of money each person kept safe rather than risking it, the researchers ranked each participant’s risk aversion on a percentile scale from 1 to 100.
The authors then linked these experimental rankings to official administrative registries, identifying each student’s first-priority application in Denmark’s centralized admission system. The team characterized each program by its official length and, using tax records from roughly 330,000 Danes born between 1975 and 1980, by its graduates’ typical annual earnings growth, how widely their salaries varied, and the share who ended up in the bottom fifth of earners.
The researchers compared the 76 programs based on the average patience and risk-aversion ranks of the students who applied to them. On its own, a 10-percentile difference in applicants’ average patience corresponded to programs that lasted nearly one and a half years longer and offered 2.4 percentage points higher annual earnings growth.
Programs that drew more risk-averse applicants tended to have fewer graduates with very low earnings and less variation in pay. Before any adjustments, a 10-percentile difference in applicants’ average risk aversion corresponded to a 6.2 percentage point lower share of graduates in the bottom fifth of earners, compared with an average share of 9.9 percent across the programs students applied to.
These relationships weakened but did not disappear once the authors accounted for school grades, parental education and income, gender, and immigrant background. With those factors included, a 10-percentile difference in patience corresponded to programs a little over two months longer, and a 10-percentile difference in risk aversion corresponded to a share of low earners about 3 percentage points lower.
Risk aversion also exhibited an unexpected link with degree duration and earnings trajectories. In both simple comparisons and models with controls, programs drawing more risk-averse applicants had longer study durations and higher earnings growth.
“Intuitively, one might assume that risk-averse individuals would avoid long, demanding university programs out of fear of failure,” Fehr pointed out. “Instead, we observed that risk-averse individuals sort disproportionately into some longer, and high-earnings-growth, programs. The reason for this is that they tend to select programs with lower downside earnings risk and lower earnings dispersion; because longer and high-growth programs also tend to have safer labor-market outcomes, risk-averse individuals consequently sort disproportionately into some longer, high-growth programs. Economics illustrates this pattern: it combines a multi-year program and high earnings growth with a relatively low probability of very low earnings.”
Comparing the predictive power of preferences to school grades highlighted their relative importance. Patience was about one-fourth as predictive of program length as school grades were, and its link to earnings growth was about one-sixth that of grades. For avoiding programs with many low earners, risk aversion was about as predictive as grades, and it was roughly twice as predictive as grades when it came to avoiding programs with widely spread earnings. These patterns suggest that sorting across degree tracks reflects personal preferences regarding time and risk, not just past academic achievement.
“The psychological footprint on career selection is remarkably powerful, rivaling traditional cognitive metrics like intelligence,” Fehr told PsyPost. He noted that in their data, which used school grades as a proxy for cognitive ability, an individual’s aversion to risk was “just as powerful a predictor – and sometimes stronger – than their academic performance” when predicting which applicants avoided fields with unstable earnings.
The findings are in line with research covered by PsyPost in 2026, which indicated that a greater orientation toward future rewards was associated with completing higher levels of education. That earlier study evaluated genetic predispositions for delay discounting rather than directly elicited behavioral preferences with cash stakes, but both studies point to a link between patience and educational investments.
“The core takeaway is that your deep-seated psychological profile – specifically your capacity for delayed gratification and your tolerance for risk – acts as an invisible architect for your career,” Fehr observed. “Highly patient individuals naturally gravitate toward marathon educational paths with steep, back-loaded rewards, while risk-averse people choose fields that offer psychological safety through predictable, stable income streams. This reveals that structural societal inequalities aren’t just born from academic talent or family wealth, but from how our minds evaluate risk and time.”
There are a few things to keep in mind when interpreting these findings. The study examined students’ first-choice applications rather than the programs they actually enrolled in or completed, and about 74 percent of applicants were admitted to their top priority. Additionally, because the main analysis evaluated programs by the average traits of their applicants, it captures sorting across fields rather than predicting each individual student’s choice. An alternative model evaluating individual-level choices yielded similar directional patterns, though the estimated effects were smaller.
Fehr emphasized that these patterns should not be viewed as direct proof of cause and effect. “A critical nuance is that our study uncovers predictive patterns rather than a strictly causal mechanism, as it is impossible to ethically manipulate a person’s core personality traits in a lab,” he explained. “Furthermore, we want to clarify that our findings do not hinge on the exact monetary amounts used in our behavioral tasks. Rather, the true value lies in the experiment’s robust psychological validity – its capability to accurately rank where individuals sit on the spectrum of risk and patience relative to their peers.”
Participation patterns and historical data also present caveats. Only 39 percent of the invited young adults logged on to take part, and participants had somewhat higher grade point averages than the general population. In addition, the earnings benchmarks were derived from graduates born between 1975 and 1980, meaning current labor market conditions could differ. The Danish setting is also distinct, as universal living stipends and free tuition reduce financial barriers that might interact differently with risk aversion and patience in systems where students face tuition fees.
Looking ahead, the researchers hope these insights help reshape economic theories and policy discussions regarding educational inequality. “Our long-term objective is to dismantle the outdated assumption that all humans evaluate risk and time identically,” Fehr concluded. “By taking into account the vast diversity in human preferences, we hope to influence how both scientists and policymakers approach systemic inequality. Ultimately, interventions designed to help people climb the socioeconomic ladder must account for individual psychological diversity rather than relying on one-size-fits-all financial incentives.”
The study, “Economic preferences predict higher-education choices,” was authored by Thomas F. Epper, Ernst Fehr, Kristoffer B. Hvidberg, Claus T. Kreiner, Søren Leth-Petersen, and Basit Zafar.

Northern Irish police to interview First Minister O'Neill over parade protest
BELFAST, Oct 9 - Northern Irish police will interview the region's first minister, Michelle O'Neill, in relation to an investigation into a protest that has blocked a Protestant parade from marching through a Catholic area for almost two weeks, O'Neill said on Friday.
Thousands of protesters, including O'Neill of Irish nationalists Sinn Fein and the party's leader Mary Lou McDonald, gathered on the Catholic Garvaghy Road, in Portadown, to stop the September 26 march after it was allowed to proceed for the first time since the contentious route was banned in 1998.
Annual attempts by the Orange Order to march through the area triggered unrest across the British-run region before the route was banned the same year the Good Friday Agreement largely ended the three decades of violence known as the "Troubles".
Police opened an investigation into what they called an unlawful protest and said they had identified people reasonably suspected of committing offences.
Sinn Fein, which leads Northern Ireland's fragile power-sharing government alongside pro-British rivals who have called for O'Neill to be prosecuted over the protest, confirmed on Thursday that a number of its representatives received correspondence from police.
"I can confirm I have received a letter inviting me for a police interview ... I will cooperate with the investigation," O'Neill said in a statement, adding that she would continue to stand with the Garvaghy Road residents.
Britain's Northern Ireland minister failed to broker a compromise with the two sides last week and is awaiting a ruling on Monday from Northern Ireland's Court of Appeal on whether residents can challenge the removal of the parade ban. REUTERS

Ex-Deutsche Bank trader has conviction for rigging interest rates quashed
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:59:38 UTC
00:59:38 KST

Former City trader Christian Bittar has become the eighth person to have his conviction for rigging interest rates quashed, just days after five other former bankers also successfully cleared their names.
Christian Bittar, who previously worked for Deutsche Bank, was convicted in 2018 of conspiracy to defraud.
On Wednesday, the court overturned the convictions of Jay Vijay Merchant, Jonathan Mathew, Philippe Moryoussef, Alex Pabon and Colin Bermingham, all of whom worked at Barclays.
This week’s acquittals come just over a year after the UK supreme court overturned a decade-old ruling against the former UBS and Citigroup trader Tom Hayes and former Barclays trader Carlo Palombo. Their victory opened the door for the other traders to challenge their convictions.
Bittar said after his acquittal: “I have waited a very, very long time for this day. Finally, the injustice of what I and others suffered has been recognised. I am so grateful for those who stood by me through this ordeal and those who worked so tirelessly to correct it.”
Bittar and the five other former traders were all sentenced to jail on charges of manipulating the euro interbank offered rate (Euribor) or the now defunct London interbank offered rate (Libor).
The Euribor and Libor rates affected the value of ordinary people’s pensions, mortgages and savings, as well as hundreds of trillions of pounds and euros worth of financial products around the world. Nine bankers accused of rigging the rates were given fraud convictions.
The supreme court overturned the convictions of Hayes and Palombo after finding faults in the original trials, ruling that trial judges had given “inaccurate and unfair” instructions to the juries, that had ultimately “deprived” the men a fair trial.
Friday’s ruling marks a further blow for the Serious Fraud Office (SFO), which brought the original charges against the former traders.
While the SFO did not contest the appeals of the five men acquitted on Wednesday, it did contest Bittar’s appeal, stating his conviction was safe.
Jason Williams, head of division at the SFO, said: “We argued for a different outcome but respect the court’s decision in relation to Christian Bittar. The SFO remains committed to tackling the most complex fraud, bribery and corruption.”
Ben Rose of law firm Hickman and Rose, who represented Bittar, said it was a “scandal that the SFO has consistently failed to uphold its duty to ensure that these trials are fair”.
Peter Johnson, the ninth former trader who was convicted of rate rigging, also intends to appeal against his conviction. He pleaded guilty to conspiring to manipulate Libor in 2014.
Ellen Gallagher, a partner at Vardags, who represents Johnson, said: “Peter’s fight to clear his name continues.
“As the court made clear today, he has taken the first steps towards that appeal by filing provisional grounds.”

Russia proposes raising maximum age for women’s military service
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:57:47 UTC
00:57:47 KST

The Russian government has submitted a bill to the State Duma, the lower house of Russia’s parliament, that would raise the maximum age for women in military service from 45 to 50. The bill appears in the State Duma’s database.
The bill would also raise the maximum age for women to remain in the reserves: to 55 for officers, up from 50, and to 50 for those with other ranks, up from 45.
The explanatory note says the bill is necessary to create “additional social guarantees for female service members.” Its authors say the current maximum age for military service does not always allow women to serve long enough to qualify for a pension and other benefits.
For example, a woman who signs a contract between ages 25 and 30 and serves in a location “where preferential pension service credit does not apply” may not receive subsidized housing or a pension after reaching the maximum age for military service.
The government also stressed that, amid the war with Ukraine, most of the personnel in medical units are women service members, “including those who have reached (or are reaching) the maximum age for military service.”
In July 2023, Vladimir Putin signed a law that raised the maximum age for remaining in the reserves by five years for certain citizens holding military ranks. The amendments set new age limits for soldiers, sailors, sergeants, petty officers, warrant officers, and midshipmen.

Kazakhstan releases Ukrainian woman detained while attempting to recover grandson from Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:56:03 UTC
00:56:03 KST

Kazakh authorities have released Ukrainian citizen Liubov Rozhanska, who had been detained in the country at Russia’s request during a trip to return her grandson to Ukraine. The independent outlet Vot Tak reported, citing Rozhanska’s lawyer Alexei Pryanishnikov, that the Ukrainian grandmother was released from a Kazakh detention facility on Oct. 4. Rozhanska then spent several days at the Ukrainian Embassy in Astana before leaving for Odesa.
“The detention period expired. Since no pretrial restriction was imposed, she was released from the detention facility. She has left Kazakhstan. The Kazakh side acted in accordance with the law,” Pryanishnikov said.
Rozhanska was detained on Oct. 1 at Astana airport after arriving from Istanbul. The Ukrainian woman had traveled there to collect her 8-year-old grandson, who is on Ukraine’s list of children who are being unlawfully held in Russia. The boy, however, was never brought to Kazakhstan. Instead, according to the lawyer Pryanishnikov, a staged video was made by the Russian side in order to create the appearance that the boy was departing from Kaliningrad to Kazakhstan in advance of the arranged meeting. Pryanishnikov believes the episode was an FSB operation.
Rozhanska’s grandson was taken to Russia by his mother in 2021 after she married a Russian citizen. The boy’s Ukrainian father had given his permission for a temporary trip, but the mother never returned to Ukraine. In 2022 both she and the boy received Russian citizenship. The father went to a Ukrainian court, which ruled that the boy should live with him. According to Pryanishnikov, that ruling provides a legal basis for returning the child to Ukraine.
At the same time, a separate case over the father’s contact with the boy was heard in Kaliningrad, where the child lives with his mother. “In the end, a court in Kaliningrad issued a ruling allowing the father, who serves in the Armed Forces of Ukraine, to have in-person contact with his son during the summer holidays on the territory of the Kaliningrad Region,” Pryanishnikov told The Insider on Oct. 2.
The boy had already been promised to be returned to Ukraine in 2023, and two Ukrainian citizens traveled to the Kaliningrad Region to pick him up.
“But those people were detained and accused of attempting to abduct the child, and then they were hit with espionage charges as well. They were put under heavy pressure there, forced to give up their lawyers and sentenced to 15 and 16 years in prison. At the same time, Rozhanska, who was detained in Kazakhstan, was declared by a Russian court to be the organizer of the ‘abduction’ — although charging a grandmother with trying to abduct her own grandson is very strange,” the lawyer said.

In Russian-Occupied Oleshky, Civilians Struggle to Survive as Hunger Deepens
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:54:00 UTC
00:54:00 KST

Lyudmila often has to call her sister about 40 times before the line connects. When she finally gets through, she can barely make out what her sister is saying.
"I hear occasional words, sometimes they're incomplete. The main thing is that I hear her voice," Lyudmila, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, told The Moscow Times.
A refugee now living in Europe, Lyudmila comes from a village on the Ukrainian-controlled right bank of the Dnipro River in the Kherson region. Her sister lives across the river in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky, where relentless bombardment has plunged the town into a deepening humanitarian crisis.
Conditions in Oleshky have continued to deteriorate since late 2025. Roads leading in and out of the town are heavily mined and badly damaged, leaving its 2,000 remaining residents, including an estimated 50 children, largely cut off from food, water, gas, electricity and medicine, residents and volunteers told The Moscow Times.
"She says everything is destroyed, houses are often burning and strikes land nearby every five to 10 minutes," Lyudmila told The Moscow Times.
With a pre-war population of 24,000, Oleshky served as a satellite town to Kherson city over the Dnipro River. It became a frontline town after Russian forces retreated across the Dnipro in late 2022.
Today, Russian forces use positions on the occupied bank to strike Ukrainian cities, while Kyiv targets Russian forces on the other side of the river in response, defense analyst Konrad Muzyka said.
Months of bombardment have destroyed much of the town’s infrastructure, according to a representative of a Russian organization that evacuates civilians from frontline areas.
"Everything has been smashed by drones. Residential buildings without damage can be counted on one hand. It's practically impossible to get in or out," the representative told The Moscow Times, speaking on condition of anonymity to discuss a sensitive matter.
There have been no food deliveries by road since June, when a delivery driver hit a mine and died.
"For the past two months, people have been eating grass," said a resident who escaped the town on foot on Wednesday.
"Food can only be bought in Radensk," he told The Moscow Times, referring to a small settlement 23 kilometers (14 miles) away.
Every few days, Lyudmila's sister makes that journey by foot to buy food while her husband, who is recovering from a shrapnel wound sustained in a drone strike, waits anxiously at home.
"By the time she gets back, her legs are completely swollen," Lyudmila said.
"To blow up on a mine or die of hunger? People from Oleshky are forced to choose between two deaths," Ukraine's Commissioner for Human Rights Dmytro Lubinets said in a post last week.
Drone footage shared by Lubinets earlier this week showed about two dozen of Oleshky's remaining residents trying to flee the city on electric bikes, bicycles and even on foot.
Tetiana Hasanenko, the exiled head of the Oleshky city military administration, said 12 people who fled the town last month had reached Ukrainian-controlled territory. Other evacuees remain in nearby towns in Russian-occupied southern Ukraine.
Ukraine blames Moscow for the deepening crisis in what Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha described as a Russian "siege."
The Kremlin has acknowledged the situation in the town as "critical," but accused Kyiv of preventing civilians from leaving.
With Moscow prohibiting humanitarian bodies and international organizations from working in Ukraine's occupied territories, evacuating civilians is left to small volunteer groups. The groups often undertake days-long journeys through Russia and Belarus to repatriate people.
"We work wherever access is possible, but in Oleshky, it's the hardest," the volunteer, who was last in the town over a month ago, said.
Ukraine’s military used drones to deliver another batch of food and medicine to Oleshky on Sunday following an initial operation in late September. The latest delivery consisted of nearly 400 packages weighing almost 4 metric tons, Sybiha said.
Neither Lyudmila’s sister nor the resident who escaped on Wednesday received any of the aid, they said.
"Where they sent it and to whom is unknown. No one in their area received anything," Lyudmila said.
After the first delivery on Sept. 27, Hasanenko accused Russian forces of taking some of the supplies.
It is difficult to establish how many people have been killed in Oleshky. By the end of June, the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine recorded at least 29 civilians killed and 54 injured in Oleshky and neighboring Hola Prystan in 2026.
Separately, Vladimir Saldo, the Russian-appointed governor of the occupied Kherson region, said Wednesday that 68 people had been killed across the entire region so far this year.
Efforts to arrange a safe evacuation from Oleshky have yet to produce a breakthrough, Ukraine’s human rights commissioner’s office said Thursday. It said talks with Russia were ongoing and that Kyiv had offered a localized ceasefire, a safe evacuation route and arrangements to receive residents in Ukrainian-controlled territory.
On the ground, people who spoke to The Moscow Times were reluctant to discuss military activity in detail. The man who escaped Oleshky said some people in the town blame Kyiv for the constant drone attacks.
"Ukrainian drones show no mercy, even to civilians," he said.
Others, like Lyudmila's sister, blame Moscow for occupying the town, and then turning it into a wasteland.
"The Russians came and created this crisis. Now, my sister and her husband are waiting for Ukraine to save them," she said.

EU takes 'crucial first step' toward rebalancing trade with China: Trade commissioner
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:53:12 UTC
00:53:12 KST

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The EU has taken a "crucial first step" toward rebalancing trade relations with China after reaching an understanding on hybrid vehicle exports, EU Trade Commissioner Maros Sefcovic said Friday.
Speaking at a news conference in Beijing, Sefcovic said the understanding could pave the way for reducing Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the European market by more than half.
"This opens the prospect of cutting China's export by more than a half," he said, describing the understanding as the first tangible outcome of trade and investment consultations between Brussels and Beijing.
Sefcovic said the EU had sought to rebalance trade relations with China amid a growing trade deficit and concerns over global industrial overcapacity.
He said the understanding was particularly important for Europe's automotive industry, which was under significant pressure.
The negotiated solution was fair and consistent with World Trade Organization methodology, he added.
"For the first time that China has accepted to moderate its export without going through the phase of prior trade tension," Sefcovic said, welcoming the outcome of the negotiations.
He said the understanding covered seven specific tariff lines and could reduce Chinese exports of hybrid and plug-in hybrid vehicles to the EU by several million cars over four years.
Sefcovic added that the EU would proceed with the relevant procedures once the understanding received endorsement from the bloc's leaders.
"This is far from the end. It's a crucial first step, but only a first step in the process of rebalancing," he said.
Trade between China and the EU remains heavily weighted in Beijing's favor.
According to European Commission data, the bloc imported approximately $650 billion worth of goods from China in 2025, compared with exports of $232 billion, leaving a merchandise trade deficit of around $418 billion.
Machinery and vehicles accounted for more than half of manufactured imports from China, according to the data.
The imbalance has become a central concern in Brussels, which has urged Beijing to open its market further to European companies and address what it describes as unfair competition and industrial overcapacity.
The two sides agreed to hold their next ministerial-level meeting in March 2027, preceded by a video conference in January.

Pensions without a future: Why Ukraine can no longer sustain its pay-as-you-go system
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
18:51:43 EEST
00:51:43 KST

Svitlana Dovhalenko, Economist at CASE Ukraine, PhD
Ukraine’s pay-as-you-go pension system is reaching its limits
Ukraine’s pension system is facing a long-term challenge as demographic constraints increasingly determine its financial sustainability. Will the country have enough contributors to meet its pension obligations to future generations of retirees?
The current system operates on a pay-as-you-go basis: contributions from the economically active population finance benefits for those who have already left the workforce. This makes the pension system heavily dependent on demographic trends. As long as the number of contributors and their incomes grow sufficiently, the system can maintain adequate benefit levels. But when the contribution base shrinks while the number of beneficiaries rises, the resulting deficit ceases to be a temporary budget shortfall and becomes a structural problem.
Ukraine is moving in precisely this direction.
The Pension Arithmetic No Longer Adds Up
Ukraine's population is ageing while fertility rates have fallen far below the level needed to maintain a stable population.
The United Nations ranks Ukraine among the countries with the world's lowest fertility rates, with the figure falling to approximately one child per woman. According to the Global Change Data Lab, Ukraine's total fertility rate stood at just 0.98 children per woman in 2023.
Maintaining a stable population without migration requires a fertility rate of approximately 2.1 children per woman. Ukraine's figure is less than half that level. The generation expected to enter the labour market in large numbers two decades from now will be significantly smaller than today's workforce. This implies a future shortage of contributors to the Unified Social Contribution (USC), which finances pensions.
At the same time, the balance between working life and retirement is changing. According to the United Nations Population Fund, life expectancy at birth in Ukraine in 2025 was approximately 70 years for men and 80 years for women. The standard retirement age starts at 60. Currently, around 67% of the population is aged 15–64, while approximately 19% are older adults. Meanwhile, the share of younger generations continues to decline.
War Has Deepened the Demographic Crisis
Since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion, Ukraine's birth rate has halved. Deaths now outnumber births by nearly 3.6 to one. In the first half of 2026, Ukraine registered more than 73,000 births, compared with approximately 260,000 deaths.
Ukraine is also losing part of its working-age population through migration. According to the United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR), 5.68 million refugees from Ukraine were registered worldwide as of 30 June 2026. Eurostat reports that 4.4 million people who fled Ukraine are under temporary protection in EU countries. Adult women account for 43.4% of this group, adult men for 27%, and minors for 29.6%. In other words, more than 70% of Ukrainians abroad are either potential or actual participants in other countries' labour markets.
For the pension system, this means losing part of its future tax and social insurance contribution base. Fewer people work domestically, less income is subject to Ukrainian taxation, and fewer contributions flow into the pay-as-you-go system.
A System Running a Structural Deficit
Before the full-scale invasion, spending on the Pension Fund was the largest expenditure item in Ukraine's consolidated public finances. In 2021, Pension Fund expenditure amounted to UAH 520.9 billion, equivalent to approximately 35% of the country's total expenditure. Of this amount, UAH 177.6 billion was financed directly from the state budget.
Even before the war, contributions from insured workers were insufficient to sustain the system independently. The shortfall had to be covered through general budget revenues.
Today, pension spending is the second-largest expenditure category after national defence. In 2025, approved expenditure by the Pension Fund of Ukraine rose to UAH 1,020.9 billion, nearly doubling over five years.
By comparison, education spending increased from UAH 302.3 billion to UAH 394 billion, a rise of approximately 30%. This illustrates the opportunity cost: every additional hryvnia committed to pension obligations comes at a potential cost to human capital, infrastructure and economic growth.
The pay-as-you-go system is no longer financed solely through contributions from current workers. A substantial share of its cost falls on the state budget. When resources are insufficient, the government seeks additional revenue sources.
For example, Ukraine levies specific charges on passenger car purchases, real estate transactions and mobile telecommunications services. Between January and July 2026, these charges generated UAH 10.6 billion in state budget revenue.
The pension deficit is therefore not merely a problem for the Pension Fund. It is a public finance challenge. And the longer Ukraine maintains a single-pillar pension system, the more heavily the state budget must bear responsibility for its solvency.
Raising Taxes Is Not a Sustainable Solution Either
The government is allocating an increasing share of public resources to pensions, requiring ever-greater revenues. For the pension system, this means one of three things: more contributors, higher declared incomes, or higher tax and social insurance contributions.
The first depends on demographic trends, which are moving in the opposite direction.
The second depends on productivity improvements and economic growth.
The third has inherent limits.
Increasing the tax burden on labour makes formal employment more expensive. The OECD notes that high social security contribution rates, combined with weak enforcement of labour income reporting, create incentives to underreport official wages.
CASE Ukraine estimated the shadow economy at up to 40% of GDP in 2021 and identified undeclared wages, commonly known as envelope salaries, as one of the main channels of economic informality. The resulting budget losses are estimated at up to UAH 262 billion.
Attempting to close the pension deficit indefinitely by increasing the tax burden on labour would therefore be counterproductive. Beyond a certain point, higher contributions could shrink the very formal employment and wage base from which pension revenues are collected.
Political Cycles Are Shorter Than Pension Obligations
The pay-as-you-go system has another structural weakness: its particular vulnerability to political cycles.
Pensioners constitute a large and politically active group of voters. This makes promises of higher pensions especially attractive to politicians.
In 2012, Nataliia Korolevska promised an average monthly wage of €1,000 and a pension of €500. Yuliia Tymoshenko pledged to bring pensions up to the level of average wages.
The problem is not simply whether such promises are realistic, but the long-term fiscal commitments they create.
Politicians can reap immediate electoral benefits by appealing to pensioners, while the financial consequences emerge much later, leaving public finances burdened with obligations for years to come.
The failure to reform the pension system, combined with political populism, has contributed to a situation in which Ukrainian pensioners are becoming poorer even as Pension Fund expenditure continues to rise.
Ukrainians May Reach Retirement Age Without Qualifying for a Pension
Social pressure is likely to intensify as limited fiscal resources become sufficient only to finance meagre benefits, while older people remain among the most politically active voters.
The outlook is troubling. An actuarial assessment of Ukraine's Pension Fund, analysed by the International Labour Organization, suggests that by 2040, only around 40% of people aged 65 and over may qualify for a state old-age pension.
An increasing number of Ukrainians will lack the required contribution records because of low participation in formal employment.
The longer Ukraine postpones reform, the more expensive and disruptive the transition will become.
Efforts to move beyond an exclusively pay-as-you-go model towards a system in which part of retirement income is generated through individual savings began in the early 2000s. Yet, in 35 years of independence, Ukraine has never fully implemented a mandatory funded pension pillar.
Draft Law No. 2683 on mandatory funded pension provision, registered in 2019, has still not resulted in an operational second pillar. Draft Law No. 9212 was returned for revision in April 2024. As of 2026, Draft Law No. 2683 has once again been placed on the parliamentary agenda.
For years, policymakers have debated pension savings while the pay-as-you-go system has remained the principal source of future retirement income.
What Needs to Change?
Ukraine does not need a radical overhaul that abolishes the pay-as-you-go system overnight. It needs a carefully managed transition towards a multi-pillar pension model.
First, a portion of existing social insurance contributions should gradually be redirected into individual retirement savings accounts for younger workers, without introducing an additional payroll tax.
For older age groups, the transition should be more gradual, with government support or co-financing to ensure that people approaching retirement do not bear the costs of reform on their own.
Under this model, the pay-as-you-go pillar would remain the foundation of social insurance, while the funded pillar would begin building personal retirement assets.
Second, pension savings must be invested rather than left idle.
A portion of these funds could be invested in government bonds, but the system must ensure diversification, independent supervision, transparent fees and protection of assets from political interference.
Individuals should be able to track their contributions and investment returns and have the right to pass their accumulated savings on to their heirs.
Third, the parameters of the pay-as-you-go system need to be reviewed.
In 2026, Ukrainians must have 33 years of qualifying insurance contributions to retire at 60, 23 years to retire at 63, or 15 years to retire at 65.
Looking ahead, Ukraine should consider gradually moving towards a retirement age of 65 and a qualifying contribution period of 39–40 years, while providing a lengthy transition period for those approaching retirement.
Fourth, tax policy should focus on reducing the cost of formal employment rather than continually increasing it.
Proposals to lower the effective tax burden on wages, previously discussed by figures including Danylo Hetmantsev and CASE Ukraine experts, make sense only if accompanied by expenditure discipline.
Lower labour taxation should not translate into a larger fiscal deficit. Instead, it should encourage a broader formal tax base, higher employment and greater capacity for individual retirement savings.
Finally, voluntary pension savings should benefit from tax incentives. Individuals need a financial incentive to set aside part of their income for retirement rather than assuming that the state will provide for them in 30 years.
The Cost of Inaction
Ukraine is entering a demographic reality in which the pool of potential pension contributors is shrinking, migration is draining part of the workforce, and the cost of existing pension commitments continues to rise.
The state budget is already covering the gap between contributions and pension expenditure. Establishing a funded pension pillar can therefore no longer remain merely another topic of parliamentary debate.
A funded pension system will not eliminate demographic risks or automatically guarantee generous pensions. Its purpose is different: to ensure that part of an individual's retirement income comes not from contributions paid by the next generation, but from personal savings accumulated throughout working life and the returns earned on their investment.
Without a second source of retirement income, Ukraine will become increasingly dependent on the government's ability to plug pension funding gaps through the state budget, contributions from younger workers and resources that would otherwise be available to future generations.

2020 was an annus horribilis. Covid stalked the land. Lockdowns, curfews and social distancing were the order of the day. But there was a silver lining: European countries showed themselves to be capable of great solidarity, jointly procuring vaccines and then agreeing on a mammoth post-Covid recovery fund, the Recovery and Resilience Facility (RRF). That fund has disbursed €450 billion in grants and loans to EU member states since 2021. As the RRF enters its crucial final phase, we take stock of the situation with Pierre Moscovici, the French member of the European Court of Auditors (ECA).
The ECA has just presented a report on the health of the EU's finances, which also talks about the implementation of the RRF.
Moscovici says that the creation of the Covid recovery plan "was a crucial decision. Some people, and I was one of them, had been arguing for Eurobonds, for common borrowing, in order to invest together in Europe. And this was never possible due to some political positions between member states and the EU Commission. And finally, because of Covid, this was done. This was called Next Generation EU. It was the idea that we could borrow together some €750 billion in order to sustain growth, to be capable of facing the consequences of Covid. And this was absolutely a success. Some countries, for example Spain or Italy, massively benefited from this fund and were able to recover swiftly."
Moscovici elaborates: "The question is, is this a one-off, or should we do that again? Should it become permanent? Should it also inspire the Multiannual Financial Framework (the EU's long-term budget) that the member states and the Council are now preparing? Because if we want to do that again – that's what Mario Draghi (the author of a seminal report on EU competitiveness) is proposing that we do massively. He believes that we need to have €1.2 trillion worth of investments in defence, in greening the economy, in order to face the future. But to do that, we also have to know what has been working in the RRF and what has not been working."
Moscovici sums up: "The Recovery and Resilience Facility now also has to be evaluated not only on what has been disbursed, but also on the results. And that's what the European Court of Auditors is wondering or examining or evaluating with facts and findings. So our main concern and our motto is 'let's go to results'."
Moving onto broader economic issues, Moscovici highlights the problem of debt, both at the EU and at the national level.
"There two different things," he explains. "The one thousand billion euros of debt (that is projected to be reached in 2027) refers to the European Union. And then there is the problem of national countries. In France we have a debt-to-GDP ratio of 120 percent. That means that the servicing of debt is over €90 billion a year. The consequences of that are clear. When you have so much to reimburse, you cannot finance pensions, health, research and innovation, or schools. We are now in a in a crisis with education. We are in a crisis with the price of energy. That's the consequence when a country is indebted. The EU is not in the same situation. It still has a triple A (rating). But what the European Court of Auditors has flagged is that the EU has a debt as well. It is significant. The repayments will last for decades. And we must take care of that debt."
