Cody unveils Badger missile and Ordnance One factory plans
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:50:37 BST
00:50:37 KST

A British company founded in February has announced its first missile and the factory it intends to build it in, aiming at a replenishment cycle of under a year against the three years it currently takes to replace a stockpile, its founder told the UK Defence Journal at Apex Europe in London.
Henry Price spent fifteen years at primes and tier one suppliers before setting up Cody Aerospace and Defence, and the frustration that came out of it is what he says drove him to start the company.
He told me: “Fifteen years working for the bigger companies, producing amazing capability, but the cost and the lead time, and having to apologise to end users for those issues running some of the programmes, is kind of the frustration that drove me to say, okay, let’s go and do this ourselves, and we can prove that capability and offer something to the end users that they really need, in the timescales they need, at the right cost.”
The number he keeps returning to is the one that defines the market he is entering. “If you look at the problem statement of seven to ten days of stockpiles on the shelf for the UK in intensive warfare, and three years to replace it, that’s all we need to solve,” he said.
“We today released Badger, which is our ground-to-ground strike missile, in a containerised launcher, so an ISO container converted for that use,” he said. “And then a couple of years after that, being realistic, we’re also looking to integrate an interceptor missile into that same strike package. So from a commander’s perspective, you’ve got both strike and intercept capability in the same platform, which I think is quite a unique proposition.”
Radar and fire control come with the package, and his pitch is that the customer gets a complete capability instead of a product they then have to integrate themselves.
The factory was announced on the same day as the missile and the launcher. “All underpinned by our factory, which is called Ordnance One, which we’re also announcing today, and that’s going to be the key in terms of the industrialisation that we need to do for the product,” he said. The plant is intended to build Cody’s own designs and to produce other companies’ and other countries’ equipment under licence.
Badger is in the design phase and the company is raising pre-seed capital. “We’re looking to raise capital to bring that to a development maturity within eighteen months, two years, including the testing,” he said, with key components taken off the shelf from existing suppliers of seekers, rocket motors and guidance to reach a high technology readiness level quickly.
Those timings add up to his argument against buying off the shelf from the United States. “If you added that into what’s the replenishment cycle look like, we’re targeting under a year. I’d love to say six months, but say a year. So if you do the two years plus the year of replenishment, you’re actually under three years, if you go and buy off the shelf from the US or all those countries today,” he said.
American orders also carry a complication British buyers have run into before, “The other piece with the contracts from the US side is they’ve got DPAS ratings in terms of who gets the priority, and it’s generally given to the US customer first, as you’d understand,” he said. “So that three years could become four or five quite quickly, as we’ve seen with what’s going on in the world today.”
Sovereignty is the third strand of the business, and he was careful not to overclaim on it. Partnerships are being put in place with British suppliers for energetics and the rocket motor, though he was clear that rare earths and composites run into supply chains nobody in Europe fully controls.
He said: “I’m cognisant of just coming out of a UK factory isn’t necessarily all sovereign, but it’s better than we’ve got today. If it was all purely UK, there’ll be three, four times the cost. That’s what we’ve been told by the supply base, and it’s a reality today.”
Obsolescence management is where he thinks the real time is lost, and he gave an example from his own career. “It’s a seven dollar chip, very small, and the replacement is ten dollars, and that is the difference between two and a half years or six months. So the qualification is the key piece,” he said. Cody intends to fire Badger with old and new components in it to prove changes quickly and hold the design authority itself.
He put the same point more plainly a moment later, and it is the line his engineers will recognise. “I want engineers to be delivering capability, not managing obsolescence,” he said.
His read of the customer base starts from how thin the stocks are. Most NATO members have a multiple launch rocket system capability and can therefore tick the box, with inventories somewhere between twenty and eighty depending on the country, and the rule of thirds puts one third in maintenance, one third in training and one third on the front line. From there he moved to a challenge aimed at the alliance as a whole, he says.
“Why do we not have a standardised effector? If you take Ukraine as an example, you’ve got three different systems from three different countries with similar sized munitions. They can’t fire each other’s product,” he said, arguing that a commander on the front line should have the flexibility to fire a similar-sized munition from whatever launcher is to hand, in the way that artillery shells and small arms ammunition already allow.
Cody’s software and fire control will be open source, he said, whether or not the company ends up shooting anybody else’s rounds.
His message to the Ministry of Defence was also pretty clear, he said “We’re not saying as industry we want more budget, which might be a strange thing for me to say,” he said. “We want to spend the money in a better way. The Defence Investment Plan was explicit. There was eleven point one billion pounds earmarked for stockpiles. My challenge to MOD is we can help you spend that money better. Let’s start with one product named Badger with the containerised launcher. Let’s go to the interceptor. Let’s go into the air-to-air domain. Why is it two million pounds every time you fire an air-to-air missile? They’re very capable, but you’ve got to wait three years to get another one.”
Torpedoes are on his list too.
Asked where the company should be by Apex Europe in 2030, he was modest about it. “I’m probably being conservative and maybe British in my approach to growth. A lot of companies out there will show thirty products. I’ve come from this world, I know the pain it takes to do the integration and the development, so I’m saying let’s start with a handful,” he said.
Longer ranges would follow, and products built for snow, sand and water instead of designed around one war. Other ideas he is turning over include airdropping the Abode launcher and moving it on uncrewed vehicles, since shoot and scoot is how artillery survives and taking the crew out of that lowers the risk case.
He finished on where he thinks all of this work should be happening, telling me “My frustration is we keep sending it to other parts of the world. Let’s do it in the UK. Let’s use the testing houses that we know are here. We’ve got the catapults. We’ve got the universities. We have everything in the UK,” he said.
“If the government wants to talk about growth and the agenda of defence, let’s back companies like Cody, and we can actually make that difference.”

Belgium 'strongly condemns' new US sanctions against International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:50:26 UTC
00:50:26 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Belgium “strongly condemned” new US sanctions against the International Criminal Court on Friday, calling for EU action to protect the court's independence and those supporting its work.
"I strongly condemn the new US sanctions against the International Criminal Court," Foreign Minister Maxime Prevot said in a statement posted on US social media platform X.
"Seeking to cripple the Court's work denies victims a path to justice and puts those responsible for the gravest crimes beyond its reach," he added.
Prevot said Belgium had initiated discussions on support for the court with EU counterparts, with the issue set to be addressed Monday and at the forthcoming European Council.
"We will press for concrete protection. The Court's independence cannot depend on whom it investigates," he said.
The Belgian foreign minister called for the activation of the EU Blocking Statute to protect the court and those supporting its work.
"Europe must act," Prevot said, stressing that the bloc must defend its ability to uphold international law without allowing foreign sanctions to dictate its decisions.
His remarks followed an announcement of new sanctions against the court by US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
Rubio threatened to "end the ICC" unless it stopped what he described as its "threats."

Franco-German MGCS Tank Program Fails Due to Germany’s Withdrawal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:50:25 UTC
00:50:25 KST

The joint Franco-German program to develop the next-generation main battle tank, the MGCS, has failed due to Germany’s withdrawal from the project.
This was stated by General Fabien Mandon, Chief of the French Defence Staff of France, during a parliamentary hearing, according to POLITICO.
The French military leader acknowledged that the attempt to develop a joint next-generation tank with Germany did not live up to expectations.
At the same time, Fabien Mandon urged that the project not be considered a complete failure, as the militaries of both countries had done significant work in defining the concept for the future tank.
The Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) program was developed to replace the French Leclerc and German Leopard 2 tanks.
The project envisaged the creation not just of a single combat vehicle, but of an entire integrated land combat system.
The MGCS industrial consortium included the French company Thales, as well as defense giants KNDS France, KNDS Germany, and Rheinmetall.
However, in recent years, the program has regularly faced prolonged delays, industrial disputes, and political tensions between France and Germany.
Germany’s withdrawal from the MGCS came just a few months after another Franco-German program, the FCAS, aimed at developing a next-generation fighter jet, was abruptly terminated.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron concluded that Dassault and Airbus would be unable to reach a compromise on the development of a joint combat aircraft.
As a reminder, the French Ministry of the Armed Forces plans to select a model for a new next-generation tank as early as 2026 as an interim replacement for the Leclerc tanks.
Setting a specific deadline is necessitated by the need to synchronize equipment replacement with delays, and, now, the cancellation of the MGCS project.

Cars overturned, two people injured as ‘unprecedented’ tornado hits Sicily
- A tornado hit Marsala and nearby Sicilian towns after a summer heatwave, overturning vehicles, destroying a house, and damaging a school and other buildings.
- Two people were seriously injured, and a couple caught while driving were taken to hospital in serious condition.
- Officials said the event was almost unprecedented for Sicily, linked to extreme weather and the climate crisis, and special funds were promised for the emergency.
AI generated
MARSALA, Italy - Vehicles were overturned and two people seriously injured on Oct 9 when a tornado swept through the Sicilian city of Marsala and neighbouring towns, in what experts said was an almost unprecedented event for the Mediterranean island.
The whirlwind caused panic among residents as it destroyed a house and damaged a school and other buildings in Marsala and nearby Petrosino and Mazara del Vallo.
“It was almost like an American tornado, nothing this violent has been seen in living memory,” the head of Sicily’s Civil Protection agency Salvatore Cocina told Reuters.
Early in September the agency issued a warning saying the sweltering summer had led to a buildup of heat that could trigger extreme weather events in autumn.
“It once again highlights the issue of extreme weather events, a characteristic of recent years due to the climate crisis,” Cocina said.
Videos shown on local media showed a Marsala school with blown-out windows and a partially collapsed ceiling, while elsewhere in the town cars and trucks lay on their sides and power polls hit by the winds were strewn on the ground.
A couple caught in the tornado while driving were taken to hospital in a serious condition.
Sicily’s regional president Renato Schifani promised to allocate special funds to address the emergency, and an alert for possible extreme weather events remained in place for Oct 10, as rains and storms continue to affect the island. REUTERS

Israeli opposition needs Arab lawmakers to form government as majority oppose their participation: Poll
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:47:48 UTC
00:47:48 KST

Lina Altawell
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Israel’s Jewish opposition would need the support of Arab lawmakers to form an alternative government to Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s, while a majority of Israelis oppose Arab parties joining the next government, according to a poll published Friday.
Poll results indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition would be able to form a government on its own in the election scheduled for 17 days from now.
Such a scenario could lead to another election several months later, an option Netanyahu may prefer if he fails to form a government.
A poll published by the Israeli newspaper Maariv showed that, if elections were held today, Netanyahu’s bloc and the Jewish opposition would each win 52 seats in the 120-member Knesset.
Arab parties would secure 12 seats, while the Reserve Party, led by Yoaz Hendel, would win four without having declared which bloc it would support.
A government requires the support of at least 61 lawmakers in the 120-seat Knesset.
Most leaders of the Jewish opposition parties have rejected cooperation with Arab lawmakers to form an alternative government to replace Netanyahu’s. 
Seat distribution
According to the poll, Netanyahu’s 52-seat bloc would comprise his Likud party with 20 seats, Itamar Ben-Gvir’s Jewish Power with eight, United Torah Judaism and Shas with seven each, Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism with six and Ofer Winter’s Amcha Israel with four.
The Jewish opposition’s 52 seats would be divided among Gadi Eisenkot’s Yashar party with 21, Naftali Bennett’s Together party with 13, Yair Golan’s Democrats with nine and Avigdor Liberman’s Yisrael Beiteinu with nine.
Arab parties would win 12 seats, with the Joint List led by Yusuf Jabareen taking seven and Mansour Abbas’ United Arab List securing five.
Hendel’s Reserve Party would take four seats without committing to either bloc.
The results indicate that support from Arab parties could enable the Jewish opposition to form a government in the event of a continued tie between the two main blocs. 
Majority oppose Arab parties joining government
The poll found that 59% of Israelis oppose an Arab party joining the government after the election, compared with 36% who support such participation, while 5% said they did not know.
By comparison, 53% supported the participation of an ultra-Orthodox Haredi party in the next government, while 41% opposed it and 6% were undecided. 
Preferred prime minister
In a direct contest between Netanyahu and former Israeli army chief Gadi Eisenkot, 46% said they preferred Eisenkot as prime minister, compared with 40% for Netanyahu, while 14% gave no clear answer.
Israel’s prime minister is not directly elected but is the person able to form a government backed by at least 61 lawmakers.
When respondents were asked to choose among several candidates for prime minister, Netanyahu received 38%, followed by Eisenkot with 24% and Bennett with 14%. All other candidates received less than 10% each.
Maariv said the poll was conducted by the private Lazar Research Institute among a random sample of 700 Israelis, with a margin of error of 3.7 percentage points.

30,000 bottles of wines from the 2023 vintage were taken from the Marchesi Antinori warehouse. Police suspect a professional criminal group.
In Tuscany, unknown perpetrators robbed the wine warehouse of the famous family company Marchesi Antinori, which has been operating since 1385. The criminals took around 30,000 bottles worth approximately €5 million in total. Italian media are calling it the largest wine theft in the country’s history, UNN reports, citing Bild.
Details
According to investigators, at least seven masked people broke into the warehouse in the city of Cortona last Saturday. They disabled the alarm system and surveillance cameras, then used the company’s forklifts to load wine onto two trucks. The theft was discovered only on Monday morning, when employees arrived at work.
The stolen wine included Solaia, Tignanello, and Guado al Tasso. All the bottles were from the 2023 vintage. In particular, the criminals took around 10,000 bottles of Solaia—one of Tuscany’s best-known and most expensive wines. Depending on the brand, one bottle costs approximately €120–300, while rare examples can be considerably more expensive.
Company head Renzo Cotarella believes that a professional criminal group may have been behind the robbery and could be linked to similar thefts at other wineries. He hopes the shipment can be found: two trucks carrying such a quantity of wine would be difficult to sell unnoticed.

INTERVIEW - Our goal is to ‘unseat’ Netanyahu; Arab turnout above 70% could prevent his return, Joint List leader says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:41:54 UTC
00:41:54 KST

- Yusuf Jabareen tells Anadolu alliance’s main goal is to unseat Netanyahu government in Oct. 27 election
- ‘Arabs will determine identity of next prime minister in Israel,’ he says
- Joint List leader says position on backing Gadi Eisenkot would be decided after election results and based on opposition’s political program
Joint List leader Yusuf Jabareen said a turnout of more than 70% among Arab citizens in Israel could prevent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu from forming another government in the Oct. 27 Knesset election.
“There is a strong and serious desire among Arab citizens to bring down this government through the ballot box,” Jabareen told Anadolu in an interview, describing Netanyahu’s government as “fascist and occupying.”
Recent opinion polls have projected about nine seats for the Joint List in the 120-member Knesset.
The alliance brings together the Democratic Front for Peace and Equality, the National Democratic Assembly and the Arab Movement for Change.
Netanyahu has headed the current government since late December 2022. 
‘We have suffered greatly’
“If the turnout among Arab citizens rises above 70%, Netanyahu will not be able to form a government,” Jabareen said.
“Over the past four years, we have suffered greatly: a genocidal war on the Gaza Strip, terrorism by Israeli occupiers in the occupied West Bank, policies of repression and restrictions on freedoms, land confiscations and home demolitions,” he said.
“Arab citizens have increasingly become aware of the danger posed by the government and its policies,” Jabareen said. 
“There is a strong and serious desire to bring down this government by going to the ballot box, and we hope turnout will reach unprecedented levels,” he said.
He argued that a strong Joint List showing would help prevent the return of a government led by Netanyahu with National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir and Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich.
Recent polls indicate that neither Netanyahu’s bloc nor the Jewish opposition bloc is currently projected to secure the 61 seats required to form a government.
Jabareen said that gives Arab lawmakers a potentially decisive role.
“Arabs are the ones who will determine the identity of the next prime minister in Israel,” he said.
“Polls show Netanyahu’s bloc receiving around 52 seats and the opposition bloc the same number. Therefore, we in the Joint List will undoubtedly be an important force in deciding several questions, including who will be Knesset speaker and who will form the government.”
“The alliance would use any parliamentary strength it gains to protect the issues of our people including equality for Palestinians inside Israel and broader Palestinian concerns,” he said. 
Backing opposition not decided
Polls suggest the Jewish opposition would need support from Arab parties to form a government, although most opposition leaders have rejected such cooperation.
Asked whether Arab lawmakers would be prepared to support Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot in forming a government, Jabareen said it was too early to announce a position.
“After the results are announced, we will assess the situation and see how the different blocs take shape,” he said.
“We want to hear the political program of whoever seeks to be the alternative to Netanyahu.”
Jabareen stressed that simply replacing one political figure with another without changing policies would not be enough.
“We are seeking real change, and we hope to hear an actual change in the political positions of the opposition parties,” he said. “We will make the responsible leadership decision based on what serves our people.” 
Goal is to unseat Netanyahu government
Jabareen said the parties making up the Joint List agree on one central objective: “Unseating Netanyahu and removing his government from power.”
He described the government as “far-right and fascist,” saying the alliance viewed its potential return as a serious threat because of its wars, discrimination and what he called “apartheid policies.”
“We feel these elections are decisive and may even be existential because they relate to our status as Palestinians inside Israel and also to the future of the Palestinian people as a whole,” he said.
Asked whether the Joint List could significantly boost participation among Arab voters, Jabareen said the alliance was seeing growing interest.
“In all our meetings with our people, we hear this desire, and we also hear their assessment of the danger of this government and its policies,” he said.
“Arab turnout in the previous election did not exceed 55%,” Jabareen said.
“We are optimistic that there is growing awareness among our voters of the importance of raising turnout,” he said. “A turnout exceeding 70% could truly be the guarantee for bringing down this government.”
“We are working around the clock to achieve unprecedented turnout in this election because that is the only thing that will guarantee that this extremist, racist and occupying government does not return,” he added.
The United Arab List, led by Mansour Abbas, is contesting the election separately and is projected by polls to win five seats.
Arab citizens make up around 20% of Israel’s population of 10 million, while polls project Arab parties to secure between 12 and 14 Knesset seats.
Higher Arab voter participation could also affect the ability of smaller right-wing parties to clear the electoral threshold, potentially reducing Netanyahu’s chances of assembling a governing coalition.
The Oct. 27 election comes as Netanyahu faces corruption charges, including bribery, fraud and breach of trust.
The International Criminal Court issued an arrest warrant for Netanyahu in November 2024 on charges of war crimes and crimes against humanity in the Gaza Strip.

Britain leads biggest NATO undersea effort since Cold War
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:40:40 BST
00:40:40 KST

Britain is the lead nation for a NATO programme to bind frigates, uncrewed underwater vehicles, surface relay nodes and satellite links into a single interoperable network, described by the officer running it as the alliance’s most significant undersea domain awareness initiative since the Cold War, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Commodore David Burton, who directs the anti-submarine warfare Smart Defence Initiative and advises the Royal Navy on the AUKUS second pillar, set out the problem the Allied Underwater Battlespace Mission Network exists to solve, and did it in one line.
He said: “I like to say we’re trying to deliver an Internet of Things in the underwater landscape. The problem is we’ve got lots of things and no internet.”
The physics of the ocean is what makes the undersea battlespace different, whether the task is protecting critical underwater infrastructure, hunting submarines, clearing mines or fighting on the seabed itself. What the programme aims at is a federation of bottom-mounted sensors, uncrewed underwater vehicles, uncrewed surface vessels and air vehicles, working alongside conventional warships.
Commodore Burton was blunt about what happens if the alliance lets the market take its own course. “The growth in uncrewed systems is exponential, and the challenge as an alliance is, do we sit back and allow that to happen and to take shape? And if we do so, I think there’s only one thing we can guarantee, and that is that we won’t be interoperable,” he said.
The architectural shift underneath that is the one navies have been circling for a decade. “How do we transition from what I describe as a small number of very large assets, conventional assets, to a very large number of small assets? Architecturally, it’s totally different,” he said.
Open architecture is a phrase he has little patience with on its own. “People blandly talk about open architecture, but the truth is we need something that truly is open and something that we can test and validate against. And that’s the piece of the jigsaw that’s missing,” he said, and the same logic governs the next stage of the work. “Standards alone are not good enough. We need to be able to validate them, and that’s the test and reference environment.”
Twelve nations sponsor the programme and he expects that to reach fifteen, with Australia, Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Portugal, Spain, Sweden, the United Kingdom and the United States taking part, and Finland, Belgium and Greece either joining or observing. NATO’s maritime research centre and Maritime Command are signatory stakeholders.
Industry comes in through the Mangrove consortium, led by Saab Kockums and running to ten partners. British involvement is substantial, with Saab UK, BlueBear, S2IX and the University of Plymouth alongside Fincantieri’s IDS, CETENA, FlySight, GraalTech and Miraya.
The reference architecture was delivered this year, and the programme has now moved into a second phase worth more than thirty million to build and validate the test and reference environment, running to 2028. The architecture is intended to end up codified as an alliance-wide standard.
Validation of all of it happens at sea, against a calendar that is already set. REPMUS 27 in Portugal anchors the trials, Dynamic Mongoose 27 covers operational integration in the North Atlantic, and Task Force X Arctic takes high-latitude uncrewed underwater operations into the High North next July, with interim events in November and February.
The sheer number of these is becoming a problem of its own, he says. “Everywhere we look, there are operational experiments popping up. This is a big drain on industry, and we really have to orchestrate these to maximise the impact of them,” he said, describing them as good opportunities for companies to prove what they can do.

Who Is Angela Paxton? Ken Paxton’s Estranged Wife Wades Into Texas Senate Battle—Without Mentioning Him
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:40:21 UTC
00:40:21 KST

Angela Paxton, the estranged wife of Texas Attorney General and Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton, has waded into the state’s hotly contested Senate race by encouraging Texans to vote Republican in the midterm elections—while avoiding directly mentioning her husband.
Angela Paxton—who filed for divorce last year, alleging adultery—long remained mum on the race, in which her husband is facing off against Democrat James Talarico. Over the summer, she declined to share with the New York Times whether she would vote for Ken Paxton in the November election.
But as Talarico continues to hold a slim lead over her husband in most polls and Election Day draws closer, she has been speaking out to urge voters to back the GOP when they head to the voting booths next month.
In a speech to a group of Republican women in mid-September, she said that the Republican Party has “some vulnerabilities on our ballot,” but urged them to still vote for the party’s candidates “even if we’re mad at it.”
“I’ll be honest with you, I think Republican women will decide this election, because some of those vulnerabilities, I think, have been particularly alienating to women that hold our values,” she said. “When I say we have to win, I mean we have to win all those races. We have to keep all of those seats.”
“It’s not the people—it’s the seat,” she continued. “Because we have more control over that seat and the future when we control the seat, when it’s still in the family, even if we’re mad at it. But if we lose it to the other team, the nuances that we want to fix with maybe a certain candidate are nothing compared to what it’s going to take to get it back.”
And she is now sharing a similar message in a new ad, in which she talks about, in her own words, “the elephant in the room.”
“People have asked my thoughts about this election and it turns out, I have some. Let’s talk about the elephant in the room,” Angela Paxton opens the ad by saying.
“In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team—it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” she says. “Either we hold every Republican seat or we hand the future of Texas to the other team. That’s why I’m voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3. Let’s hold the line together.”
She does not speak about Ken Paxton or the Senate contest outright in the ad. The ad was funded by Texas PAC, which is tied to a super PAC that backs a Republican majority in the upper chamber.
Here’s what to know about Angela Paxton, and the significance of her wading into the midterm elections.
Who is Angela Paxton?
Angela Paxton, a Republican, has served in the Texas state Senate since 2019. She was previously a math teacher and school counselor.
She and Ken Paxton have been married for nearly four decades, but last year, she announced that she filed for divorce “on biblical grounds,” stating that, “in light of recent discoveries, I do not believe that it honors God or is loving to myself, my children, or Ken to remain in the marriage.”
In her divorce petition, Angela Paxton alleged that her husband “has committed adultery” and said that the two of them had stopped living together “as spouses” by June 2024.
A spokesperson for the Texas state senator told the Times over the weekend that the divorce proceedings are still underway.
What is the significance of Angela Paxton wading into the Texas Senate race?
Political experts tell TIME that the ad featuring Angela Paxton suggests that the Republican Party is worried about her husband’s chances of winning the Senate race.
“The fact that the need was felt to reach out to [Texas state senator Angela Paxton] to obliquely vouch for her now estranged husband is pretty remarkable, and an indication of the extent of concern that Republicans are feeling in this race,” says Joshua Blank, the research director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas at Austin.
Most polls show that Paxton is trailing—by a very slim margin—behind Talarico. If Talarico wins the Senate race, it would be the first time that a Democratic candidate has won a statewide election in Texas in more than three decades.
Paxton’s campaign has been shadowed by several scandals and controversies that have arisen throughout his political career, including allegations of infidelity, a fraud indictment, and an impeachment trial on charges of bribery and abuse of office. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing. The fraud charges against him were ultimately dropped after prosecutors and Paxton agreed to a deal, and he was acquitted of all charges against him in his impeachment trial by the Texas state Senate.
Political experts say that President Donald Trump’s low approval ratings—particularly how voters feel about his handling of the economy—could also be impacting Paxton’s performance in the polls, as well as an unusually tight gubernatorial race in Texas.
“Nationwide, we know it’s a difficult environment for Republicans. That’s playing out in Texas too, though Texas is more Republican than most states and so there’s more of a buffer,” says Kirby Goidel, a professor of political science at Texas A&M University.
According to data shared by CNN Chief Data Analyst Harry Enten on air earlier this month, Paxton’s net popularity is the lowest among several Republicans vying for key Senate seats next month.
“[Paxton is] in a tight race like other Republicans, but he’s in a tighter race in a worse situation because, I think, of the baggage that he brings to the campaign,” Goidel says.
Goidel says that, if you’re the Republican Party looking at these polls, “you say, what does Ken Paxton have to do to win this race?”
“Well, the first thing he has to do is secure Republican support,” Goidel continues. “I think having his wife come on and send that message that this is the team game, not an individual game, and we need all the players on the field, is a … signal [from the party of] ‘Hey, we need you all to come on board and vote for this guy; you may not like it, but we need you.’”
Blank also says that the ad featuring Angela Paxton “is not so indirectly addressed at giving women, but in particular Republican women who might have apprehensions about supporting Ken Paxton, with permission to do so.”
A New York Times/Siena University poll conducted at the end of September found that more men who are likely voters in Texas said they would vote for Paxton than women who are likely voters in the state, at 51% compared to 40%. Blank points out, though, that there’s a gender gap in partisanship in American politics more generally—women tend to be more likely than men to align themselves with the Democratic Party, while men tend to be more likely than women to align themselves with the Republican Party.
Blank notes that “polling has indicated a consistent gap in enthusiasm among Republican voters.”
“Republican women in particular might be a soft spot in the coalition, and if anything, this ad indicates that that’s likely the case,” Blank says.

Myanmar’s Leaders Tried to Erase My Rohingya Identity 11 Years Ago
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:39:00 UTC
00:39:00 KST

In July 2015, I was invited to the residence of U Aung Thaung, a senior and influential leader of Myanmar’s Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP), in Naypyidaw. We discussed the approaching general elections and parliamentary nominations for the constituencies in northern Rakhine state.
What happened during that meeting has remained outside the public record for more than 11 years. I want to disclose it now because the political question at its center – the recognition of Rohingya identity and rights – remains unresolved. It is also relevant to how ASEAN engages with Myanmar’s military leadership today.
I was elected to Myanmar’s house of parliament, the Pyithu Hluttaw, from Buthitaung township of Rakhine state in November 2010 as a USDP candidate. In the summer of 2015 I was preparing to secure my office for another term. But, during our private conversation, U Aung Thaung proposed a condition that went far beyond ordinary electoral politics.
As I recall it, he told me that he, the USDP leadership, President U Thein Sein, and then Commander-in-Chief Min Aung Hlaing did not accept “Rohingya” as an ethnic identity. He urged me to stop advocating for that identity and to persuade my constituents to identify themselves as “Bengali” instead. He presented this change as a pathway toward obtaining citizenship documentation and restoring political participation. He also advised me to give a media interview stating that “there is no Rohingya but Bengali,” without mentioning our private meeting and his name.
My parliamentary nomination, he indicated, depended on my willingness to support that position.
I refused.
I could not ask my constituents to surrender their identity in exchange for the possibility of receiving documents, voting rights, or another parliamentary term. Political representation should protect the rights of a community, not become an instrument for bargaining those rights away.
U Aung Thaung encouraged me to consult my constituents and reconsider. I subsequently informed community leaders and constituents about the conversation. They supported my position and we were all on the same page. I did not disclose the meeting to the media at that time because of the political consequences of making such an account public while living in Myanmar.
During my visit, I saw large portraits of President Thein Sein, Min Aung Hlaing, and nationalist Buddhist monk U Wirathu in an office at the residence. An assistant told me that the office also served U Wirathu whenever he comes to Naypyidaw. These are my recollections of what I saw and I was told 11 years ago.
The statements about Thein Sein and Min Aung Hlaing were made to me by U Aung Thaung. I cannot claim that I heard either man personally authorize the proposal. But U Aung Thaung confirmed the proposal with Union Immigration Minister U Khin Yi, today’s USDP chairman and speaker of Pyithu Hluttaw, over the phone in front of me.
The central proposition was unmistakable: I was being asked to abandon public advocacy for the identity of the people I represented as a condition of continuing my political career.
On August 4, 2015, I resigned from the USDP. Two days later, I applied to contest the upcoming Pyithu Hluttaw election as an independent candidate for Buthitaung.
On August 22, the Maungdaw District Election Subcommission rejected my candidacy. Its decision concluded that my parents had not been Myanmar citizens at the time of my birth in 1965. I appealed, together with concrete documents, to the Rakhine State Election Subcommission, which upheld the rejection on September 1, 2015. The Union Election Commission subsequently affirmed the decision, communicating its ruling in a letter dated September 6, 2015.
This outcome presented a profound contradiction in my political life.
The same Union Election Commission had formally recognized me as an elected member of parliament following the November 7, 2010 election. Its recognition certificate, dated January 10, 2011, identified me as the elected representative of Buthitaung and recorded my citizenship card.
Five years later, election authorities found me ineligible to stand for the same parliamentary seat because they now considered the evidence of my parents’ citizenship insufficient.
The State Election Subcommission acknowledged that my father possessed a national registration card, which serves as a primary document for full citizenship, and that my maternal grandparents also held national registration cards. Nevertheless, it concluded that those records did not adequately establish the citizenship qualifications required under the election laws.
I maintained that I had submitted the same family citizenship documentation in both electoral processes. The surviving recognition certificate and 2105 rulings represent contrasting official outcomes, although a complete comparison of the underlying applications would require examination of the original 2010 candidate file.
I believe the circumstances of my exclusion cannot be separated from the political pressure I experienced over my Rohingya identity. But the official election decisions do not themselves establish that my refusal of U Aung Thaung Thaung’s proposal caused my disqualification.
In November 2015, I publicly described the disenfranchisement of Rohingya voters and candidates in an opinion article for the New York Times. What I did not reveal then was the private conversation that had proceeded my departure from the USDP. I am revealing it now not simply to revisit my personal experience, but because it illuminates a continuing political problem.
For decades, Rohingya identity has been contested by successive Myanmar authorities, often through the characterization of the community as “Bengali” migrants. Questions of citizenship, documentation, and political participation have been intertwined with that dispute. The consequences extended beyond elections.
The mass atrocities committed against Rohingya in 2017 drove hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people into Bangladesh and intensified international demands for accountability. The Myanmar military coup in February 2021 subsequently plunged the country into wider political and humanitarian crisis.
Today, the Rohingya question cannot be treated as an isolated refugee-management problem. It is connected to Myanmar’s broader failure to establish an inclusive political order in which citizenship and fundamental rights are protected without discrimination.
This why ASEAN’s diplomatic engagement with Min Aung Hlaing deserves close scrutiny.
Regional governments have legitimate reasons to maintain channels of communication concerning humanitarian access, armed conflicts, migration, and regional security. Diplomatic contact is not necessarily equivalent to recognition or endorsement. But engagement must be judged by what it achieves for people affected by Myanmar’s crisis.
For Rohingya, discussions of repatriation are incomplete unless they address the conditions that forced people to flee and the rights they must be able to exercise upon return. A refugee cannot be expected to regard return as durable when questions of identity, citizenship, personal security, and political belonging remain unresolved.
ASEAN should therefore make these issues substantive elements of its discussions with Myanmar’s authorities. They include equal citizenship rights, recognition of the right to self-identification, meaningful political participation, protection against further atrocities, accountability for grave violations, and conditions for voluntary, safe, dignified, and sustainable return. The wider realities of Myanmar’s conflict must be taken into account. The aspirations of people resisting military rule, the safety of civilians across the country, and political future of ethnic communities cannot be separated from efforts to resolve the Rohingya crisis.
My experience in 2015 taught me how readily the question of identity could become a condition imposed upon political participation. The documents from my parliamentary career show that official recognition in one election offered no assurance of eligibility in the next.
Eleven years later, I remain convinced that Rohingya rights cannot depend on whether individuals agree to relinquish the name by which they identify themselves.
ASEAN cannot settle Myanmar’s political future on its own. But it can insist that engagement address the rights and security of the people whose lives are at stake.
A sustainable future for Myanmar requires more than meetings among political leaders. It requires a political order in which no community must choose between its identity and its rights.

Edgewing opens first GCAP engineering site in Turin
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:38:06 BST
00:38:06 KST

The joint venture designing the next generation fighter for Britain, Italy and Japan has opened an engineering site in Turin, the first of three planned facilities, with British and Japanese sites due to follow in the coming months, according to Edgewing.
Turin is the first additional Edgewing site to open for engineering work since the joint GCAP Agency and Edgewing headquarters was established in Reading last year. All three global sites will play the same role as engineering hubs contributing to delivery of the programme.
The company says the site will sustain thousands of highly skilled engineering jobs in the region through its workforce and supply chain. Engineers from all three nations will work there, with the initial cohort made up of secondees from Edgewing’s three partner companies, some of whom have moved their lives and families as far as ten thousand kilometres from Japan to Italy.
Edgewing set out what the aircraft they are working on is meant to do. The fighter will feature sensing and communications equipment, artificial intelligence support for pilots and the latest stealth technology, flying surveillance and strike missions at long range in heavily contested airspace. It will also contribute to the strategic operating picture and direct drones and other assets in the battle as a flying team captain.
Marco Zoff, the chief executive of Edgewing, said: “Our new site in Italy is the latest step in Edgewing’s rapid growth as an organisation, as we scale up the company across our three nations. Ready to disrupt the defence industry by delivering dramatically quicker than previous generation programmes, the innovation and energy we can access here in Turin will underpin our acceleration.”
Giuseppe Lupoli, general manager of Edgewing in Italy, said: “GCAP represents the next generation of technology, and this new site represents an opportunity for many to join Edgewing and work on some of the world’s most advanced digitally-driven engineering. I look forward to welcoming colleagues from across our three partner nations to Turin as we embark on this journey together.”
Lorenzo Mariani, chief executive and general manager of Leonardo, said: “GCAP will ensure technological sovereignty for generations to come and I am proud that hundreds of engineers here in Turin, and thousands more around the country, will contribute to its success. Leonardo is proud to support Edgewing as the programme continues to drive technological development and long-term economic growth.”
Edgewing launched in 2025 as the industrial lead and design authority for the GCAP aircraft, and signed international contracts worth more than six billion euros with the three-nation GCAP Agency this year. The company is delivering the programme’s advanced concept and assessment phase while scaling to bring work together from the three national programmes, with the design and development phase to follow.
Ownership is split equally between BAE Systems in the United Kingdom, Leonardo in Italy and Japan Aircraft Industrial Enhancement Co in Japan, and the company will remain the design authority for the aircraft throughout its service life.
In Italy the new site has been placed alongside Leonardo, which has a long history of combat air technology research and development in Turin that Edgewing says it will draw on.
The United Kingdom site is one of the two still to open, and will sit alongside the Reading headquarters instead of replacing it. BAE Systems does the bulk of its combat air work at Warton and Samlesbury in Lancashire, where the Tempest demonstrator has been under construction. The programme replaces Typhoon in Royal Air Force service and F-2 in Japanese service, with an in-service date of 2035, and the three governments established the GCAP Agency in 2024 to act as the single customer.

French students vow to keep up protests as UN voices 'concern' over violence
French student unions vowed on Friday to keep up the fight even as the government registered a "marked slowdown" in a protest movement that has rattled the country for over a week. The UN human rights agency called for de-escalation, voicing concern over violent clashes with police that have caused severe injuries among teenage protesters.
Students in France were largely back in the classroom Friday following days of protests demanding better education and school conditions, as the UN voiced "concern" over the sometimes violent clashes.
Tens of thousands have taken to the streets across France since students in late September began blocking entrances to high schools, which led to squads of riot police being deployed.
The students – most aged 15 to 18 – have complained of absent teachers, overloaded timetables, dilapidated classrooms and buildings that cannot cope with rising temperatures.
More than 6,800 people have been detained since the start of the demonstrations, of whom 86 percent are minors, the justice ministry said Friday.
A government source told journalists that the cost for damage caused by the demonstrations was "at least 30 million euros".
The United Nations said Friday it was watching the events "with concern" and urged people on all sides to remain peaceful.
"We are following with concern incidents related to the student protests and high school blockades in France, some of which have turned violent," said Shabia Mantoo, spokesperson for the UN human rights agency.
Read moreFrance suspends the use of stun grenades after student protester loses hand
While the demonstrations have been largely peaceful, some protesters have started fires and vandalised bus shelters.
In response, police have used tear gas, batons and blast balls, leading to accusations from rights groups and the students themselves of a disproportionate use of force.
Police have opened 18 internal investigations into allegations of misconduct.
After a 15-year-old lost a hand on Monday after police fired a stun grenade, the government has suspended the use of the weapon.
'Marked slowdown'
The government source said Friday the authorities were seeing a "marked slowdown" in the movement, and told journalists that most of the injured high school students "were not hurt by police action (but were) students who injured themselves accidentally" during the protests.
But many students told AFP they were not relenting. Organisers have called for large-scale demonstrations next week.

Yabloko was the only party that campaigned in the September 18–20 elections with anti-war slogans. Portugal PM cautions judiciary not to get political over US use of air base
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:35:00 KST

Portugal PM cautions judiciary not to get political over US use of air base
LISBON, Oct 9 - Portuguese Prime Minister Luis Montenegro argued on Friday the US use of the Lajes Air Base during the Iran conflict was fully legal and urged the judiciary not to make political judgments, after prosecutors opened an inquiry last week into the government's authorisation to use the base.
The probe, triggered by a complaint from a leftist opposition party, adds a legal dimension to a politically sensitive issue. Several European nations have restricted or refused US military aircraft access to their airspace or bases in connection with the war in Iran.
The left-wing opposition has criticised the centre-right minority government for allowing US military transit flights to use the Lajes base, in the Atlantic Azores archipelago, during the Iran war. Spain, France, Italy, Austria and Switzerland have all imposed restrictions, much to Washington's chagrin.
"Obviously, everyone can make political judgments about decisions, with the exception of the judiciary, which should not make political judgments," Montenegro told lawmakers during a parliamentary debate, a day after meeting US Secretary of State Marco Rubio in Lisbon.
He added that he respected the ongoing investigation and was "very calm as regards compliance with all applicable legal rules".
The government has said Portugal was not involved in the conflict and that the use of the Lajes base complied with international law, having been authorised only after assurances from Washington that any operation would be defensive, necessary and proportionate, and limited to military targets.
Portugal's prosecutors are bound by the principle of legality, requiring them to investigate alleged wrongdoing when there are sufficient grounds to do so, unlike in some jurisdictions where prosecutors have broader discretion to decide whether a case should proceed. REUTERS

One person to ten thousand cameras, warns Augur co-founder
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:32:10 BST
00:32:10 KST

A British analytics company wants the cameras already watching the country’s critical sites to recognise hostile activity for themselves and pass what they see between each other, with no new hardware installed anywhere, co-founder and chief executive Harry Mead told the UK Defence Journal at the Apex Europe conference in London.
Asked to describe the company, Mr Mead said: “We are a national security analytics platform dedicated to integrating and connecting legacy sensor networks and pushing to the absolutely cutting edge for the purposes of beating the innovation curve of adversaries when it comes to threats to critical national infrastructure and our national security at large.”
“It’s not just visual sensors. We really can integrate any sensor or any source of structured or unstructured data, but I think there’s a huge opportunity to start with in just making our visual sensors, our CCTV, and our cameras smarter,” he said.
He put the number of attacks on critical facilities by Russian actors at around two hundred between February 2022 and April this year, with a further hundred and twenty since, a rise he described as forty per cent over six months. “This is the new playbook, and a lot of this can be spotted by an operator who is watching the right monitor at the right time,” he said.
“But the problem is, on average, we’re looking at 10,000 cameras to every one person who’s able to monitor them. We just don’t have the ability to keep an eye on every single threat that is facing us, whether it is our critical infrastructure or our streets, our transportation, our energy grids,” he said.
“For Augur, we integrate with these systems, and we change the way they reason about physical space, about human movement through physical space, and also what is anomalous behaviour,” he said. “You’re essentially creating a world in which these cameras can reason as a human would, and then talk to each other. So you’re able to create a huge level of networked intelligence.”
Asked where the company would be by the time Apex comes round in 2030, Mr Mead said the current work is integrating with as many parts of critical infrastructure as humanly possible, and the step after that is the networked piece.
“If someone does set fire to an energy grid or attack a vulnerable community, they’re not able to then rely on the fact that the state can’t conduct a fire investigation for two, three weeks, and they get out of country,” he said. “We can stop their movements there and then, and we can get a response immediately to that. We can massively improve the safety of everyday citizens and our national security without changing a single device.”
“And this is, I think, the critical final point. We do not have time to install new hardware when it comes to sensing architecture. The number of threats, the number of attacks, is just too vast. We have to learn to do more with what we’ve got, and that is the whole point of Augur. It’s taking what is existing and future-proofing it for decades to come.”
On what a customer gets by coming to Augur, Mr Mead put the weight on proving it in front of them. “First and foremost we aim to build trust with our customers. So instead of telling them this is what we do, this is what you get, trust our word for it, we say to them, give us a challenge nothing’s been able to solve, or tell us some things that your current system does not do well, and where your vulnerabilities are, and give us a week,” he said.
“And in one week, I guarantee we can turn around and show them how we can solve it, and we can integrate. Even if we’re not doing it yet, we can integrate a new capability that will solve that. That willingness to show that the technology works, but also that we’re there to solve their problems, not tell them what their problem should be, develops a real sense of trust and a real desire to use the application.”

====================================================================================================

New anti-jamming antenna on Russian Geran-4 drone resembles design by Chinese company Harxon, The Insider finds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:31:05 UTC
00:31:05 KST

Photos and video of a 32-element CRPA antenna removed from a Geran-4 drone that crashed in Ukraine have recently been circulating on Telegram. Until now, Russian drones had been equipped with devices containing no more than 16 elements. The appearance of a 32-element antenna on a Russian UAV means it could now be significantly harder for Ukraine to counter Geran and Gerbera drones using current jamming techniques.
An analysis by The Insider found that the antenna closely resembles a design associated with the Chinese company Harxon and bears factory markings pointing to Alabuga, a special economic zone in Russia’s Republic of Tatarstan that has become a major production hub for Geran attack drones.
These specialized antennas are critical to the navigation of Geran and Gerbera drones when an adversary is jamming satellite signals. The more elements an antenna has, the more electronic-warfare systems it can potentially resist (while also making the device larger, more complex, and more expensive to manufacture).
On Sept. 30, Ukrainian electronic-warfare specialist Serhii “Flash” Beskrestnov published photos of the new 32-element antenna from a Geran drone, and other Telegram channels later posted additional images and videos of the device. Observers quickly noted that the devices appeared to have been mass-produced specifically for the Alabuga plant, as the “ALB” marking was engraved into the housing rather than printed on a sticker.
After analyzing images of the new 32-element antenna from the Geran-4, The Insider concluded that its external design closely resembles products made to Harxon specifications. One indication is the similar arrangement of the antenna’s output connectors. At the same time, the rough finish on the metal section of the housing and the serial number engraved directly into the casing — a feature also seen on some 16-element antennas — suggest that production may have been localized.
An analysis of other recent images of Geran electronics posted on the Ukrainian military-trophy marketplace reibert.info indicates that components marked “ALB” are undergoing a similar evolution. An increasing number of drone-control components carry Russian-language stickers, which may indicate that they are being assembled in Alabuga (at least at the level of so-called screwdriver assembly) using Chinese-made printed circuit boards.
Based on expert assessments and analysis of images of various components recovered from Russian drones, the development model for Geran and Gerbera systems may work as follows:
- small trial batches of finished electronics are first purchased through popular online marketplaces
- manufacturers are then selected based on how well their equipment performs under operational conditions, including electronic jamming
- the electronics are subsequently ordered in large quantities directly from the factory
- and finally, the design may be licensed either for assembly in Russia from prefabricated components or for full domestic production.
Last year, The Insider found that the Chinese company Harxon had become the main supplier of multi-element satellite-navigation antennas to Alabuga. This year, The Insider published an invoice sent from Harxon to a volunteer with the Nordsint project who had posed as a procurement officer for Russia’s military-industrial complex. The invoice covered seven-, eight-, and 16-element antennas, and also made it possible to interpret customs records from the previous year more accurately, as official customs data had listed questionable per-unit prices.
The Insider also identified two Harxon employees working with Russian customers — Masha Wu and Anthony Zheng — and in correspondence, they replied that the company was developing a 32-element antenna. After that investigation, antenna manufacturer Harxon was sanctioned, prompting protests from Chinese officials. US pledges tens of millions to UN bodies in Geneva, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

US pledges tens of millions to UN bodies in Geneva, sources say
GENEVA, Oct 9 - The United States has pledged tens of millions of dollars to UN organisations in Geneva, sources said - a move diplomats said showed Washington still wanted to maintain some engagement with the global body that it has repeatedly criticised.
Two diplomats and a UN source told Reuters the US had sent pledge letters to several UN organisations, including the Geneva-based World Meteorological Organization and the CITES body overseeing trade in wildlife.
The US State Department confirmed it had made a payment to the UN without giving details on the amounts.
“This payment should not be mistaken for satisfaction with the status quo. It reflects recognition of reforms achieved — and an expectation of many more to come,” a US State Department spokesperson told Reuters.
PLEDGES COINCIDE WITH NEW US AMBASSADOR
The Trump administration had slashed funding to the UN and left many commitments unpaid, as it accused the UN of waste, inefficiency and failing to fulfil its potential to broker peace deals.
But it has been making moves this year to pay off a significant proportion of its debt, in a bid to maintain influence and also to keep up its voting rights at a time when a new Secretary-General is being chosen and when China's influence is rising.
Under Article 19 of the UN Charter, a member state can lose its vote in the General Assembly if its arrears exceed the amount due for the preceding two full years.
The new US pledges also coincide with the September arrival in Geneva of US ambassador Todd Steggerda, a lawyer and former Navy pilot.
The payments could help stabilise UN agencies that have implemented severe cutbacks in Geneva.
Delayed or unpaid US contributions can be crippling for UN bodies that have long relied on Washington as their top funder, prompting some to reassess their priorities.
The World Meteorological Organization, set up in 1951 to coordinate global weather data, confirmed it had received a 15.1 million CHF ($18.18 million), covering what the US owed to the agency for 2024. That payment maintained US voting rights in that body.
Washington also pledged an extra 2.2 million CHF to the WMO, the body said, although 2025 and 2026 fees are outstanding, a spokesperson said.
CITES confirmed it received a funding pledge from the US on September 24, without giving the amount.
A spokesperson for the International Labour Organization, owed more than 250 million CHF ($300.88 million) by Washington, said it has not received a pledge.
Diplomats welcomed the pledges, saying that it indicated some level of UN commitment and to topics such as weather and wildlife not typically seen as US priorities.
“It shows at least they have a political interest in keeping the system going,” said one diplomat.
It was unclear what portion of the overall debt to UN agencies the payments represented.
For the UN general budget, a payment of $725 million this month represented less than 20% of the more than $4 billion that the UN said in May the United States owed - though Washington has said that total figure is much lower. REUTERS

BERLIN, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The number of business insolvencies in Germany rose 6.9 percent year-on-year in the first seven months of 2026, official data showed Friday, as prolonged economic weakness and high operating costs continued to weigh on companies in Europe's largest economy.
A total of 15,185 corporate insolvencies were registered between January and July, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis).
In July alone, the number of insolvencies climbed 8 percent from a year earlier to 2,373. The number marked the highest level for the month since 2013, according to the German Chamber of Commerce and Industry (DIHK).
"Every 19 minutes, a company in Germany files for insolvency," said Marc Evers, a small and medium-sized business expert at the DIHK, warning that the figures showed the economic recovery was not reaching large parts of the economy.
Evers said the modest economic upturn risked being short-lived, as it was driven largely by debt-financed government spending rather than a broad-based improvement in business conditions.
He urged policymakers to accelerate structural reforms, saying high energy costs, labor expenses and excessive bureaucracy continued to weigh heavily on companies and hold back investment.
Destatis figures showed that transport and storage businesses were particularly hard hit, recording 85.5 insolvencies per 10,000 companies during the first seven months of the year, followed by the hospitality and construction sectors.
More recent figures indicated that insolvency pressures remained elevated. According to a closely watched insolvency tracker released Thursday by the Halle Institute for Economic Research (IWH), corporate insolvencies rose 13 percent year-on-year and 9 percent from the previous month in September.
The September figure was 85 percent higher than the average for the same month in the pre-pandemic years from 2016 to 2019, the institute said. ■

Xinhua Headlines: Drones tackle toughest rural delivery stretches in China
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
23:28:31 CST
00:28:31 KST

*Express delivery now reaches more than 95 percent of China's administrative villages. In some rural areas, however, getting a parcel to the village requires more than just one mode of transport.
*In Zizhong County in southwest China's Sichuan Province, for example, drones are being used on routes where winding roads make the last leg of the journey slow. This county currently has 131 drone routes serving 131 villages and plans to extend them to all 301 villages by the end of the year.
*Some 300 km away in Quxian County, drones are also being tested on the return journey, carrying farm produce from villages to township delivery points.
CHENGDU, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Express delivery now reaches more than 95 percent of China's administrative villages. In some rural areas, however, getting a parcel to the village requires more than just one mode of transport.
In Zizhong County in southwest China's Sichuan Province, for example, drones are being used on routes where winding roads make the last leg of the journey slow. This county currently has 131 drone routes serving 131 villages and plans to extend them to all 301 villages by the end of the year.
Some 300 km away in Quxian County, drones are also being tested on the return journey, carrying farm produce from villages to township delivery points.
SHORTER WAY IN
The route from Guide Town to Tongjiazui Village in Zizhong requires a delivery vehicle to travel 9.9 kilometers, which takes about 19 minutes, while a drone on this route covers 5.7 kilometers in roughly 6.5 minutes.
Around 85 percent of Zizhong is hilly, and many villages lie on slopes or in river valleys. Some remote villages previously received parcels only once every two or three days. In places without village service stations, residents sometimes had to travel to town to collect them.
Rao Yurong, who grows blood oranges in Yueliangxia Village, recently received a battery-powered sprayer she had bought online. It took the drone around seven minutes to fly from the township station to the village. Notably, Rao previously spent nearly an hour riding an electric bike to town and back to collect a parcel.
JD Logistics opened 78 routes in Zizhong in June and has since expanded the network to 131.
Drones handle only the last section of the journey. Trucks still carry parcels over long distances and from county-level facilities to township stations.
This service also relies on facilities and staff on the ground. Township landing sites and village collection points have been set up, with local workers handling parcel collection and sorting. Sichuan has also introduced financial support for eligible low-altitude logistics projects.
Similar services are being used where water, rather than hills, slows deliveries. In east China's Jiangsu Province, 32 rural drone routes are in regular operation. One route to Mudun Island on Hongze Lake has cut delivery time by approximately 50 minutes compared with the previous ferry-based service.
MAKING RETURN TRIPS COUNT
Most drones flying into villages still fly back empty. According to JD Logistics, about 99 percent of return flights on rural routes carry no cargo.
Quxian is trying to change this.
In August, local villager Yu Fengying sent several kilograms of peanuts and sweet potato starch noodles to relatives and friends outside the area. Instead of riding an electric scooter to town, she used a drone that had just delivered parcels to the village.
About eight minutes later, the package reached a central landing point in town and entered the conventional express network.
JD Logistics plans to expand this service across Quxian and use return flights to carry local products including daylilies, lemons and plums.
Farm produce requiring fast transit may be among the more suitable shipments.
During the 2025 sweet cherry harvest in Hanyuan County, Sichuan, drones carried fruit from mountainous areas to a mail processing center in around 15 minutes. Conventional vehicles needed one to two hours for the same trip.
In the course of a month, more than 550 flights transported 7,586 packages of cherries weighing a total of 22.76 tonnes.
For fresh fruit harvested within a short season, saving an hour or more in transport can help reduce the time between picking and onward shipment.
WHERE DRONES MAKE SENSE
The faster trip does not yet cost less.
On one Zizhong route, JD Logistics puts the comprehensive cost at roughly 5.6 yuan (about 83 U.S. cents) per parcel by drone, compared with 4.4 yuan by vehicle.
Drones carry approximately 30 percent of their available payload on average, while almost all return flights are empty.
Zhang Jianping, director of a low-altitude air traffic institute at Southwest Jiaotong University, said drones are most useful in places where mountains or water make ground transport difficult. Only a few such services have so far reached a scale that can support commercial operations, he noted, while most are still used alongside conventional transport.
Zhang said western mountainous areas have demand for transporting farm produce, daily necessities and engineering supplies, because difficult terrain, large elevation changes and limited road access can make ground transport slower or harder.
Fangxian County in central China's Hubei Province, meanwhile, is using several transport methods rather than relying on one. A national rural-delivery pilot project there uses conventional vehicles, autonomous delivery vehicles, drones and combined passenger-freight-express mail services, depending on local conditions.
Since the pilot began, average operating cost has fallen by 0.2 yuan per parcel, while daily inbound village mail volume has risen by 16.3 percent and outbound volume by 48.9 percent, according to the State Post Bureau.
In Sichuan, drones are also being used to carry matsutake mushrooms, cherries and highland strawberries, as well as bamboo, power-grid components and construction materials.
JD Logistics plans to expand rural drone services to more than 50 counties and districts across the provincial-level regions of Sichuan, Chongqing, Yunnan and Guizhou, all located in southwest China.
(Video reporters: Lu Youyi, Yang Hua and Xue Chen; Video editors: Hong Ling, Roger Lott and Li Qin)■

ASHGABAT, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Leaders of the member states of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) on Friday adopted a declaration marking the organization's 35th anniversary, which underscores the CIS's commitment to promoting strategic partnership among its member states.
The document was signed during a meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State in Turkmenbashi, Turkmenistan.
The declaration said international relations are undergoing profound changes and that the CIS is committed to promoting strategic partnership among its member states and serving as a unique platform for dialogue and cooperation based on equality and mutual respect.
In the field of security, the declaration identified key areas for joint action, including combating international terrorism, transnational crime, illicit arms and drug trafficking, corruption and money laundering, human trafficking and illegal migration, as well as preventing and responding to emergencies and combating cybercrime.

The meeting's outcome also included the decision that Uzbekistan would assume the CIS chairmanship in 2027, with Turkmenistan and Azerbaijan serving as co-chairs. The next meeting of the CIS Council of Heads of State is scheduled for October 2027 in Bukhara, Uzbekistan.

The missile is the easy part of deep precision strike
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:28:05 BST
00:28:05 KST

Defining deep precision strike as the ability to put a missile on a target hundreds of kilometres away is thinking about the problem too narrowly, a capability presentation at the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Luke Wattam, co-founder of the British company Labrys Technologies, titled his talk the missile is the easy part and spent it arguing that reach matters more than range.
He said: “Deep precision strike is not simply about range, it’s about reach. It’s about being able to sense, understand, decide and act against an adversary at distance, potentially through a combination of military, commercial, partner and proxy capabilities.”
What that definition covers is a good deal wider than a missile. It might be a long-range weapon, or sabotage conducted by a proxy, or forward-deployed systems, or local actors generating intelligence, or a partner force identifying a target that a commercial sensor then confirms before a military effector delivers the result.
His point was that none of those have the weapon in common. “The common denominator is not the weapon. The common denominator is the ability to extend trusted command and control beyond the traditional boundaries of our military network,” he said. “The easiest part of deep precision strike is actually the missile. The much harder problem is everything that has to happen before the missile is fired.”
The questions he listed are the ones a targeting cell has to answer about a source it cannot see. How do I know the person giving me this information is who they say they are, how do I know where they actually are, how do I know the image they have sent has not been manipulated, how do I know the person receiving my instruction is authorised to act, and how do I hold any of that together when they are thousands of miles away in a place I cannot physically verify.
Procurement, in his account, is not currently set up to answer any of them. “We procure radios. We procure military networks. We procure encrypted communication systems. And we ask, how secure is this radio? But we don’t necessarily ask a much bigger question, which is what is the technology ecosystem, embedded security and trust primitives that I need to conduct a full-spectrum hybrid operation?” he said.
Commercial messaging applications have become important in recent wars because they do something military systems struggle with, which he described as opening the funnel. In Ukraine the people who suddenly matter include a farmer with a drone, a civilian with a smartphone, a local soldier, a resistance network, a commercial satellite provider, a logistics company, a conventional unit, a special operations team and a government agency.
“We spend extraordinary amounts of money buying encrypted military communication systems, and then when the crisis actually happens, people reach for Signal or WhatsApp. Why? Because they’re free. They’re encrypted end to end. They are familiar. They’re easy to download. And quite critically, because you can put them into the hands of a partner, a contractor, an irregular force or a civilian in seconds,” he said. “The user has already voted. The user is telling us what they need.”
Those applications were never designed to be the command and control backbone of a military operation, which is the gap he says sits between the two options most forces actually have. One is the traditional military green box, secure and controlled but limited by the number of trusted users a force can equip, train and manage. The other is the commercial application, ubiquitous and encrypted but without any trust architecture behind the conversation.
Mobilising people at scale is where he thinks the distinction bites hardest, since a population cannot be asked to become signals specialists first. A call to arms that does not require anybody to join the military is how he put it, with someone photographing enemy equipment and that image reaching an authorised operator with its provenance attached. Farmers and hauliers already own machinery capable of blocking a route, and nobody doubts they can move a tractor.
Labrys builds a platform called Axiom around this argument, and has signed a short-range precision strike and sensor effects integration programme intended to carry the same approach from a phone out to sensors and weapons.
His conclusion was about where the advantage in all of this will actually come from. “The future of deep precision strike is not simply going to be about building a bigger missile. It’s going to be about building a wider, deeper and more trusted network around that missile,” he said. “The decisive advantage will belong to the force that can extend its reach without losing its trust.”
