Hurricane Isaias strengthens into Category 3 storm with US in its sights
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:25:27 UTC
00:25:27 KST

Hurricane Isaias strengthens into Category 3 storm with US in its sights
The major storm is expected to make landfall along the US Gulf Coast later on Friday or early Saturday.
Hurricane Isaias has strengthened into a major Category 3 storm as the Gulf Coast of the United States prepares for potentially “life-threatening” conditions.
The US National Hurricane Center (NHC) said on Friday that Isaias was packing winds in excess of 193kph (120mph) and was expected to continue strengthening over the course of the day. A Category 3 storm, considered a major hurricane by the NHC, is capable of causing devastating damage.
Isaias, the first hurricane of the Atlantic season, is expected to make landfall in the US later on Friday or early Saturday between Mobile Bay on the Alabama coast and Choctawhatchee Bay in Florida, the center said.
When it comes ashore, the storm is forecast to weaken quickly as it moves inland into the southern US. But the NHC urged local governments to quickly prepare for the dangerous conditions that Isaias could bring.
“Preparations should be rushed to completion as the weather will go downhill quickly today”, forecasters said. “While the storm is not expected to make landfall at peak intensity, it is likely that Isaias will still be a significant hurricane when it reaches the coast”.
Storm surge as high as 2.7 metres (9 feet) could impact an area extending from the Alabama-Florida border to Grayton Beach, Florida, creating “dangerous” conditions for residents who live along the Gulf shoreline. Isaias is projected to produce 10.1 to 20.3cm of rainfall (4 to 8 inches) across the coast, with possible localised totals of up to 38cm (15 inches).
“This is a life-threatening situation”, the center warned. “Persons located within these areas should take all necessary actions to protect life and property from rising water and the potential for other dangerous conditions.”
States of emergency have been issued by governments in parts of Alabama, Florida and Georgia. Several coastal counties along the Gulf of Mexico have mandatory evacuation orders.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who has requested an emergency declaration from US President Donald Trump ahead of Isaias’ landfall, warned residents in the state’s panhandle region of potentially significant storm damage.
“But the surge is really what puts a lot of people’s lives in jeopardy if they haven’t heeded evacuation orders, and does the most significant damage from these storms,” DeSantis said. “Everywhere from Pensacola all the way into the Big Bend section of north Florida, you could see storm surge. So please take caution of that.”
“And we always say you hide from the wind, but you run from the water. When the water’s rising and things are happening, it’s a very, very difficult conundrum — and you do not want to be caught in that,” he added.
On Thursday, the US Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) urged Gulf Coast residents to prepare for the hurricane and said its offices were “fully engaged”.
As of early Friday, the NHC said Isaias was centred about 386km (240 miles) south of Pensacola in Florida and moving north-northeast at 24kph (15 mph).

Russia wants NL to hand over ICC judges
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Russia has asked the Netherlands to hand over nine International Criminal Court (ICC) officials who were convicted in absentia last year.
The prosecutor’s office in Moscow requested the extradition of the court’s president, Tomoko Akane, and other staff members for their involvement in the arrest warrant of Russian president Vladimir Putin.
The ICC issued the warrant for Putin’s alleged involvement in “the war crime of unlawful deportation of children” from occupied Ukraine.
The ICC has also issued an arrest warrant against Maria Alekseyevna Lvova-Belova, Russia’s commissioner for children’s rights.
In December, a court in Moscow convicted Akane and others in absentia, sentencing them to prison terms ranging from 3.5 to 15 years.
Japan, Akane’s home country, said the request was regrettable. “Measures targeting individuals connected to the ICC are unjust and unacceptable,” Masanao Ozaki, the country’s deputy chief cabinet secretary, said.
The United States has also sanctioned 13 staff members, including Akane, over the investigation into alleged Israeli war crimes in Gaza.

Israeli settlers flank Palestinian cafe with Israeli flags

Breadcrumb
Israeli settlers flank Palestinian cafe with dozens of Israeli flags
Israeli settlers have planted dozens of Israeli flags at the entrance of a streetside Palestinian cafe in the occupied West Bank, obscuring it from one side in what its owner described as a blatant act of intimidation.
The coffee shop in the small village of Luban al-Sharqiya sits along the West Bank's main north-south traffic artery, used by both Palestinians and the approximately 500,000 Israeli settlers who live in the territory.
In recent years, settlers, some of whom have waged a campaign of violence and intimidation against Palestinians in a bid to force them off their land, have planted flags along the road and in close proximity at village entrances or near Palestinian landmarks.
When Mueiyyid Hussein went to open his coffee shop on Thursday morning, he discovered settlers had placed dozens of Israeli flags up against its entrance, packed together and obscuring it from southbound travellers.
"They are not leaving us alone. They have blocked the view of my shop," said Hussein, owner of the Luban al-Sharqiya Coffee Shop and Rest Area.
While Reuters was interviewing Hussein, a settler who he said was responsible for planting the flags drove by, filming Hussein and the shop with his cellphone. Reuters was not able to reach the man for comment.
"He drives away and then comes back to check whether I have removed any flags. He says he will come back and shut down my shop," Hussein said.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the placement of the flags.
UN bodies and most countries view Israel's settlements and settler outposts as illegal under international law regarding military occupations.
The West Bank has seen a sharp rise in settler violence against Palestinians and settler seizures of Palestinian land and resources. The military says it does what it can to clamp down on the violence, something Palestinians reject, pointing to numerous instances in which troops stand by as attacks play out.

Russian losses in the war with Ukraine.
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:22:12 UTC
00:22:12 KST

This publication is divided into two parts:
Bi-weekly Summary. A text summary, updated every two weeks, in which we report on what we have learned about recent losses and the frontline events that led to the deaths of Russian soldiers.
Interactive Infographics. The second part provides visualisations of the losses since the start of the war, showing, for example, where the dead served or which regions they came from. We update the data for these graphics, while the accompanying text is refreshed but remains largely the same.
A detailed description of our method for estimating total deaths using Probate Registry data can be found at this link.
Last update to the named list: October 9, 2026.
Last update to the Probate Registry estimate: May 9, 2026; estimate as of late December 2025
Full named list and a map of verified losses is available here: 200.zona.media.
Since September 21, we added more than 17,000 individuals to our list of Russian losses. As we explained in previous updates, this is unrelated to the current situation at the front: we process reports of missing persons and confirm the deaths of the missing via official state registries.
Additionally, for this update, we have confirmed the deaths of 20 officers during the massive missile strike on Donetsk on August 26. Read the report here:
The map below shows the distribution of casualties across Russia’s regions. These are absolute figures and have not been adjusted for population or number of military units.
You can filter the map to show total losses, losses by branch of service, or the home regions of mobilised soldiers who were killed.
In most cases, official reports or visual cues like uniforms and insignia allow us to determine a soldier’s branch of service, or how he came to be in the army (mobilised, volunteer, prisoner, etc.).
The chart below compares these different groups of servicemen.
From early summer and into the mid-fall season of 2022, volunteers bore the brunt of the losses, which is strikingly different from the situation in the initial stage of the war: in winter and early spring, the Airborne Forces suffered the greatest damage, followed by the Motorised Rifle troops.
By the end of 2022 and the beginning of the next year, losses among prisoners recruited into the Wagner PMC increased markedly. They were formed into “assault groups” to overwhelm Ukrainian positions near Bakhmut.
By March 2023, prisoners became the largest category of war losses. After the capture of Bakhmut, there have been no cases of mass use of prisoners so far.
By September 2024, volunteers once again emerged as the largest category among the KIA. This shift reflects a cumulative effect: prison recruitment had significantly waned, no new mobilisation had been announced, yet the stream of volunteers continued unabated.
By October 9, 2026, the death of 7,833 officers of the Russian army and other security agencies had been confirmed.
The proportion of officer deaths among overall casualties has steadily declined since the conflict began. In the early stages, when professional contract soldiers formed the main invasion force, officers accounted for up to 10% of fatalities. By November 2024, this figure had dropped to between 2–3%—a shift that reflects both evolving combat tactics and the intensive recruitment of volunteer infantry, who suffer casualty rates many times higher than their commanding officers.
Officers killed in Ukraine
To date, the deaths of 15 Russian generals have been officially confirmed: five Lieutenant Generals, seven Major Generals, two who had retired from active service, and one Ukrainian SBU general who had fled to Russia.
Lieutenant General Oleg Tsokov, deputy commander of the Southern Military District, was killed in July 2023—the first officer of that rank to die in the war. In December 2024, Lieutenant General Igor Kirillov, head of the Nuclear, Biological, and Chemical (NBC) Protection Troops, was killed by a bomb in Moscow. Lieutenant General Yaroslav Moskalik, a senior officer in the General Staff’s Main Operational Directorate, was killed by a car bomb in a Moscow suburb in April 2025. In December 2025, Lieutenant General Fanil Sarvarov, head of the Operational Training Directorate of the Russian General Staff, was killed in Moscow by a car bomb. On March 31, 2026, Lieutenant General Alexander Otroschenko, commander of the mixed aviation corps of the Northern Fleet, was killed in the crash of an An-26 transport aircraft in Crimea.
Two deputy army commanders, Major General Andrei Sukhovetsky (41st Army) and Major General Vladimir Frolov (8th Army), were killed in the first weeks of the war. In June 2022, Major General Roman Kutuzov was killed in an attack on a troop formation.
Major General Sergei Goryachev, chief of staff of the 35th Combined Arms Army, was killed in June 2023 while commanding forces against the Ukrainian counter-offensive in the Zaporizhzhia region. In November 2023, Major General Vladimir Zavadsky, deputy commander of the 14th Army Corps, was killed near the village of Krynky.
In November 2024, Major General Pavel Klimenko, commander of the 5th Separate Motorised Rifle Brigade (formerly the “Oplot” Brigade of the so-called Donetsk People’s Republic), was fatally wounded by an FPV drone.
In July 2025, a strike on the headquarters of the 155th Naval Infantry Brigade killed at least six officers, including the Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Russian Navy, Mikhail Gudkov.
The two retired generals on the list are Kanamat Botashev, a pilot who had been dismissed for crashing a fighter jet and was fighting for Wagner PMC when his Su-25 was shot down in May 2022, and Andrei Golovatsky, a former Interior Ministry general serving an 8.5-year prison sentence (but maintained his rank) who was killed in June 2024.
On March 17, 2026, SBU Major General Volodymyr Lyapkin was killed in the Kherson region. Until February 2014, Lyapkin headed a department in the Ukrainian special services, but after the victory of the Maidan revolution, he fled to Russia. After the war began, he served in the occupation administration of Kherson and then transferred to the “Bars-33” unit.
The date of death is known in 259,800 cases. While this data does not capture the full daily reality of the war, it does suggest which periods saw the most intense fighting.
Please note that data for the most recent months is most incomplete and will change significantly in the future.
The age of the deceased is mentioned in 261,300 reports. For the first six months of the war, when the fighting was done by the regular army, the 21-23 age group accounted for the most deaths.
Volunteers and mobilised men are significantly older: people voluntarily go to war over 30, and the mobilised are generally over 25.

Who wrote your book? ‘Human-authored’ book labels gain ground amid AI scandals

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

Who wrote your book? ‘Human-authored’ book labels gain ground amid AI scandals
- Human-authored book labels are gaining ground, as publishers and writers seek clearer proof of human writing.
- Schemes in Britain, France and Germany now certify books as human-made.
- Some in the trade welcome the labels, but others warn that they are easy to dodge and say the industry needs deeper rules on transparency.
AI generated
FRANKFURT – Initiatives to label books as written by humans, and not artificial intelligence, are gaining ground following a string of scandals where authors were suspected of using the technology without admitting it.
Several labelling schemes, including from Britain, France and Germany, were being showcased at the world’s biggest book industry fair in Frankfurt this week, where the challenges posed by AI were hotly debated.
Among recent cases where authors allegedly used AI, the most high-profile is that of Haitian-Canadian author Thelyson Orelien, which has rocked the French-language literary world. He has denied the claims.
The affair was a “real earthquake” for the French book trade, said Charlotte Allibert, co-founder of Librinova, a self-publishing company and literary agency.
The French group runs a scheme under which authors can get their books assessed and then labelled as a “human creation” for a small fee, with about 200 works so far given the stamp.
Writers who want the label have their works run through AI detection software and undergo an interview with an auditor, who also checks the book personally.
“It’s reassuring for authors to know that we’re committed to this issue,” said Allibert. “More and more, authors are afraid of being suspected of using AI – self‑published authors even more so.”
‘Organic literature’
Another scheme is from British start-up Books By People, which this week announced its certification mark for human-authored works has been registered by the country’s intellectual property office.
To get the stamp, titles have to meet the group’s “organic literature” standards, which require the writing to originate from its author while allowing limited use of AI for tasks such as spelling or grammar checks.
“We want to create a comprehensive, transparent, reliable framework that publishers and authors can fall back on,” said Esme Dennys, the initiative’s co-founder.
“Anxiety around undisclosed AI use has increased in recent months. We have been getting a lot more interest from people all over the world,” she said.
Publishers sign up to the scheme for a fee, and can then request to get their authors’ books labelled with the Books By People mark.
The scheme launched with five independent publishers, and is set to announce more members in the coming months.
In the United States, writers group the Authors Guild has introduced a “human authored” certification mark.
It is a self-certification system that requires authors to sign a licence agreement, and so far around 6,500 titles have received the stamp.
Mounting scandals
The controversy surrounding Orelien erupted in September when an anonymous X account alleged the 38-year-old used AI to write his debut novel, It Was Either That Or Die, based on analysis of excerpts by AI-detection websites.
He has denied the claims and believes the attacks on his work are racially motivated, although the scandal led to him being dropped from France’s top literary prize.
There have also been a string of other cases in recent times.
Earlier in 2026, publisher Hachette cancelled the release of horror novel Shy Girl by Mia Ballard in the US and withdrew the book from sale in Britain over allegations of AI use.
In comments to The New York Times, Ballard denied personally using AI but said an acquaintance she hired to edit the book, which was originally self-published, used AI.
Despite the mounting scandals, some in the book trade view the idea of labels with scepticism.
Current schemes mostly allow a minimal use of AI, for example for research and grammar checks, but there are worries this could be open to interpretation.
There are also concerns it could be too easy to circumvent checks in the fledgling initiatives, and pass off AI-produced books as human-written.
Sebastian Guggolz, head of the German Publishers and Booksellers Association, said the book trade was struggling with what approach to take.
“There’s no simple ‘with AI’ or ‘without AI’,” he said at the book fair, adding that basic schemes to categorise how much AI was used to produce a title could fall short.
“The question has to go deeper,” he said. “It has to be addressed to each individual and to the entire industry: How do we want to make our practices transparent?” AFP

Details
ICC Deputy Prosecutor Nazhat Shameem Khan condemned the sanctions and said they would not stop the tribunal’s work.

Washington has sharply criticized the ICC over its issuance of arrest warrants for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, as well as over its previous investigation into the actions of U.S. military personnel in Afghanistan (which the ICC later closed).

Israel a rare dissenting voice as praise pours in for Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay
Advocates of human rights and international justice cheered, even as Israeli officials fumed, after South African jurist and former UN human rights chief Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday. The 85-year-old drew wide praise for decades of work, including investigating crimes in Rwanda, Israel and the occupied Palestinian territories.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Navi Pillay, a South African-born jurist and former UN human rights chief whose career has spanned from defending the rights of an imprisoned Nelson Mandela to leading a panel that found that Israel committed genocide in Gaza, won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote international law as it comes under attack.
Her win signals a high-profile rebuke to US President Donald Trump and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who have both rejected the findings of the UN commission she led on Gaza. The leaders also have been highly critical of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court; Pillay has worked at both.
Pillay’s work “is a source of hope and inspiration to all those who seek to bring about a more peaceful world”, said Jorgen Watne Frydnes, chair of the Norwegian Nobel Committee, in announcing her win in Oslo, Norway, as part of the peace prize’s 125th anniversary.
Read moreSouth Africa's Navi Pillay wins 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
The committee said it sought to strengthen international law at a time of conflict, and Watne Frydnes said Pillay’s award was a message to those seeking to undermine “the international rules-based system and the institutions”.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Pillay, 85, received the news while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, where the trials of Nazi war criminals helped lay the foundations of international law. She was in the same room where the trials were held when the prize was announced in Norway.
“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic Courtroom 600” of the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, she said.
She said efforts to weaken international criminal justice “endanger the progress painstakingly made since Nuremberg, and they risk returning us to a world in which power, rather than law, determines whose suffering matters”.
World leaders, she added, have a “legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war”.
Pillay chaired the Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory and Israel, which was created by the UN-backed Human Rights Council. The commission a year ago concluded Israel was responsible for genocide in Gaza with a specific intent to destroy Palestinians in Gaza.
Read moreIsrael is committing 'genocide' in Gaza, UN investigators say
Gaza was among Pillay’s first comments Friday after hearing she had won. “What’s happening there is genocide,” she said in Germany, to more applause.
The commission last year also found that the Israeli president, prime minister and former defence minister "have incited the commission of genocide”. Israel, which has refused to cooperate with the commission since it was established in 2021, has strenuously denied the accusations.
Pillay has repeatedly rebuffed critics who accused her of anti-Semitism or turning a blind eye to the Hamas attacks in Israel. Under her leadership, the commission also issued reports accusing Hamas of war crimes and violations of international humanitarian law during its Oct. 7, 2023, attack.
A senior Hamas official, Bassem Naim, in a statement Friday called the Nobel for Pillay a message of hope for Palestinians, especially in Gaza, that “humanity still resists the forces of evil targeting international justice”.
The Israeli foreign ministry, meanwhile, said in a statement that “if there were an award for lies, hatred, and blood libels, Navi Pillay wouldn’t just be a contender. She’d be a frontrunner”.
The ministry added on X that the award “isn’t a recognition of justice. It’s the grotesque weaponization of an award to legitimize anti-Israel hatred and prejudice”.
Champion of international law
It was a rare dissenting voice amid a chorus of praise for Pillay and the Nobel Committee’s choice, which UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said honoured those who fight to defend international law and human rights.
“For decades, she has been a champion of international law and human rights, and a steadfast, independent voice of justice amidst some of the most historic international legal cases of our time,” Guterres said about Pillay, a former UN rights chief.
“Today's prize is a tribute to all those working to uphold and defend international law, the rule of law and human rights, and secure peace, justice and human dignity,” he said in a statement.
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk, one of Pillay's successors in that post, hailed a “particularly poignant” award “at a time when human rights are under attack on so many fronts, including from those who wield enormous power”.
He added: “It is an award to all those who, around the world, dedicate their lives to the defence of human rights — often at great risk to their security.”

Pillay's win brings renewed attention to Trump’s ongoing feud with the International Criminal Court, where she served as a judge from 2003 to 2008. The Trump administration already has sanctioned 13 of the ICC’s staff members, among them key prosecutors and nine judges, including the court’s Japanese President Tomoko Akane.
In his speech to the United Nations General Assembly last month, Trump called the court an “out of control institution” and an “anti-American tribunal with no jurisdiction” over the US. He urged member states to quit the court.

Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war

Eritrean troops in Ethiopia raise fears of a regional war
October 9, 2026
Various sources have confirmed the presence of Eritrean armed forces in Ethiopia. An AFP report quoted a foreign security source, speaking on condition of anonymity, as estimating that 5,000 to 8,000 Eritrean soldiers were present in the northenmost state of Ethiopia, Tigray.
Meanwhile, Ethiopia and Eritrea have ramped up their war talk.
According to Reuters, the government of Ethiopia has written to the UN Security Council, calling for the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean troops from its territory.
In the letter, dated Oct. 8, Ethiopian Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos said the presence of Eritrean troops in Ethiopia left "no option but to defend itself against Eritrea,"
in a post on X on October 7, Eritrean Minister of Information Yemane Meskel had accused Ethiopia of "incessantly beating the drums of war."
Two days later, he wrote in Tigrinya, a working language of Eritrea and the main language of Tigray, that "the sovereign state of Eritrea is bound by blood and law." adding "woe to those who touch it."
This comes as the regional conflict in Tigray has deteriorated rapidly in recent weeks.
Some experts have suggested that Ethiopia may have intentionally triggered the escalation. Just last week, it expelled diplomats from Egypt and Eritrea, causing the latter to sever diplomatic ties altogether.
On Monday, when Abiy Ahmed was sworn in for another five years as Ethiopian prime minister, he stated that access to the sea was a priority. The statement fueled fresh speculation that he intends to take Eritrea's strategic port of Assab by force and prompted fierce reactions from the Eritrean side.
Abiy's internal opposition: Tsimdo and the Alliance for Survival
While the Ethiopian National Defence Forces (ENDF), aided by the Tigray Peace Force milita, have made significant advances and notably recaptured the Tigray federal state capital of Mekelle, opposition to Ethiopia has found new formats for collaboration.
One is the Tsimdo movement, named after a Tigrinya term that loosely translates as "engagement."
"The Tsimdo concept initially surfaced through cross-border peace initiatives involving activists, religious figures, and local communities in the Tigray and Eritrea border villages in 2025," Dr. Jalale Getachew Birru, senior East Africa analyst with the US-based conflict monitor ACLED, told DW.
It has since undergone several reconfigurations and now encompasses diverse groups within Ethiopia, mostly defined along ethnic lines and with long-standing grievances against the federal government.
The Ethiopian Peoples' Forces Alliance for Survival, or simply Alliance for Survival, that was proclaimed in September, stems from this movement. According to Jalale, the alliance aims at removing the current government and initiating a constitutional dialogue.
The new alliance says a lot about the long history of unresolved conflict in Ethiopia, said Abdurahman Sayed, an analyst at the Horn of Africa Centre for Regional Integration.
"The fighting inside Ethiopia has never stopped," Sayed told DW.
"With the Oromo Liberation Army, it's been going on for decades, with the Amhara, it's been going on for the last three years, at least. With the Tigrayans, the Pretoria agreement about three years ago was just a cessation of hostility that would have led to some kind of sustainable peace by addressing the root causes of the conflict — but it failed to do that, so they're back to the conflict situation now."
However, of the seven groups in the alliance, ACLED data shows that only three were involved in recent fighting: The Tigrayan Defence Forces (TDF), the Amhara Fano National Movement (AFNM), and a fairly recently formed ethnic Afar group called Ugugumo.
Joint declaration by Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, Somalia
The success of the Alliance for Survival would depend in large part on the support they get through external actors, according to ACLED. Those could include neighboring Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea, and Somalia.
"All these four countries have grievances against Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed's government," Sayed said.
"The Egyptians have issues with the Nile River and how it should be administered, including the dams that are already there and those planned to be built around the Nile River. The Sudanese also have their own concerns that Ethiopians are supporting the [Rapid Support Forces] militia, which is fighting the Sudanese army."
In the case of Somalia, the issue of sea access has sparked tensions. Landlocked Ethiopia has negotiated access to the port of Berbera in Somaliland . In 2024, it signed a memorandum of understanding with the breakaway region, causing uproar in Somalia, which considers the deal a violation of its national sovereignty. Turkish mediation was needed to calm things down.
"So all those neighboring countries have their own concerns and they feel this threat that is coming from Ethiopia needs to be tackled collectively."
On October 4, the leaders of the four countries issued a joint declarationthat didn't mention Ethiopia but seemed to send a strong signal. The leaders stressed the importance of international law, "particularly respect for the sovereignty, independence and territorial integrity of the states of the region."
And they maintained that "the governance of the Red Sea is the exclusive responsibility of the littoral states."
Although the leaders of Sudan, Egypt, Eritrea and Somalia vowed to promote "peaceful solutions to conflicts," the reality on the ground may prove otherwise.

US sanctions on ICC: a 'test of resilience'
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:19:41 UTC
00:19:41 KST

International Criminal Court faces 'test of resilience' as US imposes sweeping sanctions
The Trump administration has imposed sweeping new sanctions on the International Criminal Court as part of its campaign to dismantle what it describes as a "rogue" tribunal, threatening to cripple its operations. Following the move, the European Union said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".
US President Donald Trump's administration has imposed sweeping sanctions on the International Criminal Court that threaten to cripple its operations and spark fresh transatlantic tension.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the sanctions Friday, after the Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to South African prosecutor Navi Pillay, a former judge at the ICC and other international courts.
Read moreIsrael a rare dissenting voice as praise pours in for Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay
Here's a look at the likely impact of the sanctions, possible responses, and the reasons behind Washington's unprecedented move, which the court said was an "assault on the rule of law".
What is the ICC and what does it do?
Based in the Dutch city of The Hague, the ICC tries individuals suspected of the world's worst offences – war crimes, crimes against humanity, and genocide.
Established in 2002 by the Rome Statute, it currently has 125 members. Major powers such as the United States, Russia, China, India, and Israel are not members of the court.
It is governed by a strict policy of "complementarity", meaning it can only take on cases a suspect's home country is unwilling or unable to try itself.
Since its establishment, the court has convicted 15 people, with four acquitted. Critics say the court has focused too heavily on war crimes committed in Africa and failed to convict major political leaders.
However, its most high-profile current case concerns ex-Philippines president Rodrigo Duterte, the first former Asian head of state to stand in the ICC dock.
The court, housed in a shiny glass building on the outskirts of The Hague, employs around 900 staff from 100 nationalities.
It is often confused with the International Court of Justice, also based in The Hague, which settles disputes between countries.
What impact will sanctions have?
The Trump administration has already issued several rounds of sanctions against top ICC officials but these latest actions go further, targeting the entire court.
ICC officials are concerned about access to banking, credit card facilities, insurance, and especially technology, given a heavy reliance on US systems.
"We have been extremely dependent on US technology solutions, Microsoft or systems related to Microsoft," acting chief prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang told AFP in a recent interview.
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
"We are trying to find alternative means, maybe not as effective as the US technology, but at least to be able to maintain our independence, to be able to continue to work," said Niang.
The prosecutor, himself the target of sanctions, said they crippled daily life -- he was unable to book transport, hotels, or conduct banking operations.
But expanding them to the entire institution raises questions about the ICC's ability to pay staff, conduct investigations abroad, protect witnesses, and even operate its detention facilities.
"This is a test of our resilience," admitted Niang.
What can Europe do?
As the host city, the Dutch have a special responsibility to the ICC under the terms of a "Headquarters Agreement" signed in 2008.
This obliges the Netherlands to protect ICC facilities and staff, provide "any means of communication" and ensure "freedom of financial assets from restrictions".
In an unusually fiery speech last month at the United Nations General Assembly, Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "in my country, in my city".
"How can you possibly be opposed to prosecuting the very worst crimes? I believe there can be only one response: 'hands off the ICC'," said Jetten to warm applause.
Read moreEU will 'stand firmly' behind ICC chief as the US levies new sanctions
The European Union on Friday called the US sanctions "deeply regrettable" and said it was "ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work".
One possibility would be for the European Commission to deploy a legal instrument known as the "blocking mechanism".
This prohibits European firms from obeying the US sanctions "actively or by deliberate omission", giving the EU a potential means of cushioning some of the impact.
The EU blocking mechanism is seen as the "nuclear option", said Berendsen, adding that the Netherlands had nevertheless asked Brussels to prepare it.
Why is the US doing this?
The US is furious the court issued an arrest warrant for close ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, over alleged crimes in Gaza.
It is also concerned an ICC investigation into Afghanistan could result in accusations against US personnel.
Trump has upped his rhetoric against what he has called a "rogue institution" and "evil group of people" and the US has vowed to dismantle the court "brick-by-brick".
But even under less pugnacious presidents, Washington has never been a fan of the ICC and never considered joining.
The US has a law dubbed the "Hague Invasion Act", allowing it to take "all means necessary and appropriate" to defend US personnel or allies detained by the ICC.
In a clear swipe at Washington, Jetten vowed to defend the ICC "brick by brick" in comments just hours before the sanctions were announced.

Arctic-grade diesel is a separate area of focus for Ukrnafta.

As reported, Ukrnafta became the largest diesel fuel importer for the first time in its history in September, importing 105,000 tonnes, 3.3 times more than a year earlier.
Compared with August, the company increased its purchases by 37%, marking its highest monthly volume since the beginning of the year.
Ukrnafta is Ukraine's largest oil producer and operates across the full oil and gas production cycle, including exploration, oil and gas production, oilfield services and management of Ukraine's largest network of filling stations under the UKRNAFTA brand.
The company produces hydrocarbons from 1,789 oil and 167 gas wells.
The shareholders of Ukrnafta are Naftogaz of Ukraine and the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine. Since 2022, the company has been under state management and is implementing a large-scale business transformation.
In 2025, Ukrnafta became the leader of the extractive industry with revenue of UAH 99.6 billion, according to Opendatabot's Best Enterprises Index.
The UKRNAFTA filling station network is Ukraine's largest, with about 650 filling stations, and ranks among the top three by fuel sales volumes. The UKRNAFTA brand has consolidated networks previously operating under the Glusco, Shell and U.Go brands.

Siberian teen reportedly dies by suicide after studying and working at Alabuga, where drones are assembled for Russia’s war in Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:17:28 UTC
00:17:28 KST

Siberian teen reportedly dies by suicide after studying and working at Alabuga, where drones are assembled for Russia’s war in Ukraine
A 16-year-old in Novokuznetsk died by suicide after spending four months working and studying at the Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan, where drones are assembled for the war with Ukraine, the outlet Echo reported. Echo said it has obtained an appeal from the teenager’s parents (it does not specify to whom the appeal was addressed) and a death certificate.
A source told Echo that the teenager — identified by the outlet only as T., without his full name — was interested in drones and had wanted to study at Alabuga. The source said the administration at Alabuga “pressed very hard, demanded that he fulfill the plan, and forced him to work,” and that he also faced bullying within his group, where “there was hazing, and older students beat younger ones.”
In their appeal, the parents said their son had lived under “a regime of harsh military discipline and a lack of time for sleep and food, in constant strain on his emotional and physical strength.” They said that after he returned, he “became withdrawn, stopped smiling and enjoying things, complained of constant headaches, lost his appetite, and slept poorly.”
The parents also wrote that the teenager may have been driven to suicide “in connection with his involvement with Alabuga, which is confirmed by his intercepted correspondence with unknown persons.” They gave no further details about the correspondence. The parents cited the conclusions of a psychiatrist, who said the teenager was in a deep depression “caused by prolonged stress at Alabuga amid the emotional instability of a child’s psyche.”
The source said that after the teenager’s death, his parents contacted law enforcement agencies, which “send back form responses” and have shown no interest in investigating.
The Alabuga special economic zone in Tatarstan has been assembling drones based on Iranian Shahed models since 2023. Those drones are then used to attack Ukrainian cities. The zone includes Alabuga Polytech college, which draws students into assembling drones.

====================================================================================================

Polish parliament's lower house approves nighttime alcohol sales, advertising bans
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:17:09 UTC
00:17:09 KST

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Poland’s lower house of parliament, the Sejm, on Thursday approved legislation introducing a nationwide ban on nighttime alcohol sales, a blanket ban on alcohol advertising and higher fees for alcohol sales permits, the Polish news outlet Bankier.pl reported.
The bill passed with 400 votes in favor, nine against and four abstentions.
The legislation, drafted by the Left and considered alongside a proposal from the Poland 2050 parliamentary group, prohibits alcohol sales nationwide between 10 pm and 6 am.
Restaurants and other venues serving alcohol for consumption on the premises are exempt.
It also allows local authorities to impose additional restrictions on off-premises alcohol sales, including bans between 9 pm and 10 pm or between 6 am and 9 am.
The law prohibits advertising and promoting all alcoholic beverages, including beer.
Violations could carry fines ranging from 30,000 zlotys ($8,100) to 1 million zlotys ($270,000), or result in imprisonment.
Sellers will be required to check customers’ identification if there is doubt about their age and refuse sales if valid identification is not provided.
Alcoholic beverages sold in containers of up to 300 milliliters must be packaged in glass or metal.
The packaging must also display visible health warnings about alcohol consumption during pregnancy, drinking and driving, and the risks alcohol poses to people under 18.
The legislation also doubles permit fees for alcohol sales.
The fee for beverages containing up to 18% alcohol will rise from 525 zlotys ($142) to 1,050 zlotys ($284), while the fee for beverages containing more than 18% alcohol will increase from 2,100 zlotys ($567) to 4,200 zlotys ($1,134).
The Sejm also adopted amendments addressing the definition of alcohol promotion, distance sales and permits for games of chance used in alcohol advertising under existing rules.
The law is scheduled to enter into force on Jan. 1, 2027.

====================================================================================================

Franco-German relations: Steinmeier and Macron say their farewells and create a new momentum for Europe
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:17:00 UTC
00:17:00 KST

Steinmeier and Macron struggle to revive Franco-German ties
October 9, 2026
The German delegation passed through Paris without being hindered by the student strikes taking place on the streets of Paris. The motorcades moved through the French capital without disruption. Around the Arc de Triomphe and the Champs-Elysees, however, traffic was at a standstill for hours. Due to the high-profile visit, the streets were cordoned off over a wide area.
Emmanuel Macron had decided on a special gesture to send off Frank-Walter Steinmeier, his German guest: The military honors took place under the Arc de Triomphe. And so, early in the morning, the German national anthem rang out in the heart of Paris — amid sunshine and bitter cold.
It was a generous gesture of friendship and symbolism, yet it seemed to be from a bygone era. In both countries, populists on the political fringes are gaining support. In Germany, the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) ranks first in nationwide polls. In France, Emmanuel Macron could soon be succeeded by either Jean-Luc Melenchon of the far left or Marine Le Pen of the far right.
Added to this is an economic crisis that threatens prosperity. Unresolved issues of social justice are driving younger generations into the streets. At the same time, social media is increasingly becoming a tool of disinformation and "accelerating doubts about democracy," Macron said in Paris.
While the AfD may soon form its first state government in Saxony-Anhalt, President Steinmeier remained confident. He insisted that Germany would continue to "play a leading role in Europe" in the future and that Germans would remain good Europeans. But he did not say where he drew this certainty from. Questions from journalists were not permitted at the joint press conference at the Elysee Palace.
A future, but no plan
Political scientist Jacob Ross isn't surprised by this. Both Macron and Steinmeier lack a "genuine agenda for Germany, France, and Europe." Both represent political systems that "seek to respond to 21st-century crises with 20th-century solutions," said the expert on German-French relations at the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP).
Even though Steinmeier and Macron have different political styles, Ross sees parallels — especially where their policies have failed. One example of this is strategic foreign policy issues, such as dealing with Russia. "For a long time, they pursued a policy based on integrating Russia into Europe, and then both were overwhelmed by the events of 2022 and had to adjust their course," said Ross. Since then, both have merely reacted to current affairs, according to the political scientist.
Little support for Macron's ideas
Emmanuel Macron has made some bold moves for Europe, but without support from Berlin, says Ross. Germany's political leadership has long reacted with caution to proposals from Paris.
A joint initiative that both countries recently promoted to the European Commission is aimed at combating unfair competition. Countries that gain an advantage through unfair practices should face strict European measures.
Macron joined German Chancellor Friedrich Merz in speaking out in favor of this. Although China was not explicitly named, the initiative is seen to be primarily aimed at that country. Beijing uses enormous subsidies to support its companies, whose products flood the European market, while European firms continue to face barriers when trying to access the Chinese market.
Germany and France have also long sought greater cooperation in the defense sector. Yet major joint defense projects are making little progress. When the planned joint fighter jet, the FCAS, fell through in June, officials emphasized ongoing cooperation on the future MGCS main battle tank. And yet differences on this became apparent during the state visit.
As German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius arrived in Paris, French Chief of the General Staff Fabien Mandon stated during a hearing in the French National Assembly that Germany had decided to withdraw from the tank project. A day later, Mandon clarified that he had expressed himself ambiguously. But some observers believe that such misunderstandings are a sign of dissatisfaction on both sides — below the political level — regarding cooperation with the other partner.
It is this political level that often ends up having to set the record straight in such cases. This time was no exception: Pistorius firmly refuted the claim that the project was on the verge of being scrapped. "The MGCS project is not over; it is not dead; it has not been terminated by anyone — quite the contrary. It is a core project of Franco-German cooperation on land systems," said the German defense minister.
The focus is primarily on digital information processing in combat, as well as unmanned and automated systems. Germany and France would continue their cooperation, Pistorius insisted, and MGCS is an important future project for both countries and their armed forces.
The future of defense and space
On Friday, the presidents of France and Germany visited several facilities near Bordeaux that are closely linked to space exploration and nuclear deterrence. These include ArianeGroup, a Franco-German company that, among other things, manufactures the nuclear-capable M51 missiles for French nuclear submarines. The itinerary also included visits to startups that are looking far into the future.
It was unofficially reported during the visit that this focus of the trip was a personal priority for Macron. The French president has long spoken of a European dimension to France's nuclear deterrent. Considering announcements from the US saying it would reduce its commitment to Europe, his views are gaining increasing traction.
As early as 2020, Macron proposed a strategic dialogue on the role of French nuclear weapons in European security. Several countries, including Germany, have since expressed interest. Now, further steps are being considered. The focus is on what Macron once called "forward deterrence," such as joint military exercises and visits to strategically important locations. A permanent deployment of French nuclear weapons in other countries remains off the table. Furthermore, according to French nuclear doctrine, France always retains sole decision-making authority over the use of its nuclear weapons.
Steinmeier's two-day state visit to France ended on Friday afternoon. So far, there has been little sign of new momentum in Franco-German relations. This makes it all the more urgent for the successors to the two presidents to develop a shared vision for the future of the relationship between the two countries starting next year.
Macron and Steinmeier will step down from their posts almost simultaneously in 2027 after ten years in office. The state visit to France thus also served as a final joint meeting, marked by some ceremonial farewells.
This article was originally written in German.

US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, threatens to 'dismantle' it
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:15:11 UTC
00:15:11 KST

Rabia İclal Turan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The US on Friday imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC), Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced, hours after former court judge Navi Pillay won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize. 
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans. That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court," Rubio said in a statement. 
Rubio said Washington had deferred the designation "in hopes that the ICC would change course or would otherwise be restrained by States Parties," but neither had "taken meaningful steps to address our concerns." 
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC," Rubio said, calling on US allies that are members of the court "to rein in the court." 
"If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer," he added.
The ICC strongly rejected the sanctions, describing them as an assault on the rule of law. 
The court also urged its member states to ensure its continued operation. 
The announcement came hours after Pillay, a South African jurist who served on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008, won the Nobel Peace Prize for her work in international criminal justice. 
According to a State Department statement, the court was designated under Executive Order 14203, which President Donald Trump signed in February 2025 to impose sanctions on the ICC. 
As a result of the sanctions, all of the ICC's property and interests in property in the US or under the control of US persons are now blocked. 
The measures also bar US persons from providing funds, goods or services to the court unless authorized by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC). 
The sanctions also followed intensified US pressure on the court after it issued arrest warrants in November 2024 for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Israeli Defense Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged war crimes in Gaza. 
The US has also objected to a past ICC investigation into alleged crimes by US personnel in Afghanistan, which the court has since closed. 
Washington previously sanctioned ICC judges and prosecutors, including court President Tomoko Akane in August. 
At a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on July 31, Trump himself tied the Rubio's campaign against the ICC to Netanyahu at a Cabinet meeting at Camp David on July 31, saying it was not aimed at protecting him. 
"He's trying to defend Bibi and various other people," Trump said, referring to Netanyahu. 
The ICC has 125 member states. Neither the US nor Israel is a party to the court.

Open architecture or we cannot use you, say forces
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:14:52 BST
00:14:52 KST

Equipment that cannot be plugged into the command and control system the British Army already runs is unlikely to be taken forward, however good it is, a Royal Artillery officer told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Lieutenant Colonel Chris Billups was asked for a closing message to the companies in the room at the end of a panel on deep precision effects, and he gave them one line to remember.
He said: “Please think open architecture. If we can’t plug you in, we’re never going to get everything from one single source. We’re going to need multiple things from multiple vendors. If we can’t plug you into the architecture relatively easily, it’ll be difficult for us to pitch for you and to use you on the day of the fight.”
The Army has already run into exactly this. “We are more concerned about a plug-and-play approach. If an industry partner is developing something that either operates in a silo or stovepipe, we can’t plug it into the system, or we need another standalone system to operate it,” he said.
Doing it the other way produced an effect he called data blindness. “We had that really early on where we were almost getting data blindness, because the only way you could put a new missile or system or drone in was by putting another screen there and another decision and another person to watch it,” he said. “It doesn’t matter how exquisite the kit is. If you can’t plug into the existing C2 system, then it’s almost not worth taking on.”
His second theme was depth of magazine, which he said gets far less attention than mass does. If only a small percentage of what is fired gets through an integrated air defence, then the number of rounds behind the first salvo is what decides whether a campaign can be sustained. Asked how confident he is that NATO is heading in the right direction on interoperability, his answer was short. “The confidence level that we’re moving in the right direction is high,” he said.
Training as a multinational force by default has made British formations better at multinational targeting, in his account, and he was positive about the direction of travel in Eastern Europe while describing the organisations involved as still young. For immediate combat engagements, information security matters less because the information itself is perishable. Going deeper and more pre-planned is where national caveats and policy start to bite, since data sources cannot be revealed and material at the highest classifications cannot currently be pushed onto a NATO network.
He described a recent event at which a large number of nations shared information across a data fabric largely owned by NATO, with United States Army Europe and Africa holding the mechanism that allows classification to be derived and downgraded so material can move across the system. The arrangement is new, he said, but the future of it looks positive.
The same theme ran through what the two industry speakers alongside him had to say. Lukas Koester of SE3 Labs argued that armies have to force manufacturers to work together, since every company would rather its own sensor talked only to its own effector, and that where governments set the framework, as Ukraine has with Delta, interoperability follows. Bryan Grubert of Attalon said what his company needs most is visibility of what the prime contractors above it intend to build over the long term, instead of a succession of individual requests to tender.

Ukraine Uses Updated AN-196 RS and FP-6 Long-Range Drones — Zelensky
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:13:56 UTC
00:13:56 KST

An oil refinery in Ukhta, Russia, was struck by a modified AN-196 RS Liutyi long-range strike drone, which has a range of up to 2,500 km.
This was reported by Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
The upgrades to the Liutyi UAV may involve larger fuel tanks or design optimizations to reduce aerodynamic drag.
Meanwhile, the upgraded FP-1 long-range strike drone, which struck the Omsk oil refinery the day before, has been renamed the FP-6.
This upgraded drone was first deployed by the Ukraine’s Defense Forces back in July of this year.
Visually, the FP-6 features a new trapezoidal wing with a straight leading edge and a trailing edge that tapers toward the wingtips.
This wing geometry provides lower drag at cruising speed and distributes lift more evenly across the entire surface.
This has a positive effect on fuel consumption and significantly increases the drone’s flight range.
Earlier, Fire Point co-owner and chief designer Denis Shtilerman announced the introduction of drones featuring a new wing that also serves as a fuel tank.
This design allows the FP-6 to fly farther while retaining a more powerful payload, with a flight range of up to 3,400 km.
As a reminder, on October 9, the Ukraine’s Defense Forces attacked the Lukoil-Ukhtanaftopereborka oil refinery in Komi, 1,700 km from the border, where a massive fire broke out.
And on October 8, FP-1 drones struck Russia’s largest oil refinery in Omsk, more than 2,500 km away, which has already caused waiting queues at local gas stations.

The resolution issued by Italian

Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin wins PEN Writer of Courage award

Breadcrumb
Gaza playwright Ali Abu Yasin named PEN Writer of Courage 2026
Palestinian playwright Ali Abu Yasin, whose writing attracted global attention as he continued to work against the backdrop of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, was named English PEN's Writer of Courage 2026 on Thursday.
The award was in recognition for his work depicting the plight of the Palestinian people.
Speaking to The New Arab (TNA) following his win, Abu Yasin explained the significance of the accolade, particularly after enduring three years of Israeli bombardment, displacement. and personal loss.
"Unfortunately, I left Gaza only 35 days ago, having lived through three full years of war," the 62-year-old playwright said.
Abu Yasin, a veteran actor and theatre director from al-Shati refugee camp in the Gaza Strip, also described how the horrors he endured reshaped his art, prompting him to stop writing plays and instead document life amid Israel’s devastating war on his homeland.
"When a person spends three years under bombardment, fleeing death at every moment and enduring more than any human being should have to bear, they can lose their passion for almost everything in this world, even if the award itself means a great deal."
Despite the atrocities he witnessed and endured, Abu Yasin said the award was an opportunity to raise the profile of both his work and Palestine, expressing hope that art could deepen international understanding of life in Gaza.
He said it "elevates my standing and that of Palestine".
"It may open up opportunities and doors that will allow me to continue telling our story and sharing our cause with the world, so that we can live in peace and be recognised."
"I will keep trying to help the world understand Gaza, although I believe the world is already beginning to understand," he added.
"Simply recognising Palestinians creating art – whether as a writer, through theatre or through cinema – reflects the civilisation and culture of our people. It makes others recognise that Palestinians deserve freedom and the right to live with dignity."
Abu Yasin expressed hope that art would help international audiences better understand life in Gaza.
"I will keep trying to help the world understand Gaza, although I believe the world is already beginning to understand," he told TNA.
"Simply recognising Palestinians creating art – whether as a writer, through theatre or through cinema – reflects the civilisation and culture of our people. It makes others recognise that Palestinians deserve freedom and the right to live with dignity."
Before the war
For years before the war, Abu Yasin had used theatre to explore the Palestinian experience, including everyday life under occupation, the impact of war, and the power of art in resisting violence.
His work has also faced censorship, with some of his plays banned or restricted.
In 2008, he began writing The Gaza Monologues, a series depicting life in the besieged territory and highlighting both the joy experienced by Palestinians and the oppression they face.
The works have since been performed and translated around the world.
Since Israel launched its war on Gaza in 2023, Abu Yasin has increasingly turned to writing to document conditions in the territory, working alongside actors who forcibly rehearse their lines in displacement tents.
Last month, Abu Yasin left Gaza with the support of an artist residency programme in France.
He hopes to continue using his platform to speak out about the war and Israel’s decades-long occupation of Palestinian territory.
"I want to send a message to the artists in Gaza, my extended family: remain true to your pens and remain faithful to the great stage," he said.
"Keep the theatre alive. The breakthrough will come. Hold on to hope. This night must give way to dawn, and the dawn must shine, with the sun of Palestine rising alongside it."
Abu Yasin was nominated for the award by British academic and cultural critic Jacqueline Rose, the winner of the 2026 PEN Pinter Prize.
Rose praised his work in a statement, describing him as "the consistent chronicler of the harshness and cruelty of Palestinian existence".
She added: "I am bowled over by his courage and tenacity, the way he captures moments of humanity and resilience out of the dark, firing up a new generation never to give up on the future.”
According to English PEN, the Writer of Courage award “is awarded to an author who is active in defence of freedom of expression, often at great risk to their own safety and liberty, and shares the PEN Pinter Prize with the winner”.
English PEN is the UK branch of PEN International, a global association of writers dedicated to “championing freedom of expression and literary advocacy worldwide”.
The organisation operates independently of its US counterpart, PEN America, which has faced criticism in recent years over allegations that it failed to adequately support Palestinian writers.
The controversy prompted a boycott of the organisation and the resignation of Ethiopian-American novelist Dinaw Mengestu as PEN America's president.
More than 74,200 Palestinians have been killed in Israel’s war on Gaza, according to health authorities.
This equates to approximately 3.4 per cent of the territory’s estimated pre-war population, while 1.9 million Palestinians have been displaced, with widespread destruction leaving families without homes.

US hits ICC with sanctions hours after Pillay's Nobel win
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:11:05 UTC
00:11:05 KST

The US has imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, as the court called on member states to ensure it can continue to function.
The ICC said on Friday that it will continue to "fully discharge its mandate."
The court also said US sanctions are "aimed at disrupting the court's operations and at intimidating those who work for or cooperate with the court."
The ICC's deputy prosecutor, Nazhat Shameem Khan, condemned the sanctions and said they would not halt the tribunal's work.
"The sanctions are intended to undermine the rule of law internationally and the work that an independent judicial institution is doing," Khan said.
"Our work will continue across all our situations, our investigations and our prosecutions."
The US has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.
The move would go far further by potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
"President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement ahead of the official announcement.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off its resources and crippling its ability to operate."
Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
‘International law under political attack’
The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries, including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC's Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008.
In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to "issue a reminder" at a time when "judges and institutions of international law are under political attack".
"An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account, and the victims of abuse see justice served, is a precondition for a peaceful world," the committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
He did not provide further details, but a senior State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licences "to protect American interests", an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
‘Reining in ICC’
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court's registrar, Osvaldo Zavala Giler, called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called "blocking mechanism" that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the United States had delayed its sanctions, hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and who rely on American service members for their defence, to rein in the court," Rubio said.
"We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly," Rubio said.

Electronic warfare is driving the move to autonomy
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:10:52 BST
00:10:52 KST

The spread of localised electronic warfare across the front in Ukraine is what is pushing drones towards autonomy, the head of UK land at Helsing told the Apex Europe conference in London on Wednesday.
Mike Wilmot said: “We see the action of denial of GPS leads to the reaction of flying by FPV, so you don’t need GPS. That sees the counteraction of localised EW that denies comms, and with that exponential increase of EW, we see a corresponding move towards greater autonomy.”
Full autonomy is not there yet, he said, agreeing with the Ukrainian officer who spoke before him, and most Western militaries are watching the same sequence and working out how to respond to it. The British Army’s answer is its 20-40-40 construct, which moves the balance away from exquisite survivable platforms and towards the attritable and the consumable.
What that means for suppliers is more software-defined systems and lower unit prices. “It also means what the army calls affordable mass, and what most economists call value, much cheaper systems, where the expectation isn’t necessarily that it will return,” he said, describing the question Helsing is working on as how to deliver more platforms at a lower price per unit that still do what is asked of them in a heavily contested electronic warfare environment.
“One of the points that is not actually often discussed there is the ethical element of being able to send a platform forward without a human operator, as well as the efficiency element,” he said.
“There isn’t just a financial expense of sending an F-35 across the forward line of enemy troops. There is also a potential human expense, and if we have that safety confidence in a platform to be able to deliver its task, then there does become an ethical consideration of why send a human pilot or a collection of human pilots when you could first send autonomous platforms,” he said.
Safety works the same way in his account, since there are tasks where an automated process earns more confidence than a person, air defence engagement being the obvious case.
Helsing has about fifty people in an office in Ukraine, set up in response to feedback from the Ukrainian armed forces, and runs a monthly software update to the hardware platforms it has fielded. “The hardware isn’t necessarily changing very much over a protracted period of time, but the software is, and it’s only through that proximity to the end users,” he said. “They’re not going to be pushing much feedback for us. We need to be pulling it from them.”
Western militaries will have to get comfortable with contractors working closer to the fighting than they have in recent conflicts, he suggested, which is a commercial problem as much as a military one and an area where Ukraine offers a working example.
Asked what he would tell a national armaments director, he reached for a high street. “If people buy sweets, sweet shops will open on a high street. If they buy enough sweets, a sweet factory will open nearby. And if they buy even more, then someone will open a sugar refinery, and even dentists will start popping up,” he said, citing the phrase capital follows contracts from reflections on the writing of the strategic defence review.

A man won a three-year dispute over a parking fine by using ChatGPT as his lawyer
Kyiv • UNN
Rafal Goral challenged a £100 fine for a 16-minute delay in paying for parking. ChatGPT helped prepare the defense, and the case was closed.
A man who was fined £100 for not paying for parking quickly enough managed to get the fine cancelled after a three-year battle — with the help of ChatGPT, which acted as his lawyer. The Independent reports, UNN writes.
Details
In August 2023, 45-year-old Rafal Goral travelled to the coast, to the town of Newquay in Cornwall. He left his car in a pay-and-display car park on Tower Road and joined the queue for the parking meter.
According to the man, the machine did not accept payment by bank card, so he had to download the RingGo app and create an account. Because of the poor mobile connection, the process took some time.
Two weeks later, Goral received a £100 fine from Smart Parking Limited. The notice stated that he had paid for parking 16 minutes after entering the car park.
In September 2023, the man appealed the fine, but later received a demand from a debt collection company to pay £170. According to him, over the following years he received letters demanding payment and warning of possible court proceedings.
In November 2025, another debt collection company contacted him. The man was subsequently told that the case could go to court in October 2026. By then, the fine had risen to approximately £300.
How ChatGPT helped
Throughout the process, Goral uploaded letters and emails to ChatGPT to receive advice on what to do and how to respond. According to him, the artificial intelligence also helped prepare a written defence, which he sent to the court.
On 25 September, several weeks before the scheduled court hearing, the man received an email informing him that the case had been closed and the fine cancelled.
Anthropic reported a user to the police over a chat with Claude06.10.26, 10:28 • 4365 views
Goral said that he had also contacted the Citizens Advice service repeatedly, but the help of artificial intelligence proved more useful to him.
"From beginning to end, every time I received a letter, I asked ChatGPT what to do. It told me what to reply, whom to contact, and everything else," the man said.
He also stressed that, for him, the case was less about the money than about the principle.
"If you know that you are right, then you should not pay them any money," Goral said.
According to him, he was prepared to defend his position in court to the end, but ultimately managed to have the fine cancelled without a court hearing.
