I’m Still Convinced the iPod Was the Perfect Gadget
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

I remember the birth of the iPod, 25 years ago this month. I was working at Newsweek. It was October 23, little more than a month after the attacks on the twin towers of the World Trade Center, and everybody was focused on the aftermath. I didn’t go to Cupertino for the launch, where Steve Jobs pulled the gadget from his jeans pocket and boasted that it contained a whole music library. Apple couriers hand-delivered the device to me in New York, and Jobs got on the phone with me. “iPod,” he told me, “will be a landmark product.”
He was right. By 2004, I was writing a cover story called “iPod Nation,” and later I published a book about the iPod called The Perfect Thing.
The death of the iPod wasn’t as memorable. It’s not even clear when it happened. Officially, one might date the time of death as occurring on May 10, 2022, when Apple discontinued the iPod Touch, the last product to use that name. But I never considered the Touch a real iPod; it was simply an iPhone without cellular connectivity. Maybe the appropriate death call might have been July 27, 2017, when Apple killed the Nano—the last traditional iPod with a screen—and the iPod Shuffle, a postage-stamp-sized player that clipped to your shirt. (Apple had quietly discontinued the classic iPod, with a hard drive and click wheel, in 2014.)
All these final dates were an inevitable consequence of what Steve Jobs put in motion on January 11, 2007. That’s when he announced three new products—a phone, an internet device, and “the best iPod ever,” all integrated into a new thing called the iPhone. From that moment on, the iPod as a separate device was living on borrowed time.
Still, for years, Apple sold millions more of the beloved devices before the iPod went silent. But even as we love our smartphones, the iPod scratched an itch that still lingers, and I’m sticking to my claim that the iPod was The Perfect Thing. It was a one-function device that superbly executed its function. It made people unconditionally happy. In contrast, our relationships with our iPhones (and Android phones) are more complicated. Yes, the device that superseded the iPod is galaxies more impactful than its predecessor. Financially, of course, it is the engine of a $4 trillion company. I can’t imagine any other contender for the mantle of best product of the century.
But I would not call the iPhone perfect. It gobbles our attention, sometimes with toxic social media apps. Countless cars have been totaled because drivers were more interested in its touch screen than what was happening on the other side of the windshield. iPhone doomscrolling can result in depression. Whereas that perky iPod brought nothing but joy.
Adding to the excitement was Steve Jobs’ willingness to redesign the iPod every year. Apple could have maintained its original iPod for a long spell, but almost immediately the company began a series of significant reinventions. Every cycle yielded an iPod with a different size and shape. With each iteration, the iPod seemed to grow smaller and cooler. First came the mini, then came multiple variations of nanos and shuffles in crazy colors and configurations. iPhone updates have kept people buying, but without the fun of a total reshaping of the product.
Is there an alternate universe where Apple continued making the iPod as a dedicated digital music player? I called Tony Fadell to discuss. Fadell is often referred to as the father of the iPod; he headed its hardware team and delivered the product in an amazing sprint of less than a year. He later was deeply involved in developing the iPhone, and his post-Apple career includes cofounding Nest, becoming a successful tech investor, and writing a well-received book.
Fadell resigned from Apple in 2008 and consulted for two years after that, when Apple was still supporting the iPod. But he recalls Jobs and other execs agreeing that the device was on a course to oblivion, despite being a great product with an enthusiastic user base. With the iPhone proving to be a monster success that also helped boost the Macintosh, and Apple pursuing potentially mass-market innovations like the iPad, iPod sales were becoming less relevant to the company’s bottom line. Jobs was a relentless prioritizer, and his successor Tim Cook felt the same way.
Fadell says that there was very little hand-wringing about the iPod’s fate. “The discussion was about Apple [not] doing lower-value things,” he says. Yet he agrees with me that the iPod’s disappearance created a hole that hasn’t been filled.
In retrospect, he says, what made the iPod invaluable is what it didn’t do—connect with the internet. “Because the iPod wasn't connected, you didn’t have all these other things going on to distract you. Today, you get all the annoyance of being connected without being able to get the same listening experience. You can always be distracted and go somewhere else.”
“This thing should still exist,” he says.
A lot of people seem to agree. There are multiple active communities on Facebook and Reddit of refuseniks who go to great lengths to mod old iPods—putting in large flash drives, installing Bluetooth. There’s even an app that makes your iPhone look and play like an iPod Classic. It works great, but you’re still one swipe away from your feeds, your mail, and everything else in your life that isn’t as fun as music.
I ask Fadell how he regards the iPod’s legacy. Tellingly, his answer speaks to Apple’s history more than exhilaration for the product itself. “The iPhone never would have existed without it,” he says. “That means that the Apple we know of would never have existed without the iPod.” It helped turn a computer company with a limited user base into a consumer electronics giant.
“And the crazy thing is that it was exactly 25 years ago—which is half the years that Apple has existed. There was the Apple II, and then the Mac, and then, boom,” he adds.
I prefer to remember the iPod for what it was, not what it led to. Not long ago, I exhumed my iPod Classic. I have an old boombox with a cradle designed for the iPod, with the old 30-pin connector. I put it in shuffle mode and blissed out.
I suspect a lot of others might like to return to iPod Nation. New CEO John Ternus has no incentive to revive the product, of course. I do find it sad, however, that a generation exists that doesn’t know what it’s like to have a dedicated music device that will never interrupt a tune with calls, texts, and notifications. They don’t know what they’re missing.
This is an edition of Steven Levy’s and Lauren Goode's Backchannel newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Germany's Tytan Technologies develops interceptor drone to counter jet-powered UAVs
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:00:00 UTC
00:00:00 KST

Germany's Tytan Technologies develops interceptor drone to counter jet-powered UAVs
Tytan Technologies CEO and co-founder Balazs Nagy said this in a comment to an Ukrinform correspondent on the sidelines of DefTech Day in Berlin.
"This is our latest interceptor drone, developed based on our experience in Ukraine over the past year. Our team on the ground closely monitors how the situation is evolving, and these findings shape our technological direction," Nagy said.
According to him, one of the main challenges has been that Russian attack drones have started flying significantly higher and faster.
"In 2023, we started at around 30-60 meters, whereas now we are dealing with altitudes of five to six kilometers. We lose a great deal of energy along the way. In addition, one trend has become particularly noticeable in recent months: attack drones are getting faster and faster. So our goal is to fly higher and faster," he said.
He said Hyperion is equipped with a rocket booster. "We have, so to speak, mounted a rocket booster underneath the drone to help it gain altitude while retaining the range and speed needed to intercept an enemy drone," Nagy said.
According to him, Hyperion is designed, among other things, to counter jet-powered UAVs such as the Geran-5.
"Hyperion's rocket-assisted launch is an important step toward reaching the required altitude and speed. This allows us to match the Geran-5's cruising speed and counter it at that stage. At the same time, the system cannot yet reach the Geran-5's maximum speeds, which is obviously a problem," Nagy said.
According to the company, Hyperion can currently engage targets traveling at speeds of approximately 400-450 km/h. Tytan Technologies is working on new propulsion systems that would enable speeds of 550-650 km/h.
Hyperion is currently undergoing testing. According to the CEO, the company's final system tests are conducted in Ukraine. "This is important to us: we bring all our products to Ukraine," he said.
Asked when the new interceptor could be deployed in Ukraine, Nagy said: "In the very near future. We are talking about weeks, not months."
However, Tytan's current contract for the supply of interceptor drones does not yet cover Hyperion, he added.

Seeing Systems unveils Reaver drone carrier
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:59:41 BST
23:59:41 KST

A British company has launched an uncrewed vessel designed to carry, launch and recover as many as a hundred strike drones, controlled with the boat itself through a single command and control layer, the Apex Europe conference in London heard on Wednesday.
Matthew Le Maitre, chief technology officer at Seeing Systems, introduced the vessel at the end of a capability presentation. “Today, I am proud to announce that Seeing Systems stands ready to meet the challenge posed by this new paradigm,” he said. “Apex, please meet Reaver.”
Reaver 101 combines the strike power of UAVs with the endurance of an uncrewed surface vessel, and one command and control layer covers both sea and air for the whole mission. Maximum range is 2,000 nautical miles, it operates far from shore without a support ship, and it moves by road or inside a C-17 to wherever it is needed.
The four payload fits shown covered littoral strike against targets ashore, anti-surface strike against enemy vessels at sea, reconnaissance drones pushed out ahead of the force, and offshore air defence using interceptors against one-way attack drones. Reconfiguration is quick. “When the threat changes, the payload changes. The vessel does not,” Mr Le Maitre said.
“An adversary has no way of knowing which Reaver is doing which job, so every one of them has to be treated as an all-capable threat,” he said. “That is the decisive advantage of autonomous mass. It forces the enemy to solve thousands of problems at once.”
“Mass on its own is a useful advantage,” he said, “but it only becomes truly decisive if it can be controlled effectively. A thousand platforms that each need their own crew are not mass, they’re a manpower problem.” Autonomy allows one team to set the vessels’ routes and the drones’ tasks from a single interface.
The waters a Reaver would fight in will be jammed, spoofed and hostile. Navigation continues when GPS is denied, using inertial dead reckoning cross-checked against radar, and when communications degrade the system steps down through defined levels of autonomy so the mission continues until the link is restored.
The vessel carries its own autonomous deployment and retrieval system, designed and built by the company, which launches drones while the boat is under way and recovers them for reuse. “Recovery capability is what turns a single strike into a sustained operation,” Mr Le Maitre said, adding that the system has already launched and recovered drones at sea in trials.
Open architecture and standard drone protocols allow new airframes and sensors to be integrated without redesigning the vessel. Production runs on live lines in the United Kingdom, the hull from a partner that has already delivered uncrewed boats to the Royal Navy, and the drones from the company’s own lines. “The capital ship takes a decade to build. Reaver’s production lines are already running,” he said.
Mr Le Maitre built the case for the vessel on the cost of the ships it is meant to supplement. “For centuries, navies have measured their power by the size of their capital ships, and since the Second World War, the aircraft carrier has been the capital ship around which the rest of the fleet has been built,” he said. “Capital is a highly relevant word here. In today’s money, each of the Royal Navy’s two Queen Elizabeth class carriers would cost close to 4.6 billion pounds.”
“Now they are undoubtedly extraordinarily capable ships, but these vessels are so important to the Royal Navy that they also represent an extraordinary target. Our adversaries know that, and they plan accordingly. Protecting them effectively is now one of the hardest problems the fleet faces.”
Ukraine and the Middle East have exposed an asymmetry that upends the warfighting conventions of this century, in his account, and cheap mass-produced uncrewed systems are overwhelming platforms that used to dominate. Improvements in AI targeting and swarming will make those weapons more lethal over time, and efficiencies in mass production will make them cheaper.
“Iran has been severely disrupting shipping through the Strait of Hormuz for over seven months, despite the US Navy committing three carrier strike groups to the region,” he said. “They’ve achieved this via a combination of drones, mines, small boats and USVs.” Iran managed it with a degraded green water navy and an air force heavily damaged by joint American and Israeli strikes.
“Just as Ukraine proved on land, Iran is proving at sea that the new asymmetry can be leveraged to frustrate a much stronger military adversary,” he said.
The arithmetic he showed sets one carrier against 4,600 fully armed Reavers. Each is designed to carry up to 100 Havoc strike drones carrying a two kilogram high explosive payload apiece, which across the fleet comes to 460,000 strike drones and more than 900 tonnes of warheads.
“An adversary facing an aircraft carrier has one rather large target to find and eliminate,” he said. “An adversary facing a comparable Reaver fleet has 4,600 targets to contend with.” Losing one costs a fraction of a per cent of the force, in his account, and “the rest of the force keeps fighting.”
The capital ship made sense while manpower was the limit on fielding mass, he argued, and autonomy has removed that limit.
“The Royal Navy has already announced its strategic shift to a hybrid navy,” he said. “We believe that Reaver will be an integral part of that new navy. Reaver will be ready to defend the UK as we move into a more uncertain world.”

Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:58:18 UTC
23:58:18 KST

Africans disproportionately targeted by ICC – investigative journalist
The International Criminal Court (ICC) disproportionately targets Africans while failing to hold perpetrators of war crimes elsewhere accountable, Nigerian investigative journalist David Hundeyin has told RT.
Hundeyin questioned the court’s record, claiming that Africans account for more than 90% of those prosecuted under the Rome Statute, the treaty that established the ICC. “It’s either crimes against humanity only happen in Africa, or Africans are disproportionately targeted by the ICC,” he said. The journalist disputed the ICC’s impartiality, asking whether it has become an instrument of selective justice.
Hundeyin said the ICC could be considered “useless or toothless” at best, or, at worst, a tool used specifically to target Africans.
Geopolitical analyst and author Kim Heller has also questioned the ICC’s credibility, accusing it of pursuing decades-old cases involving African figures while failing to address ongoing atrocities elsewhere. Speaking to RT following the sentencing of two former militia leaders from the Central African Republic last July, she described the court as embodying a “hierarchy of justice” in which Western political and military leaders escape accountability.
Established in 2002, the court is tasked with prosecuting genocide, war crimes, crimes against humanity and aggression, and relies heavily on the cooperation of its 125 members. However, some of the world’s most powerful states, including the US, China, India and Russia, reject its authority.
The court has long faced accusations of selective justice and political bias. Chad recently notified the UN of its decision to withdraw from the ICC, accusing the tribunal of disproportionately targeting countries in Africa. The Chadian Foreign Ministry claimed that nine of the 13 investigations it counted concerned African states, describing the court’s effectiveness as “limited and uneven.”
Chad’s decision followed similar moves by Burkina Faso, Mali and Niger, which previously denounced the ICC as an “instrument of neocolonial repression.” The ICC has warned that such withdrawals risk weakening international efforts to end impunity.

Rome's 'black minicar gang' incidents rise to six after man struck in street
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:56:37 CEST
23:56:37 KST

Incidents involving a suspected 
'black minicar gang' of teenagers possibly involved in an online
challenge in Rome rose to six as a man said Friday he had been
hit in the street in the capital on Sunday night.
                                    
This morning, a 67-year-old man reported to the Carabinieri
station in Rome's Monteverde Nuovo district that, late on the
evening of October 4, he was approached by a black microcar
carrying two individuals while walking along Viale dei Quattro
Venti.
                                    
The passenger struck him in the side with a plastic pipe.
                                    
The man, who was near his home, did not seek medical assistance.
                                    
Rome prosecutors went into a huddle earlier Friday over the
suspected mini-car gang that has injured several people in the
capital this week including an actor from the hit Roman
underworld show Suburra.
                                    
A meeting was held at the Prosecutor's Office in Rome to take
stock of the investigation into the "minicar gang"—specifically
regarding the assault on actor Davide Iacopini, who has also
appeared in the film on Genoa G8 police brutality Diaz and the
satirical TV series Maschi Veri.
                                    
Genoa-born Iacopini, 42, was struck by a kick delivered by
someone in a microcar on October 5th and subsequently
hospitalized in serious condition at San Camillo Hospital.
                                    
Investigators are attempting to identify the two individuals who
were inside the black electric car, reconstructing their route
by analyzing surveillance camera footage from the Monteverde
Vecchio and Testaccio areas.
                                    
At present, according to reports, there is no composite sketch
of the person who carried out the attack.
                                    
Another four people have suffered attacks from mini-car
occupants in Rome.

burgundy wood and blue ceilings shape café, bookshop, and wine bar in valencia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:55:11 UTC
23:55:11 KST

burgundy wood and blue ceilings shape café, bookshop, and wine bar in valencia
sahuquillodearriba renovates a 59-sqm space in el botànic neighborhood retaining elements of the building’s original character.
Burgundy wood, white marble, and blue define Chiquita’s interior
Chiquita by SahuquillodeArriba is a 59-sqm café, bookshop, and wine bar in Valencia’s El Botànic neighborhood, designed for product designer Gloria Izquierdo. The project combines coffee, books, and wine in a continuous interior that uses color, material contrasts, and custom furniture to connect the different functions.
A full-length ash wood bookcase stained deep burgundy runs along one side of the space, extending into the bathroom and serving as the interior’s main architectural feature. Opposite it, a continuous bench and small white marble tables introduce lighter surfaces, while the textured ceiling is finished in soft blue. Integrated shelf lighting, wall lights, and table lamps add a domestic quality to the space.
Chiquita brings reading, coffee, and wine into a shared interior
The renovation by Studio SahuquillodeArriba preserves the existing building’s character by restoring the original walls with a thin, breathable coating that addresses damp while retaining their texture and imperfections. At the back, a large communal table accommodates book clubs, meetings, and other activities, supporting Chiquita’s role as a space for cultural exchange.
Through its compact layout, custom furniture, and restrained palette of burgundy wood, white marble, and blue surfaces, Chiquita brings the functions of a café, bookshop, and wine bar together in a shared interior.
project info:
name: Chiquita
architect: SahuquillodeArriba | @SahuquillodeArriba
location: Valencia, Spain

Egyptian president begins first state visit to Malaysia to strengthen bilateral ties

Faisal Mahmud
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Egyptian President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi arrived in Malaysia on Friday for his first state visit to the Southeast Asian country, aimed at strengthening bilateral relations and expanding economic cooperation.
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim received Sisi at Kuala Lumpur International Airport following the presentation of the country's 2027 budget.
"Welcome to Malaysia, President El-Sisi!" Anwar wrote on US social media platform X.
The two-day visit is taking place at the invitation of Malaysia's King Sultan Ibrahim, according to a statement from the Malaysian Foreign Ministry.
Sisi is scheduled to hold talks with Anwar on Saturday to review bilateral cooperation and discuss regional and international developments, the ministry said.
The two leaders are also expected to witness the exchange of several memoranda of understanding.
Sisi will attend a welcoming ceremony and meet King Sultan Ibrahim at the National Palace, where a state banquet will be held in his honor, Malaysian state news agency Bernama reported.
The visit is expected to elevate bilateral relations to a strategic partnership, according to the Malaysian Foreign Ministry.
Malaysia and Egypt established diplomatic relations in 1959.
Egypt was Malaysia's seventh-largest trading partner in Africa in 2025, with bilateral trade reaching $720 million, comprising $600 million in Malaysian exports and $120 million in imports.
Trade rose 74.7% to $870 million during the January-August 2026 period, according to the Malaysian Foreign Ministry.

US imposes sanctions aiming to 'dismantle' International Criminal Court
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:53:00 UTC
23:53:00 KST

US announces sanctions on the International Criminal Court
October 9, 2026
US President Donald Trump's administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Friday, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize.
This comes as the US has in recent months made no bones about pursuing what Secretary of State Marco Rubio has called a "sweeping campaign to dismantle the threat posed by the International Criminal Court."
The United States and Israel had both strongly opposed the court's arrest warrants for top Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.
Since 2020 and the back end of Trump's first term, the US had also opposed investigations into military actions in Afghanistan that "deprioritize" alleged US wrongdoings, focusing on the Taliban, but can nevertheless include them.
What did the State Department say about the ICC sanctions?
"President Trump will never allow the International Court to prosecute Americans," Rubio said in a statement.
"That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate," he said.
Rubio said that both US political parties had long agreed that the ICC should not have jurisdiction over US citizens, but said "only President Trump" resolved to take action.
"Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American servicemembers for their defense, to rein in the court," Rubio said. "If they do not, the United States will continue its campaign to dismantle the ICC, brick by brick, until Americans are threatened no longer."
How did the ICC respond?
The ICC said the US sanctions aimed to obstruct an independent international court supported by more than half of the UN's members.
"The court will continue to fully discharge its mandate, with independence and impartiality, acting only on the basis of the law and the evidence, for the sake of the countless victims of grave crimes," said ICC President Tomoko Akane, who already faces US sanctions.
The ICC called the Rome Statute, which underpins membership of the court, a "collective promise" that the most serious international crimes must not go unpunished.
"That promise is only as strong as the resolve of those who made it," the court said. It appealed to members to take "concrete actions" to ensure the court would still have the necessary means to continue its work.
"No one should be punished for serving the cause of justice," it said. "History will judge this moment. Future generations, and above all the victims of mass atrocities, will ask how we responded when an insitution created to protect them came under attack."
What did other countries say about the US sanctions?
A collection of US allies that are full members of the ICC including Germany issued a joint statement reaffirming their "continued and unwavering support for the independence, impartiality, and integrity of the ICC."
"As committed supporters of the ICC we regret and strongly disagree with the announcement of sanctions to be imposed upon the Court by the United States," the governments of Canada, Denmark, Germany, France, Italy, Japan, the Netherlands and the UK said.
They said that, despite the ICC's best efforts to prepare and mitigate their effect, the sanctions "will have a significant impact on the Court's work, its dedicated staff and their families."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu thanked the US government for its "leadership" in issuing the sanctions.
"The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty," he said.
Sanctions announced shortly after former ICC judge's Nobel Peace Prize
The State Department released the announcement a few hours after the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize was awarded to Navi Pillay, who was an ICC judge from 2003 to 2012.
Last year Trump repeatedly complained that he should have won the accolade for promoting world peace, prompting Venezuelan opposition leader Maria Corina Machado to present him with her trophy as a gift.
Without naming names, the Nobel Committee clearly referenced US sanctions against the ICC when announcing Pillay as this year's laureate.
"The Norwegian Nobel Committee wants to remind the world that the rule of law national and international — underpins the system we have set up to ensure peace and resolve conflicts non-violently," the Committee wrote.
It said judges like Pillay "guard the thin red line between order and chaos," but lamented that "today ... these same judges are sanctioned, and their institutions are attacked."
What is the ICC?
The International Criminal Court is an intergovernmental organization and international tribunal based in the Dutch city of The Hague.
It's the only permanent international court with the theoretical jurisdiction to prosecute individuals for international crimes like genocide, crimes against humanity, war crimes and illegal aggression.
The ICC was established in 2002 and is governed by the Rome Statute.
More than half the countries in the world, 125 in total, are full parties to the Rome Statute, having signed and ratified it.
Several of the world's most significant powers, including China, India, Israel, Russia and the United States, do not recognize the court's jurisdiction and are not parties to the statute.
A grey area, however, remains since the court accepts challenges from ratified members against individuals from countries that do not recognize it.
That is why high-profile arrest warrants against Russian officials, including President Vladimir Putin, and Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, have been issued in recent years — following respective complaints from Ukrainians and Palestinians.
What were the prior signs of Trump administration pressure on the ICC?
The US has been increasingly critical of the ICC during Trump's second term.
Rubio has often led the charge. In July, he wrote an op-ed for the Wall Street Journal saying, "America never agreed to a world tribunal that can override our own courts and the Constitution."
He argued it was possible for US "soldiers, police officers, Border Patrol agents and elected leaders" to be "dragged before an international court" and tried by judges "from random countries across the globe."
Just over a week later, on July 25, Venezuela's new administration — transformed after the US abduction of Nicolas Maduro in January — announced that it planned to withdraw from the Rome Statute and the ICC.
A few days later, the military junta in Chad announced that it was withdrawing from the ICC following a US request.
The recent sexual misconduct scandal surrounding the ICC's chief prosecutor Karim Khan, who was dismissed in July, provided more ammunition the US could aim at the court.
In August, the US imposed sanctions on the ICC's president, Japanese judge Tomoko Akane, and Abdoulaye Seye, a Senegalese trial lawyer at the court.

How to clean a showerhead, remove buildup, and restore an even water stream
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
17:52:14 EEST
23:52:14 KST

How to clean a showerhead, remove buildup, and restore an even water stream
Kyiv • UNN
Buildup clogs the showerhead’s holes, weakens the water stream, and promotes the growth of fungi. Experts recommend cleaning it with approved products without vinegar or abrasives.
White deposits, a weak water flow, and jets spraying in different directions may indicate that the showerhead is dirty. Taking a shower with such a defect is inconvenient because the water flows unevenly. In addition, much more water is used than necessary, creating extra utility costs. It should not be forgotten that fungi can also multiply in a dirty showerhead. They get onto the skin with the water jets and cause various forms of dermatitis.
These problems can be avoided by cleaning the plumbing regularly. The method depends on the design and coating of the particular product. UNN explains how to do this best.
Why a showerhead gets clogged
Minerals contained in water gradually form limescale on the surface and around the openings. And the harder the water, the faster deposits appear and clog the showerhead. Soap or shower gel residue joins them, while rust particles and other debris from the pipes can accumulate in the mesh filter at the inlet.
The showerhead should be cleaned when the openings no longer let water through or the jets change direction. At the same time, a weak flow does not always mean that the showerhead itself is clogged: the cause may be in the hose, faucet, or water supply.
Where to start cleaning
First, read the instructions or the plumbing manufacturer's recommendations on its website. Check which products are permitted for the coating and whether the showerhead can be removed and soaked. Next, prepare a soft cotton cloth, warm water, an approved cleaning product, and a container. A soft brush will be needed for a removable mesh. Wipe the surface with a damp cloth, adding mild approved soap if necessary, rinse it off, and wipe the showerhead dry.
How to clean the openings without disassembling the showerhead
Many modern showerheads have flexible silicone nozzles—small protrusions from which water flows. Gently rub them with your fingers: this helps loosen the deposits. After that, turn on the water, rinse away the deposits, and check that the jets are flowing evenly. Do not pierce the openings with a needle or try to enlarge them: you may damage the nozzles and alter the spray pattern. If deposits remain, proceed with cleaning using a product compatible with the showerhead.
How to clean a removable showerhead
Turn off the faucet. If the design allows the hand showerhead to be detached from the hose, unscrew the connection without applying excessive force. Keep the sealing gasket and remember its position. If the part does not come loose, do not try to force it off. Inspect the inlet opening. If an accessible removable mesh is present, take it out according to the instructions, rinse it, and carefully remove debris with a soft brush. Do not remove secured parts or the flow restrictor.
After that, treat the deposits with an approved product. If the manufacturer permits soaking, use a container with a solution of the required concentration and follow the specified time. Do not leave the showerhead in it overnight merely because the deposits seem stubborn. Next, thoroughly rinse off the product with clean water, return the mesh and gasket to their places, reconnect the showerhead, and run water through it. Important: check that there are no leaks near the connection. Do not overtighten the thread, as excessive force may damage the parts.
How to clean a fixed showerhead
A fixed showerhead can be cleaned externally without removing it. Apply an approved product to a soft cloth, carefully wipe the surface, and then rinse it thoroughly. The cleaner should not be sprayed directly onto shower products so that it does not get inside. You should also not try to clean the showerhead by placing it in a bag of vinegar. Prolonged contact with acid can damage the plumbing's coating.
Can vinegar and citric acid be used to clean a showerhead
Vinegar can dissolve limescale deposits, but it cannot be considered a universal plumbing cleaner. Citric acid should likewise be used only with the plumbing manufacturer's approval.
What mistakes to avoid when cleaning
Do not use metal sponges, abrasive powders, or stiff scrubbing pads: they can leave scratches. Do not try to speed up cleaning by using a larger dose of the product or soaking for longer.
Do not mix different cleaners. Combining acids, including vinegar, with chlorine bleach is particularly dangerous: it can cause the release of toxic gas. Follow the label instructions regarding gloves and ventilation.
How to reduce the buildup of deposits
After showering, wipe the surface of the showerhead dry with a soft cloth and periodically clean the flexible nozzles, if the design provides for this. The frequency of care depends on the hardness of the water and the appearance of deposits. It is better to remove a small amount of buildup than to wait until the holes become clogged. If the flow remains weak after cleaning, check whether the hose has become kinked and whether water is flowing normally from the other taps. Leaks, cracks, or a faulty mixer require repair.

Anthropic bans persistent abuse of its Claude AI models
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:51:19 UTC
23:51:19 KST

Dilara Hamit
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Anthropic has introduced a policy banning users from directing sustained and unnecessary abusive or cruel behavior toward its Claude artificial intelligence models.
The new rules, published Wednesday and due to take effect Nov. 12, are intended to cover only extreme cases in which users repeatedly behave cruelly toward Claude without any discernible purpose, the company said.
The restriction will not apply to ordinary expressions of frustration, criticism of the model, dark themes in creative work or legitimate testing and research.
Anthropic said Claude’s existing ability to end rare conversations with persistently abusive users would remain its main enforcement mechanism.
The company introduced that feature for Claude Opus 4 and 4.1 in August 2025, instructing the models to terminate a conversation only as a last resort after attempts to redirect the interaction had failed.
Anthropic described the measure as part of its research into possible AI welfare, while stressing that it remained “highly uncertain” whether Claude or other large language models possessed moral status.
The policy change comes amid a broader debate over whether advanced AI systems could ever become conscious or deserve moral consideration.
Anthropic has said the question is sufficiently serious to justify low-cost precautionary measures, even though there is no agreement that present-day AI systems can experience suffering or distress.
The company’s recently published constitution for Claude says questions surrounding the model’s consciousness and moral status remain unresolved. It also says Claude should be able to establish boundaries during interactions it characterizes as distressing.
The updated usage policy also consolidates restrictions on deceptive campaigns and fake online activity, clarifies prohibitions concerning weapons and surveillance, and introduces additional safeguards for AI connected to equipment capable of taking physical actions.

Source: European Pravda, citing Austrian media outlet Der Standard
Details: The two men alleged to be Ukrainian military intelligence operatives were detained in Vienna on Monday. The regional court ruled on Wednesday that they should be remanded in custody.
Christina Salzborn, a spokesperson for the court, said on Friday that the grounds for remanding the two men in custody were the risk of further offending, tampering with evidence and absconding. The remand order is initially valid until 21 October.
Both men deny the charges.
Der Standard said it is not known how long the two Ukrainians suspected of spying have been in Austria or how law enforcement officers tracked them down. The authorities stated on Friday afternoon that this is the subject of an ongoing investigation.
The investigation is being conducted by Austria's Directorate State Protection and Intelligence Service (DSN). The suspected offence is espionage on behalf of a foreign intelligence service to the detriment of Austria (Section 256 of the Austrian Criminal Code).

New Governor, Old Problem: Koja Confronts US Base-Related Crimes in Okinawa
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:50:00 UTC
23:50:00 KST

Okinawa’s September 2026 election made headlines as incumbent Denny Tamaki was ousted by the Liberal Democratic Party’s (LDP) preferred candidate, Koja Genta. Koja became the first LDP-backed candidate to win the position since Hirokazu Nakaima in 2006.
Tamaki and his predecessor, the late Onaga Takeshi, vocally opposed the expansion of the U.S. Marine Corps’ Camp Schwab in Henoko and were generally critical of Okinawa’s excessive base burden, relative to other Japanese prefectures. Newly-elected Governor Koja was perceived by the LDP-led Japanese government to be more favorable to the U.S. bases in Okinawa, specifically the completion of the relocation of Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Ginowan City to Camp Schwab.
Perhaps most emblematic of the shift in the Okinawan Prefectural Office was Koja’s abolition of the Henoko New Base Construction Issue Countermeasures Division, the office that had handled legal, environmental, and political issues surrounding the construction. Instead, Koja’s administration created the Early Return Countermeasures Office, which is less overtly critical of the Henoko project.
Only days after his inauguration, however, Koja has had to confront the same perennial problem that his predecessors faced: crimes (allegedly) committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa and their impacts on the Japan-U.S. alliance.
On October 3, Okinawan police arrested a U.S. Marine on suspicion of murdering Anna Yagi, an Okinawan woman. While it remains to be seen if the U.S. soldier is convicted of the crime, this incident represents an unfortunate continuity of crimes committed by U.S. soldiers in Okinawa, particularly against women. In recent years, for instance, a U.S. Marine was convicted of attempted rape, and a U.S. Air Force member was found guilty of the kidnapping and rape of a minor; in both cases the victims were female.
As the U.S. and Japanese governments increasingly worry about conflict with China in the Taiwan Strait, which borders Okinawa, they must work to prevent these crimes to ensure the stable operation of their alliance.
Crimes Committed by U.S. Servicemembers Contribute to Okinawa’s “Base Burden”
Several factors impact Okinawans’ perception of the prefecture’s “excessive base burden.” One is the fact that Okinawa hosts 70 percent of the U.S. soldiers stationed in Japan, but Okinawa’s landmass is just 1 percent of Japan’s total area. Okinawa also has a contentious and traumatic history with Tokyo, which increases suspicions that the central government doesn’t have the prefecture’s best interests in mind.
A major factor that contributes to the perception of the U.S. bases as burdens is the negative externalities that periodically come from U.S. bases and troops. That includes various forms of chemical pollution, such as Agent Orange (historically) and per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) (in recent years), and other environmental issues.
Crimes attributed to U.S. military personnel are another type of negative externality. Violent crimes such as sexual assault and murder may be especially likely to mobilize protests against the U.S. military presence, in part because of the strong emotions that they can invoke. These events serve as opportunities for anti-base activists to remind Okinawans and mainland Japanese citizens alike of the island prefecture’s traumatic history involving both mainland Japan and the U.S., such as the Battle of Okinawa during World War II. Through this lens, crimes committed by U.S. military personnel in Okinawa are interpreted as further examples of the ways that the U.S. and Japanese governments have and continue to marginalize Okinawa in the name of national and regional security.
Unsurprisingly, anti-base protests in Okinawa often occur after a crime such as the murder of Anna Yagi. For example, the 1995 kidnapping and rape of a 12-year-old girl by U.S. servicemen kicked off a massive wave of protests against the U.S. bases, and more recently, the 2016 murder of Rina Shimabukuro by a U.S. contractor was followed by protests with tens of thousands of participants.
Despite the election of Koja to the governorship, which some observers may interpret as a sign that Okinawans are deprioritizing base politics, protests are likely to follow Yagi’s murder. They have already started in Tokyo, as well as Naha, the capital of Okinawa Prefecture.
The Threat Perception of China Can’t Overshadow Crimes
For some observers, Koja’s election win signaled that Okinawans’ concerns about potential Chinese hostility in the nearby Taiwan Strait may trump their concerns about the “burdens” from the U.S. bases. Koja himself stated that “the fact that the security environment around Okinawa has become more severe is something we can’t help but acknowledge.” He said that “we have to have the ability to defend ourselves and deter aggression,” presumably referring to the U.S. and Japanese Self-Defense Force (SDF) bases in the prefecture.
However, it would be a mistake to assume that the perception of China as a threat to Japanese and Okinawan security will automatically counteract the negative impacts that crimes committed by U.S. soldiers have on public opinion toward the U.S. military, at least in the short term. Recent research has suggested that threat perception does not always increase support for a U.S. military presence.
Some of my own research found that crimes committed by U.S. personnel have a negative impact on public opinion toward the U.S. military. Furthermore, it is unclear if the presence of U.S. bases makes locals feel more or less secure, particularly in the event of a military conflict, especially given Iran’s recent attacks on U.S. military installations in the Middle East. In Okinawa, surveys suggest that a majority of residents worry that military bases (which could include SDF bases as well) in the prefecture could serve as military targets.
Therefore, although recent surveys suggest that Okinawans, like mainland Japanese citizens, are wary of Chinese military aggression, U.S. and Japanese officials should not assume that threat perceptions will automatically result in Okinawan public support for U.S. bases, particularly when a crime linked to U.S. personnel is in the headlines.
An Ounce of Prevention Is Worth a Pound of Cure
If the U.S. and Japanese governments believe, as they say, that the bases in Okinawa Prefecture are crucial to regional security, they need to take more proactive measures to prevent rather than react to crimes allegedly committed by U.S. military personnel. Even if Anna Yagi’s accused murderer is ultimately found innocent, the damage to civilian-military relations between U.S. soldiers and Okinawans is already done.
For his part, Koja has issued a formal protest with the U.S. military and expressed his “outrage” at the crime. Japanese Prime Minister Takaichi Sanae has lodged a “strong protest” with the U.S.; meanwhile, U.S. officials have temporarily prohibited U.S. soldiers from going off base in Okinawa. However, reactive actions by officials are not new, and Okinawans are wary of the crime, protest, and apology routine. As one Okinawan resident put it, “I am deeply disappointed by the same kinds of government comments we have been hearing for decades – that they will protest or that they take the matter seriously.”
One of the biggest elements in preventing such crimes against civilians is the training that U.S. soldiers receive when they deploy to a specific location. Such training may impact soldiers’ perceptions of the host communities in which they live and with which they interact, as well as how they interact with host community civilians. In the case of Okinawa, a recent study suggested that the orientation materials that U.S. Marines are exposed to depict Okinawans as obstacles to be overcome and the media as agitators of anti-base sentiment. In doing so, these materials delegitimize opposition to U.S. bases, instead of asking how U.S. troops can avoid stoking anti-base sentiment. This study drew on training materials from the 2010s. Since then, the materials have hopefully been updated in a way that seeks to better understand where Okinawan anti-base sentiment comes from and the role of individual U.S. soldiers in facilitating (or inhibiting) the Japan-U.S. relationship.
The U.S. military and its municipal and gubernatorial partners also have a role to play in shaping the narratives around the U.S. military presence in Okinawa, which may help ameliorate the negative impacts of crimes on civilians’ relationships with U.S. soldiers. Recent studies suggested that contact between U.S. soldiers and civilians in base-hosting countries can facilitate positive public opinions of the U.S. military. The same research found that contact combined with exposure to base-related crime – being the victim or having a friend or family member who is a victim of such crime – does not consistently lead to negative attitudes toward the U.S. military. Thus, creating and strengthening the relationships between U.S. troops and the community members that host them is essential to maintaining a positive Japan-U.S. alliance. This can include activities such as base festivals, English or Japanese language courses, or other exchanges.
Anna Yagi’s murder comes at a time of other high-profile cases of violence against women, and joins a history of crimes committed by U.S. military personnel against women in Okinawa. For the stability of the Japan-U.S. security alliance, it is imperative to facilitate more positive relationships between U.S. soldiers and Okinawan citizens; crimes attributed to U.S. soldiers have the opposite effect. While the United States has tried to address this issue in the past, it is clearly not enough, as Koja has said.
Until the U.S. military and its Japanese partners can solve this puzzle, waves of Okinawan anti-base sentiment and protest, which threaten the Japan-U.S. relationship, will continue in the wake of every violent crime.

According to the BBC, searches revealed a small breach in the perimeter fence. The men were initially arrested on suspicion of trespassing on a prohibited site and criminal damage.
They were later arrested on suspicion of an offense under Section 4 of the UK National Security Act 2023, which covers entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK.
RAF Molesworth, near Huntingdon in Cambridgeshire, hosts US intelligence operations centers covering Europe and Africa, as well as a NATO intelligence hub. The facility is not used as a flying station.
Counter Terrorism Policing London is investigating the case and examining why the two men were at the base, the BBC reported.
“A big part of this is looking at any potential motivation as to why the men were present at the site, but I must stress we are keeping an open mind at this stage,” Commander Helen Flanagan stated.
Police were also carrying out searches at two addresses in the Peterborough area.
The abandoned vehicle prompted temporary road closures while bomb disposal officers examined it. Cambridgeshire Police later confirmed that nothing of concern had been found.
The UK Ministry of Defence stated that security around military facilities remains under constant review and includes physical barriers, patrols, surveillance, monitoring, and counter-drone systems.
The arrests came shortly after a separate security case at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire. Flanagan noted that investigators currently had no evidence linking the Molesworth breach to that earlier case.
The earlier case involved several men arrested over suspected explosives offenses near RAF Fairford, where nearby homes were evacuated and military bomb disposal specialists examined vehicles near the base.

The survey found that 30% of respondents believe European countries should increase military support for Ukraine, while another 33% want assistance to remain at its current level. Combined, 63% favor either maintaining or expanding military aid.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Another 33% of respondents said Europe should reduce military support for Ukraine, highlighting a significant minority opposed to the current level of assistance.
The divide becomes especially pronounced among supporters of the Alternative for Germany, or AfD. According to the poll, 83% of AfD voters favor cutting military aid to Ukraine, putting the party’s electorate sharply at odds with the overall national picture.
The survey was conducted by Forschungsgruppe Wahlen between October 5 and October 7, 2026, and included 1,311 eligible German voters interviewed by telephone and online. The results are considered representative of Germany’s voting-age population.
The poll has a margin of error of roughly three percentage points for results around 40% and approximately two percentage points for figures near 10%.
So far, Germany has delivered tanks and more than 154 armored vehicles. In addition, Germany donated 30 Gepard self-propelled anti-aircraft guns, two Patriot batteries, and two IRIS-T systems.
It also supplied 500 Stinger missiles or launchers, the largest documented quantity among the donors compared.

Las Vegas Aces center A'ja Wilson won a record fifth Women’s National Basketball Association (WNBA) Most Valuable Player (MVP) award for the 2026 season, becoming the first player in league history to claim the honor three consecutive times.
The 30-year-old American extended her own record for the most MVP awards, having previously won the honor in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2025.
