US imposes sanctions on International Criminal Court, hours after former judge wins Nobel
- The Trump administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court, hours after former judge Navi Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize, deepening tensions with European allies.
- Marco Rubio said the US will ban transactions with the “rogue court” and cut off resources, over ICC cases involving Israeli officials and past scrutiny of US troops in Afghanistan.
- The ICC and EU allies face pressure to respond, as the court prepares for wider sanctions that could hit banking, software and services, while Washington demands the court “rein in” its actions.
AI generated
WASHINGTON – US President Donald Trump’s administration imposed sanctions on the International Criminal Court (ICC) on Oct 9, hours after one of its former judges won the Nobel Peace Prize, putting Washington on a diplomatic collision course with European allies.
The Trump administration has long been hostile to the court and has previously imposed sanctions on its prosecutors and judges.
The Oct 9 move would go much further, potentially punishing companies that provide services to the court itself.
“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a statement reviewed by Reuters ahead of the official announcement.
“That is why, today, the United States is sanctioning the International Criminal Court. We will ban transactions with this rogue court, cutting off their resources and crippling its ability to operate.”
Washington has long been angry over ICC arrest warrants issued for Israeli officials, including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, and over a past investigation into the actions of US soldiers in Afghanistan, which the ICC has since closed.
The court, founded in 2002 to prosecute war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide, counts 125 countries as member states, including all EU countries and all members of the NATO alliance apart from the US and Turkey.
It has received strong public backing in the past from member countries, including major US allies, and is based in the Netherlands, an EU and NATO member.
Navi Pillay, the South African jurist who won the Nobel Peace Prize on Oct 9 for her work in international criminal justice, served as a judge on the ICC’s Appeals Chamber from 2003 to 2008. In its citation, the prize committee said it had sought to “issue a reminder” at a time when “judges and institutions of international law are under political attack”.
“An international legal system in which war criminals are held to account and the victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world,” the committee said.
Rubio said the sanctions had been structured to give the court and its member states an opportunity to address US concerns.
He did not provide further details, but a senior State Department official said the US Treasury would issue a set of licences “to protect American interests”, an apparent reference to temporary exemptions to some sanctions.
US expects allies to ‘rein in the court’
US sanctions typically bar all US-based companies from any work with a sanctioned organisation, forcing banks to shut accounts, insurers to end coverage and software companies to halt cooperation.
The Trump administration previously imposed targeted sanctions on court officials during Trump’s first term, which were rescinded under then president Joe Biden. Washington announced new sanctions just days after Trump returned to office in January 2025.
Court officials have been preparing for months for the prospect of sanctions on the court itself, shifting office computers from Microsoft software to open-source equivalents and making new arrangements for banking and health insurance.
The court’s registrar, Osvaldo Zavala Giler, called earlier this week for the EU to be prepared to use a so-called “blocking mechanism” that lets it shield European countries from the extraterritorial effects of sanctions.
In his statement, Rubio said the US had delayed its sanctions, hoping that the ICC and the countries party to its founding Rome Statute would address US concerns, but they had failed to do so.
“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC. We expect our allies, many of whom are part of the ICC and that rely on American service members for their defence, to rein in the court,” Rubio said.
“We have structured this action to provide an opportunity for States Parties to negotiate and present a solution to address our concerns. If these efforts do not bear fruit, we will continue to adjust accordingly,” Rubio said. REUTERS

EU aviation body widens Saudi airspace warning after Houthi strikes
Oct 9 - Europe's EASA aviation safety body said on Friday it had expanded the area of Saudi Arabian airspace where it recommended airlines not to operate, after Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthis attacked Riyadh airport.
In an update to a conflict zone information bulletin first issued on September 30, the EU regulator said recent attacks demonstrated the Houthis' ability and intent to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital. EASA added an area in northwestern Saudi Arabia to the advisory.
Saudi Arabia's civil aviation authority said earlier on Friday that three Saudi nationals were killed and several people were injured in two attacks on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh on Thursday.
The Houthis have renewed threats against airlines flying to Saudi Arabia and said on Thursday they had struck the capital's airport with two cruise missiles.
"These recurrent missile and drone attacks, together with the activation of air-defence systems, create an increased risk of misidentification of civil aircraft, as well as risks associated with missile and drone overflights, interception activity and falling debris," EASA said.
OPSGROUP, a membership-based organisation with almost 10,000 aviation professionals that shares flight risk information, sent a "do not fly" warning for Saudi Arabia to its members on Friday, citing risks of sustained missile attacks and "misjudgment" in defensive responses.
"We now recommend avoiding operations in Saudi Arabia entirely, including the use of Saudi airports as en route alternates," it said in the memo shared with Reuters.
AIRLINES SUSPEND FLIGHTS
Following Thursday's attacks, Lufthansa Group and three Indian airlines said they would suspend flights to Riyadh expected in the coming days.
Gulf airlines were also affected with Etihad Airways cancelling six flights between Abu Dhabi and Riyadh's King Khalid International on Friday and two more planned for Saturday citing "operational disruption at Riyadh airport".
"Flights to Riyadh and Yanbu have been cancelled up to and including 10 October, while flights to Abha have been cancelled up to and including 11 October," a flydubai spokesperson said.
King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is Saudi Arabia's second-busiest airport after Jeddah. It handled 296,800 flights in 2025, equivalent to about 813 a day, according to Saudi Arabia's General Authority for Statistics.
Global flight tracker Flightradar24 showed 131 flights to and from Riyadh had been cancelled by 1305 GMT on Friday after hundreds of cancellations the previous day. REUTERS

Ethiopia accuses Eritrea of ‘all-out invasion’
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of sending troops deep into its territory and warned that it must defend itself against an “all-out invasion,” escalating a confrontation between the former allies.
Foreign Minister Gedion Timothewos alleged that Eritrean forces, including mechanized units, had advanced up to 60 km into Tigray. His October 8 letter was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and circulated to other UN Security Council members, Reuters reported Friday. The letter described the incursion as a “blatant act of aggression” and sought international support for Ethiopia’s right to self-defense.
Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said on Thursday that Gedion briefed UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina J. Mohammed on what it called Eritrea’s “continued aggression,” demanded the immediate withdrawal of Eritrean forces and urged a “clear and principled UN response.”
In separate talks with senior UN officials, Ethiopian State Minister Berhanu Tsegaye alleged direct Eritrean military involvement “across different fronts along the border” and called for the UN to unequivocally condemn the “flagrant violations of sovereignty.”
Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel rejected Ethiopia’s accusations on Friday, calling them “audacity and duplicity in their most extreme forms.” He accused Addis Ababa of pursuing a war of aggression for more than three years, citing statements by Ethiopian leaders about acquiring sovereign access to the Red Sea and taking control of the port of Assab.
There are fears that renewed clashes between federal forces and Tigrayan fighters could plunge northern Ethiopia back into war. The Tigray People’s Liberation Front (TPLF), which formed an alliance with six other armed groups seeking to overthrow Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed’s government, declared a “defensive war” last month. Its forces seized airports in Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, and the cities of Axum and Shire, prompting Ethiopian Airlines to suspend flights to the region.
On Sunday, the government-allied Tigray Peace Force announced it had retaken Mekelle following the TPLF’s withdrawal. The TPLF said it had decided to “temporarily leave” and operate from another location while continuing military operations.
Conflict monitor ACLED reported suspected Ethiopian drone strikes against Eritrean forces near the border town of Adigrat on Wednesday and Thursday. A resident told Reuters that explosions continued overnight into Friday.
Ethiopia has accused Eritrea, Egypt, and Sudan of supporting the rebel alliance. The three countries have rejected the allegations. Last week, Addis Ababa expelled ten Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara, prompting Eritrea to sever diplomatic ties. Eritrean troops previously backed Ethiopia’s federal army during the 2020-2022 Tigray war, which ended with the Pretoria peace agreement.
Relations with Eritrea have deteriorated over Ethiopia’s pursuit of sovereign access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia became landlocked when Eritrea gained independence in 1993, and Asmara views Addis Ababa’s ambitions as a threat to its sovereignty.
The African Union has urged restraint, while UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres has called for dialogue to resolve the disputes between the Horn of Africa states and prevent further escalation.

Canadians ‘worried’ about US travel as Trump’s policies make travelers feel unwelcome: Former premier
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:03:15 UTC
23:03:15 KST

Fahri Aksüt
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
US President Donald Trump’s immigration and border policies make Canadians uneasy about traveling to the US for the first time, a concern reflected in tourism figures, former Canadian Prime Minister Justin Trudeau said.
Trudeau, speaking at the opening session on Friday of the World Travel & Tourism Council’s (WTTC) 26th Global Summit held in the Maltese capital of Valletta, stated that for the first time, many Canadians are “worried” about crossing the border.
“In the past number of years, the US hasn’t been very good at making travelers feel welcome, whether it’s the thickening of the borders, the worries about what can happen if you get arrested at the border,” he said. “Because, for decades, generations, Canadians and Americans criss-crossing our shared border, the longest unmilitarized border in the world, has been something we almost took for granted, and the family, personal, and business connections have been huge and strong.”
Trudeau stated that the real issue is Washington’s attitude towards Canada, particularly “this disrespect that the president has shown, in terms of saying it’s not a real country.”
“I think, first of all, (it’s important to) understand that some governments get along, some governments don't get along, and that's the reality,” he said. “Looking at what, how people are feeling — like, even when we were facing difficulties with the United States, we didn't impose penalties or raise prices or make it more difficult for people to travel to the United States, for example.”
The former prime minister noted that the number of Canadians traveling to the US declined by more than 20% and that, to compensate, American tour operators, airlines, and hotels lowered their prices, but to no avail in changing Canadians' travel preferences.
“At places like Florida, Arizona, even nearby places like Maine or elsewhere, (they’re) coming to tell Canadians, ‘it’s okay, we still like you, Please come back’ — we know Canadians still like Americans, Americans still like Canadians, but conflict between governments and disrespect from the US government has caused Canadians to say, ‘Okay, let's look at other places to go,’ and that has been a really important shift, but also a telling one, that how the mood of a country, how people are made to feel welcome, is an extremely important part of tourism,” he said.
He recalled that early bookings for the North American World Cup were affected because travelers felt hesitant about entering the US.
“Now, the US actually was very successful in welcoming lots of people from around the world who had a wonderful experience discovering North America, discovering how wonderful and nice Americans are. But at the same time, in the run-up to the World Cup, we saw that bookings were down, we saw people worried about going to the United States, not sure if they wanted to go to the United States, and there was a point at which people were worrying that it might not be a huge success. It ended up being a success, but countries need to be a little more consistent. If they want tourism dollars, they have to show themselves as being open to the world, which is something that Canada always did well,” he added.

Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:58 UTC
23:02:58 KST

Who is Navi Pillay, winner of the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize?
The 85-year-old South African judge has spent decades fighting apartheid and genocide.
South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize, becoming the fifth South African to win it.
Making the announcement on Friday, the Norwegian Nobel Committee praised Pillay for her decades-long efforts to prosecute genocide and war crimes, which have been marked by “judicial rigour, personal integrity and considerable courage”.
From defending activists in apartheid-era South Africa, to more recently overseeing a United Nations inquiry which declared Israel responsible for genocide in Gaza, the 85-year-old, who is also a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ), has specialised in international law for decades.
Here’s what we know about her life and why she has been awarded the world’s top peace prize:
Who is Pillay?
Navanethem Pillay, known as Navi Pillay, was born in the racially segregated city of Durban in South Africa’s Natal province in 1940 to parents of Tamil descent.
After earning a law degree from the University of Natal, she became the first woman in Natal province to start her own law firm. Early in her career, she helped defend numerous anti-apartheid activists in the country.
She later became the first woman of colour to sit on the High Court of South Africa. She went on to preside over the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda (ICTR), which prosecuted those charged with humanitarian crimes during the 1994 Rwandan genocide.
Pillay was the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights (OHCHR) from 2008 to 2014. More recently she chaired the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory which determined last year that Israel is responsible for carrying out genocide in Gaza.
Currently, Pillay is a judge on the International Court of Justice, acting in a case in which Myanmar is accused of genocide against its mostly Muslim Rohingya minority.
What work is she best known for?
Pillay has spent much of her life advocating for human rights in her home South Africa and abroad. While studying, she took part in boycotts and marches against apartheid. She later joined the legal defence of some of the country’s most prominent anti-apartheid figures, such as Phyllis Naidoo and Strini Moodley.
In 1973, Pillay took on a case that helped secure basic rights, including legal access, for political prisoners on Robben Island, where Nelson Mandela was jailed.
In a 2016 interview with the Diplomatic Courier, Pillay said her early human rights work was “shaped by what (she) had experienced under apartheid”.
“I used many of the challenges to my advantage, I had to learn international humanitarian law so as to defend cases of racial discrimination,” she said.
Pillay oversaw a UN commission of inquiry which concluded in 2025 that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
In a statement on the report, Pillay urged UN member states to do everything they can to establish a ceasefire in Gaza and to “ensure justice and accountability for all victims”.
What has she been awarded the Nobel Prize for?
The Nobel committee said Pillay was being honoured for her “efforts to promote peace and international law”.
It called her one of “the great defenders of international legal principles in our time”, having helped hold states and national leaders to account and bring “hope to victims of violence and conflict”.
The committee stressed the role Pillay played in the Rwandan genocide tribunal, saying her influence helped establish “that rape and sexual violence could constitute a crime against humanity – as well as genocide”.
“In the same case, Ms Pillay was instrumental in a separate legal breakthrough: for the first time, a defendant faced charges of incitement to commit genocide purely on the basis of spreading propaganda,” said the committee.
Why is her win so significant?
The committee said honouring Pillay is especially important at a time when international law “is under tremendous pressure and its institutions are under attack”.
That message was echoed by rights advocates and international officials.
The UN’s rights chief, Volker Turk, said her award was “a recognition, a reaffirmation that human rights, the rule of law and justice and accountability are fundamental to everything, to peace, to security and prosperity”.
International Criminal Court (ICC) President Tomoko Akane said the award carried special significance “at a time of profound challenges to the international legal order and the rule of law”.
South African President Cyril Ramaphosa praised the award as a tribute to Pillay’s “courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice”.
Haakon Gjerlow, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo, said it “sends a clear message that peace depends not only on political leadership, but on strong, credible international institutions and the courageous people who dedicate their lives to defending them .”
Ashok Swain, a professor of peace and conflict research at Uppsala University, told Al Jazeera that the selection of Pillay was a “pleasant surprise” and the “best possible choice”.
He said the Nobel committee likely took into consideration Pillay’s lifelong record fighting genocide and apartheid. He added that the award to the South African jurist could also be read as a message to United States President Donald Trump, who has long argued that he is deserving of the peace prize and whose administration has clashed with South Africa over debunked claims that white Afrikaners are facing “genocide”.
Furthermore, last year, the Trump administration issued sanctions against members of the ICC in what many critics saw as an attack on the system of international law.
The ICC had previously issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant for alleged war crimes and crimes against humanity.
The ICC responded by describing the US sanctions as a “flagrant attack against the independence of an impartial judicial institution” and the victims of war crimes around the world. It said it would continue its work “without regard to any restriction, pressure or threat”.
How has Pillay responded?
Pillay appeared to learn of the award as media reports circulated, telling a group of supporters applauding her: “I don’t know about this. So my question is: Is it true?”
She also jokingly referenced Trump, saying, “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.”
Once the news was confirmed, Pillay said she would dedicate the award to “all of the survivors of international crimes”.
“This award strengthens my conviction that we must stand together in defence of the rule of law, in defence of independent courts and an international legal order based on principle.”
Earlier, the Nobel committee said it had struggled to get in touch with Pillay to notify her. “If you see a Norwegian number calling, please pick up,” said committee chair, Jorgen Watne Frydnes.

Ukraine Strikes Russian Missile Launch Institute and Intercontinental Ballistic Missile Disposal Facility
Ukrainian forces struck two Russian missile-related facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region overnight on October 9, targeting infrastructure involved in missile launch systems and the disposal of intercontinental ballistic missiles.
The General Staff of the Armed Forces of Ukraine confirmed the strikes, identifying the targets as a branch of the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes and a facility responsible for dismantling intercontinental ballistic missiles.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
According to the General Staff, Ukrainian forces hit a facility belonging to the Barmin Research Institute of Launch Complexes, a branch of the Center for Operation of Ground-Based Space Infrastructure, near the settlement of Dalneye Konstantinovo-5.
The institute specializes in the development, maintenance, and operation of missile launch positions, fueling equipment, and missile control systems, making it part of Russia's missile infrastructure.
In a separate operation, Ukrainian forces targeted the Center for the Disposal of Intercontinental Ballistic Missiles near the settlement of Surovatikha, also in the Nizhny Novgorod region.
The General Staff said the strike was intended to weaken Russia's military-industrial capacity to produce explosives and components used in rocket propellants.
In addition to the two facilities in the Nizhny Novgorod region, Ukraine's General Staff confirmed a strike on the Redkino Experimental Plant in Russia's Tver region.
The Redkino Experimental Plant is a major chemical production facility in Russia’s Tver region, specializing in small-batch manufacturing of specialty chemicals. The enterprise produces more than 40 types of chemical products supplied to Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Its product range includes ferrocene-based compounds used as combustion catalysts in solid-propellant rocket engines, alongside specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These substances serve both civilian industrial purposes and military production needs.
Ukrainian forces also targeted the Lukoil-Ukhtaneftepererabotka oil refinery in Ukhta, Russia's Komi Republic, approximately 1,700 kilometers from the Ukrainian border, as Kyiv continues strikes against Russian energy facilities in response to Moscow's attacks on Ukrainian territory.

Fjord Details a Family’s Sudden Nightmare in Norway
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:02:05 UTC
23:02:05 KST

Romanian filmmaker Cristian Mungiu makes thoughtful movies about social issues that cross international borders: In 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days, a young Romanian woman risks her life for an illegal abortion. R.M.N. explores xeno-phobia in a small Transylvanian village, dissecting the complexity of spontaneous human impulses in the process. Mungiu’s films can spur us to think anew about issues we’d rather keep in the background, and they can at times be deeply moving. They can also feel dreary and instructive, in an eat-your-vegetables way.
Mungiu’s Fjord, which won the Palme d’Or at Cannes earlier in the year, offers a healthy dose of very nutritious vegetables, and in places the story almost—almost—stretches the bounds of believability. But its actors, including Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve, as well as two young newcomers, make you believe in one family’s sudden nightmare. Do the authorities entrusted to protect our children always know what’s best for them? Fjord suggests, provocatively, that the answer may not always be yes.
Mihai Gheorghiu (Stan), who is Romanian, and his Norwegian wife Lisbet (Reinsve) have just relocated with their five children from Romania to Norway, to be closer to Lisbet’s parents. Mihai and Lisbet are also deeply religious, and appear to be raising their children in a sometimes strict but undeniably loving home. One day, at the children’s new school, an instructor charged with protecting the students’ welfare notices a bruise on the shoulder of the eldest Gheorghiu daughter, Elia (Vanessa Ceban). The administrator takes swift action, and before Mihai and Lisbet can fully grasp what’s happening, their children—including their infant, who’s still breastfeeding—are whisked into foster homes. Their struggle to reunite their family involves risky twists and a great deal of frustrating bureaucracy.
Unless you know Norway’s judicial system, you might be tempted to wonder: Could one family really be broken up that fast, with so little evidence? Mungiu’s premise seems somewhat far-fetched, intensified for dramatic reasons, though it’s worth noting that his script is based on a real-life case in Norway. And recently, in the U.S., Child Protective Services interviewed the children of former Secretary of Transportation Pete Buttigieg, separating the children from their fathers for 24 hours, after receiving a tip alleging that they were at risk. The report was proved false, but the incident shows how easily a system designed to protect kids might be manipulated.
Regardless, the plausibility of Fjord’s premise is academic in the context of the performances given by Stan and Reinsve. Reinsve (so terrific in 2025’s Sentimental Value) is resolutely unglamorous here, a dutiful wife and mother decked out in dowdy clothes. But her distress over the loss of her children crosses the planes of her face like a muted shadow; you sense some anger beneath that meek veneer. And Stan, who is Romanian American, gives layers of complexity to Mihai as a father figure. He clearly loves his kids, but he also has a temper. Stan doesn’t make Mihai easy to read, just as the movie around him doesn’t offer any easy conclusions.
Yet amid all the child-custody drama Fjord lays before us, a subplot involving the deepening friendship between Elia and a neighbor couple’s daughter, Noora (Henrikke Lund-Olsen), ends up being the film’s most powerful and moving element. These two young teenagers aren’t just navigating a new friendship; they’re exploring feelings that may or may not be the roots of romantic love. Sometimes kids tell us what we need to know about life, even if it’s not always the lesson we expect or want. And sometimes they steal a movie away from the grownups. Fjord, perhaps unbeknownst even to the man who made it, really belongs to them.

Palantir’s Thiel slams Pope Leo’s AI warnings
Pope Leo is tapping into public fears of artificial intelligence to distract people from the Catholic Church’s latent child sex abuse scandals, Palantir co-founder Peter Thiel has claimed. The gay US tech billionaire also accused former President Barack Obama of exploiting opposition to AI for political gain.
The remarks come as AI developers themselves warn that the technology could soon spiral beyond human control. OpenAI chief Sam Altman and xAI owner Elon Musk have backed calls to slow the development of increasingly powerful AI models after Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned that rogue systems could seize control of vast swathes of the internet within months, causing hundreds of billions of dollars in damage.
The warnings have fueled demand for the tougher oversight of AI, with rival tech giants calling for safeguards against a technology they fear could evade human control.
During a series of closed-door lectures in Nashville, Thiel singled out both leaders while stepping up his warnings about the Antichrist, a prophesied figure traditionally associated with deception and opposition to the teachings of Jesus. Thiel has argued that such a figure could exploit fears of AI and other catastrophic threats to halt technological progress and impose a heavily regulated “one world government.” His remarks, delivered on September 28 and October 5, were revealed by Politico on Thursday.
“Many people know that AI is politically unpopular and want to leverage that to boost their own popularity,” Thiel said. “Both Obama and the pope fall into this category. Obama knows the Democrats have no ideas, but they can at least oppose AI.”
Obama recently urged Democrats to develop a more comprehensive strategy on artificial intelligence.
The openly gay Republican surveillance company billionaire went on to accuse Leo XIV of using the debate over AI to shift attention away from decades of sexual abuse scandals within the Catholic Church.
“He needed something politically popular to distract from the church’s child sex abuse scandals, and he found it in AI,” Thiel said, referring to the pope’s first encyclical, published in May.
Leo XIV has made AI a major focus of his papacy, warning about the dangers of unchecked development and its impact on human dignity, individual freedoms and the concentration of power.
Earlier this week, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman told Politico that the world should accept some “bad things” from AI, including hacks, scams and misuse, in exchange for its benefits. However, he drew the line at “the really catastrophic risks,” including “a serious loss of control to AI.”
Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates has also called for government regulation, warning that AI in the hands of malicious actors could trigger events causing “a billion deaths.” Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton has similarly warned that increasingly powerful systems could eventually escape human control, with catastrophic consequences for humanity.

BERLIN — Former German intelligence chief August Hanning angrily challenged his successor after learning that the agency he once headed, the BND, had passed allegations that he was a Russian spy to investigators.
In a three-page letter sent on Aug. 17, less than three months before his arrest this week, Hanning demanded answers to 11 questions from BND President Martin Jäger.
In the letter, obtained by WELT — which, like POLITICO, is part of the Axel Springer Global Reporters Network — Hanning complained that the BND had passed allegations by a former intelligence agent that he was a Russian spy to investigators without consulting him.
Advertisement
Jäger did not respond to the letter at the time, according to Hanning, who spoke to WELT before his arrest.
Hanning’s subsequent arrest, including on suspicion of attempted treason, has caused considerable concern abroad. Grzegorz Malecki, the former head of Poland’s foreign intelligence service, told WELT that the case was “extremely concerning” and could deepen allies’ distrust of the BND. He warned this had the potential to undermine intelligence-sharing with Germany.
The BND has also raised eyebrows within Germany’s intelligence community over allegations that it allowed Hanning’s former chief of staff, who is also in custody, to work for Hanning outside his official duties.
While civil servants are generally permitted to take on outside employment, any approval allowing a member of the BND to work for Hanning would have had to be decided at the senior management level, said Günter Heiss, a former intelligence coordinator under former Chancellor Angela Merkel. “Without knowing the details, I would never have approved anything like this had I been in a position of responsibility at the BND.”
Bernd Schmidbauer, a former minister of state and intelligence coordinator under Chancellor Helmut Kohl, told WELT that Hanning had made major contributions to Germany’s national security. The affair was therefore “not only a tragedy for the German intelligence services, but also for the former senior official himself,” Schmidbauer said.
Hanning was among Schmidbauer’s closest aides during the 1990s and went on to lead the BND from 1998 to 2005.
Dirk Banse is an investigative reporter at WELT. Philipp Fritz is WELT’s Eastern Europe correspondent. Uwe Müller is a freelance reporter based in Berlin.

The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) on Friday recommended airlines not to operate in additional portions of Saudi Airspace in an updated bulletin.
The EASA said recent attacks had demonstrated the ability and the intent of the Houthis to strike targets deeper inside Saudi territory, including the capital.
On Thursday, the Iran-backed Houthis warned employees at Saudi oil facilities that oil installations remain a target.
The Saudi-Houthi conflict: What to know
The Houthis have fought a Saudi-led coalition since 2015, when the kingdom entered Yemen's civil war to reinstate the internationally backed government in Sanaa. Houthi rebels took control of the capital in 2014.
But ever since, the Saudi-led coalition has found it hard to turn the tide of the war that quieted under a UN-brokered ceasefire in 2022.
In the last weeks, the Houthis stormed down Yemen's coast, capturing a wide swath of territory that has given them greater control of the Bab al-Mandab Strait.
A Saudi-led coalition has pressed a counteroffensive against the Houthis fighters and recaptured several areas along the strait, Yemeni officials have said. But the fighting appears to be far from over.

Kyiv has 700 generators, but they cannot power city's main facilities
Ukraine

Kyiv has 700 generators, but they cannot power city's main facilities
Around 700 generators are currently installed at Kyiv's heating and water supply facilities. However, the city's largest and most critical facilities require separate power plants to ensure a reliable backup power supply.
Source: Petro Panteleiev, acting First Deputy Head of Kyiv City State Administration, at a press briefing on 9 October
Details: The generators are used at boiler houses, heating substations, local pumping stations and other facilities. For example, 155 public drinking water pump rooms, which provide an additional source of drinking water in the event of temporary disruptions to the centralised system, are equipped with them.
"However, backup power for the main heating and water supply facilities can only be provided by building new diesel power plants or cogeneration units," Panteleiev said.
He noted that some backup power projects under Kyiv's Resilience Plan are already up and running, while the rest are scheduled to be completed by the end of the year, in line with the original plan.
Panteleiev added that utility workers are gradually stabilising the water supply in the city's Holosiivskyi, Sviatoshynskyi, Solomianskyi and Shevchenkivskyi districts, where reduced pressure has been recorded.
Background:
- President Volodymyr Zelenskyy previously said that Kyiv's city authorities have almost completely failed to implement the necessary measures to protect energy infrastructure.
- The government has unblocked payments for some projects under Kyiv's Resilience Plan, specifically backup heating supplies, the construction of cogeneration plants and measures to ensure an uninterrupted power supply to water infrastructure.

South African human rights lawyer Navi Pillay awarded 2026 Nobel Peace Prize
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:37 UTC
23:00:37 KST

South African human rights lawyer Navanethem “Navi” Pillay has been awarded the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize for her work promoting international justice and accountability for serious crimes.
The Norwegian Nobel Committee announced the award Friday in Oslo, recognizing Pillay’s contributions to prosecuting war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.
The committee praised her courage and integrity in advancing international law and defending human rights.
“Navi Pillay has held states and national leaders accountable and brought hope to victims of violence and conflict,” the committee said.
Pillay, 85, began her legal career in South Africa during apartheid, challenging racial discrimination and defending people who opposed the system.
Her clients included Nelson Mandela, who later became South Africa’s first Black president and received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1993.
Pillay subsequently served in South Africa’s judiciary, the United Nations International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda and the International Criminal Court.
She also served as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, overseeing international efforts to protect fundamental rights.
According to the committee, Pillay has consistently emphasized that individuals and governments must respect the rule of law.
The committee said the award was intended to highlight the importance of legal institutions in maintaining peace and resolving conflicts without violence.
The Nobel Peace Prize includes 12 million Swedish kronor, approximately 8 million DKK.
The prize was established under the will of Swedish inventor and chemist Alfred Nobel.
It recognizes individuals or organizations whose work has made significant contributions to peace, in accordance with the principles outlined in his will.

====================================================================================================

I hitchhiked from Sydney to Perth, and found comfort in the company of strangers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:33 UTC
23:00:33 KST

I’m alone, hunched over by a dusty road junction, and feeling the bite of the morning sun. I’ve already been waiting here, on the outskirts of Esperance on the south coast of Western Australia, for more than three hours. Another wave of traffic approaches. I smile, stretch out my arm and raise my thumb.
Most drivers who pass wave or give me a thumbs up. One gives me the finger. There isn’t much traffic. Someone tosses a water bottle out their window at me.
Just as I start to catastrophise in the dust, a four-wheel-drive quietly pulls off the road and comes to a stop behind me. I hoist my backpack around my shoulder, run over and jump in the passenger seat, thanking the driver profusely.
One of my stranger interests is hitchhiking. I’m drawn to the idea of abandoning control and finding comfort in a stranger’s company. It’s a subculture, an art, and a way of travel that satisfies wanderlust like no other trip. Plus, it costs nothing.
Once a popular way to travel in the 70s and 80s, these days it’s pretty rare to see a hitchhiker on the side of Australian roads. For starters, its reputation was overwhelmingly tarnished by its association with serial killer Ivan Milat, who murdered several hitchhikers in the early 90s. Australia is also one of the few countries in the world that make it legally fraught to hitchhike, with laws explicitly naming hitchhiking as an offence, though legislation differs between state and territories.
According to Hitchwiki (Wikipedia for hitchhiking), most jurisdictions essentially prohibit a pedestrian from standing on or moving on to a road to hitchhike, though the wording and what legally constitutes “the road” varies. However, in the ACT hitchhiking is legal in most circumstances and Tasmania removed any reference to hitchhiking from its road rules in 2019.
But safety and legal baggage aside, there are some signs hitching is making a comeback. Online resources such as the hitchhiker community Hitchwiki and its offshoot, Trustroots, which has more than 120,000 members, are steadily growing. And according to the University of Western Australia’s Dr Fang Liu, who studies adventure tourism, social media accounts sharing extreme ways of travelling are demystifying and normalising hitchhiking.
“Young international travellers are seeing people online and think, ‘Oh, I can do that too,’ but they may be unprepared and unaware of the risks,” she says.
“In a lot of places there’s no [phone] signal and you might have to wait hours for someone to stop. By then you’ve probably already dehydrated. Social media doesn’t convey that.”
Inside strangers’ cars
I introduce myself to my latest ride. The driver is Doug Hilton, the boss of Australia’s national science agency, CSIRO. His job will make for good conversational fodder, but more importantly, he’s driving 500km west to Albany, his car has air conditioning, and the dusty intersection is in the rear-vision mirror.
I’ve hitchhiked in Australia a few times before, once up Tasmania’s east coast and across Flinders Island on the Bass Strait, and another time from Canberra to Sydney. But never as far and never as ambitious as this latest leg – the plan is to go all the way from Sydney to Perth, mostly inside strangers’ cars.
It’s the final leg of my journey and things have taken a fortunate turn.
‘Here we feel so safe’
Five days earlier I’m fresh and clean-shaven, standing outside Broken Hill in outback New South Wales. I wait just five minutes before an SUV with a bull bar doubles back and offers me a ride.
Inside is Miranda and her two children, originally from Zimbabwe. The car is crammed with pillows and baggage, but they find room for me. While I ram my backpack into the boot, Miranda’s teenage daughter moves to the backseat, squishing in beside her younger brother and an Esky packed with yoghurt cups and juice boxes.
The family immigrated to the US a few years ago, but because of gun violence and immigration crackdowns decided to leave. “I never would have picked up someone there, but here we feel so safe,” Miranda says, the desert rushing by.
They now live in the regional Queensland town of Chinchilla, where Miranda says they’ve been embraced by the community. “We are so happy here,” she says. “Every day I thank God for where we have ended up.” From the backseat, her daughter says she wants to study medicine when she finishes high school.
After four hours of meandering conversations between long silences, we part ways somewhere in rural South Australia. They’re headed to Adelaide to visit a family friend and make the most of school holidays. I’m going west.
‘Milat changed things’
Soon I’m racing through rolling hills of green oats and yellow canola flowers draped in golden afternoon light. Hulking wind turbines spin on the hilltops. Mike, 67, is in the driver’s seat of his Toyota troop carrier. He spends his retirement restoring century-old farm tractors and is headed to Cowell to pick up some engine parts. He says by sundown we’ll be in Jamestown, a small town with a pleasant campground by the river.
“You’re the first hitchhiker I’ve seen in decades,” he says. “Milat probably changed things.”
Ivan Milat was convicted of the murder of five female and two male backpackers between 1989 and 1992 in NSW, several of whom had been hitchhiking. It’s alleged he’s responsible for dozens more unsolved murders or disappearances.
There’s no denying the act of hitchhiking is inherently risky. But I am a white male. Whatever the risks I face, they are not the same dangers a woman or female-presenting person can encounter hitchhiking alone. Hitchwiki offers specific safety advice for female hitchers, but maintains “you have a right to be respected and it is not true that while hitchhiking you expose yourself to a risk at your own wish”. They also point out that women will usually spend less time waiting to be picked up.
On my journey I follow the general rule of thumb when it comes to hitching safely: I stand well off the road, in places with good visibility, with enough room for cars to pull over, and slow-moving traffic. I stick to footpaths where I can.
When a car does pull over I give the driver a once-over and follow my gut. If I feel uncomfortable or unsafe, I know I’m under no obligation to get in the car. Though that’s a hypothetical. Every experience I’ve had has been positive so far.
Over beer and dinner at the Jamestown pub, I learn about Mike’s extended family and how proud he is of his overachieving daughter. The next morning I tag along with him further west, snaking up a mountain pass before plunging into a treeless and barren plain below. Across the Spencer Gulf, grey and faint in the distance, is the Whyalla steelworks. Last month more than 500 of the plant’s employees lost their jobs.
“People are feeling pissed off – there’s only bad news now and the major parties have no solutions,” Mike says. Talking about politics is a staple of the journey, though in a stranger’s car I prefer to do most of the listening. “Still, we are a lucky country, it’s just a lot of us don’t realise how lucky,” Mike says. An hour later we part ways.
‘Middle of everything’
By midday I meet Neil, a 79-year-old widower on the final leg of a four-month road trip across the continent. Neil, who lives in Geraldton in Western Australia, has stopped in his ute. His first joke is about hitchhiking.
“A hitchhiker gets into a car,” Neil tells me. “He says to the driver, ‘You’re fairly brave picking up a hitchhiker these days. For all you know, I could be a mass murderer.’
“The driver turns to him and says, ‘Well, what are the chances of us both being axe murderers?’”
As we get comfortable, Neil’s running commentary begins. There’s a “ripper” wheat crop over there and another a few kilometres later, much the same. Over there is a slag heap from an abandoned iron ore mine. But where are all the sheep? And what could that truck be hauling?
I learn about his life, too. Marrying at 21, raising a family, working 96-hour weeks driving trucks and saving prudently. We talk about relationships, love and getting to the “pointy end”. His motto is: “If you never go, you never never know.”
At dusk we pull off the Eyre Highway at a truckstop and Neil disappears into his camper trailer for the night. I pitch my tent beside it. The ground is gravel and my sleep is restless. In the morning we set off at dawn and I doze off in the passenger seat.
By the time I wake the sun is high and the landscape has transformed, thickets of silver saltbush and red dirt as far as the eye can see. We’ve reached the Nullarbor, a vast arid plain stretching 1,200km across southern Australia. “Middle of nowhere,” I say. “Nah mate, middle of everything,” Neil replies, road trains swooshing by endlessly.
Towing his camper, Neil sticks to about 80km/h for safety and fuel efficiency, so it’s slow going. In the afternoon we drive down the 90 Mile Straight, the longest straight road in the southern hemisphere, and that night, under a gibbous moon, we share a dark beer, dinner and a Magnum mini vanilla ice-cream by the fire, all courtesy of Neil.
Three days and 1,900km since we met, Neil pulls up outside a campground in Esperance. We take a selfie and exchange a warm handshake. I know it’s probably the last time I’ll see him.
A birding detour
I don’t know it yet, but Doug from the CSIRO, 62, will be the last driver to pick me up before I hit Perth.
I bookend my journey by talking to Doug about his passion for moths, his dream of inventing a way to eradicate feral cats, and the benefits of therapy to his mental health. Among other scientific pursuits, he’s on his way to Albany to meet with two Menang Indigenous elders who co-authored a paper with him about moths in the region, including three newly discovered species of primitive jaw moths.
In the afternoon I take up his invitation to join him bird watching by the ocean. We park at a headland, Doug grabs a Nikon Z9 with a huge telephoto lens out of the boot, and we start walking through thick coastal scrub. At sunset we witness a brown blur scurry across a dirt track. Doug misses the photo but is nonetheless ecstatic and wraps his arm around me in joy.
Apparently we’ve just seen one of Australia’s rarest birds, the noisy scrubbird, presumed extinct until it was rediscovered in 1961. The significance of the sighting is lost on me but Doug assures me I’ve just hit the peak of my bird-watching career. I didn’t know I’d started it.
We pull into Albany at dark and Doug drops me off at a hostel. It reeks of marijuana and there’s no hot water but I’m just happy to be sleeping on a thick mattress. When I wake up it’s miserable outside so I make the call to take the bus for the final six hours of the route to Perth. I’m comfortable, but it’s decidedly dull as the sprawling suburbs of the world’s most isolated capital city start rolling by. I’ve spent 4,360km travelling across the most isolated inhabited continent on Earth, yet for all the distance, I’ve rarely felt alone.

Hacker retained access to Danish CPR register for nearly 22 days before breach was discovered
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:32 UTC
23:00:32 KST

An unauthorized user had access to Denmark’s national Civil Registration System (CPR) for nearly 22 days before authorities discovered the security breach, according to documents obtained by TV 2.
The access began September 10 and was stopped October 2, lasting 21 days and 17 hours.
However, preliminary investigations suggest the unauthorized activity ended September 20, approximately 10 days after it began, according to a report submitted by the CPR office to the Danish Data Protection Agency.
The Ministry of Research, Education and Digitalization announced Monday that personal information belonging to approximately 8.8 million people had been exposed, including names, addresses and CPR identification numbers.
The breach occurred through a small Danish company with legitimate access to the register.
According to DR, the company is based on Funen and shares ownership and an address with a larger business. Its identity has not been publicly confirmed.
Authorities discovered the incident after receiving an unusually large invoice for searches conducted through the company’s account.
Approximately 14 million CPR searches had been made using its access credentials.
“The number far exceeds the company’s customer base, and the company has indicated that they did not perform the lookups themselves,” the CPR office stated in its report.
Private companies and organizations can pay to access certain CPR information.
Research, Education and Digitalization Minister Christina Egelund of the Moderates party acknowledged that security measures had been inadequate.
She has requested a security review of the register following the breach.
The company had not responded to DR’s requests for comment as of Friday morning.
`123456’ password used in massive Danish CPR data breach
At least three accounts at the company linked to a major breach of Denmark’s CPR register reportedly used the password “123456”, including an administrator account.
At least three user accounts at the Funen-based IT company Pays used the password “123456” when hackers gained access to Denmark’s CPR register, Politiken reports.
One of them was the company’s administrator account.
The breach exposed information linked to around 8.8 million CPR numbers. The CPR system is Denmark’s central civil registration database and contains personal information on people living or previously registered in Denmark.
The newspaper Politiken reviewed data from the breach that the hacker allegedly used to gain access to the system.
Jens Myrup Pedersen, professor at Aarhus University’s Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, described the company’s password security as “hopeless”.
“There is really no security, it is an open door. A password like ‘123456’ is one of the very first things you would guess if you took a list of common passwords,” he told Politiken.
“I find it hard to see that you could have worse security. It was a matter of time before things went wrong.”
Pays ApS, based in Odense, confirmed to TV 2 on Friday that it was the company whose access had been compromised.
“We can confirm that we are the company that has been subjected to an attack where our legal access to search for information in the CPR system has been abused,” managing director and owner Sophie Laursen said in an email to TV 2.
The hacker had access to the CPR register from 10 September for a total of 21 days and 17 hours.
An anonymous hacker told Politiken on Thursday that they were behind the attack and claimed gaining access had not been particularly difficult.
According to the hacker, access was initially obtained using a leaked password belonging to a former employee of a small Danish company. The hacker then allegedly created two computer programs to retrieve information from the CPR system and store it externally.
The hacker told Politiken that there were no plans to sell or publish the information.
Private companies and associations can be granted access to information in Denmark’s CPR register when they have a legitimate need, for example to obtain address information about customers or members.
According to Denmark’s Central Business Register, Pays ApS had two employees as of July 2026.
One in four Danish driving penalty points linked to mobile phone use
Danish motorists received almost 21,000 penalty points for using handheld mobile phones while driving last year – the highest number in four years.
Mobile phones are playing a growing role in traffic offences in Denmark.
In 2025, motorists received 20,910 penalty points on their driving licences for using a handheld mobile phone behind the wheel, according to figures from the police case management system POLSAS.
That means mobile phone use accounted for roughly one in every four of the 84,056 penalty points issued for traffic offences during the year.
The number of mobile-related penalty points increased by 7.5 percent compared with 2024 and reached its highest level in four years.
On average, police issued 57 penalty points every day for handheld mobile phone use.
Britta Bjerregaard, claims director at insurance company Alm. Brand, described the development as deeply concerning.
“Most people know full well that the phone should stay put while driving. Still, it can be tempting to just answer a call, reply to a message, or change the song,” she said.
“Traffic does not pause while you look at the screen.”
89 metres without watching the road
The Danish Road Safety Council considers inattention one of the major risks on Danish roads, with mobile phones posing a particular problem.
“The mobile phone takes an incredible amount of attention if you use it behind the wheel,” deputy director Karina Petersen said.
“If you look at the screen for four seconds at country road speed, you are driving 89 metres blind.”
However, Petersen cautioned that the increase in recorded offences does not necessarily mean that more drivers are using their phones.
The rise could also reflect more police checks or improved camera equipment used for traffic enforcement.
What are the rules in Denmark?
Using a handheld mobile phone while driving in Denmark results in a DKK 1,500 fine and a penalty point on your driving licence. An additional DKK 1,000 contribution to the Victims’ Fund is also charged.
The rule applies even when the car is stationary in traffic or waiting at a red light.
Drivers may briefly operate a phone if it is securely mounted, and using a vehicle’s built-in screen is also permitted.
The ban on handheld mobile phone use also applies to cyclists, electric scooter users and drivers of other motorised vehicles.

Sardine sales surge in Copenhagen as social media skincare trend gains popularity
Canned sardines are selling rapidly across Denmark, particularly around Copenhagen, as supermarkets report rising demand and occasional shortages.
Four major grocery retailers, Coop, Salling Group, Nemlig.com and Dagrofa, confirmed significant sales increases to TV 2 Kosmopol.
Coop, which operates 365, SuperBrugsen, Brugsen and Kvickly, reported a 170 percent increase in sardine sales in Denmark’s Capital Region between June and September 2026 compared with the same period last year.
Nationwide, Coop’s sales rose 163.5 percent.
Jacob Herbst Lassen, Coop Denmark’s press manager, said the sudden popularity has left some shelves with fewer products while purchasing teams work to replenish supplies.
Salling Group also reported pressure on availability, although spokesperson Alma Lyhne Kristensen said the company remained adequately stocked overall.
Online supermarket Nemlig.com said Greater Copenhagen and North Zealand accounted for 75 percent of its sardine sales.
Dagrofa, which operates Meny and Spar stores, reported that sales in the capital area had more than doubled compared with last year.
The surge may be connected to the social media trend “eat your skincare,” which promotes foods believed to benefit skin health.
Sardines have attracted attention for their omega-3 fatty acids, collagen and protein.
However, dermatologist and researcher Cæcilie Johansen cautioned that evidence linking sardine consumption directly to healthier skin remains limited.
She said some studies suggest omega-3 fatty acids may help with eczema, but the research involved large quantities.
Johansen emphasized that avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol and using sunscreen are more important measures for protecting skin health.
Denmark resumes citizenship and immigration cases after criminal records error
Denmark’s Ministry of Immigration and Integration has resumed processing citizenship applications that were suspended because of errors in the country’s Central Criminal Register.
The ministry announced the decision in a press release after the National Police concluded that the errors had only a very limited impact on the register.
Immigration authorities have also been instructed to restart affected cases involving permanent residence permits and family reunification, according to an update from the Danish Immigration Service.
The applications had been placed on hold September 7 while authorities investigated the problem.
The errors became public in early September when National Police Commissioner Lasse Boje informed politicians at Christiansborg, the seat of Denmark’s parliament, that some criminal records had been deleted incorrectly.
Authorities had discovered the problem in June.
The National Police said further investigations would determine whether the errors had affected decisions made by other public authorities.
If problems are identified, police will work with the relevant authorities to determine how those cases should be handled.
The errors also disrupted the issuance of child protection certificates, which are background checks used to identify certain criminal convictions relevant to working with children.
Applications for these certificates were temporarily suspended while police reviewed the affected records.
The National Police reopened applications September 18.
During its review, police restored 43 decisions that had been removed from the Criminal Register earlier than they should have been.
Those decisions were relevant to child protection certificates.
The ministry has not specified how many citizenship, permanent residence or family reunification applications were affected by the suspension.
Danish court rejects detention request for two Kosovo prison officers accused of assault

Fire near Aarup disrupts train services across Denmark throughout Friday

Banedanmark has not yet said when normal train services are expected to resume.

According to DSB, Denmark’s national passenger railway operator, all trains between Fredericia and Copenhagen are experiencing delays, while all regional trains between Odense and Fredericia have been canceled.
Intercity trains running between Copenhagen and Fredericia via Roskilde are only operating as far as Odense, DSB said on its website.
Rail replacement buses have been deployed to replace the canceled regional trains on Funen. According to P4 Trafik, six buses were operating between Fredericia and Odense.
Passengers traveling between Jutland, Funen and Zealand can continue their journeys using some of the other trains still running, DSB said.
DSB employees are available at Odense and Fredericia stations to assist and guide passengers.
Both Banedanmark and DSB are urging travelers to check Rejseplanen, Denmark’s national journey planner, for updates.
Government unveils security-focused budget proposal
The Danish government has presented a proposed budget for 2027 that prioritizes national security, with more money allocated to defence amid an increasingly tense international security situation.
The proposal, titled “A stronger defence of Denmark – a strengthened Denmark to defend”, was presented by Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard of the Social Democrats (S) at the Ministry of Finance on Friday morning.
The government wants to ensure that defence spending reaches 3.5 percent of gross domestic product (GDP) by 2030.
Hummelgaard said the proposal reflected the need to make “hard priorities” in response to the current security situation. He also described the Danish economy as being “in top shape”.
“The government’s proposal for the finance bill shows that we take responsibility upon ourselves, and that we lead the way in working for a greener, freer, and more equal Denmark,” Hummelgaard said.
Pia Olsen Dyhr of the Socialist People’s Party (SF), the minister for economic and interior affairs, also highlighted the security situation.
“We do not solve all the challenges we have in Denmark with this finance bill. But we are well on our way,” she said at the press conference.
“I also think everyone must remember that we are in an escalated security policy situation,” Olsen Dyhr said.
Much of the proposed budget had already been announced, either in the government’s policy platform or through statements by ministers in recent weeks.
The proposal allocates 1.2 billion DKK to children’s services and education in 2027, including Denmark’s public primary and lower secondary schools, known as folkeskole.
It also sets aside a total of 10.1 billion DKK in 2030 for tax cuts. These include abolishing the intermediate income tax and the top-top tax, as well as reducing corporation tax.
“We are simplifying the tax system,” said Taxation and Growth Minister Jakob Engel-Schmidt of the Moderates (M).
The tax measures will be negotiated separately as part of a tax reform. While the budget proposal includes tax cuts, the government also plans to freeze several tax thresholds, which would increase the tax burden for some taxpayers as incomes rise.
The liberal think tank Cepos estimates that the government’s various plans will result in a net tax cut of 2.2 billion DKK in 2030.
Business and Competitiveness Minister Martin Lidegaard of the Danish Social Liberal Party (R) highlighted investment in young people and education.
“We are significantly strengthening knowledge, general education, and formal education in Denmark, from ABC to PhD. It is good for the individual young person, but it is also good for Denmark’s future,” Lidegaard said.
Unlike in recent years, when the government’s fiscal room for manoeuvre helped fund much of its budget plans, this proposal includes several measures to find additional savings.
These include cuts to the Danish student grant (SU), savings on senior pension payments, a proposed tax on cruise ships and further reductions in state administration costs.
The government must now negotiate with other parties in the Danish Parliament, the Folketing, to secure a majority for the 2027 budget.
The proposal includes a negotiating reserve of 500 million DKK annually from 2027 to 2030, which other parties can seek to use to fund their own priorities.
Business groups warn 200 DKK cruise passenger tax could drive tourists away
Two Danish business organizations are warning that a proposed tax of 200 DKK per cruise passenger could lead cruise ships to skip Danish ports, reducing tourism revenue for cities and smaller destinations.
Dansk Industri (DI), the Confederation of Danish Industry, and Dansk Erhverv, a business organization representing companies across several sectors, are responding to the government’s proposal to introduce the tax from 2028.
“A cruise tax at this level will hit both the major cities and rural districts,” said Lars Bertolt Winther, head of tourism, culture and experiences at DI, in a press release.
Jesper Kronborg, industry director for transport at Dansk Erhverv, also criticized the proposal.
“In Dansk Erhverv’s view, it is a bad proposal, or at least a proposal that requires a very thorough analysis,” he said in a press release.
The government expects the tax to generate an additional 300 million DKK in annual revenue from 2028.
The aim is to make cruise tourism contribute more toward the costs associated with ships, including pollution, noise and congestion.
Figures from Statistics Denmark show that 1.1 million cruise passengers visited Denmark in 2025. The number of cruise ships calling at Danish ports increased by 16% compared with the previous year.
Copenhagen, Aarhus, Skagen and Rønne on the island of Bornholm are the country’s main cruise destinations. Together, they account for more than 98% of cruise passengers.
DI and Dansk Erhverv argue that cruise visitors generate local revenue through port fees and spending at shops and other businesses.
Both organizations point to Iceland, where a similar tax was introduced before being reduced.
“Following the introduction of a high passenger tax, bookings dropped significantly, especially to the smaller ports, and the tax was subsequently lowered to limit the damaging effects,” Winther said.
“There is no reason to believe that Denmark does not risk the same,” he added.
According to the industry organization Danske Havne, which represents Danish ports, Iceland now charges 85 DKK per cruise passenger, while Greenland charges 50 DKK.
Tine Kirk, director of Danske Havne, described the proposed Danish tax of 200 DKK as “unreasonably high.”
“The cruise ships can very easily opt out of Denmark. We fear that the shipping companies will either bypass Denmark completely or concentrate their port calls in the largest cities,” she said in a written comment.
Drop in exports to the US drags down Danish exports
Danish exports fell by 3.3 percent in August, driven in part by a decline in goods exports to the United States, according to Statistics Denmark.
Total exports of goods and services amounted to 194 billion DKK in August, down 3.3 percent from July. Goods exports fell by 6.2 percent, while services exports rose by 0.7 percent.
Søren Kristensen, chief economist at AL Sydbank, described the overall decline as “worryingly large”.
“But it is part of the story that a large part of the decline is concentrated around the US, where we also see fluctuations from month to month,” he wrote in a comment.
Exports of goods and services to both the US and the United Kingdom fell in August. Total exports to the US amounted to 31.7 billion DKK, down 2.8 billion DKK from July.
Goods exports to the US fell by 3.3 billion DKK, while services exports rose slightly.
Kristensen said fluctuations in the prices of products such as medicines sold by Danish companies in the US could partly explain the decline. He therefore cautioned against drawing too negative a conclusion from the latest figures alone.
The August decline followed an increase in exports in July. Overall, Danish exports of goods and services rose by nearly 19 billion DKK, or more than 10 percent, between August 2025 and August 2026.
According to Kristensen, Danish exports have so far held up despite geopolitical unrest, higher energy prices and rising interest rates.
Still, the August figures are bad news for the Danish economy when viewed in isolation.
“However, it will take several months of this development before we become worried,” Kristensen wrote.
Hacker claims simple password allowed access to 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers
An anonymous hacker has claimed responsibility for accessing nearly 8.8 million Danish CPR numbers, telling newspaper Politiken that a weak password made the breach possible.
CPR numbers are personal identification numbers used in Denmark’s national Civil Registration System to identify residents and access public services.
The hacker told Politiken that the breach occurred on September 11 through a small Danish company with access to the CPR register.
According to the hacker, a leaked password belonging to a former employee allowed entry into the system. The password was reportedly “123456.”
After gaining access, the hacker said they created two computer programs to retrieve CPR information and store it outside the system.
The person’s identity has not been made public, and their account has not been independently confirmed.
The hacker told Politiken they had no plans to sell or publish the personal identification numbers and were “really shocked” by the security weaknesses they encountered.
To describe the situation, the hacker compared it to someone leaving dangerous material unattended.
“Someone leaves a suitcase with 10 kilos of plutonium unattended at a train station. Then a homeless person steals it,” the hacker said.
“Yes, of course you shouldn’t steal other people’s suitcases. But you also shouldn’t leave nuclear material at a train station.”
The hacker provided Politiken with a file containing the CPR numbers.
The newspaper forwarded the file to Emil Hørning, an IT security expert at Danish cybersecurity company Defend Denmark.
Hørning said the hacker’s account appeared credible and that the described method was plausible.
Politiken conducted its interview with the hacker in English through an encrypted communication service.
Danish government proposes tighter senior pension rules to save 800 million DKK annually
The Danish government wants to change how workers qualify for senior pensions, potentially saving 800 million DKK annually by 2030, according to Jyllands-Posten.
Currently, people whose health limits their ability to work to 15 hours a week or less can receive a senior pension up to six years before reaching the state retirement age.
Their work capacity is assessed against their most recent job. Under the proposal, applicants would instead be assessed against all types of employment.
The Finance Ministry estimates savings of 200 million DKK in 2028, rising to 800 million DKK in 2030.
The proposal has divided political parties and organizations.
Anders Vistisen of DF, Dansk Folkeparti, the Danish People’s Party, said his party would oppose the changes.
“We are not going to cut for the worn-out,” he told Jyllands-Posten, citing Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen’s promises of more dignified retirement.
Ældre Sagen, Denmark’s senior citizens’ advocacy organization, also criticized the proposal.
Deputy Director Michael Teit Nielsen warned that applicants could face longer assessments to determine whether they could work in another profession.
However, Dansk Industri, the Confederation of Danish Industry, Denmark’s main employers’ association, welcomed the proposal.
Deputy CEO Søren Kryhlmand said assessing workers against the entire labor market would allow those capable of other jobs to remain employed.
The government also plans to increase the separate Arne early retirement pension by approximately 3,000 DKK monthly. Its current maximum is 15,650 DKK per month.
Changing the senior pension scheme, introduced in 2019, requires agreement among the parties behind it before a general election.
Finance Minister Peter Hummelgaard is scheduled to present the budget proposal today.
University of Copenhagen to merge and reorganize faculties from 2028
The University of Copenhagen is changing how its academic departments are organized, with several faculties set to merge or split over the next three years.
The university announced that its Faculty of Theology and Faculty of Humanities will merge into a single Faculty of Humanities and Theology on January 1, 2028.
The Faculty of Law and Faculty of Social Sciences will also combine into a Faculty of Law and Social Sciences on the same date.
Further changes will follow on January 1, 2029.
The Faculty of Health Sciences will be divided into two faculties: Clinical and Public Health Sciences, and Health Sciences. The new divisions will focus on clinical and preclinical subjects, respectively.
The Faculty of Science will also split into two. One will cover traditional natural sciences, while the other will focus on biological, environmental and geosciences.
Despite the restructuring, the university will retain six faculties.
A faculty is a major academic division responsible for particular subjects and degree programs.
The university said most students would not be affected because the content and structure of their degree programs would remain unchanged.
Rector David Dreyer Lassen said the changes were necessary because the university’s faculties had developed differently in size and complexity over the past 15 years.
“When the differences become very large, it challenges our balance, leadership power, and cohesion,” he said.
The University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479 with four faculties: theology, law, medicine and philosophy.
Its faculty structure has changed several times since then.
Today, theology students can pursue studies leading toward the priesthood, while humanities programs include history, English, education and rhetoric.
Danish government faces criticism over student grant cuts affecting 18,000 families
Around 18,000 Danish families that received government financial assistance earlier this year could lose student grants for young adults living at home under a new proposal.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats defended the planned changes Thursday during the opening debate in the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
“Fundamentally, as a Social Democrat, my view is that when you are a young person and attending school or an education, I think it is a good idea that you have a job where you earn your own money,” Frederiksen said.
The proposal concerns SU, Denmark’s state education grant, which provides financial support to students, including those living with their parents.
According to figures from liberal think tank Cepos reported by TV 2, approximately 18,000 families that qualified for a one-time government payment to offset rising living costs could now lose these student grants because of their household income.

The proposed SU cuts could cost affected households up to 12,000 DKK annually.
The apparent contradiction has drawn criticism from opposition parties.
Alex Vanopslagh, leader of Liberal Alliance, described the government’s approach as “schizophrenic.”
Leila Stockmarr of the Red-Green Alliance, a left-wing Danish political party, also questioned why families previously considered financially vulnerable would now lose support.
Frederiksen explained that the food checks were introduced to help households manage higher prices for necessities such as food and gasoline.
Asked whether the student grant reductions would outweigh the earlier payments, Frederiksen rejected the comparison.
“Those are two different issues,” she said.
Prison unit at Kærshovedgård could take five years to complete
The government’s planned prison unit at Departure Centre Kærshovedgård may take four to five years to become operational, the Ministry of Justice told Danish public broadcaster DR.
The ministry is also working to establish temporary prison spaces at the centre. These are expected to be ready within a few years.
Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen of the Social Democrats announced the plan Tuesday during her speech at the opening of the Folketing, Denmark’s parliament.
The proposed unit would hold Kærshovedgård residents sentenced to prison for offences such as repeatedly violating their reporting obligations.
“For far too many years, you have seen your local area marred by theft. Drug dealing. And reckless driving,” Frederiksen said.
Kærshovedgård operated as a prison from 1951 until it became a departure centre in 2016.
It now houses foreign nationals who have been deported or whose asylum applications have been rejected but who have not left Denmark.
Some fear persecution or torture in their countries of origin, while others cannot return because their home countries will not cooperate with Danish authorities.
Several parties, including the Danish People’s Party, have called for residents to be prevented from leaving the centre. The government has rejected that proposal because residents who are not serving sentences cannot legally be detained.
The planned prison unit would apply only to residents convicted of criminal offences.

“The big question is now how much of the rabies boost will hold into 2027. Infection among animals fluctuates from year to year, so next year will face a tough comparison,” he wrote in a comment.
Bavarian Nordic sells travel vaccines against diseases including rabies, TBE and chikungunya, a disease spread by mosquitoes.
The company also sells vaccines for countries’ preparedness against outbreaks, including mpox, previously known in Danish as “abekopper.”
