A brief history of Israeli ceasefire violations, from 1948 until today
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:00:00 UTC
23:00:00 KST

On August 18, 2026, 10 months after the so-called ceasefire between Israel and Hamas had come into effect, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner, held a marathon meeting with Benjamin Netanyahu in Jerusalem. The discussion centered around efforts to advance the US-drafted “peace plan” in Gaza, but reports circulated that Kushner also requested Netanyahu “draw down attacks in the Strip.”
The following day, the Israeli military would strike a seaside cafe in Gaza City, killing at least seven people, including a child. Fourteen more were wounded, many critically. This time, as on many occasions before, the US remained silent. What should have been seen as a major breach, one akin to a declaration of war, has instead become normalized in Gaza. As it stands, Israel has killed over 1,400 Palestinians since the ceasefire came into effect on October 10, 2025, striking the enclave every single day.
While the number of violations have been egregious, the injustice of post-ceasefire Israeli aggression is nothing new. In fact, what has played out in the last year fits into a broader historical pattern, one that innocent civilians across the Arab world have borne witness to time and time again.
A long precedent
From late 1947 onwards, after the UN voted to partition Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states, Zionist militias began an expulsion campaign known as the Nakba. After British control formally expired on May 14 1948, Israel declared independence the same day, and the ethnic cleansing of Palestinian villages accelerated. Active fighting would only end with the 1949 Armistice agreements, the first major ceasefire in Israeli history. The agreements prohibited military action and established the Green Line between the nascent Jewish state and neighboring Egypt, Jordan, Syria and Lebanon. Despite a UN commission set up for each treaty to ensure compliance, cross-border violations were recorded from the outset.
In the post-Nakba years, thousands of Palestinian refugees would be killed after crossing the demarcation line, often after attempting to return to their farms to harvest crops, visit family or retrieve lost items. Dubbed ‘infiltrators’ by the Israeli state, military commander Yigal Allon implemented a free-fire buffer zone along the border, issuing a directive that “every stranger found will be shot, without interrogation.”
While Palestinian-led attacks also occurred, Israeli troops would routinely respond with disproportionate force. One of the deadliest episodes took place in 1953, in the Jordanian-Controlled West Bank village of Qibya. Following an attack that killed three Israelis, the army unleashed a raid which came to be known as the Qibya massacre, murdering 69 Palestinians, two-thirds of whom were women and children.
Although cycles of violence were common, it was only in 1967 that the original agreements collapsed decisively, after Israel launched a strike on Egyptian airfields, igniting the Six-Day War. Israel would go on to advance well beyond the demarcation line, occupying the West Bank, Gaza, the Sinai and the Golan Heights.
Despite boasting a far more powerful army, inflicting over 16,000 casualties and tripling its territory, Israel successfully framed the pre-emptive attacks as a matter of national survival. Years later, Menachem Begin, who went on to become Prime Minister, admitted that there was no proof of an incoming attack, yet maintained that “This was a war of self-defense in the noblest sense of the term.”
The outcome of the Six-Day War transformed the relationship between Israel and the US. Once a political afterthought, the American administration now viewed the Jewish State as a principal ally in the Middle East, one capable of countering Soviet influences in the region.
This newfound allegiance would give diplomatic cover for the violence that was to be unleashed, permitting Israel to both entrench its occupation of the West Bank and Gaza, and later violate ceasefires without consequence.
Such was the case in Lebanon. In July 1981, the US brokered a ceasefire between Israel and the PLO, who at the time were exiled in Beirut. While the goal was to end escalating cross-border violence, Israel repeatedly broke the truce in hopes of drawing a reaction that could lead to a war. Although that effort proved feckless, Israel invaded eleven months later after the attempted assassination of their ambassador to England, an endeavor the PLO played no part in. By the time another ceasefire would come into effect, over 17,000 Lebanese had been killed.
As part of the agreement, the PLO agreed to relocate to Tunis, and did so at the end of August 1982, under supervision of an international peacekeeping force. The following month, despite the PLO’s evacuation, Israeli forces broke the ceasefire, entering West Beirut and encircling Sabra and Shatila, two Palestinian refugee camps. Sending in a Lebanese Christian militia, Israeli forces watched on, as the right-wing Phalange executed up to 3,500 men, women and children over the course of 40 hours.
News reports and eyewitness accounts of the massacre sparked widespread condemnation, both internationally and within Israel. Despite the pushback, which included mass protests in Tel Aviv and a UN resolution condemning the massacre as an “act of genocide,” the military remained undeterred. Israel would go on to occupy southern Lebanon for 18 years, later enforcing an “Iron Fist” policy aimed at crushing any resistance to their presence.
Two decades of strikes
Given their history of violence across the region, Israel’s actions in Gaza — particularly after blockading the Strip in 2007 —were merely the continuation of an established practice.
Between 2008 and 2023, Israel launched four successive wars on Gaza, on top of several smaller military operations. While each would be temporarily halted via a ceasefire, humanitarian pause or a hudna — an Arabic term for low-intensity truce — such agreements meant little to the occupying force, which would often carry on striking with impunity.
During this period, 5,278 Gazans were killed, and more than 140,000 were injured. Over 1,000 of those deaths came outside the four major military operations. Furthermore, weekly UN reports showed that Israel routinely struck Palestinian militants during periods in which a ceasefire had taken effect, often harming civilians in the process.
For Israeli historian Ilan Pappé, a misaligned view of the Palestinian liberation movement played an important role in shielding Israel from accountability. “Whether leftist and secular or Islamist in nature, the Western perception was that they were already guilty of “irrational” and “intransigent” behaviour,” he told Mondoweiss.
This distorted perception permitted Israel to perpetually frame Palestinians as the aggressors, a position that Ilan Pappé explained is detached from reality. “Facts on the ground showed precisely the opposite,” he said, emphasizing the “continued willingness of Palestinians, including Hamas, to allow for a long ceasefire to enable a genuine process of reconciliation, which Israel always rejected.”
This dynamic unfolded in 2017 when Hamas updated its charter, accepting a Palestinian state along 1967 borders. Instead of welcoming the agreement as a step towards peace, Benjamin Netanyahu declared that “Hamas is attempting to fool the world, but it will not succeed.”
In the past three years since October 7, 2023, Hamas officials have also repeatedly told mediators that they would lay down their weapons if the occupation comes to an end.
But for many of Israel’s allies, the belief that Hamas is incapable of political compromise was cemented on October 7, and has also served as a justification for the genocide that Israel has carried out since.
The death toll in Gaza since October 2023 has now surpassed 74,000 with over 175,000 injured. Since the ceasefire was signed, 5,000 more Palestinians have been injured, on top of the 1,400 killed. Israel has further breached their commitments by allowing insufficient aid to enter, severely restricting access to the Rafah crossing and occupying 65% of the enclave. And yet, many in the international community continue to insist that Hamas’ unwillingness to disarm is what’s preventing a peaceful resolution.
All the while, the conditions of the Palestinians in Gaza remain dire. Instead of halting the killings and ushering in meaningful negotiations, the ceasefire has only provided the illusion that the genocide is over and allowed Israel to continue killing with no accountability. With diminished global attention paid to the ongoing violence, Israel’s impunity may be stronger than ever.

Activity of Russian satellites raises concerns for Starlink - German general
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher

Activity of Russian satellites raises concerns for Starlink - German general
Kyiv • UNN
Russian military satellites maneuvered near an ICEYE satellite supporting Ukraine. A German general warned of risks to Starlink.
Observation of a Western satellite supporting Ukraine by a group of Russian military satellites at the beginning of this year demonstrates capabilities that could threaten commercial satellite constellations such as Elon Musk's Starlink, German Space Force Commander Michael Traut told Reuters, UNN writes.
Details
In May, Russia conducted a maneuver involving four military satellites, known as "Kosmos 2610–2613," near a commercial radar-imaging satellite, the U.S. Space Command reported. Finnish company ICEYE, which provides data to the United States and its allies, confirmed to Reuters that it was one of its satellites.
Major General Michael Traut, head of Germany's space command, described the Russian spacecraft as "pursuing" an ICEYE satellite that provides intelligence imagery.
"Russia is demonstrating ways that, if used directly against such a mega-constellation of satellites as Starlink, could affect their service life" and the quality of service for all users, not just Ukraine, General Traut told Reuters. He said the satellites' capabilities could be disrupted even without a direct attack.
"This worries me greatly," he said.
His concerns, the publication notes, highlight Western militaries' growing dependence on commercial satellite networks, raising the question of who should protect them. Traut's comments also came amid accusations by European officials that Russia is escalating sabotage activities in the region aimed at undermining support for Ukraine, including recent drone attacks and arson, as well as a plot to disable undersea cables, the publication writes.
According to Western military officials, Russia's interference with Western space systems has increased significantly since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation in 2022. They say this includes ground-based jamming and orbital surveillance aimed at gathering intelligence and testing the West's tolerance.
Russia's Defense Ministry did not respond to Reuters' questions about its satellite activities. Moscow has repeatedly warned that commercial Western satellites assisting Ukraine could become legitimate targets for retaliatory action. It denies conducting sabotage operations in NATO countries, the publication writes.
SpaceX, which operates Starlink, did not respond to a request for comment.
Russia's "gray-zone" tactics
German General Traut said that an overt attack on a Starlink satellite would constitute a serious escalation, but Moscow could use "gray-zone" tactics. He described a hypothetical scenario in which a Russian satellite drifts into Starlink's orbit and then breaks up, forcing the satellites to carry out resource-intensive avoidance maneuvers that could shorten their service life.
Two other Western officials told Reuters that Russian activity is raising concerns about Starlink, the world's largest satellite constellation.
Russia does not disclose the capabilities of the "Kosmos" satellite group, the publication notes.
The move into "close proximity" to ICEYE may have been intended for surveillance, preparation for future interference, or to provide signal-transmission capabilities, said Belinda Marchan, chief scientist at the U.S. space intelligence company Slingshot Aerospace.
ICEYE CEO Rafal Modrzewski told Reuters that the company later moved its satellite, triggering further Russian maneuvers. The episode showed how satellites can increasingly move close to one another "either for surveillance or potentially to cause harm," he said. The episode underscores the need to monitor activity in orbit, Modrzewski said, and raises questions about the need for protection.
As part of a large-scale spending plan to strengthen its own space capabilities, Germany is developing inspector satellites and considering the creation of orbital weapons capable of disrupting hostile space activity without destroying targets, Traut said.
The German armed forces have also signed a contract with ICEYE and a German company to create dozens of satellites, including to support NATO's eastern flank.

Polish prosecutors seek to drop case against South Asian men who slaughtered goat in kebab bar

Polish prosecutors have asked a court to discontinue a case against three South Asian men who were caught illegally slaughtering a goat at the back of a kebab bar.
They say that the men did not realise they were breaking the law, that such practices are normal in their home countries, and that that the meat was for their own consumption. Prosecutors therefore believe the crime was of low social harm and not worth the court’s time.

The case involves two Bangladeshi nationals and one Indian, all legal residents in Poland. The incident came to light in December 2025, after witnesses reported seeing the trio leading a goat through the centre of the city of Wałbrzych, before taking it to the back of a kebab bar.
After killing the animal, the men began butchering it for meat, which they were still portioning out when the police arrived. They told officers that the meat was intended for their own consumption. The kebab bar was closed for renovations at the time.
The men also said that such slaughter was customary in their home countries and they were unaware that, with limited exceptions, animals in Poland may generally be slaughtered only at authorised slaughterhouses, reports broadcaster RMF
A spokesman for prosecutors, Mariusz Pindera, told the Wirtualna Polska news website that the men’s unfamiliarity with Polish law did not “absolve them of the obligation to comply with the regulations”.
However, “the harmfulness of the act is relatively low, although I know that what these people did shocks many people”, he continued. “We must be realistic about the fact that the court proceedings will take some time, thus blocking the docket for other cases. A trial also entails costs for the state.”
Prosecutors have therefore asked the court for a so-called conditional discontinuation of the case, a very common procedure under Polish law. Almost 25,000 such motions were submitted last year by prosecutors, citing the low social harm of the offences involved, reports Wirtualna Polska.
The court must now decide whether to accept or reject the prosecution’s motion. In the latter case, prosecutors would be required to proceed with an indictment against the suspects and seek a conviction. No hearing date on the motion has yet been set.
Indians are now the third-largest group of foreign workers in Poland, followed by Colombians, according to new data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS).

Not all cases involving illegal animal slaughter have been treated as causing low social harm. Last month, a court in the town of Limanowa convicted three men for carrying out illegal halal ritual slaughter and selling unapproved meat.
The main suspect, a Polish man, was found guilty of overseeing the operation, while two Azerbaijani nationals were convicted of helping distribute the illegal meat. The verdicts can still be appealed.
Although it has relatively small Muslim and Jewish populations, Poland is one of Europe’s biggest producers and exporters of kosher and halal meat.
Almost a third of Poland's meat exports are halal and kosher, making it one of Europe's leading producers.

However, the country has itself been experiencing growing levels of migration in recent years. Most of the new arrivals are from neighbouring Ukraine and Belarus, but there are also growing numbers from outside Europe, too.
Indians are now Poland’s third-largest immigrant group, numbering around 25,500, according to recent data from the country’s Social Insurance Institute (ZUS). Among first residence permits issued by Poland last year, Indians (9,230) and Turks (7,533) were the fourth and fifth largest recipients.
Poland’s current government has blamed some immigrant groups for a rise in crime and has stepped up deportations of those found to have broken the law. However, data show that, overall, immigrants are less likely to commit crimes than Poles themselves.

Sierra Leone: From 'blood diamonds' to stones of hope?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Sierra Leone: From 'blood diamonds' to stones of hope?
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
"Blood diamonds" became infamous for funding the brutal civil war in Sierra Leone. Beginning 25 years ago, the Kimberley Process aimed to put an end to this illegal trade. Accused of complicity in the conflict, the diamond industry has since sought to clean up its image, emphasising an ethical shift. But a quarter of a century on, have the former "blood diamonds" truly become synonymous with development? FRANCE 24's Sarah Sakho and Simon Martin report.
Between 1991 and 2002, the civil war in Sierra Leone claimed more than 120,000 lives and left thousands of civilians mutilated. It also became synonymous with "blood diamonds". A deadly battle for control of the country's diamond mines gave rise to a parallel economy supported by major international firms. This illegal trade is estimated to have brought in up to $125 million a year, much of it used to fund the fighting.
Thanks to Hollywood, people became aware of the scandal through the 2006 film "Blood Diamond" starring Leonardo DiCaprio. The exposure forced the global diamond industry, which came under deep scrutiny, to change its rules in an attempt to restore its image.
The Kimberley Process, a system to trace diamonds' origin
Twenty-five years ago, the Kimberley Process began: a series of negotiations through which the major diamond-producing countries and international companies established a system to trace the origin of the precious stones and prevent history from repeating itself.
A quarter of a century later, the industry insists it has changed, with claims of ethical trade and the development of local communities. But in the Kono district of Sierra Leone, the epicentre of the former "blood diamond" trade, the industry's promises remain far from being fully realised.

MEPs linked to Russia oppose European Parliament resolution declaring Russia’s new State Duma illegitimate

Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09

The European Parliament has adopted a resolution refusing to recognize Russia’s State Duma as a legitimate representative and legislative body. The measure passed on Oct. 8 with 482 votes in favor, 41 against, and 39 abstentions. “The ‘fake’ ballot was held in a climate of fear and against the backdrop of Moscow’s continued illegal war against Ukraine,” read a press release put out by the European Parliament on Oct. 9.
“[The European] Parliament notes that during the recent fake ballot, there were no genuine alternative candidates, no free media, no credible observers, and no political freedoms, with critics of the regime having been either imprisoned, murdered, or forced into exile. MEPs also condemn the fact that so-called “elections” were conducted in parts of the Russian-occupied Donetsk, Kherson, Luhansk, and Zaporizhzhia regions of Ukraine, as well as in Moldova’s Transnistrian region and in the Georgian regions of Abkhazia and Tskhinvali/South Ossetia,” it added.
According to the Parliament’s roll-call voting record, lawmakers who opposed parts of the resolution included German MEP Petr Bystron, who had been suspected of receiving money from an influence network linked to Viktor Medvedchuk; Slovak politician Luboš Blaha, who has met with Russian Foreign Intelligence Service chief Sergei Naryshkin; and Czech MEP Ondřej Dostál, who traveled to Moscow at the invitation of a Russian foundation linked to the GRU military intelligence agency.
Among those voting against the resolution were 23 members of the far-right Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN) group, including Alternative for Germany (AfD) lawmakers Petr Bystron and Christine Anderson, Slovak MEPs Luboš Blaha and Milan Mazurek, Czech lawmakers Kateřina Konečná and Ondřej Dostál, and Luxembourg politician Fernand Kartheiser.
Also opposing the measure in the final vote were Polish far-right politician Grzegorz Braun and German MEPs Michael von der Schulenburg and Ruth Firmenich, who were elected on the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance (BSW) ticket. Braun had previously been stripped of parliamentary immunity in connection with a Polish investigation into his alleged denial of Nazi crimes at Auschwitz (in July 2025, Braun publicly denied the existence of gas chambers at the Auschwitz-Birkenau concentration and extermination camp).
The Insider compared the roll-call vote with published information about lawmakers’ contacts with Russian representatives. It found that four of the politicians listed above — Blaha, Dostál, von der Schulenburg, and Firmenich — traveled together to Moscow in May 2025. The trip was timed to coincide with the 80th anniversary of the end of World War II. While in the Russian capital, the MEPs met with Russian politicians and public figures.
In an official declaration published by the European Parliament, Dostál listed the Russian Peace Foundation as a third party that covered part of the trip’s expenses. Dostál said he paid for his flight, accommodation, and meals himself, while the foundation provided bus transportation from the airport.
The Insider previously reported that the Russian Peace Foundation has links to Russian military intelligence. According to internal GRU correspondence, the organization has been involved in passing information about foreign visitors to the intelligence service for assessment and possible recruitment.
In the same investigation, The Insider reported that Luboš Blaha traveled to Moscow with David Lindtner, an adviser to Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico. During that trip, Blaha met with Sergei Naryshkin, director of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). According to statements published by Blaha, they discussed the May 2024 assassination attempt against Fico, along with the activities of political opponents of the Slovak government.
Petr Bystron, another lawmaker on the list, had previously appeared in an investigation into the pro-Kremlin media platform Voice of Europe, which European intelligence services say was financed by a network linked to the aforementioned Medvedchuk. As The Insider previously reported, citing Der Spiegel and Deník N, Bystron and fellow party member Maximilian Krah were suspected of receiving money in exchange for cooperation with the platform. In 2025, the European Parliament lifted Bystron’s immunity in order to allow an investigation in a separate case to proceed.
A Transparency International database also contains records of meetings between some of the lawmakers and Russian representatives. According to the data, in May 2025 von der Schulenburg met in Moscow with Russian diplomats and State Duma representatives, and in July of that year with a representative of Russia’s mission to the European Union in Brussels. Dostál met at least twice with representatives of Russia’s permanent mission to the EU, while Fernand Kartheiser attended a forum in Sochi in November 2025 that included Russian politicians.

Energy Ministry explains regional differences in power outages
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:57:27 EEST
22:57:27 KST

Eastern, southern and central Ukraine currently face electricity deficits due to Russian attacks and the resulting damage, while most of the country's power generation capacity is concentrated in the west, where nuclear power plants are located and electricity imports from Europe enter the country, the Energy Ministry has said.
The western region could potentially generate more electricity than it consumes, the ministry said in a Telegram post on Friday.
Transmitting electricity from western Ukraine to Kyiv or Kharkiv requires high-voltage transmission lines and autotransformers, which Russia is deliberately targeting, the ministry said.
Energy infrastructure has become the main target of Russian strikes ahead of winter. Attacks on transformers and high-voltage networks carrying electricity between regions have temporarily reduced the power system's ability to transmit electricity to consumers, it said.
“As a result, damage to the transmission ‘highways’ leaves electricity ‘trapped’ in the regions where it is generated or imported,” the ministry said.
Consequently, power restrictions may be unnecessary in western Ukraine, while shortages are more acute in central, southern and eastern regions. The transmission networks lack sufficient capacity to carry such large volumes of electricity and were not designed for this level of load, the ministry said.
The situation is compounded by mass attacks, localized strikes in frontline areas and equipment failures caused by system overload. Equipment breaks down daily and energy workers repair it, the ministry said.
Differences in the duration of power outages are therefore the result of physical limitations, rather than arbitrary decisions, the ministry said.

Estonia pays family caregivers just €60 a month, with no national scheme
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:57:00 UTC
22:57:00 KST

Estonia pays family caregivers just €60 a month, with no national scheme
Thousands of people in Estonia care for loved ones at home, but caregiver benefits vary widely by municipality and average just €60 a month.
As of December 2025, 8,111 people in Estonia received caregiver benefits averaging €61.47 a month, with benefits for those caring for adults averaging €59.59.
In all, 10,180 people provided care at home last year, though the Social Affairs Ministry does not track how many were relatives of those they cared for.
Tasked with overseeing social assistance, local governments consider care needs and the burden on caregivers when determining eligibility, but set their own benefit amounts, resulting in wide variations in support across the country.
Minister of Social Affairs Karmen Joller (Reform) doesn't agree that should be the case.
"Support shouldn't essentially depend solely on where someone lives or their formal status, but on their assessed needs," Joller said, responding to an MP query.
Monthly caregiver benefits can range from €25–150 for adult care and from €30–210 for caring for a disabled child. The minister explained that eligibility may depend on the extent of care needed, the severity of the disability, whether the caregiver otherwise works or is in school, where both people live as well as what other services the person under care receives.
By comparison, round-the-clock general care in an Estonian care home costs an average of €50.37 a day last year, with public funding covering an average of €23.51 a day — or less than half of the total cost — for the nearly 16,800 people receiving such care.
Minister: At-home care needs aren't typically as high
Joller highlighted that public funding has increased since the nationwide care reform, with care recipients and their loved ones previously left to pay for about 80 percent of care home costs. In 2025, their share of the bill had fallen to an average of 53 percent.
The ministry has not calculated how the public cost of caring for someone at home compares with care home services for someone with similar needs.
The minister, however, said care home residents generally require round-the-clock help and supervision, while those being cared for at home typically don't need the same level of support, making the comparison difficult.
Joller said the state hasn't considered a nationwide benefit system that would automatically pay relatives a set share of care home costs when they care for an older or disabled family member at home, nor does the Ministry of Social Affairs intend to take over caregiver appointments and benefit payments.
Local governments appoint caregivers and may pay them benefits at their own set terms and rates, she noted, while also having the flexibility to arrange support through home care or other services that support people continuing to live at home.
Care reform review due by year-end
Joller said Estonia's care reform has increased municipal funding, with nearly €70 million in additional funding expected this year. The money is intended to help cover both care home costs and support services for people living at home.
Asked whether the ministry believes the current support system for family members and caregivers is sufficient, Joller said work to improve it is ongoing, with an analysis of the care reform's impact and a repeat study on the population's caregiving burden both due by year-end.
"Based on those findings, we will assess which problems require additional solutions and whether any changes are needed in service provision, funding or legislation," she said.
At the ministry's request, the Estonian Chamber of Disabled People (EPIKoda) has also developed an online platform for family caregivers, and also offers counseling and support groups.
"It's crucial to support family caregivers' own well-being, health and ability to work and ensure that the burden of care doesn't fall on relatives alone," Joller said.
The goal, she added, is to ensure that caring for a loved one doesn't force people to quit their jobs, undermine their financial security or come at the expense of their own health.

Swiss train maker Stadler secures CHF300m Saudi contract
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Swiss train maker Stadler secures CHF300m Saudi contract
Swiss train manufacturer Stadler Rail has been awarded the second part of a major order from Saudi Arabia. The Saudi Arabian Railways (SAR) has ordered a further ten Intercity trains worth CHF300 million.
With this order, the SAR has exercised an option under the contract signed two years ago, worth around CHF600 million. This doubles the fleet of trains specially developed for Saudi Arabia to a total of 20, Stadler announced on Friday. The existing maintenance contract will be extended to cover the additional trains.
The Intercity trains, which are around 175 metres long, have been designed for the climatic and operational conditions in Saudi Arabia. They feature two independent power cars and numerous redundant systems.
Special protection and filtration systems have been incorporated for operation in extreme heat and sandy conditions.
The trains, which can accommodate around 320 passengers, are to be deployed on the SAR’s east-west line. They will connect the regions of Riyadh, Hofuf, Abkaik and Dammam.
The new trains will be produced largely at Stadler’s factories in Switzerland. The car bodies for the power cars will come from the Stadler factory in Valencia, Spain.
Production will follow on directly from the manufacture of the first series, which began in April 2026. Commercial passenger services are expected to commence in the second half of 2029, according to Stadler.

The online platform used for France’s Socialist and social democratic primary was targeted in a cyberattack on Friday, disrupting some voters’ access, although the integrity of recorded votes was not compromised, French broadcaster LCP reported.
“The e-votez platform, the provider for the Socialist and Democratic primary vote, has been the victim of a cyberattack since it opened this Friday morning at 8 a.m. (0600 GMT),” Patrick Mennucci, head of the primary’s organizing commission, said in a statement.
Mennucci said the platform had remained operational and voting had continued without interruption since it opened.
He described the attack as a “massive and fictitious influx of connections,” saying bots were being used to maximize the number of simultaneous connections.

Organizers said they had taken measures to maintain the vote and assist voters experiencing connection problems.
A support line remained available to help them access the platform.
The first round of voting opened at 8 am Friday (0600 GMT) and is scheduled to close at 8 pm Saturday (1800 GMT).
The political organizations involved condemned what they described as an attempt to disrupt the democratic process and said they would refer the matter to the courts.

Yair Golan calls Khamenei killing a mistake, says Iran war left Israel worse off
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:55:54 UTC
22:55:54 KST

Yair Golan, leader of Israel's opposition Democrats party, said Friday that the assassination of Iran's supreme leader, Ali Khamenei, at the start of the latest war was a "mistake" that ultimately harmed Israel's strategic interests.
Speaking in an interview with journalist Yossi Yehoshua at a cultural event in Rishon LeZion, Golan said he firmly believed eliminating the Iranian leader had been the wrong decision. "I unequivocally believe that killing the elder Khamenei was a mistake," he said. "Not because he didn't deserve to die, but because it doesn't serve the interests of the State of Israel. There is always a certain advantage to having an elderly, long-serving leader. And he was already 86."
Golan also argued that Operation Roaring Lion, Israel's latest military campaign against Iran, had weakened the country's long-term strategic position. "My impression is that Khamenei's son, if he is functioning at all, is controlled by the most extreme elements of the Iranian leadership," he said. "After we eliminated the top layer of leadership, we were left with people who are more extreme and more violent."
"Israel was at the height of its achievements against Iran at the end of Operation Rising Lion. From a long-term strategic perspective, Operation Roaring Lion worsened our position because Netanyahu himself set an unrealistic objective that was never achieved: overthrowing the Iranian regime."
During the same interview, Golan also described Israel's ultra-Orthodox population as "parasitic," saying the goal should be to transform it into a productive, educated population with professional skills.
‘Netanyahu squandered an extraordinary strategic opportunity’
In a post on X following the interview, Golan expanded on his criticism of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, arguing that the failure was not the military operation itself but the absence of a diplomatic strategy to capitalize on it. "This is the failure I'm talking about, and it rests entirely with Netanyahu," he wrote. "The killing of the elder Khamenei could have been a historic turning point. But Netanyahu, through his arrogance and considerations of political survival, squandered an extraordinary strategic opportunity."
"Instead of leading a regional diplomatic initiative that would guarantee Israel's security, he sold the Americans illusions about overthrowing the Iranian regime, without a diplomatic strategy to secure what would come the day after," Golan wrote.
He argued that removing Iran's veteran leadership had strengthened more radical figures within the country's security establishment. "Under Netanyahu, Operation Roaring Lion worsened our strategic position instead of improving it," he wrote. "Responsibility for setting the objectives, managing the campaign and its results lies with Netanyahu. This is how a historic military achievement is turned into a severe strategic failure. Netanyahu must be held accountable for the decisions he made and the outcome he left behind."
From praising Khamenei's killing to calling it a mistake
Golan's latest remarks stand in contrast to his initial response to Khamenei's assassination in late February, when he publicly welcomed the operation and praised the Israeli and American forces involved. At the time, he described the killing as "a dramatic and significant step," saying the two countries had demonstrated "intelligence superiority and impressive operational capabilities."
"Ali Khamenei was the architect of regional terrorism, the man who made Israel's destruction a goal, financed and armed terrorist proxies and deepened instability across the Middle East," he wrote on X. He also addressed the Iranian people, saying: "You have been freed from a cruel tyrant who oppressed you for decades, and a real opportunity for freedom and a better future has opened."
By early April, however, about a month and a half later, Golan had begun questioning the decision. "It is possible that the assassination was a mistake and harmed Israel's security," he said at the time. His latest comments Friday went further, portraying the assassination and broader military campaign as a missed strategic opportunity for which he holds Netanyahu directly responsible.

Pete Hegseth’s plan to livestream execution puts US in dubious company
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:55:07 UTC
22:55:07 KST

If the US defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, goes ahead with plans to livestream the execution of a soldier radicalised to extremist Islam who killed 13 people at a military base in Texas, his country will join a motley assembly of lesser powers and rogue actors who have conducted public executions in recent years.
Only two countries currently systematically carry out capital sentences in public: Iran and Afghanistan. In 2025, the Taliban authorities carried out six such killings and the regime in Tehran 11, according to Amnesty International.
In April last year, the Taliban executed four men accused of murder in three different cities. All were shot dead in crowded public sports stadiums. Such events were common when the hardline Islamist militia movement was in power in the late 1990s. Then as now, the Taliban claimed a due court process had been followed.
In July, two young men accused of killing police officers were hanged by Iranian authorities in the central square of Isfahan, Iran. Human rights monitors have reported about 30 public executions in Ithe country in the last five years, with an intensification in recent months after massive popular unrest earlier this year and the war with the US and Israel. Historically, many hangings have been carried out using a crane as a makeshift gallows.
Saudi Arabia appears to have ended the practice after decades of beheading convicted criminals in a square in the capital, Riyadh, and sometimes publicly in provincial cities.
Legal experts and historians argue that public executions perform different functions. If the rule of law is shaky or there is doubt about the efficacy of the criminal justice system, they offer authorities seeking to win support a way of convincing the community that criminals will be punished. Such public spectacles can also be a way of cowing a population through terror.
Armed militant groups have frequently resorted to public executions – often in an effort to assert their authority.
Islamic State, which ruled a swath of Iraq and Syria between 2014 and 2019, conducted thousands of executions for alleged offences ranging from homosexuality to theft. Many of the executions took place in public or were videoed. A large number were deliberately choreographed to provide a spectacle for broadcast to terrorise enemies and potential dissidents as well as to radicalise IS supporters and attract new ones.
In October 2025, as Hamas sought to reassert its control over the population of Gaza, it carried out a public execution of six men apparently accused of collaborating with Israel. In 2017, the group had executed three men accused of the same crime, partly livestreaming the event on Facebook.
The execution of Maj Nidal Hasan, a former army psychiatrist, at Fort Hood in Texas would be the first public execution in the US in many decades.
In the US, the practice of public executions was largely stopped in the 1930s, though in 2001, some survivors and victims’ relatives were allowed to watch the execution by lethal injection of Timothy McVeigh, convicted of the 1995 bombing of a government office in Oklahoma City.
Hasan’s execution has been scheduled for 3 December. Hegseth, who has the authority to decide the conduct of the killing, has said that “of course” it would take place at the same time and in the same place as Hasan’s attack 17 years ago and would use firearms, as Hasan did.
Hasan can launch appeals within the civilian federal court system that could delay the execution for many years.
In 2025, Amnesty International recorded 2,707 executions, the highest total globally since 1981, and an increase of two-thirds on the previous year. The sharp rise was mainly due to more than 2,100 executions by Iran, its highest number of executions in decades.
Amnesty said authorities had placed the death penalty “at the centre of flawed public security and ‘tough on crime’ narratives to assert control, project state power and score political points”.
“This trend was strongest in countries where the authorities have tightened their grip on power by restricting civic space, silencing dissent and displaying disregard for protections established under international human rights law and standards,” the campaign group reported.

EU and China clinch deal over cars after heated trade talks as Brussels pushes to rebalance trade
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:51:44 UTC
22:51:44 KST

EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič described the deal as marking the end of the “first phase” of negotiations. Brussels is pushing for a fundamental rebalancing in trade relations with Beijing.
EU Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič announced a deal with China on Friday to curb imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles into the EU and facilitate access to rare earths.
While the understanding signals a preference for a diplomatic resolution to the growing trade imbalance, European leaders are pushing for stronger measures to level the playing field. They are expected to review the details at a summit in Brussels next week.
The EU has also floated retaliatory measures if the outcome falls short of expectations.
Šefčovič travelled to Beijing on Wednesday for two days of intensive talks with his Chinese counterpart, Wang Wentao, in a bid to rebalance EU-China trade relations.
The EU is facing a record trade deficit with China of €1 billion a day, as a surge in low-cost Chinese imports threatens entire sectors of European industry.
“We have reached a shared understanding to moderate China's export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the European Union,” Šefčovič said. “This opens up the prospect of cutting China's exports by more than half.”
The commissioner said the deal would also improve access to the Chinese market for a range of EU products, from “car parts to olive oil and footwear”, representing almost €4 billion in current export value. It should generate at least €225 million in duty savings, he added.
Market access has been at the heart of EU-China discussions since negotiations began last June. Beijing has been reluctant to relinquish access to the EU's 450-million-consumer market, which provides an outlet for its excess production.
Meanwhile, Brussels has proposed several legislative measures aimed at restricting Chinese companies' access to the European market, while pressing Beijing to open up its own market to EU businesses.
Šefčovič also said China had agreed to facilitate exports of rare earths, which are essential to Europe's green technology, defence and automotive industries.
“We have reached a shared understanding to further facilitate China's export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets,” he said.
The EU has accused China of “weaponising” its dependence on Chinese rare earths after Beijing restricted exports in 2025 amid a trade war with the US.
Šefčovič described the agreement as the conclusion of a “first phase of negotiations”.
The deal comes ahead of a meeting of EU leaders in Brussels next week, with expectations running high for concrete results from negotiations led by the European Commission on their behalf since last June.
A consensus on China has been emerging across the EU this week.
All EU countries now run trade deficits with China. On Monday, Germany and France urged the European Commission to take strong action against unfair Chinese trade practices that cause severe market distortions.
In a joint document, Paris and Berlin called for measures that could include “an immediate cut-off from the internal market if needed”.
On Wednesday, MEPs overwhelmingly adopted a resolution calling for resolute measures against Beijing.
Meanwhile, 44 EU industries, including chemicals, machinery, metals, solar, glass and cement, issued a joint statement on Friday warning that “Europe cannot maintain and grow its industrial base, quality jobs, and attract investment without the ability to respond effectively to unfair trade practices and distortions”.

Drones attack two Yandex data centers in two days, damaging major facility in Kaluga
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:51:00 UTC
22:51:00 KST

A Ukrainian drone strike has caused damage at a second data center belonging to Russian tech giant Yandex, knocking out several modules at a facility in the Kaluga region, the company’s press service stated earlier today. On Oct. 8, a drone strike and a fire caused the data center in Sasovo, Ryazan Region, to halt operations. The company had previously called the Kaluga facility its most powerful data center in Russia, The Insider found.
Yandex said specialists are still assessing the scale of the damage in Kaluga. The attack has caused interruptions across some of the company’s digital services; however, the specific systems that were affected and whether the disabled modules can be restored have not been announced. Preliminary reports do not mention any human casualties.
Construction of the Kaluga data center began in 2022 on the territory of the Grabtsevo industrial park. Yandex’s original project was designed to house more than 3,800 server racks, with a total design capacity of 63 MW — one and a half times that of the company’s most powerful data center at the time of announcement. The site is intended both for Yandex’s own services and for customers of the Yandex Cloud platform.
According to official documents of the Kaluga city administration, the first phase of the facility was commissioned in December 2023. In October 2024, the System Operator of the Unified Energy System reported the connection of Yandex’s largest data center to the power grid with a maximum power consumption of 49 MW, though the company has not disclosed the amount of server equipment at the site at the time of the attack.
The day before, drones knocked out a data center in the Ryazan Region
Overnight into Oct. 8, Ukrainian drones attacked Yandex’s data center in the city of Sasovo in the Ryazan Region, located on the grounds of the Sasta machine-tool plant. The strike caused a fire at the facility, forcing the management to suspend operations. As of the evening of Oct. 8, the company could not confirm whether the damaged equipment could be restored.
The data center in Sasovo opened in 2014 and is designed to house tens of thousands of servers. It is currently home to two of Yandex’s three supercomputers, which the company uses to develop and train artificial intelligence models, including YandexGPT. The extent of damage to these assets remains unknown.
On Oct. 8, large-scale disruptions occurred in the operation of Russian internet services. As The Insider reported, users ran into problems opening the websites of Russian media outlets, Russian Railways, the real estate platform Cian, the classifieds portal Avito, and other platforms. Cian confirmed that the disruptions were linked to an incident at a facility of its infrastructure partner. Problems were also recorded in the operation of Yandex’s own services.
On the Yandex Cloud status page, the company reported that the ru-central1-b zone, associated with the data center in Sasovo, was completely unavailable. Customers were advised to move their workloads to other availability zones. At the same time, the outage imposed restrictions on creating new virtual machines, Kubernetes clusters, and databases.
On Oct. 8, the independent outlet Verstka also found that Yandex had concealed satellite images of its four cloud data centers, including the facilities in Sasovo and Kaluga. On Yandex Maps, the sites are blurred, and when searched by address, the service does not indicate that data centers are located there. When and why the company hid the images remains unknown.

52-year-old Russian political prisoner Igor Yakovenko dies in Krasnodar detention center after being returned for “palliative care”
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:50:44 UTC
22:50:44 KST

Igor Yakovenko, a 52-year-old political prisoner, died in Krasnodar’s Pretrial Detention Center No. 1, according to a report by Memorial’s Support for Political Prisoners project. Yakovenko is at least the ninth political prisoner to die in Russian custody since the start of 2026, according to a count by The Insider. Human rights advocates said he had been diagnosed with an inoperable brain tumor.
Several days before his death, Yakovenko underwent medical examinations and was then returned to the detention center “for palliative care.” Memorial also said Yakovenko had been beaten at the facility before he was sentenced.
On Oct. 3, 2025, the Southern District Military Court sentenced Yakovenko to five years in prison on charges of preparing to take part in the activities of a terrorist organization. Prosecutors alleged that on May 28, 2025, he began corresponding with a person involved in recruiting Russians for the Freedom of Russia Legion, which Russian authorities have designated a terrorist organization. Yakovenko allegedly planned to travel to Ukraine, sending the person a completed application form to join the Legion. FSB officers detained him two days later. Authorities did not disclose how they learned about the correspondence.
Memorial recognized Yakovenko as a political prisoner. The movement’s human rights advocates said they did not have access to the case files and therefore could not determine whether he genuinely intended to join the Legion or if had been the victim of an entrapment scheme. Memorial noted that only two days passed between Yakovenko sending the application and his arrest:
“Such a rapid sequence of events may indicate that from the outset he wrote to one of the Legion’s fake websites and sent his application there as well.”
In addition to Yakovenko, at least eight other political prisoners have died in Russian custody since the start of 2026:
- Roman Sidorkin died on Jan. 9 in the Saratov Region. The former employee of a defense company in the Kursk Region had been convicted of treason after investigators accused him and his former wife of passing technical documentation and samples of military products to Ukrainian intelligence. Sidorkin developed bronchitis-like symptoms in December 2025, and later pneumonia. He was hospitalized only four days before his death.
- Oleg Tyryshkin, a former miner and trade union activist from Kemerovo Region, died on Feb. 4 at age 64. He had been sentenced to two years in a penal colony over a comment posted on the social network VK about the 2004 death of Akhmat Kadyrov, the first president of Chechnya and the father of its current leader, Ramzan Kadyrov. Activists who corresponded with prisoners said heart problems were the cause of his death. Tyryshkin had previously complained about his health, including about a brain cyst.
- Alexander Dotsenko died on Feb. 19 after a massive heart attack. The jewelry artist had been sentenced to three years in a penal colony in a case involving anti-war postcards left in a Lenta supermarket in St. Petersburg. His wife, Anastasia Dyudyayeva, received a 3½-year sentence in the same case. After Dotsenko’s heart attack, prison officials failed to inform his relatives and lawyer about his condition for several days.
- Vladimir Osipov died in March at a pretrial detention center in Ukhta, where he had been transferred from the Moscow Region. The 56-year-old had been sentenced to 6½ years in a penal colony over posts made on Odnoklassniki about the Russian military and Vladimir Putin. Ambulances were called for Osipov several times during his trial, and at one hearing the judge refused to postpone his final statement despite complaints of high blood pressure.
- Andrei Akuzin, a 53-year-old artist from Komsomolsk-on-Amur, died by suicide on April 8 at a local pretrial detention center — six days after he was arrested. His friend said the criminal case stemmed from an online comment. Russia’s financial monitoring agency, Rosfinmonitoring, added Akuzin to its registry of “terrorists and extremists” only after his death.
- Vegan Khristolyub Bozhiy, formerly named Dmitry Kuznetsov, died on April 17 at Penal Colony No. 2 in Voronezh. The 43-year-old preacher and YouTube blogger, whose name can be loosely translated as “Vegan Christ-Lover of God,” had been sentenced to three years in prison over videos criticizing the invasion of Ukraine, the Soviet army, and Islam. It later emerged that he had been found hanged in a punishment cell and that, according to media reports, a negligence case was opened against the prison’s employees. His relatives did not believe the official account of suicide.
- Vladimir Yarotsky was found dead on the morning of May 7 at Penal Colony No. 9 in Khadyzhensk in Russia’s Krasnodar Region. The artist had been sentenced to five and a half years in prison on charges of spreading “false information” about the Russian armed forces and “desecrating symbols of military glory” over posts that included a caricature of Putin featuring a penis and a St. George ribbon. Authorities said Yarotsky died by suicide. Another prisoner said the artist had complained of pressure from the prison administration.
- Ibragim Kudzhanov, a 52-year-old resident of Ukraine’s Luhansk Region, died at Penal Colony No. 8 in the Omsk Region. His death became known in July. Kudzhanov had been sentenced to 5½ years in prison for serving as a driver in Ukraine’s Aidar Battalion in 2018 and 2019. His daughter said he had been tortured with electric shocks after his detention and that he died from a second heart attack accompanied by an aneurysm and kidney failure. His son, Artyom, is also imprisoned in Russia after being sentenced to 12 years in a penal colony on espionage charges in 2025.

New horizons open for Iran-Afghanistan economic co-op during Iran’s trade delegation’s trip to Kabul
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:50:26 UTC
22:50:26 KST

New horizons open for Iran-Afghanistan economic co-op during Iran’s trade delegation’s trip to Kabul
TEHRAN- During the trip of a trade delegation from the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture (ICCIMA), led by Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Chamber, to Kabul, the capacities for Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining and mineral industries, agriculture and conversion industries, technology transfer, and the creation of production and processing chains were examined.
Meetings with Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, and Haji Akhtar Mohammad Mohammadi, First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production, along with participation in the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition and B2B negotiations between Iranian and Afghan traders, formed the main axes of this trip.
Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining, mineral industries emphasized
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, during the trip to Kabul at the head of a trade delegation, in a meeting with Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, referred to Afghanistan’s mineral capacities and emphasized the development of Iran-Afghanistan cooperation in mining and mineral industries.
Azizi, referring to the issue of mining machinery, welcomed the expansion of relations and economic cooperation with Iran.
In this meeting, attended by Hamed Asgari, Deputy for International Affairs of the Iran Chamber; Mahmoud Omati, Vice President of the Mashhad Chamber; Hossein Beykzadeh, Vice President of the Karaj Chamber; Arash Alavi, member of the Board of Representatives of the Iran and Kerman Chamber; and Mohsen Amini, member of the Food Industry Committee and member of the Board of Representatives of the Iran Chamber, the capacities for economic cooperation between the two countries were examined.
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, considering Afghanistan’s mineral capacities, emphasized the necessity of strengthening interactions and developing cooperation between the economic actors of the two countries in mining and mineral industries, and considered the existing capacities in this sector as a basis for expanding Iran-Afghanistan economic cooperation.
Then Nooruddin Azizi, Afghanistan’s Minister of Industry and Commerce, referring to the issue of mining machinery, emphasized the importance of cooperation in this area and welcomed the development of relations and expansion of economic cooperation between Afghanistan and Iran.
In this meeting, emphasis was also placed on using existing capacities to deepen economic relations and develop private sector cooperation between the two countries, especially in mining and mineral industries.
At the meeting of the Vice President of the Iran Chamber with the First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Agriculture Chamber, it was raised:
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, met with Haji Akhtar Mohammad Mohammadi, First Deputy of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production, and discussed the capacities for developing economic and agricultural cooperation between the two countries.
In this meeting, Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber; Kamaluddin Tawhid, President of the Afghanistan-Iran Joint Chamber of Commerce; Mohsen Amini, member of the Food Industry Committee of the Iran Chamber; and Ali Asghar Beigi, Vice President of the Yazd Chamber; a number of representatives of Iran’s parliament; and members of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production were present.
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, referring to existing capacities in Afghanistan’s agriculture and livestock sector and the country’s need for technology and production inputs, emphasized the readiness of Iran’s private sector to develop cooperation, transfer technology, and use joint capacities.
The head of Afghanistan’s Chamber of Agricultural and Livestock Production also emphasized the development of economic and trade relations with Iran and focused on expanding cooperation between the two chambers and using the private sector capacities of both countries.
Later in this meeting, Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to Afghanistan’s high capacity in agriculture and livestock, proposed the development of technical cooperation, technology transfer, and the creation of production and processing chains.
He also emphasized increasing imports from Afghanistan and said: “These imports can be developed with a focus on goods needed by Iran, including oilseeds, animal feed, and legumes.”
The President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to measures taken in agriculture and pest control, including sending specialized teams to Afghanistan, considered cooperation capacity broad in sectors such as industrial livestock farming, poultry farming, production and processing of agricultural products, and related industries, and emphasized the need for greater support and organization to activate these capacities.
Focus on Afghanistan’s capacities in agricultural processing and conversion industries required
Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, on the sidelines of the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition of Afghanistan and at the B2B negotiations ceremony of traders and economic actors of Iran and Afghanistan, emphasizing the extensive economic capacities of the two countries, said: “Iran’s view of Afghanistan should not be merely as a market for supplying Iranian goods; rather, it should move toward joint investments.”
At this ceremony, Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber, referring to the extensive presence of Iranian companies and firms in this year’s exhibition, stated: “Last year, when I came to Afghanistan to attend the Abu Hanifa Exhibition, I did not witness such a crowd and welcome from the economic actors of the two countries, but this year, with the efforts of the Iranian chambers and the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment, the presence of Iranian companies and firms has increased, and the level of the exhibition has significantly differed from last year.”
He thanked the Afghan side for hosting and planning, and added: “Alongside the historical, civilizational, and cultural ties between Iran and Afghanistan, there are serious fields for activity, joint investment, and trade exchanges between the two countries.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber continued: “In recent years, Iranian industrial goods in various fields, including electricity, energy, oil, petrochemical materials, and conversion industries, have been used in Afghanistan, and this shows that Iranian goods, industry, and firms are present in Afghanistan’s economy.”
Qiyafeh considered one of the important obstacles to developing economic relations between the two countries to be the issue of financial, monetary, and banking exchanges and said: “Part of the obstacles exists on the Iranian side and part on the Afghan side, and one of the serious obstacles is the issue of financial and banking exchanges.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber expressed hope that with follow-up by friends in the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment and given the promises made by Afghan authorities, in the future we will witness the establishment of a branch or representation of one of the Iranian banks in Afghanistan’s capital and, in return, the establishment of a branch of an Afghan bank in Iran, so that monetary and financial exchanges between the two countries are facilitated.
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber, emphasizing the need to change the view toward economic relations between the two countries, said: “We should not see Afghanistan only as a susceptible market for Iranian goods; our view should be toward joint investments, because joint investment can also guarantee the future of exports.”
He considered Afghanistan’s capacities in processing and conversion industries, especially agricultural conversion industries, significant and added: “A significant part of Afghanistan’s economy depends on agriculture, and this sector can be a suitable ground for developing joint cooperation.”
Qiyafeh also referred to the development of Afghanistan’s steel industry and said: “Today, steel production and melting factories have been established in Afghanistan and supply part of the country’s needs, but there is still a broad field for technical and industrial cooperation between the two countries.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber called mining and mineral industries one of the attractive areas of cooperation between Iran and Afghanistan and said: “Afghanistan enjoys very extensive mineral capacities, and in a correct expression, many elements of the periodic table exist in this country.”
He continued: “Iranian companies, with the experience and technical knowledge gained over several decades, can be present in this sector in Afghanistan. This cooperation can begin with exploration and continue through extraction, processing, and production of the final product.”
Qiyafeh, emphasizing that the development of mining and mineral industries requires the provision of necessary infrastructure, added: “If mining and mineral industries in Afghanistan are to develop with investment from other countries, especially Iran, the construction of new roads, development of railway lines, and establishment of power plant units are necessary.”
He said: “Solar, hydro, wind, and thermal power plants can help supply the energy infrastructure needed by this sector.”
Emphasis Qiyafeh, referring to the public ownership of mineral resources in Afghanistan, said: “Just as in Iran mines are recognized as public property and belong to all the Iranian nation, Afghanistan’s mineral resources also belong to the people of Afghanistan.”
He proposed: “Part of the minerals should first undergo primary processing inside Afghanistan, and from the revenue and profit obtained, processing capacities and industrial units should be developed.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber emphasized: “With the method adopted today, one cannot expect a serious transformation in Afghanistan’s mining sector in the near future, and it is necessary to plan for developing the value chain and processing of minerals inside the country.”
Readiness of Iranian companies for investment
Qiyafeh, referring to the presence of Iranian companies at the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition of Afghanistan, said: “Among the Iranian companies present at this exhibition, more than 10 groups are interested and ready to invest in Afghanistan, and some of them have announced their readiness to invest in conversion industries.”
Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber of Commerce, emphasizing the existing capacities for developing economic cooperation between the two countries, said: “Afghanistan’s current conditions, especially continued security and industrial and production growth, have provided a suitable ground for entering a new phase of economic partnerships between Iran and Afghanistan.”
Making the remarks at the gathering held jointly by the joint chambers of commerce of Iran and Afghanistan, he focused on the sustainability of security and the continuation of Afghanistan’s industrial and production growth and spoke of readiness to enter a new phase of trade and investment cooperation between the two countries.
Mahmoud Siyadat, President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to the presence of representatives of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Parliament at this event, emphasized: “The presence of individuals who are influential in policymaking and policies related to Afghanistan and see the country’s conditions closely is valuable at this ceremony, and we hope their perceptions and views are considered in future policies and decisions.”
He continued: “I hope we enter a new phase of partnerships. The Iran Chamber made great efforts so that part of Iran’s capable economic forces attend this round of the Abu Hanifa Exhibition, so that Afghan economic actors become closely acquainted with these capacities and the path for more cooperation is paved.”
Siyadat also, referring to the presence of Afghan exhibitors at the exhibition, said: “For offering goods and services, this opportunity may be a unique opportunity, and I recommend they have a more active presence during the exhibition days.”
He added: “We have considered places for holding meetings and sessions, and we are ready to cooperate in legal and contractual areas.”
The President of the Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, referring to the capacity of joint chambers and economic organizations of Afghanistan, said: “The Iran-Afghanistan Joint Chamber, the Afghanistan-Iran Joint Chamber, and Afghan economic organizations are three chambers at the head of which is the Afghanistan Chamber of Commerce and Investment, and these collections are ready to cooperate as wings of flight.”
Siyadat noted: “Fortunately, the will of the rulers of both countries is also on developing relations, and we hope this exhibition is the beginning of a new season for deeper, broader, and more lasting cooperation between the two countries.”
Referring to the ties between the Iranian and Afghan peoples, he said: “I don’t think we can find in the world two peoples and two countries with this level of closeness, affinity, and common roots that exist between Iran and Afghanistan.”
Alireza Beykdeli, Ambassador of Iran in Kabul, while attending the gathering of the joint chambers of commerce of Iran and Afghanistan, said: “Traders of the two countries, while trading and earning profit, bring closer the brotherly peoples of Iran and Afghanistan, who are truly one nation in two countries, and this approach will bless the wealth of all economic actors.”
Iran’s Ambassador in Kabul, referring to the transformation in economic cooperation between the two countries over the past two years, said: “During the two years I have been here, I have witnessed a transformation in the concept of economic cooperation. The day I came, most questions were about how to obtain a visa and how to see facilitation in this area, how to pass a container through the border, and how to access a company; but today conditions have changed greatly and we are witnessing a rise in the level of exchanges.”
He continued: “Today, trade elders talk about a pipeline for transferring crude oil to Afghanistan, a refinery, the Herat-Mazar-e-Sharif road, and the construction of a factory and kiln. Grand ideas are proposed; ideas worthy of two nations.”
Beykdeli, stating that good days await Iran-Afghanistan relations, said: “I thank all those who join hands in this path with good intentions, and I hope we witness an ever greater increase in the level of relations between the two countries.”
Turning neighborliness into economic partnership in Iran-Afghanistan relations needed
Following the dispatch of the Iran Chamber’s trade delegation headed by Ghadir Qiyafeh, Vice President of the Iran Chamber of Commerce, Industries, Mines and Agriculture, to Kabul, delegation members attended the opening ceremony of the Fifth Abu Hanifa International Exhibition.
Qiyafeh at this ceremony, emphasizing the capacities for economic cooperation between Iran and Afghanistan, considered the presence of economic actors at this event beyond an exhibition presence and said: “The presence of economic actors at this exhibition shows Afghanistan can be more than before at the center of regional economic cooperation and play a role as part of the region’s production, trade, transit, and investment network.”
Referring to the importance and position of the Abu Hanifa International Exhibition in the region, he stated: “The importance of this exhibition lies precisely in the point that joint investments can be formed here. An exhibition is not only a place for offering and introducing products; sometimes it can be a place where a new economic geography takes shape.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber continued: “The political geography of countries is known and fixed for all, but economic geography can be built; together and with our Afghan kin, we can define and rebuild this geography.”
Qiyafeh, stating that borders can become trade routes, said: “Borders can be turned from stopping points into trade routes, and neighborliness can be turned into partnership.”
Referring to the economic capacities of countries around Afghanistan, he added: “Countries around Afghanistan each possess part of an economic system. Some of these countries have different resources and capacities, and each has advantages. The important issue is that we can put all these advantages together.”
Qiyafeh, referring to the capacities for cooperation between the economic actors of Iran and Afghanistan, stated: “Today, Afghan and Iranian investors can together create an economic event. Iran has very good and successful experiences and knowledge in developing mines and also in agriculture.”
The Vice President of the Iran Chamber concluded: “As your Iranian brothers, we once again extend our hand for cooperation, and we hope next year when we attend this exhibition, we will witness investments coming to fruition and future horizons opening.”
Based on what was raised in these meetings and gatherings, the development of Iran-Afghanistan relations is no longer limited to the exchange of goods; rather, both sides emphasize joint investment, technology transfer, the creation of production and processing chains, the removal of financial and banking obstacles, and turning neighborliness into economic partnership. If this approach is realized, the Abu Hanifa Exhibition can become a starting point for shaping a new economic geography and more lasting cooperation between the private sectors of the two countries.

OpenAI and Anthropic poach Trump officials as industry fights for Washington’s trust

2026-10-09

This report is from this week's The Tech Download newsletter. Like what you see? You can subscribe here.
Anthropic and OpenAI are poaching officials from the Trump administration for senior roles as the AI sector scrambles to strengthen ties to Washington, with frontier tech increasingly viewed as a national security issue.
This year, Anthropic has appointed at least two former Trump officials, one to its board and another as the head of its frontier compute strategy. OpenAI has hired at least three from the president’s administrations to work across strategy and special projects.
Companies developing frontier AI have been racing to build relationships with the U.S. President Donald Trump’s White House, amid growing calls for regulation and in the wake of a number of cybersecurity incidents caused by rogue AI systems.
"Frontier AI companies are aware that the Trump administration has a lot of levers over their business, from federal procurement and supply-chain designations to export controls and everything in between, and that it's willing to use them," said Michelle Nie Duncan, visiting fellow with the technology and national security program at the Center for a New American Security.
"They have learned from the Anthropic episode that it pays to be on the good side of the White House," she told CNBC. A U.S. appeals court upheld a Pentagon designation of Anthropic as a supply chain risk in September, after a public spat between the two parties at the start of the year.
OpenAI directed CNBC to previously released statements about two of its former Trump official appointments when approached for comment. Anthropic and the White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Ties to Trump
While Trump has called AI safety concerns a "hoax" and advocated for self-regulation from AI companies, he has also said the Department of Justice and other law enforcement bodies could "rein" in AI.
Anthropic, in particular, has had a particularly antagonistic relationship with the Trump administration this year, but CEO Dario Amodei has looked to smooth his relationship with the U.S. president in recent times. He joined a lunch between Trump and AI bosses as well as dining with Trump in September.
Sihao Huang joined Amodei's AI lab in September as head of frontier compute strategy. He was previously a senior policy advisor for AI and emerging technology at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP). Huang's website states that he was responsible for leading the "AI team at OSTP & coordinating national security, science policy, and semiconductor issues."
He'll be working on Anthropic's infrastructure expansion and "planning for rapid AI progress," Huang said in a post on X in September.
The company appointed Chris Liddell, who served as the deputy White House chief of staff during Trump's first term, to its board of directors in February.
Anthropic has been racing to ink AI data center deals big and small as it looks to secure the infrastructure it needs to train and serve its models. Anthropic had struck a roughly $45 billion cloud deal with neocloud Nscale, CNBC reported in August.
Leverage
Both Anthropic and OpenAI are also currently hiring for multiple political engagements roles.
"With companies like OpenAI and Anthropic gearing up for some of the largest IPOs of all time, many also see this as a chance to be part of something historic," said Nie Duncan, adding that the companies are often able to offer attractive compensation packages beyond what would be possible in the public sector.
"The AI labs are becoming some of the most consequential institutions in the world, and for officials who are serious about shaping the future of AI governance, inside the labs is where a lot of leverage currently lies."
OpenAI confirmed last week that Thomas Lind, who had led AI policy at the Office of the National Cyber Director (ONCD), has joined the company to lead on cyber and strategic risk on its national security policy team. The ONCD is the principal advisor to the president on cybersecurity policy and strategy.
"[Lind's] expertise is even more important as AI becomes central to the national security agenda, with the Office of the National Cyber Director playing a growing role in shaping AI policy," said Sasha Baker, who leads OpenAI's national security policy team and served as deputy under secretary of defense for policy in the Biden Administration.
Dean Ball, who served as a senior policy advisor at OSTP in 2025 and was involved in drafting the Trump administration's flagship America's AI Action Plan, joined OpenAI in July as head of strategic futures.
Ball will "help us pressure-test our assumptions and think through issues ranging from frontier safety and the economic impacts of increasingly capable systems to the evolving relationship between governments, companies, and society," said OpenAI Chief Strategy Officer Jason Kwon.
OpenAI also hired Peter Bowman-Davis to work on model training and hardware engineering in March, according to his LinkedIn page. He previously served as Chief AI officer at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Invalid signatures halt Swiss vote to ease solar power plant rules
A Swiss popular initiative aimed at loosening planning rules on solar power plants has failed due to a high number of invalid signatures. The 18-month deadline for collecting 100,000 valid signatures has now passed.
The construction of solar power installations in Switzerland is often blocked by heritage conservation bodies or townscape committees.

The federal popular initiative “For solar installations exempt from planning permission” had not been submitted with the required number of signatures by October 8, 2026, the Federal Chancellery announced on Friday in the Federal Gazette. The deadline for collecting signatures had therefore expired.
