The initiative committee did not include any nationally recognised figures. The Federal Gazette lists seven private individuals from an interest group. The committee is based in Basel-Country.
The association’s website states that 117,500 people are said to have signed the petition. During the verification process in July and August, it emerged that almost 20,000 signatures were invalid, said Roland Weiss, one of the initiators of the initiative, in response to an enquiry from the Keystone-SDA news agency.

“Our lawyer is currently investigating the circumstances.” It is currently being clarified how such a high number of invalid signatures could have arisen despite the involvement of signature-collection firms.
The initiative, which has now failed, called for a new constitutional article to be enshrined for solar installations on buildings and structures.
For such installations, no planning permission would have been required either within or outside protected townscapes and landscapes.
Exceptions would have been possible for installations on cultural monuments of national or cantonal significance, as well as on historic sites. In such cases, a planning permission could have been granted subject to certain conditions.

EU to face worst winter gas shortage in 15 years — Politico
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:49:35 UTC
22:49:35 KST

BRUSSELS, October 9. /TASS/. European Union countries are bracing for their most severe winter gas shortfall in 15 years, the European edition of Politico reported.
The shortage is projected to reach up to 14 billion cubic meters (bcm) of natural gas, representing roughly 7% of the bloc's total demand - an amount equivalent to the energy consumption of 10 to 12 million European households.
EU gas reserves have dwindled to their lowest levels for this time of year since record-keeping began in 2011. Concurrently, a report by the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA) notes that European gas prices have surged to four-year highs.
The tightening crunch will force European nations to buy gas at high prices on increasingly volatile global markets or require consumers to curb energy demand. According to an IEEFA expert, even if the EU avoids depleting its storage entirely this winter, it will face a massive and costlier refilling challenge next year, locking the bloc into a vicious cycle of low inventories and elevated prices.
Analysts attribute the crisis to mounting tensions in the Middle East and the EU's impending ban on long-term contracts for Russian liquefied natural gas (LNG). While US LNG exports offer an alternative, the cost of these shipments has jumped 12% compared to last year.
Under European Commission regulations, EU member states must fill their gas storage to 90% between October 1 and December 1 annually. However, a 10% flexibility margin is allowed under adverse market conditions. Consequently, net injections into European storage must hit at least 68 bcm to meet the target for the 2026-2027 winter season. Nevertheless, hoping for a mild winter, Brussels is prepared to lower the mandatory storage threshold to 80% for the current year.

Nobel Peace Prize winner Navi Pillay dedicates award to survivors of international crimes

South African jurist Navi Pillay, the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize winner, has dedicated her award to survivors of international crimes and called on world leaders to uphold international law and protect human rights.
“Let me dedicate this award to all of the survivors of international crimes,” Pillay told a news conference on Friday in the historic courtroom in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were prosecuted after World War II.
The 85-year-old said the setting held particular significance as she received news of the award.
“Perhaps it was meant to be that I was in this historic courtroom ... when the announcement was made and I was informed of the award,” she said.
Pillay, who has spent decades working in international justice, warned that legal institutions and human rights protections were facing growing political pressure.
Pillay warns against attacks on international courts
“We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” she said, pointing in particular to criticism of the International Criminal Court (ICC).
“This worsening reality is particularly visible with the attacks on the International Criminal Court,” she added.
US President Donald Trump last month urged countries that are members of the ICC to withdraw, denouncing the court as a “rogue institution.”
Pillay called on political leaders to respect their legal responsibilities and avoid actions that undermine international protections.
“My message to leaders, political leaders, is that ... you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war,” she said.
A career shaped by international justice
Pillay has held several prominent roles in international law. She headed the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, which prosecuted those responsible for the 1994 genocide, and currently serves as a judge at the International Court of Justice (ICJ).
She is also serving in a case in which Myanmar faces allegations of genocide against the Rohingya minority.
Pillay previously presided over a United Nations commission that concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.
Her award comes amid continuing international debate over the enforcement of international law, the accountability of states and the independence of judicial institutions.
Pillay used her Nobel recognition to reiterate that protecting survivors and upholding human rights must remain central responsibilities for governments worldwide.

However, the agency noted that rising social spending and large-scale infrastructure projects could put pressure on public finances.

In August, Fitch Ratings affirmed Mongolia's long-term issuer default rating at B+ with a stable outlook. In October, Moody's Ratings affirmed the country's long-term sovereign credit rating at B1, also with a stable outlook.
Mongolian officials view the assessments by the three major international credit rating agencies as an important indication of international confidence in the country at a time of heightened global uncertainty. They also see the ratings as a positive signal to international investors that could help attract greater investment into Mongolia. ■

Loneliness linked to greatest quality-of-life decline among young Australians: study
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
21:48:40 CST
22:48:40 KST

MELBOURNE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Loneliness hits young Australians aged 15 to 24 harder than any other age group when it comes to their overall physical and mental wellbeing, a study has found.
Young people experience greater quality-of-life losses from loneliness than older adults, despite receiving less attention, according to a statement released Friday by Australia's Monash University.
The study, published in Value in Health, analyzed more than 53,000 observations from almost 22,000 Australians aged 15 and over across four rounds of a national survey.
Researchers examined how changes in loneliness and social isolation were associated with changes in their health-related quality of life over time, accounting for factors including employment, income, physical and mental health conditions and major life events.
Loneliness was reported by 18 percent of people aged 15 to 24, compared with 12 percent of those aged 65 and over. In contrast, social isolation alone was more common among older Australians, the study showed.
The study measured health-related quality of life on a standardized scale ranging from 0 (death) to 1 (full health). Among young people aged 15 to 24, loneliness was associated with a 0.079-point reduction in health utility, the largest decline associated with loneliness across the age groups studied.
Across all age groups, health utility was 0.061 points lower among people experiencing loneliness alone, compared with those experiencing neither loneliness nor social isolation. The reduction was 0.020 points for social isolation alone and 0.102 points for people experiencing both.
Lead researcher Fikru Rizal from Monash University said the findings reinforced the importance of recognizing loneliness across the lifespan and distinguishing it from social isolation, which refers to objectively having fewer relationships and less frequent social contact. ■

Helsinki moves to restrict high-emission travel ads to meet climate goals
China

2026-10-09
21:48:34 CST

HELSINKI, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Finland's capital Helsinki has decided to ban outdoor advertisements promoting airline flights, cruises and fossil-fuel-powered cars on city-controlled advertising spaces as part of efforts to meet its climate goals, Finnish media reported Friday.
According to Finnish daily Helsingin Sanomat, the Helsinki City Council approved the move on Wednesday. The restrictions would cover commercial billboards in public spaces, including advertising displays at public transport stops.
The ban, however, will not take immediate effect. According to city documents, Helsinki's existing outdoor advertising contracts run until March 31, 2035, and cannot be unilaterally amended. The restrictions are expected to be incorporated into future contracts, with their precise scope and implementation details yet to be determined.
The move comes as Helsinki steps up efforts to meet its climate targets. The city aims to cut direct greenhouse gas emissions by 85 percent from 1990 levels by 2030 and achieve net-zero emissions by 2040, according to the city government.
Commenting on the decision, Mia Eloranta, communications manager at Finnish national carrier Finnair, told Finnish newspaper Hufvudstadsbladet that much of today's advertising takes place on digital platforms, including mobile phones, adding that the airline would comply with the rules.
The proposed ban has also raised concerns in the tourism industry. Noora Lofstrom, CEO of Visit Aland, told Finnish broadcaster Alands Radio that restrictions on airline and ferry advertising could make it harder for visitors to learn about travel options to the Aland Islands, an autonomous region of Finland. She expressed hope that regular passenger ferry services would be exempted from the ban.
Marika Nojd, communications director at ferry operator Tallink Silja, said that the company welcomed Helsinki's efforts to promote sustainability but stressed that any advertising restrictions should be applied consistently. She added that the company was developing new biofuels that could become available by 2035.
The move follows similar initiatives elsewhere in Europe.
In neighboring Sweden, Stockholm proposed a new advertising policy in September that would restrict promotions for fossil fuels and high-emission transport, including hybrid vehicles, on city-controlled advertising spaces. The proposal is currently undergoing public consultation.
Helsinki's initiative also draws on approaches adopted in Amsterdam and The Hague, where local authorities have moved to restrict advertising linked to fossil fuel consumption. ■

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China has overtaken the euro area to become South Africa's largest trading partner in manufactured goods, the South African Reserve Bank (SARB) said on Thursday in its September 2026 Quarterly Bulletin.
The SARB said it periodically revises its effective exchange rate (EER) indices to accurately reflect changing trade patterns and developments in the domestic economy, and the EER measures the rand against a weighted basket of currencies of South Africa's major trading partners, with each partner assigned a weight based on its trade relationship with South Africa.
"China has been South Africa's fastest-growing trading partner since 2003, moving from sixth position in the 2003 EER revision to second position in the 2014 and 2020 revisions, and to first position in the 2026 revision. China's trade weight increased from 24.5 percent in 2020 to 28.6 percent in 2026," the SARB said.
Over a longer period, China's weight rose from just 3.1 percent in 1999 to 28.6 percent in 2026, it added. At the same time, the euro area's trade weight declined from 35.7 percent in 1999 to 26.01 percent in 2026, moving it into second place.
South Africa is China's largest trading partner in Africa, while China has remained South Africa's largest trading partner for 17 consecutive years, with bilateral trade reaching 53.58 billion U.S. dollars in 2025. ■

The proposed amendment to the Drugs Rules, 1945, seeks to make prior approval of the federal government mandatory for advertisements relating to medicines listed under Schedule H, H1 and X.
The draft amendment has been notified through a Gazette notification dated Sept. 28, 2026, following consultations with the Drugs Technical Advisory Board.
The measure is expected to reinforce safeguards relating to medicines that require appropriate medical supervision, including certain antibiotics, psychotropic medicines and other prescription-only drugs, the ministry said.
According to the ministry, the move is aimed at curbing unauthorised promotion of prescription medicines and strengthening safeguards for public health.
In India, Schedule H, H1 and X drugs can be sold only under specific conditions, usually with a doctor's prescription. These rules help regulate medicines that may have serious side effects or carry a risk of dependence or misuse.
The ministry has invited objections and suggestions from stakeholders and members of the public within 30 days from the date on which copies of the Gazette containing the draft rules are made available to the public. ■

Africa CDC urges heightened regional preparedness as Ebola cases reach 8,750

2026-10-09

22:48:09 KST

ADDIS ABABA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (Africa CDC) has called for strict regional preparedness to avert further spread of the ongoing Ebola outbreak, as the number of confirmed cases has reached 8,750 alongside a mounting death toll.
Addressing an online press briefing on Thursday evening, Wessam Mankoula, an Africa CDC official, lauded Kenya's preparedness and ongoing response efforts, as the country became the latest country to record a Bundibugyo Ebola case.
Calling for enhanced regional preparedness and solidarity, he highlighted that the East African country's prior investments in preparedness have enabled it to respond quickly to the imported case and strengthen contact tracing.
"Ebola is crossing another border. However, at the Africa CDC, we are calling for vigilance, not banning," said Mankoula.
Kenyan authorities are currently tracing contacts linked to its first imported case and have enhanced disease surveillance to avoid the potential spread of the virus, after a 40-year-old patient, a Kenyan citizen who had lived in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) for seven years, died from the disease in a Nairobi hospital on Monday.
Africa CDC officials stressed that the imported case has triggered concern over the disease's spread. The patient moved across the DRC, Uganda, and Kenya before testing positive, highlighting how quickly the virus can cross borders and threaten regional health security.
Mankoula said the current crisis, regarded as the fastest-growing and second-largest Ebola outbreak on record, at week 21, has recorded 4.1 times more cases and 3.7 times more deaths than the next-highest comparator, the 2014-2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak.
The latest data from the African Union's specialized continental public health agency showed that confirmed cases in the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak have reached 8,750, with more than 4,208 deaths and a case fatality rate of 48.1 percent. Some 2,288 patients have recovered from the deadly disease, while 1,066 patients are currently in isolation.
Beyond the DRC, Uganda, and Kenya, 10 other countries across the continent have been previously designated as high-risk: South Sudan, Rwanda, Zambia, the Central African Republic, Tanzania, Ethiopia, Angola, the Republic of the Congo, Burundi, and Somalia.
The Africa CDC declared the ongoing Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak a public health emergency of continental security on May 18, one day after the World Health Organization declared the situation a public health emergency of international concern.
Ebola is highly contagious and can cause fever, vomiting, diarrhea, generalized pain or malaise, and, in severe cases, internal and external bleeding. ■

French police have recovered two paintings by French artist Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in the southern French town of Cagnes-sur-Mer last month, French broadcaster BFMTV reported Friday.
The paintings, Madame Colonna Romano (Mrs. Colonna Romano) and Jeune femme au puits (Young Woman at the Well), were recovered Thursday, Oct. 8.
The two works were estimated to be worth between €8 million ($9 million) and €10 million ($11.2 million).
The theft took place on Sept. 8, when two burglars entered the Renoir Museum, the artist’s former residence, through a hole cut in the garden fence.
The suspects stole four artworks but abandoned two as they fled when police arrived.
The four targeted paintings were the museum’s most valuable works, according to the prosecutor’s office.
Six people were arrested Wednesday in the southern Alpes-Maritimes department, the Herault department in southern France and the Jura department in eastern France.
Two of the suspects are believed to have carried out the burglary.
Cagnes-sur-Mer Mayor Bryan Masson described the suspects as “real professionals” after the theft, saying they had worn helmets, gloves and masks and appeared to have detailed knowledge of the museum.
Following the recovery, Masson congratulated the Marseille Interregional Specialized Court and the law enforcement agencies involved in the investigation, including units specializing in judicial investigations and the trafficking of cultural property.
“These two paintings are not simply works of art. They belong to the history of our town, our heritage and the legacy left by Auguste Renoir in Cagnes-sur-Mer,” Masson said.
He described their recovery as a “great relief” for local residents and those attached to the museum.
The investigation into suspected organized theft and criminal conspiracy is ongoing.

Eggs cost nearly 20 times US prices in occupied Oleshky, where Ukraine’s ombudsman says people die of hunger every day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:45:10 UTC
22:45:10 KST

People in Russian-occupied Oleshky, a town in southern Ukraine, are running out of food and medicine and have no way out, a local resident told RBC-Ukraine. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman told the outlet that civilians there are dying of hunger every day.
The part of Kherson Oblast across the Dnipro River has been under Russian occupation since 2022, with civilians facing food and medicine shortages and restrictions on leaving. The UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine has documented deteriorating conditions in Oleshky and neighboring Hola Prystan. There has been no practical breakthrough toward an organized evacuation, though 358 people who need help to leave Oleshky and nearby settlements have been verified. About 2,000 people remain in Oleshky, Kherson Oblast head Oleksandr Prokudin estimated.
The resident, who spoke anonymously, said food is extremely scarce, and residents are waiting for a humanitarian corridor to leave. The local market offers mostly vegetables and fruit, such as tomatoes, cucumbers, zucchini, pears, and apples. Russia made its ruble the only legal currency in occupied Kherson Oblast from 1 January 2023, pushing out the Ukrainian hryvnia. Prices at the market start at 500 rubles (about $6), and "if you're lucky, 10 eggs can be bought for 3,000 rubles" (about $36), the resident said. That is about $3.60 an egg, nearly 20 times the US average of about $0.19, or $2.27 a dozen in August, US government data show.
Russian troops enter homes and threaten starving Oleshky residents for food and alcohol, officials say
Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, told RBC-Ukraine that civilians in the occupied area were dying every day.
"There is a humanitarian catastrophe there. Ukrainian civilians die there every day because they lack even basic food and water. There have been no medicines there for a long time. According to our information, there is simply hunger there," he said.
Practically no medicines
The resident said there were practically no medicines available. Expired drugs were being sold at about 100 rubles (about $1.20) a pill. His father has Parkinson's syndrome and has been concussed twice. The resident said he was forced to reduce his father's dose by 25% so the supply would last at least until the new year.
Thousands are starving in occupied Oleshky. People have no food, no way out, and Russian forces bomb incoming aid
The resident's apartment had burned down, and his house remained damaged. His family had made the house livable and was living there, he said. His wife had lost more than 40 kilograms while the family relied on vegetables and fruit.
Beyond Oleshky: villages with no transport or aid
Four villages in the Hola Prystan community—Kokhany, Kardashynka, Velyka Kardashynka, and Mala Kardashynka—are effectively blocked, according to the Skhid-SOS fund. The fund told RBC-Ukraine that no transport reaches the villages and no humanitarian aid has been delivered for a prolonged period, although it is difficult to get more information from the villages. Residents are forced to walk or cycle to other settlements to find food, despite the risks of mines and drone strikes.
Civilians used as a buffer
Lubinets also said Russian troops were using civilians as a buffer and as protection against the Ukrainian military, RBC-Ukraine reported. Because Ukrainian citizens remain in Oleshky, Ukraine cannot conduct active combat operations there, he said—which, in his view, allows Russia to hold civilians effectively as hostages on the front line.
Food arrives by drone, but how much reaches residents is unclear
Ukraine has delivered food to Oleshky by drone since March, Prokudin said. Nearly 400 parcels weighing almost 4 tons reached their drop-off points on the night of 4 October, Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi said. How much of the food stays with residents is unclear. Prokudin has said Russian forces shoot down supply drones, confiscate or resell the packages, and detain and beat residents who receive them.
After a previous delivery, Tetiana Hasanenko, head of the Oleshky City Military Administration, said that Russian troops take drone-dropped food and accuse those who receive it of cooperating with Ukraine, and that some residents got several packages while others got none.

Ukraine has recovered EUR 700,000 from abroad in a corruption case involving the state-owned Polygraph Combine Ukraina, the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU) has reported.
One of the defendants admitted guilt and agreed to compensate for the damage, NABU said on Telegram on Friday.
The funds had been frozen in the defendant's accounts in France. Following approval of a plea agreement by Ukraine's High Anti-Corruption Court and with the consent of France's National Financial Prosecutor's Office, the freeze was lifted and the money transferred to the state-owned enterprise's account, NABU said.
The recovery resulted from the work of a joint investigation team comprising NABU detectives, Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor's Office (SAPO) prosecutors, and law enforcement officers from France and Estonia. The team also received expert and coordination support from the StAR Initiative, Eurojust, and the OECD GLEN and GFAR Action Series platforms, NABU said.
This is the third recovery of assets from abroad in the case. In October 2025, French company SURYS transferred EUR 3.37 million to the Ukrainian state, followed by another EUR 450,000 in June 2026. The total amount recovered in the case has now reached EUR 4.5 million, NABU said.
In August 2026, Ukrainian anti-corruption authorities sent to court a case concerning an alleged international corruption scheme involving passport production, with estimated losses of around UAH 500 million.
The former head of the Polygraph Combine is accused of misappropriating the enterprise's funds, receiving an undue benefit in the form of copyright to security-feature designs used in foreign passports and ID cards, and laundering proceeds from their use. Another defendant is a former department head at the enterprise.
According to NABU, in 2013 the then-head of the combine acquired an Estonian company through nominees and made its involvement a condition of cooperation with foreign partners. The intermediary purchased holograms directly from a French manufacturer and resold them to the state-owned enterprise at prices four to six times higher, investigators allege.
Four participants in the scheme have been convicted by the High Anti-Corruption Court under plea agreements. Almost UAH 180 million has been returned to the state, nearly UAH 6 million allocated to support Ukraine's Defense Forces, and more than UAH 20 million reimbursed to the state-owned enterprise, NABU said.

====================================================================================================

Debunking Alarmist Narratives on the ‘China Air Base’ in Laos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:42:00 UTC
22:42:00 KST

The opening of the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy in Ban Keun, Laos on September 29 has sparked an intense media storm. China hawks claim that the innocuous airfield represents Beijing’s third overseas military base, following the Djibouti facility in East Africa and the Ream Naval Support facility in Cambodia, and the first Chinese air base in Southeast Asia.
International media has framed the Ban Keun facility as a “base” or an “air base,” and the training aircraft spotted on satellite imagery as “attack aircraft” or “light attack aircraft.” Further, alarmists warn that China could extend the airfield’s runway and expand its infrastructure to enable power projection across mainland Southeast Asia and beyond, or to use the facility for intelligence collection. Still others have proposed that an enlarged base could facilitate bomber operations or to out-flank or surround Vietnam.
Critically, however, whether due to intentional framing or simple ignorance, many of the above claims lack evidence and realism. This article attempts to debunk some of the more persistent and glaring narratives repeated in the media and expert commentary regarding the new airfield and its purpose.
First, images of Ban Keun airfield taken by a commercial satellite provider Vantor and shared first by Reuters show eight Chinese-made JL-8/K-8 basic jet trainer aircraft on the facility’s apron. The aircraft are termed as “light attack aircraft” or “attack aircraft” by media. That is an inaccurate framing, making the aircraft appear more threatening by nature than they actually are.
The K-8 is a joint China-Pakistan training aircraft project, operated by many countries, including in the region by China, Laos, Myanmar, and Pakistan, among others. The K-8 is primarily a basic or intermediate training aircraft. The type typically feeds into phases two and three of a flight training syllabus, like introduction to jet flight and advanced jet training, and an introduction to tactical flight, before moving on to more advanced and higher performance trainers.
In the Lao People’s Liberation Army Air Force (LPLAAF), the phase one elementary training is carried out on Chinese-build SAIC LE-500, the K-8 is used in the phase two and three basic jet training, and the Russian YAK-130 is used for phase four tactical training.
Unlike Myanmar’s air force, which has reportedly employed the K-8 in a light attack role, there is no evidence of LPLAAF use of the type in that role. Tellingly, no visual evidence of the type participating in exercises or carrying air-to-ground munitions has surfaced in the aircraft’s almost a decade of service in Laos. Thus, framing the Laotian K-8 as a “light attack aircraft” is simply an inaccurate description, which causes confusion and alarm.
In contrast, the Russian advanced jet trainer is a substantially more capable platform than the K-8 and can be armed with various air-to-air and air-to-ground munitions for ground support.
Another persistent claim suggests that Ban Keun airfield is a Chinese “air base” with a long runway and a “large” apron for aircraft parking, supposedly capable of supporting Chinese military power projection across mainland Southeast Asia.
However, the airfield’s single runway is approximately 2,000 meters in length, which, in fact, is not very long for a military airfield. Other major LPLAAF operating locations like the Wattay International Airport in Vientiane and Xieng Khouang (Phonsavan) air base have runways extending to approximately 3,000 m and 2,500 m, respectively, measured in Google Earth.
By way of comparison, neighboring Thailand’s military airfields are generally built to 3,000 m length. Similarly, the People’s Liberation Army Air Force (PLAAF) fighter bases in the Southern Theater Command area have 2,500 m runways, while bomber bases at Shaodong and Leiyang have longer, 3,000 m runways.
The 2,000 m runway at Ban Keun was not built to support power projection but, instead, to handle training aircraft.
In addition, claims that the facility has a large apron for aircraft parking and potential for significant expansion to support power projection are also incorrect. Judged from the available satellite imagery, the airfield’s apron is in fact relatively small and can only support a dozen trainers with associated sun shelters, hangars, and maintenance infrastructure.
To support sustained power projection operations, the airfield should have truly vast aprons, numerous aircraft shelters, and large fuel and munitions “farms,” which can be seen in similar imagery from Chinese air bases across the border.
None of this is visible at Ban Keun. What can be parsed out is an airfield with modest infrastructure suitable for the stated intended training role.
Some experts have proposed that together with the Cambodia-China Support Center in Ream (often framed as a Chinese naval base), the Ban Keun “air base” will help China “encircle” Vietnam. Writing for the Interpreter, Hunter Marston suggested that “Beijing has effectively pulled off an end run around Hanoi’s air and maritime flanks.”
Such statements demonstrate limited understanding of air power’s key attributes and China’s existing military posture and options to project power in the South China Sea or mainland Southeast Asia. Air power allows maneuver in the third dimension (altitude). Its key attributes – speed, reach, and ability to overfly any terrain – provide military aircraft significant operational flexibility.
The PLAAF does not have to base its combat aircraft physically in Laos to attempt to “surround” or “encircle” Vietnam. It can do so from its current bases within the Southern Theater Command and the South China Sea.
Under the Southern Theater Command, the PLAAF has an extensive network of well-equipped air bases that stretch from Hunan and Guangdong provinces in China’s southeast to Guangxi and Yunnan provinces in the south, directly bordering Vietnam, Laos, and Myanmar. In addition, Hainan Island, Woody Island in the Paracels, and Fiery Cross Reef, Subi Reef, and Mischief Reef in the Spratlys provide the PLAAF with a chain of well-equipped operating locations for any regional contingency.
Importantly, from its current bases, such as Mengzi in Yunnan Province or Bose/Tianyang in Guangxi Province, PLAAF combat aircraft can comfortably reach anywhere in mainland Southeast Asia. Moreover, operating from China’s Spratly outposts, the PLAAF can reach nearly all corners of the subregion. The reach of China’s air power can be further expanded by the growing fleet of indigenous aerial refueling aircraft.
The PLAAF’s primary combat aircraft in the Southern Theater Command area of operations – such as the JH-7A, Su-30MKK, J-16, and J-20 – are designed for long combat radius, extending from 600 nautical miles to up to 1,000 nm. The smaller J-10C can also reach more than 600 nm with drop tanks. With such operational flexibility, PLAAF strike aircraft can execute multipronged attacks against targets up to central Vietnam from their existing bases. Dispatched from Woody Island or Fiery Cross Reef in the South China Sea, Chinese fighters can easily cover the entirety of Vietnam and more, offering options for multiple approaches.
As a result, there is no reason for Beijing to position its bombers forward to the Ban Keun airfield to project power across mainland Southeast Asia and the Gulf of Thailand and Gulf of Bengal in conflict. With an estimated combat radius of 1,350 nm combined with the use of long-range precision-guided weapons, China’s H-6K bombers can cover all the above areas while operating from their home bases at Shaodong and Leiyang in Hunan Province. Any forward deployment of Chinese bombers would occur within the Southern Theater Command area, Hainan Island, or the Spratlys, offering the PLAAF multiple options and operational flexibility.
Experts have suggested also that China could deploy spy aircraft, surveillance radars, and signals intelligence gathering systems to Ban Keun. Commenting on the matter for the South China Morning Post, Abdul Rahman Yaacob proposed that China could use the facility for “keeping an eye on Vietnam” and to “monitor air activities deep into Myanmar, Thailand, and Vietnam.” Others have noted that the facility offers improved reach for Chinese spy planes to monitor U.S. military activity up to the Singapore Strait.
However, it is unclear from such commentary what the purpose of increased monitoring of mainland Southeast Asia is.
Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, and Cambodia all hold very close relations with Beijing. When it comes to Vietnam, which has maritime disputes with China in the South China Sea, Hanoi’s military bases can be easily monitored from Southern Theater Command area of operations, with little additional benefit from dispatching such capabilities to Laos.
These assertions are among the most frequently disseminated narratives regarding the Laos-China Support and Training Center. Many are pure speculation that fuels unnecessary alarmism – particularly those that lack evidence and demonstrate a limited understanding of air power, its key attributes, and China’s regional air projection capabilities.
What the official statements and available evidence suggest is that the Ban Keun facility is a joint training facility to help the LPLAAF develop its capacity for the future and meet its own modernization goals.
China has assisted the Lao air force (and the broader civil aviation sector) not just through hardware sales (i.e., the LE-500 and JL-8 for the LPLAAF and the C-909 for the Lao Airlines) but also by developing the entire aviation ecosystem, including infrastructure, management, maintenance, and training. This is the context in which the Laos-China Joint Support and Training Center and the Friendship Aviation Academy should be viewed.

Rodina wished her good health, peace and many more happy moments with her loved ones. And the messages from her former pupils in Bulgaria are a touching reminder that, even after all these years and thousands of miles, a much-loved teacher is never forgotten.

Bulgarian filmmaker Ina Sotirova receives five Caribbean Film Awards nominations
The winners will be announced on 10 October
Friday 9 October 2026 15:37
Friday, 9 October 2026, 15:37
Ina Sotirova
PHOTO imdb.com
Font size
Filmmaker Ina Sotirova is driven by a desire to help change the world around her through her work. In pursuing this goal, she strives to keep her finger on the pulse of everyday life, exploring the concerns and experiences that matter to people, even those they keep hidden or consider too personal to share. Her ability to tell stories with honesty, through the eyes of the people who live them, has earned her the admiration of audiences and recognition for her work.
Her fourth film, Stinky Mango, received several nominations at the Diversity in Cannes event, winning the award for Best Ensemble Cast in Cannes. It subsequently received an award for innovative storytelling at the Films That Move festival in Jamaica.
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
A year later, we have another reason to catch up with Ina Sotirova. Stinky Mango has received three nominations at the Caribbean Film Awards – for Best Short Film, Best Actor for Sheldon Shepherd, and the Caribbean Cultural Heritage Award. Sotirova herself is nominated for Best Emerging Director. Whether she takes home any of the awards will become clear on 10 October, at the inaugural edition of the awards ceremony in Wilmington, United States.
Her latest film, The Sisters and the Storm, has also been nominated for Best Documentary. The project was funded through a UNICEF programme:
“Last year, on 28 October, Hurricane Melissa struck the south-western part of Jamaica. It was extremely powerful and caused widespread devastation. Even today, people are still struggling to recover,” Ina Sotirova tells us.
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
“Earlier this year, UNICEF and the Jamaica Film and Television Association (JAFTA) launched an initiative to fund three short documentaries exploring the impact of the hurricane on women and children. I submitted my project, The Sisters of the Storm, and was awarded one of the three grants.
“The film tells the story of three girls who either have no families or have been removed from their homes because of domestic violence or other problems. They live in what are known as children's villages. The hurricane destroyed one of these villages, forcing them to move to a similar facility in Jamaica's capital, Kingston, where they don't feel at home.”
Filming presented an unusual and emotionally demanding challenge because of the circumstances of its young protagonists:
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
“They are children, some of whom have no parents. We had to protect their identities. This isn't a typical documentary where you see interviews with the people involved. We made it more like an audio diary.
“Because we weren't allowed to show the children on screen or reveal where they were living, we had to be very creative in how we approached that part of the filmmaking process. As a result, the film became a much more poetic and intimate portrait of these children at a particular moment in their lives.”
Filming took just five days, although editing continued for another two months:
“I think this is the fastest film I've ever made. It's only eight minutes long, but I should point out that making an eight-minute film is harder than making a fifteen-minute one, because it takes much more skill to decide what really matters.”
PHOTO Mango Magic Movie
Is there a story from everyday life in Bulgaria that our compatriot feels strongly enough about to turn into a film that could capture the interest of audiences in Jamaica or elsewhere in the world?
“Of course. Wherever you look, there are stories,” Ina says emphatically. “There are things I feel I should learn more about myself. I simply haven't yet had the time or opportunity to immerse myself in those stories.
“I'm particularly interested in communism and how its legacy continues to shape contemporary culture. So, at some point, I'll explore those stories too.”

This year’s poster, designed by Fatma Betul Okuyucu, combines imagery associated with Istanbul and cinema through a layered collage.

The festival will open with the European premiere of Simon Stone’s Elsinore. Ten productions will compete for its Best Film award, with the winner scheduled to be announced on Oct. 18.

In Paris, the Paris Opera Ballet will open its dance season Saturday with a gala at the Palais Garnier. The program will bring together the company’s dancers, Junior Ballet and Ballet School, followed by works from choreographers Juliano Nunes, Jean-Christophe Maillot and Aszure Barton.

Protesters clash with police in Brussels as unions and students march
BRUSSELS – A small group of protesters clashed with police in Brussels on Oct 9 as union members, joined by hundreds of students, marched as part of a national strike against planned government budget cuts.
A few dozen masked protesters dressed in black threw rocks and other objects at police, as anti-police slogans echoed through the streets and anti-police graffiti covered nearby walls. Firefighters extinguished several fires, including on buses, while police responded with tear gas, according to Reuters witnesses.
The clashes occurred as thousands of protesters took to the streets of the Belgian capital, including students inspired in part by demonstrations in neighbouring France. The strike disrupted public transport and air travel, while many schools and childcare facilities were also affected.
Among the demonstrators, some carried placards reading “I skipped class to defend class” and “Education is a right, not a privilege”.
The Belgian walkout is part of a wave of protests sweeping Europe, with students in France and Italy, among other countries, taking to the streets over education funding, while tens of thousands have rallied in Spain over a housing crisis.
Police said while the march itself, joined by around 30,000 people, passed off peacefully, clashes erupted near Brussels Central Station and in central Brussels where groups threw bottles, bricks, stones and fireworks at police, set fires and damaged public property.
Police said officers used water cannon and tear gas to disperse the groups and that 21 people had been detained or arrested, including 13 minors.
The strike was called by Belgium’s two largest unions, the socialist FGTB/ABVV and Christian CSC/ACV, which oppose government budget measures they say would make workers, pensioners and low-income households bear the burden of efforts to reduce the country’s deficit.
Belgian Prime Minister Bart De Wever said on Oct 8 that painful budget measures were needed now to avert a looming debt and interest-cost spiral that would otherwise leave future generations with a heavy bill.
Student groups, whose protests began earlier in October in Liege and spread to Brussels on Oct 9, say they are also protesting rising education costs, overcrowded classrooms and reforms they fear will make higher education less accessible.
“We’re not taken into account at all, and no one seems to realise that it’s hard for us too, both for workers and for students,” said Emilie L’Honneux, a 23-year-old student from Liege.
“We’re struggling too, and we are the future of this country,” she added. REUTERS

We continue to detect new protected satellite navigation antennas of a new type with 32 elements in the Shaheds attacking Kyiv. Previously, the enemy used antennas with 16 elements. The second time around: Meet the men who run the pre-owned luxury watch market
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:39:27 UTC
22:39:27 KST

After thousands of people queued around the world earlier this year to get their hands on the avant-garde Audemars Piguet x Swatch, Royal Pop collaboration, collectors have been carefully following the second-hand market. Now, two leading watch experts share their secrets of what and when to buy.
In May earlier this year, riot police were called to ensure security at Swatch stores from Paris to Mumbai when violence often erupted as queues of people stretched around the streets. The object of their frenzied desires was a €370 bioceramic pocket watch.
The Royal Pop — the first time Audemars Piguet has let the Royal Oak design out of its own factory — turned people who had never owned a mechanical watch into speculators overnight. Within hours, resale sites were carrying listings above €7,400. Bad bet. Two months later, several models were selling for less than the €370 Swatch asks in store.
Far from the chaos, hundreds of thousands of people search the same market every day. In their quest for desirability, every major brand is closely monitoring the market for vintage revivals and other signs of popular trends. So what are people actually buying, and how do you avoid getting ripped off? We asked two of the people who know best.
Rolex still the leading investment
Perhaps unsurprisingly, most people online prefer to pick up a Rolex rather than a Swatch or an AP. The brand with the distinctive five-pointed 'coronet' has settled back to around 30% of transaction volume, on the German platform Chrono24, the world's largest marketplace for pre-owned watches, according to Chrono24’s Rolex Report 2026.
"Rolex built its lead over decades," says José Gaztelu, CEO of Chrono24. "Buyers often start with a Datejust or an Oyster Perpetual and move up from there," Gaztelu says. "People discover the history, the references, the stories behind the models. It is what keeps people in the hobby," he adds.
Over at Bezel, an American platform built on in-house authentication, which carried more than a billion dollars in active listings through the first half of 2026, Rolex leads every measure too: 34% of tracked interest, 28% of orders, 35% of watches registered in client collections.
"Rolex has recognition, product depth and liquidity all at once," says Quaid Walker, the platform's CEO. "It reflects the depth of the secondary market around virtually every major model. It inspires confidence for new buyers and experienced collectors alike."
Cartier, Tudor or FP Journe gaining ground
But the Rolex shares are actually shrinking on Chrono24, after a peak above 44% in 2022. This decline, to the benefit of other brands, is seen as a "healthy normalization" of the market by Chrono24's CEO. "Buyers are spreading demand across a broader set of brands and models. This shift is particularly visible among younger buyers."
Who's benefiting? "Cartier stands out most clearly, particularly in the €5,000 to €10,000 segment," he says. "Patek Philippe and Vacheron Constantin have gained ground at the high end, while Audemars Piguet remains very strong as well. Beyond the high end, Tudor, Jaeger-LeCoultre and Longines are also worth mentioning."
What are the trending models? "The Cartier Tank and the Tudor Black Bay represent two different sides of the shift we are seeing. The Tank reflects the renewed interest in elegant, distinctive classics, while the Black Bay shows that versatile sports watches with a clear identity remain highly relevant", Gaztelu says.
Bezel's data shows the same drift. Tudor took 14% of orders, finishing second by sales, ahead of Omega. Further out, the sharpest momentum is with the independents: F.P. Journe has been trading at strong levels, as a younger and well-informed base of collectors pays closer attention to the watchmakers behind the watches rather than to established brand names alone.
Vintage has momentum, but no buying spree
The trend press spent the first half of 2026 pushing smaller cases and louder dials. "Buyers are moving towards more classical proportions and more refined, dress-oriented watches," says Gaztelu.
"Women are certainly part of this development. But men are also buying smaller watches than they did ten years ago. While 40mm remains a sports-watch sweet spot for many men, there is clearly more interest in refined dress watches with smaller case sizes. The industry has also added much more variety in the 35 to 39 millimetre range, which has become a versatile unisex sweet spot", he adds.
The order books at Bezel show that vintage watches are still far from taking over the market. References from the 2020s and 2010s gather together roughly three-quarters of all activity. Buyers kept reaching for 40–41mm steel in black, blue and silver. Steel alone took 72% of orders.
"There's clearly more energy around smaller cases and more expressive dials, but our buyers in the first half of 2026 were still concentrated around tried-and-true sizes and hues. Smaller watches aren't necessarily a fad. It just means a trend can be culturally important before it becomes the centre of the market. I'd call it a real design trend, but not yet a broad buying trend", Walker says.
Buy it because you want to wear it
Are you making a good investment? "There's no reliable way to predict whether a watch will appreciate in value, but you can get a pretty good sense of how resilient its value may be," says Walker. He starts with liquidity — how often the reference trades, how many buyers there are for it, where comparable examples are actually selling — then weighs condition, originality, production volume and the strength of the brand or watchmaker.
Walker refuses to name a 2026 good buy. "I'd start by assessing what someone already owns, what they actually wear, and the role they want the next watch to play in their collection," he says. "For a newer collector, that might mean something versatile from a brand with real history and a deep catalogue to explore."
"For a new collector, the biggest mistake is usually paying too much because a watch feels hard to get, or because the market around it is moving quickly," he adds. "Understanding the recent transaction history and buying a strong example at a sensible price will generally matter more than trying to predict which watch is going to take off next."
Gaztelu's advice is simple. "There are classics that tend to have the steadiest demand and value retention or appreciation. But I will be direct: the vast majority of people should buy a watch because they love it, not as a bet. The collectors who are happiest years later are the ones who bought something they love, at a fair price, and kept it," he adds.
Walker lands in the same place: "The best collections tend to feel personal rather than like a snapshot of whatever the market was excited about that year."
Pick the one you actually like. And make sure it's real. Bezel turned away 34% of the watches submitted for sale in the first half of 2026. Among them:a genuine Patek Philippe Aquanaut worth around $140,000 that had been stolen off a wrist in Ibiza, and a real Rolex Submariner fitted with a counterfeit dial.

Though the railways cited “operational reasons” for the cancellation, the move comes ahead of the protests called by the Cockroach Janata Party and other groups in Delhi on October 10, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over controversy surrounding the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.On Friday, the Bikaner Division of North Western Railway announced the cancellation of 13 train services bound for Delhi.Delhi Police also proposed closing entry and exit gates at 57 metro stations across the national capital and reducing train frequency at these stations.Hours after the measures disrupting the railways & metro adopted, the Supreme Court orally asked the Centre to ensure that Delhi Metro operations are not completely suspended ahead of the protest, stressing that preventive measures should not cause inconvenience to ordinary commuters.A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana expressed concern over the scheduled closure of 57 Metro stations, observing that the restrictions could affect students, employees and other people dependent on public transport.
"We are concerned with closure of metro services," the CJI-led Bench remarked, addressing Solicitor General Tushar Mehta, who appeared for the Centre."One very important principle that we follow for every citizen is the principle of proportionality… You have to prevent certain things. Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," CJI Kant further told Mehta.The solicitor general said he understands the concerns of the court and will discuss with the authorities concerned, but said that the remark of the CJI on use of a hammer was just an example and it should not be reported that the Chief Justice of India told the government that it is using a hammer to kill a fly.CJI Kant said, "Exercise caution in abundance. There is nothing wrong with that."

NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ despite earlier threats
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:38:20 UTC
22:38:20 KST

NATO asks Russia ‘not to worry’ about nuclear drills
NATO has asked Moscow “not to worry” about the US-led military bloc’s upcoming nuclear warfare drills, despite weeks of escalated war rhetoric from its member states, which are ostensibly preparing their populations for a war with Russia.
NATO’s forces will practice responding to launch orders, flying mock nuclear delivery sorties, and maintaining communications under the stress of nuclear war during its ‘Steadfast Noon’ exercises from October 13 to 23. The drill will involve 17 of the bloc’s 32 member states and will not involve live nuclear weapons.
This year alone, bloc forces have run three separate exercises on the borders of the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, after which Polish Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski suggested a further buildup of NATO forces in the area in order to keep Moscow “uncertain of what we will do.”
The Kremlin issued a stern warning in response, stating that Russia is “ready to use all its arsenal, including nuclear weapons, to defend its territory if NATO countries try to isolate Kaliningrad.”
The message apparently fell on deaf ears. On Wednesday, Estonia’s foreign minister claimed that NATO possessed the ability to close the Baltic Sea “within hours,” strangling Russia’s economic “lifeline” and creating an “existential” crisis for the country. Last week, Swedish Air Warfare Centre chief Colonel Carl Bergqvist said his country’s warplanes were ready to attack targets deep inside Russian territory in the event of a conflict with Moscow.
NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte and European governments insisted in recent weeks that Russia is waging a “hybrid war” against the West. The accusations are by their nature unprovable, and have been described by analyst Thomas Fazi as a form of “hybrid warfare” against the European public, in which “Europeans are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia.”
NATO’s nuclear policy director, Nassima Barrows, told Politico on Thursday that the fact that the drills are held every year should serve as “a clear message to nations like Russia that there is no need to worry.”
Despite Burrows’ reassurances, and NATO’s description of Steadfast Noon as “not linked to current world events and is not directed against any country,” some of the bloc’s leaders evidently view their nuclear weapons as a tool with which to threaten Russia. After watching the test-launch of France’s latest nuclear-capable ballistic missile on Tuesday, French President Emmanuel Macron released a video of the test, describing it as “a clear message…for wherever it must be received.”
Russia read the message “loud and clear,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov responded, adding that Russia will take “all necessary measures” to protect its national security.
During his speech at a session of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) in Vienna on Thursday, Russian envoy Dmitry Polyansky reiterated that Moscow “threatens no one and has no intention of attacking anyone.”
At the same time, however, the country “cannot ignore the development of plans by NATO for a direct military clash with Russia, nor the bloc’s simulation of scenarios involving a military-political blockade of Kaliningrad Region,” he stressed.
“Our response to any unfriendly moves will be swift,” Polyansky said, urging NATO not to test Russia’s patience or push the European continent “toward the point of no return.”

EU commissioner says recent Turkish actions widen gap with its EU membership goal
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:34:39 UTC
22:34:39 KST

EU commissioner says recent Turkish actions widen gap with its EU membership goal
EDIRNE, Turkey, Oct 9 - Turkey is moving further away from its objective of joining the European Union because of its recent efforts to crack down on the LGBTQ+ community and limit media freedoms, the EU commissioner for enlargement said on Friday.
Turkey has been an official candidate to join the EU since 1999, but its accession has long been frozen over issues ranging from its human rights record to democratic backsliding.
Last week, a Turkish court ordered access to independent news outlet T24's website and social media accounts blocked after authorities said it had published 118 pieces of content over the past year deemed to constitute "LGBT propaganda".
The decision was taken as part of the "My Family is Safe" investigation, a widening crackdown targeting LGBTQ+ groups which the government says aims to protect children and family values, but which has drawn sharp criticism from rights groups and the EU.
Speaking to reporters in the northwestern province of Edirne where she attended the opening of an EU-funded railway project, Commissioner Marta Kos said the bloc had a strong interest in developing a cooperative and mutually beneficial relationship with Turkey in light of "new realities" in Europe, but that concerns over democratic standards remained.
"The latest developments affecting media freedom, the rights of the LGBTQI+ people and local democracy are widening the gap with Turkey's objective of joining the EU," Kos said.
The EU's annual enlargement report, due on October 28, will reflect "our serious concerns in these areas", Kos said, adding that she would "not shy away from stating the facts publicly and clearly".
There was no immediate Turkish government reaction to Kos' remarks.
NEED FOR EU-TURKEY COOPERATION HAS GROWN, KOS SAYS
Despite the lack of progress on its membership aspirations, Turkey has been looking to increase cooperation with the EU. It has repeatedly called for the updating of its customs union with the bloc, and has asked to join various EU programmes.
These include the Security Action for Europe, or SAFE, which helps member states to make defence investments, the Single Euro Payments Area initiative, or SEPA, which facilitates cashless euro bank transfers, and its "Made in Europe" rules, which are aimed at boosting domestic manufacturing.
Kos said conflicts in the region, especially the expansion of the Russia-Ukraine war to the Black Sea, showed the importance and necessity of cooperation with Turkey.
"The relevance of Turkey today is significantly higher than it was four or five years back," she said.
Kos said the EU had two tracks of work currently ongoing with Turkey, focused on a "targeted update" of the customs union that would require legislative alignment from Ankara. The other focuses on public procurement, which she said was important for Ankara's aim of joining the "Made in Europe" rules. REUTERS

Finnish man fined for keeping parents' bodies in freezers for 30 years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:32:49 EEST
22:32:49 KST

A Finnish court has fined an 81-year-old man nearly €2,000 for keeping his parents' bodies in freezers for almost three decades at a property in Turku. The Varsinais-Suomi District Court convicted him of three offences involving the improper treatment of human remains and the violation of a grave. His 70-year-old brother also received a fine for his involvement in unauthorised digging at a family burial plot.
The parents died of natural causes in 1994 and 1995, but their eldest son, a trained physician, kept their remains in chest freezers inside an outbuilding rather than arranging their burial.
Police discovered the bodies in June 2024 during a search of the property. Investigators found the freezers surrounded by stored belongings and other items. One freezer had no electricity supply when officers arrived.
The older brother had collected his father's body from the University of Turku's pathology department in 1995, where the remains had been kept for six months. He also collected his mother's body from Åland Central Hospital and transported it by ferry to Turku.
During the trial, the man admitted storing the bodies but denied committing a crime. He maintained that he had followed his parents' wishes and intended to bury them in a family burial chamber.
He told investigators that his father wanted his body preserved for future scientific research rather than cremated or buried. The man also described plans to establish a burial chamber in Washington state in the United States.
The court rejected his defence, ruling that the parents' alleged wishes and his religious beliefs did not exempt him from complying with Finnish burial laws.
Prosecutors argued that the unlawful storage constituted a continuing offence lasting until police recovered the bodies in 2024. The court agreed, rejecting the defendant's argument that the alleged offences dated back to 1995 and had therefore expired under the statute of limitations.
The older brother received 110 income-linked day fines, with eight deducted to compensate for time spent in detention. His younger brother received 40 day fines, amounting to €640.
Both men were also convicted over digging at their family grave in Turku cemetery in October 2025. The court found that they had excavated a hole approximately 80 centimetres deep without permission.
The brothers claimed they were repairing a leaning gravestone, but the court concluded that the excavation was intended for a burial chamber.
The parents' remains were eventually buried at Turku cemetery in late 2025, with authorities from Lieto and Mariehamn arranging the burial.
The district court's ruling is not final, and both defendants have the right to appeal.

EU ‘pulling out all stops’ with minerals projects as it tries to avert China trade war
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:31:04 UTC
22:31:04 KST

The EU is “pulling out all the stops” to fend off an imminent potential trade crisis with China, the industry commissioner, Stéphane Séjourné, has said, as the bloc announced its backing for a string of critical materials projects.
Séjourné said on Friday that the EU would support 46 new strategic projects to accelerate supplies of critical raw materials by 2030 across the bloc.
“We could face a crisis in the coming months,” he said. “We may face trade tensions that could also trigger a crisis in a number of sectors. We need to be prepared for that. And we’re getting ready right now.”
The new projects include plants for supplies of lithium, gallium and rare earths needed for the auto, defence and renewable energy industries, with a funding cost of €21bn (£17.8bn).
They were unveiled just as the EU works to avert a trade war with China, with the trade commissioner, Maroš Šefčovič, continuing talks on Friday in Beijing aimed at reducing China’s “unsustainable” £1bn-a-day trade surplus with the bloc.
“We’re pulling out all the stops to move as quickly as possible. The primary objective is the targets set by law, and beyond that, there’s a geopolitical challenge that could catch up with us very quickly,” said Séjourné.
“Mines are opening, factories are being built, financing agreements are being signed, and a European value chain is emerging,” Séjourné added.
Amid some scepticism over the EU’s ability to meet its 2030 targets to reduce dependencies on China, Séjourné cited three “emblematic” projects which have previously been identified as strategic, earmarking them for accelerated permits.
These included a rare earths plant near Pau in south-western France. The Carester plant, which is expected to be up and running in late 2026, produces dysprosium and terbium, “two raw materials for which we are almost entirely dependent on China”, used in magnets for electric vehicles and offshore wind turbines.
“This single project could account for about 15% of global production of these oxides. That is no small feat,” Séjourné said.
He also name-checked a gallium plant in Greece which is already up and running.
The third, Keliber, a lithium extraction and processing plant in Finland, is also operational after €150m support from the European Investment Bank.
The 46 projects are the second batch of initiatives to receive flagship status since the Critical Raw Materials Act of 2024, which legally mandates the European Commission to reduce the bloc’s dependency on foreign countries.
The EU hopes to follow in the footsteps of Japan, which has reduced dependency on China for rare earths to 60% from 90% since 2011, when Beijing prohibited exports of about 20 materials to Japan, claiming they were being used for military purposes.
Although the flagship status does not bring the projects direct funds, it enables accelerated permitting, and help in mobilising funds.
However, there has been criticism in industry within the EU that the scheme is not strong enough to deliver targets to mine 10%, process 40% and recycle 25% of the bloc’s needs by 2030.
The French lithium refiner Viridian Lithium, which received EU strategic status in 2025, went into judicial liquidation in March this year.
Earlier this year, a group of 23 of the 60 projects designated strategic in 2025 wrote to the European Commission calling for more action to “urgently unlock projects, particularly those working towards final investment decision which face acute liquidity and market pressure and immediate jeopardy”.
Séjourné said member states had unlocked €1bn for six of the projects, with the European Investment Bank providing another €660m for eight projects.

They said Joshua Kerry, 28, researched the home or office addresses of dozens of politicians and public figures from May 2024 until the killing of Ann Widdecombe, a prominent figure in Farage's anti-immigration Reform UK party, at her home in July.
Kerry is also accused of attempting in April 2025 to get inside the home of Farage, one of the most influential and divisive figures in British politics for more than a decade. He is often credited with helping to bring about the 2016 referendum on whether Britain should stay in the European Union.

"The prosecution are likely to suggest that is demonstrated by those he took action against. He held particular hostility towards Reform," Polnay said.

A LIST OF POLITICIANS

Speaking ahead of City’s visit to Liverpool on Sunday, Maresca said he knew “exactly the effort that the club put in” to win its trophies and maintained his confidence in the club’s owners and senior management.
“The reason I joined this club is that I completely trust, 100%, the owner, the CEO, the sporting director, all the organization. So I don’t have doubt about that,” he told a news conference.
The commission found City guilty of breaches covering the 2009-10 to 2017-18 seasons, including the use of “sham” commercial contracts and misleading accounts in an alleged scheme to disguise more than £830 million ($1.1 billion) in funding.
City have denied wrongdoing and lodged an appeal, arguing that the ruling contained “clear material errors of law, principle and fact” and was unsafe.
Maresca said he had discussed the verdict with the club but suggested further comment should wait until the appeal process had concluded.
“We all trust, and probably the right moment to speak about that is when we are going to win this appeal,” he said.
The Italian added that his players would concentrate on matters they could influence.
“For me, the players, we can control just the pitch side, the football side. So we are focused on that. This is what we can do and what we can control.”
Maresca, appointed as Pep Guardiola’s successor in June, previously worked with City’s academy and served as Guardiola’s assistant during the club’s Treble-winning 2022-23 season.
City have won their opening five Premier League matches under the 46-year-old. Victory at Anfield would make Maresca only the fourth manager to win his first six matches in charge of a club in the competition.
He acknowledged that the financial ruling could result in an even more hostile atmosphere than usual on Sunday.
“It probably will be worse because of the situation but, again, it will be our duty to do our best and try to win the game,” he said. “The reason I decided to become a manager is for this type of game.”
Maresca also confirmed that striker Erling Haaland was ready to face Liverpool following the international break.

Helsinki votes in favour of banning fossil fuel adverts – but there could be a 10-year delay
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:26:52 UTC
22:26:52 KST

“Cities can’t keep working to cut emissions while allowing their own advertising spaces to encourage more flying and fossil fuel consumption.”
Helsinki has become the latest European city to vote in favour of banning advertising for fossil fuels and other carbon-intensive products and services.
The landmark proposal was brought to the City Council of Helsinki by Councillor Isaac Jyväsjärvi and 27 fellow councillors. It follows previous attempts to introduce restrictions on outdoor advertising from “carbon-intensive industries” that gained momentum in 2021 but failed to reach a majority support.
The exact scope of the restriction is to be determined ahead of the next advertising contract period, but campaigners say it could one day rid the streets of billboards promoting industries such as aviation, shipping, tourism and construction – as well as fossil fuels.
Existing advertising contracts in the city run until 2035, meaning it may take almost a decade for the ban to come into effect. Helsinki will now investigate the legal possibilities for restricting different types of advertising, as well as the potential impacts on the environment, the city’s finances and the wider media landscape.
Helsinki votes to ban fossil fuels ads
“Cities can’t keep working to cut emissions while allowing their own advertising spaces to encourage more flying and fossil fuel consumption,” says Niklas Kaskeala, Helsinki-based climate campaigner and Board Member of Protect Our Winters Finland.
“Helsinki’s decision won’t make these ads disappear overnight, but it draws an important line – and every city that takes this step makes it easier for others to follow.”
Anna Jonsonn, co-founder of NGO New Weather Sweden, also welcomes the ban, adding: “It’s time to stop promoting the industries that are fuelling the climate crisis.
“With this decision, Helsinki becomes the second Nordic capital to move towards such a ban, after Stockholm. A ban on fossil fuels ads is not a question of if; it is a question of when.”
Europe’s new era of green marketing
Helsinki City Council specifically cited other European cities that have moved to restrict fossil advertising when discussing the proposal.
Earlier this year, Amsterdam stripped its streets of billboards promoting meat and fossil fuel products as part of its target to reach carbon neutrality by 2050 and halve meat consumption during the same period.
The decision to ban fossil fuel advertising... comes at a crucial moment in the fight against climate change,” Femke Sleegers, coordinator of the Reclame Fossielvrij (Fossil Free Advertising) initiative, said when the ban was first proposed in 2020.
“Adverts that portray fossil fuels as normal worsen climate disruption and have no place in a city − or a country − that has complied with the Paris Agreement.”
Over in the UK, Bristol has recently become the first British city to impose an advertising ban on fast-fashion, SUVs, airlines, cruises and fossil fuels on all council-owned sites.
Since the summer of 2026, fossil fuel advertising has also been banned across city-owned billboards and public spaces in Stockholm.

Ukraine uses up Europe’s yearly supply of thermal sensors in about five months, so two Ukrainian firms will build their own plants in the West
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:23:48 UTC
22:23:48 KST

Two Ukrainian defense-tech firms, The Fourth Law and Odd Systems, have joined forces to mass-produce thermal imaging sensors in Europe and the US, The Fourth Law told Militarnyi. The goal is to wean Western militaries off foreign suppliers, chiefly China, for the core part of every thermal camera.
Amid Russia's daily attacks, Ukrainian drone makers have been shifting production to allied countries. Linza and Zoom drones are now built in Germany, and another top manufacturer has taken its technology to Canada and Finland. Sensor plants would move a core component west, not just finished drones.
A Western answer to Chinese sensors
The project, called Project Foundation, will build long-wave infrared sensors, known as microbolometers. These chips register heat, so a camera can pick out a person or vehicle at night or through smoke. The aim, The Fourth Law said, is to "ensure the sovereignty of Western countries in the field of thermal imaging technology."
Plants in Europe and the US from 2027
The project will run two sites, First Foundation in Europe and Second Foundation in the US, from a headquarters in Eindhoven, a Dutch semiconductor hub. Mass production is due to start in 2027. Within three years, the partners want to quadruple Europe's output of these sensors and double America's.
Why Europe's supply isn't enough
Ukraine's front line burns through sensors faster than Europe can make them. "Europe currently produces less than 500,000 such sensors per year, while Ukraine consumes this amount in about five months," Odd Systems co-founder Yaroslav Azhniuk said in February, when he first announced plans for a plant able to make one million sensors a year. European sensors cost about five times as much as Chinese ones and are hard to buy at all, because Europeans need them too, he added.
Factories working for Ukraine abroad have already become sabotage targets. In March, an arson attack in Pardubice, Czechia, destroyed nearly all the production capacity of a plant making drones and thermal sights for Ukraine's army. Czech investigators are looking into a possible Russian trail behind the attack.
