Paris Motor Show Mondial de l'Auto: dates and main premieres
Kyiv • UNN
Mondial de l’Auto 2026 will take place in Paris from October 12 to 18. Citroën will unveil a new generation of the legendary 2CV ahead of the event.
From October 12 to 18, 2026, Paris Expo Porte de Versailles will once again transform Paris into the world capital of the automotive industry. The Mondial de l'Auto-2026 Paris Motor Show will take place next week. At this 91st edition, the celebration of passion for automobiles takes on an entirely new dimension, bringing together even more automakers, even more entertainment, even more exhibitions, and even more spectacular moments for all visitors, UNN writes.
Mondial de l'Auto Paris Motor Show: press day
The 2026 Paris Motor Show will begin on Monday, October 12, and run through Sunday, October 18. The first day is reserved exclusively for accredited press, industry insiders, and manufacturers' official presentations, while from October 13 the motor show will be open to the press.
Paris Motor Show: premieres of the revived Citroën 2CV, Lancia Gamma, and Opel Corsa GSE
On Sunday, October 11, Citroën plans to unveil the new legendary Citroën 2CV on the eve of the Paris Motor Show.
The Citroën 2CV, popularly known as the "two horsepower," was produced from 1949 to 1990
The original Citroën 2CV debuted at the 1948 Paris Motor Show, although the technical brief for its creation had been submitted back in the 1930s. This "umbrella on wheels," also known as the "Tin Snail," was designed to carry two farmers, a 50-kilogram (110-pound) sack of potatoes, or a basket of eggs across a plowed field at 60 km/h (37 mph) without breaking a single shell.
Throughout its remarkable 42-year production run, the iconic model, named after the two horsepower of its engine, underwent many gradual updates but retained its signature shape and unique interconnected suspension. By the time the last example left the factory in 1990, Citroën had produced 5.1 million units worldwide.
Citroën has not disclosed information about the concept's technical specifications, apart from confirming a fully electric powertrain. The new 2CV is expected to be built on a dedicated platform designed in accordance with the European Union's forthcoming regulations on affordable electric vehicles.
At the beginning of this year, Citroen CEO Xavier Chardon said that the price of the production model should be less than 15,000 euros. This will make it the most affordable Citroen car.
Italy will unveil the new Lancia Gamma, which will be presented in three versions at once.
Among them, the electric HF Integrale with 375 hp will attract the most attention and become the flagship of the model range. Following its successful presentation in Italy, the Lancia Gamma will appear for the first time at the international motor show in Paris. This crossover belongs to the C-segment and has a sloping body that emphasizes its dynamic character.
The Gamma is offered in various configurations: the hybrid LX version has an output of 145 hp, while the electric LX version provides an environmentally friendly alternative. The most powerful is the HF Integrale, equipped with two electric motors. This provides all-wheel drive, making the model appealing to fans of sporty driving.
In addition to the Gamma, Lancia will present other models at its stand. These include the electric Ypsilon HF hatchback with a 280-hp motor, as well as the Ypsilon Rally2 HF Integrale rally version, which has already won in WRC2. This will allow visitors to compare the brand’s road and sports models.
Renault Group occupies 5,000 m² in Pavilion 6 and promises six new products, four of which are concept cars. The names of the concepts have not been disclosed before press day; the media expects them to include retro concepts based on the Renault 4 and Renault 5. The Renault stand will feature 22 electrified vehicles, including the Twingo E-Tech, Renault 4 E-Tech, and Renault 5 E-Tech, while Renault Pro+ will showcase the new electric Trafic E-Tech.
Romanian manufacturer Dacia, which is part of the Groupe Renault group, is bringing two new models. The first is the new second-generation Spring, presented on September 8, 2026: RGEV platform, a 27.5 kWh battery, a range of up to 250 km according to WLTP, 60 kW (80 hp), and acceleration to 100 km/h in 12.1 seconds.
The second is the Strikerї estate crossover. Dacia will use the Paris Motor Show to present this C-segment crossover in a world premiere. Thus, the brand will expand its offering with a range of multi-energy powertrains, including hybrid, tri-fuel, and LPG versions. Its starting price will be around €25,000.
What premieres are German and Korean manufacturers preparing?
Audi will present three new models to the public for the first time: the A2 e-tron, the new Q7, and the new A6 allroad. In addition, the German automaker's program is not limited solely to presentations of future vehicles. Audi intends to properly celebrate the A3's 30th anniversary at Porte de Versailles. The compact car first appeared at the Paris Motor Show in 1996.
The A2 e-tron is a compact rear-wheel-drive electric car presented in Paris on September 7. It has a motor producing 125–240 kW (170–326 hp), three battery options of 52, 61, and 84 kWh, and a range of up to 646 km.
The Audi A6 allroad has stood out among premium estates since 1999. Since then, it has occupied a niche between a classic business estate and an SUV. The new A6 allroad can boast a significantly wider stance, is available as a PHEV for the first time, and features numerous exclusive chassis and off-road functions.
While previous generations of the Allroad often differed visually from the corresponding A6 Avant only through plastic cladding and a somewhat increased ground clearance, Audi has gone much further with the new model. For the first time, the A6 allroad has a clearly pronounced wide-body design.
The body has grown by a substantial 111 millimeters in width compared with the standard A6 Avant. The most important technical feature of the A6 allroad remains its standard air suspension. Developed specifically for this model, it offers a significantly wider adjustment range—55 millimeters compared with the optional air suspension of the standard A6 Avant.
As with the regular A6 models, the Allroad will also be available as a plug-in hybrid. However, the PHEV makes its debut in the top-end A6. The combination of a 2.0-liter, 252-hp TFSI engine and an electric motor producing up to 105 kW delivers a system output of 367 hp and 500 Nm of torque. Acceleration to 100 km/h takes 5.5 seconds, while the top speed is 250 km/h.
The updated lineup presented at the 2026 Paris Motor Show also includes the recent Q4 e-tron and Q6 e-tron, as well as the sporty RS 5.
Korean manufacturer Kia will present a significant number of new models at the upcoming Paris Motor Show. Focused on electric performance and updating its hybrid lineup, the brand's program is already taking shape as a major and diverse one.
From October 12 to 18, Kia will present its entire model range at the 2026 Paris Motor Show. The manufacturer is clearly demonstrating its ambitions by bringing together the complete lineup of all-electric GT models. Visitors will be able to see the EV3 GT, EV4 GT, EV5 GT, EV6 GT, and EV9 GT side by side.
This demonstration of strength allows the brand to claim the broadest range of electric GT models on the market. These models also feature refined sporty trim and enhanced equipment.
Another major new arrival is the Kia Seltos hybrid, which will make its European debut. This stylish C-segment SUV, which enjoys significant commercial success worldwide, will be sold in France for the first time. Deliveries will begin in November 2026.
The South Korean manufacturer is bringing the story of its compact Cee'd to a close by introducing a new hybrid offering. The new Kia K4 Hybrid will also make its debut in France. With its modern design, this compact sedan heralds an обновление of the model range in the C segment. The model's commercial launch in France is scheduled for early 2027.
Who is returning to the motor show and who will be absent
The list of participants is longer than it was two years ago: according to the organisers and L'argus, both French groups—Renault Group and Stellantis—as well as Volkswagen, Skoda, Cupra, Audi, Mercedes-Benz, Smart, Volvo, Ford, Hyundai, Kia, Honda and Toyota will have their own stands.
Honda is making a grand return to the Paris Motor Show. The Japanese manufacturer, absent from the Paris event since 2018, is returning to the motor show in 2026. The exhibition will feature the Prelude, Civic, HR-V, Jazz, a Formula 1 car and even an electric mountain bike.
This return is taking place at a symbolic time. At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Honda will celebrate 60 years of its automotive business in France.
As for the cars, four models will be presented. At the 2026 Paris Motor Show, Honda will present the Prelude Advance in Racing Blue for the first time.
Alongside it, visitors will be able to see the new Civic Sport, presented in the new Meteor Grey colour. It will be equipped with an S+ shift system, developed to enhance the driving experience by imitating the behaviour of a gearbox. The brand will also present the new HR-V Sport in Crystal Red, as well as the Jazz Advance Sport.
Motorsport fans will also have a compelling reason to visit Hall 6. In Paris, Honda will present the Aston Martin Aramco Formula 1 team's AMR26.
The programme will not be limited to cars. Honda will also showcase its e-MTB prototype—an electric mountain bike presented a few days earlier at the Sea Otter Europe 2026 exhibition in Girona. With this prototype, the brand intends to demonstrate that its thinking on electrification extends to other forms of mobility. This mountain bike combines electric assistance with a sporty approach, seeking to preserve the riding pleasure that Honda values so highly.
Mercedes-Benz is also returning for the first time in eight years and will showcase three new products—the new electric C-Class will obviously be one of the models to watch. This new generation of electric vehicles boasts a WLTP range of up to 760 km, built on an 800-volt architecture.
The public will also be able to see the new Mercedes-Benz GLA for the first time. The compact SUV was presented this summer and is now available in a fully electric version with a range of up to 657 km. It will be one of the main attractions on the stand.
This year, BMW and Mini officially declined to participate in July 2026—after warning of declining profits, the group reviewed its spending. Porsche, Ferrari, Nissan and Seat are also among those absent. Toyota will only have an innovation stand in Pavilion 5.1, without a full model display.
What the Chinese manufacturers will show
There are approximately as many Chinese manufacturers in Paris as European ones, and for Chery, Omoda & Jaecoo, Lynk & Co and XPeng, this is their first Paris motor show.
In particular, Chery is preparing to take another step forward. During its first participation in the Paris Motor Show, the Chinese brand will present two models that are new to the European market.
The Chinese manufacturer will present its Q electric city car in Europe for the first time. At the same time, the hybrid Tiggo 4 will make its debut in France, with a starting price of €23,990. The brand's entire model range will also be presented in Hall 4.
This fully electric city car will be presented to the European public in Paris for the first time. Measuring 4.19 m in length, 1.81 m in width and with a wheelbase of 2.70 m, it is significantly larger than the Renault 5 E-Tech electric car. It is ready to compete in the compact-car segment.
However, the design of the Chery Q clearly leans towards an urban aesthetic, with rounded shapes and a fairly playful silhouette. Presented as a European premiere at the Paris Motor Show, Chery also emphasises the practicality of its new model.
Q has 38 storage compartments, a 375-liter boot and an additional 70-liter compartment at the front. The V2L function also allows the car's battery to be used to power external electrical devices.
The other new development is much more specific. The Tiggo 4 HEV will make its debut in France at the Paris Motor Show, with orders opening on October 12, the first day of the show.
This 4.32-meter-long B-segment SUV sits below the Tiggo 7 and Tiggo 8 models, which are already on sale in France. For its French launch, Chery highlights the Tiggo's 2.61-meter wheelbase. Its 430-liter boot is also designed for families wishing to have a relatively compact vehicle.
The equipment list is also quite comprehensive, even in the Comfort trim, with two 12.3-inch screens, dual-zone automatic climate control, keyless entry and engine start, full-LED headlights, a rear-view camera, wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, and 18-inch alloy wheels. Seven airbags and twenty driver-assistance systems are also included as standard.
Under the hood, the Tiggo 4 uses Chery Super Hybrid (CSH) technology. The system combines a 1.5-liter turbocharged petrol engine producing 143 hp with a 150 kW electric motor and a small 1.83 kWh battery. Combined output reaches 224 hp and 295 Nm of torque.
OMODA & JAECOO, a Chery Group brand, will also be present at the 2026 Paris Motor Show.
The 2026 Paris Motor Show will give OMODA and JAECOO the opportunity to present two new models to visitors. The first will be the OMODA 4, a B-segment urban crossover. This vehicle will officially go on sale in the French market at the beginning of 2027.
The OMODA 4 boasts sharp lines and pronounced angles, with a design inspired by the "MECHA" genre, well known to science-fiction fans.
Inside, the OMODA 4 offers an immersive experience. Drivers will benefit from an 8.9-inch instrument panel and a 13.2-inch central display. The Chinese manufacturer aims to emulate the world of video games as closely as possible.
Ticket prices
As already mentioned, the 2026 Paris Motor Show will begin on Monday, October 12, and run until Sunday, October 18. Ticket prices start at €20 on a weekday and €22 on a weekend day. For children, the ticket price will be €13.

China, EU agree on dialogue, cars after trade talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:23:11 UTC
22:23:11 KST

China and the European Union (EU) reached an understanding on hybrid vehicles on Friday, as the commerce chiefs of both sides concluded talks and agreed to strengthen dialogue.
The Commerce Ministry said that both sides agreed to adhere to "procedures concerning company price undertakings" of hybrid cars.
Both sides will keep exploring the possibility of lowering tariffs on certain goods within the framework of WTO rules, and continue their dialogue on market access for medical devices, the ministry said.
It added that the discussions between Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and his EU counterpart Maros Sefcovic in Beijing on  Thursday and Friday were pragmatic and productive.
The two sides were committed to maintaining trade, and to hold a further meeting in March. (AFP/Reuters)

China sees 826mn National Day domestic holiday trips
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:22:55 UTC
22:22:55 KST

The nation saw 826 million domestic tourist trips during the recent seven-day National Day holiday, with tourism spending totaling 738.38 billion yuan, the Ministry of Culture and Tourism said on Friday.
On a daily average basis, the number of domestic trips rose 6.3 percent from the eight-day National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday in 2025, while tourism spending increased 4.3 percent, according to the ministry.
The holiday witnessed a vibrant cultural scene, with 180 large-scale performances held nationwide, including 125 concerts and 55 music festivals.
Measures to boost tourism consumption have also helped expand holiday options for visitors and enhance their travel experiences.
Under a nationwide cultural and tourism consumption campaign running from late September through October, local authorities organised a variety of activities and distributed more than 310 million yuan in consumption subsidies. (Xinhua)

'Gratitude to people for continuous blessings': PM Modi hails BJP win in Assam, West Bengal bypolls
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:22:06 UTC
22:22:06 KST

NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Friday thanked voters after the BJP secured victories in byelections to two assembly constituencies in West Bengal and a Lok Sabha seat in Assam, while its ally, the All India NR Congress, won a bypoll in Puducherry.The byelections were held on Tuesday, with votes counted on Friday.“Gratitude to the people for their continuous blessings! The Lok Sabha result of Nagaon (Assam) and Assembly results of Nandigram as well as Rejinagar (West Bengal) show yet again that the people have a deep-rooted connect with the good governance agenda of BJP-NDA,” PM Modi wrote on X.
He congratulated the victorious BJP candidates and praised party workers for their hard work.“I also congratulate our valued NDA ally, the AINRC, for their win in Thattanchavady in Puducherry,” the prime minister added.PM Modi further expressed confidence that the mandate would give the BJP “added strength” as it works “tirelessly for the welfare of the people and to fulfil their aspirations for a brighter and more prosperous future.”In West Bengal, chief minister Suvendu Adhikari vacated Nandigram and chose to retain Bhabanipur, where he defeated then-chief minister Mamata Banerjee in April.
For the bypoll, the BJP fielded Hasi Rani Rath, mother of Adhikari’s aide Chandranath Rath, who was shot dead days after the party won the state for the first time.Hasi Rani Rath secured 164,427 votes, defeating Congress candidate Milan Pradhan, who polled 41,674 votes, by a margin of 122,753 votes.In Rejinagar, the bypoll was necessitated by AJUP leader Humayun Kabir’s resignation from the seat after he chose to retain Naoda. The BJP fielded Shankharavh Sarkar, who secured 129,914 votes, while AJUP candidate Golam Nabi Azad, Kabir’s son, finished second with 54,098 votes.The BJP wrested Assam’s Nagaon Lok Sabha seat from the Congress, with its candidate Devasish Sharma leading by an unassailable margin of over 1.5 lakh votes as the final result was awaited. The constituency fell vacant in February after Pradyut Bordoloi switched from the Congress to the BJP.
Puducherry’s Thattanchavady seat fell vacant after chief minister and AINRC president N Rangasamy retained Mangalam, where he also contested and won. AINRC nominee Ashok Anand secured 13,358 votes, defeating Congress nominee E Vinayagam, who finished second with 4,876 votes.
Karan Manral is a journalist at the Times of India. He covers politics, social issues, and international affairs, exploring stories that affect people’s everyday lives. He also writes explainers to make these stories easier for readers to follow.

Slovakia secures winter gas supplies through Gazprom contract — minister
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:21:35 UTC
22:21:35 KST

BRATISLAVA, October 9. /TASS/. Slovakia has secured gas supplies for the upcoming winter thanks to its active long-term contract with Gazprom, Reuters reported, citing Slovak Economy Minister Denisa Sakova.
"We have a long-term contract with Gazprom, short-term diversification contracts, and sufficient gas reserves in storage. Consumer needs for the winter season will be fully covered," Sakova was quoted as saying.
Slovak media previously reported that the country's gas storage facilities currently hold enough fuel to generate 16.8 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity. The target inventory level, capable of producing 17.5 TWh, is expected to be reached by mid-October.
Sakova also noted that Slovakia will continue to receive Russian crude oil until the end of 2027. Amid the European Union's mandate to halt such imports by the end of next year, Bratislava is seeking alternative sources and delivery routes, with negotiations currently underway with the United States.
"From 2028 onward, Slovakia will require viable alternatives to Russian oil and gas," the minister stated. "We are holding discussions on this matter at the White House. The United States is one of Slovakia's key partners in finding alternative energy sources and supply routes.".

Robert Jenrick launches scathing broadside against ‘Kensington Kemi’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:21:14 UTC
22:21:14 KST

Robert Jenrick has launched an extended attack on Kemi Badenoch, calling her part of a metropolitan elite and saying a coalition deal with the Tories would be like being “handcuffed to a zombie”.
Reform UK’s economics spokesperson repeatedly called the Tory leader “Kensington Kemi” and claimed her party was for people who moaned about the decline of Mayfair clubs and complained that they could not find Ottolenghi recipe ingredients in the shops.
He accused his former party of handing out “bungs for Belgravia” after the Conservatives said at their autumn conference that they would exempt property from inheritance tax and extend free childcare to higher earners if elected.
Jenrick’s attack on Badenoch, whose approval ratings among the public have improved, come at a time of deteriorating relations between the Conservatives and Reform. Jenrick was the target of much mockery at the Conservative conference, where he was depicted in multiple places on a satirical Bayeux tapestry of the political landscape as a crying baby. He was kicked out of the Tories in January for planning to defect.
In her conference speech, Badenoch firmly ruled out any move to “unite the right” with a deal between Reform and the Tories, questioning who would want to join with a party that made her British-born mixed-race children feel as though they were not English.
The Reform leader, Nigel Farage, downplayed the idea of a post-election pact on Thursday, saying it was “extremely unlikely”. Jenrick took a tougher line against the Conservatives in his press conference on Friday, saying they were “nothing more than a metropolitan pressure group for the wealthiest” and likening a tie-up to being “handcuffed to a zombie”.
“Kensington Kemi knows who her people are. Millionaires, not Mansfield,” Jenrick said. “The wealthy, not workers. She’s for people who complain that Mayfair clubs aren’t what they used to be. For people who struggle to find all the ingredients for that Ottolenghi recipe. And people whose lives have got almost nothing in common with my constituents in Newark.”
Jenrick made the attacks on the Tories for having “retreated into the hinterland of Kensington and Chelsea” despite a number of senior Reform figures having lived in the area. Farage rented a house in Kensington and Chelsea during the Brexit years, paid for by the leave donor Arron Banks. Nick Candy, the party’s honorary treasurer and a property billionaire, sold his £275m Chelsea mansion this year.
Last year, Farage announced a policy specifically designed to appeal to billionaires, offering them a flat £250,000 tax rate for non-dom status to attract the wealthy to London, and he bemoaned the “very rapid exodus” from central London and how it was “tough to sell a house” in Kensington and Chelsea.
Farage is famously a member of an exclusive Mayfair club, 5 Hertford Street, while the party held its fundraiser at the trendy Oswald’s in Mayfair last year.
Asked whether Reform was also the party of billionaires, Jenrick said it was focused on delivering tax cuts for 40 million middle earners.
Jenrick also faced questions regarding the suggestion by Reform figures that Badenoch could not be English because of her Nigerian heritage. He said the debate was “pretty overblown” and that it was possible to distinguish ethnicity, cultural identity and citizenship.
“Is there such a thing as the English ethnicity? Yes. Not always easy to define,” he said. “That is different from national identity. That is whether or not you ascribe to, you assimilate to, our heritage, our culture, our norms, our manners. And that is also different to whether or not you have a British passport in your bedroom drawer.”
He said he was most concerned about people who had a British passport but “do not love our country”.
Jenrick went on to defend his comments about the “Islamification” of the UK, which have now been reported to the police and the Prevent counter-radicalisation programme. He did not address the police reports, but he doubled down by saying there had been an increase in the use of sharia law, and in instances of young girls being forced to cover their faces, and churches being turned into mosques, which he said would not happen under a Reform government.

Russia views Caspian Sea shallowing as acute problem — Putin
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:21:06 UTC
22:21:06 KST

TURKMENBASHI /Turkmenistan/, October 9. /TASS/. Russia shares the opinion that Caspian Sea shrinking is one of the most acute problems, President Vladimir Putin said at the Caspian Environmental Summit.
"We share the view of the colleagues who spoke earlier that the shrinking of the Caspian Sea is currently one of the most critical challenges. Over the last 20 years, the drying up of the Caspian coastline in the Russian sector alone, according to our estimates, amounted to 20,000 square kilometers," the Russian leader said.
"Russia has to allocate substantial budget funds annually for dredging operations to support navigation," Putin noted. "The continuation of the current trends of sea level decline, which, according to our data, averages minus nine centimeters per year, poses a whole range of disastrous ecological consequences," he stressed.
Such processes are harmful for fisheries, cause coastal soil erosion, and lead to a depletion of bioresources. "This is a major threat to us all," the head of state stressed. "The shallowing adversely impacts the socioeconomic situation in the Caspian region, reduces the investment attractiveness of trans-Caspian logistics corridors, threatens to degrade the population's quality of life, and leads to job losses and other acute crisis phenomena," the Russian leader noted.
Expert research indicates climate change is the primary driver behind the Caspian Sea's depletion, Putin said.
"The rise in average annual temperatures directly affects the intensity of water surface evaporation, precipitation levels, and the inflow of feeding rivers. The shifting wind rose further worsens the situation as the previously dominant air masses from the Atlantic are being replaced by hot dry flows from Central Asia, which also sharply increases water evaporation. The combination of these factors requires from our countries to develop joint steps to preserve the Caspian Sea ecosystem," the Russian leader added.

Three years of genocide, three years of global silence
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:20:41 UTC
22:20:41 KST

“They have nowhere to return to. Look at how it looks. And by the way, the world isn’t stopping us.”
Those were the words of Israeli Minister of Finance Bezalel Smotrich at a small gathering at his home recently. Smotrich was speaking about Israel’s occupation of Southern Lebanon at that time, but he could just as easily have said the same thing about Gaza, the West Bank, or Syria.
It hardly comes as news to Palestinians to hear Smotrich talk like this. Israeli impunity has been a permanent fixture of the dynamic that has perpetuated Palestinian dispossession since long before the Nakba even happened.
But never has that impunity been so absolute as it is now, even while Israel’s image in the world, and the global public’s opinion of it, craters.
As we mark three years since the bloody October 7 attack called Operation Al-Aqsa Flood and Israel’s genocidal actions in its wake, it is important for all of us to take stock of what Palestinians, both in Palestine and in the diaspora, have been saying: that the world isn’t stopping Israel.
The three-year, ongoing genocide has answered the question many of us have asked at times: “What would I have done during the Holocaust?”
Many have answered that they would wallow in a denial, which is, in fact, a racist cover for the fact that they support the genocide.
But for a far greater number, the answer has been either indifference or a casual, “what can I do about it” shrug.
The indifference, the denial, and the support for the genocide are all rooted in the same phenomenon: the utter devaluation of Palestinian lives.
It doesn’t stop with the genocide either. While I view the producers of the controversial Israeli documentary NAZA as very noble, it is certainly the case that they are telling the world nothing Palestinians have not been saying for decades and have been screaming from the rooftops since the genocide began.
Yet, when it comes from Palestinians, no one listens. This can’t be explained merely by claiming that the aggrieved party is assumed to be biased. So-called moderates and liberals do not devalue the testimonies of African Americans, women, or migrants, let alone Ukrainians, to the same degree, although all marginalized groups experience this sort of doubt of their experience. But Palestinians are especially unheard and disbelieved.
That is a dehumanization that extends far beyond Israel and even far beyond Zionism around the world, to people who have little real stake in either. It is that widespread.
That dehumanization has been part of the Palestinian experience since the beginning of the British Mandate. But now, it combines with a level of Israeli impunity that has helped to unleash the worst parts of the settler-colonialist, nationalist movement known as Zionism.
And that dehumanization has, in fact, been a part of the process that has expanded Israeli impunity, which has grown steadily since before the Nakba.
The impunity of the Nakba brings us to the genocide in Gaza
In 1947-48, the Zionist army was able to carry out most of the dispossession of Palestinians even before declaring the independence of the Israeli state and facing the decidedly half-hearted invasion by the neighboring states.
But at that time, the expulsion of 800,000-1,000,000 Palestinians, the total erasure of entire Palestinian towns and villages, and the destruction of Palestinian life could be carried out in relative secrecy. There were no smartphones to broadcast the tragedies Palestinians were experiencing, and only a handful of international reporters were even trying to get the news out to a Western world that, in the wake of a global conflict, was not particularly interested.
To some degree, at least, Israeli impunity depended on the majority of the world’s public being unaware of what was happening. Political leaders had no such excuse, however, and this is where we see how widespread the devaluing of Palestinian life was even at that time.
By 2023, the genocide was widely broadcast. People watch it every day. Indeed, one of the few things the people of Gaza have that others do not is ubiquitous smartphone technology and sophisticated use of video testimony.
And yet, it made no difference. Yes, people saw it, and many were outraged and acted, protesting their government’s support of such atrocities. Yet in three years since the genocide began, there have been only the most cosmetic efforts to stop it, despite the public pressure.
Indeed, even Donald Trump’s order to Israel to finally stop the full-scale slaughter in September of 2025 was precipitated not by any Israeli atrocity against the civilians of Gaza but because of Israel’s attack on Palestinian negotiators in Qatar, one of Trump’s business partners. That led to Trump’s peace plan, which Hamas accepted to stop the wholesale slaughter in Gaza.
At no point did Israeli actions against the Palestinian people prompt real action against it from any quarter that had any influence over Israel.
Making impunity absolute
Israeli impunity, already a considerable factor in its treatment of the Palestinians, was now absolute.
For decades, Israel dispossessed, occupied, brutalized, and killed Palestinians with little repercussion. Yet there was at least the perception, the concern, in Israel that there was a line they could not cross. And there was evidence that there were some limits, even if those limits still allowed Israel unprecedented leeway in gradually pushing Palestinian freedom farther away.
Israeli leaders would push the envelope, walk up to the line they perceived, and step just over it, to see if they would be pushed back. For the most part, the only country they were worried about was the United States.
And sometimes the U.S. would push back, in a limited way. Jimmy Carter pressed Menachem Begin into the Camp David Accords. Ronald Reagan opened talks with the PLO. George H.W. Bush forced Israel into the Madrid Peace Conference, while his son used a threat of loan guarantees to convince Israel to alter one controversial piece of the apartheid wall it was building in the West Bank. Bill Clinton pressured Benjamin Netanyahu into signing the Hebron Agreement.
The acceleration in impunity began in earnest not under Donald Trump or “Genocide Joe” Biden, but under Barack Obama.
It happened at the very beginning of Obama’s presidency. He came into office promising a total freeze on settlements in the West Bank. He even had the public support (privately might have been quite different) of his first Secretary of State, the notoriously pro-Israel Hillary Clinton.
But his effort failed, thanks largely to the opposition of his own party leadership to the idea. Netanyahu learned from that episode that the lines that had been drawn to limit Israeli action were imaginary.
Netanyahu had halted his bombing of Gaza that began in December 2008 in deference to the incoming president and his desire to improve relations with the Arab world that had been badly damaged by George W. Bush’s invasion of Iraq. But now that he saw that the Democrats, Obama’s own party, wouldn’t back him up even in a policy explicitly designed to promote a two-state solution and ostensibly bring peace to an Israel that had just emerged from the Second Intifada, Netanyahu knew he could push the envelope even farther than he had previously imagined.
The periodic bombings of Gaza, including the use of the torturous chemical weapon, white phosphorous, the expansion of the use of Gaza as a showcase for Israel’s newest weapons, and the increasing strangulation of the Strip followed, along with gradually accelerating settlement expansion all accelerated.
Obama, discouraged, shifted his focus away from the Palestinians after that, concentrating instead on the Iran nuclear deal. Astute Palestinians—which, almost by definition, included few of PA President Mahmoud Abbas’ inner circle—recognized that their best hope for help from Washington had evaporated.
Obama’s final message to Israel—when he abstained from a toothless vote on a Security Council resolution regarding Israeli settlements—was only a final sign of his inability to take a less biased approach to Israel and Palestine.
The Trump and Biden years were the expression of the impunity that Obama had accelerated. The Palestinians were descending into near-total invisibility as Trump moved the U.S. embassy to Jerusalem and encouraged other countries to do the same. Biden labored tirelessly to reach a deal to normalize relations between Saudi Arabia and Israel, convincing Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman to lower his asking price to some vague commitment to a “plan” for a Palestinian state at some indeterminate date in the future.
Gaza starved. Protesters in the Great March of Return were shot under the pretext that they had…well, flown kites. Settlements expanded, and settler attacks grew more common and fiercer.
The only thing that concerned the United States government and its self-proclaimed Zionist President Biden was Netanyahu’s efforts to destroy Israel’s Jewish “democracy,” which threatened to further diminish Israel’s standing among Democratic voters. Palestinians simply didn’t matter, if they were even acknowledged to exist at all.
And then came October 7.
The world changes, but indifference to Palestinian life stays the same
Governments around the world expressed outrage at the attack on October 7, 2023. Initially, a few questioned the stories that were coming out, of babies being beheaded and other fantastical atrocities. Palestinian objections to the lack of substantiation of these stories were summarily dismissed.
The reality of that attack was awful enough, but dealing with reality would also have meant dealing with context. It would have meant trying to understand why Palestinians all over the world, including those who would express outrage over the killing of civilians once that was made clear, were rejoicing at the sight of their people breaking free of the open-air prison of Gaza and setting foot on a homeland from which they had been cast out and forbidden to enter for 75 years.
It would have meant grappling with the kind of reality that settler-colonial states have been forced to grapple with, usually long after it could make any real difference.
And that is why Palestinians have been thoroughly dehumanized by so many.
When we look to explanations for why governments act so impotently about Palestine, there are numerous factors that contribute. There is the pro-Israel lobby in the U.S., and less powerful counterparts in some European states. There is still the collective guilt about the Holocaust, a guilt which, if the Western states don’t make the Palestinians pay for it, they will be forced to pay the price of their own murderous antisemitism themselves. And there is the place Israel holds in a capitalist environment increasingly dependent on weapons and tech industries, in which Israel plays an outsized role.
But what about states like China, or some in the Global South? What about the Arab monarchies, who pay just enough lip service to the Palestinian cause to quiet their own domestic audiences, but are often complicit in crimes against the Palestinian people?
I have argued for years that the reason for this behavior, the reason the Israel lobby can be so successful, is that world leaders see the Palestinian people as a major threat. Not in a military sense, not even in a fully political one.
Rather, the threat that Palestinians represent is a popular one.
Many groups of people have struggled for decades, for centuries, under the yoke of one oppressive system or another. But the Palestinians are a people who had a homeland, and were forced off it, yet they have remained, refused to surrender and move on. They have also survived, while so many other Indigenous people have been killed off, assimilated, or seen their numbers drastically reduced.
Israel is far from the only settler-colonial state in the world. But it is one of the few that is still actively fighting to eliminate the Indigenous people it displaced.
Should the Palestinian people regain their homeland, build a future, and thrive there, even if only on part of it, it would invigorate decolonization and anti-oppression movements around the world. It would give hope to the impoverished and disenfranchised, dispossessed, and oppressed people in all states around the world.
This is the reason Palestinians must be dehumanized and crushed, because a Palestinian triumph would bring hope and inspiration on a scale that few other events could accomplish.
That’s why the world “isn’t stopping” Israel. It’s why the genocidal chapter that started on October 7 continues. And it’s why the rest of us absolutely must stand with the Palestinian people.

Estonia plans to add photos of pedophile offenders to criminal records database
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:20:00 UTC
22:20:00 KST

Estonia plans to add photos of pedophile offenders to criminal records database
The Ministry of Justice has sent for approval a draft law that would display document‑style photos in the criminal records database of people who have a restriction on working with children.
Displaying a photo in the criminal records database helps employers, a child's legal representative, and the Social Insurance Board ensure that the query result concerns the correct person. The change is important, for example, when a parent hires a private tutor for a child and finds the tutor's personal identification code from public sources. A photo also helps identify a person if a job applicant states or writes their personal identification code but does not present an identity document.
The restriction on working with children applies to a person who has committed a contact sexual offense against a child, such as rape.
The aim of the amendment is to protect children better than before from sexual and other dangerous offenders. Currently, employers must check at least once a year in the criminal records database whether a person working with children has a restriction on working with children.
"The easier and more convenient it is to fulfill such an obligation, the more likely employers are to actually do it," the draft states.
Checks will become automatic and more frequent
In the future, an employer will not have to enter the name and personal identification code of a person working with children into the criminal records database once a year. Instead, the system will automatically check people working with children once a month. For this, the automatic check will be linked to the employment register, and the employer must indicate which employees come into direct contact with children.
The employer will receive the result of the check as a simple yes‑or‑no answer. If an employee has a restriction on working with children, the Social Insurance Board will also be notified and will check whether the employer has complied with the restriction.
A person working with a child is someone who, due to their job or activity, comes into direct contact with a child. This means communicating with the child, guiding, teaching, caring for, counseling, or dealing with the child while providing a service.
Such people include, for example, teachers, coaches, kindergarten staff, and others whose duties require direct contact with children. A person may also be considered to be working with children if they work in an institution not intended solely for children but still come into direct contact with children due to their job.
At the same time, not everyone who encounters children is considered to be working with children. For example, a shop assistant, customer service worker, or a regular city bus driver is generally not considered a person working with children, because their job does not require direct and continuous interaction with children.
It is different, for example, for a school bus or excursion bus driver who transports a specific group of children and comes into more direct contact with them due to their job. The final assessment is made by the employer, who must consider the person's duties and their nature.
The draft notes that in practice there have been situations where people with a restriction on working with children have ended up working as school janitors or bus drivers.
Automatic checks can only cover people working in positions where they come into direct contact with children. Therefore, a person must be removed from the list of people to be checked as soon as they stop performing such work.
The records database will not become public
The ministry refers in the draft to studies showing that public sex‑offender registries have not had a positive impact on reducing repeat offenses. Some studies do indicate that a public registry may reduce the risk of first‑time offenses. According to the ministry, adding photos may help people recognize a dangerous individual and warn their close ones.
However, adding photos does not make the registry public. Queries can still be made only by persons specified in the law: employers, institutions issuing activity licenses for working with children, and a child's legal representatives.
The planned date for the law to enter into force is 1 June 2030.

Unknown Publisher

13:19:14 UTC
22:19:14 KST

Kyiv has opened its first specialized business center, which will serve as a permanent platform for developing industrial cooperation between defense companies in Ukraine and the United Kingdom.
The report comes from the Ministry of Defence of Ukraine.
The center was established with the support of the British government as part of the centennial partnership between the two countries and with the participation of the British National Armaments Director Group.
The main mission of the Kyiv Business Centre is to facilitate British companies’ entry into the Ukrainian market, particularly small and medium-sized enterprises, for which security requirements and administrative procedures previously made it difficult to operate in Ukraine.
The defense hub will provide foreign manufacturers with the opportunity to interact with Ukrainian government agencies, the innovation sector, and investors, as well as to obtain information about the current needs of the front lines.
The center’s work focuses on three key areas: industry, innovation, and investment, which will include joint development, securing funding, and scaling up production.
The British Audere Group, in a consortium with AMS Global Solutions and Hillmont Partners, has become the operator of the platform.

Tory tax break for banks has cost UK public purse £6bn, says TUC
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:18:58 UTC
22:18:58 KST

Tax cuts for big banks have deprived the UK government of £6bn in revenues, according to campaigners, who are calling on the chancellor, John Healey, to increase taxes and force lenders to pay their “fair share” in the budget.
Calculations by the Trades Union Congress (TUC), which represents unions with more than 5.3 million members across England and Wales, shows that the public purse is billions of pounds worse off as a result of tax cuts introduced under the Tory chancellor Jeremy Hunt in 2023.
The then government agreed to slash the bank surcharge – an additional levy on lenders’ profits – from 8% to 3% that year. The move was meant to offset a rise in corporation tax from 19% to 25%, after the industry argued higher taxes would put them at a competitive disadvantage compared with other big financial centres such as New York.
However, the cuts came just as lenders started reaping handsome earnings, thanks to rising interest rates. The UK’s four largest lenders – HSBC, NatWest, Barclays, Lloyds Banking Group – have now generated £200bn in pre-tax profits over the past five years.
The TUC says the 2023 cuts ultimately robbed the UK purse of tax revenues. Its analysis of HMRC corporate tax receipts shows the UK public lost out £2.3bn in 2023-24, a further £1.7bn in 2024-25, and £2bn in 2025-26 – totalling £6bn over three years.
With banks pocketing record profits, the TUC said the surcharge should now be increased beyond its pre-2023 level at the 28 October budget. That could raise up to £60bn, which could be used to cover rising household bills as part of prime minister Andy Burnham’s drive to tackle the cost of living.
“The Tories’ tax break for banks has cost the UK public purse £6bn and counting. It’s time to end it and to make sure banks pay their fair share,” the TUC’s general secretary, Paul Nowak, said.
“At a time when families are struggling with soaring energy costs, taxing banks’ booming profits to cut bills is just plain common sense. There is a mountain of evidence to suggest that banks can afford to pay more tax – not least the record £25bn bonus pool they paid out last year.
“This month’s budget is an opportunity to put things right.”
Bank bosses have been lobbying intensively against bank tax rises, after narrowly escaping higher levies during last year’s budget. Jamie Dimon, chief executive of the largest US bank, JP Morgan, warned Burnham and Healey against further levies during a meeting last month, saying it could put investment and jobs at risk.
Earlier this year, Dimon warned that he could scrap plans for a new £3bn London headquarters if the UK government became hostile to banks.
The TUC has said raising the surcharge to 16% – double the rate prior to Conservative cuts – could raise £24bn in tax revenues over the next four years. Meanwhile, a 35% bank surcharge, which would match the windfall tax rate that Conservatives imposed on energy companies, would deliver £60bn over four years. Even reversing the surcharge cuts and setting it at 8% would raise £9bn over that same period, the union body said.
“Reversing the last government’s tax cuts is the very least this government can do to claw back some of the lost billions it’s handed to banks in recent years,” said a spokesperson for campaign group Positive Money, which has also been pushing for bank tax rises at the budget. “Banks are making record profits without lifting a finger, thanks to the higher rates being paid to them, by both customers and the Bank of England.”
David Postings, the chief executive of banking lobby group UK Finance said that a strong banking sector was essential for a strong UK economy and that profitable lenders would be able to invest in better services for customers, issue more loans, and deliver “returns” – such as shareholder dividends – that supported people’s savings and pensions.
“Banks also make a major contribution to the public finances and already face a materially higher total tax rate in the UK than in other leading financial centres,” he said.
“Further tax increases would weaken the UK’s competitiveness, discourage investment and job creation, and work against the government’s ambition to deliver growth in every postcode.”
The Treasury was contacted for comment.

Special parking spaces for drivers with young children will be introduced in Ukraine — what will change
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
16:18:35 EEST
22:18:35 KST

Special parking spaces for drivers with young children will be introduced in Ukraine — what will change
Kyiv • UNN
At least 5% of parking spaces will be designated for cars with children under three years old. Drivers must have a document confirming the child’s age.
Vehicle markings, special road markings and new traffic signs — Ukraine is introducing parking rules for drivers transporting children under the age of three. This was announced by Minister of Internal Affairs Ivan Vyhivskyi, reports UNN.
The resolution developed by the Ministry of Internal Affairs to implement the relevant Law was approved by the Cabinet of Ministers of Ukraine. I am grateful to the members of the Government for their support, because this decision is primarily about the safety and comfort of families with young children
Details
According to Vyhivskyi, new identification signs for vehicles are being introduced for drivers. Appropriate markings and signs featuring an image of a baby stroller will appear in parking areas. Such spaces must account for at least 5% of the total number, but there must be at least one. It must be located no more than 50 meters from the entrance to the parking area.
It is important that drivers who mark their vehicle with this identification sign must have an electronic or paper document confirming the child’s age. This is one of the steps toward a modern traffic management and parking system. We are working to take the needs of all road users into account in detail

Skiing: Goggia to skip Sölden, 'I need to get back to feeling well'
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:18:24 CEST
22:18:24 KST

Former Olympic downhill gold
medallist Sofia Goggia said Friday she will miss the
season-opening race in Sölden on October 24, saying that she
wants to start felling well again after a virus that has laid
her low.
                                    
Bergamo-born Goggia, 33, explained this on the sidelines of the
Italian Skiing Federation (FISI) media day in Milan, discussing
her recovery from the virus that forced her to halt her training
camp in Ushuaia.
                                    
"I'm doing better; the trend is positive. I experienced a lot of
tremors and debilitating pain; my walking and speech were slowed
down, and I lacked coordination on my skis.
                                    
"I'm still tired, I missed a crucial part of my preparation, and
I have to pin all my hopes on training in America. The primary
goal right now is to get back to feeling well as a
person—especially regarding my nervous system—and to regain my
usual mental clarity so I can ski."
"I haven't set any specific goals for this season," Sofia Goggia
added at the FISI Media Day.
                                    
"I had skied well during the first week in Ushuaia. I've built a
career by patching things together after the many injuries I've
had; but those were joint injuries, where the biological healing
times can be pushed with sheer willpower. This virus affected my
nervous system a bit; it's something different. I know the
recovery process well, but I need to be mentally sharp.
                                    
"I don't have a timeline: it could be ten days, or it could be a
month and a half. Then I'll focus on specific on-snow training."
Goggia recalled moments of "alarm" caused by the virus's
symptoms.
                                    
"I never imagined I would contract a viral infection that would
stop me in my tracks like this. It caused a lot of neurological
symptoms. I was more frightened by the pain than by the tremors
or the inability to walk down stairs; I viewed the situation
more from an athlete's perspective than a personal one.
                                    
"Simply put, I had to articulate my words much more
deliberately—I couldn't find the right words, and I would lose
the thread of what I had been saying just a moment before."
In March Goggia won her first SuperG World Cup title to add to
the four downhill World Cup titles she claimed in 2018, 2021, 
2022 and 2023.
                                    
Her trophy cabinet also includes three downhill Olympic medals,
gold in 2018, silver in 2022 and bronze at Milano Cortina 2026.

====================================================================================================

Cairo commuters give their verdict on the city's new monorail
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:16:23 UTC
22:16:23 KST

Breadcrumb
Cairo's new $4.5bn monorail has commuters asking one question: is it actually worth it?
At the entrance to Station 11 of Cairo’s four-month-old monorail, near the American University in Cairo and the Future University of Egypt in New Cairo, you will see people walking up the escalator toward the monorail, while others exit and head down.
At least, that’s what it looks like at first glance.
In reality, most people skip the train entirely. Instead, the $4.5 billion project seems to be used more as a glorified crosswalk, traversed so people can avoid the traffic below.
Instead of the highly vaunted new transport system Egypt promised, how did this gleaming symbol of Egypt’s new capital become an expensive way to cross the street?
The Cairo Monorail, first announced in 2019 and opened for operation in May of this year, was meant to connect Cairo’s new administrative regions with the rest of the city and ease "traffic congestion on major roads and axes."
Instead of extending the preexisting subway system, the Monorail was "implemented in areas where metro lines and other rail transport systems are difficult to construct, and on streets with sharp horizontal curves," according to the Office of the Presidency.
The system itself is in very good shape: the stations and trains are clean and air-conditioned. It’s also completely electric, and the Egyptian government has claimed that the monorail has "energy consumption rates 30% lower than traditional electric rail systems."
The promises invited investment from businesses around the world, from Canada’s Bombardier Inc. to Egypt’s Orascom Construction and the Arab Contractors, as well as the United Kingdom’s official export credit agency UK Export Finance.
Not for everyone
Although use is limited, problems are more prevalent. The train cars remain sparsely occupied; even four months after it fully opened, some people still rely on the system.
Habiba, a 20-year-old from downtown Cairo, rode the monorail to get to her internship with the Abu Dhabi Bank this summer.
"Uber wasn't a choice for me because it was extremely expensive," Habiba tells The New Arab. "And the buses are kind of random," as she put it, leaving the monorail as her preferred option.
During parts of this year's World Cup, the government removed the fee for tickets to facilitate travel for those coming to watch it on the big screen at Cairo Stadium, which Habiba happily took advantage of.
Yet, despite it being cheaper than Uber and other ride-sharing apps, the monorail’s sparse stations and lack of connecting metro stops in New Cairo make it unusable for many.
Marwan, who lives in the New Administrative Capital, still takes Cairo’s popular minibuses to his work at the Air Force Hospital in New Cairo, which is cheaper than the monorail, even though there is a stop directly at the hospital. When travelling elsewhere, he still avoids the monorail and feels that service is inadequate
"The monorail is limited. I don’t like it," he shares.
In many cities around the world, transportation networks are connected to allow access across the city; if one metro line doesn’t reach a destination, switching to another line brings the commuter closer to their destination.
But in New Cairo, there are no connecting lines to the monorail. Only once you reach Nasr City in Northeast Cairo is a metro available.
Taking a bus off the monorail, in addition to being a hassle and another payment, can be dangerous.
Alyaa, a student at the American University in Cairo from the New Administrative Capital, tells The New Arab, "There are lots of accidents," around where the buses stop at the monorail station near her home.
The lack of bus stops around the monorail entrances, which forces buses to haphazardly pull over on the sides of very busy streets, is a likely culprit. Others, too, reported erratic driving and parking patterns by buses near the stations.
Comfort is also an important factor in choosing whether to take the monorail. One woman who works in the New Administrative Capital as a maid said, "I already pay the same price of the monorail to get to… [the] house, but I would rather go through the transportation I’m familiar with."
For others, cost is a significant factor in their choice of transportation. A public bus typically costs 9 Egyptian Pounds (EGP), and a minibus is 14 EGP, while the monorail can range from 20 to 80 EGP, depending on distance.
Ultimately, the money saved may outweigh the monorail's fixed schedule and cleanliness.
The cost of disconnection
It wasn’t supposed to be this way.
The new capital, estimated to cost around $58 billion, is one of the most expensive city-building projects in history.
If the Egyptian government wants to ensure connectivity across the city, it needs massive infrastructure projects that offer easy, inexpensive access to the capital's disparate parts.
Designed to carry 45,000 riders an hour, the monorail’s sparse usage means that, no matter how nice New Cairo and the New Administrative Capital become, movement to the newer areas of Cairo is likely to remain limited.
A geographically split Cairo, in which only the wealthy can easily travel across the city, is a recipe for disaster.
Yet this reality is becoming increasingly likely, as public transport cannot connect the city's disparate sections.
Although expansions are planned, it remains to be seen whether they will ease the city’s traffic burden.
As Egypt’s debt reaches $164.8 billion as of June 2026, the monorail can’t afford to be a wasted investment.
Yet anyone standing near the entrance at rush hour can see that, despite President Sisi calling the monorail a "major milestone," the system remains, at best, a glorified crosswalk.
Joe Zimbler is an independent journalist and researcher covering migration, displacement, conflict, and politics across the Middle East and North Africa. His reporting draws on field research and interviews across the region, with a particular focus on the experiences of migrants and displaced communities

France student riots spiral into nationwide chaos
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:16:19 UTC
22:16:19 KST

What started as a strike over staff shortages in a high school in a Parisian suburb on September 17 has descended into violence across France after high school students joined their teachers on the picket lines.
Now entering their third week, the nationwide protests have led to thousands of arrests and over 1,000 injuries, mostly among pupils.
Rights groups, unions and students have accused authorities of using disproportionate force.
Following an October 5 incident in which a teenage protester lost a hand after an officer threw a stun grenade at him, French police suspended the use of the devices, with President Emmanuel Macron calling an emergency meeting as violence escalates.
The unrest highlights deep-seated frustration with systemic issues in France’s education system, including teacher shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating infrastructure and regional inequality — compounded by proposed budget cuts.
"The education authority is not investing enough in the suburbs. It's classist and racist," said one student demonstrator.
According to Education Ministry data, nearly 10% of classroom hours in public secondary schools went unstaffed during the 2024–2025 academic year.

Missing Israeli hiker found dead on Greece's Mount Olympus after nearly three weeks

The body of Ami Yogev, a 46-year-old Israeli man from Modi'in who had been missing for approximately two and a half weeks, was found on Mount Olympus in Greece. He is believed to have fallen from a considerable height.
His body was located by a volunteer team from the Israeli rescue organization Haverim Mechaltzim.
"We are extremely busy with operations on the ground. Our volunteer team is working in difficult conditions and preparing for nightfall," the organization said.
Yogev was last heard from on September 20, when he spoke with his mother, Shosh Debi.
"At 4 p.m., I sent him a message. He saw it but didn't reply, and since then there's been only one check mark. His phone is unavailable," she said two weeks ago.
Debi said her son had made a last-minute decision to fly from Israel to Athens.
"He was in touch with me from the moment he landed in Athens. He contacted me every day and told me he was planning to climb Mount Olympus," she recalled.
"He spoke to me during the climb and sent me photos. He also spoke to a friend and sent him pictures. After sending a photo showing that he was on his way to the summit, he stopped responding."

Unions call regional transport strike, threaten weekly walkout
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Regional bus services across the Netherlands will be heavily disrupted on Wednesday, after the FNV and CNV unions called a nationwide 24-hour strike in a dispute over a new pay and conditions deal.
If Wednesday’s strike does not shift the employers, the unions say they will hold an action day every week, and will only announce the dates shortly beforehand. Earlier this month they said they were considering weekly strikes in the run-up to Christmas.
Some 13,000 workers, mainly bus drivers, are covered by the public transport collective agreement, which expired on July 1. Staff at Arriva, EBS, Qbuzz, Keolis, Transdev and RET’s regional services are involved. City transport in Amsterdam, Rotterdam and The Hague is not affected.
Talks broke down after eight rounds of negotiations. This week an ultimatum to the employers’ organisation VWOV expired without a response.
“Employers are holding on to drastic cuts in working conditions,” FNV negotiator Marijn van der Gaag said in a statement. “In doing so, they are forcing their staff to take action.”
The unions say employers want to reduce sick pay, add more unpaid breaks to shifts and give staff less say over their rosters. Rosters are currently fixed about eight days in advance, and employers want to cut that to four days or less, Van der Gaag said.
The FNV wants a 6% pay rise. The CNV is calling for 9.5% over two years, as well as better arrangements for older workers and faster access to permanent contracts.
“We will not let employers sabotage the action by drawing up emergency rosters at the last minute,” CNV negotiator Niels Rook said, explaining why dates will not be announced in advance.

EU represented by von der Leyen's right-hand at Ukraine peace talks, sources say
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:14:50 UTC
22:14:50 KST

Editor's note: This story has been updated to clarify that European, NATO, U.S. and Ukrainian officials are taking part in peace negotiations.
BRUSSELS, Belgium — The European Commission is representing the EU at the latest round of Ukraine peace talks on Oct. 9, with Commission President Ursula von der Leyen's chief of staff, Bjoern Seibert representing the bloc, diplomatic sources confirmed to the Kyiv Independent.
The question of who represents the EU at peace talks, or if it is even represented at all, has roiled the bloc repeatedly, even as Brussels is clear that Russia is not serious about ending its war of aggression.
President Volodymyr Zelensky told journalists on Oct. 8 that the peace talks would include U.S. officials as well as Europeans and NATO.
Two EU officials said Seibert would be representing the European Commission at those talks, alongside the National Security Advisers of the E3 countries: France, Germany, and the U.K.
For the Commission, the talks are simply another part of the "constant work with Ukraine to strengthen their position while also trying to secure peace," a senior EU official familiar with the peace talks told the Kyiv Independent.
That's "even more important right now as we are seeing Russia's increasing attacks," the official added.
But the EU has never been able to agree on who has the right to represent it in peace negotiations.
Earlier in 2026, the idea of a dedicated EU peace envoy dominated discussions in Brussels, driven by speculative reporting from the EU's main media outlets.
There was a debate over whether the EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, should take on the role or for EU countries to pick a specific representative.
Then it transpired that Pedro Lourtie, the chief of staff of European Council President Antonio Costa, had opened a diplomatic backchannel to Moscow without first telling all EU countries, to which several countries have told the Kyiv Independent they took offense.
And then some EU countries objected strongly to the idea that the E3 countries could represent the bloc in peace talks, partly because France and Germany were too lax with Russia in the past, and partly because the U.K. is not even a member country of the bloc.
Seibert, representing the EU, might similarly receive some blowback from national capitals.
Diplomats from three EU countries confirmed to the Kyiv Independent that they were unaware of Seibert's role as a representative.
And the idea of von der Leyen and her chief of staff concentrating power around themselves is an oft-repeated topic on the Brussels media scene, and beyond.
However, the senior EU official aware of the peace talks notes that "there is no set way this works, it's rather ad hoc how these things happen both with Ukraine and the U.S."
And Seibert "frequently debriefs to ambassadors," they added.
Separately, another high-ranking EU official described a format that is "a little bit established" for peace talks during a briefing with journalists.
"That's now being, again, replicated in Miami as we speak," they said.
And at least one national diplomat does not see Seibert participating in the talks as a problem at all, believing that U.S. President Donald Trump has a positive view of von der Leyen.
"Kallas has done a great job being vocal about the right things, and she is doing a great job, but in difficult negotiations, you have to choose your negotiator to match the other side," the diplomat told the Kyiv Independent.

NEET cancellation despite security overhaul exposes gaps in NTA reforms: House panel
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:13:47 UTC
22:13:47 KST

The NTA's 2024-25 annual report recorded 474 court cases, including 356 concerning NEET-UG 2024. The panel said restoring confidence required "consistent, transparent, and two-way communication", rather than engagement largely restricted to portals and notifications.
NEW DELHI: Move NEET-UG to computers, build secure question banks and invest NTA's accumulated surplus in government-run test centres: a parliamentary panel has sought a sweeping overhaul of NTA after NEET-UG 2026 had to be cancelled and conducted afresh despite biometric checks, mobile jammers and AI-monitored CCTV. After the 2024 controversies, it questioned whether security upgrades alone can safeguard examinations.The parliamentary standing committee on education, chaired by Mukul Wasnik, in its 382nd report presented on Friday, said the cancellation despite strengthened safeguards demonstrated the need for "greater procedural and institutional reforms". Its 35 observations and recommendations include an independent mechanism to audit examination security, investigate candidates' grievances and report directly to the education ministry.Acknowledging that NTA conducts examinations involving around 1.2 crore candidates annually, the panel welcomed reforms introduced since 2024, including biometric authentication and coordination with states. However, it flagged structural weaknesses in staffing, accountability, outsourcing and transparency, arguing that rebuilding public trust required more than new surveillance measures.The scale of disputes has been substantial. The NTA's 2024-25 annual report recorded 474 court cases, including 356 concerning NEET-UG 2024.
The panel said restoring confidence required "consistent, transparent, and two-way communication", rather than engagement largely restricted to portals and notifications.The committee found that 16 of NTA's 39 sanctioned posts were vacant, a 41% shortfall. Existing positions are filled through deputation, limiting continuity in specialised work. It recommended permanent recruitment of experts in psychometrics, examination security, technology and logistics, while discouraging appointments to the director general's post as an additional charge.It also questioned NTA's legal status as a registered society, pointing out that it does not lay its annual report before Parliament and faces less scrutiny than a statutory body. The committee sought a framework ensuring parliamentary accountability.Private examination centres had "often proved to be a weak link in examination security", the report observed. It called for government-owned centres, bringing logistics in-house, and a national registry of blacklisted vendors to prevent disqualified firms from securing contracts elsewhere.On transparency, the panel recommended UPSC-style disclosure of NEET results, noting that centre-wise data released following Supreme Court directions in 2024 had enabled public scrutiny. It also flagged the absence of an official public record of paper leaks, FIRs and investigations.
The education ministry told the panel that no paper leak had occurred in an NTA examination from 2017 to 2025, despite malpractice and disruptions. The report noted that this assertion was "at variance with the opinion of some Members of the Committee", without concluding that the ministry's claim was false. It sought a publicly accessible account of examination irregularities and investigations.Backing a phased shift of NEET to computer-based testing, the committee sought government infrastructure in underserved areas and an independently audited normalisation method explained before implementation. It also suggested considering compensation for candidates affected by administrative cancellations and time-bound grievance redressal.
