The investigation revealed that the fishmeal industry also contributes to geopolitical tensions.
For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity. In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal, after a fisher was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fishmeal boat. Since the mid-1970s, Morocco has militarily occupied Western Sahara, a presence that more than 10 EU Court of Justice rulings and various UN resolutions have deemed illegal. Still, Moroccan ships routinely fish in Western Saharan waters, turning their illegal catch into fishmeal in Western Saharan plants, then exporting it to farms globally labeled as Moroccan. A violent clash over trucks, many of them carrying this fish and fishmeal out of Western Sahara, led to the collapse of a 29-year ceasefire between the countries in 2020. As recently as 2024, a Western Saharan fishmeal plant supplied fish oil to a French importer named S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils, which advertises supplements for animal feed on its website, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that maps seafood supply chains. S.A.S. Ch. Daudruy Van Cauwenberghe & Fils did not respond to a request for comment.
Read moreThe Saya de Malha Bank, a 'forgotten ecosystem' in need of protection
France’s greatest exposure to these problems comes less from home-grown salmon than from the more than €6 billion worth of seafood the country imports annually, including shrimp, trout, tilapia, and other forms of fish that rely heavily on fishmeal and fish oil. For example, shrimp raised on farms in Ecuador and sold at major grocers in France such as E.LeClerc, Cora, and Carrefour is fed fishmeal from plants throughout Latin America that have been tied to at least five worker deaths, 20 cases of illegal fishing, and over a half dozen instances of civil unrest from neighbours protesting the stench from fishmeal factories, the investigation found. Carrefour Group, which also owns Cora, said it was immediately launching an investigation into the issues concerning its supply chain and “will take all necessary measures in the event of confirmed non-compliance", which could include the exclusion of sources of supply “that do not meet our ethical and environmental standards". E.Leclerc did not respond to a request for comment.
More than sixty percent of the salmon eaten in France comes from farms in Norway, which rely heavily on imported fish feed made from wild-caught fish. The feed raising this salmon is linked to a range of documented impacts, including food insecurity in Western Africa, pollution from waste and chemicals, and the spread of parasites and disease to wild fish populations. A 2024 Science Advances review found that about 87 percent of global fishmeal goes to aquaculture, compared with roughly seven percent to pigs and about five percent to poultry.
The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden from the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, in particular as feed for fish, chickens, and pigs. The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets. For example, less than 30 percent of the fleet had publicly available location information, and less than 25 percent had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.
Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the vessels in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species. At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths. The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.
“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Pauly. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Natural food web 'now shaped by industrial design'
For most of human history, we ate what ecosystems produced on their own: wild fish, grazing animals, and crops grown for people. Livestock survived largely on grass and agricultural leftovers that humans didn’t eat. Today, we do something different: We grow or catch food that people could eat and feed it to animals instead, especially in industrial livestock and fish farming. These calories are converted before they’re consumed.
Read morePosidonia meadows: Lungs of the seas at risk
This global transformation has rewired the trophic chain, turning farms and oceans into engineered calorie-processing systems. The natural food web, consisting of who eats what and how energy moves from plants to animals to humans, is no longer mainly determined by ecosystems. It’s now shaped by industrial design. Animals have become less like savings accounts that turn waste into food, and more like biological factories steered by globally traded feed commodities such as soy and fishmeal. Roughly 90 percent of the catch used to produce fishmeal globally is edible for humans, according to a 2017 study published in the Fish and Fisheries journal. Most fishmeal plants around the world rely on whole fish rather than processing waste or inedible byproducts, further intensifying local protein scarcity.
The science of animal feed – combining corn, soy, grains, and ingredients like fishmeal to raise livestock faster, more efficiently, and at a larger scale – has been central to the rise of modern civilisation. Techniques of animal husbandry emerged roughly 12,000 years ago in the so-called Fertile Crescent, a region stretching from Mesopotamia to Egypt. Alongside innovations such as irrigation and the plough, the domestication of livestock enabled humans to build stable food systems, settle permanently, and eventually develop cities. As farming shifted from grazing animals on open land to penning them, humans assumed responsibility for providing balanced diets, an early precursor to today’s industrial feed systems.
In her 2021 book The Fishmeal Revolution, Kristin A. Wintersteen traces how the Humboldt Current – a cold, nutrient-rich upwelling system along the Pacific coast of South America – was reimagined as a protein mine. That shift, she argues, turned Peru into a global fishmeal superpower, responsible for roughly a quarter of worldwide production. Fishmeal became a critical input fueling the post-World War II expansion of industrial chicken and hog farming, and later aquaculture, particularly in northern Europe and the United States. Since then, this model spread far beyond Peru, including to West Africa and Southeast Asia.
Modern aquaculture does have benefits. Fish farming provides millions of people with year-round access to affordable protein. In India, for example, aquaculture is a crucial source of jobs, especially for women. In Bangladesh, fish farming has driven an overall decline in the price of fish, making it more accessible for lower-income households. Even accounting for feed ingredients like soy and fishmeal, and transportation to the US, certain farmed fish, including tilapia and Atlantic salmon, emit less greenhouse gas per pound than beef or pork.
Read moreForced labour, disease and conflict: The hidden side of industrial fishing in Saya de Malha
Harvesting bivalves, like clams, oysters, scallops, and mussels, is an especially sustainable type of aquaculture, since these species do not require feed. This kind of farming also has a very low carbon footprint and produces shells that can function as a form of carbon capture, according to a 2020 paper by Nature Food. As of 2022, roughly a third of global aquaculture did not require external feed inputs. France is the European Union’s second-largest producer of farmed seafood by volume, behind Spain, with bivalves accounting for nearly 80 percent of what the country grows.
The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fishmeal and fish oil, and especially on the use of whole fish or fish that people can eat. However, as aquaculture overall grows, so too does demand for fishmeal. The total amount of global fishmeal production is predicted to rise by nearly 10 percent, mostly from trimmings, between 2022 and 2032, according to the UN’s Food and Agriculture Organization. Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson from IFFO, the international fishmeal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system". She added that her organisation’s “role is not to advise which markets should use fishmeal and fish oil". “Sustainability frameworks won’t work if they ignore real-world economics,” she said, and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat".
France has not only been a consumer of farmed seafood. It has also tried to help find alternatives to fishmeal. In northern France, inside a vast warehouse, millions of mealworm larvae wriggled in stacked trays at Ynsect, a company that promised to mass-produce insect protein as a replacement for fishmeal in livestock and aquaculture feed. When the firm broke ground in 2021 on what was billed as the world’s largest insect farm, France’s agriculture minister hailed it as a symbol of the country’s “reconquest of protein sovereignty". Investors poured more than half a billion dollars into the company.
Read moreIn the Saya de Malha Bank, sharks are being hunted to extinction for their fins
But the fix proved harder than the pitch. By 2022, Ynsect had suffered more than $105 million in losses, largely because demand from feed buyers remained weak. In 2023, the company said it would shift away from the lower-margin business of feed for fish and farm animals, focusing instead on higher-end pet food markets. Its retreat illustrated a broader problem with alternatives to fishmeal: Even when a substitute looks promising in theory, it frequently struggles with cost, nutrition, and scale. Alternatives often lack the full range of nutrients that support the growth of farmed fish, especially omega-3. Certain “green” options, like insect meal, are expensive, and there has been limited interest among feed companies to pay a premium for them as a result.
Insects, moreover, turned out not to be as circular a solution as advertised. One of the industry’s main selling points was that larvae could be raised on waste. But in the European Union, disease-prevention rules largely bar insect producers from feeding them household food waste, manure, or catering scraps. Instead, most producers must rely on feed-grade crops. As a result, a sector promoted as a way to ease pressure on oceans has, in many cases, ended up competing with people and livestock for the same agricultural resources. The lesson from Ynsect was not that replacing fishmeal is impossible. It was that there is no easy substitute waiting in the wings.
Forced labour and land appropriation
For now, the pattern persists: Wild fish are caught and rendered into feed, while the costs of this production are left elsewhere. And reporting across several continents and oceans showed just how varied those costs can be. In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks while demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal. In Russia, fish processing workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.
The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labour and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. In 2025, France imported more than $124 million worth of seafood from China, which is rapidly expanding its aquaculture industry. China now raises more than four times the amount of fish it catches. One of the fastest-growing regions in this boom is China’s mountainous and desert inland west, particularly Tibet and Xinjiang, two regions known for intense political repression.
In Tibet, the Chinese government has relocated roughly half a million Tibetans, leveling villages and monasteries for development projects such as hydroelectric dams and fish farms. This effort often uses coercive tactics, including repeated home visits, threats of criminal prosecution, and warnings that utilities could be cut off for those who refused to move, according to a 2024 Human Rights Watch report. In response to these sorts of policies, at least 169 Tibetans have set themselves on fire, typically on camera, outside police stations, monasteries, or public squares. In Xinjiang, more than a million people have been held in detention camps, and the government has engaged in large-scale land seizures, forced sterilizations, and criminal penalties for speaking native languages or practicing religious and cultural traditions.
The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of farmed seafood annually, much of which is exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. China’s effort to promote fish farming in Tibet and Xinjiang is partly facilitated by severe state repression, including the widespread appropriation of land, intense police surveillance, and the incarceration of tens of thousands of local residents. The United States bans all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labor. No such law exists for Tibet. EU law, which applies in France, does not single out China but prohibits products made with forced labor from being placed or made available on the EU market, including imports.
Sustainability smokescreens
As the production of seafood has become more globalised, its supply chains have stretched longer, and it has become tougher for consumers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally. Most grocers who sell seafood are in the dark as well because tracking is difficult and costly. Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said this is partly because grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. The other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”
Where government regulators have proven lacking in ensuring that supply chains are free from unsustainable, illegal, or unethical practices, industry-led certification programs have sought to fill the gap. Critics say these programmes serve more as a sustainability smokescreen, giving downstream customers a way to avoid looking deeper into their supply chains. The programmes generally focus on environmental crimes, while mostly overlooking labour abuses on ships. Their biggest weakness, according to researchers, is that they do not actually track seafood fully, which results in false reassurances for consumers.
Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at the strategic litigation non-profit group Corporate Accountability Lab, said that on land – at processing plants or on farms – certification programmes rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the guarantees given by managers at the factories. Instead, the programmes frequently alert companies before inspectors show up, which gives them a chance to clean up the scene so there are no violations. At sea, these programmes also often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors directly visit and check conditions offshore on vessels, where crimes are most common. Certification programmes are rife with conflicts of interest, since they are typically funded by the companies that they are supposed to police, Brudney added.
The various organisations that make up the certification industry emphasize that each plays its own role and cannot be held accountable for others’ responsibilities. For example, Devan Meserve, a spokesperson for The Global Seafood Alliance, which runs a programme called Best Aquaculture Practices, said that her organisation represents the “most comprehensive programme for farmed seafood", partially because it covers the “entire aquaculture production chain". Protecting workers on the fishing vessels that supply feed mills is, however, an “immense challenge", she noted, because audits occur strictly at port and do not witness harvest conditions. Meserve added that her organisation helps the industry counter illegal and overfishing by requiring feed mills to source most of the fish they use in fishmeal or fish oil from fisheries accredited by certification programmes like MarinTrust and Marine Stewardship Council.
Partly bolstered by these certification programmes, seafood companies routinely make marketing claims about the ethics and sustainability of their seafood. Often, these claims fail to reckon with crimes or social concerns further up their supply chains, including on the ships or plants that produce the feed for the fish farms. This disconnect is creating growing legal risk for seafood companies and grocers. Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies across six US jurisdictions. The legal complaints focused on a common pattern: marketing claims that portrayed products as sustainable or ethically sourced, paired with supply chain evidence that suggested otherwise. Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable", “eco-friendly", “all-natural", “wild-caught,” and “from the coast of Maine", as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards.
In at least four cases, the use of fishmeal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labour on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics. During this same period, seafood companies have paid more than $2 million in settlement fees to resolve false-advertising cases. The Outlaw Ocean investigation assessed more than 800 seafood companies that made marketing claims comparable to – or stronger than – those cited in the lawsuits and found that over half of the companies had documented crimes or concerns within their supply chains.
Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with the Canadian sustainable seafood group SeaChoice, said many industries have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains. She cited sweatshop garments, blood diamonds, and fair-trade coffee as examples. Seafood, she said, has been slower to face that kind of scrutiny. But as the world searches for more protein and leans further into aquaculture, that may change, particularly if more governments begin restricting imports tied to illegality or unsustainable practices. “That’s when investors will begin to see material, not just reputational, risk,” she said, “and companies will have to adjust".
The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.
The Outlaw Ocean Project is a non-profit journalism organisation based in Washington DC that produces investigative stories about human rights, labour and environmental concerns on the two thirds of the planet covered by water. The organisation is run by Ian Urbina, an award-winning journalist who used to work for The New York Times.
Most of the stories are reported at least partially at sea. In the United States, the group publishes its stories in various news outlets, including the New Yorker, NBC News, The Atlantic and The Washington Post. The reporting is also regularly translated into other languages, particularly French and Spanish, and broadcast in partnership with dozens of foreign newspapers, magazines, radio and television outlets.

Bulgaria Rules Out Revising Conditions for North Macedonia’s EU Path
Bulgarian Foreign Minister Velislava Petrova said Bulgaria was not involved in any consultations aimed at revising the commitments North Macedonia made as part of its path toward European Union membership.
Petrova made the statement during parliamentary questioning at the National Assembly about the current state of relations between Sofia and Skopje and North Macedonia’s EU integration.
The minister rejected claims that Bulgaria was discussing or considering changes to the conditions and obligations already agreed upon by North Macedonia. She said Sofia’s position remained unchanged, with implementation of the commitments made in 2022 representing the only available route for the neighboring country to advance toward EU membership.
Petrova stressed that Bulgaria was not introducing additional demands beyond the established European framework, but was insisting that existing agreements be strictly observed and that the rights of Bulgarians in North Macedonia be guaranteed.
During parliamentary control, Petrova defended the consistency of Bulgaria’s foreign policy, saying lasting good neighborly relations and mutual trust could be established only through concrete action and fulfillment of Skopje’s commitments.

Latvia must have one of most efficient judicial systems in Europe - Kulbergs  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:54 UTC
22:00:54 KST

RIGA - Latvia must have one of the five most efficient judicial systems in Europe, Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs (United List) said Friday at the conference "The Court Beyond the Codes: The Role of the Supreme Court in the Development of the State and Society".
He pointed out that it is not the government’s role to tell the courts how to rule, but rather to ensure that the courts have the necessary resources and personnel.
At the same time, the prime minister said that he sees every day how court rulings are changing the country. Meanwhile, in the recent Saeima elections, the people have spoken in favor of change. Kulbergs pointed out that if there is a desire for change, it must also take place in the economy, and the economy must be the top priority for the next 4-8 years.
"For this to happen, investment is needed. For there to be investment, the key is a solid foundation - a fair and swift trial. I emphasize: a swift trial!" said the prime minister.
The politician cited the latest data on the trials of corruption cases as an example, noting that, on average, such cases take three years to be heard in the first instance.
Likewise, he said, for companies, the specific outcome of a court decision may not be decisive, but the speed at which the decision is reached is crucial, because during the proceedings a company may go bankrupt and disappear, and then, in the end, the whole process would be pointless.
"An effective court system is the foundation of the economy. If we have a swift and fair court system, with an emphasis on speed, then that is the key foundation for promoting competitiveness and entrepreneurship," Kulbergs emphasized.
Speaking about security, the prime minister noted that we are living in a time of hybrid operations targeting Latvia, sanctions evasion, and information operations. The rule of law serves as a line of defense in these circumstances. A country where the courts work quickly and fairly is less vulnerable, he noted.
The prime minister also emphasized that court decisions must be understandable and well-explained.
"If we want real change in the country - the change voters have voted for - then that change must also take place in the courts. And Latvia must be among the five most effective judicial systems in Europe. That must be our goal. Just as I have said about public administration," Kulbergs noted, adding that technology and artificial intelligence can certainly help achieve this speed.
Following Kulbergs’ speech, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court asked to meet with him, to which the prime minister replied with a laugh, "Only if we are going to talk about speed".
As previously reported, the conference is attended by judges - senators, presidents of regional courts and district (city) courts, judges from the Constitutional Court and the General Court of the European Union, as well as chief justices and judges from 14 European countries.
Also participating in the conference are faculty members from the University of Latvia, Faculty of Law and other faculties, officials from the judicial system, representatives from several ministries, as well as representatives from the Foreign Investors’ Council in Latvia.

Number of passengers served at Riga Airport remains flat in January-September  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

RIGA - Riga Airport served 5.32 million passengers in the first nine months of this year, which is the same as during the respective period last year, the airport informed LETA.
In the first nine months of this year, the airport handled 48,800 flights, which is 2 percent more than during the same period a year ago, while the volume of air cargo handled increased by 46 percent to 20,700 tons.
The airport notes that the proportion of transit and transfer passengers in the first nine months of this year has increased from 20 percent to 22 percent compared to the same period last year.
In September 2026, Riga Airport served 623,400 passengers, which is two percent more than in July 2025. This past July, 25 percent of passengers used Riga as a connecting airport.
In September of this year, Riga Airport handled 623,400 passengers and 5,693 flights, which is on par with last year’s levels. Meanwhile, cargo traffic continued to grow in September, reaching 1,997 tons, a 19 percent increase compared to September of last year. The average load factor in September remained stable at 78 percent.
The airport added that Latvia’s national airline airBaltic, carried 4 percent more passengers in the first three quarters of this year than in the same period last year, Polish airline LOT, by increasing flight frequency on the Warsaw-Riga route, has increased its passenger numbers by 21 percent since the beginning of the year, while the number of passengers served by Turkish Airlines in Riga has increased by 10 percent, and Finnair served 9 percent more. Meanwhile, Irish low-cost airline Ryanair served 17 percent fewer passengers in the first nine months of this year than in the same period last year.
As reported, Riga Airport handled 7.111 million passengers last year, which is at the same level as in 2024. but nine percent less than in 2019, or before the Covid-19 pandemic.
The airport handled 63,155 flights last year, which is about as many as in 2024, while handling of air cargo increased by seven percent year-on-year to 20,147 tons.
Riga Airport is the largest air traffic hub in the Baltic countries.

Klaipėda Port showcases the future of smart operations with a private 5G network trial and design  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:52 UTC
22:00:52 KST

Trials of a private 5G network at Klaipėda Port in Lithuania have successfully concluded, marking a key milestone in defining the port’s digital future. Santa Monica Networks and Latvian telecommunications provider LMT (LMT Group) have completed the comprehensive design phase for a potential port-wide private network and demonstrated concrete, practical applications directly to port company executives, illustrating how 5G technology can optimize daily workflows.
According to Mindaugas Žiūkas, Director of Santa Monica Networks, as the port increasingly digitizes its operations, reliable connectivity is becoming crucial as the foundation for a growing number of machines, devices, and daily processes, not just for human communication. "Numerous processes take place simultaneously at the Port of Klaipėda, making it clearly evident where technology can deliver practical benefits, such as boosting operational efficiency, automating more processes, and reliably managing machinery and data. For us, as a strategic IT partner, this is one of the most significant projects of recent years and an opportunity to leverage our expertise to help modernize the port that connects Lithuania to the world," said M. Žiūkas during the event.
Autonomous systems demonstrate private 5G applications
Executives and IT specialists from companies operating at the Port of Klaipėda attended the demonstration. Santa Monica Networks, LMT, and their technology partners showcased specific private 5G use cases in a real-world port environment and discussed with port representatives how these solutions could further modernize the port.
Atlas demonstrated its autonomous drone-in-a-box solution, combining AtlasNEST with the AtlasPRO unmanned aerial system to enable persistent remote monitoring and autonomous operations. The integrated system enables remote deployment, operation, recovery, and recharging of the drone, supporting inspection, situational awareness, and monitoring missions in complex and hard-to-reach port environments.
LVR Flote, a provider of port technical services in Latvian ports, demonstrated its uncrewed surface vessel, the Otter USV, which is used for hydrographic surveys of the harbor bed. LVR Flote also presented a tool to improve the transfer and processing of large survey datasets and a data pre-processing tool that applies initial filtering before detailed quality control by hydrographers. Combined with 5G connectivity, these solutions are intended to reduce manual work, shorten the time between data collection and analysis, and support faster operational decision-making in ports.
“At LVR Flote, we see strong potential in using digitalization and data more effectively to support better, data-based decisions – whether in fleet management, hydrographic surveys or other operational areas. For any digital solution to work in practice, safe, reliable and secure connectivity is essential, especially in critical infrastructure such as ports,” said Kaspars Ozoliņš, Member of the Board of LVR Flote.
According to Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority, technological development is crucial for the port not only in terms of modernization but also regarding competitiveness.
“Today’s market rewards those who are fast, reliable, flexible, and resilient. A private 5G network could unlock even more opportunities for the Port of Klaipėda by enabling the implementation of advanced solutions, process automation, and increased operational capacity, while ensuring uninterrupted connectivity and secure data transmission, even in extraordinary situations. Resilient, modern, and flexible – that is how we envision the future of the Port of Klaipėda, and that is the port we are building every day,” says Algis Latakas, Director General of the Klaipėda State Seaport Authority.
Increasing use of digital solutions in port operations
A private 5G network would give the port greater control over connectivity management. The port could independently decide which processes are prioritized, which devices can connect to the network, and keep certain sensitive operational data within its own infrastructure. This contributes to an increase in security, and would help ensure controlled communication and coordinated action during incidents.
According to Aigars Runcis, Director of the Ventures Department at LMT, the solutions demonstrated in Klaipėda represent only a fraction of the potential applications for private 5G technology in a port environment. "Private 5G is not connectivity for its own sake – it is the foundation for smarter, safer, and more efficient port operations. Demonstrations in Klaipėda show how unmanned systems and mission-critical communications can already deliver practical benefits, while the same connectivity platform can support a wide range of other solutions as the port ecosystem evolves. Our goal is to help ports build infrastructure that enables continued digitalization and automation, while boosting operational efficiency and resilience," said A. Runčis.
LMT brings practical experience in deploying private 5G networks in ports to the Klaipėda project. The LMT Group installed the first private 5G network in the Baltic states at the Baltic Container Terminal (BCT) in the Port of Riga. Covering an area of over 50 hectares, the network is already used in daily operations, ensuring connectivity for mobile machinery and facilitating mission-critical communications. The team is also applying this experience to develop solutions for other ports.

About 900 working-age people in Latvia die due to external causes each year  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:37 UTC
22:00:37 KST

RIGA - External causes of death in Latvia claim an average 1,400 lives each year, including approximately 900 people of working age, according to data from the State Chancellery and the Welfare Ministry, which were presented today at a meeting of the Council on Demographic Affairs.
As the Welfare Ministry's spokesman Egils Zarins informed LETA, at the meeting, which was chaired today by Krists Avots, Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister, representatives from the State Chancellery and the Health Ministry presented data on external causes of death, their impact on society as a whole, the country’s demographic trends, and the national economy.
External causes of death account for 24 percent of all potential years of life lost up to the age of 64. The most common causes of death in this category are traffic accidents, falls, drowning, poisoning, violence, exposure to cold, fires, and suicides.
Last year, Latvia recorded 240 suicides and 234 fatal falls. There were also 171 cases of alcohol and drug poisoning, while 121 people lost their lives in traffic accidents. Also in 2025, 92 people drowned, 72 froze to death, and 34 were murdered. Of all these cases, 629 involved alcohol consumption, while psychoactive substances were involved in 102 cases.
To reduce and prevent such deadly accidents and incidents, close cooperation is needed among the health, education, traffic safety, law enforcement, and social sectors. Experts also pointed to the need for a long-term approach that combines prevention, public awareness, and cross-sectoral cooperation.
The Welfare Ministry notes that educational issues were also discussed at the meeting. The Education and Science Ministry gave a presentation on the current situation regarding the implementation of the Program at School education funding model.
At the same time, the council discussed options for providing free meals in schools through the 9th grade.
The Council on Demographic Affairs is an advisory and coordinating state institution established to promote a unified national demographic policy and its implementation at all levels of government. The council evaluates and coordinates the implementation of the national demographic policy and informs the media about demographic policy matters.

TALLINN - Estonian Prime Minister Kristen Michal, Latvian Prime Minister Andris Kulbergs, and Lithuanian President Gitanas Nausėda sent a joint letter on Friday to European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, calling for a ban on the transit of Russian grain through the European Union.

The leaders argue that the European Union must not provide Russia with an opportunity to offset the economic consequences of its aggression. They also state that the export of grain stolen from occupied Ukrainian territories through the EU must be prevented.
To support Ukrainian trade, the leaders call for the strengthening of the European Union-Ukraine Solidarity Lanes-transport connections designed to help Ukrainian goods reach the global market.

airBaltic has canceled five more destinations from Riga for winter season  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:24 UTC
22:00:24 KST

RIGA - Latvia's national airline airBaltic has canceled five more destinations from Riga for the winter season and will reduce flight frequency on certain routes, Augusts Zilberts, airBaltic’s head of public and political relations, confirmed to LETA.
He stated that airBaltic has made additional adjustments to the upcoming winter schedule. In line with seasonal demand, flights from Riga to Bucharest, Romania; Sofia, Bulgaria; Budapest, Hungary; and Oulu, Finland, will not operate during the winter season, but are scheduled to resume during the summer season. Flights from Riga to Innsbruck, Austria, will also be suspended.
Zilberts noted that airBaltic, like other airlines, regularly reviews its route network and flight schedule, adjusting capacity to passenger demand and current market conditions. In the current situation, another key factor is the rise in aviation fuel prices, which significantly impacts the airline’s operating costs.
In addition to the five canceled destinations from Riga, the airline will also reduce flight frequency on four routes, taking into account the traditionally lower demand for travel in January and February. Among others, flights will be reduced on routes from Riga to Copenhagen, Denmark; Oslo, Norway; Vienna, Austria; and Munich, Germany, while maintaining daily service to these destinations.
The flight schedule on routes from Riga to Madeira and Prague, Czech Republic, will also be adjusted during certain months of the winter season.
Zilberts noted that affected passengers are being offered the option to rebook their flight to another available flight within 14 days before or after the originally scheduled date or to request a refund.
These adjustments are a part of regular commercial planning and seasonal route network optimization and do not affect airBaltic’s long-term development plans, Zilberts emphasized.
During the upcoming winter season, airBaltic will offer a total of more than 45 direct destinations from Riga.
Previously, airBaltic told LETA that it would suspend flights on more than ten routes within the Baltic states during the winter season, including seven routes from Riga - to Faro, Portugal; Kittila in Finland, Ljubljana in Slovenia, Malta, Marrakesh in Morocco, Salzburg in Austria, and Dubai in the United Arab Emirates. Flights to Ljubljana will continue during the summer season.
As reported, airBaltic has begun restructuring its financial obligations in accordance with the Chapter 11 procedure set forth in U.S. law.
In total, airBaltic has received binding commitments from financiers to provide up to EUR 350 million in new financing (DIP) to ensure the company’s liquidity and operations during the Chapter 11 process. Currently, airBaltic has received the first tranche of financing in the amount of EUR 140 million, of which EUR 78.925 million will be used to repurchase eight aircraft and seven engines.
The financing was arranged by SVP, and Barclays, Hayfin Capital Management, Morgan Stanley, Oaktree Capital Management, and Strategic Value Partners have committed to providing it. The interest rate is SOFR +8 percent, or approximately 12 percent at present; however, this transaction will also involve additional fees totaling up to EUR 52.5 million.
Consequently, the previous plan to raise up to EUR 257 million at an annual rate of 25 percent from bondholders will not be implemented.
Chapter 11 protection shields airBaltic from creditor claims until the restructuring of its liabilities is completed.
The company also reports that flights and customer service will continue as usual. All flights will operate according to the scheduled flight plan; existing tickets and reservations remain valid, and passengers can continue to purchase tickets and travel with airBaltic as before.
Upon completion of this process, the final outcome will be a so-called reorganization plan, which must be approved by the court. The process is expected to be completed by mid-2027.
It was also reported that airBaltic bondholders supported in August the capitalization of the next two bond interest payments, as well as several other measures that provide the airline with additional flexibility in implementing its revised business plan.
Bondholders supported the capitalization of interest payments due on August 14 and November 14 of this year, adding them to the principal amount of the bonds rather than paying them out in cash. A decision was also made to grant a temporary exemption from minimum liquidity requirements until November 2026.
The airBaltic Group’s revenue last year increased by 4.2 percent compared to 2024, reaching EUR 779.344 million. Meanwhile, the airBaltic Group’s losses last year totaled EUR 44.337 million, which is 2.7 times less than in 2024. The airline carried a total of 5.2 million passengers in 2025, which is 1 percent more than in 2024.
Last summer, Germany’s national airline, Lufthansa, became a shareholder in airBaltic. Currently, the Latvian government owns 88.37 percent of airBaltic’s shares, Lufthansa holds 10 percent, the company Aircraft Leasing 1, owned by Danish businessman Lars Thuesen, a financial investor, holds 1.62 percent, and 0.01 percent is held by others. The company’s share capital is EUR 41.819 million.

Childhood ADHD diagnosis linked to lower adult religious attendance
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:17 UTC
22:00:17 KST

A childhood diagnosis of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder is linked to lower religious service attendance in adulthood, though it does not appear to diminish private religious practices like prayer. The decline in public religious participation is especially pronounced among Black and Asian American adults. The research was published in the Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion.
Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, or ADHD, is a highly prevalent neurodevelopmental condition characterized by persistent difficulties with attention, hyperactivity, and impulse regulation. These traits frequently extend well beyond childhood, affecting educational attainment, physical health, and social relationships into adulthood. One area of social life that researchers have rarely examined in relation to ADHD is religious participation. Religious communities often provide emotional support, coping resources, and a sense of belonging for individuals and families.
Sociologists Laura Upenieks and Samuel H. Fishman of Baylor University conducted the study to better understand how neurodiversity shapes lifelong religious engagement. A person with ADHD might struggle with behavioral inhibition, emotional regulation, and working memory. These constraints can make following a structured liturgy or sitting through long sermons physically and mentally exhausting. When people repeatedly fail to meet these behavioral expectations, they might feel excluded or judged, prompting them to permanently disengage from public worship.
To explore these dynamics, Upenieks and Fishman analyzed data from the National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent to Adult Health. This large, nationally representative study tracked participants from their teenage years in the mid-1990s into early midlife, between 2016 and 2018. The final sample included 9,785 adults from diverse racial and socioeconomic backgrounds. The researchers categorized participants based on whether they had been diagnosed with ADHD before age 18, after age 18, or never. They then looked at three different measures of adult religiosity: how often participants attended religious services, how often they prayed, and how important they considered religion to be in their daily lives.
The researchers built statistical models to assess the relationship between an ADHD diagnosis and later religious service attendance. They adjusted their models to account for childhood demographics, family structure, early-life health indicators like depression, and the participants’ religious habits as teenagers. They found that an ADHD diagnosis before age 18 was consistently associated with approximately 50 percent lower odds of regularly attending services in early midlife. A diagnosis received in adulthood did not show the same association.
Next, the researchers examined private religious practices and beliefs. In initial models, individuals with a childhood diagnosis appeared less likely to pray frequently or view religion as highly important, but these associations disappeared once researchers adjusted for demographic backgrounds and adolescent religious involvement. This suggests that ADHD primarily disrupts the behavioral capacity to participate in socially structured religious settings, rather than diminishing personal spiritual commitments. Private practices like solitary prayer allow for personal control and flexibility without the interpersonal pressures required in congregational settings.
The researchers also investigated whether the relationship between ADHD and religious attendance varied across racial and ethnic lines. They built an additional model that allowed the influence of an ADHD diagnosis to interact with a participant’s race or ethnicity. They found that the decline in attendance was substantially larger for Black and Asian American adults than for White adults. Black participants diagnosed with ADHD in childhood had 78 percent lower odds of attending services weekly compared to White participants without an ADHD diagnosis. Asian American adults with a childhood diagnosis exhibited 90 percent lower odds of weekly attendance.
These outcomes might be shaped by differing congregational norms and structural inequalities. Black congregations often host much longer worship services than other religious groups, which may place higher demands on sustained attention and make regular attendance more difficult. Meanwhile, many Asian American religious traditions place a strong cultural emphasis on discipline and interdependence, which can make behavioral nonconformity stand out and increase feelings of alienation. Structural inequalities in healthcare also mean that Black and Asian American children are often under-diagnosed or face punitive disciplinary measures rather than medical treatment for behavioral struggles.
An early ADHD diagnosis serves as a marker for the presence of sustained symptoms and institutional labeling, rather than acting as a direct cause of religious disengagement. Because the study relied on self-reported diagnoses, some individuals who experienced ADHD symptoms but lacked access to a formal medical evaluation might have been grouped with those who never had the condition.
This is especially relevant for women, who are historically under-diagnosed because their symptoms often present as internal inattentiveness rather than disruptive hyperactivity. The reliance on a binary formal diagnosis means the researchers could not measure the exact severity of the ADHD traits or determine if hyperactivity and inattentiveness affect religious behavior differently.
Additionally, the study’s measures of religion primarily capture Christian traditions, which heavily dominate the United States religious landscape. The survey aggregates many non-Christian traditions into a single “other religion” category, masking important differences in worship styles and cultural expectations. Future studies will need to examine whether specific religious traditions with varied community norms might be more accommodating to neurodiverse individuals. As ADHD diagnoses continue to rise, religious institutions may need to consider offering sensory-friendly spaces, shorter service options, and more flexible expectations to support all members of their communities.
The study, “Paths of Faith and Focus? ADHD, Adult Religiosity, and Moderation by Race in the Add Health Study,” was authored by Laura Upenieks and Samuel H. Fishman.

China Wants to Sell The World on Xinjiang-Farmed Fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:03 UTC
22:00:03 KST

When Chinese state television hailed inland salmon as a miracle in 2018, many viewers saw something more familiar: not a wonder, but a sales pitch.
The segment, aired by China Central Television that May, celebrated salmon farming in western China. Over images of sleek fish cutting through clear water, the narrator marveled that “a precious fish like salmon, which typically lives in the open ocean,” could now be raised inland, in the country’s barren western hinterland. The message was unmistakable. Technology had made the improbable possible. “The land is the same land, and the people are the same people,” the program declared, “but when technology is brought in, miracles are born.”
Online, viewers began poking at the claim almost immediately.
Was that salmon at all, many asked, or just rainbow trout dressed up as something fancier? On Chinese social media, the mood turned from curiosity to irritation. “People expect Atlantic salmon, but we’re getting freshwater rainbow trout that costs half as much,” one Beijing-based WeChat account complained. “How could you not be angry?” Science writer Fang Shimin dispensed with niceties: “This is cheap rainbow trout being passed off as expensive salmon. If you don’t want to deceive consumers, just call it rainbow trout.”
Such anxieties would only grow larger as China worked to sell an idea that, not long ago, might have sounded implausible: seafood from the desert. As China has rapidly expanded its fish farms as part of a state policy aimed at self-sufficiency, it has developed at least 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang, a historically restive region located in the country’s mountainous and desert inland. The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization in Washington, D.C. that I founded and run, mapped these farms as part of a sweeping investigation showing how much seafood is reaching the U.S., including government facilities, in violation of the Uyghur Forced Labor Prevention Act (UFLPA).
The distrust was not irrational. The United Nations’ Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) said this year that while there is no official global estimate for seafood fraud, empirical studies suggest it may exist in up to 20% of the worldwide trade, sometimes appearing as species substitution and other kinds of misrepresentation.
For most people, seafood comes with an expected geography. Salmon belongs to Norway or Alaska. Cod evokes the cold North Atlantic. Shrimp suggests warm coasts and estuaries. Xinjiang, by contrast, calls up deserts, surveillance, cotton fields, and the Chinese government’s mass detention, forced-labor, and assimilation campaign against Uyghurs and other predominantly Muslim minorities, along with the long, hard distances of the country’s far west. The most landlocked patch on the planet, Xinjiang is among the last places many people would associate with premium fish.
And yet for years, Chinese officials, state media, and seafood companies have been trying to teach consumers to do exactly that. They have promoted “Xinjiang seafood” as one of the small wonders of a new China: fish raised in glacial meltwater, in cold mountain reservoirs, in alkaline lakes, and at farms built against the edge of the desert. The imagery is always some variation on the same promise. Geography is no longer destiny. Harsh landscapes can be made productive. A remote frontier, disciplined by engineering, can become a source of delicacy and pride.
In that sense, Xinjiang seafood is not merely an agricultural product. It is a narrative achievement. The state-led campaign to create that narrative matters because it offers a rare window into Beijing’s worries about food security and its methods for redirecting Western attention away from its human rights problems. It also showcases China’s larger ambitions of using industry to help settle a historically restive region. This campaign saw its zenith in 2023, when Xinhua News Agency reported that the “Xinjiang seafood” label had surged in prominence on Chinese social media. Government data from that year show Xinjiang as China’s second-largest producer of “salmon,” trailing only Qinghai Province on the Tibetan Plateau. Its success is also relevant to what Americans eat, as the Outlaw Ocean Project found that seafood from Xinjiang ends up in the U.S. in violation of federal law. One company, called Tianyun, now ships to 14 countries, including the U.S., and distributes to food companies that supply military bases, public schools, and U.S. congressional cafeterias, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.
Xinjiang Tianyun said in a statement that claims of systemic forced labor “are completely factually unfounded” and described the UFLPA as an unreasonable and politically motivated framework that violates the principles of fair international trade. Xinjiang Tianyun insists that it strictly abides by China’s laws on labor and contracts and resolutely protects the legitimate rights and interests of every employee.
The 2018 salmon dispute exposed how fragile China's narrative of achievement in Xinjiang can be. To some consumers, the issue was simple: they feared they were paying salmon prices for a cheaper fish. But the outrage ran deeper because it also touched food safety. That same year, the Chinese food-safety expert Zhong Kai warned against serving trout raw, citing parasite risks common in freshwater fish. “I do not recommend eating it raw,” he said, advising thorough cooking. Online commenters accused state media of misleading the public. This was “not the salmon ordinary people think of,” they wrote. Masami Takeuchi, a food-safety officer at the FAO, noted that illnesses caused by eating raw freshwater fish can be serious, even when symptoms arrive late or are hard to trace.
The fear, then, was not simply that consumers were being overcharged. It was that they were being sold an aspirational image that obscured material differences in the fish itself.
That anxiety found ready soil in a country where food scandals have repeatedly taught the public to distrust official reassurance. China’s aquaculture industry has expanded at staggering speed, and with that expansion have come the familiar pressures of industrial animal farming: crowding, disease, waste, chemical intervention, and a recurring mismatch between the pastoral language used to market food and the industrial realities that produce it. A 2020 study in Nature found that aquaculture has the highest antibiotic-use intensity per kilogram of biomass among major animal-production sectors, exceeding use in both humans and land-based livestock.
Chinese researchers have warned for years about severe antibiotic abuse in the industry. Sedatives have posed another problem. Diazepam, sometimes used to calm fish during transport, has repeatedly shown up in official inspections despite being prohibited. In 2021, China’s Ministry of Agriculture and Rural Affairs began requiring routine diazepam testing, and a 2023 paper in China Food Hygiene Journal described diazepam residues as “widely detected” in water and seafood products. In 2025, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration issued an alert after detecting residues of prohibited substances—including malachite green, a carcinogenic veterinary drug—in seafood shipments from China, citing “significant public-health concerns.”
None of this proves that Xinjiang seafood as a whole is fraudulent or unsafe. But it helps explain why the category has struggled to inspire a durable sense of consumer trust. In a food system often shadowed by contamination scares and labeling disputes, grand claims end up feeling less like reassurance than marketing. The more insistently officials and companies promoted inland salmon, trout, whitefish, caviar, and other products from China’s far west as a new high-value frontier, the more some consumers wondered what, exactly, they were being asked to believe.
The answer, in part, was a story the state had been helping to write for years.
As early as 2011, Vice Minister of Agriculture Niu Dun was urging officials to “enhance brand building and awareness of the market expansion of Xinjiang’s seafood enterprises.” A 2017 government Action Plan for Fisheries Poverty Alleviation and Aid to Xinjiang and Tibet and Xinjiang went further, instructing local offices to “strengthen communication and coordination with mainstream media” and to “systematically publicize the progress of fishery poverty alleviation,” thereby creating what it called “an environment of positive public opinion.” The phrasing was telling. Fisheries in Xinjiang were to be built, yes. But they were also to be narrated.
That narration took many forms. Officials promoted fish-themed tourism. In Wenquan County, a local attraction described as “Xinjiang’s first cold-water fish theme park” invited visitors to tour a museum, sample whitefish sashimi and caviar, and even catch fish on site, weigh them, and bring them into town for processing. The scene was faintly surreal: a region associated abroad with coercion and repression recast domestically as a place of family outings, provincial pride, and specialty delicacies. The politics were never absent. They were simply plated more attractively.
Then, in late summer 2023, the campaign accelerated.
Posts about Xinjiang seafood surged across Chinese social-media platforms. Hashtags such as “Xinjiang welcomes everyone to come eat seafood” and “No joke—Xinjiang really does produce seafood” climbed Weibo’s Hot Search List. On Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok, interactions tied to Xinjiang seafood jumped spectacularly. A seafood industry report later said that videos associated with “Xinjiang seafood” and “Xinjiang salmon” amassed more than 150 million views in 2023. One widely circulated Douyin clip, “Xinjiang Salmon ‘Leaps’ onto the World Table,” drew more than 2.7 million views and helped touch off the frenzy. Like many of the videos that followed, it lingered on crystalline mountain water, gleaming facilities, and the visual incongruity of prized fish emerging from the country’s interior.
Soon, the theme leapt beyond China’s own internet. YouTube, which is banned in China, saw a sharp rise in Xinjiang seafood videos that fall. The message was no longer meant only for domestic audiences. Xinjiang seafood was being staged for foreign consumption, too—not just as food, but as an emblem of innovation, abundance, and purity.
The timing was hard to miss. On August 24, 2023, Japan began releasing into the Pacific Ocean treated wastewater that had accumulated since the Fukushima nuclear disaster. Beijing denounced the move as “selfish and irresponsible” and imposed a blanket ban on Japanese aquatic products. In the tense weeks that followed, content promoting Xinjiang seafood leaned heavily on purity: glacial melt from the Tian Shan, cold inland reservoirs, waters safely removed from allegedly contaminated seas. Xinjiang seafood was being sold not only as novel or upscale, but as patriotic, safe, and strategically desirable.
To some analysts, the speed and scale of the online surge suggested something more coordinated than ordinary virality. Fergus Ryan, a senior analyst at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute, said the pattern bore the hallmarks of top-down and algorithmic amplification rather than grassroots enthusiasm alone. In his view, the campaign may also have served another purpose: redirecting attention from mounting scrutiny of China’s seafood sector after an October 2023 investigation by the Outlaw Ocean Project reported that seafood plants in Shandong had used thousands of Uyghur labor transfers to process fish destined for major Western markets. Against that backdrop, Ryan argued, the flood of upbeat Xinjiang seafood content functioned as a kind of information flooding, crowding search and recommendation systems with stories of “fishery miracles” rather than forced labor.
Whether every post was centrally directed matters less than the political usefulness of the category itself. Xinjiang seafood offered the state an unusually supple symbol. It could suggest scientific prowess, dietary upgrading, regional development, ecological management, and ethnic harmony all at once. It could showcase “clean” water, advanced facilities, and smiling workers. Most of all, it could recast one of the world’s most scrutinized frontiers as a landscape of abundance.
That ambition extends beyond domestic image-making. Beijing plainly hopes to export not just Xinjiang seafood but the idea of Xinjiang seafood. Yet that effort faces an obvious obstacle: In the United States, the UFLPA presumes that goods made wholly or partly in Xinjiang are produced with forced labor unless importers can prove otherwise, while in Europe, a 2024 forced-labor regulation will bar products made with forced labor from the E.U. market once it begins applying in December 2027.
This is where the events depart from a conventional tale of food fraud. In many countries, misleading labels thrive because supply chains are opaque and enforcement is weak. In Xinjiang, opacity was part of the business model. The product itself was being woven into a larger political narrative about what the region was and what it was becoming. Fish farms were not merely farms. They were exhibits.
Part of the effort to promote Xinjiang seafood involved government-orchestrated media tours for foreign journalists and vloggers, often called “frontier influencers” or “global stringers,” to visit Xinjiang, including its fish farms. After being shepherded to government-run facilities and through regions like Tibet or Xinjiang that are typically off limits to most other journalists, these influencers tend to create seeing-is-believing style videos that offer “happy life” testimonials from locals, while showcasing the region as a high-tech and indispensable hub for global development and “green” innovation.
By 2025, Xinjiang seafood had become a recurring stop on that circuit. A state-funded outlet released a video featuring an American vlogger identified as Jack exploring what it called the “agricultural miracle” of a fish farm on the edge of China’s largest desert, the Taklamakan. That same month, a British creator toured a reservoir in Alar City and praised its role in both flood control and local fish production. A Russian student, one of the better-known foreign influencers working this terrain, filmed herself at a salmon farm in Nilka, announcing cheerfully that she had come to be “an employee for a day” and see the industry for herself. Some of the footage circulating during this push featured Tianyun, one of the companies caught up in the earlier inland salmon labeling dispute.
Even some of the industry figures tied to those disputes were later recast as patriotic exemplars of frontier development. In 2025, one prominent executive from Xinjiang’s salmon business was honored in Beijing by the Communist Party as a “National Model Worker,” then pledged to help expand China’s salmon industry and improve the skills of workers from all ethnic groups. The symbolism was familiar by then. Commercial actors were being folded into a larger state story about modernization, unity, and progress in the far west.
All of which points to the larger feat behind Xinjiang seafood’s rise. China did not simply have to learn how to raise cold-water fish in unlikely places. It had to construct a category and teach consumers how to feel about it. It had to make fish from a landlocked, desert-heavy, politically burdened region seem not only possible but desirable: clean rather than contaminated, premium rather than ersatz, modern rather than improvised, harmonious rather than coercive. That required hatcheries, reservoirs, feed, transport networks, and technical expertise. But it also required softer definitions, confident reassurances, staged tourism, influencer testimony, and a steady current of triumphal images.
In the end, Xinjiang seafood is best understood not simply as a product of ponds, pipes, hatcheries, and feed, but as a product of narrative force. Fish flash through cold inland water; cameras glide across reservoirs; influencers smile into the desert light; officials speak of innovation and harmony. The image holds. Until, somewhere behind it, the old questions return: What is this fish, really? Where did it come from? What story is being wrapped around it? In Xinjiang, those questions do not fade when the meal arrives. They sit there at the table.
(The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project. Ian Urbina is the founder and executive editor of The Outlaw Ocean Project.)

Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Here’s a look at the Nobel Prizes for science
Catching neutrinos, controlling brain cells and the mystery of mirror image molecules won
It’s Nobels season — that time of the year when we find out which groundbreaking, paradigm-shifting, world-changing achievements beat out the rest to win what is arguably the most prestigious award on Earth.
From a light switch for the brain to the discovery of an ultra-elusive subatomic particle hailing from beyond our solar system to a solution to one of the most enduring puzzles in all of organic chemistry, the researchers behind this year’s scientific prizes each revolutionized the ways that scientists understand the world around them.
Take a look at the science behind each of this year’s awards.
Shining a light
A galaxy of nearly 90 billion neurons exists within a single human brain. But unlike stars in the void, neurons communicate with one another via some 100 trillion connections, allowing the human mind to learn, adapt and interact with its surroundings.
For scientists to understand how individual actions arise from such complexity, they needed a tool to directly link neural circuits to specific behaviors, said Abdel El Manira, a neuroscientist at the Karolinska Institute in Stockholm. “Neuroscientists dreamed of a neuronal switch, a tool to turn specific neurons on or off with great precision,” El Manira said during the Oct. 5 announcement of this year’s prize in physiology or medicine by the Nobel Assembly at Karolinska Institute.
Enter the bright idea that won. It’s a technology called optogenetics, which involves using light to precisely activate specific cells, like neurons, and watch how behavior changes. For their foundational contributions to optogenetics, biophysicists Peter Hegemann of Humboldt University in Berlin and Georg Nagel, of the Julius-Maximilians-Universität Würzburg in Germany, and neuroscientist Karl Deisseroth of Stanford University shared this year’s prize.
The prize winners’ story starts in an unlikely place: the eye spot of a single celled green alga called Chlamydomonas. In the early 2000s, Hegemann, then at the Max Planck Institute for Biochemistry in Martinsreid, Germany, and Nagel, at the Max Planck Institute for Biophysics in Frankfurt, discovered a unique protein in the alga’s eye spot. When illuminated, the protein generated an electrical impulse, enabling the organism to move. Further research revealed that when the protein, called channelrhodopsin, was exposed to light, it opened like a pore, allowing positively charged ions to flow into a cell, generating the electrical impulse. “They had just discovered the switch neuroscientists had long dreamed of,” El Manira said.
Building on the Hegemann and Nagel’s work, Deisseroth began testing whether channelrhodopsin could be used to activate brain cells. He and his colleagues first inserted the gene for channelrhodopsin into cultures of rat nerve cells and found that the cells reacted to light instantaneously. They then introduced the gene into nerve cells in the brains of living mice, along with optical fibers fed through the rodents’ skulls. By beaming blue light through the fibers, the researchers were able to control the movements of the rodents’ whiskers. This technology gave researchers the ability to test the links between certain brain circuits and behaviors.
“The technology, which soon became known as optogenetics, transformed neuroscience,” El Manira said. In addition to exposing the inner workings of healthy brains, he noted, “it has also helped reveal how brain circuits are disrupted, with implications for conditions such as blindness, depression and dementia.”
For example, the technology has been used improve vision in some patients with retinitis pigmentosa, a disease that degrades light-sensing cells in the retina. It’s also helping researchers investigate the role that a person’s heart plays in how they experience and interact with their surroundings.
Capturing a ghost
At the South Pole, there exists a block of ice unlike any other on Earth. Buried deep beneath the surface of the Antarctic ice sheet, a cubic kilometer of ice is threaded with thousands of beadlike sensors. Known as the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, this immense instrument enables researchers to detect the most elusive particle in the universe — the neutrino.
Detecting neutrinos from beyond our solar system had been a goal of scientists for decades, as that could help understand where and how the universe accelerates particles to extraordinary energies.
The researcher who led the creation of the Antarctic observatory, physicist Francis Halzen of the University of Wisconsin–Madison, received this year’s Nobel Prize in physics. Halzen was awarded “for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin,” Mark Pearce, a physicist and chair of the Nobel committee for physics, during the Oct. 6 announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
Neutrinos are subatomic particles that are chargeless, incredibly small and so ethereal that they often pass through objects without interacting. In fact, billions of neutrinos pass through each of us every second, most of which are formed by nuclear fusion reactions in the sun. But some of these ghostly particles were thought to have originated much farther away, in high-energy particle collisions so distant as to lie beyond the limits of observations. Because neutrinos are not deflected by magnetic fields and rarely interact with matter, the detection of a high-energy neutrino’s trajectory could enable the identification of its distant source. An instrument capable of that task could therefore open a new window into the cosmos.
In the 1980s, Halzen realized that the South Pole was an ideal location for detecting the rare flashes of light that are generated when neutrinos collide with atomic nuclei. Ice deep inside the Antarctic ice sheet presented a large, transparent medium plunged in darkness, in a spot free from earthquakes and biological interference. It was the perfect stage for a neutrino lightshow.
Halzen’s vision was realized in 2011, when IceCube completed construction. “The biggest risk we took is that nobody knew whether a kilometer-field detector was actually large enough to discover neutrinos beyond our atmosphere from the universe,” Halzen said in a phone call during the announcement ceremony. “It only took us two years to detect them.”
And the discoveries didn’t end there. In 2018, researchers using IceCube data reported that they had traced a neutrino back to the brilliant core of a distant galaxy, called a blazar, thereby identifying a source for the energetic particles for the first time. And in 2023, researchers used a decade of IceCube data to produce the first map of the Milky Way using anything besides light, simultaneously reporting the first evidence of high-energy neutrinos hailing from within the galaxy.
Plans for a global network of neutrino detectors are now in motion. So scientists will soon be even better equipped to pinpoint and demystify the distant cosmic accelerators that launch the mysterious particles across the vast reaches of space.
Giving chemistry a hand
In nature, the building blocks of life exhibit a striking pattern. Many can exist in two versions that are mirrored images of one another, much like your right and left hand. Such molecules are said to be chiral. However, they overwhelmingly occur as just one of these chiral forms — for instance, amino acids are nearly always left-handed.
This uniformity, known as homochirality, had long puzzled scientists. When chemists first attempted to produce chiral molecules in the lab, they ended up with even proportions of right- and left-handed molecules, or enantiomers.
“It is this puzzle that this year’s laureates have solved,” Heiner Linke, chair of the Nobel Committee for Chemistry said during the Oct. 7 Nobel Prize in chemistry announcement by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences.
Henri Kagan, of the Université Paris-Saclay, and Kenso Soai, of the Tokyo University of Science, split the prize for discoveries leading “to a chemical reaction that spontaneously, without the involvement of other chiral molecules, creates only one mirror image,” said Linke, a physicist at Lund University in Sweden. “This is the first time this had happened since the processes that led to the chirality of life billions of years ago.”
Putting aside the laureates’ impact on one of organic chemistry’s greatest mysteries, their research has immensely benefitted the development of pharmaceuticals. So many active drug molecules are chiral, and one enantiomer of a drug might have the desired therapeutic effect while its other might have no effect or even be harmful, Linke said.
A notorious example of such harm occurred in the 1950s, when thousands of babies with severe birth defects were born to women who had taken a sedative called thalidomide. It was later revealed that one of thalidomide’s enantiomers was the source of the birth defects. Even making the drug with only the “safe” orientation didn’t solve the problem: It could switch handedness in the body.
In 1986, Kagan and his colleagues became the first to report chemical reactions that produced specific enantiomers in proportions far exceeding what chemists previously assumed was possible using catalysts.
Nine years later, Soai and his colleagues reported that they had figured out how to make a chiral catalyst that could, in turn, be used to form itself. That allowed them to perform reactions that resulted in products made almost entirely of one enantiomer. “This is not the final answer,” Soai said of his groundbreaking work on chirality, while calling into the ceremony from Japan. Speaking to future generations, he said “the study of chirality should be more and more developed.”
Even so, as Nobel committee member Peter Somfai, a chemist at Lund University in Sweden, said during the ceremony: “This is probably the coolest experiment in organic chemistry.”
