There’s a Danish app in English for getting help when you feel unsafe on the way home
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

“They feel insecure and a lot of those people we ask and they felt like there was no help to get.” That was one of the problems Lennart Nielsen kept hearing about when talking to young people who felt unsafe at night, particularly when heading home after being out in the city. His response was SafeCircle, a new Danish app designed for those moments when the walk home suddenly does not feel quite right.
The app allows people who feel unsafe, for example because someone is following them or approaching them in a threatening way, to alert people they know as well as other verified SafeCircle members nearby. And because the problem is not limited to Danish speakers, SafeCircle is available in English too.
“It’s not only the Danish people who have this problem. It’s everybody living in Denmark,” Nielsen, the app’s founder and CEO, said. “That’s the reason we made it both in Danish and in English.”
SafeCircle was created by Nielsen together with cofounder Nanna Liv Nielsen and app developer Elliot Gawn. Nielsen said the idea grew out of conversations with young people about what happens when they feel unsafe and there is nobody immediately around to help.
“It was originated when young people have trouble in the nighttime, for example, when they’re going home after the city,” he said. “So we made this app so you can use the app. You can get help from other people you don’t know.”
What happens when you press the alarm
Users first download the app and verify their identity through MitID, Denmark’s national digital identification system. They add a photo and can give the app permission to start recording when they activate an alarm.
“All the members are MitID approved,” Nielsen said. “So you know exactly who’s going to help you.”
If someone feels they are being followed or otherwise threatened, they can press the alarm button. Nielsen gave the example of someone leaving a train station and realizing that another person is following them.
“You press the app. The app sends out a notification to SafeCircle members in 2 km,” he said. Those members can either accept or decline the alert. “If you accept, you get a map precisely where this person is,” Nielsen said.
At the same time, the phone of the person who raised the alarm starts recording audio and video and uploading the material to a secure server. “The person who activated the SafeCircle app started recording on her phone sound and video,” Nielsen said. “Started to upload to a safe server.”
The aim, he said, is to create documentation while the situation is still unfolding. “The thing is when you activate the app it also starts recording sound and video,” Nielsen said. “So you can take a picture or a video of the guy approaching you or girl. And it’s going to be encrypted and it’s going to upload to servers.”
That material could later help document what happened. “So we have documentation of people trying to do things that they’re not allowed to do,” Nielsen said.
Help without confrontation
SafeCircle does not rely only on strangers nearby. Users can create their own network of people who will also receive an alert when the alarm is activated.
“You have your own SafeCircle network,” Nielsen said. “That means your parents, your sisters, and your friends, they also get a notification.” “So friends, family, and SafeCircle members is going to come to your aid.”
But Nielsen stressed that the idea is not to create a group of people who rush in and physically confront someone. “We don’t want people to intervene,” he said.
Instead, SafeCircle members responding to an alert can help document what they see. “They start running down, taking their phones up trying to video film also,” Nielsen said. “They can make a description if they see a guy or girl jumping into a car. They can give the license plate or description how the person looks.”
The person who activated the alarm can stop it using a personal PIN code. The recordings are not streamed live to other SafeCircle users.
“No. Because of GDPR rules,” Nielsen said when asked whether other users could watch the video being recorded. “They just record and it’s going to upload all the video and sound to a case file who gets encrypted.”
According to Nielsen, the person who activated the alarm can later access the material, and it can also be made available to police. “The police also get a file where they can download from the person who activated but also the persons who comes to help,” he said.
The app is intended for users aged 15 and older.
An English version for people living in Denmark
Making the app available in English was a deliberate part of the project. For Nielsen, whether somebody was born in Denmark or moved to the country from abroad makes little difference if they find themselves alone at night and feel threatened.
“It’s not only the English people who has this problem,” he said. “It’s everybody living in Denmark.”
For internationals, the English version means they can use the same functions without having to navigate a Danish-only service during a potentially stressful situation. “That’s the reason we made it both in Danish and in English,” Nielsen said.
SafeCircle was launched last week and is available for Apple and Android phones. For now, the app is free. Nielsen said the aim is to get enough people using it for the network behind it to become useful.
“We have tried in the beginning to make it free for everybody, so we get a lot of people on it,” he said.
The current plan is to introduce a subscription next year at DKK 9 per month. “I think next year it’s going to be like you need to pay for it, but we have turned down the prices so it’s 9 kroner a month,” Nielsen said. “It’s not a lot. So this is for everybody.”

The hidden cost of farmed fish: Pollution, forced labor and the depletion of wild fish
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

- Click here to listen to this article
-   Share via
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
- More than half the seafood eaten worldwide is farm-raised, but much of it fed ‘fishmeal,’ a product made from wild-caught fish.
- Farm-raised fish feed millions and the farms provide employment. But a global investigation into fish farming found overfishing, pollution and labor abuses.
- The investigation found that fish farming is often worsening the very problem it hoped to solve and harming the people it was meant to help.
As of 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten worldwide was farm-raised rather than caught at sea, a fact that has been praised as evidence that fish farming can meet a growing demand for seafood while slowing the collapse of the oceans.
But the unbridled embrace of aquaculture as a sustainable answer to feeding the planet ignores some very real costs.
The most popular types of farmed seafood — salmon, shrimp, trout, seabass, seabream — are fed “fishmeal,” a protein-rich powder or pellet made from the very kinds of wild fish that aquaculture is thought to save.
In fact, fishmeal is fed to two-thirds of global farmed fish. Before they reach market, some farm-raised salmon eat more than six times their weight in wild-caught fish.
With thousands of fish farms worldwide, aquaculture provides millions of people with year-round access to affordable protein. Fish farming is also a crucial source of jobs, especially for women in India.
But a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a nonprofit news organization based in Washington, D.C., has found that the aquaculture industry’s answer to worries about the world’s oceans — “grow more fish so we can catch less” — is often making the very problem it hoped to solve worse and harming the people it was meant to help.
The investigation
The business of fishmeal — often out of public view — can involve using forced labor, poisoning communities, and eradicating the livelihoods of local fishermen.
Fishmeal production has led to chronic chemical exposure, violent protests — typically spurred by the stench from fishmeal factories — and escalating transnational tensions as countries compete for catch. That price is paid primarily by the poorer countries where the main ingredient of fishmeal is harvested and processed.
The Outlaw Ocean Project mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries. The effort involved dozens of journalists from over 15 countries who visited factories and farms and boarded fishmeal ships at sea.
Using certification documents, ownership records, trade data, audits and government lists of licensed fishing ships, the reporting team was able to connect ships to the plants they supplied and pin down which species were being targeted for fishmeal. This allowed them to determine which fishmeal plants were connected to ships engaged in illegal or unsustainable fishing. Then, they traced the fishmeal to the fish farm and to where the seafood was sold by retailers.
The investigation found that more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of those ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.
For example, less than 30% of the fleets had publicly available location information, and less than 25% had a unique vessel identification number. Such opacity makes the ships difficult to police.
At least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels are classified by scientific studies as “overexploited” or worse. Most of these vessels are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of non-target species.
At least 165 of the ships were bottom trawlers, a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their path.
Concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. In Gambia and Mauritania in western Africa, the industry drives food insecurity as fish that once sustained local communities are diverted into fishmeal factories.
In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, farms and in factories. In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and protests sparked by the water pollution or the stink from factories cooking tons of decomposing fish.
In Chile in 2024, several hundred demonstrators burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks to protest the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.
In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so they increasingly are selling — or repurposing — their boats to ferry migrants to Spain’s Canary Islands, a stepping stone to Europe. This perilous journey of roughly 930 miles claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.
“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisherman in 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he tried to sail to Spain capsized, killing 30.
The fishmeal industry also contributes to transnational tensions. For example, in 2021, a dozen Turkish bottom trawlers fishing illegally in the Aegean Sea tried to ram a Greek research vessel when the scientists began filming their activity.
In 2018, riots broke out in Saint-Louis, Senegal, after a fisher was shot and killed by Mauritanian coast guards, during what the Mauritanians said was a cross-border raid by a fishmeal boat.
The politics of protein
In her 2021 book “The Fishmeal Revolution,” Kristin A. Wintersteen traces how the Humboldt Current — a cold, nutrient-rich upwelling system along the Pacific coast of South America — was reimagined as a protein mine. That shift, she argues, turned Peru into a fishmeal superpower, responsible for roughly a quarter of worldwide production.
Fishmeal helped fuel the post-World War II expansion of industrial chicken and hog farming, particularly in Europe and the United States. Since then, this model has spread worldwide.
The feed industry has emphasized that it is decreasing its reliance on fishmeal and fish oil — and especially the use of whole fish or fish parts that can be eaten by people. However, as aquaculture grows, global fishmeal production is predicted to rise by nearly 10% by 2032, according to the Food and Agriculture Organization, a United Nations agency.
For example, five of the world’s largest salmon companies increased their use of fishmeal and fish oil made from whole wild fish by as much as 39% between 2020 and 2024, according to a report from the Farm Animal Investment Risk and Return Initiative.
Asked about sustainability concerns tied to her industry, Véronique Jamin, a spokesperson for IFFO, the international fishmeal association, said that fish farming is “the most efficient animal protein system.” She added that her organization’s “role is not to advise which markets should use fishmeal and fish oil.” Attempts to make the industry more sustainable must consider market forces, she said, and seafood companies have to respond to “what people actually want to buy and eat.”
Efforts to move away from fishmeal and fish oil have struggled. Researchers have identified potential alternatives — including seaweed, cassava waste, single-cell proteins produced by fungi and even sewage.
But none are being produced affordably at scale, and the alternatives often lack the nutrients that support the growth of farmed fish.
The role of forced labor
For those toiling at fishmeal plants and fish farms, the work and conditions can be brutal, the investigation found.
In Russia, fish processing workers were held captive in secluded company towns or stuck on ships far from shore. “People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker told President Vladimir Putin, who participated in a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant in 2016. A second worker pleaded: “Please, help us.”
In China, the aquaculture industry is expanding rapidly in the country’s mountainous and desert areas inland, particularly in Tibet and Xinjiang, two areas known for political repression, with criminal penalties for speaking native languages or practicing religious or cultural traditions.
Because the U.S. government found human rights abuses to be pervasive there, Congress enacted a law in 2021 that banned all goods produced “wholly or in part” by workers in Xinjiang or by ethnic minorities from the region on the presumption that they were made with state-sponsored forced labor. No such law exists for Tibet.
The investigation mapped more than 1,000 fish farms in Xinjiang and Tibet that produce an estimated half-billion dollars’ worth of seafood annually, much of it exported to more than a dozen countries, including the United States. Despite the 2021 law banning goods from Xinjiang, the investigation found that farm-raised fish from that region have reached the United States.
For example, the Xinjiang Tiayun fish farm, which produces 40% of China’s domestically produced salmon, is tied through supply agreements to a brand of seafood called Aqua Star sold by Walmart and the world’s largest food service company, Sysco, which in the U.S. distributes to public schools, military bases and congressional cafeterias.
Sysco said it was unaware of the link to Xinjiang. “We hold all suppliers across our global supply chain accountable” to uphold U.S., international and local laws, and Sysco suspends contracts when they do not, said Ramit Plushnick-Masti, a company spokesperson. Aqua Star and Walmart did not respond to a request for comment.
Xinjiang Tianyun said in a statement that claims of forced labor “are completely factually unfounded.” The Chinese government did not respond to a request for comment.
More than 80% of seafood eaten in the U.S. is imported, and 9% of that comes from China.
Another major supplier of seafood to the U.S. is India, which produces roughly a third of the shrimp that Americans consume, almost all of it grown with fishmeal. The investigation found at least 18 instances of civil unrest and at least 20 cases of water or air pollution tied to Indian fishmeal plants.
In November 2020, Indian government investigators found hidden bore holes where the operator of the United Marine Products fishmeal plant in Goa had been covertly disposing of toxic waste, thereby contaminating groundwater. The plant owner denied wrongdoing.
Shrimp sold by Sysco and at Kroger and Safeway is fed fishmeal from United Marine, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that maps seafood supply chains. Kroger and Safeway’s parent company, Albertsons, did not respond to a request for comment.
Sustainable practices
Though problems with fish farming have arisen worldwide, for some countries, it aquaculture has been a boon.
In Bangladesh, aquaculture has driven down the price of fish. Even accounting for fishmeal and transportation to the U.S., the production of certain farmed fish, including tilapia and Atlantic salmon, emits less greenhouse gas per pound than beef or pork.
Harvesting bivalves, like clams, oysters, scallops and mussels, is especially sustainable because these species do not require feed. This type of aquaculture also has a low carbon footprint and the shells function as a form of carbon capture, according to a 2020 paper by the scientific journal Nature Food.
In the United States, at least 16 factories processed fishmeal as of 2025, along the Chesapeake Bay in Virginia, the Gulf Coast in Mississippi and Louisiana, and in California, Oregon and Alaska.
Most of these factories use inedible offcuts from fishing because nearly every U.S. state has outlawed the targeting of whole fish for fishmeal. The factories also tend to be better regulated than plants elsewhere in the world.
Long supply chains
As the production of seafood has become more globalized, its supply chains have stretched longer, making it tougher for consumers and grocers to know whether it was harvested sustainably or legally.
Robert K. Stumberg, professor at Georgetown Law and supply-chain expert, said grocers typically buy from wholesalers and rarely track their suppliers. One other reason may be plausible deniability, he added. “Companies can escape blame or the need to fix problems if they’re unaware of them.”
With government oversight of supply chains sometimes lacking, industry-led certification programs have sought to fill the gap and root out unsustainable, unethical or illegal practices.
But critics say these programs generally focus on environmental crimes and overlook labor abuses on ships. On land, at processing plants or farms, certification programs rarely conduct true spot checks to authenticate the reassurances given by managers, said Allie Brudney, a senior staff attorney at Corporate Accountability Lab, a strategic litigation nonprofit.
Instead, the programs frequently alert companies before inspectors show up. At sea, these programs often rely on self-reported information from ship captains rather than having auditors inspect vessels offshore.
Devan Meserve, a spokesperson for the Global Seafood Alliance, which runs the Best Aquaculture Practices program, defended the value of such inspection programs. She said that her organization represents the “most comprehensive program for farmed seafood,” partly because it covers the “entire aquaculture production chain.”
Protecting workers on the fishing vessels that supply feed mills is, however, an “immense challenge,” Meserve added, because audits occur at port. She added that her organization helps the industry counter illegal and overfishing by requiring feed mills to source most of the fish they use in fishmeal or fish oil from fisheries accredited by certification programs like Marine Trust and Marine Stewardship Council.
The risk of false advertising
“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at the University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”
Since 2020, at least nine lawsuits alleging false advertising have been brought against six seafood companies in six U.S. states. Plaintiffs challenged language such as “sustainable,” “eco-friendly” and “wild-caught,” as well as claims of superior worker-safety standards. Five of the lawsuits resulted in settlements, and the companies paid the plaintiffs more than $2 million.
In at least four cases, the use of fishmeal or fish oil and their link to industrial fishing and ecosystem depletion were central to arguments that the products were not environmentally sustainable. Additional allegations included forced labor on fishing vessels and reliance on harmful pesticides and antibiotics.
The Outlaw Ocean investigation assessed more than 500 seafood companies that made marketing claims that were comparable to — or stronger than — those cited in the lawsuits. Over half of those companies had supply chain ties to fishmeal producers involved in crimes, misconduct and unsustainable fishing practices.
Dana Cleaveley, a research consultant formerly with SeaChoice, a Canadian sustainable-seafood group, said that many industries have already had to begin reckoning with the human rights and environmental abuses buried in their supply chains. She cited “sweatshop garments,” “fair-trade coffee” and “blood diamonds” as examples.
Seafood has been slower to face such scrutiny, though, as the world leans further into aquaculture, that may change, she said, particularly if more governments begin restricting imports tied to illegality or unsustainable practices. She added: “That’s when investors will begin to see material, not just reputational risk, and companies will have to adjust.”
But in some quarters, the troubling costs of fish farming remain unaddressed.
In April 2025, President Trump signed Executive Order 14276, “Restoring American Seafood Competitiveness,” which instructed government officials to reduce regulatory burdens and boost the commercial fishing and aquaculture sectors in the United States.
It made no mention of feed or fishmeal.
Urbina is executive editor of the Outlaw Ocean Project. The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at the Outlaw Ocean Project.

Ukraine’s Ground Robots Rescued 45 Soldiers Under Fire, Commander Says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:57:06 UTC
21:57:06 KST

Ukraine’s ground robots rescued 45 soldiers from under Russian fire and transported more than 41 tons of supplies to frontline positions during the summer of 2026, according to the Artan special unit under Ukraine’s Military Intelligence Directorate (HUR).
Artan commander Col. Viktor Torkotiuk, call sign Titan, said crews operating the unmanned ground vehicles (UGVs) worked continuously along the front, according to RBC-Ukraine.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
During the summer campaign, the platforms covered a combined distance of approximately 4,258 kilometers (2,646 miles), with tasks ranging from supporting frontline logistics to evacuating wounded Ukrainian troops and transporting captured Russian soldiers.
Robots enter areas too dangerous for vehicles
The ground platforms allowed Ukrainian forces to evacuate wounded troops from exposed positions without sending additional personnel or conventional vehicles into areas monitored by Russian drones.
Torkotiuk said the drones help free up valuable resources.
“Technology is transforming the combat capabilities of units on the front line,” Torkotiuk said. “Innovative logistics frees up capabilities and forces for active operations and offensive actions,” he added.
The unit did not specify how many vehicles took part in the missions, how many individual journeys they completed, or which ground-robot models they used.
Ground robotic systems vary in size and configuration. Some transport ammunition, food and other supplies, while others can carry wounded soldiers, conduct reconnaissance, clear mines or operate mounted weapons.
Russia Steps Up Production of Improved Su-34 ‘Fullback’ Bombers
Ukrainian troops have said such platforms are particularly useful inside the so-called kill zone, where ordinary evacuation vehicles can quickly be detected and targeted by surveillance and attack drones.
Frontline soldiers have previously told Kyiv Post that robots are not replacing troops but are increasingly performing the most dangerous logistical and medical evacuation missions.
Artan operates in Zaporizhzhia and near Lyman
Artan said its main area of operations is currently the Zaporizhzhia front in southern Ukraine, a region where over 70 percent is under Russian occupation, most of which since 2022.
The unit also participated in one stage of Ukraine’s Operation Vivaldi near Lyman in eastern Ukraine during the spring and summer campaign. The operation recovered at least 125 square kilometers (48 square miles) of territory and disrupted Russian attempts to advance toward Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
Analysts suggest the operation has reversed Russian gains made in 2026 and thwarted Moscow’s goal to capture eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region.
The HUR special operations unit was formed on June 1, 2022. Its personnel have fought in some of the war’s most contested areas and participated in land and Black Sea operations, including the 2023 campaign that helped open the road to Klishchiivka and create an escape route for Ukrainian forces encircled by the Russians in the Donetsk region’s Bakhmut.
Ukraine expands its robotic army
Ukraine is rapidly increasing its use of ground robots to reduce the number of soldiers exposed during supply runs and casualty evacuations.
President Volodymyr Zelensky set a target to provide the military with at least 50,000 ground robotic systems by 2026.
The systems are becoming a regular part of frontline operations as Ukraine seeks to compensate for personnel shortages and adapt to a battlefield where drones can detect and attack conventional vehicles several kilometers behind the contact line.

Cyberattack on software supplier affects Bern pension funds
An external software supplier to the Bern Pension Fund and the Bern Teachers’ Insurance Fund in Switzerland has fallen victim to a cyber attack.
The Swiss canton has no evidence that any data has been stolen.
The cyberattack took place at the end of September, the Department of Finance and the Department of Education and Culture jointly announced on Friday. The affected company, which has not been named, immediately filed a criminal complaint. The Office of the Attorney General is investigating.
According to the statement, the two pension funds are in contact with the relevant departments. It cannot be completely ruled out that data may have been stolen. Should this prove to be the case “contrary to all indications”, the pension funds will provide further information, the statement added.
The pension funds in question provide cover for, amongst others, cantonal staff, staff at cantonal universities and teachers in the canton of Bern. According to their own figures, as at the end of December last year, a total of more than 63,000 insured persons were members, in addition to more than 28,000 pensioners.

Israeli forces kill renowned journalist Wael Dahdouh’s nephew in Gaza
Israeli forces killed the nephew Al-Jazeera's Gaza office director Wael Dahdouh on Thursday, just a day after the three-year anniversary of the start of the war on the enclave.
Dahdouh, a renowned veteran journalist, has reported on successive Israeli wars on Gaza and became known internationally for his bravery amid Israel’s latest ongoing offensive on the enclave.
Israeli forces killed several members of his family, including his wife, three children and a grandchild. He was also severely wounded and is still recovering in Doha, Qatar, where he has been based after he was evacuated in January 2024.
“There is not much else to say in these moments; one really is conflicted on what to say. Even looking at photos is painful. Just now, I received a message that informed me that my nephew has been killed in Deir al-Balah in the centre of Gaza,” he said in an interview with Al-Jazeera Arabic.

— قناة الجزيرة (@AJArabic) October 9, 2026
“This is a martyr, someone who had a mother; this was a family that was turned upside down after three years of genocide, displacement, and bombardment. And in this moment, we remember all these things with such pain,” he continued.
He added that journalists, despite the Israeli attacks and killings targeting them, remain “messengers of the truth” in Gaza.
“If it weren’t for the journalists, Gaza would have been obliterated and erased with no one seeing or taking notice of it – because the Israeli operation has closed off and isolated Israel, separating it from the rest of the world and not letting any foreign reporters in. Even electricity, water, and telecommunications have been forbidden,” he added.
Dahdouh said it was the insistence of Palestinian journalists and their commitment to their role that helped get the message out to the world over the atrocities committed by Israeli forces in the enclave.
At least 263 journalists have been killed by Israel since October 2023, marking the highest toll of reporters in modern times.
Al-Dahdouh noted that journalists in Gaza have been targeted in their places of work, at home, in displacement camps, in vehicles, and their family members have also been attacked.
“If it wasn’t for the journalists in Gaza, we would not have known about all of these crimes and the pain, and we would not have seen change in stance around the world when it came to Israel and its global image. However, as civilians, journalists, victims, we have no hope left if Israel is not held accountable,” he said.
An further two Palestinians were killed, and several others wounded on Thursday, the official Palestinian WAFA news agency reported. It said that an Israeli drone targeted a car near the Jordanian Field Hospital, located southwest of Gaza City, citing medical sources on the ground.
The two people killed have been identified as Hussam Abu al-Atta and Majdi al-Ayyoubi.
At least 74,250 Palestinians have been killed and 175,278 injured in the Gaza Strip since the beginning of the Israeli aggression in October 2023.

Central China's Hubei unveils investigation report on major fireworks accident
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:49 CST
21:55:49 KST

WUHAN, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The emergency management department of central China's Hubei Province on Friday released an investigation report regarding a fatal fireworks accident that occurred in the city of Yicheng in the province on Feb. 18.
The accident took place at approximately 2:22 p.m. at a store located in Jinpu Village in this city, which caused 12 deaths and direct economic losses of 12.79 million yuan (about 1.9 million U.S. dollars).
According to the investigation, the direct cause was that a customer surnamed Xie illegally test-fired a firework in front of the store, which ignited a large quantity of fireworks displayed outside the store, triggering a chain of explosions and fires both outside and inside the premises.
People outside fled into the store, but the front door was blocked by the burning fireworks and the rear rolling shutter door was closed, preventing timely escape and resulting in heavy casualties.
The investigation pointed to a number of problems exposed by the accident, including illegal and irregular operations at fireworks and firecracker retail stores, lax government oversight of permit approval, ineffective performance of duties by local Party committees, governments and departments, and inadequate supervision of the flow of oversized or over-dosage products into the market.
The report noted that Xie has been arrested by public security authorities on suspicion of negligently endangering public safety by dangerous means. As the store's actual operator, surnamed Lin, had died in the accident, no criminal responsibility is recommended.
Yang, a co-operator of the store, is recommended to receive administrative penalties, with suspected criminal conduct transferred to public security authorities. ■

China's finance ministry pledges vigorous, effective implementation of more proactive fiscal policy
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:45 CST
21:55:45 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Finance said on Friday it would vigorously and effectively implement a more proactive fiscal policy, step up counter-cyclical adjustments, and introduce additional measures in a timely manner in response to macroeconomic developments.
In a report on the implementation of China's fiscal policy in the first half of 2026, the ministry said it would make full use of existing policy measures while planning and rolling out practical and effective new measures as needed, with a focus on expanding domestic demand, improving supply and safeguarding people's livelihoods.
The ministry said it would accelerate the allocation and use of fiscal funds, optimize the structure of government expenditure, and improve spending efficiency. It also pledged to expedite the issuance and use of government bonds to support project implementation.
Special treasury bonds will be issued to inject capital into eight central financial institutions, strengthening their resilience to risks and ability to serve the real economy, according to the report.
China has pledged to continue implementing a more proactive fiscal policy in 2026, with the deficit-to-GDP ratio set at around 4 percent and the total government deficit at 5.89 trillion yuan (about 875 billion U.S. dollars), this year's government work report noted. Expenditure in the general public budget is, notably, projected to reach 30 trillion yuan for the first time.
China's gross domestic product, meanwhile, grew 4.7 percent year on year in the first half of 2026, the National Bureau of Statistics has revealed.
During this same period, China's general public budget expenditure rose 1.5 percent year on year to 14.33 trillion yuan, with spending on healthcare and on social security and employment increasing by 10.8 percent and 7.6 percent, respectively, official data showed.
By the end of June, the central government had allocated 9.4 trillion yuan in transfer payments to local governments, accounting for 90.3 percent of the annual budget. Authorities also allocated 125 billion yuan in subsidies for consumer goods trade-in programs, helping generate roughly 1.1 trillion yuan in sales.
Fiscal policy support has also been reinforced via closer coordination with financial measures to stimulate investment and consumption.
This year, the central government earmarked 100 billion yuan for a package of six coordinated fiscal and financial policy tools aimed at boosting domestic demand. In the first seven months, these measures supported more than 20 trillion yuan in newly extended credit to relevant sectors, up 4.5 percent year on year, finance ministry data revealed.
Four investment-focused measures supported approximately 1.51 trillion yuan in private investment, while two consumption-focused measures supported around 1.88 trillion yuan in household consumption during the same period.
Authorities have also expanded interest subsidies for personal consumption loans and loans to micro, small and medium-sized enterprises and service-sector businesses, while introducing a new mortgage interest subsidy policy for eligible first-time homebuyers.
The mortgage policy, which took effect on Oct. 1 with a tentative implementation period of one year, provides an annualized interest subsidy of 1 percentage point on eligible commercial mortgage loans for first homes, with the subsidy period extending up to five years. This measure is intended to reduce borrowing costs for eligible homebuyers and support housing demand.
Looking ahead, the ministry said it would also support efforts to expand domestic demand on all fronts, promote technological and industrial innovation, safeguard and improve people's well-being, prevent and defuse risks in key areas, and deepen fiscal management reforms. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China saw 826 million domestic tourist trips during the recent seven-day National Day holiday, with tourism spending totaling 738.38 billion yuan (about 109.67 billion U.S. dollars), the Ministry of Culture and Tourism said on Friday.
On a daily average basis, the number of domestic trips rose 6.3 percent from the eight-day National Day and Mid-Autumn Festival holiday in 2025, while tourism spending increased 4.3 percent, according to the ministry.
The holiday witnessed a vibrant cultural scene, with 180 large-scale performances held nationwide, including 125 concerts and 55 music festivals.
Beyond cultural performances, the integration of tourism with culture, commerce and sports continued to deepen. Mass-participation sports events and digital innovations offered visitors new experiences and helped drive tourism-related consumption.
Meanwhile, around 40 percent of tourists visited revolutionary sites or took part in activities such as flag-raising ceremonies and patriotic performances.
This trend takes on added significance this year, which marks the 90th anniversary of the victory of the Long March (1934-1936). The arduous journey helped lay the foundation for the eventual victory of the Chinese revolution.
Dai Bin, president of the China Tourism Academy, said the flow of visitors to revolutionary landmarks reflects people's emotional identification with revolutionary traditions.
When they travel, they don't just want to see history. They also want to draw deeper inspiration from the revolutionary legacy for their lives today, Dai noted.
Measures to boost tourism consumption have also helped expand holiday options for visitors and enhance their travel experiences.
Under a nationwide cultural and tourism consumption campaign running from late September through October, local authorities have organized a variety of activities and distributed more than 310 million yuan in consumption subsidies. ■

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Ding Yexian, former deputy head of the standing committee of the People's Congress of the Xizang Autonomous Region in southwest China, has been expelled from the Communist Party of China (CPC), China's top anti-graft agency announced on Friday.
Upon the approval of the CPC Central Committee, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection (CCDI) and the National Commission of Supervision (NCS) had conducted an investigation into Ding's case, according to a statement by the CCDI and NCS.
The investigation found that Ding had lost his ideals and convictions, and resisted an official inquiry and investigation of his case, said the statement.
Ding was also found to have used his position and influence to benefit others in matters concerning company public listing, project contracting and business operations. In return, he accepted huge sums of money and valuables, the statement noted.
Ding violated the political, organizational and integrity discipline of the CPC, committed serious duty-related crimes and is suspected of bribery, the statement said.
In line with Party regulations and laws, a decision has been made to expel him from the Party, revoke his entitlements, terminate his capacity as a delegate to the 10th Party congress of the Xizang Autonomous Region, confiscate his illicit gains, and hand over his case for judicial proceedings. ■

South Africa withdraws asylum directive after violent anti-migrant protests
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:28 CST
21:55:28 KST

JOHANNESBURG, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- South Africa's Department of Home Affairs on Friday withdrew a directive instructing its Refugee Reception Offices to process asylum applications following a Constitutional Court ruling, amid violent anti-migrant protests in Johannesburg and Durban on Thursday.
In a statement, the department said Director-General Livhuwani Tommy Makhode had withdrawn the directive issued on Sept. 28 concerning the intake of asylum seeker applications following the Constitutional Court's July 7 judgment in the Scalabrini of Cape Town case.
The department said that implementing the ruling had "immediately led to serious consequences" that the court order could not have foreseen, adding that within days, refugee offices were overwhelmed, officials were placed at risk, and serious threats to public safety and order emerged.
It stressed that the directive was "a purely operational attempt to support the implementation of the Court's order" without the knowledge of the Home Affairs Minister or any other political office-bearer, rejecting claims that the decision was politically motivated.
The department said it would start a fresh process to find an appropriate and sustainable way to comply with the court's order. It also reaffirmed its respect for the judiciary and the rule of law.
The withdrawal came after violent protests on Thursday in Johannesburg's Soweto township and Durban, where demonstrators opposed the processing of asylum applications and demanded tougher action against irregular migration.
South African police said 10 vehicles were torched in Soweto and another 14 in Durban during the unrest. Foreign-owned shops were also looted, while three foreign nationals were arrested in Durban, according to police. ■

China Focus: New high-speed rail lines carry holiday crowds, energize Chinese cities
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
20:55:26 CST
21:55:26 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Liu Zengyuan, a railway engineer, watched familiar fields slip past the train window. This time, he was not heading to a construction site, but going home for the National Day holiday on the high-speed line he had helped build, just days after it opened.
This line, which officially entered service on Sept. 28, links Xiong'an in north China's Hebei Province with Shangqiu in Henan Province in central China. For Liu, it has cut the trip from Renqiu, his workplace in Hebei, to his hometown of Heze in east China's Shandong Province, from four or five hours to only two.
On the same day, China opened three other high-speed rail sections, connecting Xi'an with Ankang in Shaanxi Province in northwest China, Yichang with Xingshan in central China's Hubei Province, and Harbin with Yichun in Heilongjiang Province in the country's northeast. During the National Day holiday, from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, these new lines made it easier for people to visit relatives, and brought new vitality to tourism along the routes.
During the holiday, a Beijing resident surnamed Wang took his family by high-speed rail to Hengshui Lake, a national nature reserve in Hebei Province. He was pleasantly surprised to find the journey so convenient, as the trip took less than two hours, and a shuttle bus at the station took them straight to the scenic area.
This new line ended the history of Hengshui having no high-speed trains directly running to Beijing. Thanks in part to the new rail line and local promotions, 32 A-level scenic spots across Hengshui received 715,000 visitors during the holiday, soaring 202.84 percent year on year.
"Cities are much closer now, not just on the map but in everyday life," said Qu Xiaoyuan, an Ankang cultural and tourism official. His brother, who works in Xi'an, called him the day the Xi'an-Ankang high-speed railway opened, joking that he could dash to Ankang for a nice meal at home and still be back in Xi'an that night.
The line has cut travel time between the two cities from three hours to as short as 45 minutes. Ankang, a mountainous city in southern Shaanxi, is rich in ecological resources, and the new railway has taken a growing number of holiday travelers to its forests and rivers.
Ankang West Station, a new station built for the high-speed line, handled 50,800 outgoing passengers during the holiday, which was more than expected. The city also launched shuttle services linking the station with major scenic spots, where visits rose over 40 percent year on year.
As these new lines draw passengers from a wider area, weekend and short-holiday tourists may increase significantly, driving demand for multi-purpose and experience-oriented tourism products, Qu said.
Further east, the Yichang-Xingshan line brings destinations like southwest China's Chongqing and central China's Wuhan and Zhengzhou within two hours of Xingshan, weaving the Three Gorges, dense forests and cloud-shrouded peaks scattered along the route into easy, spontaneous trips.
Xingshan Station handled 14,216 outgoing passengers during the seven-day holiday, up 54.61 percent year on year. Local businesses in the city used high-speed rail tickets to link hotel discounts and reduce or scrap scenic spot admission fees.
Meanwhile, the northernmost high-speed railway in China connects Harbin, a major ice-and-snow tourism destination, with Yichun, a popular summer retreat and forest tourism spot. It cuts railway travel time between these two cities from about seven hours to roughly two hours, making it easier for more tourists to include Yichun in their holiday plans.
"Yichun used to be a 'maybe' destination because getting there was a hassle, but thanks to the new high-speed rail, it's now a 'must-go'," said a Shanghai visitor surnamed Zheng, adding that the new line has made the stay of his family in Heilongjiang more colorful.
Wang Wei, director of the Yichun Municipal Bureau of Culture, Radio, Television and Tourism, said the new railway will bring Yichun into Harbin's "two-hour economic circle," creating new opportunities for its winter tourism, forest study tours and forest wellness tourism.
Ma Botao, of the China Railway Economic Planning and Research Institute, said for cities newly connected to the railway network, seizing the opportunity depends on how well they position themselves.
"Generally, large cities focus on research and development, finance and headquarters economy, while small cities should leverage their local agriculture, ecology, tourism and distinctive industrial strengths to undertake supporting manufacturing, agricultural product processing, and wellness and cultural tourism, serving as both industrial supporting bases and leisure backyards for central cities," Ma explained.
Behind these expectations lies a network that keeps growing. By the end of 2025, the country's total operating railway mileage had reached 165,000 km, including more than 50,000 km of high-speed rail.
Under national plans, China's high-speed rail network is projected to hit 70,000 km by 2035, featuring eight north-south vertical lines and eight east-west horizontal lines. Once complete, the network will connect major cities, city clusters and key economic zones across the country. ■

SANAA, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Warplanes launched a new round of airstrikes on Yemen's Houthi-held capital Sanaa on Friday afternoon, the Houthi-run al-Masirah TV reported, attributing the attacks to what it called "Saudi aggression."
Residents told Xinhua that a series of powerful airstrikes hit sites in southern and western Sanaa, with explosions reverberating across the capital as warplanes flew intensively overhead.
The locations and nature of the targets were not immediately clear, and there were no immediate reports of casualties.
The latest strikes came amid a rapidly intensifying exchange of attacks between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia, with the group stepping up missile strikes against the kingdom and Saudi Arabia intensifying airstrikes on Houthi-held areas in Yemen.
Meanwhile, heavy fighting has continued between the Houthis and government forces, supported by the Saudi-led coalition, in southwestern Yemen, particularly near the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait.
Earlier on Friday, Yemeni government forces renewed an offensive against Houthi positions near Bab al-Mandab, seeking to expand recent gains and push deeper into Houthi-held areas overlooking the vital international shipping route, a government military official told Xinhua.
The official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the new push began on Friday morning from positions in Dhubab district in southwestern Yemen's Taiz province.
The official claimed that dozens of Houthi fighters had been killed in Friday's clashes, adding that government forces had called on Houthi fighters remaining in the area to surrender.
The al-Masirah TV, however, gave a conflicting account, saying Houthi forces had repelled government troops advancing from the neighboring province of Lahj toward the southern approaches to Bab al-Mandab, claiming dozens of casualties among the advancing forces and the destruction or disabling of several military vehicles.
Yemen has been embroiled in conflict since late 2014, when the Houthis seized Sanaa and much of the north. A Saudi-led coalition intervened in 2015 in support of the internationally recognized Yemeni government, now based in the southern port city of Aden.
The renewed fighting marked a major escalation after a UN-brokered truce in 2022 largely halted major hostilities. ■

WINDHOEK, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- Chinese contractors China Railway Seventh Group and Zhongmei Engineering Group, along with local partner firms, have completed two major infrastructure projects, delivering critical dual carriageway and corridor upgrades in Namibia's Khomas and Erongo regions.
Namibia's Minister of Works and Transport Veikko Nekundi on Thursday officially commissioned one of the projects, the 231.6 million Namibian dollars (13.9 million U.S. dollars) final stretch of the Southern Link dual carriageway outside the capital, Windhoek.
"The completion of this project marks the realization of a strategic investment in connectivity, mobility, economic growth, and public safety. It demonstrates the government's continued commitment to developing modern transport infrastructure that supports national development and improves the quality of life of our people," he said.
Though measuring just 1.5 km, the newly opened dual carriageway plays a pivotal strategic role in unifying southern Windhoek's transport network by seamlessly integrating the Auaspoort Interchange, key bridges, and surrounding road networks.
Nekundi commended the contractor, China Railway Seventh Group-Onamagongwa Trading Enterprises Joint Venture, and all 15 small and medium-sized enterprises for delivering complex engineering works under challenging conditions.
"I also extend my sincere appreciation to the project teams, engineers, technicians, safety personnel, machine operators, and laborers for their dedication and hard work," he said.
The commissioning of the Southern Link follows the official opening on Oct. 2 of the 498.6 million Namibian dollars Karibib-Usakos trunk road upgrade.
The 31.2 km expansion, upgraded to a 2+1 carriageway, was delivered by main contractor Zhongmei Engineering Group, with local Namibian partner companies holding a 25 percent share of the contract work.
Namibia's road infrastructure connects all major domestic regions and links the port of Walvis Bay to neighboring landlocked African nations via strategic transnational corridors. ■

Berlin rejects claim it dropped Franco-German tank project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:54:39 UTC
21:54:39 KST

Berlin rejects claim it dropped Franco-German tank project
BERLIN, Oct 9 - Germany on Friday dismissed remarks by the head of the French armed forces who said Berlin had decided to quit a troubled Franco-German tank project.
The dispute is the latest sign of strain in Franco-German defence cooperation after the two countries scrapped a joint next-generation fighter jet project in June.
The project involves tank maker KNDS, a holding company created between France's Nexter and Germany's Krauss-Maffei-Wegmann (KMW). Germany's Rheinmetall and France's Thales are also involved.
Berlin and Paris agreed in 2017 to work on the Franco-German Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) tank to succeed the German Leopard 2 and the French Leclerc, but the project has been marred by delays and infighting between the countries.
"Germany and France announced several months ago that they would adjust their joint Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) cooperation program, thereby incorporating the lessons learned from Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine," a spokesperson for the German Defence Ministry said.
"This does not mean the MGCS project has failed. On the contrary: We remain committed to equal partnership in the MGCS and are focusing on future technologies for armored combat."
The head of the French armed forces, Fabien Mandon, had described the result of the joint programme as "not good" at a parliamentary committee hearing on Thursday.
"We have noted that the Germans have decided to drop out of the project," he said.
Later, the French Defence Ministry issued a statement on behalf of Mandon, stressing the work on the joint tank had not been in vain.
It said the programme was continuing and retained "major importance, with a renewed focus on enhanced connectivity, collaborative combat, automation and robotics".
In June, Germany and France scrapped a major project to develop and build a new-generation fighter jet, bowing to industrial rivalries over Europe's most ambitious defence programme.
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron had concluded that there was no prospect of breaking months of deadlock between arms firms involved in the plan, German officials said at the time. REUTERS

Breadcrumb
Greens' Polanski loses key London by-election, Wali-Abdi becomes first Somali-born UK MP
UK Green Party leader Zack Polanski failed to secure seat in parliament on Thursday after losing the Holborn and St Pancras by-election to the Labour Party's candidate.
Sagal Abdi-Wali, the leader of the local council, won the central London constituency's seat with 12,292 votes, compared to Polanski's 8,928.
The defeat follows a media storm over the party's decision to pass the 'Zionism is Racism' motion at its annual conference—a vote which Polanski abstained from.
The 43-year-old former actor and hypnotherapist has moved the party leftwards, criticising Israel's genocide in Gaza and calling on the government de-proscribe direct action group Palestine Action.
While critics suggest Polanski’s defeat will put his leadership under question, the Green leader told Britain's Sky News he would stay on in his role, describing the result as part of "Andy Burnham's honeymoon".
Former leader Caroline Lucas who struggled to contain her anger over what she said was his lack of leadership over the motion on Zionism at last week's conference.
Under former prime minister Keir Starmer, Labour ceded ground to the Green Party, which made record gains in London in May's local elections as its appeal widened among younger, left-leaning voters in the capital and other urban areas.
The Greens have fallen back in opinion polls since Burnham made policy pitches that boosted Labour's standing among left-leaning voters, including a tougher line on Israel and a more ambitious approach to relations with the European Union.
The Greens have positioned themselves as an alternative to Labour for left-liberal voters and gained momentum after beating the governing party in a by-election last year in one of its northern England strongholds.
Thursday's by-election came after Starmer, stood down as a lawmaker in September after being ousted as leader in July.
Who is Sagal Abdi-Wali?
Abdi-Wali, who came to Britain as a child refugee from Somalia after escaping the Somali Civil War, said she was honoured to represent an area that had given her opportunities in life.
"I hope this moment also says something about who gets to belong," said Abdi-Wali. "For people who look like me, I hope they see themselves reflected in this place and know that their path too belongs here."
The MP made history in May, becoming Camden's first black female leader in the local elections, after being first elected as a local councillor in 2022.
She also served as the Cabinet Member for Better Homes, managing the borough's housing and neighbourhood development.
Critics have accused Abdi-Wali of being silent on Israel's genocidal war on Gaza since October 2023, as well as dodging questions on the subject during her campaign.
The former councillor did not sign the Palestine Solidarity Campaign pledge that called on the local candidates to work to end complicity in genocide.
Abdi-Wali also skipped a local elections hustings organised by the Camden Muslim Network, which Polanski and Liberal Democrat candidate Patrick Stillman attended, and later attended a similar event hosted by the Board of Deputies of British Jews.
Agencies contributed to this report.

Malaysia shuts schools as haze from Indonesian fires chokes Southeast Asia
Kuala Lumpur’s Air Pollutant Index says air quality at unhealthy levels amid smog from forest fires.
Malaysia has closed schools in its capital and several states as smoke from Indonesian forest fires pushes air pollution to unhealthy levels.
Schools were ordered to close on Friday across Kuala Lumpur, the administrative capital Putrajaya and in the states of Johor, Malacca, Negeri Sembilan, Pahang and Selangor.
The move, which affected roughly two million students, came as Kuala Lumpur recorded an Air Pollutant Index (API) reading of about 170. The API is a government-run measure of air quality.
Singapore, at the southern end of the Malay Peninsula, saw its air quality fall into the “very unhealthy” range, according to IQAir.
“The haze issue is indeed at a worrying level,” said Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim. He added that he had spoken to Indonesia’s President Prabowo Subianto, who had agreed to take “the necessary steps”. However, he offered no details on what that might entail.
Anwar said he had asked Malaysia’s minister of foreign affairs to push for an urgent meeting of ASEAN environment ministers. Kuala Lumpur is stepping up cloud seeding to trigger rain, he added.
“Appropriate measures must be taken by the relevant ministries and agencies to protect schoolchildren and students, including senior citizens and patients with respiratory illnesses,” King Sultan Ibrahim said. He declared that schools should close when API readings hit 150 or higher.
Under Malaysian guidelines, API readings above 100 are classified as unhealthy, above 200 as very unhealthy, above 300 as hazardous, while readings beyond 500 constitute the threshold for declaring a local emergency.
Education Minister Fadhlina Sidek promised parents more advance notice of closures in future.
In August, Indonesia’s coordinating minister for political and security affairs said that El Nino conditions were threatening more fires during the dry season.
A month later, smoke started to blanket the region as the country experienced its worst fire season in over a decade.
Fires have burned across six provinces, with at least 200,000 hectares scorched, Al Jazeera’s Jessica Washington reported.
Indonesia’s Ministry of Health has recorded more than 170,000 respiratory infections, but the actual figure is likely higher as it only covers those who sought out healthcare, she noted.
The haze has also worried organisers of Singapore’s Formula One weekend, which is set to start on Friday and end on Sunday.
Organisers have insisted that they will race regardless and will have masks and extra medics, adding that it is “not a threat”.

Consumer prices in Ukraine rose by 2.1% in September 2026, following increases of 0.1% in August and 0.3% in July, the State Statistics Service reported Friday.
The statistics agency recalled that prices had risen by just 0.3% in September 2025. As a result, year-over-year inflation reached 10.0% in September 2026, up from 8.1% at the end of August, 7.7% at the end of July and 7.2% at the end of June.
Core inflation also rose to 2.0% in September 2026, compared with 0.5% in August and 0.3% in July. Given that core inflation stood at 1.3% in September 2025, the year-over-year rate increased to 8.8%, up from 8.1% at the end of August.
According to the State Statistics Service, food and nonalcoholic beverage prices on the consumer market rose by 1.9% in September compared with August of this year. Eggs saw the largest increase, surging by 43.6%. Prices for sugar, rice, grain products, lard, milk, nonalcoholic beverages, fish and fish products, sunflower oil, meat and meat products increased by between 1.7% and 8.3%. Meanwhile, fruit and vegetable prices fell by 5.7% and 2.3%, respectively.
Clothing and footwear prices increased by 8.5%, including a 9.4% rise in clothing prices and a 7.6% increase in footwear prices. Prices (tariffs) for housing, water, electricity, gas and other fuels rose by 0.8%, mainly due to increases of 5.6% in water supply tariffs and 5.5% in sewerage tariffs.
Healthcare prices rose by 1.7%, primarily due to a 2.6% increase in pharmaceutical product prices. Education services became 17.4% more expensive, including increases of 23.3% for higher education and 14.3% for secondary education.
Fuel and lubricant prices increased by 5.2%, while fares for road passenger transportation rose by 2.5%.
As reported, the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) lowered its inflation forecast for 2026 to 10.0% from 9.4% in its previous forecast issued in April, while revising its forecast for 2027 to 6.9% from 6.5% in late July.
However, NBU Deputy Governor Volodymyr Lepushynsky subsequently noted in a column for Interfax-Ukraine that the July forecast update did not take into account new attacks on and the destruction of logistics infrastructure, which have led to additional increases in consumer prices that the central bank estimates at 0.4-0.6 percentage points (pp).
Later, the NBU estimated that a further increase in fuel prices would add 0.3 pp to inflation.

Private firms driving lunar development, but competition for resources poses risks: Space executive
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:52:31 UTC
21:52:31 KST

Tugba Altun and Emir Yildirim
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Private aerospace companies are playing an increasingly important role in developing infrastructure for future operations on the Moon, but competition for limited resources and suitable locations could create international disputes without clear regulations, a space industry executive told Anadolu.
Stirling Forbes, CEO of Forbes-Space, said the growing involvement of commercial companies marked the beginning of a "second space age," distinct from the government-led competition of the Cold War era.
Speaking on the sidelines of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya, Forbes said private companies were increasingly building infrastructure for both government and commercial use.
"These commercial companies are contributing to the construction of a shared, sustainable infrastructure that will generate returns for Earth," he said.
Forbes pointed to companies developing launch vehicles, lunar rovers, power systems, communications infrastructure and landing facilities.
"These missions range from, of course, the rockets from SpaceX or Blue Origin, down to the rovers of Astrobotic or Lunar Outpost, even to the infrastructure of power systems, communications, even landing pads," he said.
The growing range of commercial projects, he added, was laying the groundwork for a more diversified lunar economy.
Moon could become refueling hub for deeper space missions
Forbes said advances in artificial intelligence and robotics would be essential for future lunar operations, particularly in environments where machines must function autonomously without constant human intervention.
Such technologies could reduce risks to astronauts during early exploration and generate innovations with applications in industries on Earth, he said.
One potential business model involves using the Moon as a refueling station for spacecraft traveling farther into the solar system.
"I think, with the construction of more of this infrastructure on the Moon, one of the main business models is for the Moon to essentially be used as a fuel station," Forbes said.
He envisioned spacecraft stopping at lunar facilities to refuel before continuing toward Mars, the asteroid belt and other destinations.
Forbes also welcomed the growing participation of countries beyond the traditional space powers, citing Türkiye's planned lunar mission as an example.
"We live in a very exciting time of this commercialization, but also democratization of space," he said.
He described Türkiye's lunar program as "a fantastic example of new nation-states getting involved in this race for the Moon," while emphasizing the potential economic and technological benefits of space exploration.
Competition for lunar resources raises concerns
Despite the opportunities, Forbes warned that the concentration of valuable resources and suitable terrain in limited areas of the Moon could lead to disputes over access.
He estimated that only about 6% of the lunar surface offered favorable conditions for future infrastructure, based on factors such as access to water ice, solar energy and relatively flat terrain.
That concentration, he argued, could encourage powerful countries to seek control over strategically valuable locations, potentially excluding smaller nations and private companies.
Forbes called for transparent international regulations to ensure sustainable and nondiscriminatory access to lunar resources and infrastructure.
"We have to be very vigilant that this does not happen, and we have to build the regulations and structure to help the Moon go in a commercially sustainable direction rather than increasing militarization," he said.
He warned that allowing powerful countries to dominate lunar development could prevent emerging space nations and companies from benefiting from future opportunities.
Forbes said commercial companies should play an active role in shaping the rules governing lunar activities rather than leaving decisions exclusively to national governments.

“Accountability cannot be buried under the rubble,” said Agnes Callamard, Secretary General of Amnesty International.

Kidnappings and Home Invasions Soar as French Syndicates Extort Crypto
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:51:00 UTC
21:51:00 KST

Reported by
A father beaten and forced into a car trunk. A magistrate and her mother held hostage for 30 hours. A family terrorized overnight in northern France for digital cash. Over the past two years, a violent wave of kidnappings and home invasions has swept across France targeting cryptocurrency executives, influencers, and their loved ones, as criminal networks increasingly turn to physical torture to extort digital fortunes.
Organized criminal networks increasingly turn to home invasions, physical torture, and abductions to extort digital fortunes. Authorities have recorded 77 such incidents so far this year, up from 67 in 2025 and roughly 20 in 2024, according to data from France’s National Prosecutor’s Office for Organized Crime, known as PNACO.
While the early wave of violence primarily targeted high-profile industry executives and wealthy influencers, law enforcement officials warn that criminal syndicates are increasingly hunting ordinary citizens suspected of holding digital wallets. Just weeks ago, four armed intruders held a family captive overnight in the northern town of Vendin-le-Vieil, forcing the father to hand over about 40,000 euros, or $47,000, in cryptocurrency.
"This phenomenon, initially characterized by high-profile attacks on prominent figures in the sector, such as influencers, entrepreneurs, or platform executives, now appears to be spreading to a wider audience," PNACO said in a statement to OCCRP. "Perpetrators may indeed target individuals who are little known or entirely unknown to the general public, provided they identify them, rightly or wrongly, as holders of crypto-assets."
The home invasion in Vendin-le-Vieil is part of a chilling sequence of physical extortion cases across the country. In December 2024, the father of a Dubai-based French crypto influencer was kidnapped, beaten, and forced into the trunk of a car. In May 2025, the daughter of a cryptocurrency exchange founder narrowly escaped a broad-daylight abduction attempt in Paris when her partner and bystanders intervened. In February, a French magistrate and her mother were held hostage for 30 hours to exert leverage over the magistrate’s partner, the head of a cryptocurrency firm.
French law enforcement currently has 13 active judicial proceedings underway, with 95 suspects—including 13 minors—placed under formal investigation for offenses that include organized kidnapping, false imprisonment, aggravated violence, and money laundering.
Investigators say the spates of violence are rarely the work of lone actors. Instead, inquiries have revealed compartmentalized networks managed by shadowy masterminds who use social media to hire young operatives, often with prior criminal records, through digital intermediaries.
"The different participants do not necessarily know each other, and the perpetrators may be recruited only for a one-off operation," PNACO noted. "This multi-level organization complicates the identification of sponsors and the reconstruction of the entire criminal chain."
The international reach of these networks has already prompted cross-border crackdowns. Following intelligence supplied by French authorities, a key suspect arrested in Morocco was sentenced to 25 years in prison.
Prosecutors point to data leaks, public social media disclosures, and targeted phishing scams as the primary avenues through which criminals identify potential victims. Once a target is secured, the unique properties of digital currency make it an uniquely attractive target for violent coercion.
"Unlike a suitcase of notes, a transaction can be carried out very quickly," PNACO said, emphasizing that the speed of blockchain transfers allows perpetrators to drain millions within minutes before law enforcement can intervene.

CJP protest on October 10: SC's order on Delhi restrictions explained in 10 points

21:50:16 KST

The Supreme Court on Friday pushed back against sweeping transport restrictions in Delhi ahead of the Cockroach Janata Party (CJP)’s October 10 protest, observing that security measures should not bring the city’s public transport network to a standstill.The bench cautioned that an entire city cannot be shut down in the name of managing a protest, warning that blanket curbs on metro and train services could cause severe hardship to ordinary citizens.
READ ALSO: 'Anti-monopoly, not anti-business': Rahul Gandhi demands 'level playing field' for corporationsA bench led by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant, with Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana, was hearing petitions challenging the proposed closure of 57 metro stations and the cancellation of long-distance trains to the capital.Here are 10 key takeaways from the proceedings and the court’s directions:
1. No complete shutdown of metro services
The court made clear that metro trains cannot be completely stopped. “There shall be no complete prohibition on the movement of metro trains,” it said in its order.
2. Authorities must reconsider restrictions
Solicitor general Tushar Mehta told the bench he would urge the authorities to allow metro and other railway services to operate in a suitably regulated manner.
3. Public convenience must be protected
The bench highlighted the impact on students, employees, senior citizens and other commuters who rely on public transport to reach Delhi from neighbouring areas.
"Exercise caution. Exercise an abundance of caution. There is nothing wrong with that. You are responsible for maintaining law and order. But that responsibility is not merely about protecting State property", it said.
4. Security measures must be proportionate
Chief Justice Surya Kant said authorities could restrict unruly movement but should not deprive ordinary citizens of transport facilities.
5. Court invokes proportionality
"One very important principle that we follow for every citizen is the principle of proportionality. You have to prevent certain things. Take measures only to the extent necessary to prevent them. But that does not mean you should use a hammer to kill a fly. That principle must be kept in mind," the CJI said.
6. Train cancellations raised in court
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal flagged the cancellation of long-distance trains, arguing that passengers scheduled to arrive during the notified period would be unable to reach Delhi.
The bench said authorities should examine which areas required regulation and which did not, stressing that “there should be a free flow of traffic”.
8. Traffic advisory ordered
The court directed Delhi authorities to issue a traffic advisory for people travelling within the city by road.
9. Revised decisions must be publicised
Authorities were directed to give wide publicity to decisions on regulated metro and railway operations to minimise further inconvenience to commuters.
10. Centre asked to consider an alternative protest venue
The court asked the Union government to consider identifying a suitable location with adequate facilities for peaceful and lawful protests.The CJP protest is scheduled for October 10 at Jantar Mantar, with organisers demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar over alleged electoral roll irregularities.
