Poland: Lifeline for Ukrainian refugees confronts donor fatigue and online abuse as anti-Ukrainian sentiment grows
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

Poland: Refugee lifeline faces funding drop and online abuse
October 9, 2026
Hours after Vladimir Putin announced his "special military operation" in Ukraine on February 24, 2022, Russian troops began attacking Kyiv's Antonov Airport close to the home of Nastya Podorozhnya's family.
Nastya was 24 at the time and living in Krakow in neighboring Poland, having recently graduated from the city's Jagiellonian University.
Alarmed by the reports coming out of Ukraine and fearful of what was to come, Nastya rushed back to Ukraine two days before the invasion to be with her family and help her sister and her three children cross the border to safety in Poland.
Helping compatriots fleeing Ukraine
Nastya realized she could use her experience of living in Poland — how to get a doctor's appointment or simply buy a tram ticket — to help the many women and children arriving in the country from Ukraine.
Poles were offering help and food at the border, but some people sought to take advantage of the vulnerable arrivals.
"I spoke to activists engaged in anti-human trafficking and they said what was happening at the border in the first weeks after the invasion was like Christmas, Easter and birthdays rolled into one for traffickers because people were so easily trusting the volunteers," Nastya told DW in a two-bedroom apartment in central Krakow her organization uses to provide shelter to vulnerable women refugees escaping domestic abuse or trafficking.
Hotline still fields 100 calls a months
Named Martynka, after Nastya's youngest niece, the organization also runs a hotline. It has received more than 5,000 requests for help since March 2022 and now gets about a hundred every month.
Her small team provides psychological and moral support in four languages as well as legal assistance and counselling.
"One of the very young women who lived with us for a long time was drugged by her boyfriend who she met as a teenager when she escaped the full-scale invasion and after years of relationship she found out that he has been drugging her and selling sex with her to other people" she said.
Nastya said she was motivated to help partly because of a traumatic experience of her own. While studying in Krakow, a Ukrainian man tried to rape her outside of her dormitory.
After a long and difficult legal process, during which police detained the suspect before releasing him, he was eventually found guilty of violating Nastya's bodily autonomy and given a restraining order.
"This terrible, traumatic experience not only gave me horrible PTSD, which later on sort of helped me be empathetic and understand survivors with PTSD, but also it put me through the system of justice and how survivors are being treated," she added.
Aid cuts and donor fatigue
Since 2022, around 100 women and children have found shelter in the apartment. Her team's work relies largely on donations from international organizations.
But cuts to USAID have led to increased competition for grants, while donor fatigue has forced the team to cut its one-to-one therapy sessions.
"Ukraine is not in the headlines anymore," says Nastya. "The international attention has moved elsewhere. For all of summer 2026 we have been running a very challenging fundraising campaign. It is so hard to convince people to donate to a Ukrainian organization right now. There is something called exhaustion, donor exhaustion, fundraising exhaustion."
The UNHCR's acting representative for Poland, Czechia and Slovakia, Jun Shirato, confirmed the difficult situation in the aid sector.
Speaking to DW in Warsaw, she said that funding cuts last year have forced UNHCR to scale back its staff in Poland by two thirds, from 120 at its peak in the months after the invasion to 40 now. The UNHCR has now closed three of its regional offices opened in Krakow, Lublin and Rzeszow after Russia's invasion of Ukraine. Its sole remaining office in Poland is in Warsaw.
Changing attitudes to Ukrainians
Nastya's fundraising efforts increasingly meet with online abuse, too.
Attitudes toward Ukrainians in Poland have changed. In the months after the invasion, many Poles opened their homes to refugees, including Nastya's sister and her daughters.
The situation is now very different. Earlier this year, new rules restricting access to child benefits and free healthcare for refugees who don't work were introduced.
In the first half of this year, reports of hate crimes committed against Ukrainians in Poland rose by a third according to Polish police statistics.
Historical disputes fuel tension
At the same time, historical disputes between Poland and Ukraine, have resurfaced, fueling further hostility toward the Ukrainian community, which accounts for more than three quarters of all foreigners living in Poland.
In May, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's decision to name a military unit after the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA), which took part in the murder of tens of thousands of Poles during the World War II, triggered outrage in Poland.
Polish President Karol Nawrocki stripped Zelenskyy of Poland's highest state honor, the Order of the White Eagle.
While Poles focus on the UPA's massacre of Polish citizens, many Ukrainians view the UPA and nationalist leaders like Stepan Bandera as heroes because they fought against the Soviet occupation after the war.
"This week we are supporting a family of Ukrainians whose car was completely destroyed. No windows left in the car and with spray paint someone wrote 'Bandera people go back where you came from,'" said Nastya, adding, "I think it is so devastating and I've recorded a video about it. We have hundreds of comments there, of people wishing me death, wishing me to go back where I came from. It is very tough emotionally."
Animosity stoked by Russian bots
Nastya said the hostility is also driven by Russia using online bots to stoke tensions between Poles and Ukrainians.
"They do not want us to be together, or to remember who our common enemy is. They don't want Ukrainian refugees to integrate or feel welcome," she said.
Despite the strain, Nastya remains optimistic that she and her team can continue their work.
"For some reason I am — and this is the weirdest thing. I love my job so much. I want to do this beautiful thing. I would easily send my mother, my sister, my best friend to Martynka for support. I know there are few organizations that could provide such wonderful help."

Why Is China Proposing Reciprocal Nuclear Laboratory Visits?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:50:00 UTC
21:50:00 KST

On October 6, CNN reported that the United States and China are engaged in informal, preliminary discussion on reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities. According to the report, the idea was first raised by the Chinese side in meetings with U.S. officials this year, during which the two sides discussed U.S. Department of Energy national laboratories and their Chinese counterparts. The same source also indicated that the U.S. side is willing to discuss visits to nuclear test sites.
At the China-U.S. leaders’ summit held in September, the two sides agreed to build “a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness, and reciprocity.” According to CNN, however, they didn’t discuss reciprocal nuclear facility visits at the summit.
Reciprocal laboratory visits could serve to test the feasibility of limited nuclear transparency and give the broad political goal of “strategical stability” something concrete to work on. The question is whether the two sides can learn about each other’s nuclear institutions, their roles, and some of their activities, without harming their own national security.
In the mid-1990s, the United States and China set up the “U.S.-China Lab-to-Lab Technical Exchange Program” (CLL). Nuclear weapons laboratories under the U.S. Department of Energy and Chinese institutions including the China Academy of Engineering Physics participated in the project. The exchanges were conducted by scientists from both countries responsible for the technical management of nuclear forces, under the supervision of both governments, and were initially limited to nuclear arms control and nonproliferation. The program listed a shared goal: the exchange of information about the operation and management of nuclear facilities, while safeguarding the national security interests of both countries.
China hosted American scientists at its nuclear weapon laboratory and the Lop Nur test site, and showed them a variety of facilities. According to a U.S. participant, the United States authorized only small scale, restricted exchange on nuclear material protection and nuclear arms control verification technologies. Although the U.S. side had initially expressed a willingness to host Chinese scientists at the Nevada Test Site on a reciprocal basis, it withdrew that commitment later.
The two sides also ran into other obstacles. In 1996, for example, regarding a joint analysis plan for seismic data from mining activities on both sides, the China Academy of Engineering Physics declined to participate because the work was outside its scope. The Northwest Institute of Nuclear Technology also declined, out of concern that the data might be used to estimate the yields of China’s past nuclear tests.
In the late 1990s, the program was halted as China-U.S. relations worsened. In particular, a 1999 U.S. Congressional report accused China of stealing nuclear technology, which Beijing allegedly used “to fabricate and successfully test its next generation of nuclear weapons designs.” Scientists from both sides tried to revive the program during the administrations of Presidents George W. Bush and Barack Obama, without success.
This history shows that laboratory exchanges were a form of contact China and the United States have tried before, where information sharing and confidentiality requirements coexisted. While the experience of the 1990s cannot directly explain China’s current motivation for reviving the idea of reciprocal visits to nuclear facilities, it left a precedent. Whether the concept of reciprocal visits described in the CNN report aligns with the experience of such limited exchanges needs to be considered together with China’s current position on nuclear transparency.
China’s official position stresses transparency of intentions, but it also insists on protecting national security. The 2025 White Paper on Arms Control stated: “Given the current international security situation, transparency in intentions and policies is the most practical significance.” The 2026 NPT Compliance Report noted, however, that “inappropriate transparency may also undermine strategic stability” and advocated that nuclear weapon states should raise transparency step by step, in accordance with their own security environments and actual circumstances.
The report also noted that in March 2026, China organized a visit by permanent representatives to the United Nations, disarmament ambassadors, and high-level representatives from nearly 20 countries to the decommissioned 816 nuclear facility in Chongqing. Beijing included this in the section on “transparency and confidence-building measures.” A visit to a decommissioned facility does not prove that China would open an active nuclear weapon laboratory in the same way. But it shows that China already uses facility visits as a way to explain its nuclear policy to other countries.
Visits to active laboratories, however, may sit in a middle ground between policy transparency and transparency about nuclear forces. Nuclear weapons research institutions also undertake specialized work in areas such as arms control and nonproliferation. The earlier CLL program set out to explore ways of sharing selected information about nuclear materials and facilities while protecting sensitive national security information. The exchanges at that time covered how a nuclear weapons research institution can organize its arms control work, staff its operations, and carry out management. These issues go beyond a nuclear policy statement, but there is no need to discuss the number of warheads, deployment locations, or readiness status.
In addition, professional exchanges among nuclear agencies can foster a better understanding of each other’s working methods. Following the 1997 CLL program export control workshop, a Chinese representative stated that the workshop had given him a clearer understanding of the functional relationships among the U.S. government, laboratories, and technical experts. If the new reciprocal visits include such substantive dialogue, the laboratories could serve as a starting point for limited transparency: providing access to institutions and personnel in the nuclear field without immediately delving into discussions regarding the numbers, deployment and use of nuclear forces.
Such professional engagement could also become part of China-U.S. strategic nuclear dialogue. Chinese expert Li Bin has suggested that strategic nuclear dialogue could take place at various levels and involve different partners, and that Track 1.5 dialogue could include diplomatic departments, the military, and nuclear weapons laboratories. He also stressed that transparency should be a tool for achieving strategic stability.
Finding a form of openness that both sides can accept is only the first step. Laboratory visits could also allow each side to ask direct questions about specific work and hear the other side explain the purposes of its activities and technical judgments. If these discussions can correct misunderstandings and are carried forward by participants into their respective policy debates, they may reduce overreactions stemming from misreading. This is also where limited transparency can contribute to strategic stability.
Laboratory visits will not automatically resolve the conflict between nuclear strategy and the security interests of China and the United States. But they could serve as a limited test for the China-U.S. nuclear relationship in a new period. While the two sides still disagree on the size of nuclear forces, deployment, and the path of arms control, can they first exchange meaningful information on certain technical issues and keep talking afterward? If so, this limited transparency could provide a concrete example of the “strategic stability” called for by the leaders of both countries.

No, the French army did not deploy tanks against protesting students
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:49:32 UTC
21:49:32 KST

No, the French army did not deploy tanks against protesting students
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on: Modified:
France's student protests have sparked a wave of misleading content online. A viral TikTok falsely claimed the French army had deployed an armoured vehicle against protesters, when it was actually returning to a nearby military base. Other posts recycle 2023 footage of retirement protests as current events, while an AI-generated image was falsely presented as showing a police officer being attacked. Vedika Bahl examines how old, out-of-context and AI-generated content is fuelling misinformation.
France's student protests continued on Thursday, blockading schools and marching through cities across the country against underfunding, poor school conditions and a lack of teachers. The demonstrations have been violent in places, with hundreds of students, law enforcement officers and teachers injured. The violence has triggered discourse surrounding some protesters' use of violence, as well as accusations of heavy-handed riot police, as rights groups accuse them of using excessive force against children.
But alongside the protests, a wave of misleading content has been circulating online, including claims that the French army has deployed armoured vehicles against students.
One TikTok video, viewed more than 2 million times, appears to show an armoured vehicle driving past a group of protesting high school students. Captioned: "They brought back the tank", the video prompted outrage among internet users who believed the army was being deployed to suppress the demonstrations.
Whilst the video is genuine, its context is misleading.
The FRANCE 24 Observers geolocated the footage to a car park opposite Bernard Palissy High School in Gien, central France. The location matches details visible in the video, including the school building, a dividing wall and a nearby house with several chimneys.
But if it's not linked to the student protests, why was a French army vehicle passing directly outside the school?
Around 500 metres from the school's campus are the barracks of the 12th Equipment Support Base, a military unit responsible for maintaining armoured vehicles for the French army. The vehicle in the video was travelling back to the nearby barracks. There is no evidence that it was deployed against the students or that its presence was connected to the demonstrations.
The French Ministry of the Armed Forces confirmed this to FRANCE 24, describing the journey as a "routine journey with no connection to current events at the school".
The misleading video is part of a broader wave of content circulating around the protests, including old footage, images taken out of context and AI-generated material.
One viral post, for example, claims to show protesters "seizing" the Paris Stock Exchange, describing the footage as the beginning of a "global revolution".
But the video predates the current student protests. It has been online since 2023 and shows protesters entering the offices of Euronext, the company that operates financial markets including the Paris Stock Exchange.
The footage was filmed during protests against the French government's decision to raise the retirement age and predates the current student demonstrations by several years.
AI-generated imagery has also been presented as authentic footage from the protests.
One Facebook post claimed to show a policewoman being chased and beaten during a high school blockade. The image attracted thousands of comments and likes.
However, the image was generated using OpenAI tools, with its digital watermark indicating that it was AI-generated.

Annual inflation in Ukraine rises to 10%

Annual inflation in Ukraine rises to 10%
Consumer prices in Ukraine rose by 2.1% in September compared with August and by 10% year on year.
Source: a new express report by the State Statistics Service of Ukraine
Details: Core inflation stood at 2% compared with August 2026 and 8.8% compared with September 2025.
Prices for food and non-alcoholic beverages rose by 1.9%. Eggs saw the sharpest increase, rising by 43.6%.
Prices for sugar, rice, grain products, milk, non-alcoholic beverages, fish and fish products, sunflower oil, meat and meat products rose by between 1.7% and 8.3%.
Meanwhile, fruit and vegetable prices fell by 5.7% and 2.3% respectively.
Clothing and footwear prices rose by 8.5%, with clothing up by 9.4% and footwear by 7.6%.
Prices for housing, water, electricity, gas and other household fuels rose by 0.8%, mainly due to increases in water supply tariffs (5.6%) and sewerage tariffs (5.5%).
Healthcare prices rose by 1.7%, primarily due to a 2.6% increase in medicine prices.
In addition, fuel and lubricant prices rose by 5.2% in September, while fares for road passenger transport increased by 2.5%.
Finally, education services became 17.4% more expensive, with prices for higher education rising by 23.3% and secondary education by 14.3%.
Background: In September, the National Bank of Ukraine decided to raise its key policy rate to 16% amid mounting inflationary pressures.

Ukrainian petrol stations fortified with sand and concrete to keep operating amid Russian attacks
Ukrnafta, Ukraine's largest state-owned oil and gas company, is installing sand-filled protective barriers at its petrol stations in Kyiv and says it has secured enough fuel supplies for the winter even if demand rises by an expected 10-15%.
Source: Reuters, citing Lesia Zharska, director of Ukrnafta's petrol station network
Details: To protect its stations in the capital, the company has installed gabions – metal structures filled with sand. It plans to install them in other cities soon. Ukrainian fuel retailers are increasingly equipping petrol stations with protective barriers and concrete shelters.
Russian strikes have damaged at least six Ukrnafta petrol stations in Kyiv in recent weeks. Zharska said some stations have been able to resume operations within a few days of being attacked.
The company has already equipped its petrol stations with generators and secured supplies of sufficient volumes of imported fuel to prevent supply disruptions, Zharska said.
During air raids, petrol stations suspend operations and customers are asked to leave the premises, while staff head to shelters.
Background: Russian forces attacked one of Ukrnafta's petrol station complexes in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast twice. No casualties were reported.

Case over alleged UAH 129 mln embezzlement during water pipeline reconstruction sent to court
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:47:37 EEST
21:47:37 KST

A prosecutor from the Specialized Anti-Corruption Prosecutor’s Office (SAPO), based on an investigation by the National Anti-Corruption Bureau of Ukraine (NABU), has sent an indictment to court in a case involving the alleged embezzlement of UAH 129 million allocated for the restoration of critical infrastructure in Kamianske district, Dnipropetrovsk region.
Seven people have been charged, including a local businessman alleged to have organized the scheme, the head of the municipal enterprise that commissioned the reconstruction, the director and deputy director of the company that won the tender, the head of an intermediary company used for procurement, a deputy head of the design organization and an employee of a company controlled by the alleged organizer, SAPO said in a Telegram post on Friday.
According to the investigation, members of an organized group helped a company controlled by the alleged organizer win a 2022–2023 tender for reconstruction of a water pipeline in Kamianske district.
Under the contract, the winning company was required to purchase pipes. Investigators found that the pipes were bought from the manufacturer at market prices and then resold to the municipal enterprise at prices more than three times higher, SAPO said.
The alleged scheme caused losses of more than UAH 129 million to the municipal enterprise. The suspects allegedly took control of the funds and disposed of them at their own discretion, the anti-corruption prosecutor’s office said.
The alleged organizer and people under his control subsequently laundered the funds by transferring them to accounts of other related companies, SAPO said.
The beneficial owner of the company that won the tender was a prominent local businessman who was wanted by the US Federal Bureau of Investigation for property crimes, SAPO added.

Russia has a plan for Ukraine this winter, Ukraine says: intercepted document reportedly outlines up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting 60 critical infrastructure sites
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:46:56 UTC
21:46:56 KST

Russia is planning a winter strike campaign involving up to 1,000 missiles, drones, and bombs targeting, among other facilities, electrical substations, hydroelectric and thermal power plants, and boiler houses. The information is contained in a document that, according to sources cited by The New York Times, Ukraine's Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal presented as an intercepted Russian plan to destroy energy infrastructure systematically. The newspaper reported on 2 October.
Russia has been striking critical infrastructure across Ukraine since the beginning of its full-scale invasion. Such attacks have become particularly frequent ahead of and during winter. Ukraine's recent battlefield gains may have prompted Putin to reconsider his strategy and attempt to force Ukraine to surrender through winter strikes, analysts at the Institute for the Study of War (ISW) suggest. Russia's reported plans to attack Ukraine's energy, water supply, and sewage systems could threaten the basic living conditions of millions of people. Such strikes could increase pressure on civilians and the Ukrainian economy while forcing the state to divert more resources to emergency infrastructure repairs instead of defense needs.
The New York Times was unable to verify the document's authenticity independently, but noted that it was written in Russian and dated August.
Warehouses, a home-improvement store, a farm: Russia’s strikes aimed past the grid at Ukraine’s civilian economy
A representative of Ukraine's defense-industrial sector who has reviewed the document believes it is more of a calculation than a finalized Russian military operations plan, according to Schemes, an investigative journalism project by Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), in a report published on 8 October.
60 targets: how Russia could attack Ukraine's critical infrastructure
The document outlines how many missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to deprive Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa of electricity, heating, water, and sewage services, Radio Liberty reported on 9 October. The document's full list of priority cities also includes Dnipro, Zaporizhzhia, Mykolaiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryvyi Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskyi, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk.
According to the document, Russia plans to begin by attacking substations near Ukraine's western border, through which the country receives electricity from Europe. Hydroelectric power plants could be targeted next, followed by facilities intended to shut down Ukraine's three operational nuclear power plants, Radio Liberty reports. The document lists a total of 60 key targets.
According to Schemes, the document states that Russia would need up to 770 Molniya and Geran drones, Dan-T/Banderol missile-drones, 170 FAB guided aerial bombs, and 75 Kinzhal and Iskander-M ballistic missiles to carry out the attacks.
Sewage systems could become Russia's next target
The document devotes particular attention to water supply and wastewater systems. These include pumping stations, treatment facilities, and other infrastructure essential for cities to provide residents with water and dispose of wastewater.
Russia has not previously attacked such facilities on a similar scale, The New York Times notes.
Preparing for possible attacks on water supply and sewage systems is significantly more difficult than protecting energy infrastructure, Oleh Popenko, head of the Ukrainian Union of Utility Services Consumers, told Current Time, RFE/RL's Russian-language network.
“Sewage is a very complex system. There are specific challenges: where to discharge wastewater, how to organize treatment facilities, and so on. Some work is also underway in this sector, but it will be much more difficult here than with district heating utilities,” Popenko says.
Creating alternative routes in case sewage pumping stations are destroyed is an expensive and technically challenging task, he adds. Such construction could cost billions of hryvnias.
14 dead in Pryluky, two each in Kyiv, Kremenchuk, and Oleksandriia: Russia’s night of 70 missiles
The priority is to equip water utilities with backup power sources so they can continue operating during power outages. However, if Russian strikes damage the sewage system itself, resolving the problem quickly will be much more difficult, Popenko believes. Specific solutions, including wastewater disposal and the operation of treatment facilities, will have to be determined according to the extent of the damage.
Sewage pumping stations play a particularly important role. They pump wastewater onward for disposal and treatment. If such a station is put out of operation by a strike, the city needs an alternative way to divert wastewater while the damaged facility is being repaired, Popenko says. Bypass pipes or channels could be installed for this purpose, but setting up such a system during wartime is far from easy.
Air defenses remain crucial to Ukraine's winter preparations
Preparations for winter are underway, but protection for energy infrastructure remains inadequate, Popenko believes. The main concern is large substations that transmit electricity from nuclear power plants and distribute electricity imported from Europe.
At the same time, some protective measures are already proving effective. Despite drone attacks over two days, one of Kyiv's substations withstood the strikes, and the city did not lose power, although scheduled outages were in effect, the expert says.
Popenko considers a repeat of last winter's scenario, when parts of Kyiv went without heating for weeks, entirely possible. Russian forces continue to attack energy facilities, and in his assessment, strengthening air defenses in Kyiv is the only way to protect its combined heat and power (CHP) plants from large-scale attacks.
“There are no other ways — for example, building some sarcophagi around CHPs or constructing shelters — because Russia can destroy these facilities again through massive strikes. And then the city risks being left 50–60% without heat,” Popenko believes.
Residents are also preparing for winter, but their options vary, he says. Some homeowners' associations participate in government programs to insulate apartment buildings and purchase backup power supplies for elevators and pumping stations. Owners of private houses are buying generators, among other measures. However, such equipment and preparations require substantial funds, meaning not everyone can afford them, he notes.
Ukraine has already experienced prolonged power outages during previous winters, particularly in 2022 and 2023. At the time, some regions went without electricity for 18–20 hours a day, the expert says. This experience may help people prepare for possible disruptions, but it does not eliminate the risk of further attacks and infrastructure damage.

University president reveals clash with Kisch amid Oct. 7 mourning, warns of academic brain drain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:46:51 UTC
21:46:51 KST

It has been a tumultuous term as chairman of the Association of University Heads Prof. Daniel Chamovitz. Now, as he prepares to step down, Chamovitz reveals what took place between him and Education Minister Yoav Kisch, discusses the brain drain from Israeli academia and questions why tens of millions of shekels promised to help students serving in the military reserves have yet to arrive.
"I was convinced he was calling to ask how he could help," Chamovitz recalled of a phone call from the education minister about two weeks after the October 7 massacre. "By then, it was already clear that we had lost so many people and that students had been kidnapped, and he asked me why I had signed a letter opposing his decision. I was in the middle of a shiva mourning visit for one of our students.
"I said, 'What? Yoav, I thought you were calling to see how the university was doing.' He said, 'No. Why did you sign it?' I said, 'Yoav, do you understand what happened here?' He replied that things had happened throughout the education system. What happened next was not my most presidential moment."
The letter in question was written by the Association of University Heads, known by its Hebrew acronym VERA, and signed by university presidents ranging from those of Bar-Ilan and Ariel universities to the Weizmann Institute of Science and the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
The letter opposed Kisch's attempt to require universities to expel students who expressed support for terrorism, arguing that the universities were already taking action against such students on their own.
"While we are burying our dead, visiting the families of those we have lost and dealing with a very small number of cases involving expressions of support for murderous terrorist organizations, you are advancing such a decision? We have lost confidence in you," the university presidents wrote.
Clashes from the start
Chamovitz said his first conversation with Kisch focused on appointments to the Council for Higher Education.
"He told me, 'The only thing I have is appointments.' I tried to explain to him that there are public appointments and scientific appointments to the Council for Higher Education, and that the public appointments are his to make. He replied, 'I want them to be my appointments.'
"What do you mean, yours? Do you know who is a good biologist and who isn't? How can an education minister know which scientist is suitable to serve on the Council for Higher Education?
"When you start making appointments based on loyalty, you begin putting the system at risk. There were people whose appointments we ultimately agreed to because we thought they were qualified. But it makes no sense for a politician to say, 'I want Professor A or Professor B on the Council for Higher Education.' That's never how it worked."
Chamovitz then turned to the main challenges facing Israeli academia.
"Israel has fallen in the OECD rankings for funding per student since 2000, and that's why we're beginning to see a significant brain drain. No university wants to talk about the numbers because they're troubling.
"I'm talking about researchers who already held professorships here, with grants and laboratories, who decide to go on sabbatical and never come back. Over the past three years, Israelis leaving academia in Israel for positions abroad has become more than just an isolated curiosity. It's a worrying phenomenon."
Do you have data on this?
"It's more than just a feeling. You can see it happening. Let's call it social science rather than exact science."
Isn't it natural for an outstanding researcher to receive offers?
"It's happening more than it used to. The Finance Ministry's Budget Department sees higher education funding as an engine of growth for the country. They're doing everything they can not only to protect the higher education budget but even to increase it. But it's not among the government's political priorities."
According to Chamovitz, there is also a threat from elements within the government seeking to restrict academic freedom.
"There's absolutely no doubt that some members of the outgoing government are uncomfortable with universities having the freedom to ask questions. There have been legislative proposals aimed at restricting universities, such as the one introduced by Knesset member Avichai Boaron, which Minister Kisch supported. Academia and research thrive when universities have the freedom to operate and conduct research."
He added: "People confuse freedom with loyalty. Around the world, we see forces demanding that universities be loyal, whether in Turkey, Russia, China or certain U.S. states.
"And loyal to whom? Loyal to the ruler. Every time that happens, academia collapses. Look at what happened in Hungary, Turkey, Russia and Germany 100 years ago.
"Academia and research thrive when universities have the freedom to operate and conduct research without thinking about what the ruler wants. When we came under attack, it was because people interpreted statements or positions as disloyalty. Universities are not partisan."
"All the politicians who attack us in the media have no problem calling and saying, 'Hi Danny, this is Knesset member so-and-so. My daughter is amazing. She wants to get into medical school. She's just 50 points short.'"
Ben-Gurion University has seen its share of controversies. One example involved Knesset member Almog Cohen, who barged into a humanities and computer science class taught by Dr. Sebastian Ben Daniel, a lecturer who had made statements against IDF soldiers.
Chamovitz, however, appears unfazed.
"It's very convenient for politicians to attack academia. But there's something really, really funny about it: All the politicians who attack us in the media have absolutely no problem calling me and saying, 'Hi Danny, this is Knesset member so-and-so. Listen, my daughter is amazing. She wants to get into medical school. She's just 50 points short,'" he said.
The missing millions
Three years of war have taken a toll on universities, and especially on students, with military reservists bearing the brunt of the burden.
"As chairman of the Association of University Heads, I was involved in the various assistance programs. The government was supposed to transfer a relatively small sum of 10 million shekels to the universities to help reservists for the 2020-21 academic year, and we never received it. There's also a signed agreement with the chief reserve officer for 80 million shekels, and none of that money has arrived."
According to Chamovitz, although some reservists are frustrated by the situation, most have not dropped out of school. Universities have made accommodations and provided them with benefits.
"They actually performed better academically than the average student," he noted.
Education Minister Yoav Kisch responded: "He's quick to point out others' faults while ignoring his own. Since taking office, I have led significant decisions at the Council for Higher Education to benefit combat soldiers and students serving in the reserves, and advanced a historic legislative change giving them priority in admission to higher education. I strengthened academia, particularly in Israel's peripheral regions, worked to expand medical education in Israel and opened four new medical schools within two years.
"Professor Daniel Chamovitz and some of his fellow university presidents opposed every attempt at change for political rather than substantive reasons. They fought against opening additional medical programs, even at the cost of having fewer doctors in Israel.
"When faced with incitement and expressions of support for terrorism on campuses, they took a weak and cowardly approach. At the same time, they fought to keep control of the Council for Higher Education in their own hands.
"They had grown accustomed to education ministers who simply rubber-stamped their decisions.” That era ended when I took office."
"It's amusing that Chamovitz, of all people, gave an interview to Yedioth Ahronoth on Thursday and lectured me about the politicization of academia. There is no limit to the hypocrisy."
The Defense Ministry also responded regarding funding for students serving in the reserves:
The ministry allocated 10 million shekels for the 2025-26 academic year to assist undergraduate students studying STEM subjects — science, technology, engineering and mathematics — who serve in the military reserves and qualify for the A+ classification.
"The ministry instructed universities to submit the necessary approvals and documentation for the financial assistance they have already provided to students. Once the required documentation is received, the transfer of funds can be completed in accordance with the government decision."

The Palace of Italian Institutions in Tangier through the lens of photographer Massimo Listri
Italy
Unknown Publisher

14:46:20 CEST
21:46:20 KST

There is a thread linking Marrakech and Tangier, and on Thursday evening it passed through the halls of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech. A thread of light, of images, of shared memory. As part of the 6th edition of the “Les Rencontres de la Photographie de Marrakech” initiative—dedicated this year to the Bicentennial of Photography, 1826–2026: Two Centuries of Light—the preview of the art book dedicated to the Palace of Italian Institutions in Tangier, featuring the unique perspective of Massimo Listri, took place. A collaborative evening, organized in partnership with the Italian Embassy, the European Institute of Sardinian Studies, the Italian Cultural Institute in Rabat, and the YSL Museum in Marrakech, to celebrate what photography does best: bringing together heritage and the present, on opposite shores of the same Mediterranean. The event opened with heartfelt remarks from Alexis Sornin, director of the Yves Saint Laurent Museum in Marrakech: “We are delighted to host a project that builds a cultural bridge between two iconic cities, Marrakech and Tangier. This is the very essence of our work.” Next came remarks from Pasquale Salzano, Italian Ambassador to the Kingdom of Morocco. “This is a book we care deeply about,” Salzano told the audience. “Tonight in Marrakech, we wanted to offer an intimate first glimpse of it. Then it will return home: it will be officially presented in December in Tangier, right inside the palace it depicts.” A thought for the absent maestro, Massimo Listri, who was unable to attend the event: “We would have been happy to share this moment with him.” And thanks to Serena Cinquegrana, director of the Italian Cultural Institute in Rabat, who guided the audience on a visual journey through the palace’s rooms, vistas, and light. “The Palace of Italian Institutions is much more than a historic building,” Salzano noted. “It is the former palace of Sultan Moulay Abdelaziz, which has served as the seat of the Italian State in Morocco since 1926. It is a place where histories, cultures, and generations have intersected. A living heritage that continues to speak when we look at it, share it, and pass it on.”

EU paid €7.9bn for Russian Arctic LNG amid record imports
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:45:20 UTC
21:45:20 KST

Continued Russian LNG imports undermine the credibility of the EU’s promise to sever its energy ties with Moscow, particularly as Russia continues its war against Ukraine.
Europe paid around €7.88 billion for liquefied natural gas (LNG) from Russia’s Arctic energy project in the first nine months of 2026 despite Brussels’ efforts to phase out gas from Moscow, according to the campaign group Urgewald.
The figures, compiled by Urgewald using data from the market intelligence firm Kpler, expose just how reliant the EU remains on Russian energy, with a record of 12.18 million tonnes reaching European ports between January and September this year.
The EU has been trying to wean itself off Russian energy for a while, and this year introduced a number of measures to end its reliance on Moscow. Brussels introduced a ban on new Russian energy contracts at the beginning of 2026, with a complete ban on Russian LNG taking effect on 1 January 2027.
Meanwhile, the Trump administration recently announced the Lindsey Graham Act, giving the US the power to sanction Russian LNG deliveries to Europe before the EU's import ban kicks in.
This comes at a time when Europe's gas storage levels are at a record low, and the bloc faces a brutal energy crisis, leaving Brussels increasingly vulnerable to decisions from Washington, the EU's major LNG supplier.
European LNG imports from the Russian Yamal project rose 9.5% year-on-year between January and September, with EU ports receiving 85% of Yamal’s recorded deliveries.
France received nearly three-quarters of September’s EU deliveries, with the Dunkirk and Montoir ports receiving 571.716 million tonnes of Arctic LNG, according to Kpler.
The Netherlands imported 146.461 million tonnes of LNG and Portugal 74.263 million tonnes. No cargoes were recorded in Spain or at Belgium’s Zeebrugge terminal.
The persistence of the Arctic LNG trade into Europe shows the difficulty of translating a long-term phase-out commitment into an immediate commercial break.
Ineffective short-term bans
The figures also raise questions about the effectiveness of the EU’s initial restrictions on Russian LNG.
A ban on imports under existing short-term contracts took effect on 25 April, but September deliveries reached 792,440 tonnes, slightly above the level a year earlier.
The EU’s full ban on Russian LNG under eligible existing long-term contracts is scheduled to take effect on 1 January 2027.
Until then, continued purchases generate revenue for Russia's war against Ukraine and expose the limits of restrictions that target some contracts without immediately stopping the wider trade.
"We have always assumed that the impact would not be particularly significant, since most of the export capacity is tied up in long-term contracts anyway," Sebastian Rötters, energy campaigner at Urgewald, told Euronews.
"In addition, export volumes are generally lower in the summer due to maintenance work at the terminal and LNG shipments to Asia via the Northern Sea Route," Rötters added.
The real litmus test for Yamal will be the EU’s phase-out starting in 2027, Rötters said, noting it may lead to noticeable reductions in exports due to the increased logistical challenges.
Call to strengthen 22nd sanctions package
The German-based NGO Urgewald is calling for the upcoming 22nd EU sanctions package to close loopholes, particularly those supporting the specialised Arc7 ice-class tanker fleet needed to transport LNG from the Arctic.
Yamal’s reliance on specialised vessels makes its export system vulnerable to restrictions on transport and associated services.
European ports are also geographically convenient destinations, allowing tankers to unload and return to the project relatively quickly.
Urgewald argues that disrupting those logistics could pile pressure on Russia’s ability to sustain Arctic LNG exports.
"The EU should not wait passively for the 2027 embargo to take effect. The next sanctions package should close the remaining loopholes, above all those that keep the indispensable Arc7 LNG tanker fleet operating. Washington, meanwhile, now has the power to sanction this trade at any time before then,” reads Urgewald's statement.
However, such measures would require political coordination among the EU and its member states and could complicate European gas procurement before the import ban takes effect and ahead of an unpredictable winter season.
The data provided does not establish how much of the trade could be redirected to other buyers or what the consequences would be for European gas prices, but any additional trade disruption on top of the loss of LNG from the Middle East would have an impact.
Trump gains another lever over the EU’s energy security
US sanctions under the Lindsey Graham Act could disrupt trade before the EU's ban on Russian LNG takes effect, forcing European governments and buyers to respond.
The US administration faces an 18 October deadline for its first review under the law. However, the deadline should not be mistaken for an automatic ban on Yamal deliveries, Urgewald say, as the law’s practical impact depends on how the administration exercises its powers.
"The US President must compile a list of ships transporting Russian LNG by October 18. These ships will then be subject to sanctions unless Trump issues so-called waivers. This is possible and, given Trump’s track record regarding Russia, not unlikely," Rötters told Euronews.
EU imports from Yamal will depend on the goodwill of the US President from 18 October until the final embargo takes effect in 2027, Rötters stressed.
US sanctions have already severely restricted Russia’s Arctic LNG 2 project and the Northern Sea Route, while Yamal LNG continues to supply Europe.
Data from Kpler shows that 706.473 million tonnes of LNG were destined for China, South Korea and Taiwan in September this year.

Seals and sea lions undergo hearing tests in Australian research
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:45:16 UTC
21:45:16 KST

Two sea lions and two fur seals learned to press a paddle whenever they heard a tone, receiving fish as a reward for correct responses. The study, reported on 9 October, found the animals were most sensitive to sounds around 3.2 kilohertz. Researchers say the results provide a starting point for assessing noise from ships, aircraft and coastal construction.
The findings are particularly important for the endangered Australian sea lion, whose population is estimated at just 12,000. These animals rely on hearing to communicate, find food, navigate and detect danger.
Lead researcher Christine Erbe, from Curtin University, said scientists first needed to establish which sounds the animals could hear before measuring their impact. The results could help guide environmental assessments and noise controls as maritime industries expand. Researchers now plan to investigate how underwater noise affects the animals' hearing and behaviour.

Unknown

US lawmakers push green card bill for Hongkongers, but observers doubt success
Broad Republican opposition to immigration expansion and tight legislative calendar expected to derail Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act
Two US lawmakers are pushing for a bill that would allow Hongkongers in the country to apply for permanent residency, but authorities and observers have dismissed it as a political move unlikely to succeed.
Senator Jeff Merkley, an Oregon Democrat, and Representative James McGovern, a Massachusetts Democrat, announced the Hong Konger Promise of Refuge Act, seeking to provide a pathway to green cards and ultimately citizenship for Hong Kong residents in the US currently protected under the Deferred Enforced Departure (DED) programme.
Introducing the bill, Merkley accused Beijing and Hong Kong authorities of continuing to “undermine the fundamental rights and freedoms of Hongkongers”.
“The United States must protect Hong Kong residents who have sought refuge in America,” he said. “Congress must take action and enact our legislation to ensure Hongkongers residing in the US do not have to fear deportation.”

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. Russian troops liberated five communities in the Kharkov, Sumy and Zaporozhye Regions over the week of October 3-9, including one community during the past 24 hours in the special military operation in Ukraine, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup North units took control of the settlement of Annopolye in the Kharkov Region through active and decisive operations. In addition, Battlegroup North forces established control of the settlement of Novaya Kazachya in the Kharkov Region and yesterday they gained control of the settlement of Kiyanitsa in the Sumy Region. <…> Over the past week, Battlegroup East units continued their advance deep into the enemy’s defenses and liberated the settlements of Samoilovka and Golubkovo in the Zaporozhye Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian troops deliver eight precision strikes on Ukrainian military sites over week
Russian troops delivered one massive and seven combined strikes by precision weapons and unmanned aerial vehicles on Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, telecommunications centers, ammunition, fuel and materiel depots over the week, the ministry reported.
"On October 3-9, 2026, the Russian Armed Forces delivered one massive and seven combined strikes, hitting military-industrial enterprises, logistics and telecommunications centers, energy and transport infrastructure facilities used to support the Ukrainian army’s operations, military airfields, sites producing and storing unmanned aerial vehicles, ammunition, fuel and materiel depots, and also temporary deployment areas of Ukrainian armed formations and foreign mercenaries," the ministry said.
In addition, some infrastructure facilities of Ukraine’s ports used to receive, store and distribute military cargo, and also fuel and lubricants for the Ukrainian army were degraded, it said.
"During the week, 14 dry cargo ships and a tanker involved in the delivery of Western weapons, military hardware, fuel and equipment for the needs of the Ukrainian army were hit," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarts enemy attempts to break out of encirclement in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North thwarted all the Ukrainian army’s attempts during the past week to break out of the encirclement in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Battlegroup North units continued tightening the ring of encirclement of enemy formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region and expanding the outer area of control. <…> All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement were thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North destroys over 275 Ukrainian troops surrounded in Kharkov area in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North destroyed more than 275 Ukrainian troops in a pocket of encirclement in the northeast of the Kharkov Region over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the week in that area, the enemy lost more than 275 troops, three armored combat vehicles, two motor vehicles and three ground robotic platforms," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North liberates 414 sq. km since encircling Ukrainian troops in Kharkov area
Russia’s Battlegroup North has liberated 414 sq. km of territory and eliminated over 1,360 Ukrainian troops since surrounding enemy armed formations in the northeast of the Kharkov Region, the ministry reported.
"Overall, 414 sq. km of territory and 20 communities have been liberated since the Ukrainian combat group was surrounded in the northeast of the Kharkov Region. Battlegroup North units have destroyed over 1,360 [Ukrainian] troops, 35 armored combat vehicles, 21 motor vehicles, 18 all-terrain vehicles and 34 ground robotic platforms," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicts over 1,850 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup North inflicted more than 1,850 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 15 enemy armored combat vehicles in its areas of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week in the Kharkov and Sumy Regions, Battlegroup North units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of five mechanized brigades, two motorized infantry brigades, two airmobile brigades, an unmanned systems brigade, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army, three territorial defense brigades and a National Guard brigade," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,850 personnel, 15 armored combat vehicles, 134 motor vehicles, six field artillery guns and eight electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in the areas of responsibility of Russia’s Battlegroup North over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicts over 1,565 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup West inflicted more than 1,565 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 13 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"During the past week, Battlegroup West units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of four mechanized brigades, an assault brigade of the Ukrainian army and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,565 personnel, 13 armored combat vehicles, 93 motor vehicles, nine field artillery guns, a US-made HIMARS multiple rocket launcher and five electronic warfare stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicts over 1,215 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup South inflicted more than 1,215 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 10 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup South units improved their forward positions and inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of three mechanized brigades, a motorized infantry brigade, a mountain assault brigade, two airmobile brigades of the Ukrainian army, a marine infantry brigade and two territorial defense brigades," the ministry said.
The Ukrainian army lost more than 1,215 personnel, 10 armored combat vehicles, 162 motor vehicles, nine field artillery guns and three electronic warfare and counterbattery radar stations in that frontline area over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center advancing in Dobropolye in Donetsk region
Russia’s Battlegroup Center units are advancing in the western and eastern parts of Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, the ministry reported.
"In Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, units of the 51st Army are developing an offensive in converging directions in the town’s western and eastern parts. All the enemy’s attempts to break out of the encirclement or rotate troops have been thwarted," the ministry said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center forces have eliminated over 520 enemy troops, an armored combat vehicle and six pickup trucks since surrounding Ukrainian armed formations in Dobropolye in the Donetsk People’s Republic, it said.
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicts over 3,415 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Center inflicted more than 3,415 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 23 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
"Over the past week, Battlegroup Center units gained better lines and positions and inflicted losses on formations of five mechanized brigades, an assault brigade, a jaeger brigade, an airborne brigade, an unmanned systems regiment of the Ukrainian army, two marine infantry brigades, two National Guard brigades and the Azov special operations brigade [outlawed as a terrorist group in Russia]," the ministry said.
Overall, the Ukrainian army lost more than 3,415 personnel, 23 armored combat vehicles, 69 motor vehicles, six field artillery guns and 13 electronic warfare stations in the responsibility area of Russia’s Battlegroup Center over the week, it specified.
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicts over 1,845 casualties on Ukrainian army in week
Russia’s Battlegroup East inflicted more than 1,845 casualties on Ukrainian troops and destroyed 14 enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.
During the past week, Battlegroup East units "inflicted losses on manpower and equipment of a mechanized brigade, an assault brigade, three air assault brigades, two assault regiments of the Ukrainian army and a marine infantry brigade," the ministry said.

Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminates 245 Ukrainian troops in week
Russia’s Battlegroup Dnepr eliminated roughly 245 Ukrainian troops and destroyed three enemy armored combat vehicles in its area of responsibility over the week, the ministry reported.

Russian air defenses intercept 7,389 Ukrainian UAVs, 17 cruise missiles over week

France, Germany try to save face on joint tank project
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:42:32 UTC
21:42:32 KST

PARIS — Defense ministers from France and Germany insisted their joint tank project is going well Friday, one day after the French chief of defense staff said it had faltered because of Berlin.
The Main Ground Combat System (MGCS) “remains a relevant project,” Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said, speaking near Bordeaux alongside her German counterpart Boris Pistorius.
“I can only wholeheartedly agree, dear Catherine. The MGCS project is not over, it is not dead, it has not been terminated by anyone,” Pistorius echoed. “Quite the contrary: It is a cornerstone project of Franco-German cooperation in land systems.”
Advertisement
France’s chief of defense staff, Gen. Fabien Mandon, told lawmakers Thursday that Germany had pulled out of the project. His comments landed especially awkwardly as German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is currently on a state visit to France.
Later in the evening, Mandon tried to backpedal in a written statement, arguing the project was only delayed to the late 2040s.
In recent years, Franco-German defense industrial projects have repeatedly failed. MGCS — which involves KNDS France, KNDS Germany, Rheinmetall and Thales — has been bogged down by years of delays, industrial disputes and political tensions. POLITICO reported in June that France and Germany would most likely build separate tanks.
Now, Pistorius has said the two countries will still work together on “unmanned systems and automated processing.”
The German minister pledged that the project wouldn’t meet the same fate as the Future Combat Air System, the joint next-generation fighter jet program that collapsed before the summer. “The crucial point is that we learn from our mistakes. That is why MGCS is in no way at risk and remains an important future project for our two nations and our two armed forces,” he said.
But the imbroglio highlights strains in the defense relationship between Paris and Berlin, and an increasing number of French lawmakers are now calling for Paris to look for other partners.
“Defense cooperation with Germany is at an all-time low, since Germany is going it alone,” a French lawmaker working on defense policy told POLITICO on condition of anonymity.
Rixa Fürsen contributed to this article from Bordeaux, France.

President Volodymyr Zelensky criticized Kyiv’s city authorities over their failure to implement resilience measures as Russian strikes caused significant damage to Ukraine’s power grid and electricity transmission infrastructure.
In a Telegram post on Friday following a conference call with military and government officials, Zelensky said restoration work was proceeding around the clock, with repair crews, energy workers and regional authorities working to restore the energy system.

Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
He added that Ukraine had updated its requirements for energy equipment and air-defense packages.
The Foreign Ministry and the presidential office were preparing communications with international partners, and Zelensky said he would speak with world leaders.
Zelensky also issued a sharp warning over delays in implementing regional resilience plans, saying that any delay was “absolutely unacceptable.”
He said the Infrastructure Ministry and regional administrations bore personal responsibility for carrying out the work.
Kyiv was singled out for criticism, with Zelensky saying the city authorities had failed to take the necessary steps “in almost all respects.”
Zelensky also addressed the situation in Pryluky, in the Chernihiv region. He instructed officials to prepare a comprehensive package of solutions by the end of the week, taking into account issues discussed with local residents.
Zelensky Says Ukraine Is Aware of US-Russia Economic Discussions
The president did not specify the extent of the damage to the power grid, the number of people affected by electricity disruptions or the precise measures he expected Kyiv authorities to complete.
Klitschko defends Kyiv’s preparations
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko has said the capital is in “survival” mode ahead of winter as intensified Russian strikes hit infrastructure, bridges and the energy grid, causing power cuts and disrupting water supplies.
In an interview with AFP, he said the city was preparing for the cold months by building backup heating systems and stockpiling fuel, food and drinking water, but warned that preparations alone might not be enough.
“No matter how well we prepare, if air defense does not work, we could end up in a bad scenario,” he said.
Klitschko defended Kyiv’s preparations amid repeated criticism from Zelensky’s government, arguing that municipal authorities faced a “very difficult” task with “limited time, limited funding, a limited number of workers.”
“Finding scapegoats won’t make people warmer,” he said.
The mayor warned that Russian attacks on bridges across the Dnipro River were disrupting traffic and threatening the city’s ability to function. Kyiv was developing alternative pontoon crossings to ease congestion, he said, while damage to water infrastructure could trigger a “quite large-scale” crisis.
Klitschko urged residents who have friends or relatives outside the capital to consider temporarily relocating, while insisting he was not calling for a full evacuation.
Zelensky reports progress near Dobropillia
The conference call also covered the battlefield situation, particularly in the Donetsk region, including the areas around Kostiantynivka, Dobropillia, Sloviansk and Kramatorsk.
According to Zelensky, Ukrainian forces had made progress in eliminating Russian “infiltrations” in the Dobropillia area. He said officials had also identified measures to be implemented over the coming weeks.
Zelensky thanked Ukrainian units carrying out their assigned tasks but did not provide further operational details or quantify the reported gains.
Power cuts disrupt essential services
The latest warnings follow water supply disruptions on Kyiv’s right bank on Thursday, when Russian attacks on the energy grid interrupted electricity supplies to water facilities and reduced pressure in the network. City authorities reported problems in parts of four districts, while emergency power cuts had already disrupted scheduled outages earlier in the week.
International partners have also announced additional winter assistance. The UK pledged £54 million in support, approximately $71 million, including funding for emergency grid repairs, backup generators and solar power. The package also covers heating and water systems, alongside direct cash assistance.

Pezeshkian urges Caspian states to unite on long-term environmental protection plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:41:20 UTC
21:41:20 KST

Pezeshkian urges Caspian states to unite on long-term environmental protection plan
TEHRAN – Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has proposed developing and implementing a long-term regional plan under the Tehran Convention to address the declining water level of the Caspian Sea.
Speaking at an extraordinary summit of Caspian littoral states in Turkmenistan on Friday, Pezeshkian said environmental cooperation could serve as an important platform for building trust and strengthening regional convergence at a time when the world is grappling with multiple crises, geopolitical rivalries, wars, unilateral sanctions, and the weakening of multilateralism.
He noted that the Tehran Convention and its protocols provide a comprehensive framework for cooperation among the Caspian littoral states on a range of environmental issues, including oil pollution, land-based sources of marine pollution, biodiversity conservation, transboundary environmental impact assessments, climate change, and the decline in the Caspian Sea’s water level.
Iran believes that the first principle in addressing the crisis should be reliance on science, shared data, and regional cooperation, Pezeshkian said.
He acknowledged that a comprehensive and definitive understanding of the relative contributions of various factors to the Caspian Sea’s declining water level had yet to be achieved. Climate change, rising temperatures and evaporation, shifting precipitation patterns, changes in river flows, and human interventions must all be examined within an integrated scientific framework to identify effective solutions and mitigate the consequences, he added.
Given the rapid pace of change, the region must move beyond merely observing and describing the crisis toward a new phase of joint crisis management, Pezeshkian stressed.
He also said lasting peace, stability, and security in the Caspian region could be ensured only if the littoral states respected one another’s sovereignty and legitimate interests and prevented the strategic water body from becoming an arena for destructive rivalries or the presence and interference of extra-regional powers.
The entry of fuel and pollutants into the marine environment, damage to coastal habitats, contamination of water and sediments, and harm to biodiversity could have consequences extending far beyond the immediate site of an incident, he warned.
Iran therefore emphasizes the importance of preserving the Caspian Sea’s peaceful character and protecting its environment even in situations of armed conflict, the president said.
Pezeshkian underscored the central role of the Tehran Convention, which was signed by the five Caspian littoral states in 2003 and serves as the region’s principal legally binding framework for protecting the marine environment of the Caspian Sea. The convention recently marked the 20th anniversary of its entry into force, with the seventh meeting of its contracting parties held in Tehran with the active participation of all littoral states.
Welcoming the summit’s decision to establish a high-level commission comprising deputy heads of government from the Caspian littoral states, Iran proposed developing and implementing a long-term regional plan under the Tehran Convention to address the declining water level.
According to Pezeshkian, the proposed plan should cover at least seven key areas:
 
1. Joint scientific monitoring of the factors contributing to the decline in water levels, alongside the development and implementation of a comprehensive regional action plan.
 
2. Stronger joint mechanisms to combat marine pollution and protect biodiversity.
 
3. A strengthened role for the Tehran Convention, including more effective implementation mechanisms.
 
4. Adaptation of coastal infrastructure and ports to future changes.
 
5. Protection and restoration of wetlands, habitats, and ecologically sensitive areas.
 
6. Support for local communities, fisheries, and livelihoods of the millions of people who depend on the Caspian Sea.
 
7. Mobilization of financial and technological resources to implement environmental protection and adaptation measures.
Pezeshkian said the region faced a historic choice: either passively observe the Caspian Sea’s declining water level as a natural and inevitable process and wait for its consequences, or draw on science, regional cooperation, and political will to reduce the damage and strengthen the resilience of this unique ecosystem.
Iran’s choice, he said, was cooperation, science, and the protection of the Caspian Sea, as well as preserving the shared heritage for future generations.
He called on the littoral states to turn the Caspian Sea into a new symbol of regional cooperation, describing it as a bridge connecting nations rather than a dividing line.
“The Caspian is not just a sea; it is a shared heritage,” Pezeshkian said, adding that protecting this heritage was a shared historic responsibility for all the countries of the region.

Iranian president suggests CIS+1 format be established

TURKMENBASHI /Turkmenistan/, October 9. /TASS/. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has proposed to establish a CIS+1 format to expand cooperation between the Commonwealth of Independent States and Tehran.
"A format 'Commonwealth of Independent States + Iran,' or CIS+1, should be established as a flexible and efficient mechanism for dialogue and cooperation," he said at the CIS summit, as quoted by the Fars news agency.
According to Pezeshkian, regional diplomacy "should serve as an instrument of crisis management, maintaining ties, preventing the spread of conflicts, and fostering practical cooperation." Iran, in his words, wants "communication rather than fragmentation, cooperation rather than destructive competition, interdependence rather than unilateral dependence, and security based on trust and shared interests rather than security based on threats."
Iran is a "gate" from Central Asia to the sea, with Iranian ports in the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman providing access to South Asia, Africa, and Europe, he noted, adding that the North-South and West-East corridors are not rivals but "elements of a common regional network." He also expressed hope that this summit will be a "practical step toward forming a region where Central Asia, the South Caucasus, and Iran will be part of a unified network of cooperation rather than a collection of separate areas."

- The case comes amid rising settler violence in the West Bank, where UN bodies view settlements as illegal and Palestinians say the army does too little to stop attacks.
AI generated
LUBAN AL-SHARQIYA, West Bank - Israeli settlers have planted dozens of Israeli flags at the entrance of a streetside Palestinian cafe in the occupied West Bank, obscuring it from one side in what its owner described as a blatant act of intimidation.
The coffee shop in the small village of Luban al-Sharqiya sits along the West Bank’s main north-south traffic artery, used by both Palestinians and the approximately 500,000 Israeli settlers who live in the territory.
In recent years, settlers, some of whom have waged a campaign of violence and intimidation against Palestinians in a bid to force them off their land, have planted flags along the road and in close proximity at village entrances or near Palestinian landmarks.
When Mueiyyid Hussein went to open his coffee shop on the morning of Oct 8, he discovered settlers had placed dozens of Israeli flags up against its entrance, packed together and obscuring it from southbound travellers.
“They are not leaving us alone. They have blocked the view of my shop,” said Hussein, owner of the Luban al-Sharqiya Coffee Shop and Rest Area.
While Reuters was interviewing Hussein, a settler who he said was responsible for planting the flags drove by, filming Hussein and the shop with his cellphone.
Reuters was not able to reach the man for comment.
“He drives away and then comes back to check whether I have removed any flags. He says he will come back and shut down my shop,” Hussein said.
The Israeli military did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the placement of the flags.
UN bodies and most countries view Israel’s settlements and settler outposts as illegal under international law regarding military occupations. Israel rejects this, viewing the territory as disputed rather than occupied.
The West Bank has seen a sharp rise in settler violence against Palestinians and settler seizures of Palestinian land and resources. The military says it does what it can to clamp down on the violence, something Palestinians reject, pointing to numerous instances in which troops stand by as attacks play out. REUTERS

Expert: Longer lifespans should mean longer working lives
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:39:00 UTC
21:39:00 KST

Expert: Longer lifespans should mean longer working lives
The retirement age in Estonia must rise together with life expectancy so that the pension system remains sustainable and different generations spend roughly the same amount of time in retirement, says Lauri Leppik, professor of social and population policy at Tallinn University.
"If people live longer, then they must also work longer. We see that as of 2026, Estonia has about 315,000 old‑age pensioners. If we add other types of pensions, then almost every fourth person in Estonia is a pensioner," Leppik said.
"Of course, this is a burden on the state. If the retirement age had not been raised, then soon every third person here would be a pensioner. So this decision was necessary from the standpoint of the burden on the working population."
In 2026, the retirement age in Estonia is 65, applying to people born in 1961. Starting next year, the retirement age will be tied to the expected life expectancy of people aged 65.
"This means that if 65‑year‑olds live longer than before, then the retirement age will rise accordingly. In other words, it is specifically the life expectancy at age 65 that is taken into account," Leppik explained.
A nuance that was overlooked
When the law on old‑age retirement was adopted, a transition to a new system was also foreseen, where the retirement age is determined by calendar years. The minister of social affairs approved the retirement age for the next two years: 65 years and 1 month in 2027, and 65 years and 3 months in 2028.
"But it turns out that only people born from January to November 1962 can retire in 2027. Those born in December 1962 will reach retirement age only in 2028, when it will not be 65 years and 1 month, but 65 years and 3 months. This means they can retire only in March 2028 — their retirement age is two months higher," Leppik said.
"It's hard to say why this happened; I did not participate in those discussions, but it seems that when the transition to the new system was being discussed, this nuance was not noticed," he added.
Out of 100 men, 80 will reach retirement age
After the restoration of Estonia's independence, women retired at 55 and men at 60 for some time. Now the ages have equalized.
"Women's retirement age has risen by 10 years during this period, and men's by five. But average life expectancy has also risen significantly over 30 years. In 1995, women lived an average of 74 years, and now more than 83. For men, average life expectancy in 1995 was only 61 years, and now more than 75. So women's average life expectancy has increased by almost 10 years, and men's by 14," the professor explained.
According to Leppik, men's chances of reaching retirement age are now much higher — almost 80%. That means out of 100 men, 80 will reach retirement age, and for women the figure is 91%.
"Of course, people's lives differ: there are long‑lived individuals who reach 100, and there are those whose lives are quite short. There are significant individual differences in life expectancy," he added.
Historically, women's retirement age in Estonia was lower than men's. Now the ages have equalized because Europe follows the principle of gender equality.
"At the same time, men who reach 65 have about 16 years left based on average life expectancy. Women have more than 20. So in retirement age, the difference in life expectancy is about five years," Leppik said.
Estonia has a lot of working retirees
Estonia ranks among the top European countries in employment rates among people of retirement age.
"In many cases, people are forced to work to ensure a sufficient standard of living. On the other hand, people with higher education — for example teachers or doctors — can continue working and choose to do so in retirement. There are also many in Estonia who lose their jobs before reaching retirement age and cannot continue working either for health reasons or because they cannot find work," he said.
"It is also true that the indicator of healthy years is low. But subjective factors influence it as well — for example, Estonian residents tend to be quite critical when assessing their own health."
Leppik noted that no sharp improvements in Estonia's state pension system are expected, so people must prepare themselves and use all available opportunities before reaching retirement age.
