India's 'cockroaches' vs Election Commission: What you need to know ahead of CJP's October 10 protests
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:23:00 UTC
21:23:00 KST

Why are India's 'cockroaches' protesting again?
October 9, 2026
India's Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has called for a nationwide march on New Delhi on Saturday, after its ultimatum demanding the resignation of the country's election chief was ignored.
In the days leading up to the planned gathering, authorities have been clamping down on protesters gathering at Jantar Mantar, the 18th-century observatory that serves as the Indian capital's designated protest site.
Those arrested include members of the general public, student activists and opposition leaders, including the Indian National Congress' Rahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra.
CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke urged people to turn out in huge numbers, while adding that the police were already detaining protesters: "The more people you detain, the more people will show up!"
The stakes remain high: the credibility of the body that runs the world's largest elections is on the line.
What is the controversy about?
Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar is currently in the hot seat after the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that revealed that fellow election commissioners, Sukhbir Singh Sandhu and Vivek Joshi, had raised at least 14 formal objections over 10 months to decisions concerning voter registrations, deletions and restorations, as well as control of electoral-roll data.
In one of the objections, Sandhu complained that the Election Commission of India (ECI) had acted against the written advice of the two commissioners and claimed its action was "unauthorized and illegal."
Kumar became the CEC in 2025 after being chosen by a selection panel led by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi. Rahul Gandhi, who was also a member of the panel, had opposed Kumar's appointment.
Now, Kumar, along with Sandhu and Joshi, is responsible for overseeing the Special Intensive Revision (SIR), a nationwide re-verification of the electoral rolls requiring voters to prove their eligibility to remain on them.
The ECI says the process is meant to remove errors in India's electoral rolls, such as the names of deceased individuals or people who have permanently moved abroad and duplicate entries — as well as avoiding the "inclusion of the names of foreign illegal immigrants."
But critics say the ECI it has gone far beyond that remit.
The Indian Express report says more than 130 million names were removed from electoral rolls across the country. Before this India had some 970 million eligible voters. For scale, Germany has about 60 million eligible voters in total.
Who are the 'cockroaches' and what do they want?
The CJP, an ironic riff on the name of Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), is a youth-led movement that emerged in May after the chief justice of India, Surya Kant, referred to unemployed young people as "cockroaches" in an offhand remark during an unrelated court hearing.
The move backfired, with young people embracing the tag and turning it into a channel for their disillusionment over what they see as failings in the country's education system and its massive youth unemployment problem.
The CJP has since amassed nearly 25 million Instagram followers, more than double that of the BJP's 9.9 million.
Modi's account, however, remains far ahead with 106 million.
A campaign protesting multiple competitive exam leaks launched the CJP into nationwide relevance, securing the resignation of the then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
Now, the CJP is demanding:
- Kumar's resignation and initiation of criminal proceedings against him
- An immediate hold on upcoming elections, and a freezing of the SIR
- The repeal of the 2023 law on the appointment of election commissioners of India
Is CJP really leading the protests?
The CJP is not alone in its call for protests.
For days ahead of the planned October 10 march to Jantar Mantar, student activists, civil society members — including former high-ranking government officials — and leaders of opposition have called for accountability and Kumar's resignation.
The CJP has been joined by representatives of several student associations, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (AISA) and its breakout star Neha Bora, who has been leading protests in the capital all week.
Dramatic scenes emerged from New Delhi whenleaders from the opposition INDIA alliance, including the Gandhis, were detained by authorities.
Bharatiya Kisan Union spokesperson and farmers' rights activist Rakesh Tikait also extended his support to the march and vowed to join on October 10. Tikait was part of the leadership behind the 2020-2021 farmers' agitationthat forced the Indian government to repeal three laws intended to liberalize the agricultural sector.
The other side
Amid heavy police presence and barricading near the ECI offices in lush central Delhi, the electoral body has rejected any suggestion of a split and Kumar's overreach, maintaining that all decisions, including on the SIR, were unanimous.
It also addressed allegations that opposition parties had not been allowed to meet with its officials on Tuesday, saying that till "4.00 pm today, no political party, through its representatives, had sought an appointment for a meeting with the Election Commission."
A day earlier, a delegation of retired senior bureaucrats had also attempted to approach the office of the ECI to submit a charge sheet and impeachment notice against Kumar on behalf of the public, but were unable to reach the premises.
Delhi police said no permission has been given for the October 10 protests, calling them illegal.
"I request everyone to refrain from participating in this protest," Delhi's Deputy Commissioner of Police Shrishti Pandey told news agency ANI.
Some BJP politicians had previously referred to the CJP as a "cross-border influence operation" aimed at destabilizing India, with Parliamentary Affairs Minister Kiren Rijiju accusing them of seeking social media followers from archenemy Pakistan and the "anti-India gang."
What to watch for on October 10
New Delhi has been turned into a fortress, with the government deploying close to 43,000 security personnel ahead of the protests, local media reported.
Several independent journalists and others associated with the last round of CJP protests have claimed that authorities have been using intimidation tactics to keep them from joining the march.
CJP national spokesperson Deepak Baliyan was taken into police custody on Thursday, but released hours later.
In the last round of CJP protests, the police used tear gas, sticks and pellet-firing shotguns to subdue the demonstrators.

Interpol operation seized 2,800 illegal firearms across Europe and Asia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:22:34 UTC
21:22:34 KST

An Interpol-coordinated operation conducted across 17 countries in Europe and Asia this summer allowed the seizure of 2,823 firearms and over 40,000 pieces of ammunition.
A substantial amount of illegal weaponry linked to former or ongoing armed conflicts in eastern Europe, the Balkan region and Nagorno-Karabakh was seized by what is presented as a first-of-its-kind Interpol-coordinated operation.
From 22 June to 5 July, the INTERPOL-coordinated Operation Trigger X targeting illicit firearms trafficking across Europe and Central Asia has permitted to seize "2,823 small arms and light weapons, almost 400 hand grenades and explosives, and over 40,000 pieces of ammunition", according to an Interpol press release.
More than 152 people were arrested in relation to firearms possession or trafficking, but also for drug trafficking, migrant smuggling and robbery.
Participating authorities arrested 15 individuals subject to Interpol Notices, including five fugitives wanted internationally under Red Notices.
Conflict zones illicit firearms trafficking
Many firearms linked to conflicts in eastern Europe and countries in Central Asia were seized by customs officers. A major seizure at the border crossing between Bulgaria and Turkey involved two heavy goods vehicles containing over 1,000 military-grade shotguns.
"Operation Trigger X has revealed the high-level risk of weapons that are used in armed conflicts being diverted into organised crime channels, where they are used to commit other crimes", said Harald Arm, Executive Director of Police Capabilities at Interpol.
"These seizures demonstrate the importance of coordinated international action to identify trafficking routes, dismantle criminal networks and prevent illicit firearms from reaching those who seek to use them for criminal purposes".
Firearms, handguns and explosives were seized during the operation. A total of 268 hand grenades were recovered, while the largest single seizure was made in Serbia, where 68 hand grenades were being trafficked from Bosnia.
Authorities also discovered a "clandestine workshop converting gas and starter guns into firearms" in Serbia.
Inflatable boats linked to migrant smuggling
The operation led to the seizure of 20 inflatable dinghies in Bulgaria that were being shipped to a western European country.
"Intelligence suggests that the shipment was linked to criminal networks involved in migrant smuggling and intended for use in clandestine English Channel crossings", says the Interpol press release.
Illegal migrants were also intercepted during the operation; one of them was in possession of an automatic rifle and several rounds of ammunition.
"Other items seized during the operation included several different types of illicit drugs, such as cocaine and marijuana, counterfeit cigarettes and undeclared textiles and food products", says the Interpol press release.

Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:22:20 UTC
21:22:20 KST

Russia forcibly removes 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied Kharkiv Oblast, ombudsman says
Russian forces forcibly removed 25 Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territory in Kharkiv Oblast to an unknown destination, Ukraine's Human Rights Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets said on Oct. 9.
The civilians, including children, young people, and elderly residents, were taken from an area of the oblast where active fighting continues. Their current whereabouts and the conditions in which they are being held remain unknown, Lubinets said.
"Russia calls this an 'evacuation.' But when people are taken away against their will, intimidated, and left with no choice, it is not a rescue. It is coercion," Lubinets said.
The ombudsman did not specify which settlement the civilians were taken from or where they had been transported.
According to Lubinets, Russian forces published footage of what they described as a rescue operation on their Telegram channels. He said the footage showed signs of intimidation and pressure on civilians who had not consented to being relocated.
The Kyiv Independent could not independently verify the circumstances of the reported removals.
Lubinets also warned that Russian occupation authorities had created a Telegram bot to collect personal information under the pretext of evacuation, potentially putting civilians and their relatives at risk.
Forcible transfers and deportations of civilians from occupied territory are prohibited under Article 49 of the Fourth Geneva Convention.
Lubinets said he had appealed to Russia's human rights commissioner, demanding information about the 25 civilians, their whereabouts and conditions, and measures to secure their return to Ukraine.
He also appealed to the International Committee of the Red Cross, the United Nations, and other international organizations for assistance.
Russia has repeatedly forcibly transferred and deported Ukrainian civilians, including children, from occupied territories since launching its full-scale invasion in 2022.
In March 2026, a United Nations commission concluded that Russia's deportation and forcible transfer of Ukrainian children amounted to crimes against humanity.

Ambassador Ferranti Visits the Italian Hospital in Armenia
Italy
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
14:22:07 CEST
21:22:07 KST

The Italian Ambassador to Yerevan, Alessandro Ferranti, attended the ceremony in Ashotsk, in the Armenian region of Shirak, marking the 35th anniversary of the “Redemptoris Mater” Hospital, commonly known as the Italian Hospital. The event was attended by civil and religious authorities, including the Bishop of the Latin Rite Catholics of Georgia and Armenia, Giuseppe Pasotto, and the Mayor of Ashotsk. In his remarks, Ferranti recalled Italy’s contribution to Armenian communities following the earthquake and the hospital’s role in assisting families throughout the region, even in the most remote villages. The Ambassador emphasized the importance of preserving this legacy of collaboration and solidarity for future generations.
                                    
Built by Italian companies and workers, the facility was inaugurated on October 7, 1991, at the behest of John Paul II, to assist the population affected by the earthquake of December 7, 1988. Healthcare services have been entrusted to the Camillian religious order and supported over time by Caritas Italiana, the Italian Episcopal Conference through “otto per mille” funds, the Camillian Order, and parishes, associations, and benefactors.
                                    
According to data presented by Father Mario Cuccarollo, from January 1993 to December 2025, the hospital admitted 62,459 patients and performed 32,855 surgical procedures. In addition to the hospital’s activities, there are 21 outpatient clinics in the surrounding villages, which have provided 427,900 outpatient visits, 174,390 home visits, and 82,225 vaccinations.
                                    
Care was provided entirely free of charge until December 2012. Since January 2013, approximately 45% of patients have continued to receive free care, particularly the neediest families and patients in the pediatric, maternity, and emergency departments. For others, a copayment of approximately 20% of the average cost of local healthcare facilities is required. Meals and medication remain free for all inpatients.

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Clashes broke out near Brussels Central Station during Friday's demonstration organized by Belgium's socialist trade union ABVV against the federal government's austerity policies, with police using tear gas and water cannons to disperse rioters, according to local media reports. 
Hundreds of young people, many dressed in black and wearing masks, threw stones, glass bottles, wooden beams and trash cans at police, public broadcaster VRT and news agency Belga reported. 
Police deployed tear gas and water cannons at demonstrators and made several arrests. 
At least 21 people have been arrested, including 13 minors and five adults among those taken into judicial custody, Brussels police said in a statement. 
Police said the trade demonstration itself proceeded peacefully and had completely ended, stressing that the subsequent incidents in several areas were unrelated to the protest's demands or conduct.  
At Brussels-South station, clashes escalated when groups of youths attempted to move toward the city center but were stopped by police using a water cannon. 
Youths threw stones and fireworks at police, while a large fire was lit at an intersection. 
Similar incidents were reported near Brussels Central station, where police were targeted with fireworks, wooden beams and stones. 
Officers responded with tear gas and multiple water cannons, while small fires were set and roads blocked with piles of scooters and bicycles. 
A public transport bus at Brussels-South was extensively vandalized, and a bus stop near the station was also heavily damaged. 
Authorities also seized potentially dangerous items, including Molotov cocktails, gasoline, pyrotechnic devices, a knife, a hammer, lighters and gloves. 
At Brussels-South, most station entrances remained closed, forcing passengers to take detours. 
The unrest occurred as ABVV held a national demonstration in Brussels, beginning at 10 am local time (0800GMT), with protesters marching from Brussels Central Station toward Brussels South Station under the slogan "Stay out of our pockets." 
Police said 30,000 people participated in the demonstration, while ABVV had earlier estimated attendance at 50,000. 
The union is protesting the federal government's austerity measures as officials consider a new budget. 
It opposes potential measures affecting purchasing power, the wage indexation system and value-added tax (VAT), as well as plans to introduce annualized working time. 
ABVV Chairman Bert Engelaar warned before the march that a nationwide strike could take place in November if the government crosses the union's "red lines." 
Meanwhile, the Christian trade union ACV organized a separate protest on Friday involving hundreds of activists at the Brussels headquarters of Belgium's governing coalition parties. 
Public transport and airport services were severely disrupted amid the demonstrations.

Lithuanian Minister Condemns Intimidation Campaign against Investigative Reporters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:21:00 UTC
21:21:00 KST

Reported by
Lithuanian Culture Minister Lukas Alsys condemned the harassment of journalists and editors on Thursday after being asked about growing pressure on 15min staff following the news outlet’s joint investigation with OCCRP into the crypto-finance firm Bankera.
“Any persecution of journalists or editors aimed at intimidating or frightening them is completely intolerable,” Alsys told Žinių Radijas, adding that relevant authorities should “draw conclusions.”
The joint investigation revealed that more than 45 million euros raised during Bankera’s 2017–2018 token sale was transferred to Pacific Private Bank in Vanuatu, an offshore entity acquired by Bankera’s three co-founders. Records showed the bank subsequently issued millions of euros in loans to the founders and their companies, including funds used to purchase luxury real estate.
Lithuania’s Financial Crime Investigation Service opened a pre-trial investigation shortly after the story was published in April 2025. Vanuatu’s central bank later revoked Pacific Private Bank’s international license, though the decision was stayed pending appeal.
What followed was a systematic campaign of pressure targeting journalists and executives at 15min.
According to the newsroom, unknown actors collected personal data on staff members and their families, trailed journalists at public events, and launched a targeted smear campaign across social media, a newly created website, and outdoor billboards.
15min also reported a barrage of regulatory complaints. Lithuania’s Public Information Ethics Commission received four formal complaints against 15min in just two months—all filed by individuals linked to Bankera—compared to its usual average of about one complaint per year, national broadcaster LRT reported.
A coalition of press freedom groups—including the Internet Media Association, the Journalists’ Professional Association, the Lithuanian Journalists’ Union, and the National Press Association—issued a joint statement calling the tactics a strategic lawsuit against public participation (SLAPP) campaign designed to exhaust and intimidate critical media. The groups urged state institutions to step in.
Bankera acknowledged filing regulatory complaints but denied orchestrating a harassment campaign. Co-founder Vytautas Karalevičius told LRT that the legal filings were a response to 15min’s alleged failure to present the company's position fairly. Bankera lawyer Gintaras Černiauskas added that his clients had no knowledge of any surveillance or data gathering against journalists, stating that law enforcement should investigate those claims if true.
In September, Lithuanian authorities formally named Bankera co-founders Mantas Mockevičius, Vytautas Karalevičius, and Justas Dobiliauskas as suspects in an investigation into the alleged unlawful dissipation of at least $49 million in investor funds. None of the three men have been convicted of a crime.
15min Editor-in-Chief Vaidotas Beniušis insisted that the pressure would not silence the newsroom, while the Journalists’ Professional Association called on law enforcement to help protect the reporters involved.

Türkiye and the European Space Agency (ESA) are reportedly holding talks to renew cooperation and develop joint orbital programs, a Turkish space expert told Anadolu at the International Astronautical Congress in Antalya.
Gulin Dede, partnerships director at nonprofit Space Renaissance International (SRI), said she had heard that discussions were underway and expressed optimism that they would lead to positive results and revive previous cooperation agreements between Ankara and the agency.
Dede, Türkiye's first female analog astronaut who previously worked at ESA's technology development center in the Netherlands, said European space officials were showing growing interest in expanding cooperation with Türkiye.
She also welcomed Türkiye's signing of the Artemis Accords, an international framework for cooperation in civil space exploration.
Dede said hosting the International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Türkiye had helped raise the country's profile within the global space community.
"That this event is being held in Türkiye sends a wonderful message to the global space community and ecosystem, evident from the academic contribution of the delegates and their satisfaction with the expo, the evaluation of Turkish firms' exhibits, and presentations from other countries," she said.
"I'm here myself as a committee member and our work is progressing successfully," she added.

She also said greater participation by Turkish astronauts in international missions and activities could help strengthen Türkiye's position as a partner in future space projects.

The last original mural will be preserved on the Berlin Wall
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:20:36 EEST
21:20:36 KST

The last original mural will be preserved on the Berlin Wall
Kyiv • UNN
The foundation will allocate €13,300 for the conservation of the Hands mural at the East Side Gallery. The work has remained in its original form since 1990.
Berlin will undertake the preservation of “Hands” — the only image that has survived on the Berlin Wall in its original form since 1990. The German Foundation for Monument Protection will allocate €13,300 for the conservation and other work to preserve the Berlin Wall, the organization said on October 8. DW reports this, writes UNN.
The history behind the image
The work “Hands” was created by Scottish artists Margaret Hunter and Peter Russell. In it, Hunter repeated the motif from her painting “Berlin 09.11.89” — raised hands, which she painted on the night the Berlin Wall fell on November 9, 1989. According to the artist, the image recalled the peaceful protests in the GDR that preceded the reunification of the country.
“Hands” holds a special place among the works of the East Side Gallery. During large-scale restorations of the gallery in 2000 and 2009, the other images were completely or partially repainted, while this work was only conserved. Today, “Hands” makes it possible to imagine what the images on the wall looked like in 1990. Currently, certain areas of the “Hands” paint layer are peeling and require consolidation.
Work has begun at Berlin’s East Side Gallery to preserve the last original mural and other fragments of the Berlin Wall.
Experts will examine and clean the wall
Some of the allocated funds will be used to develop methods for removing graffiti and protecting the preserved elements of the Berlin Wall. Experts will also examine the remains of the first version of the wall, which was built as a border structure in 1961.
The East Side Gallery, approximately 1.3 kilometers long, runs along Mühlenstraße in Berlin and is the longest surviving section of the Berlin Wall. In the summer of 1990, it was painted by 118 artists from 21 countries. In 1991, the East Side Gallery was granted protected-monument status. According to the monument protection foundation, around four million people visit it every year today.

India's dowry curse: Outlawed practice remains deeply entrenched
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:19:07 UTC
21:19:07 KST

India's dowry curse: Outlawed practice remains deeply entrenched
To display this content from YouTube, you must enable advertisement tracking and audience measurement.
One of your browser extensions seems to be blocking the video player from loading. To watch this content, you may need to disable it on this site.
Issued on:
India recorded 5,737 dowry-linked deaths in 2024, an average of around 16 women a day. Despite being outlawed more than six decades ago, the practice of dowry – the transfer or money or valuables from a bride's family when she gets married – remains deeply entrenched across Indian society. Our correspondents report.
Dowry refers to the transfer of money, property, vehicles, jewellery or other valuables from a bride's family to the groom or his family as part of a marriage arrangement. The practice was outlawed under India's Dowry Prohibition Act in 1961, but demands for cash and goods continue to be made before and after weddings.
This transfer is specifically done from the bride's side. India has long dealt with deep-rooted gender bias, where being born a woman is often seen as a disadvantage. Despite a legal ban on prenatal sex determination, research shows that between 2000 and 2019, nearly 9 million female foetuses were aborted in India. The preference for sons stems from rooted social attitudes: men are viewed as future breadwinners, while women are seen as financial burdens whose primary role is to be married off. And in exchange for marrying the woman who is considered a burden, men and their families demand luxury items.
In some communities, dowry demands can function like a market, with families negotiating according to the groom's education, occupation and income. Government employees and men with secure, well-paid jobs can command particularly high demands. Even families that reject the word "dowry" may accept expensive gifts presented as voluntary offerings to the bride or groom.
These demands often do not end with the wedding. Many women face pressure to continue bringing additional money, property or luxury goods from their families. Those who cannot meet these demands may face harassment, physical violence, abandonment or, in the most extreme cases, death.
A multi-billion-dollar wedding industry
Dowry is also linked to India's enormous wedding economy. Indian weddings are estimated to generate around $130 billion a year, with families spending heavily on ceremonies, jewellery, clothing and gifts.
For many families, the societal pressure is immense. Some borrow money or sell assets to meet wedding expenses and dowry demands.
Official crime data recorded 35,493 dowry-linked deaths between 2017 and 2022. Police also register tens of thousands of cases each year involving cruelty and harassment linked to dowry demands. But activists and researchers say the true scale of the problem is difficult to measure because many cases go unreported.

Northeastern Estonian cities question value of participatory budgeting
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:19:00 UTC
21:19:00 KST

Northeastern Estonian cities question value of participatory budgeting
Narva and Narva-Jõesuu are both reconsidering participatory budgeting as residents' proposals continue to prove too costly or vague to carry out.
Narva-Jõesuu has run the process nine times, spending €30,000 a year on projects including sidewalk repairs, fountains and a shorefront Wisdom Trail dotted with display boards featuring quotes from famous figures. But city officials say public interest is waning, ideas are getting repetitive and many proposals are simply too expensive.
"Over the past three years at least, the same proposal has come up again and again: let's renovate the resort hall," Mayor Maksim Iljin said, noting that €30,000 is nowhere near enough to overhaul the long-abandoned building.
"It's clear participatory budgeting has run its course in Narva-Jõesuu," he added.
Iljin said the city should instead focus on supporting local nonprofits and community organizations.
Narva, meanwhile, has spent up to €300,000 a year on participatory budgeting, but some winning projects have proved too expensive to complete, including Paju Park on Rakvere tänav and a boat ramp on Jõe tänav.
No new big projects
The city paused the collection of new proposals two years ago and now believes the annual participatory budget should be slashed to a tenth of its current size to focus on smaller projects.
"That's the problem — people come up with these big ideas that end up requiring public procurements and quotes," said Narva City Council chair Urbo Vaarmann.
He argued that unfinished projects should be completed before the city starts over with a new approach focused on "nice little projects."
In Narva-Jõesuu, the fate of participatory budgeting is on the city council agenda later this month. Narva city officials, meanwhile, are expected to make a decision within the next four months.

Command decisions: CENTCOM chief Brad Cooper's ups and downs in shaping Trump's war on Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:17:18 UTC
21:17:18 KST

While US President Donald Trump and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu make their next decisions on Iran and the Middle East conflict strategy, The Jerusalem Post now reveals the major impact that US Central Command (CENTCOM) chief Adm. Brad Cooper has had in this regard.
In April, the Post reported that Cooper has, in some ways, taken a more passive role than his predecessor, Gen. Michael “Erik” Kurilla, in communicating his broad strategy views to Trump, preferring instead to convey them to US Joint Chiefs of Staff chairman Gen. Dan Caine.
The Post can now add that, at times, some say that Cooper conveys views directly to US Secretary of State Marco Rubio or to US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, along with Caine, depending on the issue.
Cooper, the Post understands, views this as his proper role as a theater combat commander and says communicating with these top officials, rather than Trump, lets him get his concerns heard at the highest decision-making levels.
All parties credit Cooper with tremendous success as deputy chief of CENTCOM in the June 2025 war with Iran, where he worked closely with top Israeli officials and managed much of that relationship and coordination.
All parties also credit Cooper with excellent military operational planning and execution in many areas as CENTCOM chief during the early 2026 war with Iran.
They have also been impressed by his ability to capitalize on his special naval expertise during the ongoing Strait of Hormuz conflict.
However, questions remain about his role and impact in areas where the American public is critical of the war’s results.
The Post now reveals a range of Cooper, CENTCOM, US military, and Israeli military views about areas where many Americans have criticized the results of the war.
Much of Iran’s closure of Hormuz ‘fake’ until April
The biggest black eye for the Trump administration has been the Strait of Hormuz. Whether current US operational control there succeeds going forward, the US and the world economy have been shaken by Iran’s closure of the strait for much of 2026.
Many experts have slammed Trump and US military officials for failing to secure the strait in the opening plays of the war.
If questioned about why the US military did not focus its first moves in early March on cleaning up or blocking any Iranian efforts to blockade the Strait of Hormuz, the Post understands that Cooper would explain that the strait “clean up” could not happen until the main drone, ballistic missile, and large vessel Iranian naval threats were cleared.
Estimates were that this was going to take at least a month. Several US military officials argue that many observers wrongly superimpose the situation now when they go backward to analyze the state of play way back in early March.
They fail to consider the months it took to wear down the broader Iranian threats, such that there can be a more surgical focus on the strait now. In other words, there was no way to immediately neutralize the strait problem.
Based on this, Cooper would argue that such backseat quarterbacking is misinformed and irrelevant.
Questions do remain about whether the US, Israel, and CENTCOM could have pursued a different operational strategy, as Gen. Kenneth Franklin McKenzie Jr. told the Post on April 9.
McKenzie suggested seizing Kharg Island, or using consistent firepower to prevent Iran from operating there or around the Strait of Hormuz.
But given the limits of Trump not wanting to lose marines or hobble Iran’s non-military economic capabilities longer term, it is unclear exactly how some of those other operational options would have played out.
In addition, in a staggering revelation, when Iran announced that it had closed the Strait Hormuz in early March, Cooper would assert that this was a partially fake declaration.
Iran’s declaration was real in the sense of the danger felt by ships worldwide that stopped traveling through the strait and regarding the threat of hundreds of daily missiles and thousands of daily drones.
However, the Post can now disclose that Iran’s claims that it was already mining the strait back then were mostly fictitious.
Over time, the US Navy inspected suspicious objects in the sea and found that the vast majority of the supposed 80 mines were duds, the Post has learned.
What about reports by The Wall Street Journal, CNN, and others in early and mid-March claiming that Iran had already laid significant quantities of mines in the ocean and that the US was facing difficulty in removing them?
According to American sources, while the missile and drone threats were real and the US military was dealing with those from the start of the conflict, it later turned out that any reports backing Iran’s claims of heavily mining the strait in early March were untrue.
The Post can now disclose that it understands that Iran did not deploy mines in Hormuz before the April 7 initial ceasefire.
This might seem like too convenient an answer for US sources to give, since they can blame any shortcomings on the absence of continuous military operations.
But one significant piece of evidence for this narrative is that no reports show ships damaged by sea mines. By May 2026, CENTCOM said it had destroyed over 90% of over 8,000 Iranian sea mines (many were destroyed before they could be deployed).
New dimensions to the Cooper call to Zamir to eliminate Tangsiri
It has recently been reported that around March 19, Cooper made a secret call to IDF Chief of Staff Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir to request that Israel eliminate IRGC Navy chief Alireza Tangsiri, considered a serious threat to Hormuz and the naval conflict in general.
Zamir approved, and on March 26, Israel assassinated Tangsiri.
This incident raises the question: Why would Cooper secretly call Zamir on March 19 to ask him to remove Tangsiri as a threat, if US sources want to claim that Iran was not carrying out significant, real sea mining until the conflict paused sometime in mid-April?
The Post has learned that the US was confused and had varying levels of confidence when it learned of Iranian discussions about what Tehran was really thinking about doing regarding mining.
Whatever the concerns were, both Israeli and American sources have acknowledged that they were not the same as issuing actual orders on the matter.
In that sense, the Post understands that Cooper’s call to Zamir was, in many senses, a call for a preemptive move to head off a possible future strategic problem.
The Post also reported earlier on Thursday that some top Israeli officials worried Tangsiri could emerge as the next head of the IRGC and that he would be a much tougher adversary than Ahmad Vahidi, who eventually became the new IRGC chief.
In contrast, many top Israeli officials viewed Tangsiri as a highly creative and resourceful commander. Vahidi was largely seen as a deputy to a deputy of top commanders, lacking the power to shape the broader security posture.
What role or influence has and will CENTCOM have on the war’s strategic goals over time?
There are multiple parts to this question, starting with resolving the Hormuz crisis. The other parts involve regime change and Iran’s nuclear program.
Regarding regime change, even at the start of the war, American voices opposing or doubting that regime change plans pushed by Israel would pay off leaked out.
As the war has drawn out, the divergence between US and Israeli strategy and focus on these issues has grown even larger.
Even the targeting carried out by the two militaries during the main conflict saw Israel assassinating Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and other top Iranian officials. At the same time, the US mostly stayed away from that, focusing on degrading Iranian military capabilities.
A disconnect on the US side over regime change complicates the picture.
Trump himself has repeatedly made comments encouraging regime change or using metaphors about wiping out Iran as a functional nation.
However, the Post has learned that behind the scenes, Trump and his other top lieutenants have given zero directives to the military and CENTCOM about making efforts toward achieving this.
Also, US sources would note Trump has made at least as many or more statements demurring from regime change as a goal – it just happens to be that this American president does not try to keep a consistent public message on the issue.
However, the nuclear dilemma is different.
All US officials and most of the world know that getting Iran to make nuclear concessions (once negotiations were viewed as having failed) was the minimum primary strategic goal and starting point for the war with Iran.
In that sense, the purpose of striking Iran’s drones, missiles, and navy has been to remove Iran’s strategic threats that have held back the US, the West, and Israel from confronting it about the nuclear program more directly all these years.
Striking Iran’s military programs had benefits on their own, but the real goal was to pressure Tehran into nuclear concessions.
How would Cooper and CENTCOM judge overall success on these goals at this point?
The jury is out, but the story isn’t over yet.
What does that mean?
It means that Cooper and CENTCOM, like Israel and much of the world, are waiting to see what Iran’s breaking point is, given all of the economic and military pressure it has been under.
This last point may make sense after a few weeks or a few months, but seems problematic after seven months.
Yes, Iran has been hit much harder. But American bases, soldiers, allies, and the US and world economy have also been hit hard for seven times longer than Trump publicly promised this conflict would go on for.
Is there a point where Cooper and CENTCOM would press Trump harder and more directly to either end the conflict or reengage militarily to break the logjam?
The Post’s understanding is that even if this conflict is stuck for a full year or even a few years (however unlikely), Cooper’s and CENTCOM’s position would not change: strategic feedback should come only through lower channels, including Caine, Rubio, and Hegseth.
Former CENTCOM chief McKenzie warned US bases would be vulnerable to sustained Iranian attacks
In 2024, McKenzie, discussing American military bases in the region, warned that “the United States will not be able to maintain these bases in a full-throated conflict, because they will be rendered unusable by sustained Iranian attack.”
Previously, the Post and others have reported that CENTCOM and the US in general did not heed McKenzie’s warnings.
Cooper only took over CENTCOM fully in August 2025, so there is only so much he could have done, but his previous efforts on the issue had not been reported in any significant fashion.
In contrast, the Post has learned that there is a counter-narrative on the issue.
According to it, the winding down of many US bases and assets in the region did start before the war, especially in Iraq and Syria.
Since the war, more winding down has occurred in Iraq and Syria, and eventually in Kuwait as well. Notably, the US has not talked about reducing its footprint in Jordan and Saudi Arabia, though its bases there have been hit hard and repeatedly.
Another area where Cooper’s and CENTCOM’s narrative would likely differ from the narrative reported by most of the media to date relates to how unexpected the billions in damage to US bases from Iran have been.
Another disconnect within the administration is that Hegseth has often publicly denied the extent of the damage and has been accused of trying to cover it up.
But the CENTCOM view would be that such damage was, in fact, expected.
CENTCOM would ask rhetorical questions like: Since when has there been a war with no damage to one of the sides?
In addition, CENTCOM would note that a modern war in which bases were spread like peanut butter across a region was obviously vulnerable, and anyone who did not recognize this grossly misunderstood the weaknesses of America’s basing posture, a leftover from earlier eras of warfare.
But decades of basing cannot be changed overnight, especially in the enormous US military, which is known for being slow to transfer large forces between bases or military theaters.
It seemed to be implied that the much more recent expanded and evolving drone threat changed the security posture for US basing much more rapidly and radically than the decades-old missile threat.
Alternatively, elements of the Trump administration may not have thought Iran would succeed at firing off as many missiles at US bases as it did.
In contrast, Cooper would take significant pride in the success of America’s regional air-defense architecture with its Middle Eastern allies.
Meanwhile, the war might have heavily degraded the US supply of interceptors for missiles and drones. Some internal US defense establishment reports have said there could be shortages if there is a war in the near future with another adversary like Russia or China.
Cooper might have communicated this risk to Caine and Hegseth. However, both the US defense secretary and Trump have denied any combat impact from interceptor shortages – without explaining how a shortage would affect combat readiness.
In addressing these problematic byproducts of the war, the Post understands that Cooper’s view is that what matters most is that Iran was hurt by the war exponentially more than the US.
Put simply, Iran lost $200-$300 billion in its defense sector from US and Israeli attacks, while the US lost only around $5b.
In addition, some have said that absent the superior US-allied air defenses, Iranian missile fire could have potentially killed millions of people in worst-case scenarios.
Other estimates put the risk from Iranian missile fire more in the tens of thousands. But either way, the point about how ready Iran was to commit mass murder across the region, absent strong CENTCOM regional air defense, remains clear.
Some American sources have questioned whether this is the right way to evaluate the mission’s and the war’s success or failure.
They ask: What if Washington had an option to achieve its strategic goals with Iran without losing $5b. in damages to its bases?
US military sources believe that part of the problem with the public perception of the war could be that portions of them thought the Iran war would go as quickly and as easily as America’s effective coup in Venezuela in January of this year.
Unspoken by US military officials in this criticism, but obvious from public comments by the US president about how surprised he has been that Iran did not “crack” sooner, is that many military officials believe that Trump himself was swept up by the quick “win” in Venezuela.
Trump administration claimed Iran's ballistic missile threat would soon be eliminated
During the war, Trump, Caine, and Hegseth repeatedly made public claims indicating that Iran’s ballistic missile apparatus had been decimated and that its threat would almost entirely disappear within days or weeks.
Israeli defense and intelligence officials also told the Post in March and April that Iran’s missile capacity had fallen to possibly as few as several hundred missiles.
Iran fell from 2,500 missiles to 1,600, and its production capacity fell from an expected 2,000 by the end of 2026 to original pre-war estimates that, absent outside intervention, it might reach 6,000 missiles by the end of the year.
In that sense, the Post has learned that CENTCOM’s view would be that Iran’s missile threat is substantially weaker now than pre-war.
However, the predictions by Trump, Caine, and Hegseth seem substantially off base.
Even the predictions by Israeli defense and intelligence officials have turned out to be significantly overly optimistic.
If Iran is “not the same Iran,” as CENTCOM and Israel would both argue, it has still managed to fire dozens of ballistic missiles and drones at will throughout the Middle East. This includes firing on American ships during any period of renewed military conflict between Tehran and Washington.
These missile launches have paled in comparison to the hundreds of missiles and thousands of drones Iran was able to launch per day at the start of the war. They have been far more than the drizzle that some American and Israeli officials predicted, and remain a strategic-level threat.
Certainly, Iran cannot threaten the region as a “bully” the same way it could before. But the US and Israel are still refraining from going directly to control Iran’s remaining nuclear assets by force out of fear of what remains of the Islamic Republic’s capabilities.
All of this paints a nuanced picture of CENTCOM under Cooper as the region’s lead shaper in some respects, but one that avoids sticking its neck out too much in others.
Many top American generals who have spoken up when they disagreed with some aspect of Trump’s or Hegseth’s ideas have been summarily dismissed in numbers unseen in years.
Cooper’s preference for conveying his views through Caine, Hegseth, and Rubio has not only been a way of operating within the chain of command, but has also saved him so far from the rash wave of firings.
It will be years before history can fully judge the mix of undeniable major contributions Cooper has made to Middle East security, alongside major dilemmas where he steered clear of rocking the boat too much.
In the meantime, much of the region is thankful that, even if Trump and Washington are wildly unpredictable, they have the benefit of Cooper’s steady hand.

Middle Israel: Remember October 7 by building a stronger western Negev - opinion
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:17:18 UTC
21:17:18 KST

“Jews!” called Emanuel Ringelblum to his brethren, “write it down!”
A historian trapped in the Warsaw Ghetto, Ringelblum understood the value of documenting what he was witnessing, and so secretly recorded, with other scholars he assembled, everything they learned and saw about the unfolding Holocaust.
Ringelblum was murdered along with his family after managing an escape and getting caught, but much of what he documented was found stuffed in tin containers after the war, and became a priceless contribution to the Holocaust’s documentation.
He was but one link in a long chain of reporters who chronicled the Jewish people’s calamities, harking back to the Book of Lamentations’ description of Jerusalem’s sack in 586 BCE, and to Deuteronomy’s command “Remember what Amalek did to you” more than five centuries earlier.
It was a clarion call that the Jewish people repeatedly fulfilled.
“Father of Mercy,” a call for divine revenge written after the Crusader massacres of 1096, is said in synagogues throughout the world every Shabbat morning, to this day. After the 1648-49 massacre in Ukraine, for centuries millions of Jews fasted on the anniversary of its largest pogrom. Following the Holocaust, the Jews established more than 700 museums, monuments, and research institutions worldwide.
October 7 massacre raises new challenges for Israel's tradition of remembrance
Expectedly, Hamas’s massacre in the western Negev three years ago this week triggered this time-honored Jewish instinct. However, this trauma’s commemoration has raised dilemmas that previous disasters did not evoke.
Commemoration initiatives began days after the massacre. Makeshift monuments, laughing youngsters’ photos nailed onto fence poles above flower pots and little Israeli flags sprouted in multiple locations along Route 232. In the Re’im Forest, where the Nova music festival’s partygoers were mowed down, a whole forest of such photos became a makeshift pilgrimage site.
Then came commemoration projects.
Kinneret Gat, who was murdered in Kibbutz Be’eri, and her daughter Carmel, who died as a hostage in Gaza, are memorialized by a social start-up launched by their husband and father, Eshel, who collects unsold fruit and vegetables and distributes them to the needy. There are countless such initiatives countrywide: parks, stools, scholarships, concerts, and whatnot.
National commemoration, however, has been trickier. The dilemma began with the designation of the catastrophe’s memorial date. The Hebrew date was impossible because it falls out on Simchat Torah. The Gregorian date was also impossible, because Israeli remembrance days are all defined by Hebrew dates, and rightly so.
Ultimately, the government decided on the day after Simchat Torah, which will now be etched in Jewish memory alongside the dates that commemorate the Babylonian destruction, the Roman destruction, and the Holocaust.
Israel establishes national October 7 memorial day following public debate
Legislated as a National Memorial Day for the Massacre and Heroism of 22 Tishrei – October 7, the government initially tried to avoid including the word “slaughter” in its name. Public wrath, inspired by Jewish memory, changed that, and the bill passed along with instructions that flags be lowered to half-mast, ceremonies be held in schools, and a central memorial monument be built in the western Negev.
Though there were scandals en route to this formula (see “Miri Regev’s Ministry of Truth,” August 30, 2024), this part of the commemoration effort has been resolved. Not so the communal dilemma.
The big problem was what to do about the houses that Hamas disfigured and torched. There were three alternatives: repair and rebuild; destroy and build from scratch; turn the ruins into monuments, and rebuild elsewhere.
Kibbutz Nir Oz decided to destroy all its 400 damaged buildings and build from scratch, preserving only sporadic reminders of the carnage, to be integrated in a memorial complex. Kibbutz Be’eri took a similar decision, but decided to preserve one of the destroyed houses as part of a new memorial site.
In Kibbutz Kfar Aza, however, the dilemma caused a big debate between the “destroy” and “preserve” camps. The former won the vote, but a group of bereaved parents appealed last spring to the Supreme Court to block the demolition. A ruling has yet to be issued.
Commemorating October 7 in the western Negev is a shared national responsibility
It’s a heartbreaking communal debate in which outsiders are unable to participate. That cannot be said of the areas between, around, and beyond these kibbutzim. There, in the western Negev, the commemoration is every Israeli’s concern, obligation, and opportunity.
Some 50 KM. long and 20 kms. deep, the region abutting the Gaza Strip was part of a massive settlement project launched in the 1950s, becoming a great success, with 30 moshavim, 24 kibbutzim, and three cities.
In this part of the country there never were Palestinians, or, in fact, any human settlements until Israel turned it into a lush breadbasket. The virginity of its soil is what made it ideal for the organic agriculture in which some of its farms specialize, exporting more than 100,000 tons of highest-quality potatoes annually to Germany, Holland, Britain, and France.
Like its immaculate soil, the region’s inhabitants defied Israel’s political divisions, with secular and religious farmers regularly cooperating and living peacefully alongside the proletarian populations of Netivot, Ofakim, and Sderot.
In all, this region’s 57 communities were home to 60,000 Israelis when Hamas invaded and killed 278 in its rural communities, and 96 in its urban towns. Three years on, the population is 66,000, and growing.
This improbable momentum should be accelerated. The western Negev should inhabit 250,000 Israelis, connected by a spinal hikers’ path extending from Yad Mordecai in the North to Kissufim in the South.
Stretching along this trail on the massacre’s annual anniversary, the colorful march of thousands, winding between blossoming fields, handsome houses, and bustling towns, will say better than any prayer, monument, poem, or book: We remember. We remember that they came to kill, and we came to live; that they came to destroy, and we came to build; that they came from hatred’s bowels, and we came back from the dead.
The writer, a Hartman Institute fellow, is the author of the bestseller, The Jewish March of Folly (Yedioth Books 2026), now available in English on Amazon.

Russia's Uralvagonzavod eclipses 100,000 tanks made in 90-year history

MOSCOW, October 9. /TASS/. Russia’s Uralvagonzavod defense manufacturer (UVZ Group, part of the Rostec State Corporation) has produced 100,000 armored vehicles over its history, setting an absolute record in global tank manufacturing, the company’s press service reported on the occasion of UVZ 90th anniversary, which will be marked on October 11.
"In total, over the course of its history, UVZ has produced <…> more than 100,000 combat vehicles, which is an absolute record in global tank manufacturing," the press service stated.
It noted that Uralvagonzavod’s tanks have been purchased by 77 countries around the world. These achievements are the result of the efforts of more than 550,000 people who have worked at the plant over the course of nine decades.
"From the very beginning, Uralvagonzavod has proven that it can handle any task. In the 1930s, UVZ’s first heavy-duty open-top railcars immediately set the standard for the industry. During WW II, it was our assembly line that produced the largest number of the legendary T-34 tanks, which became a symbol of Victory. In the challenging 1990s, the plant did not falter, it persevered and found new strength. All of this was achieved thanks to the Ural spirit, the determination, and the talent of the plant’s workers. "Our plant is unique. It has received eight state awards, two of which were awarded in recent years. This means that we are not resting on our laurels but are successfully moving forward," emphasized UVZ CEO Alexander Potapov, whose remarks were cited by the press service.
It noted that in the fall of 1941, the world’s largest tank factory--the Ural Tank Plant No. 183--was established on the premises of Uralvagonzavod and 12 other enterprises that had been evacuated to the Urals. By the end of the year, the first batch of 25 T-34 tanks had already been sent to the front. Starting in May 1942, a T-34 rolled off the assembly line every 30 minutes. A total of 25,914 tanks were produced during the Great Patriotic War (1941-1945). The Ural Tank Plant surpassed the combined output of all German factories (23,000 tanks) in the production of mass-produced medium tanks. Every second T-34 that saw combat rolled off the Nizhny Tagil assembly line.
The company emphasized that every Uralvagonzavod tank can be described as "the first," "unique," and "one of a kind." The T-54 was a true breakthrough: its 100-mm rifled gun possessed muzzle energy that was unmatched at the time. The T-55 was the world’s first tank with a comprehensive anti-radiation protection system. The T-62 was the world’s first tank equipped with a smoothbore gun capable of firing armor-piercing sub-caliber shells at high muzzle velocity. Armor capable of withstanding the impact of such a projectile did not appear on NATO’s main battle tanks until the 1980s. The T-72--the most widely produced tank of the modern era--is in service with 45 countries worldwide. The T-90S is the most commercially successful tank of the 21st century.
T-90S tank
UVZ noted that at the turn of the century, the company’s major achievement was a contract to supply Russian T-90S tanks to India. "It became a turning point not only in the plant’s history but also served as an impetus for the revival of the domestic tank industry. During the extremely complex work on its implementation, it became clear that an industry-wide scale was necessary to preserve and develop the scientific and technical potential of tank manufacturing," the company added.
In 2007, the Uralvagonzavod Research and Production Corporation, which included design bureaus and research institutes, developers and manufacturers of armored vehicles, assemblies, components, and electronics, as well as repair plants was established under Russian presidential decree.

In Denmark, IKEA stores could become shelters amid Europe’s increasing preparedness
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:16:28 EEST
21:16:28 KST

In Denmark, IKEA stores could become shelters amid Europe’s increasing preparedness
Kyiv • UNN
IKEA stores in Denmark could become shelters or temporary hospitals during crises. Europe is involving businesses in civil preparedness.
Europe is strengthening its readiness for emergencies amid acts of sabotage by russia. As Reuters reports, IKEA stores in Denmark could become shelters, while in Estonia a law requires 300 companies to support the provision of critical services during a crisis, reports UNN.
Details
In the event of a power outage, flooding, or an attack on critical infrastructure facilities in Denmark, IKEA could turn its stores into temporary accommodation centers or even temporary hospitals. Restaurants could provide food, generators could keep the buildings operating, and additional beds could be assembled from kits taken from warehouse shelves.
The media outlet emphasizes that this idea reflects broader changes in Europe’s approach to security issues: governments are increasingly focusing not only on the armed forces and emergency services, but also on businesses capable of helping maintain the functioning of society during a crisis.
These efforts have gained relevance amid a wave of alleged acts of sabotage, cyberattacks, and other incidents that European officials link to russia’s hybrid war. Danish intelligence warned that russia is likely to intensify such activity against NATO countries and other Western states in the coming months — an accusation moscow denies.
The European Union encourages member states to cooperate more closely with businesses במסגרת the Union Preparedness Strategy, launched in March 2025.
Additionally
IKEA is part of the Danish Corporate Crisis Preparedness Coalition — a network that keeps track of resources that private companies can provide in emergencies: from beds and food supplies to trucks and specialized personnel.
"IKEA is a very good example, because intuitively no one would include this company on a list of crisis resources... An IKEA store has space, goods, food outlets, and generators," noted Maja Brolos, head of the network.
This concept is not purely theoretical. During the devastating floods in Valencia, Spain, in October 2024, IKEA turned one of its stores into a shelter for more than 600 people.
Representatives of the retailer said that the company does not have a global emergency preparedness program, and that such measures are organized separately in each country.
Other Danish retailers are also preparing for emergencies. Salling Group, Denmark’s largest supermarket operator, is opening the first of 51 stores designed to operate for 48 hours without electricity or internet access.
This trend is also spreading beyond Denmark. In Estonia, a law requires 300 companies to support the provision of critical services during a crisis, while Finland has a network of government agencies, non-governmental organizations, and companies responsible for security of supply. In Poland, some companies are legally required to provide the armed forces with their vehicles, equipment, and property in the event of a crisis.
The Danish network includes more than 200 companies employing more than 300,000 people — from retail businesses and construction groups to telecommunications operators.
"In the event of a crisis, the authorities will have a single point of contact to turn to, and we will identify companies capable of helping," Brolos said.
According to her, a state compensation system is currently being developed, with the amount of reimbursement to be determined individually in each case.
This voluntary network has already participated in emergency preparedness exercises together with government agencies, but it has not yet faced a real large-scale crisis.
However, there has already been an incident demonstrating how an IKEA store in Denmark can serve as a shelter.
In December 2021, because of a snowstorm, six customers and around two dozen employees were forced to spend the night in an IKEA store in Aalborg and sleep on beds displayed in the sales area.
The very next morning, the staff changed the bed linen, and the store resumed operations for visitors.

Ukraine abolishes one-year driving experience requirement for BE, C1E, CE licences
Ukraine
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:15:16 EEST
21:15:16 KST

The Ukrainian government has abolished the requirement for drivers to have at least one year of driving experience in a base vehicle category before obtaining licences for categories BE, C1E and CE, the Ministry of Agrarian Policy and Food said.
Under the decision, holders of category B, C1 or C licences will be eligible for the corresponding BE, C1E or CE category after completing the prescribed retraining programmes and passing a practical driving test at a territorial service centre of the Interior Ministry.
The change will apply during martial law and for six months after it is terminated or lifted, the ministry said.
Category BE covers passenger cars towing trailers with a maximum authorised mass exceeding 750 kg. Category C1E covers medium-duty vehicles in category C1, with a mass of 3.5 to 7.5 tonnes, towing trailers exceeding 750 kg. Category CE covers category C trucks towing trailers or semi-trailers exceeding 750 kg.
The ministry said the change would help bring more drivers into the freight transport sector and eliminate the need to wait an additional year before qualifying to drive vehicles with trailers.
“For the agricultural sector, this is an important decision, as a shortage of drivers directly affects logistics. When there are not enough people behind the wheel, it becomes harder to transport the harvest on time and deliver produce to elevators, processing facilities, ports and border crossing points,” Agrarian Policy and Food Minister Taras Vysotsky said, according to the statement.
The changes do not affect statutory age requirements or the basic legal right to drive, the ministry said. They simplify procedures for driver training, retraining and qualification certification.
The decision extends earlier government measures to ease access to the driving profession. Since 2022, drivers holding category B licences have been permitted to drive category C and C1 vehicles during martial law. The government has also simplified access to category CE licences for drivers who already hold category C licences.

Tolkien’s Elvish languages live on through global fan communities
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:14:09 UTC
21:14:09 KST

Aybuke Inal and Irmak Akcan
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The fictional Elvish languages developed by British author and philologist J.R.R. Tolkien continue to be studied and used by fans decades after their introduction in works including The Lord of the Rings, The Hobbit and The Silmarillion.
Tolkien designed multiple languages for the peoples of Middle-earth, giving them distinct grammar, vocabulary and sound systems as well as imagined histories showing how they changed over time.
Among the best known are Quenya and Sindarin. Quenya was conceived as an older, ceremonial language associated particularly with the Elves of Valinor, while Sindarin was more commonly spoken among the Elves living in Middle-earth.
Tolkien drew inspiration from real languages when developing them. Finnish and Latin influenced Quenya, while Sindarin was shaped partly by Welsh.
Although Tolkien did not complete every element of the languages, enthusiasts have continued studying his manuscripts and other writings to reconstruct and use them.
Norwegian author and philologist Helge Kare Fauskanger told Anadolu that his interest began when he encountered the Elvish script in The Lord of the Rings as a young reader.
He said the 1987 publication of The Etymologies, a document included in The Lost Road, greatly expanded scholars’ understanding of Tolkien’s languages by providing thousands of words and linguistic roots.
According to Fauskanger, Tolkien first imagined a primitive Elvish language and then developed separate branches by applying different sound changes. This allowed Quenya and Sindarin to appear related while retaining their own characteristics.
Many familiar Middle-earth names, including Aragorn, Galadriel, Minas Tirith, Mordor and Gondor, have roots in Sindarin, he said.
Learning the languages can nevertheless be challenging because Tolkien repeatedly revised their structure during his lifetime.
“Rather than pieces from a single puzzle, what we have is a mixture of pieces from countless puzzles,” Fauskanger said, explaining that individual documents often reflect Tolkien’s thinking at a particular moment.
A student with a linguistic background could understand the fundamentals of Quenya grammar within a week, he said, although learning its vocabulary would take considerably longer. Gaps also remain in the known vocabulary.
“There is a word for rat, but none for mouse,” he said, adding that future publications could fill some of those gaps.
Despite the difficulties, online communities continue to use Quenya and other Elvish languages.
“They generally try to translate phrases intended for tattoos or inscriptions on rings, or share poems and other short texts,” Fauskanger said.
For many fans, he added, the languages and Tolkien’s writing systems are inseparable from the broader aesthetic and cultural appeal of Middle-earth.

UN rights chief hails Navi Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize as recognition of global human rights struggle

Pillay, who previously served as UN High Commissioner for Human Rights, also chaired the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, which concluded during her tenure that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza.

Anadolu’s documentary Salda: A Bridge to the Red Planet was screened on Friday on the public day of the 77th International Astronautical Congress (IAC) in Antalya.
The 72-minute film, produced by AA Productions, looks at Lake Salda in the southwestern Burdur province and its geological similarities to Mars, as well as the need to protect the lake.
It features scientists, biologists, earth scientists, divers and experts from Türkiye and NASA, from the US.
Salda has attracted scientific interest because its magnesium carbonate formations resemble those found in Mars’ Jezero Crater, an ancient lake basin where NASA’s Perseverance rover is investigating the planet’s geological history and searching for evidence of past microbial life. Studying similar formations on Earth can help scientists interpret geological evidence collected on Mars.
An IAC attendee from South Africa told Anadolu the documentary gave an insight into potential life on another planet. “Hopefully it will happen in our lifetime. But if not, at least one has an idea that there is potential for life on another planet after Earth,” the person said.
A visitor from the Netherlands, who was hearing about Lake Salda for the first time, said the film had “many nice shots.” 
“Now I really want to go there,” he said.
The attendee’s Turkish companion, who visited the lake 10 years ago, recalled how the lake had attracted public attention that time, both as a tourism destination and because of its scientific significance.
Reflecting on the documentary’s broader themes, he said the film brought together “nature, future of humankind, or past, and space.”
The congress, for which Anadolu is the global communications partner, ends Friday at the NEST Congress Center.

====================================================================================================

India’s Energy Transition Is Complicated, But Progressing
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
12:12:00 UTC
21:12:00 KST

Across Western climate commentary, India is frequently portrayed as a coal-dependent laggard whose rising emissions threaten to offset progress elsewhere. This framing obscures a more complex reality: While coal continues to dominate India’s power supply, the country is also building clean energy at one of the fastest rates in the world. Understanding this contradiction requires reassessing how climate progress is conventionally measured.
The concerns behind India’s continued use of coal are real. India recorded the world’s largest absolute rise in emissions in 2024, and thermal power still generates around 70 percent of its electricity. Yet these figures describe where India stands today, not where it is heading.
At the 2015 Paris climate conference, India pledged that 40 percent of its installed power capacity would come from non-fossil fuel sources by 2030. It reached that goal in November 2021, almost a decade early. After raising its target to 50 percent, India crossed that threshold in June 2025, this time five years ahead of schedule.
As those figures suggest, India’s renewables expansion is significant. India’s non-fossil fuel energy capacity passed 300 gigawatts in July 2026, more than half of its total installed capacity. The country added a record 55 gigawatts of clean capacity in the 2025–26 financial year and now ranks third in the world for installed renewable energy. On July 29, 2025, renewables met more than half of India’s electricity demand, a record share and, in the Indian government’s words, “a remarkable sign of change.”
Many of today’s high-income economies industrialized on coal for over a century before shifting to cleaner energy. India is attempting to do both simultaneously, expanding electricity access and industrial growth for 1.4 billion people while building one of the largest clean-energy systems in the world.
Yet significant challenges remain. The largest is the gap between capacity and generation. Although more than half of India’s installed capacity is now non-fossil, these sources produce under a third of the electricity the country consumes. Solar output peaks in the afternoon while demand often peaks in the evening, and the storage and transmission networks needed to bridge this gap are still under construction. Until they are complete, coal will remain the backbone of reliable energy supply.
Rising demand compounds the difficulty. Rapid economic growth, urbanization and more frequent heatwaves are driving up electricity consumption, which is why India’s total emissions continue to climb even as its power mix becomes cleaner. Clean capacity is being added quickly, but demand is rising almost as fast.
Heavy industry presents a further hurdle. Steel and aluminum are among the hardest sectors to decarbonize. Indian exporters now face carbon border rules in key markets; the Global Trade Research Initiative estimated that Indian steel and aluminum exporters may need to cut prices by 15 to 22 percent to remain competitive in Europe. Smaller firms struggle the most with the cost of measuring and reporting emissions.
Finance is the final, perhaps most binding, constraint. A transition of this scale requires enormous investment, much of it in grids and storage with long payback periods. At COP29, India objected to the new climate finance goal of $300 billion a year, which was less than one-fourth of the $1.3 trillion that developing countries had demanded.
Still, India continues to push forward. Its national carbon market became operational in January 2025, providing industry with a price signal to reduce emissions. The growth of India’s fossil fuel emissions is projected to have slowed sharply in 2025.
Energy transitions are rarely linear, as recent Western experience shows. During the 2022 energy crisis, several European countries temporarily returned to coal to maintain supply before renewable growth resumed. This was a reasonable response to an emergency, and it illustrates that every country balances climate goals against energy security and affordability. India faces the same trade-offs at a lower income level and with more people still gaining reliable power.
International partners can also play a constructive role. Expanded financing for grid infrastructure and battery storage would directly address India’s generation gap. Mechanisms that recognize domestic carbon pricing, such as India’s carbon market, could ease the burden of border carbon rules on smaller exporters. The International Solar Alliance, which India co-founded, already offers a strong base for wider cooperation on clean technology and supply chains
Coal will remain part of India’s energy mix for some time, and the obstacles ahead are real. But measuring climate commitment through coal dependence alone risks misreading one of the world’s largest clean-energy transitions.
Assessments of India’s climate performance should therefore shift their focus. Rather than asking whether India still uses coal, the question should be whether it is moving decisively away from it. A fairer yardstick would weigh a country’s direction of travel, per capita emissions, and historical responsibility alongside its current energy mix. After all, the average Indian emits about 2.2 tonnes of carbon dioxide a year, less than half the global average, and India has contributed under 4 percent of cumulative carbon dioxide emissions since the industrial revolution.
Future analysis of India’s climate role should account for both its achievements and the constraints shaping its choices.

Court fines man for storing dead parents in freezers for 30 years
Finland
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
15:11:49 EEST
21:11:49 KST

A court in Turku has fined an 81-year-old man about 2,000 euros after finding him guilty on three counts of violating the sanctity of a grave, as well as the unlawful concealing of an unburied body.
Police discovered last year that the man had stored the bodies of his parents in freezers for over 30 years.
The case first came to the police's attention when the defendant, a trained physician who is also listed as an executive at a firm described as offering funeral services, was found digging up a family grave last autumn.
His 70-year-old brother was also charged with and convicted of violating the sanctity of a grave in relation to that incident, and the court fined him a total of 640 euros.
Decades-long concealment
The court heard that the brothers' parents died of natural causes in 1994 and 1995 and their bodies were released to the family for burial.
However, the older of the two brothers took possession of their parents' remains in 1995 when he collected one body from a hospital and the other from the University of Turku's department of pathology.
Police found the bodies in an outdoor storage unit at a detached house in Turku in 2024.
The 81-year-old defendant told the court during the trial that he was "only acting in accordance" with his father's wishes.
When police found the bodies, the electricity had been cut off to one of the freezers.
"The photographs presented by the prosecutor show that the freezers were under various pieces of junk amid general disorder, and had lain undisturbed for a long period," the court's ruling noted.
The court further found that the parents' wish for their bodies to be frozen did not absolve the man of criminal liability, as he was found to have violated statutes intended to protect people's basic understanding of how the dead should be treated.
Finnish legislation concerning the violation of the sanctity of a grave changed in 1999. Before the change in the law, the offence was called unlawful concealment of an unburied body.
Because the timeline of the crimes preceded and followed the law reform, the man was found guilty of both offences.
The court's ruling is not yet final, meaning it can be appealed to a higher court.
