Iran’s presence in world’s top 2% of scientists nearly doubles
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:52:14 UTC
20:52:14 KST

Iran’s presence in world’s top 2% of scientists nearly doubles
TEHRAN – The number of Iranian researchers included in the world’s top 2% of scientists has nearly doubled, rising from 1,154 in 2020 to 2,678 in 2026, according to Scopus data provided by Elsevier.
An analysis of the rankings shows a steady upward trend in the number of Iranian researchers recognized among the world’s top 2% of scientists over the past several years.
The number rose to 1,701 in 2021 and 1,941 in 2022, before increasing to 2,137 in 2023 and 2,514 in 2024. The figure reached 2,678 in 2026, ISNA reported.
The majority of Iranian researchers are from 30 universities and scientific centers; the University of Tehran, with 123 researchers, is placed first. Followed by Tehran University of Medical Sciences (112), Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (75), and Iran University of Science and Technology (74).
Tabriz University of Medical Sciences with 66 researchers, Iran University of Medical Sciences with 64 researchers, University of Tabriz with 61 researchers, and Tarbiat Modares University with 56 researchers are placed fifth to eighth.
Also, the number of highly cited Iranian researchers in the career-long index has experienced threefold growth, rising from 433 in 2020 to 1,380 in 2026.
Some 794 out of 1,380 researchers, amounting to 57.5 percent, are from 30 universities and scientific centers. University of Tehran (with 91 researchers), Sharif University of Technology (53), Amirkabir University of Technology and Tehran University of Medical Sciences (each with 48 researchers), and Iran University of Science and Technology (45), University of Tabriz and Tarbiat Modares University (each with 40 researchers) rank first to fifth.
Stanford University’s list of “World’s Top 2%” scientists is based on a 2 percent or above percentile rank, or the top 100,000 by c-score (with and without self-citations). This prestigious list identifies the world’s leading researchers, representing approximately 2 percent of all scientists worldwide.
It encompasses standardised data on citations, h-index, and a wide range of bibliometric indicators. Researchers are classified into 22 scientific fields and 174 sub-fields, drawing from Scopus data provided by Elsevier through ICSR Lab.
The esteemed ranking, derived from Scopus database data, highlights researchers whose work has had a significant impact across various scientific disciplines.
The ranking is based on a composite indicator (c-score) calculated from six citation metrics: Total citations (NC), H-index (H), Hm-index (H-index adjusted for the number of authors), Citations to single-author papers (NCS), Citations to single or first-author papers (NCSF), Citations to single, first, or last-author papers (NCSFL).
The c-score combines these metrics to provide a comprehensive measure of a scientist’s impact, accounting for both the quantity and the quality of their contributions.
The list provides two separate rankings, each offering a different perspective on a researcher’s impact:
 
Career-long impact ranking: This evaluates a researcher’s cumulative citation performance over their entire career to date.
 
Single-year impact ranking: This focuses on the citation impact of research produced in the most recent year.
Iran ranks first in key scientific output among Islamic countries
Iran ranks first among Islamic nations in key fields of scientific output such as quantum science, cognitive sciences, artificial intelligence, biotechnology, and advanced materials, the head of the Presidential Affairs Office at the Islamic World Science Citation Center (ISC) announced in August.
The country is in close competition with Turkey and Saudi Arabia in these fields, IRNA quoted Saeed Bakhtiari as saying.
He made the remarks in a press briefing on August 17, noting that the development of science in these fields has also been emphasized in national development plans.
Based on the reputable Web of Science database, Iran ranks first among Islamic countries in scientific output in some of these fields, while placing second or third in others. Overall, however, Iran holds the top position, he said.
Bakhtiari noted that in advanced materials—a multidisciplinary field spanning physics, chemistry, mechanics and materials science—Iran ranks second among Islamic countries and ninth worldwide.
He added that Iran ranks third in artificial intelligence, behind Saudi Arabia and Turkey, while in quantum science it ranks second, after Saudi Arabia.
The ISC official further said that Iran holds the top position among Islamic countries in scientific output in cognitive sciences and ranks first overall.
According to Web of Science (WoS) data, over a five-year period (from 2021 to 2025), Iran (with 32 documents) ranks first in cognitive sciences among Islamic countries.
Turkey, with 23 documents, and Saudi Arabia, with 22 documents, are placed second and third, respectively, IRNA reported.
From 2014 to 2023, Iran ranked either first or second in most fields of cognitive sciences among Islamic countries. Over the course of the decade, the country ranked first in cognitive neuroscience, cognitive rehabilitation, and cognitive linguistics with 387, 156, and 30 documents, respectively.
It ranked second in cognitive psychology (124 documents), cognitive education (561 documents), philosophy of mind (34 documents), and cognitive evaluation (898 documents). The country’s best ranking globally was in cognitive neuroscience; it ranked 15.
Tehran University of Medical Sciences, with 73 documents, University of Tehran, with 39 documents, and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences, with 32 documents, ranked first to third in cognitive neuroscience. In cognitive psychology, University of Tehran(10 documents ), Ferdowsi University of Mashhad (7 documents), and Allameh Tabatabai University (6 documents) were the top three universities.
In cognitive linguistics, University of Tehran (with 3 documents), Al-Zahra University (3 documents), Allameh Tabatabei University (2 documents ) ranked first to third. In cognitive education, Tehran University of Medical Sciences, Iran University of Medical Sciences, Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences were placed first to third, respectively.
In cognitive rehabilitation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences (21 documents), University of Tehran (16 documents), and Iran University of Medical Sciences (12 documents) ranked first to third. The best three universities in philosophy of mind were University of Tehran, Isfahan University, and Amirkabir University of Technology.
In cognitive evaluation, Tehran University of Medical Sciences ranked first with 196 documents. Iran University of Medical Sciences (105 documents) and Shahid Beheshti University of Medical Sciences (91 documents) ranked second and third.
The country is placed second in quantum (with 216 documents) and advanced materials (with 5975 documents), after Saudi Arabia, with 283 and 6160 documents in quantum and advanced materials. Malaysia (with 154 documents) and Egypt (with 3151 documents) are placed third in quantum and advanced materials, respectively.
Despite illegal sanctions, Iran secures first place in cognitive sciences among Islamic nations and ranks ninth globally in advanced materials. Numerous prestigious Iranian universities and institutions are included in international rankings. These accomplishments underscore the country’s scientific capabilities, IRIB quoted Science Minister Hossein Simaei-Sarraf as saying, addressing the 7th Turkey Educational Technologies Summit (known as TETZ 2026), held in Istanbul from June 26 to 28.
Iran serves as a great opportunity to invest in higher education and modern technologies. The country has one of the largest higher education systems in the region, with more than three million students and over seventy thousand faculty members and researchers.
Highlighting that the rapid development of emerging technologies, including AI, is fundamentally transforming human relationships and higher education systems around the world at an unprecedented pace, Simaei-Sarraf said that effective use of smart technologies requires the establishment of a system based on algorithmic transparency, educational justice, accountability, protection of learners’ rights, and responsible data governance.

Pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger Mikhail Zvinchuk arrested in Montenegro
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:51:18 UTC
20:51:18 KST

A leading pro-Kremlin Russian military blogger with reported ties to Russia’s intelligence services has been arrested in Montenegro, after warnings of attempts to destabilise the Balkan country, officials have said.
Mikhail Zvinchuk, the founder of the influential Rybar war blog, was detained on Friday alongside his wife and three other Russians by police and security agents in the Adriatic resort town of Risan, on suspicion of spreading Russian influence, local media reported.
Montenegro’s prime minister, Milojko Spajić, confirmed Zvinchuk’s detention in a post on X, saying it followed warnings that the country would face attempts at destabilisation and hybrid warfare.
The Montenegrin news outlet Vijesti reported later on Friday that Zvinchuk and the other detainees were to be expelled from the country on national security grounds.
The Russian Telegram news channel Baza said officers detained Zvinchuk at the luxury Mövenpick hotel in Risan. It said the group was taken to Podgorica, Montenegro’s capital, for questioning and their phones and passports were confiscated.
Founded in 2018 by Zvinchuk, a former press officer at Russia’s defence ministry, Rybar is one of the most popular Russian military blogs covering the war in Ukraine, with more than 1.5 million subscribers on Telegram. It forms part of a sprawling online media ecosystem that promotes Vladimir Putin’s invasion of Ukraine.
But Rybar’s activities extend well beyond Ukraine, with the channel promoting pro-Kremlin narratives in Africa and the Middle East. More recently, it has been accused of amplifying far-right narratives surrounding the migration crisis in Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in north Africa.
“At the moment, the project team is in contact with Russia’s foreign ministry, which is working to resolve the situation. Since there were no violations of local legislation, we expect all detainees to be released,” the channel said on Telegram.
Britain sanctioned Zvinchuk and Rybar in December 2025 over their role in spreading Kremlin propaganda and undermining support for Ukraine. The British government said Zvinchuk received funding from the Russian state-owned defence conglomerate Rostec, and worked with members of Russia’s intelligence services.
The US has separately accused Zvinchuk of attempting to interfere in the 2024 presidential election, offering a reward of up to $10m for information about those involved.
Days before his arrest, Zvinchuk boasted on social media that he had managed to enter Montenegro despite being subject to western sanctions and an entry ban. He mocked a border guard who, he said, had searched his belongings but failed to check his name against a database.
The Kremlin spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said Moscow was aware of Zvinchuk’s detention and would work to secure his release.
Russia’s former president Dmitry Medvedev suggested Moscow could detain European and American citizens to use in prisoner exchanges to secure Zvinchuk’s release. “We will probably have to replenish our pool of prisoners for exchange with European and American idiots in order to get our own people back,” he wrote on social media.
The arrest is likely to further strain relations between Montenegro and Russia, which have long been tense. In 2016, Montenegrin authorities accused Russian operatives of plotting with Serbian ultranationalists to stage a coup, allegations Moscow denied.
Montenegro, which joined Nato in 2017 and is seeking membership of the EU, imposed sanctions on Russia after its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
The country recently approved plans to end visa-free travel for Russian citizens from 1 November, closing off a popular holiday destination for Russian tourists as it brings its visa policy into line with the EU.

China says it reaches ‘understanding’ with EU on hybrid cars
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:50:29 UTC
20:50:29 KST

EU and China clinch deal to curb hybrid car exports
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič says the agreement could prevent millions of Chinese vehicles from entering the European market over the next four years.
The European Union and China reached an agreement on Friday that will curb China’s booming hybrid car exports, delivering a breakthrough in negotiations aimed at rebalancing their trade relationship.
The announcement came as Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič wrapped up two days of talks in Beijing, the culmination of a push launched in June to narrow the bloc’s €1 billion-a-day trade deficit with China.
The deal marks a win for the EU executive, which has been under pressure to secure concessions from Beijing. Going into the talks, France and Germany strengthened Šefčovič’s hand by calling for the EU to take tough action on trade if China failed to curb a growing export glut.
Advertisement
Speaking in Beijing, the commissioner said the two sides had reached an agreement that would help to shield European automakers from low-price Chinese competition. He declined to enter into specifics before EU leaders officially mandate the EU executive to move forward.
“We have reached a shared understanding to moderate China’s export of hybrids and plug-in hybrids to the European Union. This opens the prospect of cutting China’s exports by more than a half,” Šefčovič told reporters.
The estimate was based on projections of how Chinese exports would grow over the next four years without the agreement. In practical terms, it would mean that “several millions of car exports from China to the European Union” would be prevented, he explained.
China’s Commerce Ministry highlighted the understanding on hybrids in a parallel 16-point statement, but offered no details on how exports would be restrained. It said the two sides “will continue to strengthen communication and cooperation under the trade monitoring mechanism and further leverage dialogue mechanisms to enhance mutual understanding.”
Šefčovič declined to elaborate when asked whether the deal would allow the EU to impose safeguards — a mixture of import quotas and tariffs — a step that Brussels has been considering. He said the arrangement would comply with the rules of the World Trade Organization.
First step
Šefčovič said that Beijing had also agreed to lower duties on European goods worth €4 billion, ranging from olive oil to footwear, a move that would save exporters €225 million.
Advertisement
“It is a crucial first step,” he said. “But only a first step in the process of rebalancing.”
The Slovak commissioner said he would report back to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, along with EU leaders, when they meet for a summit in Brussels next Thursday.
He had focused on cars as a key deliverable going into meetings in Beijing with Commerce Minister Wang Wentao and Vice Prime Minister He Lifeng.
Chinese auto exports to Europe have been booming, accounting in August for one in eight cars sold in the bloc — mainly driven by sales of hybrids. Europe’s own automotive industry is feeling the pressure, with Volkswagen and Mercedes-Benz recently announcing job cuts and plant closures.
Aside from the deal on hybrids, Beijing said in its statement that it was “willing to continue” fast-tracking licenses to export rare earth elements to the EU. Automakers had been forced to shut down assembly lines after China temporarily restricted exports in response to U.S. tariffs last year. China dominates the production and processing of rare earths.
“We have reached a shared understanding to further facilitate China’s export licensing for rare earths and permanent magnets,” Šefčovič said.
Advertisement
Road ahead
Brussels sees the agreement on hybrid electric vehicles as a blueprint that could be replicated to shield further EU sectors currently under strain, such as chemicals or machinery. The two sides plan to meet again in March 2027, and will hold a video call in January.
The agreement on one of the EU’s top negotiating targets significantly reduces the risk of an escalation in trade tensions that could have led to a tit-for-tat round of retaliation. It remains to be seen whether the EU will act swiftly on the Franco-German call to empower Brussels to shut out exports from countries that destabilize its single market.
“Public opinion and the leaders clearly expect very fast action from our side. I am glad to say that the Chinese partners appreciated this very strong political argument, and therefore, we can proceed through the negotiated solution,” said Šefčovič.
Other areas of agreement include exploring easier market access for European medical devices, as well as promises by Beijing to scale back sweeping disease-control measures that have restricted European meat and livestock exports.
While the deal will cool the most immediate tensions, a wider resolution to the economic imbalances that fueled the conflict remains distant. The EU’s trade deficit with China totaled nearly €360 billion in 2025, and is already up 12 percent so far this year.
China’s automotive exports to the EU, which totaled €15.1 billion last year, are only a fraction of that.

Self-driving Razorback UGV carries drone-killing turret
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:50:11 UTC
20:50:11 KST

- Forterra and Hypercraft are showing the Razorback unmanned ground vehicle with AutoDrive autonomy and a 9 Mothers Edda counter-drone turret at AUSA.
- The companies say the vehicle targets contested logistics, but no customer, contract or test schedule has been announced.
Forterra and Hypercraft are showing a driverless off-road vehicle built for military resupply at the Association of the U.S. Army’s annual meeting in Washington, pairing Hypercraft’s Razorback unmanned ground vehicle with Forterra’s AutoDrive self-driving system and a counter-drone turret from 9 Mothers.
The companies say the vehicle is aimed at contested logistics, moving supplies through areas where a human driver would be under fire. Neither company has announced a military customer, contract or price for the combination.
“We’re going after contested logistics and other missions where a driver is the most exposed person on the battlefield,” Forterra Chief Growth Officer Scott Sanders told Tectonic. “Razorback and AutoDrive combine to deliver a platform that can go further, over more complicated terrain, and power platforms in ways that traditional UGVs cannot.”
Razorback is the first complete vehicle from Hypercraft, a company in Provo, Utah, that started out building electric powertrains for commercial vehicles before moving into defense. Hypercraft unveiled the vehicle earlier this year. It is more than 4 meters (13 feet) long and, according to the company, can carry up to 1,814 kg (4,000 pounds), drive about 800 km (500 miles) and supply up to 38 kilowatts of electricity to other equipment. Hypercraft designed it to take third-party sensors, radios, weapons and mission payloads, and it has already shown the vehicle with Fortem Technologies’ counter-drone radar.
Sanders said Razorback was designed for autonomy from the start, which made it an easy fit, since many unmanned ground vehicles are crewed trucks with self-driving kits added after production.
Forterra, formerly Robotic Research, does not build vehicles. Its AutoDrive package combines software, sensors and computers that can turn an existing vehicle into a driverless one. The company says AutoDrive has been integrated into more than 50 vehicle types, used on more than 1,100 missions and put under contract for more than 258 systems. Those include Polaris Ranger 1500 utility vehicles used in Ukraine, Oshkosh Joint Light Tactical Vehicles for the U.S. Marine Corps’ ROGUE-Fires anti-ship missile launcher and Ford F-250 pickups for the U.S. Army.
The vehicle at AUSA carries 9 Mothers’ Edda turret, a roughly 23 kg (50-pound) counter-drone system from Austin, Texas. Edda listens for the sound of small drone rotors, tracks the target with cameras and fires a shotgun at drones about 18 cm (7 inches) across at ranges of 10 to 100 meters (33 to 328 feet). In August, the U.S. Army tested the same turret on a Forterra-equipped, self-driving Ford F-250 during a live-fire exercise at Fort Bragg, North Carolina.
Forterra said it chooses partners that solve real operational problems, can scale to production and understand that autonomy reaches beyond software into the vehicle, sensors, computers, communications and operator.
“Get any of those wrong, and the system doesn’t get fielded,” Sanders said.
Forterra is also one of six companies the U.S. Army selected in August for its Infantry Last Tactical Mile prototype effort, which is testing robotic vehicles for front-line resupply and casualty evacuation, using its MESA vehicle built on a Polaris Ranger.

20:49:48 KST

Shein, the online fast-fashion retailer founded in China, increased sales in the UK by just over a quarter last year, overtaking its British rival Asos.
The company, whose global parent group listed on the Hong Kong stock exchange valued at just over $26bn (£19.6bn) last month, increased sales at its UK division by 26% to £2.58bn, according to accounts filed at Companies House.
Pre-tax profits rose 18% to £45.2m even as the number of people employed by the group in the UK, mostly in sales and marketing, rose to 113 from 91 a year before. The company paid £11.2m in current tax – understood to be mainly corporation tax – up from £9.6m a year before.
Shein said sales had been helped by a marketing partnership with the Wireless and Creamfields music festivals, a pop-up shop on London’s Oxford Street and Christmas gift events in Edinburgh, Manchester and Liverpool as well as London.
Asos’s sales were £2.47bn in the year to 31 August 2025 – although this figure includes revenues outside the UK, unlike Shein UK’s comparable statistic.
Shein’s strong trading figures are likely to increase pressure on the government to bring forward action to change the “de minimis” rule that has underpinned the rise of the fast-growing online specialists Shein and Temu.
Fears about China’s retailers and manufacturers dumping goods in the UK have grown since the US last year revoked its own de minimis exception for Chinese-made goods, crimping Shein’s expansion there.
The retailer’s model is based on shipping orders of cheap clothes from Chinese factories to homes so that each order is low enough in value to avoid import duties.
Under the US exemption, which was scrapped last year, parcels with a value of less than $800 (£600) shipped to individuals had been spared from import tax.
The EU is also phasing out its exemption on customs duties for low-value parcels. It began in July by replacing the €150 de minimis relief with a flat €3 customs duty.
The former UK chancellor Rachel Reeves said she would get rid of the UK’s rule, which allows overseas sellers to send goods valued at £135 or less direct to British shoppers without paying any customs duty, by 2028. However, major retail bosses have said the government should move sooner.
Investors’ concerns about global government regulatory changes meant Shein’s value was far lower when it listed on the stock market than had been expected several years ago.
It reached a valuation of $100bn in an April 2022 fundraising round, making it the third most valuable startup in the world, and then considered a £50bn ($66bn) float on the London Stock Exchange in 2024 before eventually launching in Hong Kong.
Shein, founded by the entrepreneur Chris Xu, runs most of its operations from China but sells all its goods outside the country. It moved its headquarters to Singapore at the start of 2022 and has recently begun manufacturing in other countries including Turkey and Brazil.
After forced labour concerns were raised, Shein said it had tightened its supplier policies, enforced through regular audits, with any child or forced labour violations becoming grounds for immediate termination of contract.
Last week, Shein reported a 67% fall in group quarterly profits to £173m in its first results since the float, blaming higher oil prices and freight rates linked to the war in Iran.

‘Nobody is listening to us’: on the school protest frontline, I heard why France’s students feel disowned | Alexander Hurst
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:48:58 UTC
20:48:58 KST

When adolescents protest that the government is failing to uphold their right to an education, and the government’s response is to send in riot police, the government has lost the plot. People outside France may have spent the past week watching the student protests in Paris and other cities, and thought, “Well, France has a long tradition of insurrection” or, “That’s just the French being French.”
But the situation that has provoked the high-school walkouts and teenage anger is most likely not one they would immediately associate with the France of their imaginations. In place of its lost plot, the French government has a collection of anecdotes and statistics that it should be ashamed of: 27th place in the most recent OECD education rankings, schools with ceilings collapsing and rats in classrooms and, in a school in Bagnolet, no drinkable water; an increase in the average number of students per class from 27 in 2010 to over 30 today; half of primary and high schools missing teachers at the start of the school year – many of them with no substitutes or replacements.
Julie, a 34-year-old teacher who joined the demonstrations, told me that staff shortages were the fault of “low salaries and poor treatment.” She has to commute for an hour and 45 minutes each way between Paris and the school on the city’s outskirts where she accepted a post last year after switching careers. All for €2100 (£1,780) a month, plus some overtime pay. Teachers’ salaries in France are only 56% of what they are in Germany – even as over €200bn in public subsidies finds its way annually to businesses.
So it could easily have been a teacher-led revolt – instead, the high-schoolers themselves cracked first.
They paid a high price for refusing to accept a failing education system: a 16-year-old has lost the use of an eye, a 15-year-old has lost a hand, a 14-year-old has a broken jaw – all from police munitions. Hundreds more have been injured in some way. In total, 4,400 people, the vast majority minors, have been arrested in a little over a week, almost half the number of arrests made during the months of gilets jaunes chaos. It might be incoherent that protesting students shoot fireworks at high school buildings, while at the same time denouncing the poor facilities they have to study in. But the far greater incoherence belongs to a government that has disinvested in its youth, and has chosen to answer bin fires with police charges.
“Sure some people were burning trash cans,” Fatoumata Sylla Wague, a 17-year-old in her final year at the Lycée Paul Éluard in Seine-Saint-Denis, where pupils were among the first to set up blockades outside their campus, told me. “But trash cans can’t feel anything.” She and her fellow students, on the other hand, certainly felt the teargas that the police launched in response.
Despite “unlivable” temperatures in the school buildings, extreme heat and extreme cold, walls covered in mould, electricity cuts and often not enough tables or chairs for everyone, Fatoumata would rather have been in class than out braving the riot police. But she wants to teach history some day and felt compelled, in a moment in history, comparable to May 1968, to take part. “If I’m fighting for our rights today, it’s because I really want to teach, but in good conditions. And so this is for the next generation of students and teachers.”
I can’t imagine how hard it must be to be a teenager in general today. In 2021 The Lancet found that 75% of French 16-25-year-olds exhibited signs of eco-anxiety, telling researchers they were “frightened” about the future. In France and beyond, students and young workers actively dislike AI and feel pessimistic about the future it portends. As for Fatoumata, she worries about the rise of far-right political movements, both in France and elsewhere.
For years, successive French governments have dealt with problems in some of France’s most troubled urban areas by unleashing heavy-handed policing that all too frequently targets young people with random checks that can be personally degrading. Centralised policymaking has also produced a national education system that often sends its least experienced teachers to these same areas, while granting more senior teachers priority in requesting transfers to other, less difficult, schools.
A future far-right government, the kind Fatoumata says she worries about, would almost certainly ramp up these kinds of tensions. Already, in response to the protests, rightwing politicians have called for harsher sentences and more law and order. But this is not a problem that will be solved with more police and more batons, any more than it already has been.
Because none of it signals a government that truly wants to listen – it signals that society at large does not really claim these places, or these teenagers, as its own. On n’est pas mal éduqué, on n’est pas écouté (“We’re not poorly educated, we’re just not being listened to”), read one sign I saw brandished at Paris’s Place de la République on Tuesday.
Responding to the crisis is going to require some tangible acts, such as upgrading dilapidated facilities. Arnaud Richards, 50, head of student services at Iqbal Masih middle school in Saint-Denis, offered me the example of how thoughtful architecture can have more impact than one might expect. The technical high school he previously worked in – Gabriel Péri, in an extremely poor area – reopened in 2022 after a total reconstruction, which, according to Richards, led to a calmer climate for both students and teachers. “Having the school itself be a beautiful place made the community feel more respected,” he told me. That in turn “created a calmer environment” for both students and staff.
But a real answer doesn’t stop with better facilities. Showing up to cut ribbons on new construction, or renovations, isn’t enough. During Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power, his government has, on any number of issues, successively failed to listen in a way that makes people feel deeply seen and heard.
As Fatoumata said: “Honestly, I don’t think the government cares, they just want to shut us up with false promises. We know nothing will change, because the government doesn’t listen to us.” Of all the things going wrong for France at the moment, this underlying lack of a feeling of “togetherness”, the feeling that nobody is really listening, is going to be the most difficult to deal with.
- Alexander Hurst writes for Guardian Europe from Paris. His memoir Generation Desperation is out now

The National Gallery of Art hosts an exhibition featuring Bauhaus-trained architect Vladas Švipas  - The Baltic Times
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:47:16 UTC
20:47:16 KST

On 9 October, at 5:00 PM, the National Gallery of Art of the Lithuanian National Museum of Art (LNMA) opens an exhibition celebrating the life and professional legacy of the architect Vladas Švipas (1900–1965). Titled Vladas Švipas: Pušalotas > Bauhaus > Kaunas > New York, the display tracks the path of Lithuanian Bauhaus alumnus from interwar Kaunas to a German Displaced Persons camp, and into New York, where he had to adapt to an émigré fate.
On the same day, from 3:00 to 4:30 PM, the opening of the exhibition is preceded by an international symposium on the interwar relationship of the Bauhaus and the Baltics. Dr Marija Drėmaitė (Vilnius University), Dr Anke Blümm (Erfurt University), and Dr Julia Secklehner (Masaryk University, Brno) will present at the symposium. Dr Birgitte Franzen, Director of the Bauhaus-Archiv/Museum, is expected to take part in a roundtable discussion moderated by Gabrielė Radzevičiūtė (NDG).
“Exhibitions based on recent research and introducing as-yet-unseen layers of Lithuanian culture and art are among the priorities in the exhibition programme of the National Gallery of Art. We are delighted to present, together with the architecture historian Marija Drėmaitė, a new page in the history of Lithuanian architecture and its international contexts,” says Dr Lolita Jablonskienė, director of the National Gallery of Art of the LNMA.
Lithuanian Bauhaus adherent: a civil servant who promoted ideas of modernism
According to the exhibition curator Dr Marija Drėmaitė, Švipas remains a relatively unfamiliar figure even within the Lithuanian art and architecture community – most likely because he designed only five residential buildings in Kaunas. However, his professional legacy highlights an entirely different side of a modernist architect’s career – his public service, his involvement in regional and territorial planning, and his work developing rules and regulations.
“In the 1930s, serving as head of Construction Department at the Chamber of Agriculture, Vladas Švipas acted as public promoter of Bauhaus ideas. He integrated these principles into modernization programmes of Lithuanian countryside, new settlers’ homestead designs, the plan of the campaign for “Brick Lithuania”, and the search for an ideal residential house. The exhibition illustrates how architectural practice reaches beyond an individual artistic creation, including also regular work of a modern-minded civil servant and technical expert,” says Drėmaitė.
The exhibition places Švipas’s architecture within a broader historical and cultural context of a modern state construction. The newly independent Lithuanian state (1918-1940), emerging from wars and the collapse of empires, was in great need of modern professionals. State scholarships encouraged young people to study in Western Europe, yet only one Lithuanian student-scholarship recipient chose the Bauhaus, the most avant-garde school of design of its time. The life and work of Vladas Švipas reveal the making of a new type of modernist architect and his role in shaping a modern state.
Studies and connections with celebrated 20th-century artists and architects
Švipas’s professional links with the leading figures of global modernism highlight the bold ambitions of interwar Lithuanian artists. Between 1924 and 1926, Švipas studied in Wassily Kandinsky's Wall-Painting Workshop (Wandmalerei), in 1928, he completed an internship at the Bauhaus Architecture Office under Hannes Meyer and Hans Wittwer. Returning to interwar Kaunas, he developed ideas of rational planning both through his public service and theoretical work.
During the Second World War, Švipas navigated between the Soviet and Nazi occupation regimes. At the end of the war, he withdrew to the West and lived from 1945 to 1949, in Dillingen DP camp in Germany. With the help of former Bauhaus director Walter Gropius and his fellow student Xanti Schawinsky, he later emigrated to the United States to begin a fresh chapter of his professional life in New York. Another Bauhaus colleague, Marcel Breuer, helped him with the search for work, while surviving Švipas’s correspondence with Gropius reveals warm ties between the former Bauhaus student and his mentor.
Švipas’s biography sparks questions about an architect’s desire to extend rational order into the landscape and navigate the realm of politics. More broadly, the exhibition tells a story of professional migration – showing how as historical ruptures and political regimes break and make ideas, knowledge, and connections. The exhibition is accompanied by a bilingual, Lithuanian and English, book by Maria Drėmaitė Vladas Švipas: Pušalotas > Bauhaus > Kaunas > New York by Lapas.
Curator-guided tour: Saturday, 10 October at 4:00 PM
Lecture by Dr Maria Drėmaitė: 19 November.
Produced by: Kultūros projektų asociacija Documentum
Project Manager: Lina Pranaitytė
Sponsor: Lithuanian Council for Culture
Curator: Dr Marija Drėmaitė (Vilnius University)
Architect and Designer: Vika Pranaitytė (O-D-A Architecture studio)
Photographer and Curator: Lukas Mykolaitis
Image editor: Ieva Austinskaitė (aust.studio)
Models: Urtė Šimkutė

Čiurlionis Museum of Art, Vilnius University Library, The Wroblewski Library of the Lithuanian Academy of Sciences, Martynas Mažvydas National Library of Lithuania, Lithuanian Central State Archives, Lithuanian National Museum, Ąžuolynas Kaunas County Public Library, Vaga Publishers, Alfonsas Švipas, Bernd Freese, and Galerie Berinson (Berlin).

Houthi attack on Riyadh airport killed three Saudi nationals
Saudi Arabia has seen several attacks by the Houthis in recent days, with the airports appearing to be the primary target.
Saudi Arabia has said that three people including a pilot were killed in Thursday’s Houthi attacks on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport.
In a statement on social media on Friday, the General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said attacks on the airport killed an airline pilot and two other Saudi citizens, while several people “of different nationalities were wounded”.
“It is with profound sadness that Saudia announces the passing of Captain Hamoud Ali Alkalthami,” the flag-carrier said in a statement, citing an “incident” at the Riyadh airport.
Dozens of people wounded in the missile attacks suffered minor to severe injuries. The attacks also caused material damage, including to a plane operated by national carrier Saudia, GACA said. Airport operations have now resumed and air traffic has returned to normal, according to Saudi media reports.
Saudi Arabia has seen several attacks by the Houthis in recent days, with the airports appearing to be the primary target.
GACA said Wednesday that attacks earlier in the week had killed three civilians and injured 36 at Abha and King Khalid airports. At least three people were also wounded in other attacks on Jazan and Najran airports near the Yemen border.
A Houthi military spokesperson said on Thursday that the armed group had launched a ballistic missile towards King Khalid Airport, claiming that the missile had successfully hit its intended target, causing damage and disrupting air traffic.
The Houthi military campaign appears to be a revival of a tactic seen last month. On September 18, Saudi-led coalition forces said they intercepted and destroyed a suspected Houthi ballistic missile fired towards King Khalid airport. A day later, at least one explosion was heard near the airport in Riyadh, and a large plume of black smoke was seen rising from a fuel storage area.
The Iran-backed Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah (Arabic for Supporters of God), have warned aviation companies to avoid using Saudi airspace, saying any aircraft operating there, except over the holy cities of Mecca and Medina, is a target.
Al Jazeera’s Yousef Mawry, reporting from Sanaa in Yemen, said the Houthis want to impose a blockade on all Saudi airports.
“This is part of the blockade-for-blockade equation, the airport-for-airport equation. Because Sanaa remains besieged by Saudi Arabia, the Ansar Allah Houthis want to impose a blockade on all Saudi airports”, Mawry said.
The Houthis say the strikes are in retaliation for Saudi attacks on Yemen’s Sanaa International Airport and the airport in Hodeidah, he said.
Fighting intensifies in Yemen
The resumption of attacks on Saudi Arabia’s airports comes as Yemeni forces continue a counteroffensive against the Houthis.
Late on Friday, air strikes were reported in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa, which remains under the control of the Houthi movement, which seized the city in 2014.
Loud explosions were also reported in the southern port city of Aden, where the internationally-recognised Yemeni government is based.
The Saudi-led coalition supporting Yemen’s government also said on Friday that it had destroyed three rocket launch platforms that were used by the Houthis “to threaten regional security”.
Coalition spokesman Colonel Turki al-Maliki declared that all Houthi attacks on civilians and civilian facilities “will be met with resolve” by the Saudi-led coalition.
The push by Yemeni forces and the Saudi-led coalition was launched after the Iran-aligned rebel group last month seized a broad swath of territory in Yemen along the strategic Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which connects the Red Sea to the Gulf of Aden, in a sudden push.
Yemeni government forces this week claimed key gains around the Bab al-Mandeb coastline, but intense fighting continues.
The conflict, which was frozen for years but reignited after the United States and Israel’s war on Iran, has stoked further upheaval in a region already destabilised by Israel’s wars on Gaza and Lebanon.
It now threatens to draw other states into the conflict, with Pakistan and Turkiye having agreed to deploy troops under a mutual defence pact signed with Saudi Arabia earlier this year.
Pakistan’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs spokesman Sajjad Haider Khan said on Friday that the country now has a “substantial number of forces as well as resources … in Riyadh”.
Pakistani military personnel “would not be crossing the borders of the other side for an attack on the Houthis, but of course [are acting] in the defence of the territory”, he noted.
UN Security Council members condemn Houthi attacks
Meanwhile, at the United Nations on Friday, Yemen’s internationally recognised government and Saudi Arabia asked the Security Council to take action to address the escalating situation in Yemen.
“The increasing targeting of civilians, the continuing threats to the security of navigation in the Red Sea and Bab al-Mandeb Strait, and the resulting repercussions that extend beyond Yemen and the region negatively affect international peace and security,” Saudi Arabia’s UN representative, Abdulaziz al-Wasil, told the council.
Abdullah Ali Fadhel al-Saadi, the UN representative for Yemen’s internationally recognised government, said that the threat posed by the Houthis, “is no longer an internal Yemeni affair that can be contained within our borders”.

South Korean opposition lawmakers have proposed legislation to end automatic eligibility for alternative military service for Asian Games gold medalists following controversy over athletes' celebrations at the 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Games, local media reported Friday.
The bill, introduced by Rep. Joo Ho-young and nine other lawmakers from the main opposition People Power Party, would remove Asian Games gold medals as a qualification for alternative military service, according to The Korea Times.

The debate intensified after South Korea's men's football team celebrated winning its fourth consecutive Asian Games gold medal.
Player Yang Min-hyeok acknowledged that avoiding military service had been his primary motivation, while teammate Park Seung-soo posted a photograph of himself wearing a military discharge cap.
Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul told lawmakers Wednesday that his ministry aimed to gradually reduce and ultimately abolish the exemption program.
Culture Minister Chae Hwi-young had earlier pledged a comprehensive review of the system following public criticism, according to Yonhap News Agency.
South Korea requires most able-bodied men to serve between 18 and 21 months in the military.
Under the existing system, qualifying athletes and artists can fulfill their obligations through alternative service arrangements rather than regular military duty.

Gaza's people need shelter as El Niño threatens flooding: IOM

Breadcrumb
Almost all Gaza's people need shelter as El Niño threatens flooding: IOM
Almost all of Gaza's population needs tents or help with shelter ahead of winter, with the El Niño weather phenomenon expected to bring heavier rainfall, while supplies remain scarce due to Israeli restrictions, the UN migration agency said on Friday.
The El Niño — which the UN weather agency says could be the strongest ever — could further weaken unsafe buildings and cause flooding amid the enclave’s heavily damaged drainage systems, the IOM said.
Almost two million people inside the enclave, largely devastated by a genocidal war launched by Israel in October 2023, require assistance, but only about 17% of the needs for winter shelter supplies have been met by humanitarian actors, IOM Director General Amy Pope said.
"Families who have already endured repeated displacement and devastating loss must be able to face the winter in safety and dignity," Pope said, adding that constraints by Israeli authorities are making it hard for agencies to scale up their responses.
Some 8,600 emergency shelter kits, comprising wood, a tarpaulin and some basic materials, have not been allowed by Israeli authorities to enter Gaza, as they have been determined to be dual-use, the IOM said.
COGAT, the Israeli military arm that oversees aid flows into Gaza, did not immediately respond to Reuters request for comment. Israel cites security concerns for its curbs on Gaza.
IOM said they had been able to bring in some tarpaulin and tents, but that it was not enough at the current scale needed in Gaza.
More than half of all tents and makeshift shelters in the enclave need replacing as they are in poor condition, the IOM said, warning that there are few alternatives with war-damaged buildings posing safety risks.
In August, the IOM identified more than 3,600 structures as dangerous and at risk of collapse, while around 1.8 million people are living in displacement sites — most in flood-risk areas.

German drone maker STARK and Thales Australia have agreed to fit STARK’s Cascade loitering munition to the Bushmaster armored vehicle, giving the Australian-built truck a launcher for one-way attack drones that the company says can hit targets up to 100 km (62 miles) away.
The two companies signed a memorandum of understanding on Oct. 7 at the Land Forces 2026 exhibition in Perth, Western Australia, where Thales Australia unveiled its latest Bushmaster configuration a day earlier. STARK said the partnership is meant to promote the development, production and deployment of loitering munitions in Australia. Neither company has announced a customer, and the Australian Army has not said it plans to buy the combination.
Loitering munitions are small drones that fly to a target area, search for a target and then dive into it with an explosive warhead. Cascade is launched from a tube, which STARK says makes it easy to add to vehicles and other platforms and lets small mobile units carry their own long-range strike weapon. The company offers it in configurations with ranges of 40 km, 60 km and 100 km, carrying a payload of up to 4.5 kg (10 pounds), and says the launcher can be ready to fire in under a minute.
On the Bushmaster, the drones would be carried in a multi-cell launcher on the rear deck of the new dual-cab version, allowing several to be fired in coordinated groups. Thales Australia says the munitions would let small units strike targets such as command posts, logistics hubs, artillery positions and air defense systems far behind the front line. The same Bushmaster variant shown in Perth also carries Thales’ RapidStriker counter-drone system, so a single vehicle could defend against enemy drones and launch its own.
The Bushmaster is a mine-protected wheeled vehicle built by Thales Australia in Bendigo, Victoria. It has served with the Australian Army for more than two decades and is also used by the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and Japan, and Australia has sent more than 100 to Ukraine since 2022.
STARK, founded in Germany in 2024, unveiled Cascade in June at the ILA Berlin air show. It has since launched the drone from its Vanta unmanned surface vessel, and in September British vehicle maker North Defence said it would integrate Cascade on its light vehicles and unmanned ground vehicles. The company’s larger Virtus loitering munition, which takes off vertically, has been tested by the German Bundeswehr, including in an AI-enabled drone swarm exercise in April, and Germany’s parliament approved a purchase of Virtus and Helsing’s HX-2 in February.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham delivers a speech during the The Innovation Nation Summit at Bruntwood SciTech on October 09, 2026 in Manchester, England. | Christopher Furlong/Getty Images
LONDON — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham confirmed Friday he will legislate to ease restrictive non-compete clause rules for workers — but stopped short of committing to a ban.
Burnham said in a speech in Manchester that he wants to "make sure that non-compete clauses will no longer be a barrier to hiring for our most promising start-ups and scaling firms" — but did has yet to set out the extent of the crackdown.
The scope of the new rules will come later, ahead of legislation. POLITICO first reported the planned crackdown Thursday.
Advertisement
The government's action would be the "Bosman ruling for the innovation sector," Burnham said at a government-backed innovation summit in Manchester. That's a reference to a 1995 European Court of Justice decision that changed how star players are transferred between football clubs.
Potential changes to non-compete clauses in workers’ contracts began in 2025 under Burnham's predecessor Keir Starmer. The proposals ranged from a total ban on non-compete clauses to a partial ban, such as allowing non-compete clauses only for workers earning more than a set salary threshold, or limiting their length.
The vow from Burnham comes after intense lobbying lobbying for and against the restrictions in workers' contracts. U.K. tech start-ups claim the curbs are undermining economic growth, while City firms and trade bodies, including TheCityUK and the Managed Funds Association, are against any changes.

French investigators recover 2 stolen Renoir paintings
October 9, 2026
Two paintings by by Pierre-Auguste Renoir that were stolen from a museum in France last month have been found, authorities said on Friday.
Police have arrested six people in connection with the crime.
The two stolen paintings were the Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano (1910) and Jeune fille au puits (1886). Both belong to Paris' Orsay Museum and were on loan.
"These two paintings are not simply works of art. They are part of our city's history, our heritage," said Bryan Masson, the mayor of Cagnes-sur-Mer, where the Renoir Museum is located. "Knowing they have been recovered is an immense relief."
According to AFP news agency, police have arrested five people so far as part of the investigation. Authorities said at the time of the robbery that it was clear that the thieves were not first-time offenders
The heist followed a string of high-profile robberies from European museums, including the theft of crown jewels from the Louvre in Paris last year.
No details on paintings' discovery
Authorities did not immediately respond to questions about how the paintings had been recovered. A a press conference had been scheduled for Thursday afternoon, but it was ultimately cancelled in order to not interfere with the investigation.
The robbery took place in the early morning of September 8, when thieves broke into the grounds of the Renoir Museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer through a hole cut in a garden fence and entered through a window.
They had also stolen two other paintings, Madame Pichon and Coco Reading, a portrayal of Claude, Renoir's young son. But they dropped those in the gardens as they were running away from the police, who had arrived on the scene, alerted by alarms.
"This news is a source of immense joy and a great relief for the town of Cagnes-sur-Mer and its residents," mayor Bryan Masson said in a statement.

Trump envoy kept financial ties to firm behind $15 billion Hormuz-bypass oil pipeline plan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:41:58 UTC
20:41:58 KST

Thomas Barrack, a top US diplomat in the Middle East, advocated for a firm run by his business partner to take part in the development of an oil pipeline from Iraq to Syria, three people said, activities which appear to violate federal ethics rules.
In July, Iraq and Syria signed memorandums of understanding with a consortium made up of the company, Californian investment group TI Capital, along with Chevron and Qatar’s UCC Holding, to carry out technical and financial studies in preparation for rehabilitating the pipeline, which would skirt the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint.
Barrack, US presidential special envoy to both Iraq and Syria as well as Ambassador to Turkey, has a longstanding business relationship with TI Capital and its founder Ziad Ghandour. At the time of his confirmation hearings in 2025 he had a financial interest entitling him to as much as a fifth of the profits from a real-estate venture near San Francisco, California and managed by TI Capital - with Ghandour as chief executive - that he said he intended to retain, public records show.
During engagements with Syrian and Iraqi officials after the start of the war in Iran, Barrack pressed for Ghandour's firm to be included in the project, according to two of the people, who have direct knowledge of the discussions.
On June 16, a month before the consortium agreement was signed, Barrack and Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi issued a joint statement that commended Iraq's decision "to advance a memorandum of understanding with TI Capital to rehabilitate the Kirkuk-Baniyas Pipeline." The statement made no mention of Chevron or UCC in connection with the pipeline.
Reuters found no evidence that Barrack stands to profit from the pipeline or other projects. His ties to Ghandour would not constitute a criminal conflict of interest unless he stood to directly profit from the pipeline itself, two ethics lawyers told Reuters.
However, Barrack's relationship with Ghandour makes such advocacy "a serious problem" under the regulation that prohibits officials from participating in matters that call into question their impartiality because of a personal or business relationship, said Richard Painter, a former chief White House ethics lawyer and a professor at the University of Minnesota Law School.
The impartiality rule, which is not a criminal statute, can be triggered by the involvement of a business associate in a project, regardless of whether the official has a financial interest of his own.
“The ethical concern is the appearance of a conflict of interest," said Ann Skeet, interim executive director at the Markkula Center for Applied Ethics in Santa Clara University.
Asked what Barrack would have needed to do to comply, Painter said: "Have nothing to do with this pipeline. Completely recuse. Say this is not a matter I participate in."
Don Fox, a former general counsel and acting director of the US Office of Government Ethics, said that promotion of TI Capital by Barrack would additionally violate a regulation prohibiting officials from using their office to endorse any enterprise or for the private gain of people they are affiliated with.
Barrack has not filed a conflict-of-interest waiver with the US Office of Government Ethics regarding his ties to the company as it participates in the project, according to a Reuters records request. Waivers allow officials with potential conflicts of interest to participate in matters that would otherwise require the employee be recused.
In a signed ethics agreement before his confirmation hearings last year, he committed to recusing himself from matters directly affecting the financial interests of the real-estate venture unless he first obtained such a waiver.
Barrack’s office and Chevron declined to comment. TI Capital, Ghandour and UCC did not respond to requests for comment.
In a July 17 post on X, Barrack said the involvement of US companies in Iraq and Syria was “a new paradigm” aimed at bringing clarity and opportunity to the region.
A fourth ethics lawyer said it was up to the State Department to decide whether its employee's financial holdings create a potential conflict of interest.
"Ambassador Barrack has no affiliation with, role in, or financial interest in the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline project," a State Department spokesperson told Reuters, while acknowledging Barrack’s relationship with the TI Capital real-estate venture.
His public comments on the pipeline reflect "long-standing, publicly stated US policy interest in regional energy integration," the spokesperson said, adding that Barrack was certified to be in compliance with ethics rules.
The disclosed interest: Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment
In a financial disclosure filed with the US Office of Government Ethics in March 2025, before assuming his diplomatic roles, Barrack declared an equity stake in ACD-TI Oakley Investment LLC, a venture building a large housing project near San Francisco. The filing did not disclose the size of the stake, but said he was entitled to 20% of the company’s profits when the earnings reach an established minimum.
ACD-TI is managed by TI Capital and headed by Ghandour, California state corporate records show. Reuters was unable to find contact details for a company representative and did not get a response to questions sent to its postal correspondence address.
The filing said the profit-sharing arrangement was in return for services he provided to the company. Barrack also disclosed to the OGE a paid consulting role with the venture in 2024. The filing does not say whether or how much he was paid.
In a separate signed ethics agreement dated March 7, 2025, three weeks before his Senate confirmation hearing, Barrack listed ACD-TI Oakley among assets he would retain rather than sell.
Bypassing Hormuz via the Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline
The historic Kirkuk-Baniyas pipeline, which for decades moved Iraqi crude to Syria's Mediterranean coast, faced sporadic shutdowns from the early 1980s and has been out of action since the US invasion of Iraq in 2003. Mothballed plans to revive it received new impetus this year when, under US attack, Iran restricted traffic through Hormuz, pushing oil prices higher.
Several people told Reuters in August the pipeline would take at least four years and cost $15 billion to build.
The idea of bringing TI Capital into the regional project was raised by Barrack in May at the Milken Institute Global Conference in Los Angeles, a third person with direct knowledge of the conversation told Reuters. The discussion, they added, took place on the sidelines of the event.
With the US war on Iran raging, Barrack and Ghandour also participated in an invite-only panel at the conference, where they discussed in more general terms the need for new energy supply lines in the Middle East, the person said.
A Milken Institute spokesperson declined to provide details of the panel discussion, saying it was closed to the media.
Barrack has engaged in business with Ghandour since at least 2020, when the two men created a $250 million blank-check SPAC that was dissolved after Barrack was arrested in 2021 on charges of acting as an unregistered agent of the United Arab Emirates. He was acquitted in 2022.
The Iraqi cabinet named TI Capital later in July as part of another consortium with UCC Holding and ConocoPhillips to assess the Akkas gas field, one of Iraq's largest undeveloped reserves. On its website, the firm claims involvement in projects at Syria's Tartous port, without providing details. Syria’s port authority did not reply to questions about TI Capital, and Reuters could not verify its role in Tartous. ConocoPhillips did not reply to a request for comment.
A person close to Barrack said the ambassador trusted Ghandour to help implement US President Donald Trump’s regional strategy of bringing Iraq and Syria closer to the US. “Ziad is the chosen man. Hand-picked by Barrack,” the person said.
The White House referred Reuters questions to the State Department.

Just how sunlike is the sun?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:41:08 UTC
20:41:08 KST

Is the sun a sunlike star?
If you’re not an astronomer, the obvious answer is yes. That’s tautological! Sunlike stars are stars like the sun. The sun is the sun, so it’s the most sunlike of them all!
Astronomers, though, can be persnickety. When asked that question, they immediately shoot another right back: What do you mean by “sunlike”?
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
That’s a fair response. If the definition is too broad, the sun starts to look a little funny, appearing quite unlike other stars. For a much tighter definition—well, it’s still a little off but not nearly as much.
So why ask this question in the first place?
Astronomers like to look at large populations of objects because bigger sample sizes should better reveal trends in their properties. This can lead to greater insights on their structure, their characteristics and the physics that underlie it all.
We already know a lot about the sun, given that it’s the nearest star in the universe to us. If we then compare it with other, similar stars, we can extrapolate the properties we know to those we may not, thus learning more about them, too.
For example, when compared with stars of similar mass, the sun sits right at the average in terms of its temperature and the amount of energy that it emits. In those cases, it’s quite normal.
But stars have other properties! An important one for a star is its amount of magnetic activity, which depends on the strength and variability of its magnetic field and the effect that field has on the star and its immediate surroundings. Research published in the journal Science in 2020 suggested that the sun was not normal when compared with the magnetic activity of other, similar stars. Our very own star was instead something of an underachiever.
Magnetic fields are extremely complex phenomena. They can, however, be explored in stars using a surprisingly simple method: looking at star spots—sunspots on other stars.
At the risk of oversimplifying, magnetism is created when charged particles (such as electrons, protons or ionized atoms) move around. In general, the more coherently these particles move as a group, the stronger the magnetic field is. All of them ping-ponging around higgledy-piggledy won’t generate a magnetic field, but a cloud of them moving along together will.
The sun and stars like it aren’t just miasmas of incandescent plasma. They have internal layers, such as each’s core, where energy is generated by thermonuclear fusion power. At some distance above that, material heated by the core rises up, just like warm air rises in Earth’s atmosphere, flowing upward until it reaches the star’s surface. It then radiates its heat into space, cools and sinks back down in a process called convection. It’s like a conveyor belt of heat, and there are many thousands of such towers of upward-and-downward-flowing cells in the sun.
But that gas is hot enough to have electrons stripped from its atoms, making it ionized. Each vast tower of flowing material therefore creates its own magnetic field, which it drags along as it flows vertically. Sometimes, the magnetic fields from neighboring convection cells get tangled together, and when these tangles reach the surface, they prevent material from easily flowing back down. So that stuff spends more time at the surface, where it cools a bit more than usual. Cooler gas doesn’t glow as brightly, so these patches are a little bit darker than the surrounding material. These are the aforementioned star spots. And besides looking menacingly dark, they are sites of enhanced magnetic activity.
It’s easy to see them on the sun, but detecting them on distant stars is much harder. It is possible, however, because stars rotate. As one does, star spots spinning into view can slightly dim the star, as seen from afar, with bigger spots or groups of spots causing greater dimming. The star brightens again when the spots rotate back out of view. By carefully measuring the star’s fluctuating brightness, we can get a measure of its star spot activity and use that as a proxy for its magnetic field.
This is more important than you might think because a star’s magnetic field isn’t constant. The sun, for example, has a roughly 11-year cycle in which the magnetic field waxes and wanes in strength. When it’s strong, the number of sunspots increases. At the peak of the cycle, the sun blasts out more solar flares, as well as coronal mass ejections, immense explosions of material that scream outward into the solar system. These can profoundly affect our orbiting satellites and power grid, so understanding the sun’s magnetic activity actually very much impacts us here on Earth.
And this is where the sun appeared anomalous in the 2020 research: it didn’t show as much magnetic activity as similar stars. So maybe the sun is a magnetic weakling.
A team of astronomers wanted to take a closer look at this. The scientists used data from NASA’s exoplanet-hunting satellite Kepler, which searched for exoplanets via very precise, high-cadence brightness measurements of hundreds of thousands of stars. Those measurements, it turns out, can be used to look for star spots as well.
Their results, published in 2023 in the journal Astronomy and Astrophysics, is that the sun is indeed less active compared with other stars in a broad range of characteristics such as temperature and mass. But by narrowing the range of these parameters—for instance, by only looking at stars whose temperature was within 100 degrees Celsius of that of the sun—they found our home star is only a tad bit less active, well within the range of normal.
So the sun is a sunlike star.
Still, why are the other stars stronger at all? If they have the same properties as the sun, what makes them more magnetically excited?
The answer, the team found, is that the stars observed by Kepler are composed of somewhat higher levels of heavy elements. Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, with much smaller amounts of elements like iron, carbon, and so on. But these trace elements can have an outsize effect on overall stellar characteristics.
For example, heavy elements are better at absorbing heat from the core, which affects the size of a star’s convective layer. More heavy elements make the convective layer deeper, allowing it to generate a more powerful magnetic field.
Surprisingly, this also affects a star’s rotation. Stars like the sun blow a wind of subatomic particles; in the case of the sun, we call it the solar wind. As the star spins, the magnetic field coming out of the surface catches that wind and sweeps it up. This imparts a drag on the star—imagine spinning around on your heels while holding an open trash bag; the bag will act like a parachute, slowing you. Over millions and billions of years, the drag from a star’s magnetic field slows its rotation, and in fact, the astronomers found that stars with stronger magnetism tended to rotate more slowly.
So that dash of heavier elements in other stars has wide-ranging effects and shows that, in the end, it’s not so much that the sun isn’t sunlike but rather that astronomers need to do a little extra bookkeeping when they compare it with other stars.
It’s reassuring to know the sun is sunlike after all. And while that might seem like a silly question, it actually reveals a lot of fascinating science behind stars and their behavior. It also forces us to question our assumptions, something every scientist (and everybody) should do.

In Pictures: Weirdest and most thought-provoking statues of Donald Trump over the years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:40:41 UTC
20:40:41 KST

Following the headline-grabbing statue "The Orange Plague" by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, which was displayed this week at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, we take a look back at some of the ways artists have depicted Trump in satirical, humorous and thought-provoking ways.
Donald Trump has been immortalised by artists on countless occasions, with creatives using their talents to poke fun, criticise, educate, and even warn.
From signs and murals to carnival floats, the divisive POTUS has inspired many to remind the public that the arts are a vital way to comment, inform and inspire.
One artform which has been an effective favourite for many wishing to represent Trump is the sculpted figure. It makes sense since Trump has shown a clear preference for classical and gilded aesthetics; statues play on the man’s perception of monumentalism as being a reflection of power. Artists therefore use oversized or flashy statues to better reflect and lampoon Trump’s ego, as well as comment on the pitfalls of gaudish effigies which so often betray a sense of narcissism.
In effect, the momuments strike at the heart of Trump's sensibilities and symbolically cast him as the eagle in Aesop’s fable – a figure undone by a self-infliction. In this case, a marked proclivity for oversized effigies.
The latest example has been "The Orange Plague", the 2.6-meter statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt.
Coated with 23-karat gold, the artwork also known as “The King of Injustice” shows a nude Trump holding a comically sized golf club in one hand, a set of scales in the other, all while sitting on the back of a smaller, frailer man.
Beneath the statue is a plaque which reads: "I am sitting on the back of a man. He is sinking under my burden. I will do anything to help him. Except stepping down from his back. - The King of Injustice."
According to Galschiøt, the work is a “satirical outcry” against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies.
The statue was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the COP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year. It has just finished its short stint at the European Parliament building in Strasbourg and is heading to the COP31 UN Climate Conference next month in Antalya, Türkiye.
Before we see “The Orange Plague” once more, here are other notable statues of Trump which have amused spectators and sought to reflect what certain people think of the current leader of the free world.
"The Emperor Has No Balls"
Artist: Indecline
Year: 2016
Original location: Cleveland, Los Angeles, New York City, San Francisco, Seattle

A theft worth €5 million has occurred
at the Marchesi Antinori facility in Cortona (Arezzo), as
thieves made off with 30,000 bottles produced by the Florentine
winery—all from the 2023 vintage—including 10,000 bottles of
their most prestigious product Solaia, Corriere della Sera and
the Financial Times reported Friday.
                                    
According to the Italian newspaper, this is the largest wine
heist by value ever to take place in Italy.
                                    
A group of at least seven people carried out the operation last
Sunday night, managing to haul away a shipment of Solaia,
Tignanello, and Guado al Tasso—wines ranging in price from €120
to €300 per bottle.
                                    
After disabling the alarm system and putting the cellar's
security cameras out of commission, the thieves reportedly
entered with two trucks and loaded the bottles using the
company's own forklifts.
                                    
The theft was only discovered on Monday morning when employees
arrived and found the wine missing.
                                    
"It is certainly a highly organized gang," Renzo Cotarella, CEO
of Marchesi Antinori, told Corriere.
                                    
"Perhaps the same one that has targeted other wineries in Italy
in recent months. A theft of this magnitude and value has
certainly never happened in Italy before."
The stolen stock could be destined for collectors or venue
owners, though it is likely to raise suspicions—particularly
regarding the Solaia, of which only about 60,000 to 70,000
bottles are produced annually.
                                    
"We are informing our customers around the world," the company
explained—as reported by the Italian newspaper—"we want to warn
them to be wary of offers made outside official channels."
"We still hope to recover the wine; two trucks cannot simply
vanish," Cotarella told the FT.
                                    
"These wines are highly valuable, and I don't understand how
they could be sold worldwide without being detected," he added,
noting that Antinori also aims to "protect the market" by
warning potential buyers that bottles offered by unusual sources
at attractive prices could be stolen goods.

'Grand odysseys': Why historic travel and legendary journeys are trending for 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:40:21 UTC
20:40:21 KST

Skyscanner’s 2027 travel trends report points to growing demand for historic trails, ancient ruins and iconic destinations brought to life on screen, as travellers look to the past for a sense of connection in a fast-paced world.
It’s the season when travel companies start to reveal their predictions for the following year, and now Skyscanner has launched its 2027 Travel Trends report.
Pairing global search insights and research from more than 28,000 travellers, the report uses data from the likes of TikTok, ClassPass, Wise, Universal Music Group for Brands, and AllTrails.
Among the new trends for 2027 is history-focussed travel, which follows on from a trend which has already seen significant traction this year thanks, in no small part, to The Odyssey, Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster adaptation of Homer's epic poem.
Skyscanner has called this particular trend “Grand Odysseys”, and suggests that its popularity is down to travellers trying to escape a fast-paced world. They’re seeking out history which offers context and grounds them in timeless human stories.
Next year will see tourists following sacred walking trails, exploring legendary ruins and turning to the past to enrich their often overwhelming present.
Skyscanner’s research found that cinematic releases have been driving real-world bookings, with films and TV shows including The Odyssey and Gladiator proving particularly inspiring.
Data from TikTok backs this up, too, showing that video views for cinematic travel content are up +346% year on year, while posts featuring #HeroJourney are up some +452%.
The Odyssey reportedly prompted a third of people to plan a trip inspired by the epic, and the data shows that almost half – 43% – of Millennials have been inspired by films and TV set in antiquity, from Troy to the tales of Ancient Greece.
And 24% of them have taken it further and travelled in the footsteps of ancient stories, a figure which rises to 30% among Gen Z.
The top historic hikes for 2027
Among Skyscanner’s partners for the report was the app AllTrails, which revealed its top five walking trails to experience historical travel on foot in 2027.
In first place is Corfu’s Cape Drastis Loop. The popular route on the Greek island is said to be ancient author Homer’s mythical land of Phaeacia, where a shipwrecked Odysseus shared the story of his epic 10-year journey home.
Next up was the route between Horcones Viewpoint, Horcones Lagoon and Espejo Lagoon in Argentina. Walkers can experience shimmering glacial lakes as they walk in the shadow of Mount Aconcagua, South America’s highest peak.
In third place was China’s Xi’an City Wall. Here, visitors can stroll along impressive Ming Dynasty walls where ancient gateways, sweeping views and centuries of history unfold below.
In fourth is Monte Santa Caterina in Favignana, Italy. Adventurous travellers can climb to Favignana’s highest point, which is home to a historic castle with a rich history linked to the island, long associated with Odysseus’ legendary voyage.
Finally, Rizes Cave, or the Cave of Eumaeus, in Ithaca, Greece continues The Odyssey theme. Here, walkers will pass through olive groves above the Ionian before arriving at a cave where Odysseus sought refuge after returning home in the epic tale.
“It’s grounding to visit a trail and realise you’re seeing the same rugged peaks, ancient forests, and horizons that travellers did thousands of years ago,” said Shelby Eagleburger, head of data integrity at AllTrails.
“Historic routes remind us that exploring the outdoors is a universal human experience, and it connects us across generations. How we travel evolves, but the pull of natural landscapes stays the same.”
Skyscanner’s top trends for 2027
Grand Odysseys is one of seven trends featured in the Skyscanner report, all of which show a shift in traveller behaviour.
The prediction trends also include “Signal Severance”, which is linked to the fact that one in four Gen Z travellers plan to disconnect in 2027.
Many of us are craving a less connected world and are seeking out remote travel spots, or places where it’s possible to switch off entirely.
Skyscanner found that digital detox spots in Finland, including Kittilä and Rovaniemi, are seeing rising demand.
Most of us like to bring back a keepsake from a trip – whose fridge isn’t covered in magnets? But for 2027, Skyscanner believes that the best souvenirs are the ones you have to travel for, with travellers increasingly building itineraries around unique regional apparel, artisanal crafts and location-exclusive items.
One in four travellers have taken a trip specifically for items they couldn't buy online, including the vastly popular Trader Joe's tote from the United States and merchandise from the Ritz Paris.
Weddings and travel often go hand-in-hand and, increasingly, couples are choosing to move away from gendered celebrations and are embracing the “sten do”, a combination of stag and hen parties. The report shows that 25% of travellers are opting for these combined celebrations abroad as they’re more fun, less expensive and easier to organise.
If you’re into fitness and wellbeing, you may already be an aficionado of the gym-cation, but it’s set to be a huge trend in 2027.
The report found that 67% of millennials are more likely to book a hotel which serves a nutritious breakfast, and 40% of Gen Z travellers said they prioritise hotels with gyms. TikTok data also showed a +659% year-on-year increase in video views for "Gym Hotel" content.
Increasingly, many travellers are opting to base a trip around seeing live music and experiencing unusual events.
Cultural immersion is a priority as traditional carnivals rank highly for both Gen Z (33%) and Millennials (30%), while 25% of those surveyed said the setting of a concert is almost as important as the set list, with fans hoping for gigs held in the likes of ancient caves or pyramids.
Finally, the “currency chasers” trend is set to be huge in 2027. Those keen to save cash are plumping for destinations where they can take advantage of positive foreign exchange rates.
According to the data, 45% of Gen Z and 40% of Millennial travellers have switched destinations to get more bang for their buck. Vietnam is a particularly popular choice for this trend, as the currency means tourists can spend relatively little while making the most of the beautiful Asian nation.
