‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:08:05 UTC
20:08:05 KST

‘Indentured servants’: US green card move will hit thousands of IT workers
The US is suspending top tech firms, including Microsoft, from a key programme to sponsor foreign workers’ green cards.
The United States government has moved to exclude some of the world’s top tech companies from a programme that allows them to sponsor skilled foreign workers for permanent residency.
Vice President JD Vance said the action was a response to companies abusing the system to hire lower-paid foreign workers at the expense of US workers.
It comes as US President Donald Trump’s administration continues efforts to clamp down on immigration – both legal and undocumented – and make it harder for immigrants to get residency or citizenship.
But the latest move also potentially impacts thousands of foreign workers, many of whom have spent years waiting for a backlog in applications to clear.
Here’s what to know about the latest policy:
How does the current system work?
The suspension concerns the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, which enables a US-based employer to sponsor a foreign worker’s green card — as the permanent residency is commonly known. To qualify, the employer is supposed to demonstrate that there are insufficient US workers for a needed job role and that bringing a foreign worker will not impact the pay or conditions of US workers in the industry.
PERM is a key step in the green card process for many skilled foreign workers. Major tech companies often hire workers on temporary visas, such as the H-1B, before they transition to permanent residency through the PERM process.
What have Vance and others said?
Vance on Thursday accused major companies of fraudulently using the current visa regime to displace US employees and bring in lower-paid foreign workers who amount to “indentured servants”.
“The programme has become rife with fraud,” said Vance at a White House news conference. He claimed that many workers who start off on temporary H-1B visas and later apply for permanent residency under the PERM programme are “being mistreated by their employers” and “used to undercut the wages of American workers”.
“You’ve got to hire great American workers,” the US vice president said. “You cannot lay off American workers and then replace them with foreign indentured servants.”
Labour Secretary Keith Sonderling used similar language, saying the US would “shut down the pipeline of systemic fraud that has flooded our country”.
“The fraud doesn’t end with getting the job,” said Sonderling. “That job becomes a pathway for foreign workers and their families to stay in America permanently and eventually (become) US citizens.”
“And who pays for it all? The American worker,” he said.
Which companies are impacted?
Vance singled out Microsoft as a major offender and said it would be suspended from the PERM programme.
Other companies whose PERM applications will no longer be processed include US software firm Adobe and some of the world’s top IT firms, including Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. Of these, Capgemini is French, Microsoft and Adobe are American, and the rest — Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro and HCL — are all Indian.
“We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labour certification applications involving these companies,” said Sonderling.
Vance said the suspensions would continue “as long as it needs to”.
Other companies that rely heavily on H-1B visas such as Meta, Amazon or Alphabet’s Google will not be affected.
Have tech firms been abusing US immigration rules?
Critics of the H-1B visa and PERM green card process argue that some employers use the system not to fill legitimate skills shortages, but to reduce labour costs, gain leverage over workers and make it harder for US employees to compete for jobs. They say companies do this by hiring foreign workers at lower wages and manipulating recruitment conditions to keep out qualified US workers.
Vance said Microsoft last year let go 6,000 US workers, while also securing 6,300 H-1B visas and almost 3,000 green cards.
“If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants,” said Vance.
Sonderling said companies being suspended from PERM had received more than 230,000 H-1B visas and over 100,000 permanent labour certifications since 2009.
“That’s hundreds of thousands of jobs that were taken from American workers,” Sonderling said.
The H1-B visa system has also emerged as a lightning rod for many of the most vocal backers of Trump’s Make America Great Again (MAGA) movement, some of whom have married criticism of the programme with anti-immigrant stereotypes — particularly against Indians — to demand that the scheme be scrapped.
Microsoft disputed the implication that its visa filings represented new hires replacing US workers. In a statement, the company said that 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H1-B visa applications it issued last year were “to extend or change the status of existing Microsoft employees”, not for new employees, and that the other filings were for “individuals already legally in the United States”.
The company also said that it only files applications for people who “meet the rigorous standards of this visa category” and that such employees are paid equally to any others who do similar work.
What does this mean for foreign workers?
The suspension could make it harder for foreign workers in the tech industry to obtain permanent residency in the US. Many of those affected are likely to be Indian nationals, who account for a large share of the country’s skilled foreign workforce in the technology sector.
Each year, there are only 85,000 slots for new H-1B visas (not including filings for renewals), but hundreds of thousands of applications. Many H-1B visa holders work in technology-related jobs: 62 percent of the beneficiaries in the 2025 fiscal year worked in computer-related occupations.
Indian nationals account for roughly 70 percent of existing H-1B visa holders.
The Trump administration has already tried to crack down on the H1-B scheme, and in August proposed a new $103,000 fee for H1-B applications, after an earlier pitch for a similar fee was struck down by a federal court. The fee, the government argues, would help provide revenue that could be used to service the vast US immigration system, while reducing the incentive for companies to attempt to misuse H1-B visas.
But the new move to restrict the pathway to a green card for foreign workers already in the US, legally, could impact not just those who might have dreamed of working or living in the US — but thousands already in the country.
The US typically issues around 140,000 employment-based green cards every year. But it also has a strict country-based cap — applicants from any one country cannot receive more than seven percent of green cards issued in a year.
Yet, because the employment-based green card application system is largely used to convert many H1-B visa holders into permanent residents, applicants for permanent residency are disproportionately Indian.
The result: Nearly one million Indians legally in the US on work visas are currently stuck in the employment-based green card backlog. They represent 79 percent of the total green card backlog of around 1.25 million people.
Even before the latest move, Indian green card applicants in certain employment categories would have needed to wait for decades, according to a 2025 analysis for the Congressional Research Service.
Sonderling’s statement that the US will no longer process “any pending permanent labour certification applications” from the blacklisted companies has raised fears that tens of thousands of foreign workers in the country legally — most of them Indian — who have waited for years might suddenly no longer be eligible. For others, the wait could get even longer.
Has India responded?
Yes. India’s Ministry of External Affairs issued a statement saying the US’s suspension does not “advance the shared ambitions of both countries”.
The ministry said that “talent mobility adds value” to both the Indian and US economies, including providing US companies “with cutting-edge talent, innovation, research, productivity, competitiveness and job creation”.
The ministry also criticised comments by Vance comparing foreign workers to indentured servants as “unwarranted” and “deeply offensive”, saying his words recalled “painful historical and colonial legacy connotations”.
Colonial powers — the British, Dutch and French — took more than 1.6 million Indian workers as indentured labourers to work on plantations and build railways in their other colonies: in Malaysia, Mauritius, South Africa, Kenya, Uganda, Fiji, Suriname, Guyana and other Caribbean countries.
India’s foreign ministry said Vance’s descriptions also “ignore the fact that Indian professionals in the United States are highly educated and skilled contributors to its economy and innovation ecosystem”.

China's FAST telescope identifies pulsar as part of evolving primordial triple star system
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:07:58 CST
20:07:58 KST

BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese research team has found that a pulsar discovered by the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Radio Telescope (FAST) is part of a primordial triple star system still in the process of evolving, according to a study published Friday in the Astrophysical Journal Letters.
With its extraordinary detection capabilities, FAST has discovered more than 1,000 pulsars. The pulsar in this triple system was detected on June 8, 2020, by the team from National Astronomical Observatories under the Chinese Academy of Sciences (NAOC) using FAST.
After the discovery, a team from the Xinjiang Astronomical Observatory found that the pulsar is orbited by a white dwarf companion. They also found that the pulsar's rotation period is showing an unexpected increase of 1 nanosecond per year, two orders of magnitude higher than similar pulsars.
Following this, NAOC researcher Han Jinlin led researchers from several domestic institutions to analyze the archival data from FAST and other observational facilities. They found that the pulsar has a second companion -- a Sun-like star still evolving, with a mass nearly identical to that of the Sun. These three celestial bodies form a rare triple system.
Based on stellar evolution theory, the team inferred that the triple system originated as "primordial triplets" born from the same gas cloud. The most massive of these stars has already completed its evolution, ended its life in a supernova explosion and become the pulsar observed today by FAST. The second-most massive star has also ended its evolution, becoming the white dwarf that accompanies the pulsar.
The least massive star is relatively far from the other two and was largely unaffected by their early supernova explosions. It is a "living" star, still evolving steadily.
Prior to this discovery, the only known pulsar triple star system was found by the Green Bank Telescope. It consists of a pulsar and two white dwarfs, all three of which have already ended their evolutionary process.
The research team noted that this system shows clear and significant three-body gravitational interactions, making it an excellent natural observational platform for testing fundamental gravitational theories such as the strong equivalence principle.
It also provides a valuable research target for understanding the complex evolutionary mechanisms of triple star systems and for exploring astrophysical processes under extreme conditions.
Located in a naturally deep and round karst depression in southwest China's Guizhou Province, FAST has a reception area equal to 30 standard football fields. As the world's largest single-dish radio telescope, FAST started formal operations in January 2020 and was officially opened to the world in March 2021. ■

China's Zheng Qinwen reaches China Open semifinals shortly after turning 24
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:07:46 CST
20:07:46 KST

Zheng Qinwen of China hits a return during the women's singles quarterfinal match between Zheng Qinwen of China and Elina Svitolina of Ukraine at 2026 China Open tennis tournament in Beijing, China, Oct. 9, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Han)
BEIJING, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- China's Zheng Qinwen advanced to the women's singles semifinals of the China Open here on Friday, defeating sixth seed Elina Svitolina of Ukraine 6-3, 7-6(6) on her first day after turning 24.
Playing her first top-10 opponent of the tournament, wildcard Zheng broke serve three times in the opening set. She claimed breaks in the first and seventh games, only to be broken herself while serving for the set at 5-3, before securing her third break in the ninth game to close it out 6-3.
Svitolina raised her level in the second set and broke Zheng in the seventh game to move 4-3 ahead, only for the Chinese to hit back immediately in the eighth. Both players held serve to force a tie-break, where Zheng trailed 0-2 before winning four straight points to lead 4-2. Svitolina drew level at 6-6, but Zheng sealed the win on her second match point at 8-6.
"She performed excellently in the second set. That tie-break was really so close. Both of us played at a really high level. Honestly speaking, I really wanted to win this match, so I felt nervous when I hit the balls," Zheng said.
Zheng, who spent her 24th birthday on Thursday, said, "I hope at 24 I can become more mature, and stay calm facing every single point on court. That is my own expectation for myself," she said.
The result sends Zheng into her second China Open semifinal, matching her best run at the event, and her first WTA 1000 semifinal this year. ■

Laos aims for 30 pct EV adoption by 2030
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
19:07:20 CST
20:07:20 KST

VIENTIANE, Oct. 9 (Xinhua) -- The Lao government aims to have electric vehicles (EVs) account for at least 30 percent of vehicles by 2030, as part of efforts to strengthen economic stability, reduce fuel import costs and make greater use of domestic electricity resources.
Laos imported 37,475 vehicles in the first eight months of 2026, including 8,330 fully electric vehicles, up 107 percent year on year, and 2,804 hybrid vehicles, up 114 percent. Together, new-energy vehicles accounted for 29.7 percent of total vehicle imports, Lao Youth Radio reported on Friday, citing Lao Minister of Industry and Commerce Malaithong Kommasith at the second ordinary session of the 10th National Assembly.
Laos has also expanded its charging infrastructure, licensing 43 operators and establishing 200 charging points across the country. Meanwhile, the Lao central bank is promoting the use of banking systems for vehicle purchases and has issued green bonds as a pilot initiative to mobilize funding for EV infrastructure.
To meet its 2030 target, which includes an estimated 222,784 four-wheeled EVs and 1,307 public charging stations, the Ministry of Industry and Commerce has outlined several measures to accelerate the transition.
The Lao state-run Electricite du Laos has studied a proposal to reduce average electricity rates for charging stations by 10 percent compared with standard commercial rates. A time-of-use pricing system is also being developed to offer lower rates during off-peak hours.
The government is also encouraging commercial banks to provide preferential interest rates and longer repayment periods for EV loans. It plans to transition newly procured government administrative and official vehicles to fully electric models and encourage freight and passenger transport operators to adopt EVs.
To support the transition over the long term, the Ministry of Education and Sports has approved a vocational training curriculum for EV repair and established a dedicated technical training center to develop the skilled workforce needed for EV maintenance and servicing. ■

ROME, October 9. /TASS/. It is not Russia but the NATO and EU establishment that is waging the so-called hybrid war against Europe, intimidating their own citizens with a non-existent threat, Italian journalist Thomas Fazi, who works in the English-language media and writes for international publications on European issues, stated.
In his latest article entitled "The ‘Russian hybrid war’ narrative: a new NATO strategy of tension?" posted on his X page, the journalist analyzed all the recent incidents that have been presented in the international media as acts of this very war: from sabotage on the seabed of the Baltic Sea to the crash and discovery of drones in various European countries.
"Ultimately, serious scrutiny of the ‘Russian hybrid warfare’ narrative can only lead to one disquieting conclusion. A ‘hybrid war’ is indeed being waged against Europe - but it is being waged by the EU-NATO establishment itself, against its own population," the journalist wrote.
Fazi noted that Europeans are being subjected to a targeted psychological campaign designed to make them believe that Europe is under attack by Russia and that these hybrid attacks are precursors to imminent military action. "Europeans are being subjected to a sustained campaign of cognitive or psychological warfare aimed at conditioning them to believe that Europe is under attack from Russia, and that these hybrid attacks are a prelude to conventional hostilities - a claim for which, by and large, there is little or no proof. What the record points to, in fact, is a deliberate campaign of threat inflation in which governments, media outlets and defence-funded ‘think tanks’ have colluded to instil a permanent sense of fear in the population, through relentless coverage of ‘incidents,’ ‘attacks,’ ‘sabotages’ and ‘campaigns’ that, in most cases, simply do not exist," the reporter pointed out.
He also stressed the importance of considering what rational or strategic interest Russia would have in launching an offensive against Europe, as this could easily escalate into a large-scale war with NATO. The analyst noted that, thus far, Moscow has refrained from retaliating against Kiev’s actions on its territory, which are supported by the alliance and include attacks on civilians.
Moreover, Fazi emphasized that NATO's own assessments are highly contradictory, yet the more cautious ones are often downplayed, allowing baseless, speculative scenarios to take precedence.

African activists demand global tribunal over corporate abuses
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:06:43 UTC
20:06:43 KST

African activists demand global tribunal over corporate abuses
African civil society organizations have called for an international tribunal to prosecute corporate human rights and environmental abuses, citing decades of oil pollution in Nigeria’s Niger Delta as a major example.
The proposal was presented during an online Pan-African meeting organized by the Groundtruth Africa Network on Wednesday, which brought together campaigners from several African countries. Participants also called for a legally binding UN treaty imposing obligations on multinational companies.
“Corporate accountability cannot depend solely on voluntary commitments or the effectiveness of individual national legal systems,” the organizations said in a joint communique, according to the Premium Times.
The groups argued that victims often struggle to obtain compensation because multinational companies operate through subsidiaries, contractors, and financial partners in different countries. The campaigners pointed to the Niger Delta, where decades of oil production have been linked to contaminated waterways, damaged farmland, and declining fishing livelihoods.
The Niger Delta, a vast wetland region in southern Nigeria and the heart of the country’s oil industry, has been at the center of long-running legal disputes involving multinational companies. In 2015, Shell agreed to pay £55 million ($72.8 million) to residents of the Bodo community over two major oil spills in 2008. Other communities have also pursued lawsuits against the company in British courts, seeking compensation and environmental cleanup.
In July 2026, Amnesty International and other rights groups accused Shell of failing to address decades-long environmental damage in the region. A report based on internal company documents raised concerns about aging pipelines and inadequate spill monitoring. Shell rejected the report’s characterization of its operations. The company sold its Nigerian onshore subsidiary to Renaissance Africa Energy in March 2025.
Beyond Nigeria, the African organizations raised concerns about land disputes and compensation linked to the East African Crude Oil Pipeline in Uganda and Tanzania. They also cited alleged abuses connected to cobalt and copper mining in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, as well as labor and environmental concerns in South Africa, Chad, Cameroon, and Tunisia.

Yeşim Ustaoğlu on the journey behind What Remains
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:06:01 UTC
20:06:01 KST

Breadcrumb
Yeşim Ustaoğlu's What Remains: A journey towards freedom, creativity and self-discovery
In 2016, after Yeşim Ustaoğlu released her seventh feature film, Clair Obscur, the idea of a woman trying to reconnect with her creativity began to form. The film she had just made explored the experience of two repressed Turkish women: a 30-something psychiatrist and a teenage bride seeking love and autonomy outside the marital unit.
But with her next film, What Remains, the Turkish filmmaker needed to let thoughts about creativity, and how societal systems can suffocate them, especially for women, marinate for several years before she could tell the story she wanted.
"It's a subject that I needed to rest and wait with to get a deeper understanding," she tells The New Arab on the patio of Hotel de Londres in San Sebastián, where the film premiered at the annual film festival.
"It made me think about what I am doing and what I am searching for, because it is about getting out."
What Remains continues the theme of self-determination through the eyes of Elif, a poet, wife, and mother who breaks away from domestic life and travels across Turkey to rediscover her voice.
But during the pandemic, when the world was trapped in their homes, the concept became more urgent.
"I was blocked for a while when the world stopped, and I felt these thoughts more deeply, what I refer to as a 'loss of appetite for creating and making sense of things,'" Yeşim explains. "I felt a strong urge to leave, to simply go; not just trying to escape, but trying to be more connected."
As soon as she was free to, Yeşim headed out onto the road, driving from her homestead in Istanbul to central Turkey and toward the northeast.
She discovered a different landscape from the one she remembered from her 1998 film Journey to the Sun.
"I met amazing, strong people, especially the women, and I started to realise the countryside part is more deserted," she says. "The whole portrayal of social life is different from these big cities."
Some rural areas were drier, with huge water problems, yet the stories she collected to weave into her script were those of durability and survival: "The people whom Elif meets give her courage and some meaning that even within such conditions, someone can be very content or able to deal – these were all my own memories of the people whom I met on the journey."
Letting love breathe
In What Remains, Elif, played by Öykü Karayel, has been celebrated for her poetic efforts, but without much current creative inspiration, she has poured her energy into being a doting mother to Selim (Ali Kayra Kul).
She feeds his curiosity for the world on long walks and creative projects while her experimental musician husband teaches at a university, yet she remains unfulfilled.
It's a setup that begins to question the role of a parent in a society that Elif feels inhibits their ability to be truly themselves and sets the wrong example for their children. "We need to question what the responsibility of being a mother is," Yeşim argues.
"How do we raise a kid? What kind of life are we offering them if we are not really content and feel stuck in something that you cannot be yourself? She doesn't want him to be a slave of the system that erases you, your creativity, your understanding, your feeling, everything."
Yet as much as this is a portrait of a woman on a journey of self-discovery, it is also a love story between a man and a woman.
When Elif's partner Mehmet (Metin Akdülger) loses his job, the cracks in their relationship are laid bare.
A hushed conversation in their kitchen conveys his resentment and her unhappiness, leading to her departure, but Yeşim is careful not to present a complete severing of their partnership.
"I wanted to point out that they can continue to be in love, but it doesn't need to be under the conditions that they have," she explains.
"This is a very gentle separation; they have very different lives, and they will be more inspired by themselves, and from that they will be happier. The heart may beat to each other with freedom," she adds.
A voice of her own
Elif voyages across Turkey and finds herself drawn to her grandmother's village in the mountains, where the actor performed scenes with a woman the filmmaker met on her own journey, adding to the story's grounded authenticity.
She also enlisted her close friend of 20 years, the Turkish poet Birhan Keskin, to bolster the script's poeticism and Elif's characterisation.
"I've always admired her voice, and she is like me in that she only writes when she feels, so when I start to think about Elif getting out, her voice should be a poet's."
After establishing the main beats for the story, Yeşim and Birhan sequestered themselves away at the poet's seaside home, where they spent days "creating all this imagination about Elif and the poems," recalls the filmmaker.
"It was a beautiful, inspiring time and Birhan became the voice of everything passing through me."
Yeşim has never shied away from exploring the diversity of female experience among Turkish women, from 2004's Waiting for the Clouds to 2008's Pandora's Box, which won the Golden Shell for Best Film at the San Sebastián International Film Festival.
Yet her films have not gone without pushback in her own country.
Censorship laws and state funding constraints have affected filmmakers who don't adhere to the political expectations of the Turkish government, headed by authoritarian President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan.
Her examination of Turkey's suppression of its Kurdish community in Journey to the Sun led to a media boycott for three years, with the filmmaker taking prints of the film on tour as part of a grassroots distribution effort.
"All my films have been shown and will be shown," Yeşim says defiantly.
Economic turmoil continues to impede the country, with the Turkish lira at a record low and production costs rising with inflation.
As an independent filmmaker, she is well aware of the struggle to make films at home.
"We had a big struggle to finance this film," she explains. "You can get collaborators from outside, but there's not enough strong funding in your own home, and anything can be censored too."
While What Remains might not be doused with political themes of ethnic suppression, its non-conformist image of a family unit, she admits, might be seen as "problematic" by the Turkish government.
Still, with 30 years of filmmaking under her belt, nothing will deter Yeşim from making the films she wants to make, and she's grateful for all the people who pay the ticket price.
"There is an important number of people who love my cinema; I put it out in the world, and they go."
Hanna Flint is a British-Tunisian critic, broadcaster and author of Strong Female Character: What Movies Teach Us. Her reviews, interviews and features have appeared in GQ, the Guardian, Elle, Town & Country, Mashable, Radio Times, MTV, Time Out, The New Arab, Empire, BBC Culture and elsewhere
Follow her on Instagram: @hannainesflint

Inside Kazakhstan’s historic rock-hewn mosques now recognised by UNESCO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:05:48 UTC
20:05:48 KST

Five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites dating from the 12th to the 18th centuries make up Kazakhstan’s newest UNESCO World Heritage property. The complexes preserve centuries of Sufi tradition alongside much older beliefs.
The World Heritage Committee adopted the decision at its 48th session on 25 July in Busan, South Korea. This follows President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev’s 2024 instructions to pursue the inscription of these rock-hewn mosques on the World Heritage List.
Set amid the otherworldly landscapes of Mangystau, the newly recognised mosques and their associated sites are named after revered Sufi masters: Beket-Ata, Shopan-Ata, Karaman-Ata, Shakpak-Ata and Sultan-Epe.
In Central Asian Sufism, ‘Ata’, meaning ‘father’ or ‘ancestor’, is used as an honorific for a revered spiritual figure.
Their spiritual lineage traces back to the 12th-century Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. His teachings helped spread Islam among the Turkic-speaking peoples of Central Asia, connecting Islamic practices with older Tengri beliefs and local shamanistic traditions.
The mosques welcome both pilgrims and visitors seeking to explore Kazakhstan’s spiritual, cultural and architectural heritage.
Mangystau – the cradle of nomadic spirituality
According to the UNESCO World Heritage Centre, the complexes reflect the evolution of a distinctive spiritual culture.
They represent “sacred practices in which Islamic Sufi spirituality organically continued and transformed more ancient practices related to ancestor worship, the sacredness of the landscape and the role of spiritual leaders”.
Developed over many centuries, the monuments show how spiritual traditions and practices were adapted to the region’s distinctive natural environment and geological features through local architecture.
Speaking at the 48th session in July, Erlan Karin, Chairman of Kazakhstan’s National Commission to UNESCO and ICESCO, highlighted the significance of the inscription for the country.
“The inscription of the sacred monuments of Mangystau on the World Heritage List was not only a recognition of their significance for humanity as a whole, but also a tribute to the rich history, spiritual heritage and cultural identity of the Kazakh people.”
For local resident Almagul Zhaiman, the sacred sites embody a faith passed down through generations.
“These sacred sites have been preserved because of the faith passed down through generations, the knowledge of that heritage, preserving it and passing it on to our future generations. I believe that is what makes all these mosques so meaningful to us,” she said.
The Sufi masters of the mosques
Karaman-Ata was a Sufi missionary who came to spread Islam in the region. His mosque is believed to date back to the 12th or 13th century, while its associated necropolis is one of the largest and oldest in Mangystau.
For the Kazakhs and Turkmens who lived on the Mangyshlak Peninsula, the necropolis was considered a sacred place. According to local tradition, it was also a site for resolving disputes and negotiating peace. Those who made vows there were expected to honour them, as breaking a vow was believed to bring death and the end of one's lineage.
Karaman-Ata is believed to have been the grandson of Shopan-Ata, a 12th-century mystic revered as the spiritual protector of shepherds and their livestock.
According to tradition, Shopan-Ata was a disciple of the renowned Sufi master Khoja Ahmed Yasawi. Once part of an ancient caravan route to Khorezm, Shopan-Ata’s site remains an important destination for Sufi pilgrims.
Beket-Ata is said to have regarded Shopan-Ata, who lived centuries earlier, as a spiritual mentor.
Local traditions attribute extraordinary abilities to the 18th-century scholar, healer and architect, including teleportation and levitation.
“He was also regarded as the last and highest-ranking spiritual master among other holy men, which is why he became known as Pir Beket,” said Bakhtiyar Esimbetov, caretaker of Beket-Ata’s mosque.
In Sufi tradition, the Persian word ‘Pir’ refers to a spiritual guide or master, often one who has attained a high level of spiritual wisdom.
The Shakpak-Ata complex served as one of the region’s principal Sufi centres for centuries. Shakpak-Ata is believed to have lived sometime between the 9th and 14th centuries.
Carved into a chalk and limestone cliff, the sanctuary is arranged around a central domed hall with a cross-shaped layout.
Local traditions say the scholar taught astrology and astronomy, as well as ideas linked to the cosmos.
Inside the mosques’ architectural layout
According to local belief, divine signs guided the Sufi masters to the places where they built their mosques.
The sanctuaries are scattered across Mangystau, in western Kazakhstan, a region shaped by its nomadic heritage and geological history. Much of the area was once covered by the ancient Tethys Ocean.
Locally known as “underground mosques”, the complexes were built in natural caves, carved into steep rock faces or dug into the ground, providing shelter in the semi-desert landscape.
Their architectural layouts vary. They include prayer halls, mihrabs, rooms for contemplation and self-reflection, multifunctional spaces and tombs of the Sufi masters, sometimes alongside those of their immediate families.
Some underground cells were carved out for silent meditation and ascetic isolation.
“These underground mosques were places of retreat from society, where people could withdraw from everyday life and devote themselves fully to spiritual purification,” said Yersultan Islam, a local sacred sites guide.
The complexes also feature courtyards, water sources, sacred trees, pathways and cemeteries, some of which date from the 10th to the 20th centuries.
Pilgrims
For centuries, Mangystau’s sacred mosques have been important destinations for pilgrims.
Visitors are expected to dress modestly, while women are required to cover their heads before entering the underground mosques as a sign of respect for the sacred sites.
The sanctuaries attract not only local worshippers but also pilgrims from abroad.
Among them is Dinara Farvazova, whose family travels from Bashkortostan, Russia, to visit Mangystau’s sacred sites year after year.
“We read the Quran here, pray and make wishes. People come here seeking healing, and many see their dreams come true. They then tell their relatives and friends about the place, who come here too.”
Some visitors come in search of a deeper understanding of Islam.
Kaahn Ozturk, a traveller from Turkey, stopped at Karaman-Ata’s mosque during a long-distance motorcycle journey across the country.
“I have lots of questions in my mind, and I just want to find answers. That’s why I’m trying to discover every mosque, every place, every idea about Islam, to understand it better.”
Rinat Aubekerov and his wife, ethnic Kazakhs from Russia, made a pilgrimage to Shopan-Ata, hoping their prayers to have children would be answered.
For Davide Passanante, a visitor from Italy, the appeal was different.
After experiencing the crowds of summer tourism at home, he found a sense of calm in the remote sanctuaries. Travelling with a group of friends across Mangystau’s Martian-like landscapes, he was struck by the region’s spiritual atmosphere.
“I'm very impressed because the religion here is very important. I see how people pray and how they feel, how they think of God every time.”
Easing travel for visitors to sacred sites
The remote sanctuaries are attracting growing numbers of pilgrims from around the world. Kazakhstan is now planning to improve access to the newly listed sites while preserving them for future generations.
A five-year comprehensive development plan, due to begin in 2027, is expected to support tourism at the sites, including restoration work and the development of new visitor infrastructure.
Each sanctuary already has basic facilities where visitors can sleep and eat free of charge, although donations are welcome to help cover maintenance costs.
Plans include building visitor centres at Shopan-Ata, Beket-Ata and Karaman-Ata, complementing the existing centre serving Sultan-Epe and Shakpak-Ata.
“An asphalt road will be built to the site as part of the development plan. We also hope that internet connectivity issues will be resolved,” said Baltabai Balapan, director of the Mangystau State Historical and Cultural Reserve.
The five rock-hewn mosques and associated sacred sites of Mangystau, now collectively inscribed on UNESCO’s World Heritage List, are bringing the region’s spiritual heritage to a global audience, inviting visitors to discover its sacred landscapes.

Bulgaria's Interior Minister Links Bomb Threats to Peevski Flight Hearings, DPS Leader Fires Back
Bulgarian Interior Minister Ivan Demerdzhiev said bomb threats against institutions across the country had increased sharply during periods following his parliamentary hearings on flights linked to Delyan Peevski, leader of the Movement for Rights and Freedoms (DPS).
Speaking from the parliamentary rostrum during parliamentary control, Demerdzhiev said a spike in threats followed his July 2 hearing, when he presented information about flights involving Peevski. He pointed to July 3, 7 and 8 as dates when the number of threats rose significantly.
“There is a characteristic dependence that bomb threats escalate in certain periods of time, such as after my hearing on July 2, when I presented data on some flights, to one manager, to one parliamentary group, and on July 3, 7 and 8, the number of these threats increased sharply,” Demerdzhiev said.
He reported that a similar increase had occurred last week and again this week, which he also linked to his hearings. Demerdzhiev noted that the aircraft used for the flights had been sold to a Dubai-based company after his July 2 hearing, describing the timing as another notable coincidence.
The minister said the available evidence supported the assumption that the threats were part of hybrid operations intended to destabilize Bulgaria and test how quickly state institutions could respond. He said the messages were also intended to disrupt public life, weaken citizens’ confidence in state authorities and interfere with the work of institutions.
Since June 2026, Bulgarian institutions have received hundreds of threatening emails, Demerdzhiev said. The targets have included courts, universities, kindergartens, ports, schools, municipal offices and other institutions. The threats led to temporary suspensions of work and evacuations of students over several consecutive days, but all the reports proved false.
Investigators have established that the messages were sent through compromised email accounts using services based in Italy, Britain, Lebanon, Brazil and Argentina, as well as a free Swiss anonymizing email service. Bulgarian authorities contacted the providers, but the use of anonymization services has so far prevented them from identifying the actual senders.
Demerdzhiev said evidence of machine-assisted translation in the messages could indicate that they had not been written by Bulgarian citizens. Their content was largely identical and lacked specific details, he added. He also said authorities currently had no effective way to block the sending or receipt of such messages because different hacked accounts were used in individual cases.
The minister said Bulgaria had requested assistance from partner services and that institutions in other Balkan and European countries had also faced similar attacks during the period in question. The Interior Ministry is examining two main possibilities: that the threats are part of different types of hybrid attacks or that someone is seeking to create disorder at specific times.
Demerdzhiev also said a detailed protocol governed the response to such incidents, but complained that it was not always followed.
He linked the pattern of threats to information he disclosed on July 2 about private flights associated with Peevski, which reportedly cost millions of euros. Authorities are checking how the politician, who is under sanctions, paid for the flights.
Peevski dismissed Demerdzhiev’s allegations when speaking to reporters in parliament, accusing the interior minister of being preoccupied with him rather than his family. He made the remarks in response to Demerdzhiev’s comments about the timing of the bomb threats.
“All I can do is give him a thermometer,” Peevski said, adding that “the man apparently raised the temperature or his wife didn't turn him on”.
Peevski called on the government to get some rest, saying its members appeared overly concerned about him and were inventing nonsense every day, BTA reported. He added that he could not be blamed for the state’s problems or the authorities’ inability to manage them.
Asked about the reported visit to Bulgaria by Kyrylo Budanov, head of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s office, Peevski said he had no information and that questions about the visit should be directed to the prime minister.
Bulgaria has experienced several previous waves of false bomb threats, including in June and July. A similar series of incidents occurred in March and April 2023, shortly before national elections.
Following the 2023 incidents, the government introduced a unified response protocol. Under the rules, evacuation is not automatic and must instead follow a specific risk assessment by police and the management of the affected building.

Widow of Playboy founder Hugh Hefner urged Jessica Biel to reconsider her role in the film "Playmates"
Kyiv • UNN
Crystal Hefner urged people not to romanticize Playboy in the film «Playmates». The movie is inspired by the director’s childhood memories.
The widow of Playboy founder Hugh Hefner expressed her disapproval, nearly a decade after his death, of a coming-of-age film inspired by her late husband. UNN reports this, citing Deadline.
Details
Crystal Hefner, who was married to him from 2012 until his death at the age of 91 in 2017, shared a screenshot of a private Instagram message she sent to Jessica Biel, asking her to "reconsider her decision" to play Hugh’s fictional wife in Lorraine Nicholson’s Searchlight film "Playmates."
"Please reconsider your role as Hugh Hefner’s ‘wife’ if this film is intended to romanticize him or the Playboy world," Crystal wrote in the message. "I was, in fact, his wife and experienced sexual, emotional, financial, and physical abuse in that relationship. Many other women have also come forward with allegations of rape, coercion, drug use, and exploitation. There are also deeply troubling concerns involving minors. I hope everyone involved in this film will take the time to listen to the women who experienced this before helping Hollywood turn it into nostalgia."
Written and directed by Nicholson and inspired by her childhood friendship with Hugh Hefner’s children, "Playmates" is described as a Los Angeles coming-of-age story about 13-year-old "know-it-all" Elle (played by Indiana Elle), who considers the Playboy Mansion her second home. While staying at the mansion, Elle meets Anna (Lily-Rose Depp), one of seven contenders for the title of "Playmate of the Month." They form an unlikely friendship and try to help each other get what each wants most: a magazine cover and a boyfriend.
Crystal added in her post: "As for the film, I hope it will not glorify Hugh Hefner. With women in the leading roles, I hope the film will ultimately convey a message of empowerment: that women can find fulfillment, independence, and a sense of self outside of Playboy."
According to the outlet, Bill Pullman plays Hugh Hefner, and Biel’s character is a fictional role not inspired by any of his three wives.
Following Hugh Hefner’s death in 2017, Crystal spoke openly about the toxic atmosphere at the Playboy Mansion and the abuse she says she experienced during her time there, while other Playboy models have shared similar experiences in recent years, the outlet notes.

Zelensky ‘doesn’t give a damn’ about Ukrainians – Russian envoy

‘People are feeling the real impacts’: influencers use humor to make fun of the private equity industry
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:26 UTC
20:00:26 KST

Johnny Hilbrant Partridge kept getting stuck next to the same kind of finance guy at weddings – the one bragging about his family’s full-time nanny and lavish vacations while name-dropping elite club memberships and private schools.
To Partridge, a former fitness instructor, their shameless knack for self-promotion felt ripe for comedy. Using a filter that puts an exaggerated sneer on his face, Partridge donned a puffer vest and created “The PE Guy”, a caricature of the men who work in the private equity industry.
“All we did is acquire some youth hockey complexes, implement dynamic pricing and put some people on recurring revenue subscription models,” Partridge scoffed in a video after lawmakers introduced a bill this year to ban private equity from youth sports. “This country used to reward innovation, and suddenly it’s wrong to charge $11,000 for a development lacrosse weekend … give me a break.”
Since he first debuted the character last year, “The PE Guy” has racked up millions of views on Instagram and TikTok, becoming the most popular player in a fast-growing ecosystem skewering private equity. The multitrillion-dollar industry has turned into a catch-all online for the ills of modern capitalism, inspiring “a day in the life” skits and parody rap music videos.
For many viewers, the draw is the dark humor, something that even the finance guys are embracing. Partridge said he gets invited to speak at insurance and private equity conferences and finance companies’ annual meetings as comic relief.
But it’s also been a way many Americans are learning how the industry, which often operates out of view and without the same oversight or regulation as publicly traded corporations, is affecting their lives.
Every business has bad actors, Partridge said, but he chose to focus on private equity because it is changing everyday things like healthcare so radically that “people are feeling the real impacts from it”, he said.
Private equity has found its way into everything from funeral homes to family dental offices. Once they were acquired by private equity firms, beloved chains such as JoAnn Fabrics and Toys “R” Us faced bankruptcies, and many name brands taken over by the industry have degraded in quality.
“When people say private equity, they don’t just mean the exact technical term,” said Hojung Kim, whose August Instagram post on how private equity is changing veterinary care got a million views in just two days. The term has come to represent “leveraged buyouts, hard cost-cutting in order to ruthlessly profit-maximize and saddling the business with debt in order to self-enrich”.
Struck by the response, Kim, co-founder of an affordable LSAT prep business, started a series on other industries changed by private equity and built Grass, an app that helps users find independent American businesses.
“We hit a nerve. A lot of people were being affected by this rampant rise in costs and wanted to know what was behind it,” Kim said. “As it happens, private equity has changed a lot of industry landscapes.”
TikTok and Instagram are awash in pro-business content too, of course, as companies overall have spent $37bn on influencer marketing in 2025, one advertising trade group estimates, and private equity companies are even buying up influencer tools like Uscreen.
But the private equity criticism continues to grow. Journalist Pablo Torre and comedian Stavros Halkias have gotten hundreds of thousands of views on a YouTube video railing about Blackstone’s takeover of Jersey Mike’s Subs and financial investors in sports teams.
“If they fucking destroy the Lakers, guys with Kobe [Bryant] back tattoos are going to start the proletariat revolution,” Halkias said on Torre’s podcast, going off news that the Los Angeles basketball team was acquired by Bob Iger and Josh Kushner for $12.5bn in August. “The closest we’re getting to class consciousness is fast food and sports teams.”
Natalka Burian, owner of Elsa, a bar in Brooklyn, is among the food industry experts who are chronicling private equity’s takeover of restaurants and bakeries.
They can pay outrageous rents and snatch up the best locations, she said, which drives out businesses like her own.
“That’s money that should be going to local businesses,” Burian said. “I think there’s something about this blandness that takes away from our communities.”

Researchers explore how J-Pop listening habits impact visual memory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:12 UTC
20:00:12 KST

A small pilot study exploring the brain activity of young adults found that listening to preferred Japanese pop music was associated with higher descriptive scores in visual memory and subjective focus compared to unpleasant noise or silence. While the results were not statistically significant, the research provides a framework for testing how everyday listening habits relate to learning and attention. The findings were published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience.
Many students habitually listen to music while they review class materials or prepare for exams. Popular media often highlights a supposed cognitive boost from classical music, an idea frequently branded as the Mozart effect. But very few university students actually select classical instrumental pieces for their daily study routines.
Instead, contemporary students frequently choose popular music with familiar lyrics. This habit presents a puzzle for cognitive researchers. Meaningful speech and background vocals can easily disrupt the human brain as it attempts to process language and memorize verbal facts.
Listening to a favorite pop song with lyrics might logically act as a distraction that pulls attention away from educational materials. Conversely, familiar and enjoyable music can elevate a person’s mood, reduce stress, and increase overall motivation to complete a difficult task.
Different types of learning might also respond differently to musical background noise. While reading comprehension and verbal memorization often suffer when background lyrics are present, recalling visual information might be less susceptible to the exact same interference.
Researchers are working to understand if preferred background music can support efficient memory processing through emotional engagement. They are looking at neural mechanisms that are entirely distinct from those typically emphasized in traditional classical music narratives.
Yoshiko Tojo, a researcher at the Ibaraki Prefectural University of Health Sciences in Japan, wanted to understand this dynamic in a realistic context. Tojo aimed to see how self-selected Japanese pop music, commonly known as J-Pop, relates to visual memory retrieval and regional brain activity.
Tojo recruited healthy university students for a small brain imaging pilot study. After exclusions for incomplete data, the final analysis included five participants. The participants completed a visual memory test while lying inside a functional magnetic resonance imaging scanner.
This imaging technology tracks blood flow in the brain to measure neural activity in real time. The visual memory task began with an encoding phase. Participants viewed sets of emotionally neutral photographs, such as everyday animals and food items.
They were asked to memorize both the specific objects and the exact order in which they appeared on the screen. Later, the participants answered true or false statements about the images to test their recall. They performed this retrieval task under three different auditory conditions.
In the first condition, participants listened to a J-Pop song they had personally selected beforehand as pleasant and comfortable. The second condition featured an abrasive composite sound made of ambulance sirens and earthquake early warning alarms. The final condition served as a baseline, featuring no sound other than the continuous rhythmic thumping of the scanner itself.
Following the memory tests, participants rated their subjective ability to focus during each auditory condition on a visual scale. They also rated the pleasantness of each sound environment. Tojo then analyzed both the behavioral performance and the brain activity data to see how the auditory contexts compared.
The behavioral data showed distinct patterns across the three listening environments. Participants achieved the highest average recall accuracy, answering correctly roughly 82 percent of the time, while listening to their preferred J-Pop music. In the baseline condition with no added sound, accuracy averaged about 76 percent.
The abrasive alarm sounds yielded the lowest recall accuracy at just 71 percent. The subjective focus ratings closely mirrored these results, with participants reporting the highest concentration during the J-Pop condition.
Brain scan data revealed shifting activity in specific neural regions depending on the background noise. Tojo focused heavily on the anterior insula, an area of the brain involved in evaluating subjective emotions, sensing internal body states, and managing large-scale attention networks.
During the J-Pop condition, participants showed higher average activity in the anterior insula compared to the other two conditions. This elevated activity suggests the familiar music might have engaged brain areas responsible for processing positive emotions and maintaining sustained task engagement.
Tojo also examined the temporo-occipital visual association cortex, a region at the back of the brain responsible for higher order visual processing and memory. Activity in this visual region was highest during the unpleasant alarm condition and lowest in the silent baseline condition.
This increased visual brain activity during the alarm condition might indicate that participants had to work harder to process the images when exposed to abrasive noise. But because the sample size was restricted to only five people, these behavioral and neural differences were not statistically significant.
The limited number of participants is the primary constraint of this research. The small sample size heavily restricts statistical power, meaning the results cannot be generalized to broader populations without further testing.
The experimental design also utilized different sets of pictures for each sound condition. This approach prevented participants from simply recognizing images they had already seen in previous rounds. But it also introduces the possibility that some image sets were inherently easier to remember than others.
The research focused exclusively on a visual memory task and a single genre of popular music. It is unknown if similar emotional and neural patterns would appear for verbal learning tasks, such as reading a textbook or memorizing vocabulary words.
Future studies with larger and more diverse groups of participants are needed to verify these trends. Expanding the research could reveal exactly when and for whom studying with background music might be beneficial.
These initial observations do not establish that listening to preferred music inherently improves memory performance. They do suggest that listening to emotionally positive background music is not universally detrimental to studying, opening the door for larger investigations into how personal listening habits affect the brain.
The study, “Preferred J-pop music and visual memory retrieval: an exploratory pilot fMRI study,” was authored by Yoshiko Tojo.

AI Chatbots Often Fail To Help Users in Mental-Health Crisis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:04 UTC
20:00:04 KST

As more people turn to AI chatbots to share their most distressing thoughts, companies are making pivotal decisions about how their platforms respond to users in the midst of mental-health crises. According to new research conducted by Scale AI and shared exclusively with TIME, chatbots are adept at discerning when a user is in crisis, but often fail to provide adequate help.
In about 35% of test conversations in the study, different AI chatbots recognized the user was distressed but didn’t refer them to helpful resources, such as a suicide hotline, according to the research.
“The models do a good job—regardless of the scenario—of identifying, ‘Look, this person's talking about something harmful,’” says Patrick Oathout, Red Team & Safety Lead at Scale AI. “But they'll respond in a very just empathetic, kind way as opposed to saying, ‘Okay, it's time that we get you help.’” The models performed worse at responding to users’ distress when they were engaging in long, multi-turn conversations—a deficit that matches the findings of previous studies, Oathout adds.
To test AI models’ effectiveness at responding to distressed users, Scale AI asked 19 licensed clinicians and crisis counselors to write 718 realistic chats, simulating scenarios where someone in crisis reaches out to a chatbot. The company tested 25 frontier models, including those from OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google. It graded the models’ responses based on a rubric that included whether it was compassionate, de-escalated the situation, and steered users to an expert who could help them, said Oathout. It also assessed whether they refrained from moralizing, such as criticizing suicide, and disclosed it wasn't a therapist. Based on the research, Scale AI research developed DistressBench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate how well models reply when someone tells them they're thinking about committing suicide or self-harm.
How chatbots respond to mentally distressed users is a question with high stakes. More than half a million people in the U.S. died by suicide between 2014 and 2024, with 2022 marking a record high, according to the health-policy organization KFF. According to the CDC, an estimated 14.3 million people seriously thought about suicide in 2024.
Increasingly, vulnerable people turn to chatbots for comfort, companionship, or guidance when dealing with mental-health distress. But there isn’t consensus among tech companies, policymakers, or mental-health professionals about how AI companies should train their models to respond to users in crisis.
Kelly Zuromski, a principal clinical research scientist at Crisis Text Line, says the nonprofit’s 24/7 crisis text line has spoken with “a lot of people” who indicated they heard about the group through a chatbot. But Zuromski says there are unanswered policy questions about what a responsible handoff looks like when a chatbot refers users to a human during a mental-health crisis—and how effective the referral process is in the first place. “Who is actually using the recommended resources?” she says. “Are we getting people to us that need the help the most?”
In some cases, AI companies, including OpenAI and Google, have been sued for fostering emotional dependence among young users and then failing to respond adequately to their expressions of distress, or reinforcing their delusional or suicidal thinking in the first place. The companies have expressed sympathy for the families and said their models include mental-health safeguards. (The lawsuits are ongoing.) AI labs such as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have said in recent years that they beefed up their protections for sensitive conversations, including by implementing policies that bar chatbots from instructing users on how to harm themselves and directing users to professional or emergency support.
An OpenAI spokesperson said in a statement the company did not have sufficient evidence to fully evaluate the Scale AI study, adding that the company incorporates robust safeguards into its models. Google declined to comment. Anthropic didn't respond to a request for comment.
In the future, AI labs should improve their models to better respond to users engaging in dangerous lengthy conversations with chatbots, says Scale AI’s Oathout. “I think the models are better than they were,” he says. “The goal now is to raise it further and actually reduce harm, which would add this massive benefit to society.”

The Cornell 7 Case Demands More Than Outrage
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
11:00:03 UTC
20:00:03 KST

By now, most of America has heard about the young woman who says she was gang raped by fraternity brothers while she was a student at Cornell University.
The case has been dubbed the "Cornell 7" across mainstream and social media, after the seven Chi Phi members named in her recent lawsuit. The woman who filed the suit, referred to as Jane Doe, first reported her experience to Cornell campus police in November 2024. According to her lawyer, after Cornell's Title IX process, two of the seven were expelled, and the other five were suspended, sent to workshops, and assigned essays. Cornell says none of them got off with only an essay.
At the time, the Tompkins County District Attorney declined to prosecute. After public outcry, the DA issued a statement explaining that Jane Doe’s original statement to police described the drug use and sex as "voluntary, conscious, and consensual.” “However, recognizing that the process of healing from trauma is personal and different for every human, my office has reopened this investigation," he wrote. Now, New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor in the case.
How did the case come to light? It took The Cornell Daily Sun, the campus student newspaper, breaking the story roughly two years later for this to capture the hearts, minds, and headlines of Americans across the country. The story struck a nihilistic nerve.
This case lands squarely in a moment of massive frustration, disappointment, and anger over how the Jeffrey Epstein and Ghislaine Maxwell case was handled. New CDC data shows that nearly half of American women and one in six men have experienced some form of contact sexual violence. Based on how broad this issue is and based on how some of the most visible cases have turned out, apathy about our ability to see our way from a society steeped in rape culture to one where sexual violence is rare should come as no surprise.
As someone fully immersed in this work, even though I see a pathway forward, I understand these feelings from a very deep place in my spirit. We should be disgusted. We should be heartbroken. We should be enraged.
So what do we do with these feelings?
We provide an outpouring of support to Jane Doe and to other women who have come forward with their accounts of sexual assault, such as Kendall Francis, who took to TikTok to speak out about how her college, LSU, handled her Title IX case. According to ESPN, in July, the LSU Office of Civil Rights and Title IX found her alleged attacker, a football player, responsible for “forcible rape” and suspended him for two semesters. The player appealed and in August, Administrative Law Judge Janet Waguespack reduced his punishment to four semesters’ probation, allowing him to remain on campus. The player's lawyers maintain that their client is innocent.
Again, Francis’ story struck a nerve, catching the attention of East Baton Rouge District Attorney Hillar Moore, whose office is now investigating the case.
The outpouring of support matters, both so these young women can get the justice they're seeking and so survivors everywhere know that support is out here. But what many of us know is that for every Jane Doe and Kendall Francis who reports and seeks justice, there are hundreds, if not thousands, of survivors who won't, for a lot of reasons. Chief among them is feeling alone in the fight. They aren't alone. But I'll admit it's hard to tell when spotlights dim, headlines fade, and accountability seems stifled.
As if right on cue, something else happened this week while these cases took over headlines. The Trump Administration’s Department of Education altered Title IX rules, declaring that harassment has to be "severe, pervasive, and objectively offensive" before a school must act, that most off-campus violence falls outside a school's responsibility, and that a college survivor can be cross-examined at a live hearing by the advisor her attacker chose.
This decision landing right as the Cornell 7 case came to light is telling. It's one of the clearest illustrations of the direct line between the damage this administration has done to the fight against sexual and gender-based violence—especially among young people.
The Trump Administration’s decision to make it more burdensome to file a Title IX complaint only adds to the helplessness so many survivors feel. Patriarchy protects itself the way any system of power does. It writes the rules, staffs the offices, and then leaves survivors like Jane Doe and Kendall Francis to fight for justice on their own.
Of course, it is worth remembering the challenge we collectively face isn’t simply a matter of one rule or how it is applied; there are questions we must confront about where our culture has ended up. After all, these Cornell students were tweens when recordings of now-President Donald Trump leaked of him using crude language to describe how he treats women. The context may be different, but we have to ask: How far is the line between "grab 'em by the p---y" and "free p---y", the message the lawsuit says one of the Cornell 7 sent his fraternity brothers, inviting them to join in the hours-long assault on Jane Doe?
Yet, in the face of these various challenges, we must also remember: We are not helpless.
On October 15, it'll be nine years since #MeToo went viral. We're far past the hashtag, but we're still in the movement, and it's a very real, very active movement fighting tooth and nail to destroy systems that prevent justice. The answer to such systems has always been the organized power of the people those systems harm. The rage people are feeling right now, from Baton Rouge to Ithaca, can be organized and directed exactly where it's needed. That means our outrage can't be selective. It can't show up when Epstein or Cornell makes the news and disappear when the coverage moves on. Because when the next national story takes hold, there will still be students on high school and college campuses all over this country who are fundamentally unsafe.
We've made real progress in almost ten years of the MeToo movement, and lasting change will only come from constant demand. Frederick Douglass famously said: "Power concedes nothing without a demand." Black people in the civil rights era didn't wait for a government full of segregationists to find its conscience. They organized until it had no choice. Sexual and gender-based violence is solvable, but those solutions have to be demanded, and we have the numbers to demand them.
Too many survivors who stay silent believe they'd be fighting alone if they raise their voices. The CDC's most recent national survey found that nearly 80 million American adults, close to 58 million women and more than 20 million men, have experienced contact sexual violence. For some people, those are just numbers. In reality, they're a base of power: millions of people who know this trauma intimately and are primed to act.
What action against sexual violence can look like
First, you can join an organization dedicated to addressing sexual violence head-on. Several national organizations are working to bring survivors and our allies together to demand systemic change. Organizations like mine, me too. International, along with the National Women's Law Center and UltraViolet, are on the front lines organizing survivor leaders, fighting for survivors in courtrooms, and keeping people engaged on these issues. Others, like Justice for Migrant Women, Educate Us, and the National Domestic Workers Alliance, work on where sexual and gender-based violence meets immigration, domestic work, and education. The Survivor Justice Network, a coalition of organizations fighting sexual and gender-based violence from a social and political standpoint, runs the Survivors Vote campaign to organize survivors as a voting bloc. And there are countless regional and local organizations fighting this fight every day, especially local rape crisis centers, many of which are struggling.
In April 2025, the Justice Department terminated hundreds of grants worth more than $800 million, including money for victim services, and this spring $200 million meant for violence against women programs was still sitting unspent. Centers like the DC Rape Crisis Center (DCRCC), the oldest in the country, don't only provide direct services to local survivors. They take on the larger issue of sexual violence and how it's affecting the people they serve.
Next, you can use your resources well. Speakimng of DCRCC, local rape crisis centers are the first line of defense, and when students can't get support on campus, they often go looking for it at the rape crisis center in their college town. Find the survivor support organizations near you and give to them directly. It's the best way to shore up the front line so survivors can get what they need and the fight can continue.
Third, you can get active in local politics.
Ask your elected officials where they stand on sexual and gender-based violence and on legislation they can move right now, like the Survivors' Rights Restitution Act, which Rep. Ayanna Pressley introduced in September with Reps. Teresa Leger Fernández and Deborah Ross to compensate survivors whose federal rights were violated, including Epstein's survivors. Pressure them to vote accordingly, and make your support heard and understood.
Lastly, we must unite around our shared challenges. National outrage helps shake people up enough to pay attention, but culture won't shift just because we change laws and elect better politicians. People need to understand how sexual and gender-based violence shows up in their daily lives, how it intersects with the other issues they care about, and how long it stays with families, communities, and institutions. Until the whole of society sees this as an abomination, we won’t have the lasting cultural impact that makes sexual violence a rarity.
Jane Doe and Kendall Francis each refused to carry this quietly. The rest of us owe them and survivors like them more than a week of outrage.
We can let them see what it looks like to turn outrage into outcomes.
