The protests began in mid-September in the Paris suburb of Creteil, where high school students mobilized in support of teachers protesting staff shortages, before spreading to schools across France.
Students have demanded increased education funding, more teachers and support staff, improvements to deteriorating school buildings, smaller class sizes and changes to the Parcoursup university admissions system.
The demonstrations have intensified amid reports of clashes between protesters and police, including the use of tear gas and other crowd-control weapons that have left several students seriously injured.
French authorities have faced growing criticism over the police response, while the government has pledged to address students' grievances.

Feverish after a vaccine? The reason could be your gut microbiome
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:48:29 UTC
19:48:29 KST

Vaccines pack a punch: The shots save lives, but they can also often cause minor side effects such as muscle soreness, fatigue and fever. Researchers have long wondered why some people develop these reactions while others seem to skate by unaffected. The reason, it turns out, may have to do with the bacteria in our guts.
In a new study published in Science on Thursday, researchers collected stool samples from more than 170 people before and after a second or third dose of a COVID vaccine. They found that people who experienced fever after the shot tended to share similar microbiome traits.
Specifically, people with worse fever tended to have more of a protein called flagellin in their systems than those with little to no fever. Flagellin makes up the tail-like structures, or flagella, that bacteria use to move—suggesting that the fever-associated microbes had greater “motility,” or ability to move around, explains Ruth Ley, the study’s senior author and director of the department of microbiome science at the Max Planck Institute for Biology Tübingen in Germany. The participants with high-fever symptoms also tended to have greater gut inflammation than their peers.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
To investigate why, exactly, flagellin might influence fever, the researchers conducted a follow-up experiment in genetically engineered mice. They found that animals exposed to the fever-associated human bacteria showed a response equivalent to a fever in humans. This was particularly the case in those that could sense flagellin. Mice without flagellin receptors were less affected—indicating a direct link between flagellin and an immune system response.
On top of that, the levels of humans’ fever correlated with those of the equivalent reaction in mice, Ley says. “The worse the fever in the people, the more the temperature dropped in the mice,” she says. (Mice typically experience hypothermia as part of their immune response, which serves a similar function as a fever in humans.)
It’s still unclear why some people could have higher levels of flagellin in their guts than others. It may have something to do with diet: self-reported vegetarians tended to have lower flagellin levels, according to the study. But more research is needed to tease that out.
“It would make sense that, if you could tamp down the motility of the bacteria, we would predict that you wouldn’t react as strongly in terms of the fever,” Ley says. “But that’s all very much future research.”
Eventually, Ley hopes, the results could help fight this side effect of vaccines and, by extension, encourage higher vaccination rates.

Acciaierie d'Italia has announced a suspension of production in Taranto pending a ruling from Italy's Supreme Court of Cassation, with plants in Genoa and Novi Ligure also set to shut down temporarily by 15 November.
Workers at all former Ilva sites in Italy are set to go on strike on 12 October, unions have announced, following Thursday's meeting with the government at Palazza Chigo.
Meanwhile, production at the hot end of the Taranto steelworks was suspended on Friday. More than 2,000 workers in Italy remain at risk of losing their jobs.
Acciaierie d’Italia has announced plans to shut down operations at plants in Taranto, Genoa, and Novi Ligure.
The undersecretary to the prime minister's office, Alfredo Mantovano, stressed the need for an emergency decree that includes social protections for workers and provides for a wage-support scheme that would not be tied to the closure of operations but would instead help keep the business going.
The government is expected to submit it at the next council of ministers, scheduled for Tuesday.
Taranto
On Friday, all production at the hot end of the Taranto steelworks was suspended, in compliance with a ruling by the Milan Court of Appeal.
The facilities will remain on heated standby, operating at the minimum technical level required to keep them warm but without producing steel.
Acciaierie d’Italia confirmed the move in a note sent to the prefect, local authorities, and law enforcement.
The shutdown will remain in place until the Court of Cassation rules on the appeals lodged by Ilva and Acciaierie d’Italia on 20 October.
'Completely unacceptable'
The company has also announced that by "15 November" there will be a "temporary general shutdown" of the former Ilva plants in Genoa and Novi Ligure.
"The announcement of a lockout is completely unacceptable," said the mayors of Genoa and Novi Ligure, Silvia Salis and Rocchino Muliere.
"It is an untenable prospect for workers, for Genoa and Novi Ligure, and for our country’s entire steel industry," Salis warned.
For the President of the Liguria Region, Marco Bucci, and his Piedmont counterpart, Alberto Cirio, "the announced closure of the former Ilva plants in Cornigliano, Novi Ligure and Racconigi is extremely serious news, not only for Liguria and Piedmont, but for the entire Italian steel industry, which is strategic for the country’s industrial future."
The trade unions also describe the idea of closure as "unacceptable."
"The workers have shown a great sense of responsibility, and we must therefore ensure that the cost of decisions and mistakes – which are not the workers’ fault – is not passed on to all the workers at the former Ilva plants," said Michele de Palma, feneral secretary of Fiom-Cgil, who was present at the meeting at Palazzo Chigi.
According to the USB, a country’s industrial strategy "is not decided by the judiciary," with Sasha Colautti, a member of the national executive, insisting that the government’s powerlessness in the face of the courts must not become an excuse.
This situation could take a further turn for the worse if the blast furnaces at Taranto were also to be taken off heat before the Court of Cassation issues its ruling.
The permanent shutdown of the hot end would leave no possibility of a subsequent restart, marking the definitive end to production and rendering any decision by the Supreme Court null and void.
Undersecretary Mantovano has stated that the government is "assessing whether there is scope to avoid a complete shutdown so as not to cause irreparable damage to the plants," before focusing on green steel production using DRI plants (which do not use blast furnaces) and electric furnaces, provided this is part of a "credible industrial plan."

The Race Illusion: On the Reality of Racialization and the Myth of Race
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:47:00 UTC
19:47:00 KST

Is race real? Are there human races? In the contemporary debate about the metaphysics and ontology of race, the most common answer is yes. Most people are racial realists, but they disagree about whether race is defined biologically—by reference to ancestry, genetics, etc.—or socially—by reference to culture, politics, etc. Adam Hochman bucks the recent realist trend in the metaphysics of race. He argues that there are no human races. Instead, he defends a thoroughgoing, and formidable, anti-realist account of race that he calls reconstructionist anti-realism. In my view, Hochman has provided the most convincing case for racial anti-realism since the work of Kwame Anthony Appiah and Naomi Zack in the early 1990s. (This is no small accomplishment!) The book makes a case for racial anti-realism that should be taken seriously for years to come.
Hochman divides the book into two parts. In Part I, he argues against biological realism. In Part II, he argues against social realism and considers some consequences of his anti-realist account. I will summarize each part and offer a few critical observations.
In Part I of the book, Hochman defines, and argues against, increasingly sophisticated versions of the biological theory of race. In Chapter 1, he considers the traditional view that races are human populations, where a population is a group of individuals that occupy a certain area, have shared ancestry, and are likely to have shared descendants. Hochman notes several problems with this view, but I will focus on two. First, the populations view appears to change the subject; there are many human populations that we would not consider races. Second, the populations view makes races scientifically trivial; such a notion of race would not tell us anything interesting about human biological diversity. Overall, Hochman dispatches these traditional views before moving on to more serious competing philosophical views in Chapter 2.
There, he argues against the most robust contemporary biological theory of race—the genetic cluster theory of race as articulated by Quayshawn Spencer. Spencer argues that human races can have a scientifically legitimate biological basis if we think of them as genetic clusters. Specifically, we think of racial concepts as picking out genetic clusters. Against Spencer, Hochman argues that Spencer’s theory faces the same problems as traditional biological theories of race. For example, Hochman argues that Spencer’s theory changes the topic, as genetic clusters give rise to different races than the ones that ordinary people will recognize. Hochman also thinks the view trivializes the notion of race, given that there are many genetic clusters. In Chapter 3, Hochman discusses several more theories of race by major figures in this area—Joshua Glasgow, Michael Hardimon, and Philip Kitcher—and argues that these views fail for similar reasons.
Hochman’s discussion of biological theories of race is comprehensive, rigorous, and compelling. He truly attempts to confront every major view in the area, and he gives substantive, extensive arguments against each biological account. While anti-realists have argued against biological theorists in the past, this book tackles the biological theories that have been offered most recently. This matters because it is tempting to think that recent advances in biology count in favor of biological realism. Hochman’s point is that biological realism still fails as a metaphysical thesis, despite what advances in genetic sequencing and mapping there might be. One worry about Hochman’s arguments, however, is that they feel a bit too familiar. While Hochman does not simply repeat existing arguments, it is true that the kinds of arguments he deploys against the biological theorist are well known. This is not to say that his arguments are unimportant. It is only to say that his arguments may not persuade people who are broadly familiar with the existing literature.
In Part II of the book, Hochman argues against social realism about race. On this view, racial kinds are social kinds, united by a common culture, recognition, or social structure. In Chapter 4, Hochman’s main issue with social theories of race is that they have what he calls an inflation problem. If we define race by reference to the social world, then we may end up inflating the concept of race. The clearest example of this is the distinction between race and ethnicity. The idea of an ethnic group includes factors surrounding shared ancestry and appearance, on the one hand, and culture, on the other. If races are essentially social, however, ethnic groups will count as racial groups because they include elements of culture and social recognition. Hochman criticizes Ásta’s conferralist account of race for different reasons. Ásta argues that we confer racial properties onto individuals in contexts.[1] Hochman thinks this kind of view makes racial properties come too easily. To use his example: the fact that we perceive someone as a witch does not make them a witch. Similarly, thinking that races are real should not make it so. Hochman discusses other social realist accounts of race, including Chike Jeffers’s cultural account of race and phenomenological approaches to race.
Hochman’s case against social realism was less persuasive to me than his criticisms of biological realism. This is because his arguments seemed to be against social constructionism, in general, not specifically against social constructionism in the metaphysics of race. The clearest example of this is his criticism of Ásta’s conferralist theory. According to conferralism, we socially construct the world by socially conferring properties onto groups and individuals. Hochman criticizes conferralism because it seems to rule out the possibility of major error about the social world; surely the world does not have whatever properties we think it does. This is a fair critique, but (a) it is not unique to the metaphysics of race, and (b) there are more general theories of social construction—ones that appeal to essences, grounding, anchoring, truthmaking, and so on—that respond to it.[2]
There are other signs that Hochman has issues with social constructionism, more generally. He thinks that the notion of social construction is radically ambiguous, to the point of “meaningless” (95). This too is a fair criticism, but it also seems like a more general point. Or at least, I wanted to see more argument for these claims. His critique of biological realism is almost twice as long as the critique of social realism, but, as far as I can tell, social realism is the most dominant position within social ontology.
Chapters 1-4 offer arguments against biological and social realist theories of race. Hochman considers, and rejects, the possibility of a purely negative metaphysical project. He calls unreconstructed anti-realism the view that races do not exist, and we do not need an alternative to race concepts. This view seems straightforward for anti-realists; if there are no races, then there is nothing further we need to explain. Hochman rejects this view because he thinks it is both metaphysically incomplete and “dangerous” (137).
The view is incomplete because it overlooks a non-trivial fact about the metaphysics of race: namely, that racialized groups and racialization exist. The view is dangerous because it leaves us without the resources to identify racism and historical racial injustices. The unreconstructed anti-realist says there are no races. But if there are no races, how do we explain interpersonal and institutional racism? Hochman thinks anti-realism is more plausible if we have good answers to such questions.
To this end, he defends reconstructionist anti-realism, which says that we should reform our understanding of groups that are believed to constitute races. Specifically, instead of talking about races, we would be better off talking about racialized groups and racialization. Hochman defines racialization as the process by which a group comes to be understood as a biological race. Racialized groups are the products of racialization. Hochman then gives a brief account of the advantages of his reconstructionist picture. First, he notes that the concept of racialization, unlike the concept of race, is a process concept; we must think of racialization as something that is done to us by others, while race is typically understood as who we are, biologically or socially. Second, he argues that the appeal to racialization would also be more advantageous when thinking about biomedical contexts. Race realists tend to attribute certain differences in the health of populations to race. The problem is that this kind of attribution can be dangerous, as people tend to think of race as genetic. If we talk about disparate health impacts in terms of racialized groups and racialization, it is harder to make this kind of mistake.
I found the discussion of racialization and racialized groups informative and fruitful. The chapter was informative because it explains how the anti-realist seeks to fill the explanatory gap that they are usually accused of being unable to fill. (“If there are no races, how could there be racism?”) It is fruitful because it asks new, and probably more interesting, questions within the metaphysics of race. For example, Hochman thinks we need a concept of racialization, but we should not bother with a theory of racialization. Insofar as I understand the dialectic, I disagree. Metaphysicians need theories of racialization because racialization often seems more explanatory than race.[3] Independently of who is right about this matter, it seems to be a point of disagreement that pushes the metaphysics of race toward new topics. This is a good thing.
I was also particularly impressed with the way that Hochman integrated the metaphysics of race with normative concerns about racism and racial injustice. In (what I call) critical social ontology, one does metaphysics with an eye toward critiquing or addressing social injustice.[4] Of course, critical social ontology has a danger of being done poorly; either we confuse metaphysics and politics, or we do both badly. Hochman’s case for reconstructionist anti-realism is clear about the distinction between metaphysics and value theory; it is metaphysically rigorous, and the recommendations seem practically sensible. It is hard to balance normative matters and social metaphysics, but Hochman succeeds in this task.
Adam Hochman’s The Race Illusion does not settle the debate on racial realism. (In philosophy, debates are never settled!) However, it does constitute the definitive case for racial anti-realism. If you are serious about the metaphysics of race, you should read this book.
REFERENCES
Ásta. Categories We Live By: The Construction of Sex, Gender, Race, and Other Social Categories. Studies in Feminist Philosophy. Oxford University Press, 2018.
Ásta. “Critical Social Metaphysics: Metaphysics for Liberation and Social Science and Theory.” Journal of Social Ontology 11, no. 1 (2025): 264–85.
Epstein, Brian. The Ant Trap: Rebuilding the Foundations of the Social Sciences. Oxford Studies in Philosophy of Science. Oxford University Press, 2015.
Griffith, Aaron M. “Social Construction and Grounding.” Philosophy and Phenomenological Research 97, no. 2 (2018): 393–409.
Passinsky, Asya. “Norm and Object: A Normative Hylomorphic Theory of Social Objects.” Philosopher’s Imprint 21, no. 25 (2021).
Richardson, Kevin. “Critical Social Ontology.” Synthese 201, no. 6 (2023): 204.
Richardson, Kevin. “The Spatial Theory of Race.” Philosophia, ahead of print, April 20, 2026. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11406-026-00991-5.

[2] For example, see Epstein (2015), Griffith (2018), and Passinsky (2021).

German residential construction prices rise 5.5%, fastest pace in 3 years
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:46:01 UTC
19:46:01 KST

Mucahithan Avcioglu
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Residential construction prices in Germany rose 5.5% year on year in August, their fastest increase in three years, according to official figures released Friday.
The increase accelerated from 5% in May, while prices rose 1% over the three-month period, the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis) said.
The figures cover construction work on conventionally built residential buildings and include value-added tax.
Prices for structural work increased 5.4% from a year earlier, led by roofing, which rose 7.6%, and carpentry and timber construction, up 7.2%.
Concrete and masonry work, which account for the largest shares of structural work and the overall residential construction price index, became 4.3% and 4.2% more expensive, respectively.
Earthworks prices increased 6.1%.
Interior finishing costs rose 5.7% year on year, with electrical, security and information technology systems recording a 7.2% increase.
Prices for external thermal insulation systems climbed 5.7%, while heating and central hot-water systems, including heat pumps, rose 5.2%. Metalwork prices increased 5%.
Price increases also extended to maintenance and nonresidential construction.
Maintenance work on residential buildings, excluding cosmetic repairs, cost 6% more than a year earlier.
Prices for new office buildings rose 5.7%, while commercial building construction costs increased 5.5%.
Road construction recorded a sharper annual increase of 6.9%.

Heathrow’s third runway is a bottomless money pit. Stop it now | Simon Jenkins
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:45:25 UTC
19:45:25 KST

Infrastructure sends politicians berserk. Propose more money for the health service or reopening youth clubs and frowns break out all round. Can we afford it? But shout infrastructure and cheers go up. The word suggests glamour, chest-beating and “growth”. Reason flies out of the window.
The saga of Heathrow’s third runway beggars belief. A foreign-owned private company wants to make more money out of its cramped west London investment. The airlines are sceptical and passengers will have to pay surcharges higher than any in Europe. Meanwhile fields lie empty round its rival, Gatwick, and capacity at London’s third airport, Stansted, is underused.
The third runway is a nightmare. The official price tag is now a staggering £49bn but the overall budget for Heathrow’s expansion and operating expenditure could soar beyond £100bn. An unknown proportion of this will fall on the taxpayer. The proposal has been debated for 20 years and the opening constantly postponed. A date of 2035 has now become 2039. I would not take bets on 2045.
Sixty years ago, the British government agreed it was totally inappropriate for crowded and polluted Heathrow to expand in densely populated west London. Nor could an expanded Gatwick meet demand. The debate was over where to locate a new third airport. Sites in the Thames estuary and at Cublington and Stansted were researched. Stansted won. It already had an RAF base and it would service the expected growth in demand from London’s growing eastern reaches. Stansted opened in 1991.
The Tories privatised London’s airports. This turned what should have been a planned expansion into a battleground of feuding rivals. Each airport became a matter not of orderly growth but of quick profits, self-serving airline slots and a shifting army of amateur officials. Commissions came and went, in the grip of overpaid lobbyists. A Heathrow runway proposed by businessman Surinder Arora within the existing airport curtilage was brushed aside as insufficiently bold. As for Stansted, it was taken over by Manchester airport and is now hardly mentioned as an alternative to a third runway.
Airport public relations endlessly suggests it is about “business” and therefore relevant to “growth”, as if it were part of Andy Burnham’s re-industrialisation of Britain. Heathrow claims its new runway will create 100,000 jobs. But fewer than 15% of air travellers claim to be “on business”, and whatever happened to video conferencing reducing the need for intensive business air travel? As for Heathrow’s claim to be Britain’s leading cargo airport – “a quarter of all UK trade by value” – that is based, ludicrously, on the value of the gold ingots that form roughly 60% of the goods it transports. What banks shifting bullion has to do with growth is unclear.
Heathrow now has eerie echoes of HS2. Even its upper cost limit of £100bn is much the same. Both are plagued by extravagant planning horizons and consultancy-driven budgets in which each contractor has a vested interest in cost inflation. A third similar project is Hinkley Point nuclear power station, its cost currently rising through £50bn. Both the railway and the power station have been savaged by the National Audit Office. These projects are widely considered political white elephants and years from completion. Few dare say so. Meanwhile we should note that a new general hospital costs £1bn, as would rebuilding 50 secondary schools.
Stupefying sums are here being channelled into London and the south of England. That they have been born of the age of Boris Johnson’s “levelling up” and Burnham’s tilt to the north is bizarre. This week, conference politicians have cited budgets with endless savings: half a million off student exchanges here, a billion off quangos there. Yet no one mentioned that every year for the next decade John Healey’s Treasury will blow about £7bn just to relieve overcrowding on trains from London to Birmingham. This is almost 70% of his total rail investment.
The fact is that big infrastructure is monumental and sexy. No one boasts about building a care home, rather a fancy train or a nuclear power plant. One of Parkinson’s laws states that, while tiny items of corporate spending are debated for hours, big ones go through on the nod. They are too big to check and easy to promote.
It is absurd for the government to spend the next two decades upheaving Heathrow and tearing apart the M4 corridor for the profit of a band of foreign investors, when a simple alternative lies in growing Gatwick and Stansted. This whole debate is about tourism, and tourists can surely suffer the mild inconvenience of using the other two venues, as was intended half a century ago.
The rest of us – politicians not least – should realise that this is serious money. There are serious uses to which it should be put.
- Simon Jenkins is a Guardian columnist

Palestinians set to delay legislative elections due to worsening conditions, letter says

Palestinians set to delay legislative elections due to worsening conditions, letter says
PARIS, Oct 9 - Palestinian Vice President Hussein Al Sheikh has informed France that a Palestinian legislative election planned for November 28 will be postponed, possibly until September 2027, because of worsening conditions throughout the Palestinian territories, according to a letter seen by Reuters.
"The assessment concluded that the anticipated political, security and economic conditions, on which the scheduling of the legislative elections for 28 November 2026 was based, have not materialized," said the letter, which was addressed to French Foreign Minister Jean-Noel Barrot and dated October 8.
It added that "holding them under the current circumstances faces fundamental obstacles affecting their inclusiveness, freedom of participation and the integrity of the electoral process."
There had been serious doubts that the Palestinian Authority vote would go ahead in late November. The Palestinians have not held legislative or presidential elections since 2005-06, after which Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas' rival, the Islamist group Hamas, seized control of Gaza, ousting his loyalists.
Some officials within Abbas' Fatah party have demanded dialogue with Hamas and other factions to agree on a common national vision before proceeding with a vote. Others have cited obstructions to ballot boxes, election papers and ink entering Gaza, which they say would make voting impossible.
PALESTINIAN OFFICIALS SAY THEY EXPECTED US ACTION
The letter said Palestinian officials had expected conditions to improve through the implementation of US President Donald Trump's peace initiative and a UN Security Council resolution, including the deployment of international forces and Palestinian police in Gaza, the disarmament of Hamas and the withdrawal of Israeli troops.
It said the Palestinians had also anticipated US efforts to prevent further annexation of Palestinian territory in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, curb settler violence and secure the release of nearly $7 billion in Palestinian funds withheld by Israel.
"However, these steps, understandings and promises have not materialized. Rather, conditions have worsened throughout the Palestinian territory," the letter said, outlining in detail security issues in Gaza and the West Bank.
Based on their assessment, Palestinian officials recommended to Abbas "that the date of the legislative elections be adjusted by several months, and that dialogue continue to prepare the internal conditions", the letter said.
It added that Abbas had been advised to issue a decree adjusting the date for holding elections to the first half of September 2027.
Abbas, elected president of the PA in 2005, had reaffirmed plans to hold the elections during a speech to the United Nations on September 24.
FRANCE SAID ELECTIONS WERE ESSENTIAL
The letter was addressed to France after it recognised a Palestinian state in September 2025. As part of that decision France had urged that the planned legislative and presidential elections proceed, a written commitment that Abbas had made to President Emmanuel Macron and Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman.
Speaking to reporters on Thursday, France's foreign ministry spokesperson Pascal Confavreux said it was essential for the elections to take place and hailed the launch of an EU mission to observe the elections.
"These elections will enable the Palestinian leadership to champion its people's legitimate aspirations with renewed legitimacy, while preserving the two-state solution," he said.
In the more than two decades since Abbas was elected as the successor to Fatah founder Yasser Arafat, the PA's public standing has sunk among Palestinians, who have grown to view it as ineffective and corrupt.
In 2007, the PA was driven out of the Gaza Strip by Hamas militants, who had won an election there on an anti-corruption platform. Abbas has ruled by decree since his mandate expired in 2009.
A peace process meant to lead to the creation of a Palestinian state in the West Bank, Gaza and East Jerusalem collapsed in 2014, and expanding Israeli settlements have since carved up areas once slated for eventual Palestinian control. REUTERS

EU faces potential gas shortage as winter approaches: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:43:16 UTC
19:43:16 KST

Melike Pala
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
The European Union could face a natural gas shortfall of up to 14 billion cubic meters this winter, equivalent to around 7% of the bloc's demand, amid depleted storage levels and disruptions to global energy supplies, according to energy reports.
A report by the US-based Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), shared with Politico on Friday, warned that the EU's gas reserves have fallen to just above 70%, their lowest level for this time of year since records began in 2011.
The potential deficit could affect energy supplies equivalent to the consumption of 10 million to 12 million European households, raising concerns over higher electricity bills and possible energy-saving measures.
High prices have encouraged traders to sell gas during the summer rather than replenish storage facilities ahead of winter, leaving the bloc with a reduced buffer against supply disruptions.
The findings are also reflected in the 2026-2027 winter supply outlook published by the European Network of Transmission System Operators for Gas (ENTSOG).
The report warned that storage levels could fall to as low as 11% under a cold-winter scenario if liquefied natural gas (LNG) imports are limited or remain at optimal levels.
To restore reserves to 30% by the end of winter, the EU could face a situation in which gas consumption equivalent to 7% of demand would have to be curtailed or supplies withheld from consumers, according to ENTSOG.
The EU's planned ban on long-term contracts for Russian LNG, due to take effect in January, is expected to reduce gas imports by a further 7 billion cubic meters, according to the IEEFA report.
Meanwhile, winter gas demand has risen over the past two years, while imports have remained largely flat, increasing the bloc’s dependence on stored supplies.
The EU could turn to additional LNG imports, particularly from the US, to offset potential supply losses.
However, replacing the missing volumes at current prices would cost an additional €3 billion, representing a 12% increase compared with the cost of the same volumes last year, according to IEEFA.

Forgotten trail camera yields 9 months of wildlife images
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Forgotten trail camera yields 9 months of wildlife images
A farmer in South Estonia who forgot about a trail camera he had set up found a wealth of nature photo on it once he retrieved it.
Tarvo Siilaberg, a Põlva County farmer, left the trail cam in a forest earlier this year and it soon passed from his mind. But once he remembered and located it, he found the fully working camera had been "visited" by moose, deer, cranes and other wildlife — including a bear.
The camera's battery and systems were still running, and its memory had not filled up either.
"Part of it was simple absent-mindedness. We have quite a few camera traps for animals and one ended up in a spot I couldn't remember for a long time," said Siilaberg, owner of Raja Farm.
When he went looking for the camera in the forest, he found it hard to spot because of its nature as a trail cam — well camouflaged.
Some of the visitors captured on the footage were more surprising than others.
"We already knew that a moose trail passes through our land, which is why we put the camera at the edge of the bog forest," Siilaberg explained.
"The camera was up at the edge of the forest, where the ditch bank meets the meadow — we happened to place it right at an animal crossroads," he said. "Deer appear in front of the trail camera about as often as you'd see a pigeon in the city."
One of the last images the camera captured before it was retrieved was also one of the most impressive: a bear.
"That was also the first photo I saw when I took the camera down from the tree. Then I knew there was something very good here," said Siilaberg, whose farm is in Kanassaare village in Põlva municipality.
"The picture of the cranes is my favorite," he said. "I hope to forget my camera in the forest again soon — then good things will start happening, if a person keeps their hands away. The result is definitely worth it."
Of the animals he had hoped to see, Siilaberg said he had wanted footage of a lynx, but there wasn't any.

The Lublin District Prosecutor’s Office reported the findings.
An official decision lists 24 localities, including Chojny, Krzywowierzba-Kolonia, Cześniki, and Wyhalew.
However, the names of three other locations where drone debris was found have not been disclosed because the information is classified.
Some of the drones were found several dozen kilometers from Warsaw.
The drones crashed because they ran completely out of fuel during their long flights.
As previously reported, the Polish prosecutor’s office closed its investigation into the mass violation of the country’s airspace by Russian drones because it was unable to identify the individuals directly responsible.
Most of the case files, including the reasoning behind the decision to close the investigation, are classified. As a result, the prosecutor’s office has not publicly disclosed details about the identified flight paths, the methods used to control individual drones, or which specific drones were shot down by Polish and allied forces.
However, closing the investigation because the individuals directly responsible could not be identified does not mean that Polish authorities are denying the Russian origin of the drones.
A separate part of the investigation examined the actions of Polish military personnel during the interception of the drones. The prosecutor’s office concluded that the military acted within their authority and had legal grounds to open fire to destroy the aerial targets.
SIM cards issued by Polish mobile operators were also found in some of the Russian Gerbera drones that violated Polish airspace.
However, the prosecutor’s office has not disclosed whether the SIM cards were stolen or obtained illegally.

Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:40:36 UTC
19:40:36 KST

Is Trump signalling a return to war with Iran after the midterms?
US media reports suggest he may be weighing strikes before the vote but the president has ruled that out.
United States President Donald Trump has said that he does not intend to bomb Iran again until the November midterm elections, even though several US media outlets have reported that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to relaunch attacks before that vote.
Trump has been accused of misdirection on the issue in the past. The US launched its initial attacks on Iran on February 28, as talks with Iran were ongoing and despite Trump saying just the day before that he had not made any decision. One year previously, the US struck Iran towards the end of Israel’s June 2025 12-day war, despite Trump saying he would announce a decision about attacks “in two weeks”.
Still, striking Iran ahead of the midterm elections would be risky for the administration as the war remains deeply unpopular with Americans.
Resuming the war afterwards may have less of a negative impact on Trump, who is not eligible to run for another term as US president anyway.
Here’s what we know about Trump’s plans.
What has been reported by US media?
In the past two days, The New York Times, The Wall Street Journal and other publications have reported claims by unnamed officials that the Pentagon has drawn up plans to attack Iran before the midterms, if authorised to do so.
On Wednesday, US publication Axios cited US and Israeli officials saying the Pentagon has instructed US Central Command (CENTCOM) to prepare for imminent major combat operations. The Atlantic also reported along similar lines.
What has Trump said?
On Thursday, Trump posted on his Truth Social media platform that he will not order a resumption of strikes on Iran before November 3, when the US midterm elections will be held.
“I want to make it clear to everybody that, while Iran is in very bad condition…we will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the Midterm Elections to be held in the United States on November 3rd,” he said.
The president added that the US is presently “having productive discussions” with the Iranian side. However, that was also the case on February 28, the day the US and Israel first struck Iran, triggering the war.
Trump did not make any reference to preparing for potential military operations, nor did he provide more details on the state of talks.
Why might Trump be hesitant about resuming bombing before the midterms?
Trump and Republicans are worried about a voter backlash against the war at the polls. The US war on Iran is intensely unpopular domestically as Americans have had to grapple with surging prices of gas, food and other basic commodities because of the crisis in the Middle East.
Since the start of the war, surveys have shown that large numbers of Americans did not approve of striking Iran.
Now, about 65 percent of Americans say they “disapprove” of the way in which Trump has handled the Iran war overall, according to a Pew Research Center poll released on Thursday. Trump stated at the start of the war that it would go on for just a few weeks, however, it is now into its eighth month.
According to Pew, most Americans now believe the war will continue for at least another year. Even Republican or more conservative-leaning voters are growing more negative about the war, its poll found.
The conflict has also severely affected Trump’s personal ratings and eroded support for Republicans. A Reuters/Ipsos poll on Thursday found that only 30 percent of his supporters were enthusiastic about voting in the midterms, compared with 48 percent of Democratic voters.
About 13 percent of those who voted for Trump in 2024 say they are not sure who to vote for in the congressional elections.
Delaying attacks until after the elections could potentially shield Republican candidates from voter backlash, analysts say.
While analysts say Trump will see a good performance at the polls as approval for renewed strikes, a Republican defeat at the polls could equally further incentivise him to hit Iran again as he will calculate that he has little to lose at that point.
While that could further affect Trump’s ratings, the president is not eligible to run in the next presidential election in any case.
Will the US restart the war after the midterms?
In recent weeks, the US president has threatened to “end” the war with force after the elections as talks with Iran have dragged on.
At a Republican convention in September, he accused Iran of trying to affect the outcome of the midterms and said that conflict “is going to end immediately after the elections”.
In an interview with Time magazine two weeks ago, he also said it would be “possible” to ramp up bombing in Iran after the elections, but declined to elaborate. Analysts say his comments were designed to calm voters, while at the same time warning Iran of potential aggression after the vote.
Last week, the US military dispatched about 7,000 sailors and 2,000 Marines aboard several ships now sailing to the Middle East amid threats of new attacks from Trump. The vessel formation included the USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group.
The deployment increases the number of US troops in the region to 20,000, alongside hundreds of aircraft and at least three carrier strike groups.
In the past, US troop build-up in the Middle East and the Caribbean has subsequently resulted in military action.
In June, Washington and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement that quickly broke down over control of the Strait of Hormuz.
Trump has repeatedly said that the US has the upper hand in the strait, citing more oil exports and Iran’s weakened economy. He has also voiced aversion to a deal with Tehran over management of Hormuz, but said he might consider it because “they’re willing to offer us anything to stop”.
Washington rejected a recent proposal from Iran to reopen the strait based on certain conditions it wants the US to meet, including the lifting of sanctions, unfreezing Iranian assets and guaranteeing an end to attacks. Last week, Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Iran was considering a counterproposal from the US.

Excavations resume at ancient Tyana Roman Baths in Türkiye after 20-year hiatus
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:39:56 UTC
19:39:56 KST

Excavations resume at ancient Tyana Roman Baths in Türkiye after 20-year hiatus
Archaeologists in Nigde aim to uncover earlier phases of AD 213 complex and identify associated structures, including possible sports and education facilities
Ahmet Demircan and Gizem Nisa Demir
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
NIGDE, Türkiye / ISTANBUL
Excavations have resumed at the Roman Baths in the ancient city of Tyana, located in the town of Kemerhisar in the Bor district of Türkiye’s central Nigde province, after a 20-year hiatus.
The work, conducted under the Turkish Culture and Tourism Ministry’s Heritage for the Future Project, aims to identify earlier phases of the baths and uncover associated structures, such as a palaestra (an exercise area or courtyard) or a gymnasium (a center for physical and intellectual education).
Archaeologists also hope to uncover evidence of cultural activity dating to well before Roman rule.
Numerous remains and artifacts
Osman Doganay, head of the Tyana Excavation Team and a professor in the Department of Archaeology at Aksaray University’s Faculty of Arts and Sciences, told Anadolu that excavations at the Roman Baths had resumed after a two-decade hiatus.
Doganay noted that at least two other baths are believed to exist in the ancient city beyond the complex currently being excavated, adding that efforts to locate them would begin.
Tyana was a major metropolitan center in Cappadocia during the Roman period, and the baths under excavation were built by Emperor Caracalla in AD 213, he said.
"Changes were also made to the structure of these baths during the reigns of emperors who succeeded Caracalla. We can confirm this with certainty," Doganay said.
Excavations at the baths began in 2002 and continued for four years, uncovering numerous remains and artifacts. Researchers have since established the structure’s layout and confirmed that it was a public bathhouse, he said.
Located on the southern slopes of Tyana Mound, the baths were positioned to receive the greatest amount of heat, Doganay said.
He added that archaeologists believe the complex received a significant portion of the water carried by aqueducts from the Roman Pool, citing water pipes discovered during excavations between the pool and the baths.
Bronze Age layer discovered beneath baths
Doganay said the primary objective of the current excavation season was to identify earlier phases of the bath complex. Much of the work this year has focused on clearing layers of rubble and debris from the site.
Test excavations extending nearly 2 meters below the surface revealed that the baths had been built over a Bronze Age layer, he said.
"In our upcoming work, we will uncover all the sections of the baths and determine whether structures associated with sporting activities, such as a palaestra and a gymnasium, are present.
"At the same time, we expect to find important evidence of the city's cultural heritage dating to periods long before the Roman era," Doganay said.
He added that measures were being taken during the excavations to protect the structure.
The team also hopes to make the historic Roman Baths a new regional tourist attraction.
"There is no comparable bath complex of this kind in the Cappadocia region. As part of our efforts to promote Tyana as a destination for tourism and contribute to the regional economy, we are working to include the Roman Baths in visitor routes through the ancient city and establish the complex as a destination in its own right," Doganay said.

Ex-OpenAI staff say they were fired for raising safety concerns
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:39:07 UTC
19:39:07 KST

Ex-OpenAI staff say they were fired for raising safety concerns
Three former researchers pen open letter warning of ‘chilling’ effect on company culture.
Three former OpenAI employees say they have been fired due to their efforts to ensure the safety of artificial intelligence.
Safety researchers Mikita Balesni, Tomek Korbak and Jasmine Wang levelled the accusations on Thursday after their dismissals last week. The trio warned of a “chilling” effect on other staff concerned about the frontier technology’s risks.
OpenAI said they were let go due to misconduct involving the mishandling of company information.
“I believe we were fired for prioritizing safety over the near-term interests of OpenAI as a corporation,” Balesni said in a post on X.
Korbak voiced a similar sentiment, expressing his belief that he had been terminated for raising concerns that OpenAI was “losing the ability to monitor what AI agents think, one of our best tools for catching when they misbehave”.
In an open letter published in tandem with their social media posts, Balesni, Korbak and Wang expressed concerns that their dismissal would make their former colleagues “afraid to speak and operate in ways that, until last week, were an integral part of working at OpenAI”.
“We could raise safety concerns and disagree openly, and were encouraged to draw on the expertise of independent safety organizations,” they said in the letter. “This is part of what made OpenAI special, and why we are immensely proud to have been part of the team.”
The three added that “if the people closest to the risks can no longer work in high-trust, high-bandwidth ways with each other and with third parties”, then AI could not be developed safely.
“It is that culture we are writing to defend,” they stated.
The trio denied violating company policy, saying any engagement with external safety experts had been in line with the mandate of their roles.
“Given the significant safety concerns surrounding the development of AI, employees must not be left working in an environment where fear and unclear rules stymie AI safety work and weaken third-party accountability,” they said.
“Terminations such as ours, executed and communicated so abruptly, are chilling the open culture OpenAI has prized in the past.”
In a statement, OpenAI said it had uncovered “a significant breach of trust” by the former researchers that went beyond what was described in their letter and said it stood behind the decision to fire them.
“We want to be very clear that these decisions were not about raising safety concerns or speaking out,” the San Francisco-based company said.
“Safety and research debates happen every day at OpenAI, often spirited and highly critical. We actively encourage these discussions and consider them essential to making the right decisions. We cannot do the work in front of us without a high degree of trust. We will continue to be extremely forgiving of our team making good-faith mistakes.”
OpenAI added that it was saddened by the outcome.
“We appreciated Jasmine, Mikita, and Tomek’s contributions to AI safety at OpenAI and their willingness to speak up and challenge ideas,” the company said.
“We championed their voices, supported their work, and placed enormous trust in them. These decisions were not about them raising safety concerns. We have always encouraged that and always will.”
The ex-employees’ intervention comes as OpenAI and other AI companies are at the centre of intense debate about how to ensure the rapidly evolving technology does not expose humanity to catastrophic harm.
The risk of cutting-edge AI models escaping human control has been in the spotlight since July when it emerged that autonomous agents generated by OpenAI had hacked the software start-up Hugging Face.
OpenAI and its chief rival, Anthropic, have urged the international community to work together on a coordinated slowdown in AI development.
However, that suggestion has been rebuffed by the two leading AI powers, the United States and China.
Last month, OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, Meta, SpaceXAI and Nvidia endorsed a voluntary accord calling for stronger internal safeguards and the engagement of external auditors to better manage safety risks.
The accord, announced by US President Donald Trump, drew a mixed response from AI safety advocates, many of whom criticised its nonbinding nature.
OpenAI has announced a number of steps to mitigate risks in the absence of formal regulation, including scrapping the planned release of its latest-generation model, GPT-6.1 Astra.
The ChatGPT creator said it decided not to go ahead with the release after its model failed to meet company standards for acting in accordance with human wishes.

Estonian Border Guard: Migration pressure to rise in coming weeks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:36:35 UTC
19:36:35 KST

Egert Belitšev, head of the Estonian Police and Border Guard Board (PPA), has indicated that migration pressure could rise sharply in the coming weeks as migrants attempt to leave Belarus before winter sets in, reports ERR News.
Belitšev explained that Russia has deliberately relaxed entry requirements and increased the number of flights from countries such as Ethiopia. Its ally, Belarus, then facilitates the migrants' movement toward Europe. The journey is organized right up to the European Union borders and can cost up to 10,000 euros per person.
While Estonia does not share a border with Belarus, Latvia does. Almost all of the 200 migrants detained in Estonia since mid-summer entered the country via Latvia. Estonia has a population of 1.3 million, whereas Ethiopia is home to around 130 million people and hosts nearly a million refugees from neighboring countries. 
Belitšev noted that there are six direct flights weekly between Ethiopia and Moscow, and no Russian visa is required. 
The passengers' goal is to reach Europe. He emphasized that Russia has deliberately relaxed entry requirements and increased the number of flights.
People travel by bus from Moscow to Belarus. Authorities make no attempt to stop them—quite the opposite; they help them reach the border, and Russia uses Belarus to exert pressure on Europe. Belitšev asked rhetorically whether this stems from dependence on Russia or the notion that acting on the "master's" orders will bring success and prosperity, adding that this is a path Belarus has consciously chosen.
The illegal transport of people is a form of organized crime; it is highly lucrative, and Russian and Belarusian authorities take a share of the profits. Belitšev noted that for those using the route through Belarus to reach Europe, the process is not as simple as buying a ticket to Moscow and proceeding on one's own; the movement is orchestrated by criminal organizations.
On the 6th of October, reports emerged that the PPA had caught migrant smugglers in the act. Belitšev pointed out that, metaphorically speaking, it is impossible to halt these criminal activities without "cutting off the heads." Currently, the primary tactic is to apprehend migrant smugglers, arrest them, and bring them before the court as quickly as possible. Whenever possible, financial gains are confiscated. In mid-September, Estonia sentenced a migrant smuggler to seven months in prison and imposed a six-year ban on entry into Schengen Area countries.
The PPA is under significant pressure yet continues its work; however, according to Belitšev, migration pressure also complicates the operations of other institutions. Many apprehended migrants claim to be minors in an attempt to exploit the EU's child protection system. This creates challenges for the local governments responsible for providing guardianship. First-instance administrative courts are also unaccustomed to such a volume of migration-related cases. Belitšev noted that the situation could become more difficult in winter, when migration pressure typically subsides; few people wish to remain in Belarus once temperatures drop below freezing.

EU countries agree to shift oversight of major financial markets to European authority ESMA
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:36:01 UTC
19:36:01 KST

EU countries struck a deal on Friday to give the EU’s financial markets watchdog more powers, aiming to make cross-border investment easier and help businesses raise more money across the bloc.
EU countries have agreed on a package to strengthen the bloc’s financial markets watchdog at a meeting of finance ministers in Luxembourg on Friday.
The Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP) would give the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) direct oversight of major market operators currently supervised by national authorities.
While some rules are harmonised across the EU, differences in implementation, supervision and enforcement have contributed to fragmentation in financial markets.
The Irish presidency said the package aims to make it easier for savings and investments to flow across borders, helping companies access finance and giving households more opportunities to earn returns on their savings.
The package would give ESMA direct oversight of major trading venues, clearing houses and bodies that handle securities settlement, as well as crypto-asset service providers. It would also create a full-time, independent executive board within the watchdog.
Market operators could opt into a new framework for operating across the EU. The reforms would make national supervision more consistent and update rules on trading, completing transactions, managing investments and using blockchain technology.
However, some trading venues run by Deutsche Börse, which operates the Frankfurt stock exchange, may remain outside ESMA’s direct supervision.
Euronews previously learnt that Germany had secured an exemption for Deutsche Börse’s domestically focused trading venues, leaving a key part of the system under regional German supervision. The current announcement did not give details on this matter.
Dutch Finance Minister Eelco Heinen welcomed the agreement, saying: "Major step forward today in advancing the Capital Markets Union. We made more progress in 10 months than in 10 years.
This marks an important milestone in the Savings and Investments Union (SIU), which aims to channel more of Europeans' savings into investments that support the economy.
Supporters of more integrated capital markets argue that they would lower costs and improve access to funding for companies, while giving savers and investors more investment options.

Explainer: What is the International Criminal Court?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:35:58 UTC
19:35:58 KST

Explainer: What is the International Criminal Court?
THE HAGUE - South African judge Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, who was awarded the Nobel peace prize on Oct 9, has been a judge on several international courts, including the International Criminal Court (ICC).
Here are some facts about this court:
When was the ICC set up and why?
The court was established in 2002 to prosecute individuals for war crimes, crimes against humanity, genocide and the crime of aggression when member states are unwilling or unable to do so themselves.
It can prosecute crimes committed by nationals of member states or on the territory of member states by other actors. It has 125 member states.
The court's budget for 2026 is about €196 million (S$280 million)
What is the ICC investigating?
The ICC is conducting investigations in the Palestinian territories, Ukraine, African states such as Sudan, Uganda and Democratic Republic of Congo, Venezuela, Myanmar and the Philippines.
It says there have been 34 cases before the court, some with more than one defendant. ICC judges have issued 68 arrest warrants.
Who is on the court’s arrest list?
Notable ICC suspects are Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, accused of being criminally responsible for acts including murder, persecution and using starvation as a weapon of war in the Gaza conflict, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, accused of the war crime of illegally deporting hundreds of children from Ukraine.
Israel and Russia, neither a member of the court, have repeatedly denied committing atrocities in Gaza and Ukraine respectively and have argued that the ICC has no jurisdiction over them.
When it issued the warrant for Netanyahu, the ICC also issued a warrant for Hamas military commander Mohammed Deif, whose death was confirmed after the warrant was issued.
The court has also issued arrest warrants for two senior Afghan Taliban leaders, accusing them of persecuting women, an allegation that the Taliban reject.
Prosecutors have requested warrants for Myanmar’s military leader Min Aung Hlaing for crimes against humanity in the alleged persecution of the Rohingya, a mainly Muslim minority. The outcome of that request has not been made public.
What trials are pending?
Former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte is due to go on trial on Nov 30 to face charges of murder and attempted murder as crimes against humanity related to his war on drugs, accusations he denies.
A Libyan accused of overseeing a notorious prison is also awaiting trial.
Why does the US oppose the court?
While a US delegation was present for the negotiations that produced the court’s founding Rome Statute in 1998, it never became a member and always opposed ICC jurisdiction over US nationals.
In 2002, Washington even adopted a Bill nicknamed the Hague Invasion Act, which authorises the president to use “all means necessary” to ensure the release of any US citizen or US ally held by the ICC.
In the years that followed, the US supported some ICC investigations, notably into atrocities in Darfur and Uganda, but remained firmly opposed to the court looking into alleged crimes by US troops on the territory of ICC member states.
During the first Trump administration, in 2020, Washington imposed sanctions on the court’s then-chief prosecutor and another official over an investigation into whether American forces had committed war crimes in Afghanistan. That ban was lifted by the Biden administration a year later.
In early 2025, after the ICC announced arrest warrants for US ally Netanyahu and his former defence minister Yoav Gallant, Trump authorised economic and travel sanctions against ICC officials targeting the US and its allies who are not members of the court. Washington has since imposed sanctions on 13 ICC officials including nine judges.
At the UN General Assembly in September, Trump called the ICC a “rogue institution” and “an evil group of people” and urged its members to resign.
Why does the ICC claim jurisdiction over some nationals of non-member states?
Although the court is supported by many United Nations members and the European Union, other countries such as the United States, China and Russia are not members, arguing the ICC could be used for politically motivated prosecutions.
Israel is not a member and does not recognise its jurisdiction, but the Palestinian territories were admitted as an ICC member state in 2015. This, together with a ruling by judges, means the court can look at potential war crimes carried out by Hamas fighters in Israel and by Israelis in the Gaza Strip and the West Bank.
The reasoning for the warrants for Israeli officials is the same as for warrants against Russian officials for crimes allegedly committed in Ukraine: they concern alleged criminal acts that took place on the territory of an ICC member state.
Myanmar is not a member of the ICC but, in 2018 and 2019, judges ruled that the court had jurisdiction over alleged cross-border crimes that partially took place in neighbouring ICC member Bangladesh, such as deportation and persecution, and said prosecutors could open a formal investigation.
The Philippines is not currently a member but was between 2011 and 2019, when the unilateral withdrawal by Duterte became final. Under the Rome Statute, if a state withdraws, the ICC retains jurisdiction there for crimes committed during the membership period.
How many people has the court convicted?
ICC judges have issued 15 convictions and four acquittals. Twenty-three people have been held in the ICC detention centre in The Hague and appeared before the court, and 34 wanted suspects remain at large. Warrants have been withdrawn for nine suspects who died.
Of the 15 convictions, 10 have been for the court's core offences of war crimes and crimes against humanity. The others were for crimes such as witness tampering. Those 10 defendants were all African militia leaders from Democratic Republic of Congo, Mali, Sudan, Central African Republic and Uganda. Terms ranged from nine to 30 years in prison. The maximum possible sentence is life imprisonment. REUTERS

Japan’s government moves to slash food tax to ease prices
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:34:36 UTC
19:34:36 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
09 October 2026•Update: 09 October 2026
Japan’s government on Friday approved a bill to cut the consumption tax on food and nonalcoholic drinks from 8% to 1% for two years, seeking to ease pressure on households facing rising food prices.
The legislation would also introduce an income-linked cash benefit system for lower earners, Kyodo News reported.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s government has submitted the bill to parliament and aims to secure parliamentary approval during the current session, which ends Dec. 12, before implementing the tax cut in April 2027.
It would be Japan’s first consumption tax reduction since the levy was introduced in 1989.
Japan’s standard consumption tax rate is 10%, with a reduced rate of 8% applying to food and beverages, excluding alcohol and dining out.
The proposed cut is expected to reduce tax revenue by about 10 trillion yen ($63 billion) over two years, according to Kyodo News.
Takaichi has argued that the measures would provide relief from rising living costs, but the government has yet to detail how it would cover the revenue shortfall.
Opposition lawmakers have questioned how the shortfall would be covered. The plan has also raised concerns about local government finances, as municipalities receive a share of consumption tax revenue.
“We will take measures to ensure that local governments' fiscal management is not adversely affected,” Takaichi told the Senate on Friday.
On how to secure funding, Takaichi said it would be considered “given the broader framework of budgetary reforms to be pursued going forward.”

liam de la bedoyere’s inflatable chopsticks roll up into your pocket between meals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:34:10 UTC
19:34:10 KST

liam de la bedoyere’s inflatable chopsticks roll up into your pocket between meals
popsticks turns everyday tableware into portable inflatable chopsticks inspired by 1990s design.
POPSTICKS REIMAGINES CHOPSTICKS AS INFLATABLE UTENSILS
Some ideas begin with a serious problem. Popsticks begins with the possibility of finding yourself without chopsticks, which is apparently enough to justify a little design intervention. Created by designer Liam de la Bedoyere, the playful concept proposes a pair of inflatable chopsticks that can be rolled up, slipped into a pocket, and brought out when dinner calls. Instead of folding through hinges or coming apart into smaller pieces, the utensils rely on air to take shape.
The concept is as straightforward as it is unexpected. Each stick can be rolled into a compact spiral when deflated, then inflated into an elongated utensil ready for an unlikely chopstick emergency. The translucent blue forms resemble miniature pool inflatables, bringing a certain familiarity to an otherwise unusual object. Images of the concept show the chopsticks both rolled up and in use, illustrating a simple transformation that makes the act of preparing for dinner part of the experience.
PRODUCTOBER PROMPT BRINGS BACK 1990S INFLATABLE DESIGN
The idea emerged from Productober, an Instagram-based creative challenge that invites designers to respond to different prompts. For the theme ‘Inflatable,’ de la Bedoyere decided to go beyond the usual sketch and develop his proposal in three dimensions. The result explores how an ordinary dining utensil might be reconsidered through a material behavior more commonly associated with beach toys, temporary furniture, and objects that tend to disappear into storage once the fun is over.
The visual language draws directly from the inflatable furniture of the 1990s, which the designer remembers from his childhood. While CAD and KeyShot are part of his usual workflow, he turned to Vizcom to help capture the translucent appearance of those nostalgic objects. This gives Popsticks a deliberately familiar aesthetic, somewhere between a functional accessory and a miniature inflatable novelty. The design takes something as rigid and conventional as a pair of chopsticks and imagines what happens when softness becomes its defining feature.
LIAM DE LA BEDOYERE’S LATEST UNNECESSARY EMERGENCY PRODUCT
As it turns out, preparing for improbable situations is something of a recurring interest for de la Bedoyere. ‘This isn’t my first emergency product idea. About ten years ago, I created the Emergency Moustache, so I’m always thinking about the next unnecessary emergency to prepare for,’ the designer tells designboom. Popsticks follows that same line of thinking, treating a minor everyday inconvenience as an opportunity to experiment with how familiar objects might look, behave, and travel differently.
For now, Popsticks remains a concept rather than a commercially available product, leaving questions about materials, rigidity, and everyday usability unanswered. Yet its appeal lies less in solving a pressing culinary problem than in challenging the expectations attached to ordinary objects. A utensil that spends most of its time rolled up in a pocket and only takes shape when needed offers a playful alternative to conventional tableware. Whether or not inflatable chopsticks ever become a dinner essential, de la Bedoyere has found a way to make preparing for a meal a little more entertaining.
project info:
name: Popsticks
designer: Liam de la Bedoyere, Bored Eye Design | @bored_eye_design

Narrow body jets will ‘change the shape of travel’, says Dubai Airports CEO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-10-09
10:33:17 UTC
19:33:17 KST

Speaking on the sidelines of the WTTC Global Summit in Malta, Dubai Airports chief Paul Griffiths shared that he believes the expansion of regional airports will be key in the next decade of travel.
The CEO of Dubai Airports has said that aircraft technology improvements, with smaller planes able to fly longer distances, will “change the shape of travel”.
Talking at a roundtable on the sidelines of the World Travel & Tourism Council’s Global Summit in Malta, Paul Griffiths spoke about the expansion of Al Maktoum International Airport (DWC), noting that there are plans to have direct connections from Dubai to more than 600 cities.
“The great thing, of course, is aircraft technology is changing all the time, and with smaller aircraft able to fly longer distances we'll have all of those secondary cities in Europe directly connected to Dubai, so you'll be able to fly from, you know, Exeter or Valencia or Lyon or Marseille or Baden Baden, to Dubai and then on to the world, so it's going to change the shape of travel,” he said.
Dubai Airports announced plans to turn DWC into the world’s largest airport back in 2024. Once complete, the airport will have 400 terminal gates and five runways, with capacity for up to 260 million passengers annually.
The airport expansion should be completed by 2032.
“I think over the next decade or so there will be a fantastic opportunity for regional airports to expand their operations,” Griffiths added.
“With narrow body jets now capable of flying the Atlantic to minor destinations, where you don't need a wide body jet to fill to make it commercially sustainable, there'll be huge opportunities for regional airports.
“All they have to do is get their surface transport access sorted out and that will be a good place to invest and it will be great for regional economies.”
How aviation can reach net zero
Of course, you can’t talk about expansion without mentioning sustainability.
Griffiths highlighted sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) as being “probably the only way” for the industry to eliminate carbon emissions, pointing to Singapore, which has introduced a green fuel tax, as a destination to emulate.
He noted that the private sector must be persuaded to invest in SAF’s production, while governments must mandate its use, slowly increasing the required percentage of SAF blended with conventional fuel.
“My message is please balance the community impact by mitigating it through taking environmental control seriously, but setting a target and a framework to allow the expansion of the infrastructure to facilitate this increase in income from travel and tourism,” he added.
The future of airports
Griffiths said in a panel on digital identity and resetting the border experience that he believes the need for passports could be eliminated within the next five years, but he expanded on his comments in the roundtable.
Discussing the new airport, he said: “I can't comment on the technology that you see, because hopefully if you don't see any technology, then we will have done our job incredibly well.
“The idea is to make all of the process and the entire customer experience all about human contact.”
Facial recognition will be at the heart of the new experience, with no need to show your passport at the border or to present your boarding pass. AI will also be used to scan baggage.
“We can do it so much more quickly and less obtrusively,” he said. “I always think that airport security – and particularly in some airports which I won't name and shame – is probably the most intrusive process that any human being could go through outside of a hospital operating theatre, and we don't really want to do that to our customers.”

We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
Tver regional governor Vitaly Korolev later confirmed that a fire had broken out at the plant in the town of Redkino following a drone attack. He said employees had been evacuated to shelters in time, no one was injured, and emergency crews subsequently extinguished the blaze.
The Redkinsky Experimental Plant is one of the larger chemical manufacturing facilities in the Tver region and specializes in small-volume specialty chemicals. It produces more than 40 types of products used by Russia’s aviation, aerospace, and other industrial sectors.
Among its products are ferrocene derivatives used as combustion catalysts in solid-fuel rocket engines, as well as specialized materials, protective coatings, and fuel additives. These chemicals have applications across both civilian and military manufacturing.
According to Ukraine’s Security Service, the plant also produces components for Decilin-M, a specialized synthetic fuel used by Russian Kh-55 and Kh-101 cruise missiles. The facility is additionally linked to the production of additives for diesel fuel and aviation kerosene.
The Kh-101 is one of Russia’s principal air-launched long-range cruise missiles and has been used extensively in strikes against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure throughout the full-scale war.
The plant’s role in Russia’s defense and chemical sectors has already drawn international sanctions. The United Kingdom imposed restrictions on the enterprise in September 2025, citing its activities in sectors considered strategically important to the Russian government and its military-industrial base.

Multipolarity, need to remove trade barriers in CIS: Putin’s key statements

TURKMENBASHI /Turkmenistan/, October 9. /TASS/. The countries of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) unanimously support establishing a just, multipolar world order based on the principles of international law and the central role of the UN, Russian President Vladimir Putin said at a meeting of CIS leaders.
He noted that the organization could achieve far greater success by removing trade barriers.
TASS has compiled the Russian leader’s key statements.
Economic cooperation
Trade between Russia and the CIS member states exceeded 110 billion dollars last year and continued to grow this year: "We’re working on it. Notably, by the end of 2025, trade between Russia and the CIS member states had exceeded 110 billion dollars. In the first half of this year alone, it grew by another 19%."
The CIS can achieve far greater success by removing trade barriers: "Is it possible to move even faster? Probably so. What needs to be done to achieve this? We need to remove barriers."
The countries’ leaders are addressing practical issues, but it is well known that restrictions are "sometimes imposed at the national level": "We ourselves are consciously holding back the pace [of development that could be achieved]."
One of the priority areas of CIS cooperation has been and remains the economy: "The CIS countries maintain close cooperation in trade, investment, and high technology. Of course, as I’ve just mentioned, we would like to move even faster and work even more effectively in this area. That is certainly true. Nevertheless, the work is progressing."
The share of national currencies in mutual settlements between CIS member states has exceeded 90%: "A stable financial infrastructure, independent of external influence, allows us to effectively address many of today’s challenges. Virtually all mutual settlements are conducted in national currencies. Their share in commercial transactions between our states has exceeded 90%. This allows us to deepen economic cooperation, regardless of any external influences or market conditions."
Multipolarity
The CIS countries "unanimously advocate for the formation of a just, multipolar world order based on universally recognized principles of international law and the central role of the UN."
Cultural and humanitarian ties
The leaders of the CIS countries will adopt a resolution emphasizing the importance of preserving their shared history; young people must know the truth about the achievements of all the peoples of the CIS member states during the Soviet era: "I have spoken about how important the CIS countries’ joint efforts are in protecting our shared history and preventing its falsification. Without a doubt, young people must know the truth about the achievements of our peoples during the Soviet era and the heroic deeds of our fathers and grandfathers during the Great Patriotic War."
The CIS framework has enabled the member states to preserve the economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian ties built up over centuries: "Over the past three and a half decades, the CIS has truly come a long way and established itself as an authoritative regional integration organization. It is precisely thanks to this organization - and I agree with some of my colleagues who have already mentioned this today - that we have managed to preserve, and in many areas even strengthen, the economic, social, cultural, and humanitarian ties built up by our peoples over centuries of living in a single state."
Russia supports Tajikistan’s and Turkmenistan’s initiative to declare 2028 the Year of Social Development in the CIS: "The CIS has a well-established tradition of organizing thematic years, during which large-scale joint projects and events are carried out in various spheres of humanitarian and public life. We welcome the initiatives of our friends in Tajikistan and Turkmenistan to declare 2028 the Year of Social Development in the CIS and 2029 the Year of Transportation."
These thematic years, involving federal and regional authorities, the business community, the public, and the media, will help demonstrate to citizens of the member states the benefits of CIS cooperation in specific areas.
Promoting CIS on international stage
Promoting a positive image of the CIS in the media and on the international stage "is an extremely pressing task": "We expect the relevant resolution to be adopted at this meeting to help intensify efforts in this area."
Combating economic crimes
The CIS countries are effectively coordinating their efforts to combat economic crimes and are also implementing joint programs to combat the criminal use of digital technologies: "Our countries have established effective coordination in combating financial and economic offenses, money laundering, and corruption. Joint programs are being implemented to combat the criminal use of digital technologies, organized crime, drug trafficking, terrorism, and extremism."
"Close operational contacts are being maintained between law enforcement agencies and special services": "A number of new, useful decisions on criminal justice, the prevention of cybercrime, and border security have been submitted for approval at this summit and are supported by Russia.".
